chunks.t: About Ethicare
chunks.x: Our story What we believe Who we are Why we exist We didn’t start Ethicare because there was a gap in the market. We started it because people making this move deserved better than they were getting. Finding the right role is one part of a successful move. It’s everything around it that keeps people awake at night: the registration, the schools, the money, the distance from family, the friends you’re saying goodbye to. So we start there. We help you look at the whole picture before you commit to anything. Sometimes that means saying yes, this is right, let’s go . Sometimes it means saying not yet : wait a while, sort one thing out first. Telling someone to wait almost never wins us the placement. It’s usually the right thing to say anyway. That, far more than any list of company values, is who we are. A note from Sophie

chunks.t: About Ethicare
chunks.x: I never set out to build a traditional recruitment company — I came to it from inside the NHS. Most of a decade in workforce transformation at one of the country’s largest teaching hospitals, and my own move to the other side of the world and back, taught me the same thing: this is about people staying, not gaps being filled. Ethicare grew from both. Read my story ▾ I never set out to build a traditional recruitment company. For years I worked inside the NHS, most recently as Senior Service Improvement/Transformation Manager at the Royal Free London NHS Foundation Trust, one of the country’s largest teaching hospitals. I led workforce improvement programmes there: reducing temporary staffing spend, the trust’s patient engagement strategy, waste reduction. It taught me how much depends on people staying, and how often that comes down to the human things no job description ever mentions.

chunks.t: About Ethicare
chunks.x: I know what it’s like to pack up your life and start again somewhere new: a year travelling around Australia, then several years living in Wellington, where I met my partner. What bothered me was watching international recruitment treat people like a gap on a rota. Someone gets sold a role, lands on the other side of the world, and the phone goes quiet exactly when the hard part begins. That always felt backwards to me. This isn’t a vacancy being filled. It’s a person, often a whole family, changing their life. So I built Ethicare the way I wish someone had done it for me. We tell people the truth, even when it costs us the placement. We stay small on purpose, so you speak to the same people the whole way through. And we don’t disappear once you’ve landed, because that’s usually when you need us most. If you’re weighing this up, I’d be glad to help you think it through.

chunks.t: About Ethicare
chunks.x: No pressure — just a clear conversation. "Settling in is made of small moments, not big ones. That is the part nobody prepares you for, and the part we pay the most attention to." Sophie Careem Founder, Ethicare Resourcing Families matter as much as careers. The move succeeds or struggles on whether the whole family settles, not just on whether the role works out. From the other side of the world, to a place that becomes home. Open by default

chunks.t: About Ethicare
chunks.x: Recruitment agencies traditionally share information only when there is a vacancy to fill. A move to Australia or New Zealand can affect your career, your finances, your family and your everyday life. You should be able to understand what you are getting into before anyone asks you to apply for a job. So Ethicare does two things, and both of them are the business: we recruit into carefully chosen roles across Australia and New Zealand, and we get the people who take them, and the families who come with them, through registration, visas, arrival and the first year. But we don’t believe good information should only reach the people we place. Our registration guides, comparison tools and relocation resources are free to use whether you find your role through Ethicare, apply directly to an employer, or work with another agency entirely.

chunks.t: About Ethicare
chunks.x: You don’t need to have been placed by Ethicare to use our relocation support. If you have secured a role directly with an employer or through another agency, Plan Ethicare is still yours to use: our free planning tool covering registration, the visa, the budget, schools, housing and what to do when. Start planning your move →

chunks.t: About Ethicare
chunks.x: Our background is NHS leadership : planning and reshaping the clinical workforce from the inside. That order matters. We think about staffing the way the people who run services do, as something that has to hold up over years rather than weeks. Done well, this is workforce transformation, not vacancy filling . A clinician who arrives prepared and stays gives a service far more than one who covers a gap for a few months and leaves, so retention is what we design for. No health system has a workforce large enough to do this alone, and the range of experience international clinicians bring makes services stronger. Less locum reliance Workforce sustainability Retention & continuity Better patient outcomes

chunks.t: Working in Australia
chunks.x: I worked and travelled in Australia for a year, and I’ve lived in New Zealand too. What I love about Australia is how much of life happens outside. The weather makes it easy — you eat outdoors most of the year, the beach is part of an ordinary week rather than something you save up for, and people build their time around being out in it. The big cities are properly diverse, and it’s no surprise that three of the world’s ten most liveable are Australian. And the birdsong. Stepping outside and hearing such different sounds made even a familiar morning feel special. Alongside the beaches and the scenery, it’s the small, everyday pleasures that gradually become part of your life — that, and coffee taken almost as seriously as the Italians do. That’s the life.

chunks.t: Working in Australia

chunks.t: Working in Australia
chunks.x: A move this big is about far more than the job. Registration is national for the Ahpra-regulated professions: register once with your national board and every state and territory is open to you, which is what makes the choice so wide. Sonography is the exception — it is accredited through ASAR rather than registered with Ahpra, with the same freedom to work anywhere once accredited. Alongside the public system sits a substantial private sector, so the range of roles, and what they pay, is broader than most clinicians expect. On the measures that describe a life rather than a job, Australia sits in the top ten worldwide for human development, and life expectancy is among the highest anywhere. If you have children, the schooling picture is reassuring: Australian 15-year-olds perform above the OECD average in maths, reading and science.

chunks.t: Working in Australia
chunks.x: The distances are real — Perth to Sydney is a four-hour flight, and going home is further still — and renting in Sydney or Melbourne is among the most expensive in the world; the same salary buys a noticeably different life in a regional service. What people say they love once they are here, what nobody puts in the brochure and how the distance feels are the same conversation in either country. chunks.t: Can I work there? Registration for clinicians
chunks.h: Registration is more than your qualification
chunks.x: It is rarely the assessment of your training that holds people up. Every regulator also has to satisfy itself about your standing, your English, your character and your health — and it is these, the slow ordinary ones, that decide whether registration takes four months or nine. None is difficult. They simply take longer than anyone expects, so it helps to know now.

chunks.t: Can I work there? Registration for clinicians
chunks.x: You will need one from every regulator you have practised under — in New Zealand, from the last five years or since you last practised there, whichever is shorter. The authority sends it directly to the Council rather than to you, and it expires: the Medical Council wants every certificate dated within three months of the day you start work. Ask too early and it lapses; too late and everything else waits on it. There is a window, and your checklist marks it.

chunks.t: Can I work there? Registration for clinicians
chunks.x: This one surprises people who have practised in English for twenty years. It turns on where you trained and were assessed rather than on nationality, and each Board decides for itself what counts as evidence and for how long. In Australia it is one of the five registration standards every Board applies, with nursing and midwifery the exception. Worth settling before any fee is paid.

chunks.t: Can I work there? Registration for clinicians
chunks.x: Ahpra requires an international criminal history check from one of two approved suppliers if you have been primarily based outside Australia for six consecutive months or longer as an adult. You pay for it, the supplier sends the result to Ahpra directly, and it is valid for three months. New Zealand works by declaration instead: any conviction carrying three months’ imprisonment or more, and any investigation or disciplinary proceeding anywhere in the world, current or past.

chunks.t: Can I work there? Registration for clinicians
chunks.x: Both countries ask whether anything about your physical or mental health could affect your ability to practise. It is a declaration, not an examination, and a condition that is managed is not a bar — what causes trouble is a gap between what you declare and what a referee or a previous regulator says. Declaring something early is almost always easier than explaining it later.

chunks.t: Can I work there? Registration for clinicians
chunks.x: Australia’s other three registration standards, set Board by Board rather than nationally: enough recent practice, continuing professional development you can evidence, and professional indemnity insurance in place. If you have had a career break, recency is the one to check first, because it is the one with no quick fix.

chunks.t: Can I work there? Registration for clinicians
chunks.x: A thin reference is the most common reason a Board comes back with questions, and it is almost never the referee’s fault — they simply were not told what was being looked for. A short conversation with them beforehand changes what they write.

chunks.t: Can I work there? Registration for clinicians
chunks.h: And one your employer asks, not the regulator
chunks.x: Immunity and a pre-employment health declaration — measles, hepatitis B, the rest — are a condition of the job rather than of registration, handled by the employer’s occupational health service after an offer. People routinely confuse the two and chase records they do not yet need. Worth gathering anyway, because they are far easier to obtain before you leave than afterwards. Which of these bites, and how hard, is our experience rather than a rule, and we try to keep the two clearly apart. The Board’s own document list, linked from every guide and checklist, is what governs your application. The specifics above were checked against the Medical Council of New Zealand and Ahpra on 28 September 2026 — both change them, so check the date before you rely on it. Alongside registration

chunks.t: Cost of Moving Calculator
chunks.h: What people ask about the cost of moving
chunks.x: The cost of an international move is the question we are asked earliest and most often. These are the honest answers, including the parts that are harder to pin down. How much does it cost to move to Australia or New Zealand? + There is no single answer, and anyone quoting one is guessing. The cost depends on where you are moving from, who is moving with you, your profession and registration pathway, whether you ship belongings, how long you need temporary accommodation, and the rent on the home you eventually secure. That is why this tool builds the figure line by line from your own circumstances rather than offering an average. Which costs do people most often forget? + Three in particular. The cash needed to secure a rental — bond plus rent in advance — is usually the single largest cost of arriving, and most of it comes back to you later.

chunks.t: Cost of Moving Calculator
chunks.h: What people ask about the cost of moving
chunks.x: Temporary accommodation while you look for that rental adds up quickly. And the gap before your first full salary catches almost everyone: you may arrive several weeks before you are paid properly, and you still need to eat, travel and set up a home in that time. Is registration or the visa the bigger cost? + It depends on your household and your pathway. Australian visa charges apply per person included in the application, so a family of four is a substantially larger number than one person. Registration is usually the smaller figure — unless your pathway includes an examination or clinical assessment, which can cost more than everything else in your registration put together. The calculator asks about an exam separately for exactly that reason. Our registration pathway checker is the place to work out which route applies to you.

chunks.t: Cost of Moving Calculator
chunks.h: What people ask about the cost of moving
chunks.x: Will my employer pay for my relocation? + Many healthcare employers contribute, and relocation support is a reasonable thing to ask about. What matters as much as the amount is how it reaches you: paid upfront, reimbursed after you have paid, or settled directly with the supplier. A reimbursed package still means the money has to leave your account first, so the calculator shows the cash you may need available upfront as a separate figure from your eventual cost. If you are weighing up an offer, negotiating your offer covers how to raise it. Are these figures a quotation? + No. Every line is labelled with where it came from — an official fee, a figure calculated from an official rule, one of our planning estimates, or a number you entered yourself — and the estimate carries the date the data was last checked. Fees and tenancy rules change, and exchange rates move daily.

chunks.t: Cost of Moving Calculator
chunks.h: What people ask about the cost of moving
chunks.x: Treat the result as a planning document to take into a conversation with your employer, your bank or us, and confirm each amount against the official source before you commit to it. Does it cover the cost of living once I arrive? + Only the first month or so. This is deliberately a moving budget: what it takes to get there and get established, plus a buffer for everyday expenses until your first full salary arrives. Ongoing rent, groceries, childcare, insurance and transport are a different question, and our destination guides cover them city by city with local figures. Do I have to give you my details to see the result? + No. The estimate appears as you answer, and nothing is sent to us. Your answers stay in your own browser so you can come back to them, and you can print or save the result as a PDF to keep. Leave this empty:

chunks.t: Adelaide Relocation Guide
chunks.h: The capital that gives the money back.
chunks.x: Adelaide is the city where the sums work: a tertiary career, a house you can buy, the Adelaide Hills twenty minutes from the wards and the sea forty. It costs less than Sydney, Brisbane or Perth, and it does not feel like a compromise. The health system is large for the city’s size — three metropolitan networks and a statewide children’s service, anchored by one of the newest hospital-and-research precincts in the southern hemisphere. And uniquely among the mainland capitals, Adelaide counts as regional for skilled migration. The costs are a fierce dry summer, power bills among the dearest in the country, and a job market that is one city deep. This guide prices all three plainly. Welcome to the twenty-minute city. Warm regards — the Ethicare team The Torrens · a city inside a ring of parkland

chunks.x: Moving countries is a big step. It is also, for most people, the beginning of a much better working life — shorter lists, real weekends, and a country you can cross in a day. New Zealanders call it manaakitanga: looking after the people who arrive. Where pay comes up we describe how the system works rather than quoting figures — and where a number matters, we verify it against the relevant agreement before we put it in writing. chunks.t: Bay of Plenty Relocation Guide
chunks.h: The region everyone asks for by name.
chunks.x: A long, warm curve of coast facing north-east into the Pacific, wrapped around a working harbour. More than two thousand two hundred hours of sunshine a year, twenty kilometres of unbroken ocean beach, and a volcanic cone at the end of it that half the city walks around before work. Tauranga is now New Zealand’s fifth-largest city and has been its fastest-growing for most of two decades. There are two public hospitals in the region — the base hospital here and a smaller one in Whakatāne, eighty minutes east — both run by Health New Zealand | Te Whatu Ora, both serving a population expanding faster than the services around it. For a clinician the trade is unusual for this collection. The lifestyle is the best case any region in it can make. The housing is the most expensive relative to local wages. Both halves are true, and this guide does not soften either. Nau mai, haere mai ki Te Moana-a-Toi. Ngā mihi nui — the Ethicare team Mount Maunganui · the ocean beach

chunks.t: Brisbane Relocation Guide
chunks.x: For years Brisbane was described in terms of what it wasn’t — not Sydney, not Melbourne, a big country town with a river running through it. That framing is now well out of date. Two and a half million people, a rebuilt centre, a serious food and arts scene, and a decade of Olympic infrastructure ahead of it. For clinicians the draw is a hospital cluster with tertiary depth across the inner city and the fastest-growing health demand in the country to the north and south. And the arithmetic still works: a family house within half an hour of the wards is a workable plan here in a way it stopped being in Sydney a decade ago. The costs are the summer — humid, stormy, and long — and a public transport network that is good along its spines and thin between them. This guide prices both plainly. Welcome to the river city. Warm regards — the Ethicare team The Story Bridge · the city’s front door

chunks.t: Canberra Relocation Guide
chunks.x: Canberra is the city Australia built on purpose: a lake at its centre, forest and grassland reserves on every side, and a plan that still shows in how calmly it moves. It also has the country’s highest average income, some of the shortest commutes on the mainland, and — despite housing the federal parliament — a skilled migration classification that puts it alongside Perth, Adelaide and Hobart rather than Sydney or Melbourne. For clinicians, healthcare here runs as a single territory system rather than several competing networks, anchored by two hospital campuses and a research precinct that shares a fence line with the university. It also carries a job most people don’t expect: Canberra is the specialist referral centre for a wide stretch of southern New South Wales, so the caseload reaches well past the territory’s own population of under half a million.

chunks.t: Canberra Relocation Guide
chunks.x: The costs are a public-service economy that can feel like a company town, a housing market that has caught up with the income rather than trailing it, and a coastline that’s a drive rather than a tram ride. chunks.t: Central Otago Relocation Guide
chunks.h: Everyone asks about here. Very few end up here.
chunks.x: This guide covers two districts that work as one region: Queenstown Lakes — Queenstown, Wānaka, Arrowtown — and the drier inland basins around Cromwell, Alexandra and Clyde. Sixty-five thousand permanent residents, ringed by mountains, in the only continental climate in New Zealand. Two facts govern a clinical life here. There is no base hospital — care runs through small rural hospitals and a strong community network, and anything complex travels three hours to Dunedin. And Queenstown and Wānaka are the least affordable places to live in the country relative to local income, with rentals scarce as well as expensive. We say all that first because the landscape needs no advocacy. Four ski fields inside an hour, lakes you swim in, an autumn people cross the world for, and direct flights to Australia from a town of twenty-eight thousand. The question was never whether it’s beautiful.

chunks.h: The only city in New Zealand that had to decide what it wanted to be.
chunks.x: The earthquakes took the centre of Christchurch down. What went up in its place is not a copy — it is lower, greener, and organised around the river rather than turned away from it. You will still see gaps. Fifteen years on, some blocks are car parks waiting for a decision, and locals are relaxed about this in a way visitors find surprising. What you get in exchange is a city with room in it — in the streets, in the houses, in the price of things. For a clinician moving with a family, that is often the whole argument. A major tertiary hospital, a house with a garden, and the Southern Alps ninety minutes away. Nau mai, haere mai ki Ōtautahi. chunks.t: Christchurch Relocation Guide
chunks.x: From the centre the city reads flat — a grid on a plain, the Alps a blue suggestion on the horizon. It is holding something back. Fifteen minutes east, the grid simply stops at the Pacific — and there is surf. Over the Port Hills, or straight through them: a drowned volcano with a working port in it. The Alps visible from an ordinary suburban street. People say they never stop noticing it. Skis in the car before seven, on the mountain by nine, home for dinner. The nor’west arch — a strange lens of cloud over the hills — and the light once it clears. Riverside Market on a Friday evening, which is where half the city seems to be. Trams still running through New Regent Street, past a row of pastel shopfronts. Punting on the Ōtākaro Avon. Absurd, and lovely, and you will take every visitor. Gardens big enough that people use them, and eat outside in them. A short commute, which is really a way of saying the evening still belongs to you. The full radius is walked in Weekends and the outdoors ; what the commute costs you in minutes is in Getting around . What the evenings look like

chunks.t: Christchurch Relocation Guide
chunks.x: Not a permanent holiday. A working week with the daylight left over — which is the part that is hard to picture from the other side of the world. Tuesday Off at half four. The estuary loop with the dog, the light going gold over the water, and no particular reason to hurry. Wednesday Netball after school, then dinner outside — because at seven it is somehow still warm. Thursday Nothing whatsoever. A Thursday is still a Thursday, wherever in the world you decide to put it. Friday Riverside Market on the way home, then somebody’s back garden until the light finally goes. Saturday & Sunday The mountain, the peninsula, the vines, the coast. The weekend has earned a chapter of its own rather than a line here. Read the weekends chapter → Monday Back at work. The same profession, the same standards you hold now, the same you. Only the week around it has changed.

chunks.t: Christchurch Relocation Guide
chunks.x: And the bits a brochure leaves out The nor’wester will flatten a good plan several times a year, and it gives half the city a headache while it does it. Winter evenings are dark and properly cold. Plenty of Sundays are just a Sunday, spent on the washing. Picture that too — it is the same life, not a better species of one. Contents

chunks.t: Darwin Relocation Guide
chunks.h: The tropical capital of Australia’s north.
chunks.x: Darwin is the city Australia built on its harbour and rebuilt twice over: a compact, tropical capital closer to Dili and Singapore than to Sydney, home to around 150,000 people across Darwin and its satellite city Palmerston. Generations of Larrakia, Southeast Asian, Greek and Chinese communities have made it, by a wide margin, the most multicultural capital in the country. For clinicians here the pitch is unusual: Royal Darwin Hospital is both the Top End’s only tertiary hospital and home to the National Critical Care and Trauma Response Centre, the base behind Australia’s response to Bali, regional disasters and pandemics. And despite being a capital city, the whole of the Northern Territory is classed as regional for skilled migration, the same bracket as Perth, Adelaide and Hobart.

chunks.t: Darwin Relocation Guide
chunks.h: The tropical capital of Australia’s north.
chunks.x: The costs: a wet season that closes down outdoor life for months and carries real cyclone risk, a small professional community you’ll come to know quickly, and a grocery bill that carries the cost of freighting almost everything a very long way. This guide prices all three plainly. Welcome to the Top End. Warm regards — the Ethicare team Darwin’s harbour foreshore — the heart of Top End life

chunks.t: Dunedin Relocation Guide
chunks.h: The city people rule out on the map and change their minds about in person.
chunks.x: The Scots founded Dunedin in 1848 and built it in stone. Gold money made it briefly the largest and richest city in New Zealand, and the city spent that wealth on architecture that is still standing. What keeps it interesting now is the university. Around 20,000 students in a city of 130,000 is a ratio no other New Zealand city comes close to, and it shows — in the bars, in the music, in the fact that a small southern city supports a serious art gallery and three good museums. For a clinician the arithmetic is unusual. A tertiary teaching hospital and the country’s oldest medical school, in a city where a family home costs a fraction of Auckland and the commute is fifteen minutes. Nau mai, haere mai ki Ōtepoti. Ngā mihi nui — the Ethicare team The university clocktower · five minutes from the hospital

chunks.t: Gisborne Relocation Guide
chunks.h: The region we’re most careful about matching.
chunks.x: Gisborne is the most easterly city in New Zealand and the first in the world to see the sun. Around fifty-two thousand people across a district the size of a small country — three rivers meeting the sea, a surf coast running north to the East Cape, and steep hill country behind. Over half the district’s people identify as Māori, the highest proportion of any region in the country. Te reo and tikanga are part of ordinary working life here to a degree unmatched anywhere else, and iwi-led providers deliver a substantial share of care. There is one hospital, and it is a rural hospital rather than a base hospital — four hours from the nearest one, in Hawke’s Bay. That means wide scope and autonomy for the clinicians it suits, and no role at all for many hospital subspecialties. Read the healthcare chapter first. Nau mai, haere mai ki Tairāwhiti. Ngā mihi nui — the Ethicare team The coast north of the city, towards the Cape

chunks.t: Gold Coast Relocation Guide
chunks.x: The Gold Coast is Australia’s sixth-largest city and still one of its fastest-growing: around 700,000 people along fifty-seven kilometres of surf coast between Southport and the New South Wales border, an hour south of Brisbane by road or rail. For clinicians here the pitch has changed in the last decade: Gold Coast University Hospital is a full tertiary teaching hospital, paired with a health and knowledge precinct built alongside Griffith University. And the whole coast carries a regional migration classification that opens pathways the capitals don’t. The costs: a housing market that’s grown up fast, a light rail that covers the coast but not the hinterland, and a city still working out its own identity between beach-suburb reputation and the real thing. This guide prices all three plainly. Welcome to the Gold Coast. Warm regards — the Ethicare team Surfers Paradise — the heart of the strip

chunks.t: Hawke’s Bay Relocation Guide
chunks.h: The region that’s hardest to argue against.
chunks.x: Hawke’s Bay is a wide sunlit crescent on the east coast — Napier on the northern arm, rebuilt in Art Deco after the 1931 earthquake, and Hastings twenty minutes inland across the Heretaunga plain. Between them, orchards, vineyards and some of the best soil in the country. The base hospital is in Hastings, serving a hundred and eighty thousand people from Wairoa in the north to Central Hawke’s Bay in the south. Real breadth, a substantial equity agenda in the heartland of Ngāti Kahungunu, and a rural catchment that reaches a long way. On most measures a clinician feels — sunshine, commute, housing cost, what’s on the table at the weekend — this region does very well. The costs are the four hours to Wellington, real deprivation in parts of it, and a recovery from Cyclone Gabrielle that is well advanced but not finished. Nau mai, haere mai ki Te Matau-a-Māui. Ngā mihi nui — the Ethicare team Cellar doors · twenty minutes from home

chunks.t: Hobart Relocation Guide
chunks.x: Hobart is the choice people make on purpose: a mountain that stands over the wards, a harbour that still works for a living, and a health system small enough to know your name. Founded in 1804, it is Australia’s second-oldest capital, and it still runs at that scale. Tasmania runs a single statewide health service, and Hobart carries its depth — the principal referral hospital, the island’s widest range of specialist services, and the university medical school beside it. It is a system you can know personally within a year, which cuts both ways, and this guide says so. The costs are a tight rental market, older housing that wasn’t always built for a cold winter, and a Bass Strait crossing between here and everywhere else. What you get back is proximity: the mountain, the wilderness and the coast are minutes from the wards, not hours. Welcome to the mountain and the harbour. Warm regards — the Ethicare team

chunks.t: Melbourne Relocation Guide
chunks.h: For clinicians who want the system.
chunks.x: Melbourne carries the deepest concentration of tertiary and quaternary medicine in Australia, standalone specialist services that create career paths smaller systems cannot, and a biomedical research precinct of international standing sitting next to the hospitals that feed it. Around that sits a city built on trams, laneways and a century of migration — five million people, the largest tram network on earth, and the best food culture in the country. It is a city that rewards people who like cities. The costs are the weather and the price: four seasons in a day is not a joke, and Melbourne is the second-dearest capital in the country. This guide prices both plainly. Welcome to the southern capital. Warm regards — the Ethicare team

chunks.t: Moving to New Zealand
chunks.h: Most of what you need to know isn’t about a city.
chunks.x: It’s about a country. New Zealand runs one health system, one tax system, one set of tenancy rules and one school framework from Kaitaia to Bluff. Learn them once and they hold wherever you end up. That’s what this guide is for. It’s the layer underneath the regional guides — the systems, the money, the paperwork and the rhythms of the year. Dry-sounding subjects, mostly, but they’re the ones that decide whether your first six months feel manageable or bewildering. Read it in order or dip in. Nothing here is trying to sell you a move — it’s here so you can make the decision with your eyes open. Nau mai, haere mai ki Aotearoa. Ngā mihi nui — the Ethicare team Never far from the bush

chunks.t: Nelson Tasman Relocation Guide
chunks.h: The region that needs no selling.
chunks.x: Nelson Tasman sits at the top of the South Island, wrapped around a sheltered bay in a rain shadow. Around 2,400 hours of sunshine a year — the most in New Zealand — with mountains behind, orchards and vineyards between, and warm clear water in front. Three national parks are within reach: Abel Tasman’s golden beaches an hour north, Kahurangi and the Heaphy Track over the hill, Nelson Lakes ninety minutes south. No other city in the country can say that. Nelson also has an active community of working artists and more breweries per head than anywhere else in New Zealand. There’s a base hospital in Nelson serving the region, with a second in Blenheim under the same district service. The costs are housing — expensive for a city of fifty-five thousand, because half the country would like to live here — and the distance from everywhere else. Nau mai, haere mai ki Whakatū. Ngā mihi nui — the Ethicare team Kaiteriteri · the gateway to Abel Tasman

chunks.t: New South Wales Relocation Guide
chunks.x: One Australian in three lives in New South Wales. Sydney is the country’s biggest city, its main gateway and its deepest healthcare job market — and behind it sits a state of surf coasts, wine valleys, world-heritage mountains and the outback. The public system here is the largest in Australia: fifteen local health districts running more than two hundred and twenty hospitals, with the deepest tertiary concentration in the southern hemisphere in Sydney and busy referral centres across the regions. Registration is national; hiring is local. Which district you choose decides your daily life. The cost is Sydney’s housing — the most expensive in the country, concentrated exactly where most people first want to live. This guide treats that plainly, and gives the Hunter, the Illawarra and the regional cities the attention the arithmetic says they deserve. Welcome to the harbour state. Warm regards — the Ethicare team

chunks.t: Newcastle Relocation Guide
chunks.h: A working harbour that became a lifestyle city.
chunks.x: Newcastle is New South Wales’s second-largest city, home to around 170,000 people and a wider Hunter region of some 700,000, about two hours north of Sydney by car or train. It grew up around coal and steel, and its reinvention since the old BHP works closed has made it something its own. For clinicians the pitch is straightforward: John Hunter Hospital is the major tertiary referral centre for a region stretching well beyond Newcastle itself, giving a caseload that punches above the city’s own population. The Hunter carries a regional migration classification that opens pathways Sydney doesn’t. We’ll be straight with you about what to weigh: a smaller specialist bench than Sydney for the most complex cases, a still-forming post-industrial identity in some neighbourhoods, and a housing market feeling real pressure as Sydneysiders arrive for the lifestyle. This guide weighs all three plainly — alongside everything they buy you. Welcome to Newcastle. Warm regards — the Ethicare team Newcastle Beach — minutes from the CBD

chunks.t: Northland Relocation Guide
chunks.h: The region people drive through, and then move to.
chunks.x: Northland is a long peninsula with two coasts, three hundred kilometres of it, and nowhere more than forty kilometres from the sea. It is the warmest region in New Zealand, the greenest, and the one where the country’s history begins. Whāngārei is the only city — around 55,000 people on a harbour, with the region’s base hospital. Beyond it: the Bay of Islands, the Far North, and the kauri coast in the west. Around a third of Northlanders identify as Māori, the highest of any region, and te ao Māori is part of clinical practice here rather than an add-on. For a clinician the trade is clear. Generalist practice with real breadth, on the cheapest housing in this guide, twenty minutes from a beach. Against that: distance, a thin services market, and some of the highest deprivation in the country. Both halves are true. Nau mai, haere mai ki Te Tai Tokerau. Ngā mihi nui — the Ethicare team Paihia · the Bay of Islands, an hour north

chunks.t: Palmerston North Relocation Guide
chunks.h: Few people arrive with this city top of the list.
chunks.x: Palmerston North sits in the middle of the Manawatū plain, ninety minutes north of Wellington, with a mountain range twenty-five minutes east and thirty kilometres of dune coast half an hour west. It is flat, green, and almost entirely unglamorous. It is also a base hospital serving a large region, and one of a small number of centres in New Zealand delivering radiation oncology. That is a serious clinical offer for a city of ninety thousand people — and Massey University next door gives it a young, international, research-minded character it would not otherwise have. The trade here is the cleanest in this collection. National pay, among the cheapest housing of any North Island city with a base hospital, and a ten-minute commute. What you give up is the skyline and the sea. Most people find that a better bargain than they expected. Nau mai, haere mai ki Te Papaioea. chunks.t: Perth Relocation Guide
chunks.x: Perth asks you to accept isolation — a five-hour flight to the east coast, closer to Singapore than to Sydney. In return it offers the best beaches and weather of any Australian capital, and housing that still makes a family life straightforward. Professionally it is a full tertiary system with newer facilities than most of the country, in a city small enough that you will know the people who run your specialty within a year. And it is the one capital classed as regional for skilled migration, which can open visa pathways the eastern cities cannot. The cost is distance — from family, from the eastern states, from everywhere. This guide takes that as seriously as the beaches. Welcome to the western capital. Warm regards — the Ethicare team London Court · the city’s oddest laneway

chunks.t: Queensland Relocation Guide
chunks.h: The state people move to on purpose.
chunks.x: Queensland is where Australians themselves relocate: winter sun, beaches that work all year, and housing that still lets an ordinary salary buy an ordinary house. Brisbane has grown into a confident river city with the 2032 Olympics ahead of it, and the two coasts either side hold the country’s fastest-growing corridor. The public system runs as sixteen hospital and health services across the most decentralised state in the country — and uniquely, tertiary-level medicine exists far outside the capital: Townsville and Cairns anchor the tropical north a two-hour flight from Brisbane. Registration is national; hiring is service by service. The costs are summer — humid in the corner, monsoonal in the north, with a real cyclone season — and distances that make the far postings far. This guide prices both plainly, and takes the north as seriously as the corner. Welcome to the sunshine state. Warm regards — the Ethicare team The waterfront ordinary · Queensland’s housing argument

chunks.t: South Australia Relocation Guide
chunks.h: The capital that gives the money back.
chunks.x: South Australia is the state where the sums work: a major-hospital career for less than Sydney, Brisbane or Perth would cost, with the Adelaide Hills twenty minutes from the wards, the beach forty, and about half of Australia’s wine made within an hour of the city. Adelaide is elegant, walkable and ringed entirely by parklands — a festival city that turns into one long stage every March. The public system runs as ten local health networks, with a rebuilt biomedical precinct in the capital and broad-scope careers in the country networks, where the incentives are strongest. The costs are a fierce dry summer, power bills among the dearest in the country, and a job market that is one city deep. This guide prices all three plainly, and takes the country posts as seriously as the capital. Welcome to the festival state. Warm regards — the Ethicare team Rundle Mall — the capital’s everyday centre

chunks.t: Southland Relocation Guide
chunks.h: Nobody asks about Southland. They should.
chunks.x: Southland is the bottom of New Zealand — a broad green farming plain with Fiordland at one end, Rakiura across the strait, and Invercargill in the middle of it. A hundred and three thousand people in an area larger than Wales. Unlike the other far-south options, this region has a base hospital. Acute medicine and surgery, an emergency department, intensive care, maternity, paediatrics and imaging, serving the whole region, with a rural network reaching into Fiordland and out to the island. Real hospital medicine with a wide catchment. And Invercargill has the cheapest city housing in the country — not "affordable relative to income", the lowest actual prices of any city in the country. The cost is the weather: cool, changeable and windy, with a dark midwinter. If that doesn’t put you off, very little else here will. Nau mai, haere mai ki Murihiku. Ngā mihi nui — the Ethicare team Tautuku Bay · the Catlins, east of the city

chunks.h: The city that needs a clear guide.
chunks.x: Sydney needs no introduction and no selling. New South Wales runs the largest public health system in Australia, and Sydney holds the deepest concentration of it — major teaching hospitals across several districts, quaternary units taking national referrals, and research institutes beside them. Around that sits a city of five and a half million built around a drowned river valley: a hundred beaches, free ocean pools, national parks pressing in from three sides, and a ferry commute that never quite becomes ordinary. The cost is money. This is the least affordable housing market in the country, and the gap between an inner-suburb life and an outer-suburb one is wider here than anywhere else in Australia. This guide is written with that fact in the room. Welcome to the harbour city. Warm regards — the Ethicare team Ocean pools · free, tidal, and used year-round

chunks.t: Tasmania Relocation Guide
chunks.h: The island that trades scale for life.
chunks.x: Tasmania is the deliberate choice: an island of 570,000 people with the cleanest air on record, a 1,271-metre mountain standing over its capital, and forty per cent of its land in parks and reserves. Nobody drifts here — you choose it. The health system is a single statewide service — four principal hospitals rather than a metropolis full — which makes careers broad, colleagues neighbours, and new arrivals looked after. Hobart carries the depth; Launceston and the north-west coast carry lives of their own. The costs are the smallest job market in the country, winters that are cold in draughty housing, and an island premium on everything that crosses Bass Strait. This guide prices all three plainly — alongside the life that makes people stay anyway. Welcome to the island state. Warm regards — the Ethicare team

chunks.t: Victoria Relocation Guide
chunks.x: Victoria packs the second-biggest city, the second-deepest job market and the best regional-rail network in Australia into its smallest mainland state. Melbourne is laneways, trams, galleries and the country’s definitive coffee — a world city that costs meaningfully less to live in than Sydney. The public system is organised as independent health services — metropolitan clusters in Melbourne with tertiary depth to match Sydney’s, and substantial regional services in Geelong, Ballarat, Bendigo and beyond. Registration is national; hiring is service by service, and the regional cities sit on commuter rail, which changes what "regional" means. The costs are the weather — grey winters and four-seasons days — and a housing market that is only cheap by comparison with Sydney. This guide prices both plainly, and gives Geelong, Ballarat and Bendigo the attention the arithmetic says they deserve. Welcome to the garden state. Warm regards — the Ethicare team Melbourne · the terraces and the trams

chunks.h: The region people drive through, and then move to.
chunks.x: The Waikato is the part of New Zealand most people drive through. That is a mistake worth correcting: it holds a tertiary hospital, the country’s longest river, a surf coast and the seat of the Māori King. Hamilton sits at the centre of it, on a bend of the river. One of the youngest and fastest-growing cities in the country, and one that has spent a decade quietly becoming a much better place to live. For a clinician the arithmetic is unusually simple. Tertiary work and a broad rural network, ninety minutes from Auckland, in a city where a family home with a garden is an ordinary purchase. Nau mai, haere mai ki Kirikiriroa. Ngā mihi nui — the Ethicare team Hamilton Gardens · free, and better than anyone expects

chunks.x: Wellington has a tertiary hospital, a parliament, a national museum, a theatre scene and a working port — all inside a city you can walk across in an afternoon. That smallness is the whole character of the place. You will run into the same people. Your registrar will know your neighbour. The same smallness is why some people leave. We are straight about that too — the wind, the cold houses, and a professional world where everyone knows everyone. chunks.t: Western Australia Relocation Guide
chunks.x: Western Australia is a third of the continent with one city holding most of its people: Perth, the most isolated capital on earth and one of the most pleasant — the country’s best city beaches, its sunniest capital climate, and the only one where the sun sets over the sea. The south-west corner adds wine capes and karri forests; the north is another world entirely. The public system splits the way the map does: metropolitan service groups running Perth’s complete tertiary network, and a single country service spanning the largest health geography in the world. Registration is national; hiring is service by service — and the north recruits with the strongest incentive packages in Australian healthcare, verified case by case. The cost is the flight line: five hours to Sydney, a time zone of your own, and every east-coast family event a commitment.

chunks.t: Western Australia Relocation Guide
chunks.x: This guide prices that plainly — and takes the north as seriously as the city, because gone into deliberately it is the fastest financial reset in Australian healthcare. Welcome to the west. Warm regards — the Ethicare team The Kimberley · a state built for the long drive

chunks.t: Cost of living in Adelaide: the value capital, audited
chunks.x: The picture is a happy one, so let’s audit it anyway. Adelaide is the most affordable mainland capital, and there are three costs the sunshine hides that deserve to be weighed before you commit.

chunks.t: Cost of living in Adelaide: the value capital, audited
chunks.x: We used to print a weekly rent and a monthly budget table here. We have taken them out. A figure that was true when a page was written is misleading a year later, and a candidate who plans a move around a stale number is worse off than one who plans around none. What does not go stale is the shape of a month, and the judgement about which lines will surprise you. For today’s actual numbers use the calculators at the foot of the page, and use them to compare Adelaide against the city you are leaving. That is the only comparison that decides anything.

chunks.t: Cost of living in Adelaide: the value capital, audited
chunks.x: What doesn’t change is the relationship: like-for-like housing runs hundreds of dollars a week below Sydney and well below Melbourne, and it is housing that decides whether a salary feels big.

chunks.t: Cost of living in Adelaide: the value capital, audited
chunks.x: The most affordable mainland capital The proportions, for one person on a mid-range budget. Proportions move slowly; prices move every quarter. Rent is fifty-six per cent of the month — the smallest rent line of any mainland capital. Rent 56% Groceries 19% Entertainment 10% Power & water 8% Transport (metroCARD) 5% Internet 3% The line that decides it Rent · 56% The transport line is the smallest of any capital — no tolls, cheap parking by capital standards, and commutes short enough to save childcare hours. The picture here is a happy one; the chapter below prices the three costs the sunshine hides anyway.

chunks.t: Cost of living in Adelaide: the value capital, audited
chunks.x: Power South Australian electricity is among the dearest in the country, and summer cooling is non-negotiable. An efficient home and a deliberately chosen energy plan are worth real money a year — compare retailers before you sign anything. The car you’ll probably own Inner-ring and tram-corridor life can be car-free; most Adelaide lives aren’t. Price a reliable used car, registration and insurance into your arrival budget rather than discovering it in month two. Flights east If your people are in Sydney, Melbourne or overseas via the east, visits mean flights. Two or three trips a year is where most families settle — budget it.

chunks.t: Cost of living in Adelaide: the value capital, audited
chunks.x: The rent gap against the eastern capitals is the big one — for many households it covers the whole grocery bill. The small ones accumulate: no tolls, cheap parking by capital standards, commutes short enough to save childcare hours, the Central Market beating supermarket prices on produce, and the 10-cent container deposit quietly funding the coffee habit. On the income side, public-health and not-for-profit roles here can salary-package part of your pay before tax — in a lower-cost city the effect on real quality of life is significant, and many international staff don’t set it up until far too late. How packaging, tax and superannuation work is national and lives in Pay & conditions ; the Adelaide habit to copy is simply asking payroll about it on day one.

chunks.t: Cost of living in Adelaide: the value capital, audited
chunks.x: The bottom line Plan the bridge, not just the destination: temporary accommodation, a bond of up to four weeks’ rent plus up to two weeks in advance, a first car, and setting up a home. In Adelaide that bridge costs far less than in the eastern capitals — but the people who arrive calm are the ones who priced it anyway. Get today’s numbers, and compare them to home These are live and updated continuously. Put the city you are leaving in the other box. Numbeo cost-of-living calculator — the most complete comparison tool, and the one most clinicians already use. Crowd-sourced, so treat it as a ballpark. Expatistan — the same idea with a cleaner side-by-side. Worth running as a sanity check when Numbeo looks off. Australian Bureau of Statistics — official and slower, and the one to trust on the direction of travel. If what you find differs from what we say here, tell us and we will correct it. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Food, wine & the everyday in Adelaide
chunks.x: Adelaide’s everyday food culture runs through one building: the Central Market, trading since 1869 in the middle of the city grid. Around it sit the fiercely local supermarket, the surviving corner deli, and — because this is Adelaide — the assumption that decent wine is a grocery, not a luxury.

chunks.t: Food, wine & the everyday in Adelaide
chunks.h: The Market and the weekly shop
chunks.x: The Adelaide Central Market is one of the best fresh-food markets in the country — seventy-odd stalls of produce, cheese, seafood, bread and world cuisines under one roof, cheaper and better than the supermarkets for most of what matters. Hospital staff treat Thursday evening or early Saturday as the serious shopping windows; go late Saturday afternoon for the closing-time bargains. For the rest: Woolworths and Coles run full-range stores everywhere, ALDI is the cheapest weekly shop, and the local pride is real — Drakes and Foodland are South Australian institutions. The corner deli — part milk bar, part grocer, part sandwich counter — survives in Adelaide as it does nowhere else in the country. Bring your bags South Australia was the first state to ban lightweight plastic bags, and the checkout assumes you came prepared. Save your bottles The 10-cent container deposit has run since 1977.

chunks.t: Food, wine & the everyday in Adelaide
chunks.h: The Market and the weekly shop
chunks.x: A crate in the boot and a monthly depot run is a local rhythm. Farmers’ markets Willunga on Saturday morning is the flagship; the Hills and the Barossa keep their own, all inside an hour. The fritz order At the deli counter, fritz and sauce on white bread is the childhood taste of the state. Order it once, for citizenship.

chunks.t: Food, wine & the everyday in Adelaide
chunks.x: For its size, Adelaide feeds its communities well. The western suburbs carry the Italian and Greek heritage — delis, continental grocers, the long Sunday lunch; the north and north-east are the centre of gravity for Asian, African and Middle-Eastern groceries; halal butchers are easy to find across the northern suburbs; and kosher supplies, while more limited than Sydney or Melbourne, are available through the long-established community in the east. The Market fills most gaps in one visit. For newcomers this matters beyond ingredients: those shops sit alongside the associations, places of worship and weekend gatherings that make a new city feel liveable within a month rather than a year.

chunks.t: Food, wine & the everyday in Adelaide
chunks.x: Adelaide eats above its weight. The laneway small-bar scene — Peel Street, Leigh Street and their neighbours — arrived a decade ago and stayed; the pub is still the default meeting place; and the cellar doors of McLaren Vale, the Hills and the Barossa double as the city’s best long lunches, forty minutes to an hour from town. Coffee is taken seriously without Melbourne’s theology about it. The heritage list is cheerfully odd: the pie floater — a meat pie upturned in pea soup — is the late-night institution, fritz is the deli order, and every March the whole food city moves outdoors into the festival gardens. Eating out costs noticeably less than Sydney; the wine list is where Adelaide quietly shows off. The everyday, in one list Serious shop: Central Market Thursday evening or Saturday morning; supermarkets for the rest.

chunks.t: Food, wine & the everyday in Adelaide
chunks.x: Cheapest basket: ALDI; local loyalty: Drakes and Foodland; Saturday: Willunga farmers’ market. Specialist ingredients: west for Italian and Greek, north and north-east for Asian, African, Middle-Eastern and halal. Bags in the car, bottles in a crate, fritz at least once. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Adelaide at a glance: the grid, the hills and the half-hour clock
chunks.x: Before the practical chapters, orientation. Adelaide is the easiest Australian capital to read: a planned grid in the middle, parklands all the way around it, the hills on one side and the gulf on the other, and almost nothing more than half an hour away.

chunks.t: Adelaide at a glance: the grid, the hills and the half-hour clock
chunks.h: How the city is laid out
chunks.x: Where Adelaide sits, with the straight-line distance to Barossa and Victor Harbor

chunks.t: Adelaide at a glance: the grid, the hills and the half-hour clock
chunks.x: The city centre is a mile-square grid of wide streets and five public squares, wrapped completely by parkland — there is no continuous built edge between the city and North Adelaide. The Torrens runs through that green belt, with the cultural boulevard of North Terrace along the northern edge carrying the museum, the gallery, the university and the newest hospital-and-research precinct.

chunks.t: Adelaide at a glance: the grid, the hills and the half-hour clock
chunks.x: Thirty-odd kilometres of white sand run down the western edge, from North Haven through Henley, Glenelg and Brighton to Seacliff and, further south, Sellicks. Glenelg has the tram; the rest have jetties, esplanades and gulf sunsets. The beach suburbs are twenty to thirty minutes from the city and priced accordingly.

chunks.t: Adelaide at a glance: the grid, the hills and the half-hour clock
chunks.x: Behind the city the Adelaide Hills rise within twenty minutes — cooler, greener, with autumn colour and Sunday-morning fog. Beyond them the wine valleys wrap the capital: the Barossa and Clare to the north, McLaren Vale and the Fleurieu to the south, all inside an hour.

chunks.t: Adelaide at a glance: the grid, the hills and the half-hour clock
chunks.x: Hot, dry summers and mild, green winters, with the rain arriving May to September. Summer brings real heatwaves — runs of days past 40° most years — which end, theatrically, with a cool change rolling in off the Southern Ocean that can drop the temperature ten degrees in minutes. The Hills sit several degrees cooler; the coast gets the sea breeze first. Summer Dec – Feb 17–29° Dry heat · 40° runs Autumn Mar – May 12–23° Mad March · vintage Winter Jun – Aug 8–16° Cool, green, wet Spring Sep – Nov 11–22° Jacarandas · festivals Two practical notes. Older housing stock often has thin insulation and patchy heating — make a good split system a rental-search criterion, for both ends of the year. And take the heat itself seriously: hydration, sun protection and a plan for very hot days matter, especially with children or older family members.

chunks.t: Adelaide at a glance: the grid, the hills and the half-hour clock
chunks.x: South Australia runs on Australian Central Standard Time — UTC+9½, thirty minutes behind Sydney and Melbourne — and, unlike Queensland, it does observe daylight saving. The practical effects are small but constant: national meetings land at five past the half-hour, broadcast times shift, and Perth sits ninety minutes behind you in winter. You adjust within a month; your phone adjusts instantly.

chunks.t: Adelaide at a glance: the grid, the hills and the half-hour clock
chunks.x: Adelaide Airport is unusually close to the city — about fifteen minutes from the CBD, on the way to the beach. It flies direct to every Australian capital and to a handful of international hubs, so most of the world is one stop away. Melbourne is a day’s drive or a short flight; everywhere else east is a flight. The South Australia guide covers the drives out to the regions.

chunks.t: Healthcare in Adelaide: a system you can know personally
chunks.x: Registration is national; hiring here runs through three metropolitan networks. Adelaide’s distinguishing feature is a health system that is large for the city’s size, anchored by one of the newest hospital-and-research precincts in the southern hemisphere — and small enough that you will know it within a year.

chunks.t: Healthcare in Adelaide: a system you can know personally
chunks.h: How the metropolitan system is organised
chunks.x: South Australia runs its public system through ten local health networks. Three of them cover metropolitan Adelaide — broadly the central city, the northern suburbs and the south — and a fourth is a statewide women’s and children’s service based in the capital. Each network employs in its own right, so moving between them later is a fresh application rather than a transfer. Alongside them sit a substantial private and not-for-profit hospital sector concentrated in Adelaide, a state ambulance service, university-linked research institutes clustered along the city’s northern boulevard, and Aboriginal community-controlled health organisations. A new precinct The city’s western boulevard now holds one of the newest hospital-and-research precincts in the southern hemisphere — hospital, medical research institutes and university health faculties on adjacent sites.

chunks.t: Healthcare in Adelaide: a system you can know personally
chunks.h: How the metropolitan system is organised
chunks.x: Three metro networks Central, northern and southern Adelaide, each anchored by a major teaching hospital. The north is the growth corridor, where demand has risen fastest. A statewide children’s service Paediatric and maternity specialist care runs as its own network from Adelaide, serving the whole state with outreach into the regions. One national register Ahpra registration works everywhere in Australia. The process, English evidence and assessment live once in Eligibility & registration . Four employers, one city “A job in Adelaide” is a job with one of these. Each hires in its own right, so which one you apply to also decides your campus, your case mix and your commute. Central Adelaide The new precinct on the city’s western boulevard — hospital, medical research institutes and university health faculties on adjacent sites, with the state’s major trauma capacity.

chunks.t: Healthcare in Adelaide: a system you can know personally
chunks.h: How the metropolitan system is organised
chunks.x: The deepest research links in the state sit here. Northern Adelaide The growth corridor. Demand has risen fastest here and recruitment follows it, which makes this the most consistently open door for clinicians arriving from overseas. Southern Adelaide Its own teaching hospital with a network of community and specialist sites around it, on the coastal side of the city — and the shortest commute for anyone drawn to the southern beaches. The statewide children’s service Paediatric and maternity specialist care runs as its own employer from Adelaide, serving the whole state with outreach into the regions. A whole career in children’s work is possible without changing employers. Moving between them later is a fresh application rather than a transfer, so it pays to choose deliberately the first time. Registration itself is national and portable: Eligibility & registration .

chunks.t: Healthcare in Adelaide: a system you can know personally
chunks.h: What that means for a career
chunks.x: Adelaide gives you tertiary and quaternary medicine — including the state’s major trauma capacity and its teaching, research and specialist services — in a city where you can live twenty minutes from work. That combination is rare, and it is why clinicians move here. The trade is depth of market. There are fewer tertiary sites than Sydney, Melbourne or Brisbane, so a very narrow sub-specialty may have one or two possible employers in the whole city. If that describes you, check the job market for your specialty before you apply. In exchange, a smaller system means you are known by name quickly, and opportunities travel through relationships faster than through advertisements.

chunks.t: Healthcare in Adelaide: a system you can know personally
chunks.h: What that means for a career
chunks.x: One structural advantage worth repeating: the whole of South Australia — Adelaide included — is classed as regional for skilled migration, which can open extra visa pathways and points that the eastern capitals cannot. For internationally trained clinicians that is concrete, and it is why Adelaide is often the shortest route into Australia. The detail lives in Visas & the move . “ Tertiary medicine, a twenty-minute commute, and a capital that counts as regional for migration. The one-line version

chunks.t: Healthcare in Adelaide: a system you can know personally
chunks.x: Pay here follows state enterprise agreements that differ from the east coast’s — we deliberately quote no figures in this guide, and will always walk you through the current agreement for your profession instead. And once you land, arrange ambulance cover: it is not automatic in South Australia, and a state ambulance membership or insurance add-on is inexpensive insurance against a very expensive ride. chunks.t: Where clinicians live in Adelaide: the villages, the coast and the Hills
chunks.x: Adelaide is small enough that this decision is forgiving — get it slightly wrong and you’re still twenty minutes from work. That makes it one of the more enjoyable housing decisions in Australia rather than a stressful one. Here is the map as we’d draw it over coffee. chunks.t: Where clinicians live in Adelaide: the villages, the coast and the Hills
chunks.x: North Adelaide, Prospect, Unley, Norwood, Goodwood: bluestone villas and cottages on tree-lined streets, cafés on the corner, the parklands between you and the wards. This is where many hospital staff start — walkable, characterful, close to everything — and where rents run highest, though “highest” here would read as ordinary in Sydney. Apartments in the CBD itself suit short first leases while you learn the city.

chunks.t: Where clinicians live in Adelaide: the villages, the coast and the Hills
chunks.x: Glenelg, and the beach suburbs running north through Brighton, Somerton, Henley and Grange, give Adelaide something rare among capitals: sand at the end of a tram line, with city hospitals a straightforward ride away. Sunsets over the gulf, esplanade coffee, jetty swims before a late shift. Summer weekends get busy and parking with them; that is the whole complaint.

chunks.t: Where clinicians live in Adelaide: the villages, the coast and the Hills
chunks.h: The Hills and the near valleys
chunks.x: Stirling, Aldgate and Crafers sit in hill country — cooler, greener, autumn colour, a Sunday-morning fog — twenty to thirty minutes up the freeway from town. Further out, Mount Barker is one of the fastest-growing towns in the state and noticeably better value. The trade: you will drive, and on summer fire-danger days you’ll live by the warnings like everyone else.

chunks.t: Where clinicians live in Adelaide: the villages, the coast and the Hills
chunks.x: Adelaide’s growth is happening in two directions. North through Mawson Lakes and toward Gawler, and south through Seaford and Aldinga toward the Fleurieu: newer housing, bigger blocks, the most affordable family homes in the metropolitan area, and their own hospital campuses in both directions. Both corridors are rail-served, which matters more here than the distance does — the northern network is where health demand has grown fastest.

chunks.t: Where clinicians live in Adelaide: the villages, the coast and the Hills
chunks.x: The one Adelaide habit worth copying: arrive with your references, proof of income and offer letter as clean PDFs; a complete same-day application regularly beats a longer local history. Before you sign a lease Is the property inside the school zone you need? Zones run street by street here. Does the home have decent cooling and heating? Older stock often doesn’t, and the bills follow. How long is the commute at your actual shift times — and is there parking at both ends? Would a short-term rental first be wiser? Most people re-choose their suburb once they know the city. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Getting around Adelaide: the twenty-minute city
chunks.x: Adelaide’s transport story is mostly the absence of pain: no toll roads anywhere in the state, some of the shortest commutes of any Australian capital, and an airport fifteen minutes from the office. This is the chapter where the city quietly wins.

chunks.t: Getting around Adelaide: the twenty-minute city
chunks.x: metroCARD Trains, trams and buses run on one tap-on card — or just a contactless bank card. Simple, and cheap by east-coast standards. The tram One line, but the right one: free through the city centre, then out to the beach at Glenelg. It makes the coast a commute, not an outing. Trains Suburban lines reach the coast, the northern growth corridor and the south. Small network, reliable timetable, useful if you live on one. The O-Bahn Adelaide’s oddity: buses on a guided concrete track to the north-east — one of the fastest suburban runs in the country. Living car-free is practical along the tram corridor, in the inner ring and near a train line. It stops being practical in the Hills and the outer corridors — plan on a car for those from day one.

chunks.t: Getting around Adelaide: the twenty-minute city
chunks.x: Australians drive on the left, and Adelaide is the easiest capital to learn in: a flat grid, ring routes, no tolls, and rush hours that would make a Sydneysider laugh. You can usually drive on a valid overseas licence for a period after arriving, then transfer to a South Australian licence once you’re resident — the rules, and buying a car, live in Living in Australia . Two local notes. The power poles are concrete-and-steel stobie poles — unforgiving, which is partly why Adelaide drivers treat them with respect. And once you leave the metropolitan area the distances lengthen fast: fuel stops you plan rather than assume, and wildlife at dawn and dusk.

The hours this gives back are the least-discussed and most-felt advantage of living here. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Weekends in Adelaide: the hills, the coast and wine country
chunks.x: The recruiting pitch for Adelaide is really a geography lesson: almost everything worth a weekend sits within an hour of the city. This chapter is what people do with that — and the festival month the whole year bends around.

chunks.t: Weekends in Adelaide: the hills, the coast and wine country
chunks.x: Four of the world’s best-known wine regions ring the capital. The Barossa and the Adelaide Hills are inside an hour; McLaren Vale is forty minutes down the coast, where the vines run almost to the sea; the Clare Valley sits within two, its old railway now the Riesling Trail for a day’s cycling between cellar doors. The practical effect: a long cellar-door lunch is a normal Saturday, not an anniversary. Vintage, in autumn, is the prettiest time to live here.

chunks.t: Weekends in Adelaide: the hills, the coast and wine country
chunks.x: The city’s own thirty kilometres of beach handle the everyday — jetty swims, esplanade runs, gulf sunsets that make the local news. Weekends stretch to the Fleurieu Peninsula’s surf and coves, to Victor Harbor and the whale-watching season, and to Kangaroo Island — a ferry or a short flight — for wildlife, wilderness beaches and remarkable food. Maslin Beach, where the metro coast gives way to the Fleurieu

chunks.t: Weekends in Adelaide: the hills, the coast and wine country
chunks.x: Twenty minutes up the freeway the air cools and the country turns green: Mount Lofty’s summit and botanic garden, the Heysen Trail running through the ranges, Hahndorf’s German heritage main street, and a run of villages that do log fires in winter and long lunches all year. It is the closest thing an Australian capital has to a countryside on its doorstep. Three directions, all under two hours The recruiting pitch for Adelaide is really a geography lesson, and this is it: three roads out of the city, and almost everything worth a weekend on one of them. Up into the Hills Twenty minutes up the freeway the air cools and the country turns green — log fires in winter, long lunches all year. The city Stirling · 20 min Hahndorf Mount Barker · 35 min Down the coast Thirty kilometres of metropolitan beach first, then the vines running almost to the sea, then whale season.

chunks.t: Weekends in Adelaide: the hills, the coast and wine country
chunks.x: The city Henley & Brighton · 20 min McLaren Vale · 40 min Victor Harbor North to the valleys Two of the world’s best-known wine regions, and an old railway line now ridden between cellar doors. The city The Barossa · ~1 hr Clare Valley · ~2 hr Kangaroo Island is the exception — a ferry or a short flight rather than a drive. Everything else on this page is inside two hours, which is why a long cellar-door lunch here is a normal Saturday rather than an anniversary.

chunks.t: Weekends in Adelaide: the hills, the coast and wine country
chunks.x: Mad March The Fringe — the southern hemisphere’s biggest arts festival — plus the Adelaide Festival, WOMADelaide and the motorsport, all at once. The city doubles in energy for a month. Winter Illuminate lights up the city in July; the Hills do log fires and galleries; the footy fills the oval — and the Showdown derby splits every workplace in two. Spring & vintage Tasting Australia in autumn, jacarandas and show season in spring, and harvest turning the valleys gold.

chunks.t: Moving to Adelaide: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.x: Adelaide is the Australian city where the arithmetic still works: a tertiary career, a house you can buy, the hills twenty minutes from the wards and the sea forty. It asks one thing in return — that you like your city elegant and unhurried rather than enormous.

chunks.t: Moving to Adelaide: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.h: A capital built on a plan
chunks.x: Around 1.4 million people live on a grid Colonel Light laid out in 1836, ringed completely by parklands — a piece of city planning so unusual that it still shapes daily life here. The Torrens runs through the middle, the Adelaide Hills rise behind, and the gulf beaches run thirty-odd kilometres down the western edge with a tram to the middle of them. For clinicians the draw is a health system that is large for the city’s size, anchored by one of the newest hospital-and-research precincts in the southern hemisphere along the city’s western boulevard. It is a system you can know personally within a year — which cuts both ways, and this guide says so. The costs are a fierce, dry summer with real 40-degree runs, power bills among the dearest in the country, and a job market that is one city deep.

chunks.t: Moving to Adelaide: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.h: A capital built on a plan
chunks.x: What you get back is time: the shortest commutes of any mainland capital, and a weekend that starts twenty minutes from your front door. Who wrote this Ethicare is a healthcare recruitment company. This guide is free to read, asks nothing of you, and does not give visa advice. Adelaide is where the money and the life line up best of the mainland capitals, and also where “will the job market fit me?” needs the most careful answer. Where we think it’s the wrong city for you, we say so.

chunks.t: Moving to Adelaide: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.x: ~1.4M People in Greater Adelaide — roughly three in four South Australians live in or around the capital. 20 min From the city to the Adelaide Hills. The sea is about forty. This is the “twenty-minute city” people talk about. ~30 km Of white-sand metropolitan beach, from North Haven down to Sellicks — with a tram to the middle of it. 1836 Founded as a planned free settlement — no convicts, a fact locals will mention — on a grid inside a complete ring of parkland. ~50% Of Australia’s wine is made in this state, and the Barossa, Clare, McLaren Vale and the Hills all sit within about an hour. 3 Metropolitan health networks — central, northern and southern — plus a statewide women’s and children’s service. UTC+9½ The half-hour time zone — thirty minutes behind Sydney and Melbourne, with daylight saving in summer.

chunks.t: Moving to Adelaide: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.x: March The Fringe, the Festival, WOMADelaide and the motorsport all at once. Locals call it Mad March, and mean it. 10c Per can and bottle — the container deposit has run since 1977, and returning them is a local habit. North Terrace — galleries and museums a short walk from the city centre

chunks.t: Moving to Adelaide: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.h: Six things you only learn once you’re here
chunks.x: The half-hour clock is real Thirty minutes behind the east coast. National meetings land at odd times, football starts at half past, and every newcomer misses one call in their first month. Summer is dry and serious Heatwaves run past 40° for days, then break with a cool change off the Southern Ocean you can feel arrive. A good split system is infrastructure, not comfort. Power bills bite South Australian electricity is among the dearest in the country. An efficient home and a carefully chosen energy plan matter more here than almost anywhere. It’s a two-degrees city “Which school did you go to?” is an Adelaide icebreaker. Everyone seems to know everyone — which makes reputations, good and bad, travel fast. The deli is an institution The corner deli — part milk bar, part grocer — survives here as it does nowhere else, along with Foodland, the fiercely local supermarket.

chunks.t: Moving to Adelaide: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.h: Six things you only learn once you’re here
chunks.x: Nothing is far Most of Adelaide is twenty-odd minutes from most of the rest of it, with no toll roads anywhere. It resets what you think a commute costs you. A note on Country Adelaide stands on Kaurna Country — Tarntanya, the place of the red kangaroo — and the Adelaide Plains carry Kaurna names you will see in dual naming across the parklands, the city squares and health services. Acknowledgement of Country opens meetings, and health services work in partnership with Aboriginal community-controlled organisations. Take the cultural induction seriously.

Anything true of Australia generally — Medicare, visas, Ahpra registration, tax, superannuation, schools — lives once in Moving to Australia .
