chunks.t: Why Adelaide: the case for the twenty-minute city
chunks.x: Every city has a brochure. This chapter is the conversation we’d have instead: what Adelaide gives a working clinician, the arithmetic that works, what a week here plausibly looks like — and who we’d point to a bigger city.

chunks.t: Why Adelaide: the case for the twenty-minute city
chunks.x: Start with the sum most people never quite write down. Adelaide is the most affordable mainland capital: a three-bedroom family house rents for hundreds of dollars a week less than its Sydney equivalent, and buying one is an achievable mid-career plan. There are no toll roads anywhere in the state, commutes are among the shortest of any Australian capital, and — unlike Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane or Perth’s eastern equivalents — the whole of South Australia is classed as regional for skilled migration, which can mean extra visa points and pathways. Against that, salaries sit broadly in the national range for public health — the enterprise agreements differ state by state, and we’ll always walk you through the current ones rather than quote figures here. The point isn’t that you earn dramatically more in Adelaide. It’s that the same career buys noticeably more life. $0 Toll roads in the state <1 hr To the Barossa, the Vale or the Hills 100% Of SA counts as regional for migration

chunks.t: Why Adelaide: the case for the twenty-minute city
chunks.x: A week here can plausibly hold all of this. A city-hospital shift that starts without a toll-road crawl, because most of Adelaide is twenty-odd minutes from most of the rest of it. A swim at Henley or Brighton before a late start — the sea sits at the end of the tram line. A Thursday-evening shop at the Central Market, where the produce is better and cheaper than any supermarket. Saturday lunch at a McLaren Vale cellar door, forty minutes south, and Sunday on the Heysen Trail in the Hills before the working week resets. None of that is a holiday itinerary. It’s the ordinary shape of a week when a city this liveable is also this small — and it is exactly what people mean when they say their salary “goes further” here. The distance between your roster and your life shrinks. Sophie’s insight What I love most about Adelaide is how much life it offers for the money.

chunks.t: Why Adelaide: the case for the twenty-minute city
chunks.x: Having spent years in the NHS, I know how easily work can take over — and what stands out here is how close everything is. The hills, the sea and the vines are all a short drive away, and people make time for them. My advice: think about your commute, your community and what you’ll do on your days off. Those things shape your happiness more than people expect. Sophie Careem Founder & CEO, Ethicare Resourcing

chunks.t: Why Adelaide: the case for the twenty-minute city
chunks.h: When we’d point you to a bigger city
chunks.x: The market is one city deep Adelaide carries fewer tertiary sites than Sydney, Melbourne or Brisbane, so a narrow sub-specialty may simply have more room on the east coast. Ask us early if that describes you. Summer is fierce Dry heat, 40-degree runs, and a long brown February. If you wilt in heat and can’t love an early-morning life for two months a year, think hard. It’s a quiet city Adelaide is elegant, not electric. If what recharges you is big-city churn — new restaurants weekly, a giant professional scene — Melbourne or Sydney will fit better. The east coast is a flight away Melbourne is eight hours’ drive, Sydney fourteen. If your family network lands in the eastern capitals, every visit means a flight. Everyone knows everyone A small professional community is warm and quick to include you — and unforgiving of a bad first impression.

chunks.t: Why Adelaide: the case for the twenty-minute city
chunks.h: When we’d point you to a bigger city
chunks.x: Reputations travel faster here than in a big system. Where we’d steer you instead If you need system scale and sub-specialty depth, Melbourne or Sydney carry more sites. If winter sun is the whole point, Brisbane is the answer — Adelaide winters are cool and green. If it’s the country posts and the incentives that interest you, the South Australia guide covers the Riverland, the gulfs and the South-East properly. In our experience Adelaide suits clinicians who are done trading hours for postcode — the twenty-minute commute is real, and it compounds into something bigger than it sounds. The people who thrive here measure a city by their weekday evenings, not its skyline. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Cost of living in Auckland for healthcare professionals
chunks.x: Auckland is New Zealand’s most expensive city, and housing is the reason. Everything else is closer to what you’re used to than you might fear.

chunks.t: Cost of living in Auckland for healthcare professionals
chunks.x: We used to print a weekly rent and a monthly budget table here. We have taken them out. A figure that was true when a page was written is misleading a year later, and a candidate who plans a move around a stale number is worse off than one who plans around none. What does not go stale is the relationship between places — which suburb, ring or region you choose — and the judgement about which costs catch people out. For today’s actual numbers use the calculators at the foot of the page, and use them to compare Auckland against the city you are leaving. That is the only comparison that decides anything. Two things are worth saying before any numbers. First, prices here include GST — the figure on the shelf is the figure you pay, and restaurant bills carry no service charge or expectation of a tip.

chunks.t: Cost of living in Auckland for healthcare professionals
chunks.x: Second, salaries are quoted as gross annual figures and most healthcare staff are paid fortnightly. Beyond that, the summary is simple. Housing will take a bigger share of your income than you’re probably used to. Food is comparable. Fuel and cars are cheaper than the UK and dearer than the US. Eating out is reasonable, alcohol is not, and electronics cost more than they should because everything arrives by ship.

chunks.t: Cost of living in Auckland for healthcare professionals
chunks.x: Four choices, and a monthly range you can take to a conversation about salary. Who is moving Where you’d rent Add or remove Monthly range — per month, before tax and savings Indicative New Zealand dollars, July 2026. Excludes tax, KiwiSaver, student loan repayments and one-off setup costs.

chunks.t: Cost of living in Auckland for healthcare professionals
chunks.x: The quickest way to calibrate a new country is to price a week’s shopping. These are supermarket and high-street prices, GST included. Two local habits worth knowing Fruit and vegetables are strongly seasonal and dramatically cheaper in season — buying what’s abundant is how people here keep the grocery bill down. Pak’nSave is much cheaper than New World for the same basket. Bring your own bags: single-use plastic bags are banned. What moves in your favour, and what doesn’t Compared with the UK, Ireland and most of Europe. Coming from the Gulf or the United States the picture shifts, particularly on tax and on cars.

chunks.t: Cost of living in Auckland for healthcare professionals
chunks.x: Cars The used Japanese import market makes a reliable second car affordable. Being outdoors Regional parks, beaches, walking tracks and DOC campsites cost little or nothing. The default weekend is free. Club sport and children’s activities A season of junior football or netball costs a fraction of what most arrivals expect. Seasonal produce, meat and dairy Bought in season, from the right supermarket, food is very reasonable. Childcare for three to five year olds The 20 Hours ECE subsidy takes a real bite out of the bill.

chunks.t: Cost of living in Auckland for healthcare professionals
chunks.x: Rent, and by a distance This is the line that reshapes your budget. Plan it first and everything else follows. Alcohol Excise duty is high. Local wine and beer are excellent and still not cheap. Anything imported Electronics, appliances, books, cosmetics, cycling kit. Everything arrives by ship, and the price shows it. Heating an older house Insulation standards have improved, but plenty of housing stock predates them. Saturday market — in season is the whole trick

chunks.t: Cost of living in Auckland for healthcare professionals
chunks.x: Costs vary by suburb and by household. These tools will get you closer than any average. Compare cities Numbeo · cost of living Auckland prices for rent, groceries, transport and dining, against your current city. Plan your budget Sorted budget planner New Zealand’s free, government-backed budgeting tool. Official data Stats NZ living costs The Household Living-Costs Price Index, updated each quarter. chunks.t: Why Auckland: the case and the trade-offs
chunks.x: Built on forty-eight dormant volcanoes between two harbours, Tāmaki Makaurau was prized long before it was a city. Here’s what living in it feels like — and, just as usefully, when it’s the wrong answer.

chunks.t: Why Auckland: the case and the trade-offs
chunks.h: Three reasons people choose it, and one they don’t expect
chunks.x: 01 · The deepest job market A third of the country lives here, which means four major hospitals, every subspecialty, and room to move sideways without moving city. 02 · An international city More than two hundred ethnicities, which in practice means your food, your festivals and your community already exist here. 03 · An hour to everywhere Islands, surf and native bush inside an hour. Not a holiday — a Tuesday evening. 04 · The one nobody mentions How quickly the pace of your week changes. It tends to land around week three, usually on an ordinary Wednesday.

chunks.t: Why Auckland: the case and the trade-offs
chunks.x: Auckland’s real advantage isn’t the city centre — it’s how little of your life is spent getting anywhere. Choose a distance to see what the journey looks like. From the harbour to the islands, a world of lifestyle sits within forty minutes of the city centre.

chunks.t: Why Auckland: the case and the trade-offs
chunks.x: Rosters differ and no two departments are the same. But a normal week here has a shape, and it’s roughly this. Mon · Handover at 07:30 Departments here are smaller. You’ll know everyone’s name by Friday, including the porters’. Tue · A late finish Home by half six. In summer it’s still light at nine, so the evening isn’t over. Wed · Netball, football, or the pool Club sport costs very little and is how most newcomers meet people who aren’t colleagues. Thu · The weekly shop, and a plan Pak’nSave for the week. Someone in the tearoom will have an opinion about where you should go on Saturday. Fri · Dinner out, and a walk home Ponsonby Road or the Viaduct. A mid-range meal runs about NZ$25–$40, and the walk back is along the water. Sat · The market, then the coast Forty minutes west to Piha. Black sand, real surf, and thinning crowds by four. Sun · Nothing much The Domain, a bakery, and being home in time for a Monday you don’t dread.

chunks.t: Why Auckland: the case and the trade-offs
chunks.x: Know both sides before you book a flight. Nothing here should be a surprise once you arrive. What it does brilliantly Four major hospitals and every subspecialty — the widest choice of work in the country, without changing city. Food, faith and community from almost anywhere. Halal butchers, Asian supermarkets, Pacific markets, and the largest Pacific festival in the world. Islands, surf beaches and native rainforest all inside an hour of the CBD. New Zealand’s main international airport, which matters more than you think when family are far away. What takes adjusting to Housing is the most expensive in New Zealand — a three-bedroom house sits around NZ$700 a week, and more in the central and beachside suburbs. Wages are higher here too, but plan for rent first. The city is spread out. Public transport is improving and the City Rail Link helps, but most households still keep a car. February is humid. Not unbearable, but a different kind of warm from a European summer. It is far from Europe. Most people settle into one long trip home a year rather than several short ones.

chunks.t: Why Auckland: the case and the trade-offs
chunks.h: A mild year, and what you do in it
chunks.x: Warm, humid and coastal. Summers rarely get uncomfortable, winters stay mild, and frosts are rare. Rain arrives across the whole year rather than in one wet season. Summer Dec – Feb 20–24° Avg daytime Autumn Mar – May 17–21° Avg daytime Winter Jun – Aug 11–15° Avg daytime Spring Sep – Nov 15–19° Avg daytime “I thought Auckland was going to feel really busy because it’s New Zealand’s biggest city. But coming from London, it feels so much slower and more relaxed. Being able to finish work and head to the beach is something I could only have dreamed of before we moved.” Festus, Radiographer — moved from London to Auckland

chunks.t: Why Auckland: the case and the trade-offs
chunks.x: Pace of life Slower outside work, not inside it. The hospital is a hospital — busy, pressured, occasionally chaotic. What changes is the evening: shops shut earlier, people leave on time more often, and there’s a general social agreement that a weekend is for something other than work. The main adjustment is that Auckland isn’t a late-night city. If you love a midnight restaurant, that’s a loss you will feel. Diversity More than two hundred ethnicities, roughly four in ten Aucklanders born overseas, and the largest Polynesian population of any city in the world. Whole suburbs are shaped by their communities — South Asian around Sandringham and Papatoetoe, East Asian along Dominion Road and in Northcote, Pacific across the south. Practically: your food, your festivals and your place of worship almost certainly already exist here.

chunks.t: Why Auckland: the case and the trade-offs
chunks.x: Safety New Zealand consistently ranks among the safest countries in the world, and for most people arriving from a large city the change is noticeable — children walking to school, unlocked back doors in some suburbs, an unarmed police service as the norm. It isn’t crime-free. Retail and vehicle crime get discussed a lot locally. But personal safety is rarely what worries people once they arrive. Family friendliness Auckland’s strongest card. Free regional parks and beaches, cheap club sport, playgrounds everywhere, under-fives travelling free on public transport, and schools that expect children to be outside. The catch is grandparents. Being twenty-four hours from family is the hardest part of this move for most parents, and no amount of beach compensates for it entirely. Commuting Better than London or Sydney, worse than a mid-sized city.

chunks.t: Why Auckland: the case and the trade-offs
chunks.x: A car city with improving public transport — the City Rail Link and the Northern Busway have changed what’s possible, and the ferries are pleasant. Twenty to thirty minutes door to door is achievable if you choose your suburb around your hospital. Fifty is what happens if you don’t. Outdoor lifestyle The strongest single argument for the city. Fifty islands in the gulf, black-sand surf beaches forty minutes west, rainforest ranges on the doorstep, and a harbour built for sailing. All of it a Tuesday evening rather than an annual holiday. If you don’t particularly like being outdoors, you’re paying Auckland prices for something you won’t use.

chunks.t: Why Auckland: the case and the trade-offs
chunks.h: Four good reasons to choose somewhere else
chunks.x: If any of these sound like you, say so and we’ll point you elsewhere in the country. Rent is your main worry Auckland housing is the most expensive in the country. Christchurch, Waikato and the Bay of Plenty will give you materially more house for the same salary. You want to walk everywhere Wellington is compact, walkable and hilly, with the whole city inside twenty minutes. Auckland is not that, and won’t become it. You want mountains and snow Auckland is subtropical and flat by comparison. Christchurch, Central Otago and Queenstown are where the Alps are. You want small and quiet A third of the country lives here. If the appeal of New Zealand is that it’s not a big city, don’t move to the big city. Every region has its own pace, cost of living and kind of work. It’s worth reading a few before you narrow down — our New Zealand destination guides cover each one in the same detail.

chunks.t: Why Auckland: the case and the trade-offs
chunks.x: What tends to change You gain time. The commute shortens, the evening lengthens, and the weekend belongs to you. You gain access — the coast, the bush and the islands are ordinary rather than an event. You miss the density: the late restaurant, the last-minute concert, the airport that’s four hours from anywhere in Europe. You miss family, and it doesn’t fade. Most people settle into one long trip home a year rather than several short ones. These are impressions rather than measurements, and no ranking of cities is intended.

chunks.t: Why Auckland: the case and the trade-offs
chunks.x: The ones that come up most often when clinicians are weighing Auckland against everywhere else. Is Auckland too expensive to be worth it? It’s New Zealand’s priciest city, and housing is where you’ll feel it. What you get back is the deepest job market in the country, the widest choice of schools, and a coastline you don’t have to pay to use. Plenty of clinicians choose an outer suburb or the Shore and treat the extra commute as the trade. Do I need a car? In the city centre, no. Almost everywhere else, yes — Auckland is spread out and most households run one. Buses, trains and ferries keep improving and cover more of the region each year, but plan around a car unless you’re living and working centrally. How long is a typical commute? Auckland traffic is real, and the harbour bridge is the pinch point. A cross-city drive that takes 20 minutes on a Sunday can take an hour at 8am.

chunks.t: Why Auckland: the case and the trade-offs
chunks.x: Most people optimise for their hospital, not their postcode. Which suburb should I look at first if I have children? Start from the school, not the house. Work out which schools you’d want, check their zones, then search inside them. The North Shore and the central isthmus are the usual starting points, but zoning — not reputation — is what decides enrolment. Is it easy to meet people? Auckland is one of the world’s most multicultural cities, so most newcomers find a community that already feels familiar, plus a lot that doesn’t. Sports clubs, church groups and the hospital social scene do most of the work in the first few months. What surprises people most? How quickly the city stops feeling big. And how cold houses can be indoors in winter — New Zealand homes are built differently from what most arrivals are used to, so pack a warm layer even if the forecast looks mild.

chunks.t: Why Auckland: the case and the trade-offs
chunks.x: Where we’d steer you instead If the housing market is the dealbreaker, Waikato and Christchurch both carry real clinical breadth at a materially lower entry price — and neither is a compromise on the work. If you want a city you can live fifteen minutes from work in, Wellington is the answer. A smaller system, a shorter day. If the traffic is what you would come to resent, the Bay of Plenty is growing quickly and the commute is a fraction of Auckland’s. In our experience Auckland is the one place in New Zealand where the clinical scale rivals what you left. The clinicians who settle here are the ones who decided the breadth of the work was worth the price of the housing — and who chose their suburb around the commute rather than the listing. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Healthcare in Auckland: hospitals, ACC and the private sector
chunks.x: You’ll work inside this system and, sooner or later, use it. Here’s how it fits together — for you, and for your family. Public healthcare is funded through general taxation and delivered by Health New Zealand | Te Whatu Ora as a single national organisation. Auckland’s services sit across three metropolitan districts. Alongside it sit two things newcomers rarely expect: a no-fault accident scheme that covers everybody, and a private sector growing faster than anyone here can remember. The public system Free or heavily subsidised hospital care for residents and most work-visa holders. Emergency departments, planned surgery, maternity, mental health and specialist services all sit here. ACC The Accident Compensation Corporation covers everyone in New Zealand — residents and visitors — for injury from accidents, no fault attached. Treatment, rehabilitation and some loss of earnings. Private cover A large and fast-growing private sector handling mostly elective surgery, endoscopy and diagnostics. Many people hold insurance alongside the public system, and some employers contribute.

chunks.t: Healthcare in Auckland: hospitals, ACC and the private sector
chunks.x: Four major public hospitals serve the region, each with a distinct character and catchment. Which one you join shapes your commute, your caseload and your colleagues. Auckland City Hospital One of New Zealand’s largest tertiary hospitals — acute, surgical, specialist and emergency care, with Starship Children’s Hospital on the same campus. Central, so most inner suburbs are a short commute. Middlemore Hospital A major South Auckland hospital, known nationally for its trauma, burns and plastic-surgery services. Serves one of the most diverse catchments in the country. North Shore Hospital Acute, medical and surgical services for the rapidly growing North Shore. Most staff live on the Shore rather than crossing the bridge twice a day. Waitākere Hospital Medical, maternity and outpatient services for West Auckland, with the Waitākere Ranges and the west-coast beaches on the doorstep.

chunks.t: Healthcare in Auckland: hospitals, ACC and the private sector
chunks.x: Auckland’s private hospitals do mostly planned work — surgery, endoscopy, diagnostics and day procedures — funded by insurance, by ACC, by patients directly, and increasingly by Te Whatu Ora outsourcing planned operations. For a clinician this matters in two ways. Many specialists work across both sectors in the same week: a public list on Tuesday, a private list on Thursday. And private hospitals are a substantial employer in their own right — theatre nurses, anaesthetic technicians, radiographers, sonographers and recovery staff. There are around seventeen new operating theatres in train across the city. It’s worth knowing the landscape even if you only ever intend to work in the public system.

chunks.t: Healthcare in Auckland: hospitals, ACC and the private sector
chunks.x: Public and private hospitals are the two obvious employers. There are three more, and between them they account for a great deal of the clinical work in the region. Primary care General practices, most grouped into Primary Health Organisations, plus after-hours accident and medical clinics. GPs here are independent businesses rather than hospital employees. Roles: GPs, practice and specialist nurses, nurse practitioners, physiotherapists, sonographers, podiatrists. Community radiology A significant part of Auckland’s imaging happens outside hospitals, in community networks running their own MRI, CT, ultrasound and mammography. Roles: radiographers, MRI and CT technologists, sonographers, mammographers, radiologists. Often more regular hours than a hospital roster.

chunks.t: Healthcare in Auckland: hospitals, ACC and the private sector
chunks.x: Community & NGO services District nursing, home-based rehabilitation, aged residential care, hospice, mental-health and addiction services, and Māori and Pacific providers delivering care in their own communities. Roles: district and community nurses, occupational therapists, physiotherapists, speech-language therapists, psychologists, social workers. Why this matters when you’re choosing a job The same qualification opens quite different working lives here. A radiographer can be on a tertiary trauma roster, in a suburban community clinic, or moving between both. If the hours matter more to you than the acuity — or the other way round — the sector you choose matters as much as the employer. Five working lives, one qualification The sector you choose shapes the week more than the job title does.

chunks.t: Healthcare in Auckland: hospitals, ACC and the private sector
chunks.x: Same registration, same city — five quite different working lives, described here by what the week feels like rather than who the employer is. A tertiary roster Highest acuity, deepest subspecialty exposure, and a shift pattern built around a hospital that never closes. Nights, weekends and on-call are part of the deal. Planned-list work Mostly booked, mostly daytime, in the private hospitals and increasingly on outsourced public lists. More predictable weeks; a narrower and less acute case mix. Primary care Continuity rather than episodes — the same families over years, in practices that are independent businesses. Wide scope, and clinical decisions made without a hospital behind you. Community imaging Clinic-based scanning at volume, with regular hours far more often than a hospital roster allows. Technically demanding, without the acute pull.

chunks.t: Healthcare in Auckland: hospitals, ACC and the private sector
chunks.x: Community, NGO and aged care Care delivered in homes, hospices and neighbourhoods. The most autonomy of any of these, the least immediate backup, and often the closest to the community you serve. Many clinicians move between two of these over a career, or run two at once — a public list one day and a private or community list the next. Worth deciding which week you want before you decide which employer.

chunks.t: Healthcare in Auckland: hospitals, ACC and the private sector
chunks.h: Everyday care: enrol with a GP in your first month
chunks.x: Your GP is the front door to almost everything non-urgent. Enrolling with a practice near home means subsidised visits and a record that follows you; turning up as a casual patient costs considerably more. Many practices let you enrol online once you have a New Zealand address — do it before you need it, because popular practices near good schools sometimes close their books. Dental care is private for adults, and prescriptions are partly subsidised once you’re enrolled. Pharmacies are everywhere, and pharmacists here are used to advising rather than just dispensing. What things cost Indicative NZ$ GP visit, enrolled adult $50 – $70 GP visit, casual patient Higher Children under 14 Usually free Prescription, per item Small standard charge Dental check-up, adult $90 – $150 Accident-related treatment Covered by ACC Indicative, and they change. Your practice publishes its own fees. Do this in week one Enrol the whole household with a GP near home, not near work. Save 111 and Healthline in every phone in the family. Find your nearest late-opening pharmacy and urgent care clinic.

chunks.t: Healthcare in Auckland: hospitals, ACC and the private sector
chunks.h: Four numbers worth knowing before you need them
chunks.x: 111 · Emergency Police, fire or ambulance. Ask for the service you need. 0800 611 116 · Healthline Free advice from registered nurses, 24 hours a day. Use it early. 1737 · Mental health Call or text, free, any time. Trained counsellors. Moving is hard — this is not a last resort. 105 · Police, non-urgent For anything that matters but isn’t happening right now. Between the GP and the emergency department sit accident and medical clinics — walk-in, extended hours, and the right choice for most evening and weekend problems. Find your nearest one in your first week.

chunks.t: Healthcare in Auckland: hospitals, ACC and the private sector
chunks.h: Six things that work differently here
chunks.x: Not better or worse — different. Worth knowing before your first shift rather than during it. Departments are smaller Which cuts both ways: you carry a broader case mix, and you’ll know the consultant, the radiographer and the ward clerk by name. Decisions get made in corridors rather than committees. Te ao Māori is embedded, not added on Karakia at the start of meetings, te reo on signage, whānau involved in decisions as a matter of course. Orientation will introduce Te Tiriti o Waitangi and tikanga — take it seriously. Hierarchy is flatter First names, fewer titles, and juniors expected to speak up. If you’re used to a more formal culture this feels strange for a fortnight and excellent thereafter. Geography is part of clinical practice Patients travel. Retrieval, telehealth and regional referral are normal parts of the work in a country this shape, even in a city as large as Auckland.

chunks.t: Healthcare in Auckland: hospitals, ACC and the private sector
chunks.h: Six things that work differently here
chunks.x: Rosters are generally respected Pressure exists — it’s a health system. But finishing on time is closer to the norm than the exception, and annual leave is expected to be taken. Auckland is the whole spectrum From a tertiary centre with Starship next door to a hospital known nationally for trauma and burns. You can change the shape of your career without changing city. “The clinical standard here will not surprise you. What surprises people is how quickly they are trusted with real responsibility, and how normal it is to leave on time. Ask about the department, not just the job title — in a system this size, the team you join matters more than the letterhead.” Sophie Careem — Founder & CEO, Ethicare Resourcing

chunks.t: Healthcare in Auckland: hospitals, ACC and the private sector
chunks.h: The questions that are awkward to ask in an interview
chunks.x: Will my family be covered? Cover depends on your visa. Most people on eligible work visas of two years or more, and their partners and children, can access publicly funded services on the same basis as residents — but check your specific visa conditions rather than assuming. ACC covers accidental injury for everyone, regardless of status. Do I need private health insurance? You don’t need it. Many people take it anyway, for shorter waits on elective procedures and for dental and optical extras. Some employers contribute — ask before you buy your own. How quickly can I see a GP? Same-week is common once you’re enrolled; same-day is often available for urgent problems. Enrolling early matters more than choosing the fanciest practice — a full practice can’t take you at all. How do I see a specialist? You can self-refer to many private specialists, or your GP will refer you.

chunks.t: Healthcare in Auckland: hospitals, ACC and the private sector
chunks.h: The questions that are awkward to ask in an interview
chunks.x: Public specialist care is free but prioritised clinically, which means waiting if your condition isn’t urgent. Most people use a mix of both. What about mental health support? Primary mental health support through your GP is the usual route, and 1737 is free, 24-hour and staffed by trained counsellors. Relocation is one of life’s larger stressors — using it early is sensible, not dramatic. How the system is funded nationally, what ACC covers in detail and how enrolment works wherever you land is the same across the country — our New Zealand healthcare guide sets it out in full. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Eating and shopping in Auckland: coffee, food and the everyday
chunks.x: Auckland takes coffee more seriously than almost anywhere and dinner less seriously than most. Whatever you cook at home, the city almost certainly sells it — the trick is knowing which street to drive to. This is a city that eats early, brunches properly, and has excellent Asian and Pacific food at prices that make the restaurant scene look expensive by comparison. There are vineyards forty minutes from the hospital. There is also a coffee vocabulary you’ll need on your first morning.

chunks.t: Eating and shopping in Auckland: coffee, food and the everyday
chunks.h: The coffee is very good, almost everywhere
chunks.x: This is the part of daily life that most surprises people arriving from the UK. There’s no chain-coffee default here. Independent cafés dominate, most of them buying from local roasters, and the standard at an ordinary suburban café is higher than at a specialist one in a lot of European cities. Espresso is the baseline, not the upgrade. The flat white is claimed by both New Zealand and Australia, and the argument won’t be settled in your lifetime. What matters practically is that it’s the default order — espresso with steamed milk, less foam than a latte, in a smaller cup — and that ordering one correctly is a small, disproportionately satisfying milestone in your first week. The other thing to know: cafés close early. Most stop serving mid-afternoon and many are shut by three.

chunks.t: Eating and shopping in Auckland: coffee, food and the everyday
chunks.h: The coffee is very good, almost everywhere
chunks.x: Brunch, not dinner, is the meal café culture is built around, and a weekend brunch here can comfortably take two hours. Flat white Espresso with steamed milk, less foam than a latte, smaller cup. The default. Long black Closest to an Americano — espresso poured over hot water. Short black An espresso. Ask for a double if you want a double. Trim Skim milk. “Trim flat white” is a complete order. Fluffy Warm frothed milk with chocolate dust, for small children. Usually free. Long black, no water What you order when what you want is a ristretto.

chunks.t: Eating and shopping in Auckland: coffee, food and the everyday
chunks.h: The clock runs earlier than you’re used to
chunks.x: A Saturday, roughly, in a city that gets up early and eats before it gets dark. The shift in timing is one of the bigger adjustments — and mostly a pleasant one. 7am Cafés open and are already busy. Runners, dog walkers and the first flat whites of the day. 9–11am Brunch proper, and the main social meal of the weekend. Expect a wait and don’t rush it. 3pm Most cafés stop serving. If you wanted lunch at three, you wanted it at two. 6–7pm Dinner. Restaurants fill early and empty early — a 9pm booking is a late one. Late Limited. Auckland is not a late-night city, and that’s an adjustment you may never fully get used to.

chunks.t: Eating and shopping in Auckland: coffee, food and the everyday
chunks.h: Eight places, and what each is good at
chunks.x: Auckland’s best eating isn’t concentrated in the centre. Several of the most interesting streets are ordinary suburban ones, and the food is better for it. Dominion Road The city’s great Chinese street — hand-pulled noodles, hotpot and dumplings, for a fraction of restaurant prices. Sandringham South Asian, and excellent. Sweet shops, dosa, and the best-value dinner in Auckland. Ponsonby Road The polished strip — wine bars, small plates and the restaurants people book for birthdays. Karangahape Road Scrappier and more interesting. Where the newer, riskier kitchens open. Britomart & Commercial Bay Harbour-edge dining in the centre, handy after work and priced accordingly. Otahuhu & Mangere Pacific food at its best — umu, taro, and Saturday markets worth setting an alarm for. Northcote & Takapuna Korean and Japanese on the Shore, plus the beachfront cafés.

chunks.t: Eating and shopping in Auckland: coffee, food and the everyday
chunks.h: Eight places, and what each is good at
chunks.x: Titirangi & the west Village cafés on the way to the ranges, and the reason a bush walk takes all morning. The Auckland Night Markets rotate between shopping-centre car parks through the week — cheap, busy, and the best value street food in the city.

chunks.t: Eating and shopping in Auckland: coffee, food and the everyday
chunks.x: Auckland isn’t New Zealand’s most famous wine region and doesn’t need to be. What it has is proximity — four distinct areas close enough for an ordinary Sunday. Waiheke Island Forty minutes by ferry, which improves it considerably. Syrah, Bordeaux blends, and restaurants with a view over the gulf. Kumeū & the north-west Thirty minutes by car. Chardonnay, old family vineyards, and Sunday lunch among the vines. Matakana An hour north. A farmers’ market, a cinema, oysters and a cluster of small producers. Clevedon Forty minutes south-east. Quiet, rural, and the one locals keep to themselves.

chunks.t: Eating and shopping in Auckland: coffee, food and the everyday
chunks.h: Eating out is expensive. Eating well is not.
chunks.x: Restaurant prices will make you wince if you’re arriving from anywhere with cheap labour or subsidised agriculture. The compensation is that the cheap end of Auckland eating is excellent rather than merely cheap. What it costs Indicative NZ$ Flat white $5.50 – $6.50 Bakery lunch $10 – $16 Dominion Road noodles $14 – $20 Weekend brunch $22 – $32 Mid-range dinner, per person $25 – $40 Bottle of local wine, restaurant $45 – $70 Two things that surprise people No tipping, no service charge. Staff are paid a proper wage and tipping isn’t expected anywhere. The menu price is the bill. Card payments sometimes carry a small surcharge, which will be signposted. BYO is a real thing. Many smaller restaurants let you bring your own wine for a modest corkage fee, which changes the economics of eating out considerably. A third of Aucklanders were born overseas, and the shops followed.

chunks.t: Eating and shopping in Auckland: coffee, food and the everyday
chunks.h: Eating out is expensive. Eating well is not.
chunks.x: This chapter is a practical directory: where the specialist grocers are, which supermarket to use for what, how to clothe a family for a New Zealand winter, and how to furnish an empty house in a fortnight without spending a fortune.

chunks.t: Eating and shopping in Auckland: coffee, food and the everyday
chunks.h: Three things worth knowing before your first shop
chunks.x: 01 · Two groups own the supermarkets Foodstuffs runs PAK’nSAVE, New World and Four Square. Woolworths runs the rest. Competition is thin, which is a large part of why groceries cost what they do — and why the specialist shops matter so much. 02 · The price on the shelf is the price GST of 15% is already included in every ticket, everywhere, and there’s no tipping culture to budget around. What you see is what leaves your account. 03 · Produce follows the season, properly Imported fruit out of season is expensive and often poor. In season it’s superb and cheap. Cooking to what’s in the shop is the single biggest saving available to a new household.

chunks.t: Eating and shopping in Auckland: coffee, food and the everyday
chunks.x: Most households here end up splitting the week: a bulk shop at one chain, fresh produce somewhere cheaper, and a market at the weekend. PAK’nSAVE The cheapest of the big chains and the ugliest, cheerfully so. Warehouse shelving, bring your own bags, pack your own trolley. Where most families do the fortnightly bulk shop. Woolworths Formerly Countdown, renamed in 2024 — you’ll still hear both names. The most familiar layout if you’re arriving from the UK or Australia, and the strongest online delivery. New World Same owner as PAK’nSAVE, aimed higher. Better fresh counters, better bread, noticeably dearer. Useful for the things the bulk shop does badly. Asian & specialist supermarkets Frequently the cheapest fresh produce in the city, by a wide margin. Plenty of Auckland households buy vegetables, fish and rice here and everything else at a chain. Four Square & dairies The corner shop. A dairy is a small local convenience store — the word has nothing to do with milk, and it’s the first bit of New Zealand English you’ll need.

chunks.t: Eating and shopping in Auckland: coffee, food and the everyday
chunks.h: Where to buy the food you grew up with
chunks.x: Areas rather than addresses, deliberately — individual shops open and close, but these neighbourhoods have held their character for decades and will still be there when you arrive. South Asian Sandringham, Papatoetoe and Mount Roskill. Spices, pulses, fresh curry leaves, halal butchers and sweet shops. Prices well below the chains for anything you’d buy in quantity. East Asian Dominion Road, Northcote and Botany. Full-size supermarkets rather than corner shops, with fish counters, fresh noodles and produce most chains don’t stock. Pacific Ōtara, Māngere and Ōtāhuhu. Taro, green bananas, corned beef and the Saturday markets that anchor the whole community. Middle Eastern Mount Roskill and Sandringham again. Halal meat, bread, olives, cheeses and pantry staples, usually with a bakery attached. African Smaller and more scattered, largely in the south and west.

chunks.t: Eating and shopping in Auckland: coffee, food and the everyday
chunks.h: Where to buy the food you grew up with
chunks.x: Ask — the community networks know exactly where, and word of mouth beats a search engine. British & Irish Most of what you’d miss is in the chains’ international aisle. The hard ones are proper sausages, decent bacon and specific chocolate.

chunks.t: Eating and shopping in Auckland: coffee, food and the everyday
chunks.x: Weekend markets are how a lot of people here shop, and how a lot of Saturday mornings get spent. Ōtara Market · Saturday morning The largest Pacific market in the country. Produce, seafood, and food stalls that are worth arriving hungry for. Finishes by midday. La Cigale · Parnell, weekends French-market baking, cheese, charcuterie and flowers. Expensive, excellent, and the pastry queue is real. Avondale Sunday Market South and East Asian produce in bulk at prices the chains can’t approach. Bring cash and a big bag. Matakana · Saturday An hour north, and a whole morning out. Local producers, oysters, wine and a cinema next door. Auckland Night Markets Rotating between shopping-centre car parks through the week. Cheap, busy, and the best value street food in the city.

chunks.t: Eating and shopping in Auckland: coffee, food and the everyday
chunks.h: You need fewer warm clothes and much better rain gear
chunks.x: Auckland winters are mild and wet rather than cold. Thick coats mostly stay in the wardrobe; a waterproof shell and merino layers get worn constantly. Houses are cooler indoors than you’re used to, so what you wear at home matters more than what you wear outside. Where people go Sylvia Park is the largest centre in the country. Westfield Newmarket sits closest to the city hospitals, Commercial Bay is the smart end downtown, and Botany, Albany and LynnMall serve the east, north and west. All are on the rail or busway network. Brands worth learning Icebreaker for merino — the most useful thing you’ll buy in your first month. Kathmandu and Macpac for outdoor and rain. Glassons and Hallenstein for everyday. Karen Walker and Kowtow at the design end. Second-hand is unembarrassing Hospice shops, Salvation Army stores and Save Mart are good and widely used across every income bracket.

chunks.t: Eating and shopping in Auckland: coffee, food and the everyday
chunks.h: You need fewer warm clothes and much better rain gear
chunks.x: For children who grow out of things in a season, this is where sensible families shop. Ask yourself Range is narrower than a large European city and sales cycles are shorter. Shoes, children’s clothes and anything imported in small volumes cost more. If you have a size that’s hard to find, bring a year of it with you.

chunks.t: Eating and shopping in Auckland: coffee, food and the everyday
chunks.x: No fridge, no washing machine, sometimes no curtains. It catches almost every arrival out, and it’s the reason the first fortnight costs more than the budget said. Cheapest · Kmart, The Warehouse, Big Save Kmart is where most new arrivals furnish the kitchen and the children’s rooms in one afternoon. Briscoes covers homeware and is permanently mid-sale, which locals find funny and newcomers find confusing. Middle · IKEA, Freedom, Nick Scali IKEA opened at Sylvia Park in December 2025 — the first in the country, and a big change to how an empty house gets filled here. Danske Møbler sits at the better end. Smartest · Trade Me and Marketplace New Zealanders move house often, so the second-hand market is deep and unsnobbish. A good fridge or washing machine costs a fraction of new. One thing nobody budgets for Almost nothing is delivered free.

chunks.t: Eating and shopping in Auckland: coffee, food and the everyday
chunks.x: Plenty of households own a tow bar and a trailer, and trailer hire is cheap and everywhere. Factor a couple of hundred dollars of moving-things-around into your first month, or make friends with a neighbour who has a ute. What a full household month costs, including the setup, is in Cost of living . Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Auckland at a glance: the shape of the city
chunks.x: The shape of the city, who arrived when, what fills the calendar, and how people get about — the orientation that makes your first week easier.

chunks.t: Auckland at a glance: the shape of the city
chunks.h: A city on a narrow waist of land
chunks.x: The Sky Tower, lit up over the central city Auckland sits on an isthmus barely two kilometres across at its narrowest — the Waitematā Harbour on one side, the Manukau on the other. Understanding that shape explains almost everything about commuting here. Select a place to see where it sits. Waitematā Harbour Manukau Harbour Hauraki Gulf A schematic — not to scale, and not a map for navigating by.

chunks.t: Auckland at a glance: the shape of the city
chunks.x: Where Auckland sits, with the straight-line distance to Hamilton The volcanic field beneath Auckland has erupted around fifty times over the last 200,000 years, and each eruption left a cone, a crater or a lava flow. What that means today is a city interrupted, pleasantly, by hills — most of them public parks. Māori built fortified pā on the largest of them. Maungawhau (Mount Eden), Maungakiekie (One Tree Hill) and Takarunga (Mount Victoria) still carry the terracing, and the views from the top are the quickest way to understand how the city fits together. Rangitoto, the youngest cone, rose from the sea only about 600 years ago and was watched from shore as it formed. Practically speaking, it means most suburbs have a hill you can walk up before work, and that the flat run between them is where the motorways went.

chunks.t: Auckland at a glance: the shape of the city
chunks.h: How the city became this mixed
chunks.x: You will not be the first person to arrive here from a long way away. That is the single most useful thing to know about Auckland. From c. 1350 · Tāmaki Makaurau Māori settlement across the isthmus — gardens, portage routes between the harbours, and pā on the volcanic cones. The name means the place desired by many. 1840s · A colonial capital Founded as the capital of the new colony, and briefly the seat of government before it moved to Wellington. British and Irish settlers, and a port that never stopped growing. 1950s–70s · The Pacific arrives Samoan, Tongan, Cook Island and Niuean families came for work, largely to South and West Auckland. Auckland is now the largest Polynesian city in the world. 1990s onward · Asia, and everywhere Chinese, Indian, Korean, Filipino and South African communities reshaped whole suburbs — and, gratifyingly, the food. Dominion Road alone is worth the move. Today · Two hundred ethnicities Roughly four in ten Aucklanders were born overseas. In a hospital tearoom that means you are unremarkable, in the best possible way.

chunks.t: Auckland at a glance: the shape of the city
chunks.h: Four weekends worth putting in your diary
chunks.x: Dates shift year to year, so check before you plan — but these four are the ones people talk about. Jun / Jul · Matariki The Māori new year, marked by the rising of the Pleiades and now a public holiday. Dawn ceremonies, light installations, and a national pause. March · Pasifika The largest Pacific festival in the world, spread across villages in Western Springs Park — one for each nation, each with its own food and stage. Oct / Nov · Diwali Aotea Square fills with dance, food stalls and fireworks. One of several festivals the city puts on for communities it is proud of. Feb / Mar · Lantern Festival Lunar New Year, marked with hundreds of lit lanterns in the Domain and a night market that is worth arriving hungry for.

chunks.t: Auckland at a glance: the shape of the city
chunks.x: Auckland Transport runs the buses, trains and ferries under one fare system. Get an AT HOP card in your first week — it’s cheaper than paying cash and works on everything. Ferries Commuter and island services cross the Waitematā to Devonport, Half Moon Bay, Hobsonville and Waiheke. The Devonport run takes twelve minutes and is, objectively, a better commute than a car. Trains & buses Four rail lines plus frequent bus routes on the main arterials, now running through the City Rail Link beneath the centre. Driving Still how most households get about. One motorway spine, one harbour crossing, and a peak that is narrow but firm. Walking & cycling Better than its reputation, particularly along the waterfront and the Northwestern path. E-bikes have made the hills a non-issue. The full detail — licences, buying a car, running costs and the traffic — is in Getting around .

chunks.t: Auckland at a glance: the shape of the city
chunks.x: Auckland’s climate is mild — no snow, no extremes, and you can swim from December to April. What catches people is the rhythm rather than the weather: when the country works, when it stops, when flights cost double, and why a fourteen-degree winter can feel colder than a British one.

chunks.t: Auckland at a glance: the shape of the city
chunks.x: Averages for the city, so treat them as the shape rather than a forecast. Auckland’s real signature is variability — four seasons in a day is a cliché because it’s accurate. Summer Dec – Feb 20–24° Avg daytime Autumn Mar – May 17–21° Avg daytime Winter Jun – Aug 11–15° Avg daytime Spring Sep – Nov 15–19° Avg daytime Sea temperature peaks in February rather than January — the water lags the air by about a month. Summer daylight runs until around nine, which is what makes an after-shift swim practical.

chunks.t: Auckland at a glance: the shape of the city
chunks.h: For about a month, the country closes
chunks.x: From a few days before Christmas until well into January, New Zealand stops. Not slows — stops. Trades go away, offices run on skeleton staff, businesses close for two or three weeks with a note on the door, and the whole country appears to be at a beach somewhere. This is lovely if you’re on holiday and difficult if you’ve just arrived. It’s the single most important thing in this chapter for anyone choosing a start date. If you can choose your start date February or late March are the easiest months to land in. Everything is open, the weather is still excellent, school has started so the rental market has settled, and you get four good months before winter. October is the next best. Mid-December is the hardest — you’ll arrive to closed offices, no trades available and a rental market that has gone quiet.

chunks.t: Auckland at a glance: the shape of the city
chunks.h: Fourteen degrees outside can feel colder than four
chunks.x: This is the complaint you’ll hear from every British, Irish and Northern European arrival, and it isn’t imagined. Auckland winters are mild by any measure — daytime highs around fourteen, frost almost unheard of, no snow. But the older housing stock was built for a warm climate on the assumption that nobody would need central heating, and a great many houses are single-glazed, under-insulated and unheated in the rooms you’re not sitting in. Add humidity. Auckland is damp, and a damp fourteen degrees inside a still room is unpleasant in a way a dry four degrees with a radiator is not. The consequence people are least prepared for is mould — on window reveals, in wardrobes, behind furniture against an external wall. The Healthy Homes standards have improved rentals substantially, and a modern or well-renovated house is entirely comfortable.

chunks.t: Auckland at a glance: the shape of the city
chunks.h: Fourteen degrees outside can feel colder than four
chunks.x: But the habits are different from what you’re used to, and they’re learnable in a week. The winter habits nobody tells you Open windows for ten minutes every morning, even in winter. Moving air is what stops mould, not heat. A dehumidifier is standard equipment here, not a luxury. Run it overnight in the wettest rooms. Dry washing outside or in a vented dryer, never on a rack in a closed bedroom. Heat the room you’re in, and shut the door. Whole-house heating is rare and expensive. Pull furniture a few centimetres off external walls so air can move behind it. The five Healthy Homes standards a rental must meet, and what to look for at a viewing, are set out in the Moving to New Zealand guide .

chunks.t: Auckland at a glance: the shape of the city
chunks.h: The school year runs with the calendar year, not across it
chunks.x: Four terms, starting in late January or early February and finishing in mid-December, with two-week breaks between and six weeks over summer. If you’re moving children mid-year, this is the detail that reshapes your timing. Term 1 · Late Jan – mid Apr The start of the school year. New classes, new teachers, and the easiest point to join. Term 2 · Late Apr – early Jul The long grey stretch. Fine to join, but socially harder than term one. Term 3 · Mid Jul – late Sep Winter sport, and the term most families find longest. Term 4 · Mid Oct – mid Dec Short, sunny and full of end-of-year events. A difficult term to arrive into.

chunks.t: Auckland at a glance: the shape of the city
chunks.h: Timing the trip back is worth real money
chunks.x: Long-haul fares from New Zealand swing enormously with the season, and the expensive windows are predictable. Getting this right once a year is worth more than most of the savings in Cost of living . Cheapest windows February to early April, and late October to mid-November. School is in, the shutdown is over, and fares drop noticeably. Most expensive Mid-December to mid-January, and the two-week school holidays. Book six to nine months ahead or pay double. Plan for one long trip rather than several short ones Twenty-four hours of flying each way makes a ten-day visit hard on everybody. Most people here take three or four weeks and go once every year or two. Build the annual-leave request in early — hospital rosters fill months ahead.

chunks.t: Auckland at a glance: the shape of the city
chunks.h: Bring layers and rain gear, not thickness
chunks.x: The single most common packing mistake is a heavy winter coat that never comes out of the wardrobe, and no waterproof jacket. Bring Merino layers, a proper waterproof shell, sturdy walking shoes, prescription medicines with documentation, and anything in a hard-to-find size. Leave behind Heavy winter coats, thermal boots, snow gear, and most electrical appliances — the plug and voltage differ. Buy on arrival A dehumidifier, a good heater, sunscreen, jandals, and a set of togs. All cheap here, and none worth the baggage allowance. “The first Christmas is the strange one. Thirty degrees, a barbecue, everyone at the beach, and light until nine at night — and somewhere underneath it a small part of you expecting dark afternoons and the smell of a kitchen at home. Plan for it rather than being surprised by it. Ring people at their Christmas Eve, not yours. And then go swimming on Christmas morning, because by the second year that is the bit you would not give up.” Sophie Careem — Founder & CEO, Ethicare Resourcing Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Weekends and the outdoors in Auckland
chunks.x: Auckland has two coasts, forty minutes apart, and they couldn’t be less alike. Knowing which one you want on a given day is most of what there is to learn — and what you do with the rest of the weekend is the reason people move here. This is the chapter that sells the city, and also the one with the most important safety information in the guide. New Zealand’s west-coast surf beaches are beautiful and dangerous, and the sun here burns faster than almost anywhere you’ve lived. Both are worth reading properly before your first summer.

chunks.t: Weekends and the outdoors in Auckland
chunks.x: Devonport, looking out across the gulf — twelve minutes by ferry from downtown East is the Hauraki Gulf — sheltered, island-scattered, warm and calm. West is the Tasman Sea — black sand, open swell, and nothing between you and Australia. Most Aucklanders use both, for entirely different things. East · Hauraki Gulf Golden sand, shallow entry, water that reaches the low twenties in February. Sheltered by the Coromandel and a scatter of islands, so the swell rarely amounts to much. Where families swim, where people go after work, and where you can leave a toddler at the water’s edge without your heart rate changing. West · Tasman Sea Iron-black volcanic sand, cliffs, and surf that arrives with the whole Tasman behind it. Reached through rainforest, forty-five minutes from the city, and one of the great coastlines anywhere. It’s also where people drown, most years, and almost always visitors who didn’t understand what they were looking at. 40 min Coast to coast, by car 15 min City centre to the nearest swim Feb Warmest sea, not January 9pm Summer daylight, after a shift

chunks.t: Weekends and the outdoors in Auckland
chunks.x: Choosing by intention works far better than choosing by proximity — the nearest beach is frequently the wrong one for what you had in mind.

chunks.t: Weekends and the outdoors in Auckland
chunks.h: Read this before your first west-coast swim
chunks.x: New Zealand has one of the higher drowning rates in the developed world, and the west-coast beaches account for a disproportionate share of it. The water looks inviting and the danger is invisible from the sand — which is precisely the problem. As a clinician you’ll recognise the pattern: confident adults, unfamiliar environment, no local knowledge, no perceived risk. Five rules that cover almost all of it Swim between the flags. They mark the only patrolled, rip-assessed stretch of water on the beach. If there are no flags, don’t swim. Unpatrolled west-coast beaches are not a judgement call for newcomers. Learn to spot a rip. Calm, darker, flatter water between breaking waves isn’t the safe bit — it’s the current heading out. Caught in one, don’t fight it. Float, raise an arm, let it carry you out until it releases, then swim parallel to shore. Never swim alone, and never after drinking.

chunks.t: Weekends and the outdoors in Auckland
chunks.h: Read this before your first west-coast swim
chunks.x: Almost every fatality involves one or both. Surf Life Saving New Zealand publishes daily beach and hazard information at safeswim.org.nz — water quality, rip risk, patrol status, and whether the beach is currently safe at all. Aucklanders check it before they drive out. So should you.

chunks.t: Weekends and the outdoors in Auckland
chunks.h: Rainforest, thirty minutes from a hospital car park
chunks.x: Two ranges of subtropical bush sit at either end of the region, and there’s a walking track across the middle of the city itself. None of it requires equipment beyond decent shoes and a raincoat. Kauri dieback — please take this seriously A soil-borne pathogen is killing kauri, the giant native tree the Waitākere Ranges exist to protect. Many tracks are closed, permanently in some cases. Scrub your boots, use the disinfectant stations at both ends, and stay on the boardwalk — the spores travel in a gram of mud on your sole. Closures change, so check Auckland Council before you set out rather than at the gate.

chunks.t: Weekends and the outdoors in Auckland
chunks.h: The gulf is full of islands, and the ferry leaves from downtown
chunks.x: The sun The UV here is fierce — a thinner ozone layer and cleaner air mean you burn far faster than at the same temperature in Europe. It doesn’t have to feel hot. Overcast days in October catch people out routinely. Sunscreen, a hat and shade between eleven and four, every summer day. Skin cancer rates here are among the highest in the world, and you’ll see the consequences at work. “I absolutely love Waiheke Island. We spent my birthday there and visited a couple of the wineries. The vineyards are beautiful and the views are incredible. It’s probably one of my favourite days we’ve had since moving here.” Festus, Radiographer — moved from London to Auckland Here are four versions of an Auckland weekend, and all four are ordinary. Not holidays — the sort of weekend people here have most weeks, in ordinary clothes, with the washing still to do on Sunday evening.

chunks.t: Weekends and the outdoors in Auckland
chunks.x: The coast weekend Friday dinner somewhere local, Saturday morning at the market, then west to Piha by ten and swimming by half past. Home sandy and early. Sunday is the Domain, a bakery and nothing much. Furthest you travel: 45 min. Rough cost for two: modest. The island weekend Ferry to Waiheke on Saturday morning, a vineyard lunch, a swim at Oneroa, and the six o’clock boat back full of people carrying wine and sandy towels. Sunday recovers. Furthest you travel: 40 min by ferry. The city weekend Brunch that takes two hours, the art gallery, Ponsonby Road in the afternoon, dinner in Britomart, and walking home along the water. Sunday is the Coast to Coast walkway if the weather holds. The bush weekend Waitākere Ranges on Saturday for a waterfall track and a village café on the way home. Sunday up Maungawhau before breakfast, then Cornwall Park with a flask. Almost free. Costs are indicative for two adults, excluding fuel and anything you’d have spent at home anyway. The point is the shape of the day, not the arithmetic.

chunks.t: Weekends and the outdoors in Auckland
chunks.h: Six habits you’ll probably pick up
chunks.x: Not clubs and groups — those are in Finding your people . These are the things people here simply do, that you likely didn’t. Checking the tide Not the weather — the tide. Whether a beach is worth going to at two o’clock depends on it, and within a month you’ll know without looking. Keeping togs in the car Swimming becomes something you do on the way home rather than something you plan. A towel lives in the boot from November. Barbecuing on a Wednesday It isn’t an event here. Long evenings make cooking outside on a weeknight completely normal from October. Going barefoot In the supermarket, at the petrol station, at school pick-up. It stops being remarkable faster than you’d think. Owning a chilly bin And a trailer, or a friend with one. New Zealanders transport things constantly and are very relaxed about lending. Watching the weather move Four seasons in a day is accurate. You learn to go when it’s fine rather than waiting for a better day.

chunks.t: Weekends and the outdoors in Auckland
chunks.h: It would be dishonest to end on the beach
chunks.x: There’s a real trade here, and it’s worth naming before you decide rather than discovering in year two. None of these are reasons not to come. All of them are reasons to come with your eyes open. Spontaneity with family You can’t drop in on anyone. Birthdays, funerals and bad news all happen twenty-four hours of flying away, and that doesn’t get easier. The cultural depth of a big city Touring acts skip New Zealand or come once. Exhibitions are smaller. If the last Tuesday of every month was a concert, that changes. Cheap weekends elsewhere No Friday-night flight to another country for forty pounds. Travel from here is a proper undertaking, planned and paid for. Being understood immediately You’ll explain where you’re from for years. It’s friendly, and it’s also a small daily reminder that you arrived from somewhere else. “The thing that changes is not the weekends.

chunks.t: Weekends and the outdoors in Auckland
chunks.h: It would be dishonest to end on the beach
chunks.x: It is that you stop saving them up. In a big northern city a good weekend takes planning and money and a train. Here you can decide at nine on a Saturday morning to drive to a beach, and be swimming by ten, and be home for lunch. It sounds small. It reorganises how a year feels.” Sophie Careem — Founder & CEO, Ethicare Resourcing Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Where clinicians live in Auckland: 16 suburbs compared
chunks.x: Where you land shapes your commute and, if you have children, your school zone. Pick the hospital you’ll work at and the list re-sorts around it — because the right suburb in Auckland is mostly a question of which way you drive in the morning. Villa-lined streets in Devonport, on the North Shore Where will you work? Narrow it down Sort by A tip on choosing Where you live can decide which state school your children attend. Zone boundaries can run down the middle of a street, so check the exact address is in-zone before you sign. Most rentals are advertised on Trade Me Property and realestate.co.nz , and good ones move quickly. Many clinicians rent short-term first and get to know a few areas before committing to a longer lease. Rents are indicative weekly figures for a typical three-bedroom home, July 2026.

chunks.t: Where clinicians live in Auckland: 16 suburbs compared
chunks.x: Commute times are door-to-door driving estimates outside peak — add meaningfully at 8am, and more if you cross the harbour bridge. How renting works here — applications, bond, tenancy rights and the Healthy Homes standards — is the same everywhere in New Zealand, and the Moving to New Zealand guide walks through it step by step.

chunks.t: Where clinicians live in Auckland: 16 suburbs compared
chunks.x: One · Which hospital? In Auckland this decides more than anywhere else in New Zealand. The city is long, the harbour splits it, and a suburb that is twenty minutes from one campus can be fifty from another in traffic. Pick the site first, then the suburb — not the other way round. Two · Which side of the bridge? The Auckland Harbour Bridge is the single biggest variable in a commute here. Living on the North Shore and working in the central city means crossing it twice a day, and at peak that is a different proposition from the off-peak estimate. If you are going to cross it daily, drive the route at 8am before you sign anything. Three · School zone or square metres? With school-age children the zone usually decides the suburb, and the most sought-after zones carry a substantial rent premium. Families without that constraint can go further out and get considerably more house. Work out which of the two you are.

chunks.t: Where clinicians live in Auckland: 16 suburbs compared
chunks.x: Auckland is really several cities that grew into each other, and they behave differently. Central The isthmus — Mount Eden, Epsom, Ponsonby, Grey Lynn, Remuera. Villas, volcanic cones, the best-regarded state school zones and the highest prices. Walkable, and close to the central hospital campus. North Shore Across the bridge — Devonport, Takapuna, Milford, Albany. Beaches on the doorstep, strong schools, a slightly separate identity. Excellent unless you cross the bridge at peak. West New Lynn out to Titirangi and the Waitākere Ranges. Bush, black-sand surf beaches, more space for the money, and a different feel from the isthmus. South & east Manukau, Howick, Botany and the eastern bays. The most diverse part of the city, the best value on family housing, and where a large share of the health workforce lives.

chunks.t: Where clinicians live in Auckland: 16 suburbs compared
chunks.x: How renting works nationally — applications, bond, tenancy rights and the Healthy Homes standards — is the same everywhere, and set out in Renting in New Zealand . If you remember three things Choose the hospital first. In a city this size the commute defines the suburb, not the other way round. If you will cross the harbour bridge daily, drive it at 8am before you commit to a lease. With children, check the exact address is in-zone. Boundaries can run down the middle of a street. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Getting around Auckland: licences, cars and public transport
chunks.x: Auckland has changed more in the last five years than in the previous fifty. It’s still a car city — but some commutes are now faster without one. It’s still a car city Most households run at least one car, and outside the central suburbs you’ll want one. Plan on buying in your first month. But transit is improving The City Rail Link, the Northern Busway and the ferry network mean some commutes are now faster without a car than with one. And the bridge decides a lot One harbour crossing carries the whole North Shore. Whether you cross it daily is the single biggest variable in your week.

chunks.t: Getting around Auckland: licences, cars and public transport
chunks.h: You can drive on your own licence at first
chunks.x: Which takes the pressure off week one. But there’s a clock running, and the conversion is easier if you start it early rather than in month eleven. Day 1 · Drive on your overseas licence Valid for up to twelve months from the date you arrive. Carry the licence itself, plus an official English translation or an international permit if it isn’t in English. Month 1–2 · Start the conversion Apply at an AA or VTNZ agent. You’ll need identity documents, your overseas licence, an eyesight check and the fee. Before 12 months · Hold a NZ licence Depending on which country issued yours, you may convert directly or may need theory and practical tests. Check which category applies before you book anything. Four habits to pick up quickly Drive on the left. Give way rules changed in 2012 and are now closer to what most people expect, but read them once properly.

chunks.t: Getting around Auckland: licences, cars and public transport
chunks.h: You can drive on your own licence at first
chunks.x: Open-road speed is generally 100 km/h, and 50 km/h in urban areas unless signed otherwise. Rural roads are narrow, unlit and often unsealed. Journey times are longer than the distance suggests — this catches out almost every newcomer on their first road trip. One-lane bridges are real, and the sign tells you who gives way. The smaller arrow yields.

chunks.t: Getting around Auckland: licences, cars and public transport
chunks.h: Buying a car: cheaper than you expect, thanks to Japan
chunks.x: New Zealand imports a large volume of used Japanese vehicles, which keeps second-hand prices well below what most people arriving from Europe or Africa are braced for. A tidy, reliable runabout costs less here than almost anywhere comparable. Where people buy. Trade Me Motors is the default marketplace for private sales. Licensed dealers cost more but give you consumer protection and often a warranty. Car auctions are the cheapest route and the riskiest. If you’re buying in your first fortnight, a dealer is the lower-stress option — you can always sell it on in a year. Before you pay — four checks, in this order A current Warrant of Fitness (WoF) and registration. A pre-purchase inspection — the AA and others will do this for a modest fee, and it pays for itself. A money-owing and stolen-vehicle check, so you don’t inherit someone else’s finance.

chunks.t: Getting around Auckland: licences, cars and public transport
chunks.h: Buying a car: cheaper than you expect, thanks to Japan
chunks.x: Odometer history — imports occasionally arrive with an optimistic reading. What your budget buys Indicative NZ$ Older import hatchback $4k – $8k Tidy family car, 8–12 years $9k – $16k Newer SUV or hybrid $20k – $35k Pre-purchase inspection Around $150 Indicative, July 2026. Prices move — treat these as orientation, not quotes. Arriving without a car Renting for the first two to four weeks is normal and sensible. It buys you time to open a bank account, get your address confirmed and view cars without hurrying. Long-term rental deals are considerably cheaper than daily rates, and some employers can help with short-term arrangements — worth asking. If you’ll live centrally and work at Auckland City, it’s worth trying a month without one before you commit.

chunks.t: Getting around Auckland: licences, cars and public transport
chunks.x: Petrol, insurance, the annual registration and a Warrant of Fitness. None of them is large on its own. The one that catches people out is Road User Charges : diesel and electric vehicles don’t pay fuel tax at the pump, so they pay per thousand kilometres instead, bought in advance as a distance licence. If you buy a diesel, budget for it. Insurance here isn’t compulsory, which surprises people arriving from the UK. Third-party cover is cheap and comprehensive cover isn’t expensive by international standards. Get it anyway — and note that ACC covers injury from a crash regardless of fault or cover. Indicative running costs NZ$ Petrol, 91 octane ≈ $2.80 / litre Warrant of Fitness $60 – $90 Annual registration Varies by vehicle Road User Charges — diesel & EV Per 1,000 km Comprehensive insurance $60 – $150 / month AA membership Worth having Registration and Road User Charge rates are set nationally and change — check Waka Kotahi for current figures.

chunks.t: Getting around Auckland: licences, cars and public transport
chunks.h: Trains, buses, ferries: one card, one network
chunks.x: Auckland Transport runs the buses, trains and ferries under a single zone-based fare system. Get an AT HOP card in your first week — it’s materially cheaper than paying cash, and transfers between modes inside a journey are included. Trains Four lines — Southern, Eastern, Western and Onehunga — now running through the City Rail Link beneath the centre, which adds new central stations and cuts journey times across the network. If your suburb has a station, use it. Buses & the busway The Northern Busway has its own dedicated road and is often faster than driving from the Shore at peak. Elsewhere, frequent routes run every ten to fifteen minutes on the main arterials. Ferries Devonport, Half Moon Bay, Hobsonville, Birkenhead and Waiheke, all from the downtown terminal. Devonport takes twelve minutes. The best commute in the city, and the one people move suburb for.

chunks.t: Getting around Auckland: licences, cars and public transport
chunks.h: Trains, buses, ferries: one card, one network
chunks.x: Cycling Better than its reputation. The Northwestern and waterfront paths are good, and e-bikes have made the hills a non-issue. Bikes travel free on ferries and, outside peak, on trains. Fares are zone-based and reviewed regularly — check at.govt.nz for current prices. Under-fives travel free.

chunks.t: Getting around Auckland: licences, cars and public transport
chunks.x: It isn’t London or Jakarta. But it’s a city of 1.7 million funnelled through one motorway spine and one harbour crossing, and pretending otherwise does nobody any favours. Peak is narrow but firm Roughly 7 to 9 in the morning and 4 to 6.30 in the evening. Shift work often means you miss both entirely, which is a perk. The bridge is the bottleneck Everything from the North Shore crosses one structure. A twenty-minute run becomes fifty when it goes wrong, and it goes wrong without warning. School terms change everything The school holidays empty the roads noticeably. If you test a commute during a holiday you’ll get a misleadingly good answer. Rain adds fifteen minutes Reliably, across the whole network. It’s the local joke, and it’s also true. Friday afternoon starts early From about two o’clock, particularly heading north or east out of the city.

chunks.t: Getting around Auckland: licences, cars and public transport
chunks.x: Long weekends are worse — leave Thursday night or Saturday morning. Parking at hospitals is finite Staff parking is usually available but rarely abundant, and often paid. Ask about it at interview — it’s a legitimate question and affects your daily routine. “Don’t buy a car in your first week. Rent something small, get your bank account and address sorted, and use the fortnight to work out whether you need one where you have landed. A surprising number of people discover they only need a car at weekends — and that changes the budget entirely.” Sophie Careem — Founder & CEO, Ethicare Resourcing Converting your licence, the paperwork and the rules of the road are national — the Moving to New Zealand guide covers them in full.

chunks.t: Getting around Auckland: licences, cars and public transport
chunks.x: Auckland has the warmest climate of New Zealand’s main centres: mild, humid summers and gentle winters, rarely cold, with the sea always close by. What to pack Layers and a light rain jacket year-round. Auckland weather can turn quickly. Homes are often cooler indoors than newcomers expect, so pack a warm layer even for summer evenings. Summer Dec – Feb 20–24° Avg daytime Autumn Mar – May 17–21° Avg daytime Winter Jun – Aug 11–15° Avg daytime Spring Sep – Nov 15–19° Avg daytime Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Moving to Auckland: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.x: Tāmaki Makaurau — Tāmaki desired by many. A city of a million and a half people built across fifty volcanoes, between two harbours, with a rainforest on one side and an ocean on the other. The city sits on an isthmus barely a kilometre wide at its narrowest point. You are never more than about half an hour from water.

chunks.t: Moving to Auckland: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.x: Moving to the other side of the world is a big thing to do. I know, because I did it. Twenty-odd years ago I arrived in Australia on a working holiday visa, having backpacked my way across Southeast Asia, and then made my way to New Zealand. I lived and worked in Wellington. I managed a backpackers in Queenstown, where I met my partner. I stayed for years, and Aotearoa has never really left me. So when I talk to a radiographer in Manchester or a sonographer in Johannesburg who is trying to work out whether to do this, I am not reading from a brochure. I remember the particular feeling of standing in a supermarket in a new country and not recognising a single brand. I remember how long it took before it stopped feeling like a very long holiday. What I did not have, then, was anything like this guide.

chunks.t: Moving to Auckland: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.x: Most relocation material is either a list of visa requirements or a tourism advertisement, and neither of those tells you what a Tuesday looks like. That is the gap this is trying to fill: what it costs, where people live, what the winters are really like in an Auckland house, what you will miss, and what you will gain. It includes the parts that are less flattering. If Auckland is not right for you, we would far rather you worked that out here, at your kitchen table, than eighteen thousand kilometres from home. And if it is right — and for a great many clinicians it turns out to be — then this should save you a year of learning things the slow way. Sophie Careem — Founder & CEO, Ethicare Resourcing A café by the water
