chunks.x: Where a month goes The proportions, for one person on a mid-range budget. Proportions move slowly; prices move every quarter. Rent is just over half of it — against the smallest main-centre rent line in the country. Rent 52% Groceries 19% Power & water 10% Entertainment & leisure 9% Transport / petrol 6% Internet 3% Mobile plan 2% The line that decides it Rent · 52% Power and water is the line that catches people out here rather than the rent — old villas and a real winter, not a pricing problem. Budget for it and Dunedin stays the cheapest main centre by a wide margin. Indicative figures that change over time. Use them as a shape, not a quote.

chunks.t: Cost of living in Dunedin: what a clinician spends
chunks.x: This deserves its own heading because it catches almost everybody. A poorly insulated older house in Dunedin can cost two or three times as much to heat in July as it does to run in February. The same house, properly insulated with an efficient heat pump, costs a fraction of that. The Healthy Homes standards have raised the floor for rentals considerably, which helps. But if you are buying, treat insulation, double glazing and heating as part of the purchase price rather than a later project. It is the best money you will spend here. Ask for the numbers Landlords and vendors can usually produce recent power bills. Ask for a July one specifically, not an average. Look for the retrofit Ceiling and underfloor insulation, a heat pump, and double glazing in the main rooms. A villa with all three is a warm house. Sun is free heating A north-facing living room does more for your winter than any appliance. This is why aspect matters so much here.

chunks.t: Cost of living in Dunedin: what a clinician spends
chunks.x: Twenty thousand students distort the rental market. Demand peaks sharply in late January and February as the academic year begins, and slumps from November. Family homes in the hill and coastal suburbs are less affected than flats near the university — but if you can time your search for December, you will have more choice and less competition. Tax, KiwiSaver, banking and sending money home are national topics, covered in Money, tax & banking .

chunks.t: Cost of living in Dunedin: what a clinician spends
chunks.h: The bill that catches people out
chunks.x: Heating is the Dunedin budget line that surprises people, and it has almost nothing to do with how cold the city is. Dunedin winters are cooler than the North Island but not extreme; the issue is the housing stock. The city has a large inventory of Victorian and Edwardian villas — beautiful, generously proportioned, and frequently built with single glazing, no wall insulation and high ceilings. A house like that costs several times more to keep warm than a modern equivalent, and the difference shows up on every winter bill for as long as you live there. The practical advice: when you view a property, ask when it was last insulated, whether it is double glazed, and what the heating is. A well-upgraded villa is a wonderful thing to live in. An un-upgraded one is the single most common regret we hear from people who move here.

chunks.t: Cost of living in Dunedin: what a clinician spends
chunks.x: Flights home Every long-haul journey from Dunedin involves at least one connection, usually two. Budget both the fare and the extra half-day each way. Adult dental Private in New Zealand, as everywhere. A check-up runs into three figures, and work beyond that adds up quickly. Setting up Bond and rent in advance, a car, whiteware and furniture — plus, here, whatever it takes to make an old house warm. Most people spend more than they planned in the first two months. Three costs people forget Flights home. Dunedin Airport has domestic and limited trans-Tasman connections; long-haul means Auckland, Christchurch or Sydney. Add half a day each way. Heating. The single biggest local budget line. An old villa without insulation can cost several times what a modern house does to keep warm. Adult dental is private, as everywhere in New Zealand. Register early rather than in an emergency.

chunks.t: Cost of living in Dunedin: what a clinician spends
chunks.x: The short version The same national salary against the lowest housing costs in the country — provided you spend some of the difference on keeping the house warm. Get today’s numbers, and compare them to home These are live and updated continuously. Put the city you are leaving in the other box. Numbeo cost-of-living calculator — the most complete comparison tool, and the one most clinicians already use. Crowd-sourced, so treat it as a ballpark. Expatistan — the same idea with a cleaner side-by-side. Worth running as a sanity check when Numbeo looks off. Tenancy Services market rent — official bond-lodgement data by area, and the most reliable rent figure in New Zealand. Stats NZ — official and slower, and the one to trust on the direction of travel. If what you find differs from what we say here, tell us and we will correct it. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Food, shopping and the everyday in Dunedin
chunks.x: A city of 130,000 should not have this many good places to eat. It does, for two reasons: 20,000 students who need feeding cheaply, and a century of Scottish, Chinese and more recent Asian and Middle Eastern settlement that left its mark on the kitchens.

chunks.t: Food, shopping and the everyday in Dunedin
chunks.x: The Otago Farmers Market runs every Saturday morning in the car park beside the railway station, and it is the closest thing the city has to a weekly civic ritual. Producers come in from the Taieri, Central Otago and the Catlins; you go for the vegetables and stay for the coffee and the whitebait fritter. It is not a tourist market. Most of the city shops there, and after a couple of months you will recognise half the queue.

chunks.t: Food, shopping and the everyday in Dunedin
chunks.h: Six parts of the city worth an evening
chunks.x: The Octagon The literal and social centre. Bars and restaurants ring the plaza, and on a warm evening the tables spill onto the grass in front of the town hall. The warehouse precinct Vogel and Bond Streets, where the Victorian warehouses have been restored into restaurants, breweries and design studios. The best-looking few blocks in Dunedin. George Street The main shopping street, running north from the Octagon towards the university. Recently rebuilt as a slower, more pedestrian-friendly stretch. St Clair Esplanade Cafés looking straight at the surf. Breakfast here on a clear Sunday is one of the reasons people move. Port Chalmers Fifteen minutes up the harbour: a working port with a good little arts and food scene attached to it. Roslyn village The hill suburb’s own strip of cafés and shops — useful when you do not want to go down the hill.

chunks.t: Food, shopping and the everyday in Dunedin
chunks.x: Dunedin takes brewing seriously. The city has a long-established brewing tradition and a strong craft scene that grew out of it, with several breweries running taprooms you can walk between. If beer is your thing, this is one of the better small cities in the country for it. The Scottish founding still shows in the street names, the architecture, the pipe bands and a certain civic seriousness — less in the food, though you will find haggis on a menu in January if you look.

chunks.t: Food, shopping and the everyday in Dunedin
chunks.x: Supermarkets The major chains cover the city, with the larger stores on the flat and in Mosgiel. Prices are comparable with the rest of the South Island. Asian groceries Several well-stocked stores near the university and in the centre, serving the student population — the practical answer for most of the ingredients you cannot find in a supermarket. Furnishing an empty house The usual big-box retailers are on the flat and in South Dunedin. For character furniture, the city’s second-hand and antique trade is unusually good, a legacy of all those large old houses. Online Trade Me handles a great deal of the second-hand market. Delivery from the North Island takes an extra day and sometimes an extra charge — a small, persistent tax on living this far south.

chunks.t: Food, shopping and the everyday in Dunedin
chunks.x: The public art gallery is free and good. There are three museums worth your time — the settlers’ museum, the Otago Museum and the university’s own collections. The Regent Theatre and a scattering of smaller venues cover touring theatre and music, and the student population keeps live music alive in a way that cities twice the size struggle to manage. A few practical notes Finding what you grew up with. The student population supports a surprising range of Asian and Middle Eastern grocers for a city this size. Ask the community groups — faster than hunting supermarket shelves, and people share sources readily. Bring reusable bags. Single-use plastic bags are banned nationwide. The short version More good food, beer and culture than a city this size has any right to — because 20,000 students and 150 years of civic ambition both insist on it. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Dunedin at a glance: the harbour, the hills and the seasons
chunks.x: Dunedin sits at the head of a long, narrow harbour on the south-east coast of the South Island, with hills on three sides and the open Pacific on the fourth. Understanding that shape explains almost everything about how the city works.

chunks.t: Dunedin at a glance: the harbour, the hills and the seasons
chunks.h: The four parts of the city
chunks.x: The flat and the centre The Octagon, the university, the hospital and the warehouse precinct all sit on reclaimed flat land at the harbour head. Walkable, and where most of the working day happens. The hill suburbs Roslyn, Māori Hill, Mornington and their neighbours climb the western slope. Views, villas, good schools, steep streets, and a few degrees cooler than the flat. The coast St Clair and St Kilda face the open sea to the south, with a surf beach and an esplanade. Andersons Bay and Musselburgh sit behind them, sheltered and family-heavy. The peninsula and the plain The Otago Peninsula runs twenty kilometres out to Taiaroa Head; the Taieri Plain sits over the hill to the south-west, with Mosgiel and the airport. Both are commutable, in different moods.

chunks.t: Dunedin at a glance: the harbour, the hills and the seasons
chunks.x: Dunedin has a cool temperate maritime climate. The sea moderates it in both directions: summers are mild rather than hot, and winters are cool rather than freezing. The mean annual temperature is around 11°C, and hard frosts are less common than people expect from the latitude. What defines the year is not cold, it is variability and cloud. A February day can be 25°C and still. A February week can be 15°C and grey. Locals dress in layers and stop discussing it. Summer Dec – Feb 18–22°C Long evenings — light until after 9pm. Warm days are warm; cool ones need a jacket. The city is emptiest and at its most relaxed. Autumn Mar – May 12–18°C Often the best of the year. Settled, clear and golden, with the students back and the city busy again. Winter Jun – Aug 4–11°C Cool, not severe. Snow settles on the hills a few times a season and rarely on the flat. Short days are the real adjustment: dark by 5pm in June. Spring Sep – Nov 10–17°C Changeable and windy, warming steadily. The peninsula is at its best as the seabirds return.

chunks.t: Dunedin at a glance: the harbour, the hills and the seasons
chunks.x: The Octagon The literal centre — an eight-sided plaza with the town hall, the art gallery and a ring of bars and restaurants. Everything is described by its distance from here. The harbour Long, narrow and shallow at the city end, deepening towards Port Chalmers. The road along it is one of the more pleasant commutes in the country. Baldwin Street The steepest residential street in the world, in North East Valley. A useful reminder that gradient here is not decorative. Distances Christchurch 4½ hours by road or an hour by air. Queenstown 3½ hours. Invercargill 2. The Catlins start an hour south.

chunks.t: Dunedin at a glance: the harbour, the hills and the seasons
chunks.x: Where Dunedin sits, with the straight-line distance to Oamaru Dunedin sits at the head of a long harbour, with the city built up the slopes of an ancient volcanic basin. The flat central grid — the Octagon, the university, the hospital, the warehouse district — occupies the harbour floor, and everything else climbs. Out along the harbour’s northern shore the road runs to Port Chalmers, the working port. On the southern side, the Otago Peninsula stretches twenty kilometres to Taiaroa Head, with albatross, penguins and sea lions at the end of it. Behind the city to the west, the hill suburbs give way quickly to farmland and then to Central Otago. The scale is the thing that surprises people. Dunedin has the architecture and civic infrastructure of a much larger city — the legacy of the gold rush, when it was briefly the wealthiest place in New Zealand — on a population of around 130,000.

chunks.t: Dunedin at a glance: the harbour, the hills and the seasons
chunks.x: That mismatch is why the city feels grander than its size, and why housing is such good value. A few local notes On the cold. Dunedin is cooler than most of New Zealand but rarely extreme. The problem is old housing and wind chill rather than the temperature itself. On the hills. The city is built into an amphitheatre around the harbour. Which contour line you live on changes your sun, your view and your walk home. On the light. Being this far south means long summer evenings and short winter days. It affects people differently — take it seriously if you know it affects you. The thing to hold on to Dunedin is a small city in a big landscape. Nothing in it is more than twenty minutes from anything else, and the edge of it is wilder than the edge of any other New Zealand city. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Healthcare in Dunedin: the tertiary hospital and the medical school
chunks.x: How the New Zealand system is funded and organised nationally is covered in How the health system works . This chapter is Dunedin specific: where you would work, what the catchment does to your case mix, and what the teaching connection means day to day.

chunks.t: Healthcare in Dunedin: the tertiary hospital and the medical school
chunks.h: A tertiary hospital, and the medical school next to it
chunks.x: The city’s tertiary hospital serves the lower South Island, run by Health New Zealand | Te Whatu Ora. It provides the full range of secondary services for the city and the wider Otago region, and tertiary services — the complex work that smaller hospitals refer on — for a catchment reaching south to Southland and inland across Central Otago. What makes it distinctive is the university. The Otago Medical School, New Zealand’s first, sits immediately alongside, and the two are structurally intertwined: joint appointments are common, students and registrars are everywhere, and research is a normal part of the working environment rather than something you do in your own time. The practical effect is a case mix broader than the city’s size suggests, delivered by teams small enough that you will know everyone in your specialty within a fortnight.

chunks.t: Healthcare in Dunedin: the tertiary hospital and the medical school
chunks.h: A tertiary hospital, and the medical school next to it
chunks.x: A large catchment, a small city Tertiary referrals arrive from across Otago and Southland. You see complexity that a city of 130,000 would not otherwise generate. Teaching is built in Medical, nursing, dentistry, physiotherapy and pharmacy students are all trained here. If supervision and teaching interest you, the opportunity is immediate. A new hospital is being built A major rebuild of the Dunedin campus is underway — a long, publicly debated project that will run for years yet. Ask about timelines and interim arrangements for your service at interview; the picture differs considerably by department. Rural and regional links Smaller hospitals and community services across Otago, plus outreach clinics. Generalist scope and autonomy, and for many people the most enjoyable part of a southern career.

chunks.t: Healthcare in Dunedin: the tertiary hospital and the medical school
chunks.h: A tertiary hospital, and the medical school next to it
chunks.x: What the catchment means for your work Tertiary referrals arrive from across Otago and Southland, so the case mix is bigger than a city of 130,000 would generate on its own. Four consequences clinicians here describe, in the order they tend to notice them. Broad scope Smaller teams mean less subspecialisation. You will do more outside your narrowest interest than you might in Auckland — most people find this the appeal rather than the cost. Distance shapes decisions When a patient’s alternative is a four-hour transfer, thresholds and planning look different. Retrieval and transfer logistics are part of normal clinical thinking here. Access is informal You will phone the consultant rather than the department. Decisions that take a week elsewhere can take an afternoon. Seasonal swing The student population and the summer visitor influx both move demand. Winter is the pressure point, as everywhere.

chunks.t: Healthcare in Dunedin: the tertiary hospital and the medical school
chunks.h: Everyday care, for you and your family
chunks.x: Enrol with a GP early Some practices carry closed books. Enrol as soon as you have an address rather than waiting until you need an appointment. Urgent care The city has after-hours accident and medical services that handle most of what would otherwise reach an emergency department. Know where yours is before you need it. Dental is private As everywhere in New Zealand. Free for under-18s; budget roughly NZ$90–$150 for an adult check-up.

chunks.t: Healthcare in Dunedin: the tertiary hospital and the medical school
chunks.h: A second system, close at hand
chunks.x: Dunedin’s private sector is small but real — planned surgery, endoscopy, diagnostics and day procedures, funded by insurance, by ACC, by patients directly, and increasingly by Health New Zealand outsourcing elective lists. Because the city is compact, working across both sectors is straightforward: a public list in the morning and a private list in the afternoon is a ten-minute drive, not a lost day. Many senior clinicians hold appointments in both. Close to the centre The main private surgical facilities sit within a few minutes of the public campus, which makes cross-sector work about as convenient as it gets in New Zealand. Imaging & diagnostics Community radiology clinics operate across the city and into rural Otago — a meaningful employer for imaging staff, and often a route to more predictable hours.

chunks.t: Healthcare in Dunedin: the tertiary hospital and the medical school
chunks.h: A second system, close at hand
chunks.x: Aged residential care A substantial sector across the city, employing nurses, physiotherapists and occupational therapists outside the acute roster. Raise it early If cross-sector work is part of your plan, say so during the conversation, before you arrive. Arrangements vary by specialty. A sketch of the landscape; sites and ownership change. One employer, named What doesn’t change — Health New Zealand | Te Whatu Ora is the national public health employer. Pay comes from national collective agreements — your salary is the same here as in Auckland. What changes is the work — an academic centre with teaching and research woven into ordinary practice, and a catchment that stretches across Otago and Southland.

chunks.t: Healthcare in Dunedin: the tertiary hospital and the medical school
chunks.h: A second system, close at hand
chunks.x: A note on names We don’t name hospitals, trusts or private providers as places of work anywhere on this site — a named employer implies a relationship, and the post and the package get confirmed with you directly. Where a public body is named on this page, it is there as a reference point for how the system is organised. It is not an employer reference, and it does not imply we recruit for it. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Where clinicians live in Dunedin: fourteen suburbs compared
chunks.x: Fourteen suburbs, sorted by commute to wherever you will work. Dunedin is small enough that nothing is far, so the choice here is not about distance — it is about height, sun and how old you want your house to be.

chunks.t: Where clinicians live in Dunedin: fourteen suburbs compared
chunks.x: One · Flat, hill or coast? The three versions of living here. The flat is walkable and close to work. The hill gives you views, character housing and a few degrees less warmth. The coast gives you a beach at the end of the street and salt air on everything you own. Drive all three before you decide. Two · How warm is the house? The single most important question in Dunedin, and the one newcomers ask last. Much of the housing stock is a century old and was built without insulation. A well-retrofitted villa is lovely; an untouched one is hard work in July. Ask about insulation, heating and sun before you ask about the kitchen. Three · Which way does it face? On a hill this far south, aspect decides everything. A north-facing section gets sun all winter; a south-facing one in a valley may get almost none between May and August. Visit in the morning and again at four o’clock.

chunks.t: Where clinicians live in Dunedin: fourteen suburbs compared
chunks.x: Rent first, and time your search Six months of renting tells you whether you want the hill, the flat or the coast — and whether you can live with a twenty-five-minute peninsula commute. The rental market follows the university year. December and January are the easiest months to find a family home; February is the worst. Renting in New Zealand covers the application pack, the bond and the Healthy Homes standards.

chunks.t: Where clinicians live in Dunedin: fourteen suburbs compared
chunks.h: Pick your site, then read down
chunks.x: Suburbs reorder by commute to whichever site you select. Rents are indicative weekly figures for a three-bedroom house as at July 2026 — treat them as a shape, not a quote. Space, greenery and a view — the classic Dunedin hill house Commuting to Show Commutes are typical door-to-door driving times outside peak. Dunedin’s peak adds perhaps five minutes. Rents move — check current listings before budgeting.

chunks.t: Where clinicians live in Dunedin: fourteen suburbs compared
chunks.x: This is the part that surprises people arriving from Auckland, London or Sydney. A character home is attainable The grand Victorian and Edwardian housing that would be unreachable in a bigger city is ordinary stock here. Consultants routinely buy the kind of house they had stopped imagining. One car is usually enough Short distances and a walkable centre mean many households run a single car, which is a real saving over cities where two is assumed. But budget for warmth Whatever you save on the mortgage, put some of it into heating and insulation. It is the difference between loving the house and enduring it. How renting works nationally — applications, bond, tenancy rights and the Healthy Homes standards — is the same everywhere, and set out in Renting in New Zealand . Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Getting around Dunedin: driving, buses and the hills
chunks.x: Dunedin is the easiest city in New Zealand to get around, for one simple reason: there is not very much of it. The trade-off is gradient. This is a city where the question is rarely how far, and often how steep.

chunks.t: Getting around Dunedin: driving, buses and the hills
chunks.x: Fifteen minutes door to door is normal from most suburbs. Twenty-five from Mosgiel over the hill. The rush hour exists but it is a courtesy title — it means the lights take two cycles instead of one. Driving The default, and quick. Most people can be at the hospital from anywhere in the city inside twenty minutes. Hospital parking, as everywhere, is the actual constraint. Walking The flat is entirely walkable — the Octagon, the university, the hospital and the warehouse precinct are within fifteen minutes of each other. Living on the flat means you may barely use a car midweek. Buses The Orbus network covers the city and suburbs, with the main routes running frequently enough to rely on. Fares are low and a regional card makes them lower. Cycling Excellent on the flat and along the harbour, hard work anywhere else. E-bikes have changed this considerably and are increasingly common on the hill routes.

chunks.t: Getting around Dunedin: driving, buses and the hills
chunks.x: Yes — unless you live on the flat and rarely leave the city. Not for the commute, but for everything at the weekend: the peninsula, the beaches, Central Otago, the Catlins. Public transport does not reach the places that make living here worthwhile. One car per household is usually enough, which is a meaningful saving over cities where two is assumed. Converting your licence, buying a car, WOF and rego are national topics, covered in Driving & licences .

chunks.t: Getting around Dunedin: driving, buses and the hills
chunks.x: Gradient is a housing decision Some streets are steep. In a rare snow event a handful become impassable for a day. Ask locals about a specific street rather than judging from a map. Microclimates The hill suburbs are a couple of degrees cooler than the flat and can sit above or below the cloud. The same afternoon can be grey in the centre and clear in Roslyn. Views cost gradient The harbour views everyone wants are up the hill. That is the deal.

chunks.t: Getting around Dunedin: driving, buses and the hills
chunks.x: The airport Momona, about 30 minutes south on the Taieri Plain. Domestic connections to the main centres, plus some trans-Tasman services. Long-haul means connecting through Auckland, Christchurch or Australia. By road Christchurch 4½ hours, Queenstown 3½, Invercargill 2, the Catlins 1. State Highway 1 runs through the city. Plan for flying home Every long-haul trip starts with a connection. It is the single most common thing people underestimate about moving this far south.

chunks.t: Getting around Dunedin: driving, buses and the hills
chunks.x: Dunedin is built into an amphitheatre around the harbour, and the contour line you live on shapes your daily life more than the distance does. A suburb that is two kilometres from the hospital can be a twenty-minute walk uphill, and the same walk in reverse takes ten. This is the practical difference from Christchurch, which people often assume is comparable. Cycling here is hard work outside the flat central grid, and winter ice on steep streets is a real hazard that catches newcomers out. Some of the steepest residential streets in the world are here, and that is not a tourist statistic when your car is on one of them in July. The upside: the flat central city is compact and thoroughly walkable, and if you live in the inner suburbs or along a main bus corridor you can manage without a car more easily than in most New Zealand cities.

chunks.t: Getting around Dunedin: driving, buses and the hills
chunks.x: The commute Ten to twenty minutes from most suburbs. There is no meaningful peak by city standards — the constraint is topography and parking, not traffic. Buses The Orbus network radiates from the central city and covers the main suburbs and the peninsula. Reasonable on the corridors, thin in the evenings and on the hills. Parking Tighter in the central city and around the hospital and university than you might expect for a city this size. Check what comes with a rental. Winter driving Frost and occasional ice on steep streets. A rear-wheel-drive car on a Dunedin hill in July is a serious problem — locals plan around it. Out of town Central Otago and the lakes 2–3 hours, Queenstown 3.5, Christchurch 5, the Catlins 1.5. The roads are quiet and the drives are among the best in the country.

chunks.t: Getting around Dunedin: driving, buses and the hills
chunks.x: Flying Dunedin Airport, half an hour south, has frequent domestic connections and limited trans-Tasman flights. Long-haul means connecting through Auckland, Christchurch or Sydney. Getting around, practically Do you need a car? If you live in the inner city or on a main bus route, not necessarily. Anywhere on the hills or the peninsula, yes. The hills matter. Cycling here is hard work, and winter ice on steep streets is a real hazard. This is not Christchurch. Licence conversion is national — see Driving & licences . The short version The shortest commute of any New Zealand city, a car you will still want for weekends, and an airport that is close but not a hub. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Weekends in Dunedin: the peninsula, the coast and Central Otago
chunks.x: This is the chapter that persuades people. Dunedin’s weekends are not a compromise for living somewhere small — they are the reason to do it. The wildlife is world-class, the coast is wild, and Central Otago and the Catlins are close enough for a Saturday. World-class wildlife, measured in minutes Driving times from the city, to scale against each other. The marked row is the one that astonishes new arrivals: royal albatross, sea lions and penguins on an ordinary Saturday, inside half an hour of home. St Clair & St Kilda Board riders at one end, the heated pool at the other, swimmers all winter ~10 min Taiaroa Head & the peninsula Nowhere else on a southern mainland do royal albatross breed ~30 min The Catlins The quiet southeast corner, an hour from town and all but empty ~1 hour Central Otago & the ski fields Dry schist country and its vineyards — stay the night ~3½ hours Indicative driving times. The scale is the story: the first three rows fit inside a normal Saturday without planning anything.

chunks.t: Weekends in Dunedin: the peninsula, the coast and Central Otago
chunks.x: The Otago Peninsula runs twenty kilometres out from the city, and it is the single best thing about living here. At the far end, Taiaroa Head holds the only mainland breeding colony of royal albatross in the Southern Hemisphere. Along the way there are yellow-eyed penguins, little blue penguins, New Zealand sea lions, fur seals and a road that hugs the harbour the whole way. You can do all of this on an ordinary Saturday afternoon, twenty minutes from your front door. People who move here from cities where nature is a holiday activity take about a year to stop being astonished by it. Taiaroa Head Royal albatross, with a two-metre wingspan, nesting on a headland you can drive to. Also fur seals, shags and little blue penguins coming ashore at dusk. Sandfly Bay A steep dune descent to a wild beach where sea lions haul out and yellow-eyed penguins come in at evening.

chunks.t: Weekends in Dunedin: the peninsula, the coast and Central Otago
chunks.x: Keep your distance — the sea lions are large and faster than they look. Larnach Castle New Zealand’s only castle, with gardens and views down both sides of the peninsula. The harbour road Flat, scenic and popular with cyclists — one of the best easy rides in the country.

chunks.t: Weekends in Dunedin: the peninsula, the coast and Central Otago
chunks.x: St Clair and St Kilda give the city two surf beaches within ten minutes of the centre. St Clair has the hot saltwater pool at one end and a serious surf break at the other; there is a year-round swimming community that treats the cold water as a feature rather than an obstacle. Further out, Tunnel Beach has a hand-carved tunnel down to a sea arch, and the coastline south towards the Catlins is emptier and wilder with every kilometre.

chunks.t: Weekends in Dunedin: the peninsula, the coast and Central Otago
chunks.x: The local one Farmers market on Saturday morning, a hill walk that starts from a suburban street, and the art gallery in the afternoon. You will not drive more than fifteen minutes all weekend. The wildlife one Out to the peninsula early, albatross and seals at the head, then Sandfly Bay at dusk for the penguins. A full day, all of it inside half an hour of home. The Central Otago one Three and a half hours inland to schist country, vineyards, rail trails and the driest, brightest landscape in the country. Doable in a day, better as a weekend. The Catlins one An hour south into forest, waterfalls, blowholes and beaches with nobody on them. The least-visited corner of the South Island, and it starts on your doorstep.

chunks.t: Weekends in Dunedin: the peninsula, the coast and Central Otago
chunks.x: Dunedin is not a ski town, but it is closer to the snow than most cities. The Central Otago fields are within a comfortable drive for a long weekend, and Queenstown’s are three and a half hours away. Plenty of people here ski a handful of times a season without it being the organising principle of their life. Closer to home, winter means clear cold days on the peninsula, empty beaches, and a city that turns inward towards its pubs and galleries in a way that is pleasant.

chunks.t: Weekends in Dunedin: the peninsula, the coast and Central Otago
chunks.x: Honesty matters here. You give up warm ocean swimming, reliable summer heat, and the casual ability to be anywhere else in the country quickly. You give up a certain amount of choice — in restaurants, in shops, in the sheer number of things happening on a given evening. What you get instead is space, quiet, and a landscape most people only see on holiday. For the clinicians who settle here, that trade stops feeling like a trade after about a year. Being sensible outdoors The coast is cold and powerful. Southern beaches have strong rips and the water is cold year-round. Wetsuits are standard. Wildlife is protected. Albatross, penguins and sea lions on the peninsula are close and wild — keep your distance and follow the signage. Alpine weather changes fast. Central Otago and the lakes are two hours away and make their own conditions. Check the forecast and carry layers.

chunks.t: Weekends in Dunedin: the peninsula, the coast and Central Otago
chunks.x: The short version Albatross, penguins and sea lions twenty minutes from the hospital; surf beaches at ten; Central Otago and the Catlins for the weekend. Nowhere else in New Zealand puts this much wildness this close to a tertiary hospital. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Moving to Dunedin: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.x: Dunedin is the city people underestimate until they visit. It is small, it is a long way south, and it has a reputation for cold that is only half deserved. What it has is grand Victorian stone, a world-class university, wildlife you would normally have to book a boat to see, and housing costs that make the rest of the country look unserious. The Scots founded it in 1848 and built it in stone. When gold was found in Central Otago in the 1860s, Dunedin briefly became the largest and richest city in New Zealand, and it spent that money on architecture — a railway station that looks like a Flemish town hall, banks with marble floors, churches out of all proportion to the congregation. The money left. The buildings stayed. What keeps it interesting now is the university.

chunks.t: Moving to Dunedin: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.x: Around 20,000 students in a city of roughly 130,000 is a ratio no other New Zealand city comes close to, and it shows: in the bars, in the music, in the fact that a small southern city supports a serious art gallery and three good museums. For a clinician, the arithmetic is unusual. You get a tertiary teaching hospital and the country’s oldest medical school in a city where a family home costs a fraction of Auckland, and where your commute is fifteen minutes with the harbour on one side.

chunks.t: Moving to Dunedin: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.x: ~130,000 People in the city. Small enough that you will start recognising faces within a month. ~20,000 University students. The single biggest thing shaping the city’s rhythm, rents and nightlife. 1869 The University of Otago founded — New Zealand’s oldest, and home to its first medical school. 15 min A typical commute. Traffic here means waiting through two sets of lights. Lowest Housing costs of any main centre in New Zealand, by a clear margin. Same National pay. Health New Zealand pays the same agreement rates wherever you work. 20 min From the centre to albatross, penguins and sea lions on the Otago Peninsula. ~11°C Mean annual temperature. Cool rather than cold — the sea keeps the extremes off. 30 min To the airport at Momona, out on the Taieri Plain. Domestic, plus some trans-Tasman.

chunks.t: Moving to Dunedin: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.h: Seven things you only learn once you are here
chunks.x: The cold is overstated, the damp is not Winter days sit around 10°C — milder than most of the UK. The problem is the housing stock. A poorly insulated villa is unpleasant in July, and a well-insulated one is fine. Ask about heating before you ask about the view. The year runs on the university calendar The city empties in late November and refills in late February. Rentals, restaurants, traffic and gym queues all follow that curve. If you are house-hunting, arriving in December is a considerable advantage. The hills decide everything Dunedin is built into an amphitheatre. Five minutes of driving can put you 200 metres higher, into a different microclimate with a different view and a noticeably different price. Walk the street before you sign. Wildlife is not an excursion Sea lions haul out on the city beaches. Penguins come ashore at dusk twenty minutes from the hospital.

chunks.t: Moving to Dunedin: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.h: Seven things you only learn once you are here
chunks.x: People here are matter-of-fact about it in a way that takes newcomers a year to match. It is far from everywhere Christchurch is four and a half hours by road. Auckland is a connecting flight. This is the main trade-off: work out how often you plan to fly home. The student thing cuts both ways It brings music, cheap food and energy. It also brings noise in certain streets and a rental market that spikes every February. Where you live determines which version you get. People stay The retention rate among clinicians who move here is high, and it is usually the same reason: the job is interesting, the commute is nothing, and the weekend starts fifteen minutes from your door. Before you read on Who wrote this. Ethicare is a healthcare recruitment company. This guide is free to read, asks nothing of you, and does not give visa advice.

chunks.t: Moving to Dunedin: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.h: Seven things you only learn once you are here
chunks.x: Where we think Dunedin is the wrong answer for someone, we say so. That’s more useful to you than a placement that doesn’t last. Ōtepoti is Dunedin’s name in te reo Māori. Kāi Tahu is the principal iwi of the South Island, and their story runs through the harbour, the peninsula and the city’s place names. Te ao Māori at work covers pronunciation. The short version A tertiary teaching hospital and the country’s oldest medical school, in a small Victorian city where your money goes further than anywhere else in New Zealand — and where the compromise is distance, not quality of life. What follows is Dunedin-specific. Anything national — visas, registration, tax, renting, driving, schools — is explained once in Moving to New Zealand . Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Why Dunedin: the case for the southern city
chunks.x: The case for Dunedin is easy to make badly. Said one way it sounds like a compromise: cheaper, smaller, further away. Said it is a different proposition — the same national pay and a tertiary case mix, in a city where you can own a character home ten minutes from work.

chunks.t: Why Dunedin: the case for the southern city
chunks.x: Your salary goes furthest here Health New Zealand pays national agreement rates, so the number on your contract is the same as it would be in Auckland. Housing is not. That gap is the single strongest argument for Dunedin, and it compounds every year you stay. A teaching hospital, and a medical school attached to it Dunedin is a tertiary centre serving a large southern catchment, tightly bound to the University of Otago. If teaching, research or supervision is part of how you want to work, the infrastructure is already here and the door is not hard to find. The commute gives you your evening back Fifteen minutes is normal. For a lot of people this is the change they notice most — not the salary, not the scenery, but arriving home before six with the day still in it. Extraordinary nature, without the drive The Otago Peninsula starts at the edge of town.

chunks.t: Why Dunedin: the case for the southern city
chunks.x: Surf beaches are ten minutes from the centre. Central Otago and the Catlins are a comfortable day trip. You are not saving this up for annual leave. It is a real city, at a small scale A public art gallery, three museums, a roofed stadium, a live music scene and more good coffee per head than the population justifies — because 20,000 students demand it.

chunks.t: Why Dunedin: the case for the southern city
chunks.x: Not a brochure week. An ordinary one. Monday to Friday A fifteen-minute drive or a twenty-minute walk downhill to the hospital. Coffee from the same place, because there is only one you will settle on. Home by six most days. Wednesday evening Something at the university or in town — a talk, a gig, a film at the Regent. The small-city advantage is that you can decide at 6pm and still be there by 7. Saturday morning The farmers market at the railway station. This is a local institution, and most of the city goes. Saturday afternoon The peninsula, or St Clair, or a hill walk that starts from a suburban street. All of these are twenty minutes away. Sunday Slow. Dunedin does not rush on a Sunday, and after a few months neither will you.

chunks.t: Why Dunedin: the case for the southern city
chunks.h: The six things people ask us
chunks.x: Is the clinical work strong enough? The city’s tertiary hospital is also the base of New Zealand’s oldest medical school, which shapes everything — teaching is woven into the work, research is accessible, and the academic culture is unusual for a city this size. If you want to teach, publish or subspecialise in an academic setting, this is the best-value place in the country to do it. How cold is it really? Colder than most of New Zealand, and the answer is that the cold is not the problem — the wind and the old housing are. Dunedin has a large stock of Victorian and Edwardian villas, beautiful and often poorly insulated. A well-insulated modern house here is perfectly comfortable; a cold flat is miserable. Chapter five is blunt about how to tell the difference.

chunks.t: Why Dunedin: the case for the southern city
chunks.h: The six things people ask us
chunks.x: What is the student thing like? Dunedin has one of the highest student populations per capita in the country, concentrated in North Dunedin. It gives the city energy, cheap eating and a cultural life well beyond its size. It also means noise, flatting stock in poor condition, and a city that empties over summer. Where you live determines how much of this touches you. Is it isolated? Yes, more than Christchurch. Dunedin Airport has domestic connections and a handful of trans-Tasman flights, but almost every long-haul journey means connecting through Auckland, Christchurch or Sydney. Factor in an extra half-day each way when you plan a trip home. What is the housing like? The best value of any city in this guide, and the most variable in quality. You can buy a substantial character home here for less than a two-bedroom Auckland townhouse.

chunks.t: Why Dunedin: the case for the southern city
chunks.h: The six things people ask us
chunks.x: The catch is that character often means single glazing, no insulation and a heating bill. Ask when it was last upgraded, not when it was built. Is there enough for a family? Plenty — beaches, the peninsula, good schools, short commutes and a safe, walkable city. The limitation is range rather than quality: fewer sports clubs, fewer specialist activities and a smaller pool of children’s services than a bigger city. Most families find that a fair trade for the space and the pace.

chunks.t: Why Dunedin: the case for the southern city
chunks.x: The distance is real Everything is further away. Family visits mean a connection. Weekend trips to the North Island are not casual. If you need to be able to get home quickly, think hard about this one. The housing stock is old and often cold Much of the loveliest housing here is Victorian or Edwardian, and a lot of it is under-insulated. The Healthy Homes standards have improved rentals, but "charming villa" and "warm in July" are not the same claim. Partner employment is narrower Outside health, education and the university, the professional job market is small. Couples where both people need specialist work find this the hardest part of the move. Grey stretches Dunedin gets proper seasons, but it also gets weeks of low cloud. People who need reliable sun find the shoulder months wearing. Small city, small circles The professional community is tight.

chunks.t: Why Dunedin: the case for the southern city
chunks.x: That is mostly a benefit — but it means your colleagues are also your neighbours, and privacy takes more effort than it does in a bigger city. Where we’d steer you instead Want the same value but warmer? Nelson Tasman or Hawke’s Bay . Want a bigger southern city? Christchurch — five hours north, warmer housing, more services. Want the widest range of roles? Auckland . Who it suits People who want a serious clinical job without a serious mortgage, who like the outdoors close rather than far, and who are at peace with being a long way from everywhere else. In our experience Dunedin suits clinicians who want a teaching hospital’s rigour without a big city’s costs — and who like that the beach at the end of the road has sea lions on it. Pack for the weather and it gives back more than it asks. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Cost of living in Geelong
chunks.x: Housing is most of the story. Almost everything else in Geelong costs close to Melbourne prices, and a couple of things cost more — which is a more useful way to think about it than a single index number.

chunks.t: Cost of living in Geelong
chunks.h: Why we don’t print dollar figures
chunks.x: We publish rents and prices only where we have verified them against current data, and a figure that was true when a page was written is misleading a year later. Rather than print numbers we cannot stand behind, this chapter tells you the shape of the difference and where to check the current position yourself. For the national picture — tax, superannuation, Medicare, banking and what a first year costs — see Money, tax & banking in Australia .

chunks.t: Cost of living in Geelong
chunks.x: Geelong Housing — the largest single difference Melbourne Noticeably higher to rent and to buy Sydney A different order of magnitude Relative widths are illustrative of direction, not measured values. Check current listings and the ABS or state data before you budget. Housing, rented or bought The reason many people move here and stay. What a clinical salary carries in Geelong is not comparable to what it carries in Melbourne, and the difference compounds over a career. Parking and commuting Generally easier and often free outside the CBD core, a real change from Melbourne’s inner suburbs. Space for the money A family home with a garden is achievable on a single clinical income in a way it increasingly is not in Melbourne.

chunks.t: Cost of living in Geelong
chunks.x: Groceries, fuel, insurance, utilities, phone and internet all sit close to Melbourne levels. Australia is a national market for most of this, and Geelong is a large enough city to have real competition. Do not expect a regional discount on the weekly shop; do not expect a penalty either.

chunks.t: Cost of living in Geelong
chunks.x: Coastal accommodation in summer The Bellarine and Surf Coast see Melbourne-level holiday pricing from Boxing Day to late January, which is worth knowing if you are house-hunting in that window. Anything with a small local market Specialist trades, certain hobbies and niche services. Not dramatically, but the choice is narrower than Melbourne, and that shows in price.

chunks.t: Cost of living in Geelong
chunks.h: The one-off costs of the first year
chunks.x: These are the ones people underestimate, and they are the same wherever in Australia you land: visa and registration fees, flights, shipping or replacing furniture, a car, a rental bond, and the gap between arriving and your first pay. Preparing to move covers the national picture, and our relocation cost calculator will give you a personal estimate. Where to check the current position Current rental listings for the specific suburbs in Where clinicians live — the fastest reality check there is. State and ABS housing data for medians. Ask us what a role pays before you model anything. We will tell you the framework and the range. The short version Treat Geelong as Melbourne prices with a materially cheaper roof over your head, plus a premium on coastal accommodation in peak summer. The housing difference is the entire argument, and it is a large one. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Food, Pako & the everyday in Geelong
chunks.x: The test of a place is not its best restaurant. It is what an ordinary Wednesday feels like, and whether Saturday morning has a shape. Geelong does well on both, and one street does much of the work.

chunks.t: Food, Pako & the everyday in Geelong
chunks.h: Pako is the centre of gravity
chunks.x: Pakington Street in Newtown — “Pako” to everyone who lives here — is the café and shopping strip that gives the inner suburbs their social life. It is not a tourist strip; it is where people spend a Saturday morning, and the standard of coffee and casual dining is high for a city this size. Down at the water, the waterfront and Little Malop Street precincts carry most of the dinner-out trade, with views across Corio Bay thrown in. Between the two, a Saturday farmers’ market rotates through the region and is worth building a routine around. Old shopfronts and independent shops in central Geelong

chunks.t: Food, Pako & the everyday in Geelong
chunks.x: What is good Café culture, casual dining on Pako and the waterfront, and a growing wine-region influence on the local food scene. For a city of 270,000 the standard is well above what the population would suggest. What is thinner The sheer range Melbourne carries. A specific niche cuisine may still mean an hour’s drive, though the gap has narrowed noticeably in the last decade. Where the wine comes from The Bellarine Peninsula and the Moorabool Valley, both twenty to thirty minutes out — cool-climate pinot noir and chardonnay country, local by any reasonable definition. Where to find groceries from home The main supermarkets carry more than they used to, and Geelong’s size supports a good range of specialist grocers. For anything unusual, Melbourne is an hour away.

chunks.t: Food, Pako & the everyday in Geelong
chunks.h: A week, once the novelty has worn off
chunks.x: Weekdays A short commute and light left in the evening The thing people mention most is arriving home early enough for a walk along the waterfront before dinner. Saturday morning Pako, or the market Coffee and errands on Pakington Street, or the rotating farmers’ market, depending on the week. Saturday afternoon The water, or the wine Eastern Beach or the Bellarine coast if the wind allows it, a Moorabool Valley cellar door if it does not. Sunday The Great Ocean Road, or nothing at all Torquay and beyond for a proper day out, or the Barwon River trails if you would rather stay close to home.

chunks.t: Food, Pako & the everyday in Geelong
chunks.x: Geelong is large enough to have plenty of variety and small enough that joining something — a football club, a surf lifesaving club, a Deakin-adjacent community group — is a fast route in. Clinicians consistently tell us the professional community here feels close for a tertiary centre, partly because the specialist bench is smaller than Melbourne’s. On community, faith and belonging, and the smaller communities a regional city carries, see Community & belonging in Australia . The short version A good café strip, a wine region on the doorstep, and eating out that punches above the population. The change is the shape of the week — a short commute buys back the evening, and Pako gives Saturday morning somewhere to be. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Geelong at a glance
chunks.x: Geelong is easier to understand once you see it as a bay city that turned to face the water again. Almost everything about it — the waterfront, the wind, the way the suburbs spread — follows from Corio Bay.

chunks.t: Geelong at a glance
chunks.x: Where Geelong sits, with the straight-line distance to Melbourne and Torquay The city centre sits at the northern edge of Corio Bay, with the Barwon River running through the southern suburbs before reaching the sea at Barwon Heads. The Bellarine Peninsula extends south-east from the city, and the You Yangs — a granite range visible from most of Geelong — rise to the north-west. What that means in practice: the inner suburbs and the waterfront are compact and walkable, the growth corridor runs south toward Armstrong Creek, and the Bellarine towns give you the coast with a commute attached. 75 km South-west of Melbourne ~270,000 Greater Geelong Only Tertiary hospital outside Melbourne

chunks.t: Geelong at a glance
chunks.x: Geelong’s climate is temperate and coastal, with more wind than Melbourne and slightly less rain than the hills further south. The difference between a still day and a blustery one can be the difference between a beach day and an indoor one. Summer — Dec to Feb Warm to hot, with hot inland northerlies sometimes followed by a sharp cool change off the bay within hours. Autumn — Mar to May Mild and settled — arguably the best swimming and the best light on the waterfront. Winter — Jun to Aug Cool and wet, with Bass Strait weather making itself felt. The wind is at its most noticeable. Spring — Sep to Nov Changeable and windy, with wildflowers on the You Yangs and the first warm days on the coast.

chunks.t: Geelong at a glance
chunks.x: Long before Wadawurrung Country Corio Bay and the surrounding plains have been lived on and managed by the Wadawurrung people, part of the Kulin nation, for tens of thousands of years. 1830s A port on the bay European settlement followed the sheltered anchorage, exporting wool from the Western District’s sheep runs. 19th century The wool boom Geelong grew wealthy enough to build the grand civic architecture that still defines the city centre. 20th century A manufacturing city Car assembly, an aluminium smelter and an oil refinery all operated here in turn, making Geelong one of Victoria’s great industrial centres. Today A city that turned back to the water All three heavy industries have closed within the last fifteen years. The waterfront has been rebuilt around people, two state agencies relocated their head offices here, and the local health and university sectors have grown to fill the gap.

chunks.t: Geelong at a glance
chunks.h: What is here that you would not expect
chunks.x: Victoria’s only tertiary hospital outside Melbourne Two Deakin University campuses, one on the waterfront The National Wool Museum, in a former woolstore A working seaport still handling grain and fuel One of the AFL’s most fiercely supported clubs A heritage carousel and painted bollards along the promenade Cool-climate wine country twenty minutes from the CBD The start of the Great Ocean Road at the edge of the municipality Orientation, in one line A bay city that built its wealth on wool, spent a century on heavy industry, and has spent the last fifteen years turning back to the water. Work out whether you want the inner city, the growth corridor or the Bellarine, and the rest of the map follows. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Healthcare in Geelong
chunks.x: Geelong punches above its population clinically, for one structural reason: its hospital is the only tertiary centre in Victoria based outside Melbourne. Understanding that designation is the difference between reading this as a regional posting and reading it accurately.

chunks.t: Healthcare in Geelong
chunks.x: A tertiary centre The region’s principal referral hospital is the only tertiary hospital in Victoria based outside metropolitan Melbourne, and the largest hospital in regional Victoria. A large catchment Its primary catchment covers around 350,000 people, extending to roughly 500,000 for some specialist services drawn from further along the south-west coast. District services behind it Smaller hospitals and community health services across the Surf Coast, the Otways, Colac and the Bellarine refer inward for specialist and complex care. A private sector Private hospitals and specialist imaging providers operate alongside the public system, giving real choice for clinicians and patients alike. Melbourne is close, not essential An hour up the freeway if a case needs a Melbourne subspecialty opinion, but the great majority of work is managed locally.

chunks.t: Healthcare in Geelong
chunks.x: A note on names We don’t name hospitals, trusts or private providers as places of work anywhere on this site — a named employer implies a relationship, and the post and the package get confirmed with you directly. Everything above is described structurally for that reason. If you want to know exactly where a role sits, ask us and we will tell you plainly.

chunks.t: Healthcare in Geelong
chunks.h: What the tertiary role does to your work
chunks.x: A tertiary centre with a large regional catchment behind it pulls in two directions at once, and both are true of the same job. What the region gives you A case mix closer to a metropolitan teaching hospital than a typical regional posting — subspecialty exposure, teaching relationships with Deakin University’s medical and health-science programmes, and a role in the state’s health system that carries weight. What it asks of you Comfort working with a smaller specialist bench than a Melbourne teaching hospital, even while the case complexity is comparable.

chunks.t: Healthcare in Geelong
chunks.x: This is where our Australian work is concentrated, so it is the part we can speak to in most detail. As the only tertiary imaging service in regional Victoria, Geelong’s capability sits closer to a metropolitan department than a typical regional posting — a full range of modalities, and a teaching relationship with Deakin University’s health science programmes. For a technologist or radiographer that has a specific consequence: subspecialty exposure is available without a five-million-person city built up around it, and cross-training tends to be actively supported. Profession guide Radiographers in Australia Ahpra registration, the pathway in order, and what the role is really like. Profession guide Nuclear medicine in Australia The registration route for technologists, and what to expect from the work. Profession guide Sonographers in Australia ASAR accreditation, the pathway, and indicative pay. Profession guide Radiation therapists in Australia Recognition of your training, scope of practice, indicative pay.

chunks.t: Healthcare in Geelong
chunks.x: Registration is national but pay is not. In the public system, salaries are set by the relevant Victorian health system industrial agreement, negotiated between the health service and the union covering your profession — so the same role can sit on a different scale in another state. In the private sector, pay is negotiated individually and is often higher, particularly where a service is hard to staff. We do not publish figures we have not verified against the agreement that governs the role. For the indicative bands and how the frameworks work, see Salary in Australia, explained .

chunks.t: Healthcare in Geelong
chunks.x: How does the tertiary designation affect my day-to-day caseload? Which cases, if any, go to a Melbourne subspecialty service? How many colleagues sit alongside me in my specialty specifically? What is the on-call pattern, and how often is it called upon? Which modalities or sub-specialties would I be expected to cover? What CPD time and funding is provided, including travel to Melbourne? Is there a teaching component through Deakin, and is it supported? The short version Geelong is Victoria’s only tertiary hospital outside Melbourne, which is why the clinical case mix is wider than the population suggests. The trade is a smaller specialist bench than a Melbourne teaching hospital — and for imaging specifically, a full-modality service most regional cities cannot offer. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Where clinicians live in Geelong
chunks.x: Geelong is compact enough that most commutes stay under twenty minutes, which frees you to choose on lifestyle rather than logistics. The real decision is inner city, growth corridor, or the Bellarine.

chunks.t: Where clinicians live in Geelong
chunks.x: Before you look at a single listing: fix your work site. The hospital and university precinct sits close to the CBD, while some services and clinics operate further out — and while nothing here is a long drive by Melbourne standards, the difference between a ten-minute and a thirty-minute commute is worth knowing before you sign a lease. Then choose your shape of life. Inner suburbs mean cafés and walkability. The southern growth corridor means new housing and more space. The Bellarine means beach life with a longer commute attached.

chunks.t: Where clinicians live in Geelong
chunks.x: Newtown & Geelong West Leafy and established, with Pakington Street’s cafés and shops on the doorstep. Suits professionals without children or those who want to walk to dinner. Least space per dollar. Herne Hill & Hamlyn Heights Similar character a little further from the centre, with somewhat better value for a family-sized block. Highton & Wandana Heights Established and family-friendly, close to well-regarded schools and a short drive from the hospital precinct. Belmont & Grovedale Established southern suburbs near the Barwon River and the Waurn Ponds precinct, popular with families. Armstrong Creek The city’s major growth corridor to the south — the newest and most affordable family housing, with a longer commute in. The Bellarine towns Ocean Grove, Barwon Heads, Drysdale and Portarlington offer beach life with a twenty-five to forty-minute commute, and are increasingly sought after for exactly that reason. Corio & Norlane The city’s more affordable northern suburbs, close to the ring road and undergoing gradual renewal.

chunks.t: Where clinicians live in Geelong
chunks.h: Renting first is the sensible order
chunks.x: Almost everyone we place rents for six to twelve months before buying, and Geelong’s market moves with the seasons as much as anything else — competition for Bellarine rentals rises sharply over summer. Arriving with something secured for your first month takes the pressure off the decision that matters more. How leases, bonds, applications and tenancy rights work is the same across Australia and is covered once in Moving to Australia . Nothing about renting in Geelong is legally different; it is the timing and the local competition that vary. Practical, in order Fix your work site before you choose a suburb. Decide between inner city, growth corridor, or the Bellarine. Rent for the first six to twelve months, and secure something before you fly. Walk the street at the time of day you would be coming home.

chunks.t: Where clinicians live in Geelong
chunks.h: Renting first is the sensible order
chunks.x: If you are drawn to the Bellarine, drive the commute at peak on a summer weekend before committing — the traffic is real in January. The short version Nothing in Geelong is a difficult commute by Melbourne standards, so choose on the life rather than the drive. Inner city for walkability, the growth corridor for space, the Bellarine for the beach — and rent first, because the Bellarine market moves with the summer season. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Getting around Geelong
chunks.x: The summary: a car makes life easier, but Geelong is also the most train-connected regional city in Victoria, and some households manage well without a second one.

chunks.t: Getting around Geelong
chunks.x: Most trips across Geelong take ten to twenty minutes. A local bus network covers the suburbs, and the train line itself has local stops that double as inner-city transport. Parking is easier than Melbourne, though not as effortless as a small country town. Cycling works well along the waterfront and the Barwon River trails, and Geelong’s flat inner geography makes it a rideable city outside the windiest days. ~15 min Most trips across the city 1 hr To Melbourne by train or freeway ~20 min To Avalon Airport

chunks.t: Getting around Geelong
chunks.x: By road About an hour up the Princes Freeway, dual carriageway the whole way. A normal commute for some, and the reason a Melbourne evening is an easy thing to do. By train A frequent direct service runs to Melbourne’s Southern Cross Station in roughly sixty to seventy-five minutes — commutable, and some Geelong residents do it daily. By air Avalon Airport sits between Geelong and Melbourne with limited domestic and seasonal international services. For most international travel you will use Melbourne’s main airport, about fifty minutes away. By coach Regional coach services connect Geelong to the Surf Coast, the Otways and towns further west, useful if you are without a car.

chunks.t: Getting around Geelong
chunks.x: Useful, not always essential. If you live centrally and work at the hospital, the train line and local buses can cover daily life. A car earns its keep on weekends — the Bellarine, the Great Ocean Road and the wine regions are not well served by public transport, and that is where Geelong’s real lifestyle argument lives. Licence conversion, importing a vehicle, insurance and registration all work the same way across Australia and are covered once in Living in Australia . Nothing about it is specific to Geelong. First-month practicalities If you plan to live centrally and use the train, confirm your actual commute time at your real start time, not the timetable’s best case. Check whether your accommodation has off-street parking — it varies more in the inner suburbs than further out.

chunks.t: Getting around Geelong
chunks.x: If you are commuting from the Bellarine, drive the route once at your real start time before you commit to a lease. Register for the Melbourne rail service early if you expect regular trips — peak services fill. The short version Geelong is the rare regional city where you can manage without a second car. Fifteen minutes to anything local, an hour to Melbourne by train — and the car earns its keep on Bellarine and Great Ocean Road weekends, not the daily commute. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: The Great Ocean Road, the Bellarine & the weekend
chunks.x: This is the argument for Geelong that needs the least explaining. You are living at the start of one of the world’s great coastal drives, with a capital city on the other side of you.

chunks.t: The Great Ocean Road, the Bellarine & the weekend
chunks.x: The official start of the Great Ocean Road, and the spiritual home of Australian surfing. Bells Beach hosts one of the sport’s oldest professional contests, but the coastline either side is just as good for a beginner or a family. Close enough that it is a weeknight option, not just a weekend one. Summer evenings on the waterfront

chunks.t: The Great Ocean Road, the Bellarine & the weekend
chunks.h: Thirty to forty minutes: the Bellarine
chunks.x: Ocean Grove & Barwon Heads Family beach towns at the mouth of the Barwon River, popular enough that a summer weekend needs planning ahead. Queenscliff A heritage seaside town with a working ferry across Port Phillip Bay to the Mornington Peninsula — a day trip in its own right. The Bellarine wineries Cool-climate cellar doors scattered across the peninsula, most within forty minutes of the city. Portarlington & the mussel coast A working fishing town on the calmer bay side, known locally for its mussels and a slower pace than the ocean beaches.

chunks.t: The Great Ocean Road, the Bellarine & the weekend
chunks.h: Two to three hours: the Great Ocean Road proper
chunks.x: Lorne, Apollo Bay, the Otway rainforest and the Twelve Apostles are all reachable as a long day out, or better as an overnight. It is one of the world’s great coastal drives, and Geelong is where it starts rather than somewhere you fly into to see it.

chunks.t: The Great Ocean Road, the Bellarine & the weekend
chunks.h: Thirty to forty minutes inland: the Moorabool Valley & the You Yangs
chunks.x: Cool-climate wine country to the west, and an easy granite-range walk at the You Yangs with views back over Corio Bay and, on a clear day, the Melbourne skyline. The reminder that Geelong’s hinterland is not only coastline.

chunks.t: The Great Ocean Road, the Bellarine & the weekend
chunks.x: A walk or swim at Eastern Beach The waterfront carousel and painted bollards The National Wool Museum Kardinia Park on an AFL match day The Barwon River trails for cycling or running The Geelong Gallery Deakin University’s waterfront campus and public spaces A Saturday on Pakington Street “ People fly into Melbourne to drive the road that starts at the end of your street. The Great Ocean Road, in one sentence The short version Bells Beach in twenty-five minutes, the Bellarine in forty, the Twelve Apostles in a long day, and Melbourne itself in an hour the other direction. Geelong is not near the coast — it is where the coast starts , and that is what keeps people here after the job stops being new.
