chunks.t: Moving to Geelong: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.x: Geelong is the city that gives Melbourne a coastline of its own: Victoria’s second city on Corio Bay, home to the only tertiary hospital in the state based outside Melbourne, with the Great Ocean Road starting at its edge. Here it is in nine numbers, then six things nobody tells you until you have moved.

chunks.t: Moving to Geelong: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.h: A wool port that became a knowledge city
chunks.x: Around 270,000 people live across Greater Geelong, on Corio Bay about 75 kilometres south-west of Melbourne. It grew rich on wool in the nineteenth century — the reason for the grand civic architecture still standing in the centre — then on manufacturing through the twentieth: car assembly, an aluminium smelter and an oil refinery all operated here in turn. Within the last fifteen years all three closed, and the city rebuilt itself around health, education and the public sector instead. Two state government agencies moved their head offices to the waterfront, Deakin University expanded, and the local health service grew into Victoria’s largest regional provider. For clinicians the proposition is specific.

chunks.t: Moving to Geelong: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.h: A wool port that became a knowledge city
chunks.x: The region’s principal referral hospital is the only tertiary hospital in Victoria based outside metropolitan Melbourne, drawing a primary catchment of around 350,000 people and extending to roughly 500,000 for some specialist services. You get full tertiary breadth in a city of a quarter of a million, with Melbourne itself an hour up the road when you want it. The costs: a specialist bench that, while real, is still smaller than a Melbourne teaching hospital’s; a summer that brings the whole of Melbourne to the local beaches; and a wind off the bay that takes some getting used to. This guide prices all three plainly. Who wrote this Ethicare is a healthcare recruitment company. This guide is free to read, asks nothing of you, and does not give visa advice. Geelong suits people who want real tertiary work and a coastline, without needing everything a capital offers. Where we think it is the wrong fit, we say so.

chunks.t: Moving to Geelong: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.x: ~270,000 People across Greater Geelong, Victoria’s largest regional city. 1 hr To Melbourne by train or the Princes Freeway. A commute for some, a day trip for most. Only Tertiary hospital in Victoria based outside metropolitan Melbourne. 350,000 Primary catchment population for the region’s principal referral hospital. 25 min To Torquay and the start of the Great Ocean Road. 2 Deakin University campuses, including one built into the waterfront itself. 1850s When the wool boom built the grand centre that still stands today. Regional Classification for skilled-migration purposes, despite the tertiary hospital. 20+ Cool-climate wineries across the Bellarine Peninsula and Moorabool Valley. Corio Bay, the water the whole city is built around.

chunks.t: Moving to Geelong: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.h: Six things you only learn once you are here
chunks.x: The wind has opinions Geelong is breezier than Melbourne, exposed to both the bay and Bass Strait. A hot northerly followed by a cool change can move thirty degrees in an hour. It is a Cats town The Geelong Football Club runs deep here. Expect the city to notice, loudly, in September. “Pako” is a place, not a joke Pakington Street in Newtown is the café and shopping strip locals just call Pako. You will too, within a month. The referral role is bigger than the city suggests Case mix arrives from across the Barwon South West, not from Geelong’s population alone. Old industry left a waterfront, not a scar Where wool stores and a refinery once stood is now parkland, apartments and government offices.

chunks.t: Moving to Geelong: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.h: Six things you only learn once you are here
chunks.x: People still talk about “when Ford was here.” Summer means visitors The Bellarine and the Surf Coast are Melbourne’s nearest beach escape, so the roads and coastal towns get busy from Boxing Day to late January. A note on Country Geelong sits on the land of the Wadawurrung people, one of the five nations of the Kulin alliance. Acknowledgement of Country opens meetings and events across the region, as it does across Victoria.

chunks.t: Moving to Geelong: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.x: Nine chapters, all about Geelong specifically. Anything true of Australia generally — Medicare, visas, Ahpra registration, tax, superannuation, schools — lives once in Moving to Australia , so you read it once and not nine times. If you read nothing else, read Why Geelong for the case weighed up, and Healthcare in Geelong , because the tertiary role is the part most people underestimate. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Why Geelong: the case for Victoria’s second city
chunks.x: Most people who move here are trading Melbourne’s scale for a hospital they can get to know, and a coastline at the end of the street. That trade is real, and so is what you give up. Both sides, plainly.

chunks.t: Why Geelong: the case for Victoria’s second city
chunks.x: Tertiary reach without the metro grind The region’s hospital is Victoria’s only tertiary centre outside Melbourne, so the case complexity is high, but the commute is not a Melbourne commute. Seniority arrives earlier Smaller specialist teams than a Melbourne teaching hospital mean your name is on decisions sooner. A commute measured in minutes Most suburbs sit ten to twenty minutes from the hospital and the waterfront alike. Housing that leaves room Property costs materially less than Melbourne, without leaving the state’s health and education systems behind. Regional migration status Geelong is classed as regional for skilled-migration purposes despite its size — a pathway Melbourne itself does not offer. The coast is not a holiday, it’s Tuesday The Bellarine Peninsula and the start of the Great Ocean Road sit inside the everyday commute radius. The Baywalk bollards — Geelong’s waterfront, painted one figure at a time

chunks.t: Why Geelong: the case for Victoria’s second city
chunks.x: None of the following should stop you. All of them are worth knowing before you sign, because they are what people tell us they wish they had asked about. Clinical The bench is finite Depth in your specialty exists, but it is a team, not a Melbourne teaching hospital’s full department. Ask how many people sit alongside you specifically. Clinical Melbourne is the backstop for the rarest work Occasionally a case goes to a Melbourne subspecialty service. Which ones depends on your specialty, and it is worth asking about directly at interview. Practical Summer brings the whole of Melbourne to your beach The Bellarine and Surf Coast get busy from Boxing Day to late January. Locals plan around it rather than fight it. Practical The wind is a real feature, not a footnote Exposed to Corio Bay and Bass Strait alike, Geelong is a noticeably breezier city than Melbourne. Outdoor plans need a backup. Personal It is a city of 270,000, not five million A good range of cafés, restaurants and culture exists here. It is not Melbourne’s range, and some people miss that; others find it a relief.

chunks.t: Why Geelong: the case for Victoria’s second city
chunks.h: When another city is the better answer
chunks.x: If you need a large metropolitan subspecialty team around you, Melbourne is our recommendation — and close enough that Geelong can be a later move rather than a rejected one. If the draw is coastal lifestyle with regional breadth at a different latitude, Newcastle or the Gold Coast offer a similar shape. And if it is the Bellarine itself rather than Geelong specifically that appeals, the peninsula towns are worth a conversation, though the clinical roles are concentrated in Geelong, not out on the coast. “ Geelong asks you to trade Melbourne’s scale for a hospital you can get to know. What clinicians tell us, in one sentence

chunks.t: Why Geelong: the case for Victoria’s second city
chunks.x: A ten to twenty-minute drive to work. A walk along the waterfront or Eastern Beach before or after a shift. Saturday morning on Pakington Street or at the Waterfront Farmers Market. An afternoon at Ocean Grove or Barwon Heads, or the Bellarine wineries, depending on the wind. The Great Ocean Road when you want a full day out. Melbourne when you want a gig, an airport or the MCG. The short version Geelong gives you Victoria’s only tertiary case mix outside Melbourne, a commute in minutes and the Great Ocean Road at your back door, for materially less than Melbourne costs. What it asks in return is a smaller specialist bench and a city many times smaller than the capital. If that trade appeals, few places in Australia offer it this close to a state capital.

chunks.t: Why Geelong: the case for Victoria’s second city
chunks.x: Where we’d steer you instead If you want a capital’s depth and sub-specialty range, Melbourne is an hour by train and the obvious comparison. If regional Victoria is the real draw, the Victoria brief sets out the wider state and where the opportunities sit. If you would take the same deal in New South Wales, Newcastle is its closest equivalent — a coastal second city two hours from Sydney. In our experience Geelong is the rare regional city where you can manage without a second car and still reach a capital for dinner. Clinicians who settle here tend to be the ones who wanted the coast and the Otways without giving up a city’s services. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Cost of living in Gisborne: the numbers
chunks.x: Gisborne is among the more affordable regions in the North Island, and the headline numbers understate the picture in both directions. Housing costs less than almost anywhere with a hospital. Almost everything else costs a little more, because it has to be trucked in over a hill road.

chunks.t: Cost of living in Gisborne: the numbers
chunks.x: We used to print a weekly rent and a monthly budget table here. We have taken them out. A figure that was true when a page was written is misleading a year later, and a candidate who plans a move around a stale number is worse off than one who plans around none. What does not go stale is the shape of a month, and the judgement about which lines will surprise you. For today’s actual numbers use the calculators at the foot of the page, and use them to compare Gisborne against the city you are leaving. That is the only comparison that decides anything.

chunks.t: Cost of living in Gisborne: the numbers
chunks.x: Clinical pay is national. You arrive on the same salary you would earn in Auckland or Tauranga, into a market where a family home costs a fraction of theirs. Buying here on a single clinical salary is achievable, and a good number of clinicians do it within their first year or two. The complication is supply rather than price. The rental market is small, a meaningful share of the stock is older and under-insulated, and good properties go quickly. Post-Gabrielle, some housing was lost and some remains affected, which has tightened things further. Ask your employer directly what accommodation support exists before you accept anything. Within the district there is a clear ladder: Whataupoko and Wainui at the top, Mangapapa and Riverdale in the middle, Kaiti and Elgin the most affordable, and the rural settlements cheaper again.

chunks.t: Cost of living in Gisborne: the numbers
chunks.x: Wainui & Okitu The district’s premium — surf beach living, limited stock, and prices well above the city’s average. Still modest against a main centre. Whataupoko & central The best character housing in town, near the gardens and the rivers. The city’s most sought-after streets. Mangapapa & Riverdale The sensible middle — family homes, good schools, sound value. Kaiti & Elgin The most affordable housing in the city by a clear margin. Variable stock — check insulation and heating carefully. Matawhero, Patutahi & the flats Land and space for the money, ten to twenty minutes out among the vines. Up the Coast Cheapest of all, and remote. Small coastal communities with real housing quality issues in places. Where a month goes The proportions, for one person on a mid-range budget. Proportions move slowly; prices move every quarter.

chunks.t: Cost of living in Gisborne: the numbers
chunks.x: Rent takes under half of it, which is unusual in this country and most of the financial case for Tairāwhiti. Rent 47% Groceries 20% Car — petrol, insurance, running 10% Entertainment & leisure 9% Power & water 8% Internet 4% Mobile phone plan 2% The line that decides it Rent · 47% Clinical pay is national, so this is the same salary as Auckland or Wellington against one of the smallest rent lines in the North Island. The car is not optional here. Indicative prices that change over time. Note the grocery and freight lines — that is the isolation showing up in the weekly shop.

chunks.t: Cost of living in Gisborne: the numbers
chunks.x: Freight and the weekly shop Everything arrives by truck over a hill road, and it shows in the price. Groceries and delivered goods cost a little more than in a main centre, and online delivery takes longer. Flights, repeatedly The real cost of this region. Every trip out starts with a flight, and if family are overseas you will be adding a domestic leg every time. Insurance and flood exposure A live question since 2023, particularly on the river flats and up the coast. Check a property’s history and its insurability before committing. Winter heating in an older house The climate is mild, but the housing stock is variable. Paying a little more for a well-insulated home with a heat pump is usually cheaper overall.

chunks.t: Cost of living in Gisborne: the numbers
chunks.x: Compare cities Numbeo · cost of living Gisborne prices for rent, groceries, transport and dining, against your current city. Crowd-sourced, and the sample is thin for a place this size — treat it as a ballpark, not a quote. Plan your budget Sorted budget planner New Zealand’s free, government-backed budgeting tool. Official data Stats NZ living costs The Household Living-Costs Price Index, updated quarterly. Property realestate.co.nz Current Gisborne rentals and homes for sale. Look early — the market is small. Sanity check Expatistan A cleaner side-by-side of two cities. Worth running when Numbeo looks off. Official rents Tenancy Services market rent Bond-lodgement data by area — the most reliable rent figure in New Zealand. How pay, tax, IRD numbers, KiwiSaver and sending money home work is national, and covered in Money, tax & banking .

chunks.t: Cost of living in Gisborne: the numbers
chunks.x: The summary You will live cheaply here and can buy a home within a couple of years . The catches are limited housing supply — ask about accommodation support before you accept anything — and the cost of flying out of an isolated region . Neither is a dealbreaker; both belong in your planning. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Food, wine and everyday life in Gisborne
chunks.x: Gisborne calls itself the chardonnay capital of New Zealand and has the record to back it. Add citrus, sweetcorn, avocados and a coastline full of kai moana, and you have a region that eats far better than its size or its remoteness would suggest.

chunks.t: Food, wine and everyday life in Gisborne
chunks.x: The Gisborne flats are warm, sunny and fertile, and the region built its reputation on chardonnay — ripe, generous and among the best in the country. Gerürztraminer, viognier, chenin blanc and pinot gris all do well here too; this is aromatic white country rather than red. Cellar doors sit out among the flats at Matawhero and Patutahi, ten to twenty minutes from the city. They are unpretentious, cheap to visit, and rarely busy. A Saturday afternoon at one becomes ordinary very quickly.

chunks.t: Food, wine and everyday life in Gisborne
chunks.x: Citrus, sweetcorn, squash, avocados, persimmons and kiwifruit off the flats, sold at roadside stalls and orchard gates through the season for very little. This is productive country and it shows up on the table. Off the coast: crayfish, pāua, kina, snapper and kahawai, with a deep local culture of gathering kai moana — particularly up the Coast, where it is customary practice rather than recreation. Rules on species, size and quantity are real and enforced, and there is proper tikanga around it. Ask before you assume, and ask locally. The Gisborne farmers’ market on Saturday morning is the weekend fixture: producers rather than resellers, and a cross-section of the town.

chunks.t: Food, wine and everyday life in Gisborne
chunks.x: The city centre A modest but real scene — good cafés, a handful of solid restaurants, and a couple of very good ones. Small, and better than you would expect. The beach and the coast Casual food near Wainui, and up the Coast the pleasure is a bakery, a pie and a view rather than a restaurant. Groceries The main chains are here. Prices run a little above a main centre because of freight, and the fresh local produce is the offsetting bargain. Specialist ingredients The weak point — the narrowest range of any region in this collection. If a particular cuisine is central to how your family eats, check carefully first. See Finding your feet & your people .

chunks.t: Food, wine and everyday life in Gisborne
chunks.x: New Year is the region’s big moment Gisborne is the first city in the world to see the new year, and it makes something of it. The city fills, there are events and festivals, and it is good fun. Summer is hot and busy Beaches, holidaymakers, and a surf town at full tilt. The department feels it. It settles in February. Matariki and the Māori calendar matter here More than in most regions. Marae events, kapa haka, hui and tangihanga are part of the community year, and being invited into that is a privilege rather than an obligation. Community closes around you slowly, then completely A small remote city takes longer to break into than a transient one. Sport, kapa haka, the surf club, the school gate — turn up consistently and you will belong properly. Limitations Retail is limited. Serious shopping means Napier, Auckland or online, and online delivery is slower and sometimes surcharged.

chunks.t: Food, wine and everyday life in Gisborne
chunks.x: Touring music, theatre and exhibitions rarely come this far east. The region’s own festivals — and there are good ones — fill part of the gap. Specialist imported groceries are hard to find. Most people build up an order from Auckland a few times a year. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Gisborne at a glance: climate, geography and the recovery
chunks.x: Gisborne sits where three rivers meet the sea on New Zealand’s most easterly point, with steep, soft hill country rising immediately behind it. That geography gives the region its warmth, its wine and its surf — and its vulnerability.

chunks.t: Gisborne at a glance: climate, geography and the recovery
chunks.x: Where Gisborne sits, with the straight-line distance to Napier The city sits on the flats of Poverty Bay , where the Waimatā, Taruheru and Waipaoa rivers converge. Kaiti Hill rises above the harbour, and the surf beaches — Waikanae, Midway, Wainui and Makorori — run north along the coast from the city’s edge. Behind the flats, the land climbs quickly into some of the steepest and most erosion-prone hill country in New Zealand: sheep and cattle stations, and extensive pine forestry. Inland and west lie the Raukūmara Range and Te Urewera , one of the largest tracts of native forest in the North Island. North, the coast road runs to Tolaga Bay, Tokomaru Bay and Ruatōria, and eventually around the East Cape — a slow, beautiful, deeply Māori stretch of country. South, past the vineyards, the road runs to Māhia peninsula and on to Wairoa and Hawke’s Bay. Photography needed — Poverty Bay The city on the flats, Kaiti Hill above the harbour

chunks.t: Gisborne at a glance: climate, geography and the recovery
chunks.x: Summer Dec – Feb 24–30°C Hot, dry, brilliant Autumn Mar – May 18–24°C Harvest and clean swell Winter Jun – Aug 14–17°C Mild, wet at times Spring Sep – Nov 17–22°C Warming, changeable Indicative daytime highs on the flats. Inland and up the coast the hill country is cooler, and considerably wetter in a bad year.

chunks.t: Gisborne at a glance: climate, geography and the recovery
chunks.h: What the numbers don’t tell you
chunks.x: It is warm, sunny and early. Around 2,200 hours of sunshine, hot dry summers, and mild winters. Being the most easterly city in the country means the sun arrives here first — and in midsummer that is very early indeed. The hill country is soft, and that matters. The geology here is young and erodible, and much of the steep land was cleared for pasture and later planted in pine. When a big rain event arrives, the hills move. This is the mechanism behind the region’s flooding, its slips, and the forestry slash that ended up on beaches and bridges in 2023. The roads are the region’s weak point. There are effectively two ways out by land — south to Wairoa, or north around the Cape — and both cross terrain that slips. Closures happen, and when they do, Gisborne is isolated. Housing quality is variable. Prices are modest, but a good proportion of the stock is older and under-insulated.

chunks.t: Gisborne at a glance: climate, geography and the recovery
chunks.h: What the numbers don’t tell you
chunks.x: Ask about insulation, ventilation and heating, and check the Healthy Homes compliance statement — a legal requirement, covered in the national Renting in New Zealand chapter. Cyclone Gabrielle In February 2023 Cyclone Gabrielle hit Tairāwhiti as hard as anywhere in New Zealand. Rivers broke out, bridges and roads were destroyed, forestry slash and silt buried farmland and beaches, and coastal communities north of the city were cut off for extended periods. Lives were lost across the affected regions. Where things stand now: the city functions normally. Much of the road network has been repaired or rerouted, but work continues, and some communities up the coast and inland are still rebuilding. Land use, forestry practice and river management remain live regional debates. Why it matters clinically: it left a lasting imprint on rural mental health, on how services plan for isolation and access, and on trust between communities and institutions. Colleagues here lived through it. Arrive informed rather than curious.

chunks.t: Gisborne at a glance: climate, geography and the recovery
chunks.h: Where things are, in driving time
chunks.x: Across the city 10 minutes, at any hour. → Wainui & Makorori 10 to 20 minutes north. The surf beaches. → Rere Falls & the rockslide 50 minutes inland, and a regional institution on a hot day. → Tolaga Bay / Tokomaru Bay 45 minutes and 1 hr 30 north up the coast road. → Māhia 1 hr 45 south — the peninsula, the beaches and the rocket launch site. → Napier / Waikato / Auckland 4 hr, ~6 hr and 6–7 hr. Flying is usually the answer.

chunks.t: Gisborne at a glance: climate, geography and the recovery
chunks.x: Tairāwhiti The region — the coast upon which the sun shines across the water. Tūranganui-a-Kiwa The name for Gisborne and Poverty Bay. The Coast The East Coast road north towards the Cape. A place and an identity. Ngāti Porou The large iwi of the East Coast, north of the city. Slash Forestry debris. A charged word here since 2023. Wainui The main surf beach, minutes from town. Kaiti Hill Titirangi — the hill above the harbour, and the view. Chardonnay capital What Gisborne calls itself, with justification. The short version Warm, sunny and early, on soft steep country with a fragile road network . The climate and the surf are why people come; isolation and erosion are the costs, and Gabrielle made both concrete. Healthcare here is the chapter that decides it. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Healthcare in Gisborne: rural practice in Tairāwhiti
chunks.x: This chapter decides whether Gisborne is right for you, so we will lead with the two facts that matter most: this is a rural hospital four hours from the nearest base hospital, and over half the population it serves is Māori. Everything else follows from those.

chunks.t: Healthcare in Gisborne: rural practice in Tairāwhiti
chunks.x: Public hospital and specialist services across the district are delivered by Health New Zealand | Te Whatu Ora. There is one hospital, in Gisborne, serving the entire district — an emergency department, inpatient medical and surgical beds, maternity, imaging, day procedures and outpatient clinics, with visiting specialist services from larger centres. Around it sits a primary and community network that carries more weight here than in most regions: general practice, iwi and Māori health providers, community and district nursing, rural clinics up the coast, aged residential care and ambulance. In a region this dispersed, community care is not an adjunct to the hospital — it is the system. What is not here: intensive care beyond stabilisation, most surgical and medical subspecialties, oncology treatment, and complex paediatrics.

chunks.t: Healthcare in Gisborne: rural practice in Tairāwhiti
chunks.x: All of that is referred out — principally to Hawke’s Bay four hours south, with Waikato and Auckland used for tertiary services. Retrieval and air transfer are a routine part of the working week. The distance that defines the job 4 Hours to the nearest base hospital One hospital serves the entire district, and the next one south is four hours away. That is why scope here is wide, why senior support by phone matters more than anywhere else in this collection, and why retrieval and air transfer are a routine part of the working week rather than an emergency measure. Tertiary services are further again — Waikato and Auckland. What is referred, and what you stay involved in, varies by specialty: ask about yours specifically.

chunks.t: Healthcare in Gisborne: rural practice in Tairāwhiti
chunks.x: Strong fit Rural generalist medicine, general practice, emergency nursing and medicine, midwifery, radiography, community allied health, mental health and addiction, paramedicine, and public and Māori health. Possible, with planning Sonography, physiotherapy, occupational therapy, aged care, and roles combining a clinical caseload with travel up the coast. Difficult or unavailable Most hospital subspecialties, intensive care, radiation therapy and oncology. Those roles are in Hawke’s Bay, Waikato or the main centres. Autonomy Small teams, no subspecialist down the corridor, and decisions that are yours. Exhilarating if you want it, exposing if you don’t. The most meaningful equity work in the country Highest Māori population share, high deprivation, real unmet need. If closing that gap is why you came into healthcare, few places offer more. Workforce pressure is real Recruiting and retaining staff in a remote region is a standing challenge. That means openness to international clinicians, and gaps alongside it.

chunks.t: Healthcare in Gisborne: rural practice in Tairāwhiti
chunks.x: Here this is not a chapter heading — it is the working environment. Over half the district’s population identifies as Māori, the highest share in New Zealand. This is the rohe of Ngāti Porou, Rongowhakaata, Ngāi Tāmanuhiri, Te Aitanga-a-Māhaki and others, and iwi-led health providers deliver a substantial proportion of care. Practically: karakia opens meetings, te reo is used freely on the ward and in the community, whānau are present and involved in decisions as a matter of course, and marae-based clinics and outreach are ordinary. Kaupapa Māori services are not an alternative pathway here; for many patients they are the main one. You are not expected to arrive fluent. You are expected to try, and in this region the effort registers more than anywhere else in the country.

chunks.t: Healthcare in Gisborne: rural practice in Tairāwhiti
chunks.x: The national chapter Te ao Māori at work covers pronunciation, the words you will hear and marae etiquette — read it properly before you arrive. What to ask at interview What senior support is available, on site and by phone, overnight and at weekends? Ask this first. It is the single most important question in a rural hospital.

chunks.t: Healthcare in Gisborne: rural practice in Tairāwhiti
chunks.x: What is referred out, where to, and what is my role in stabilising and transferring? How much rural or coastal outreach is in the role, and how does it work when roads close? What orientation, cultural induction and te reo support is there for clinicians new to New Zealand? What professional development and study support exists, given the distance from a tertiary centre? Is there relocation and housing support, and what does the team’s retention look like? Sophie Sophie’s insight Gisborne is the region I am most careful about matching, and the one where the right person does the most good. The clinicians who thrive here came into healthcare to work where the need is greatest, and they arrive ready to learn te reo rather than expecting to be accommodated. When that lines up, it is the most rewarding placement I make. Sophie Careem Founder, Ethicare Resourcing

chunks.t: Healthcare in Gisborne: rural practice in Tairāwhiti
chunks.x: Registration with your professional body, and the visa that goes with it, are national processes and identical wherever in New Zealand you land. They are explained once, properly, in Eligibility & registration and Immigration & visas . How the health system is funded and structured — ACC, primary care, what things cost, how it differs from the NHS or a private system — lives in How the health system works . Ethicare Live roles & professions What we’re recruiting for now, by profession and by region. Nearby Hawke’s Bay The base hospital this region refers to, four hours south — and a strong option in its own right. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Where clinicians live in Gisborne: ten places compared
chunks.x: Gisborne is small enough that everywhere is ten minutes from the hospital, so the choice here is about what you want your street to be — town, beach, or the flats out towards the vines. The real constraint is not distance. It is what is available. Ten minutes from everywhere — so choose a street, not a commute Nothing in this chapter is far from the hospital. What differs is the kind of place you wake up in. A town street Character housing and mature gardens on the settled side of the water, with the gardens and cafés walkable. The settled heart of the city, and still modest money by national standards. A beach street North along the surf coast, where the day starts with a look at the water. The district’s premium addresses, with little on the market at any one time. A country road West onto the flats among the vines — land, sheds and space, still inside a quarter-hour of work. The option most regions can’t offer at all. Availability, not distance, is the real constraint here — start the search early and be ready to move on the good ones.

chunks.t: Where clinicians live in Gisborne: ten places compared
chunks.x: Palms along the river in central Gisborne Central Gisborne & Whataupoko Established, leafy streets just north of the rivers, with the city’s better character housing and the Botanical Gardens. The most sought-after part of town, and still modest by national standards. Mangapapa Solid, settled family housing north of the centre, well served by schools. A common first house for relocating families. Riverdale & Lytton West Mixed suburbs west of the river with good-value family homes and easy access across town. Kaiti East of the harbour beneath Titirangi, the city’s largest and most strongly Māori suburb, with significant deprivation alongside real community strength. The most affordable housing in the city, and where much of the region’s most important health work happens. Elgin & Outer Kaiti Affordable, working suburbs on the city’s edges. Good value, variable housing stock — check insulation carefully. Photography needed — Gisborne housing Established streets, the rivers, the gardens

chunks.t: Where clinicians live in Gisborne: ten places compared
chunks.x: Wainui Beach Ten to fifteen minutes north of the city, along one of New Zealand’s best surf beaches. The premium address in the district and, for a lot of people, the reason they came. Limited stock and priced accordingly. Okitu & Makorori Further along the same coast — smaller, quieter, more scattered. Twenty minutes to work, and the surf at the end of the drive.

chunks.t: Where clinicians live in Gisborne: ten places compared
chunks.x: Matawhero & the flats West towards the vineyards — lifestyle blocks, land, and space for the money. Ten to fifteen minutes in. Patutahi & Manutuke Small rural settlements twenty minutes from the city, among the vines and farmland. Cheap, quiet and rural. Up the Coast — Tolaga Bay and beyond Forty-five minutes and more north. Small, strongly Māori coastal communities with their own rural clinics. Its own decision, not a commute — and the part of the district most affected by road closures. Three things to sort before you commit Availability, not price. Housing here is affordable but stock is limited and good rentals move quickly. Ask your employer what accommodation support exists, and start looking early. Insulation, ventilation and heating. The stock is older than average and quality varies widely. Ask for the Healthy Homes compliance statement and look for a heat pump.

chunks.t: Where clinicians live in Gisborne: ten places compared
chunks.x: Flood and slip exposure. A live question after 2023, particularly on the river flats and up the coast. Ask directly about a property’s history and its insurability. Schooling choice is more limited than in a larger city, and popular schools are zoned by address — see Schools & education . How renting works — the application pack, bond, tenancy rights and the Healthy Homes standards — is national and covered once in Renting in New Zealand . Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Getting around Gisborne: two roads out and one airport
chunks.x: Inside Gisborne, getting around takes ten minutes and no thought at all. Getting out of Gisborne is the defining practical fact of living here, and it deserves a chapter rather than a footnote.

chunks.t: Getting around Gisborne: two roads out and one airport
chunks.x: Ten minutes from anywhere in the city to the hospital, on flat streets with free parking at both ends. Wainui and the beaches add another five or ten. There is no rush hour and no congestion. If you have come from a large city, this is the daily change you will feel most. It also means that where you live is a lifestyle choice here rather than a commute calculation.

chunks.t: Getting around Gisborne: two roads out and one airport
chunks.x: This is the part to understand properly. Gisborne has effectively two land routes to the rest of New Zealand, and both cross steep, erodible country. South — SH2 to Wairoa and Napier The main route, about four hours to Napier through the Wharerata hills. The road most often affected by slips in bad weather. North-west — SH2 over the Waioeka Gorge To Ōpōtiki and the Bay of Plenty, around two and a half hours to Whakatāne. A beautiful gorge road, and another that closes. The Coast road — SH35 The long way round the East Cape to Ōpōtiki. Slower, spectacular, and the route people take for its own sake rather than to get anywhere. When they close It happens. In February 2023 both main routes were cut, and the city was reachable only by air and sea. That is the extreme case, but shorter closures are routine in winter.

chunks.t: Getting around Gisborne: two roads out and one airport
chunks.x: What this means practically Check road conditions before any long drive, especially in winter and after heavy rain. It becomes second nature. If you have family elsewhere in New Zealand, plan around flights rather than drives. It is usually faster and always more reliable. Keep a reasonable supply of essentials at home. Locals do, not out of anxiety but out of experience.

chunks.t: Getting around Gisborne: two roads out and one airport
chunks.x: Gisborne Airport Five minutes from the city centre — it is inside the urban area, with a railway line crossing the runway. Daily flights to Auckland and Wellington. Why it matters The airport is what makes this region liveable rather than remote. A flight to Auckland is about an hour; driving is six or seven. Long-haul Always via Auckland or Wellington. Budget a full day at each end, and expect one more leg than from a main centre. Weather Small regional airport, occasional wind and fog delays. Build a buffer into anything that matters.

chunks.t: Getting around Gisborne: two roads out and one airport
chunks.x: There is a small urban bus network in Gisborne, plus limited coach services out of the region. It is useful for some routes and will not cover a clinical roster. Cycling, on the other hand, is good: the city is flat, small and warm, with shared paths along the rivers and out towards the beaches. A number of clinicians here cycle or walk to work simply because it is easier than driving. A car is still necessary. The coast, the hill country and the beaches all assume one, and most households run two.

chunks.t: Getting around Gisborne: two roads out and one airport
chunks.x: Journey Typical time Across the city 10 min City → airport 5 min City → Wainui Beach 10–15 min City → Makorori 20 min City → Rere Falls 50 min City → Tolaga Bay 45 min City → Māhia 1 hr 45 City → Ōpōtiki (Waioeka Gorge) 2 hr City → Whakatāne 2 hr 30 City → Napier 4 hr City → Auckland 6–7 hr, or 1 hr flying Times on open roads in good conditions. Always check SH2 and SH35 before setting out in poor weather. Converting your licence, buying a car, and what a warrant of fitness and registration involve are national matters, explained once in Driving & licences . Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Weekends in Gisborne: surf, forest and the East Cape
chunks.x: Gisborne’s compensation for being far from everything is that what it has, it has almost to itself. World-class surf ten minutes from the hospital, native forest inland, and one of the great road trips in New Zealand starting at the edge of town. Alone with it, in driving time Driving times from the city, to scale against each other. The marked row is the reason a meaningful number of clinicians move here at all: world-class surf inside twenty minutes, and uncrowded. Wainui & Makorori Consistent eastern-Pacific swell, surf schools and space in the water 10–20 min Rere Falls & the rockslide A natural waterslide into a river pool — bring something to slide on ~50 min Eastwoodhill Arboretum The national arboretum, extraordinary in autumn ~1 hour Beyond the chart sit the region’s two great expeditions: Te Urewera and Lake Waikaremoana to the west, and State Highway 35 right around the Cape — expeditions, not day trips.

chunks.t: Weekends in Gisborne: surf, forest and the East Cape
chunks.x: This is the main event. Wainui , Makorori and the beaches north of the city catch swell from the whole eastern Pacific, and they are consistent, varied and — the part people cannot quite believe — uncrowded. Ten to twenty minutes from your front door. Add Māhia to the south for longer point breaks, and the city beaches at Waikanae and Midway for a swim after work. There are surf schools, boardriders clubs and a strong local culture around it. A meaningful number of the clinicians who move here do so because of this paragraph.

chunks.t: Weekends in Gisborne: surf, forest and the East Cape
chunks.x: Rere Falls & the rockslide Fifty minutes inland — a wide waterfall and a sixty-metre natural rock slide into a pool. A regional institution, and exactly as good as it sounds. Eastwoodhill Arboretum The national arboretum, an hour from the city — one of the largest collections of northern hemisphere trees in the southern hemisphere. Extraordinary in autumn. Te Urewera West into one of the largest tracts of native forest in the North Island, with Lake Waikaremoana and its Great Walk. Deeply significant country, and remote. The Raukūmara Range North-west, wild and little-visited. Serious tramping for people who want solitude. Hackfalls & the hill country Farm parks, arboreta and river valleys through the back country. Slow driving, and worth it. Mountain biking Trails in the pine forests close to the city, plus the coastal and river paths for easier riding.

chunks.t: Weekends in Gisborne: surf, forest and the East Cape
chunks.x: Titirangi / Kaiti Hill The hill above the harbour, with the view over Poverty Bay and a significant pā site. The after-work walk. The rivers Three of them meeting in the city, with walkways, rowing and swimming holes along them. Tūranga and the museum Tairāwhiti Museum tells the region’s story — waka landings, Cook’s arrival, and the layered history since. Worth going early. First light People gather for sunrise here, particularly on New Year’s Day and at the solstice. It is the region’s signature.

chunks.t: Weekends in Gisborne: surf, forest and the East Cape
chunks.x: State Highway 35 runs from Gisborne north around the Cape to Ōpōtiki — around three hundred and thirty kilometres of coast road through Tolaga Bay, Tokomaru Bay, Ruatōria, Te Araroa and Hicks Bay. It is one of the great New Zealand drives and unlike anywhere else in the country: small, strongly Māori communities, empty beaches, wharves, marae and the East Cape lighthouse at the very edge of the map. It is also the part of the region most affected by Gabrielle, and some of it is still being rebuilt. Go slowly, check the road, buy your petrol and your lunch locally, and treat the places you pass through as communities rather than scenery.

chunks.t: Weekends in Gisborne: surf, forest and the East Cape
chunks.x: Māhia — 1 hr 45 Beaches, point breaks and the rocket launch site on the peninsula. Lake Waikaremoana — ~2 hr 30 A Great Walk around one of the country’s most beautiful lakes, in Te Urewera. Bay of Plenty — 2 hr 30 Whakatāne and the eastern bay over the Waioeka Gorge. Hawke’s Bay — 4 hr Napier, Hastings, the wineries and a change of pace. See the Hawke’s Bay guide .

chunks.t: Weekends in Gisborne: surf, forest and the East Cape
chunks.x: Tourism Tairāwhiti Gisborne The region’s official visitor site: the coast, the wineries, events and the Cape road. Council Gisborne District Council Local services, libraries, pools, parks and recovery updates. Outdoors Department of Conservation Te Urewera, Waikaremoana, the Raukūmara and the coast. Essential NZTA road conditions Live road and closure information for SH2 and SH35. You will use this. That’s the guide Nine chapters on Gisborne and Tairāwhiti. Everything national — visas, registration, tax, renting, driving, schools, te ao Māori — lives in Moving to New Zealand . This region suits a particular kind of clinician extraordinarily well. If that sounds like you, see what’s open now . Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Moving to Gisborne: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.x: Nau mai, haere mai ki Tairāwhiti. Gisborne is the most easterly city in New Zealand and the first in the world to see the sun each day. It is also the most Māori region in the country, one of the most isolated, and — for the right clinician — one of the most rewarding places to work in the whole collection.

chunks.t: Moving to Gisborne: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.h: The coast of the shining sun
chunks.x: Tairāwhiti means the coast upon which the sun shines across the water, and the region lives up to it: around 2,200 hours of sunshine a year, three rivers meeting at the city, and a long arc of surf coast running north to the East Cape and south to Māhia. Gisborne city holds about thirty-eight thousand people, with around fifty-two thousand across the wider district — an area the size of a small country, most of it steep hill country, forestry and farmland. This is where Cook first came ashore in 1769, and long before that where the waka Horouta and Tākitimu made landfall. That layered history is present here in a way it is not everywhere. The clinical picture is specific: there is a hospital in Gisborne, run by Health New Zealand | Te Whatu Ora, serving the whole district.

chunks.t: Moving to Gisborne: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.h: The coast of the shining sun
chunks.x: It is a rural hospital rather than a base hospital — the smallest catchment of any hospital-served region in this collection — and complex work travels to Hawke’s Bay, Waikato or Auckland. What that buys you is scope, autonomy and a close team. What the region asks of you is a tolerance for isolation. Napier is four hours by road, Auckland six or seven, and there is no practical alternative to flying if you need to be anywhere quickly. Gisborne is also one of the most deprived regions in New Zealand, and the health need here is substantial. Who wrote this Ethicare is a healthcare recruitment company. This guide is free to read, asks nothing of you, and does not give visa advice. Gisborne is the region we’re most careful about matching. It suits a particular kind of clinician enormously well and is a poor fit for others. Where we think it’s the wrong answer, we say so.

chunks.t: Moving to Gisborne: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.x: ~52,000 People across the Gis­borne district, in an area larger than some European countries. ~38,000 In the city itself. Everything else is small settlements, hill country and coast. ~53% Of the district’s people identify as Māori — the highest proportion of any region in New Zealand. This shapes everything about the work. 1 hospital A rural hospital in Gisborne serving the whole district, with complex work referred out of the region entirely. ~4 hrs To Napier, the nearest base hospital. Waikato is around six, Auckland six to seven. 2,200+ hrs Of sunshine a year. This is one of the sunniest and warmest corners of New Zealand. First light Gisborne is the first city in the world to see each sunrise. It is a real thing here, not a slogan — people gather for it. Affordable Among the more affordable regions in the North Island, though tighter than the raw numbers suggest because supply is limited. Feb 2023 Cyclone Gabrielle. Tairāwhiti was among the worst-affected regions in the country, and the recovery is ongoing.

chunks.t: Moving to Gisborne: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.h: Six things you only learn once you’re here
chunks.x: Te reo is everywhere With over half the population Māori, te reo and tikanga are part of ordinary working life here to a degree unmatched anywhere else in New Zealand. It is the single biggest cultural adjustment, and the most rewarding. The isolation is real This is not "a bit far from things". Four hours to the nearest base hospital, over roads that close. If that would worry you clinically or personally, weigh it now. The surf is world class Makorori, Wainui and Māhia. excellent, uncrowded, and a fifteen-minute drive. A significant number of people move here for this alone. Housing is cheap but scarce Prices are modest by national standards, but stock is limited and quality is variable. Finding a good rental takes longer than the price suggests. Gabrielle changed the region Roads, bridges, forestry slash, whole communities.

chunks.t: Moving to Gisborne: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.h: Six things you only learn once you’re here
chunks.x: Two and a half years on the recovery continues, and it is part of daily conversation and clinical work. The community closes around you A small, remote city where people know each other. Slower to break into than a transient town, and far deeper once you are in. A note on names Tairāwhiti is the region’s name in te reo Māori — increasingly used ahead of "Gisborne district", including officially. The area is the rohe of Ngāti Porou to the north, Rongowhakaata, Ngāi Tāmanuhiri and Te Aitanga-a-Māhaki around the city, and others along the coast. Here more than anywhere in this collection, effort with te reo matters. You are not expected to arrive fluent. You are expected to try, and people will notice either way. Te ao Māori at work covers pronunciation, the words you’ll hear on the ward and marae etiquette.

chunks.t: Moving to Gisborne: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.x: Nine chapters, all of them about Gisborne and Tairāwhiti specifically. Anything true of New Zealand generally — visas, registration, tax, renting law, driving licences, schools — lives once in Moving to New Zealand . If you read nothing else, read Healthcare here , because a rural hospital four hours from a base hospital is a different job, and Why Gisborne , which is candid about who this region suits. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Why Gisborne: the case for Tairāwhiti
chunks.x: Gisborne is the region in this collection with the clearest answer to "who is this for". It suits some clinicians profoundly and others not at all, and the difference is not about how good you are — it is about what you want from the job and from the place.

chunks.t: Why Gisborne: the case for Tairāwhiti
chunks.x: Clinical pay in New Zealand is set nationally. You earn the same in Gisborne as in Auckland or Christchurch. Housing here is among the more affordable in the North Island, so on paper the money goes further. But the real trade in this region is not financial. It is scope for isolation. You get a wider clinical remit, more autonomy, and work that matters more visibly than almost anywhere else in New Zealand — in exchange for being four hours from a base hospital, in a small team, in a region with real need and limited resource. For a rural generalist, a GP, an emergency or community clinician, or anyone who came into healthcare to work where the need is greatest, that is an extremely good deal. For a subspecialist who needs volume and colleagues, it is not a deal at all.

chunks.t: Why Gisborne: the case for Tairāwhiti
chunks.x: Monday to Friday Ten minutes to work from anywhere in the city. Free parking. No traffic in any meaningful sense. Before work A surf at Wainui or Makorori, fifteen minutes out, in the first daylight on earth. This is how a lot of people here start the day. After work The rivers, Kaiti Hill for the view over Poverty Bay, or the beach again. Long light evenings for most of the year. Saturday The Gisborne farmers’ market, then a chardonnay cellar door or the coast road north. Sunday Te Urewera and the redwoods inland, Rere Falls and the rockslide, or Māhia for the beach and the rocket launch site. A long weekend The full East Cape road, Hawke’s Bay for a change of pace, or a flight to Auckland or Wellington.

chunks.t: Why Gisborne: the case for Tairāwhiti
chunks.h: The six things people ask us
chunks.x: What is the hospital like to work in? Small, busy, close and broad. It is a rural hospital with an emergency department, inpatient beds, maternity, some surgical and outpatient services, imaging and a strong community and primary network around it. You will carry a wider caseload than in a larger centre, make more decisions yourself, and stabilise and transfer more. Healthcare here sets out which professions this suits. Is the isolation manageable? For most people, yes — with planning. Flights connect Gisborne to Auckland and Wellington daily, the city has everything you need day to day, and the community is warm. What is not manageable is pretending the distance isn’t there: if you need specialist care, a particular school, or frequent long-haul travel, that is a serious constraint. Will I be out of my depth? The answer is that you will practise at the top of your scope.

chunks.t: Why Gisborne: the case for Tairāwhiti
chunks.h: The six things people ask us
chunks.x: Good services here provide real senior support, orientation and phone backup, and we push hard on those questions before placing anyone. Ask them at interview. Clinicians who thrive here are the ones who wanted that breadth, not the ones who tolerated it. Is it a good place with children? For an outdoor childhood, wonderful — surf, space, safety, sunshine and a strong bicultural upbringing. The caveats are real: secondary schooling choice is limited, and some specialist paediatric and allied health services mean travelling to Hawke’s Bay or beyond. How is the region after Cyclone Gabrielle? Still recovering, more than most. Tairāwhiti was among the hardest-hit regions — roads, bridges, forestry slash and whole coastal communities. Much is repaired, some is not, and the effects on rural mental health, access and isolation are live clinical realities. It is worth arriving informed.

chunks.t: Why Gisborne: the case for Tairāwhiti
chunks.h: The six things people ask us
chunks.x: Will I fit in as an international clinician? Yes, and Gisborne has recruited internationally for years. What it asks in return is engagement — with te reo, with tikanga, with whānau-centred care. Clinicians who arrive curious do very well. Clinicians who treat it as background noise struggle, and that is fair to say plainly.

chunks.t: Why Gisborne: the case for Tairāwhiti
chunks.h: Who we’d steer to a bigger centre
chunks.x: Your specialty needs a base hospital Most hospital subspecialties do not have a role here. The nearest base hospital is four hours away, and this is the plainest fact in this guide. You need services close by For you or your family. Complex care means Hawke’s Bay, Waikato or Auckland — a flight or a long drive. You want a city Gisborne is a small, friendly, remote city. Retail, culture and dining are limited, and everything larger is a flight away. You travel internationally often Every long-haul trip needs a domestic leg first. From here that is a long travel day. You’d find the need heavy This is one of New Zealand’s most deprived regions, and the caseload reflects that. Many clinicians come specifically for it. Others find it wearing, and knowing which you are matters.

chunks.t: Why Gisborne: the case for Tairāwhiti
chunks.h: Who we’d steer to a bigger centre
chunks.x: Where we’d steer you instead Want the same sunshine and coast with a base hospital and a bigger region? Hawke’s Bay , four hours south. Want similar generalist breadth with a tertiary hospital nearby? Waikato . Want rural and coastal practice with strong Māori health work, closer to a city? Northland . In our experience Gisborne suits clinicians who want their skills stretched and their work to count double — the autonomy is real, and so is the welcome. The isolation isn’t a rumour; the people who stay longest came for the community, not despite it. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Cost of living on the Gold Coast
chunks.x: The Gold Coast’s cost of living sits between the big southern capitals and the rest of Queensland: no longer the bargain it once was, but still generally ahead of Sydney or Melbourne for the same money.

chunks.t: Cost of living on the Gold Coast
chunks.x: We used to print a weekly rent and a monthly budget table here. We have taken them out. A figure that was true when a page was written is misleading a year later, and a candidate who plans a move around a stale number is worse off than one who plans around none. What does not go stale is the shape of a month, and the judgement about which lines will surprise you. For today’s actual numbers use the calculators at the foot of the page, and use them to compare the Gold Coast against the city you are leaving. That is the only comparison that decides anything. Where a month goes The proportions, for one person on a mid-range budget. Proportions move slowly; prices move every quarter. Rent is over sixty per cent of it — the largest share of any destination in this collection.

chunks.t: Cost of living on the Gold Coast
chunks.x: Rent 62% Groceries 17% Entertainment 8% Power & water 6% Transport / fuel 6% Internet 2% The line that decides it Rent · 62% That rent share is why the Gold Coast is no longer the bargain it once was — though it still sits ahead of Sydney or Melbourne for the same money. The suburb you choose does most of the work here. On the payslip Pay and allowances vary by role, employer and agreement, so we won’t quote figures here — ask us directly and we’ll talk you through the range for your profession. Our national living-in-Australia guide covers pay packaging and the wider picture. Get today’s numbers, and compare them to home These are live and updated continuously. Put the city you are leaving in the other box. Numbeo cost-of-living calculator — the most complete comparison tool, and the one most clinicians already use. Crowd-sourced, so treat it as a ballpark.

chunks.t: Cost of living on the Gold Coast
chunks.x: Expatistan — the same idea with a cleaner side-by-side. Worth running as a sanity check when Numbeo looks off. Australian Bureau of Statistics — official and slower, and the one to trust on the direction of travel. If what you find differs from what we say here, tell us and we will correct it. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Food & the everyday on the Gold Coast
chunks.x: Food on the Gold Coast runs from beachside brunch culture to hinterland farm-gate produce, with the coast’s dining scene maturing about as fast as everything else here.

chunks.t: Food & the everyday on the Gold Coast
chunks.x: Burleigh Heads The coast’s best-known dining strip — breakfast culture, cafes and some of its most-loved restaurants. Miami Marketta A Friday and Saturday night market with street food stalls and live music, a local institution. Hinterland farm-gate Tamborine Mountain’s wineries and farm stalls make the drive up the range worth it for more than the view. Fresh seafood Local co-ops and fish markets along the coast keep the catch close to the table. Burleigh Heads or Miami Marketta Photography to come

chunks.t: Food & the everyday on the Gold Coast
chunks.x: Woolworths and Coles cover the full range across the coast; ALDI is the cheapest weekly shop; IGA and independents fill in around the edges, especially in the hinterland. The coast’s café and dining scene is a major drawcard — casual, outdoor and built around the beach, whatever the day. The Goldy The informal, affectionate nickname most Australians use for the Gold Coast. The Strip Surfers Paradise’s beachfront core, around Cavill Avenue. The M1 The Pacific Motorway to Brisbane — and the road everyone complains about on long weekends. The Hinterland The elevated rainforest country behind the coast — Tamborine, Springbrook, Lamington. Schoolies The school-leavers’ festival held on the coast every November — worth knowing about if you’re arranging accommodation that month. Sophie’s tip Book ahead for Burleigh’s better-known cafes on weekends — the coast’s food reputation is well and truly out, and the queues prove it. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: The Gold Coast at a glance
chunks.x: The Gold Coast is a single coastal strip with a rainforest spine behind it, built fast and still building. Here’s the geography, the history and the people, in brief.

chunks.t: The Gold Coast at a glance
chunks.h: A subtropical coast, most of the year
chunks.x: Four seasons exist here more as a formality than a felt experience — the real distinction is between a long, warm, sometimes-humid stretch and a shorter, mild, drier one that draws the crowds. Summer Dec – Feb 21–29° Hot, humid, storm season Autumn Mar – May 17–25° Warm, drier, easing off Winter Jun – Aug 10–21° Mild, sunny, the dry season Spring Sep – Nov 16–25° Warming, humidity building Winter is the coast’s best-kept secret: mild days, low humidity and clear skies, which is exactly why the tourist season peaks then rather than in summer. Summer brings the heat, the humidity and the storms — and, some years, an ex-tropical system to plan around.

chunks.t: The Gold Coast at a glance
chunks.x: Before European settlement Yugambeh Country The Gold Coast sits on the land of the Yugambeh-speaking peoples, including the Kombumerri clan group. 1800s Timber and sugar Early settlement centres on timber-getting and sugar cane along the coastal strip. Mid-20th century The tourism boom Post-war Australia discovers the coast; the “Gold Coast” name and the high-rise skyline both take shape. 2018 The Commonwealth Games A turning point for infrastructure and international profile, including the light rail’s expansion. Today Australia’s sixth-largest city Still one of the country’s fastest-growing, with a health and knowledge precinct to match its population.

chunks.t: The Gold Coast at a glance
chunks.x: Where Gold Coast sits, with the straight-line distance to Brisbane A young, growing population One of the country’s fastest-growing cities, skewed toward working-age arrivals and young families. A magnet for interstate movers A steady stream of Australians relocate here from Sydney and Melbourne, drawn by lifestyle and cost. Two university communities Griffith and Bond bring a student population and academic health precinct. Tourism, health and construction The coast’s three biggest employers, and the clearest sign of a city still being built. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Healthcare on the Gold Coast
chunks.x: Healthcare on the Gold Coast has grown as fast as everything else here: from a modest regional service to a full tertiary teaching campus in barely a decade, with the system still catching up to the population around it.

chunks.t: Healthcare on the Gold Coast
chunks.x: The tertiary teaching hospital A full tertiary teaching hospital at Southport, one of the largest in the country, paired with Griffith University’s health precinct. A second public campus A public-private campus serving the southern coast, easing pressure on the tertiary centre. A large private sector Several major private hospitals along the strip add real depth and choice to the system. A young, expanding system Still building its specialist bench — some highly specialised tertiary care is referred to Brisbane. A note on names We don’t name hospitals, trusts or private providers as places of work anywhere on this site — a named employer implies a relationship, and the post and the package get confirmed with you directly. Where a public body is named on this page, it is there as a reference point for how the system is organised. It is not an employer reference, and it does not imply we recruit for it.

chunks.t: Healthcare on the Gold Coast
chunks.x: Rapid growth means opportunity and responsibility earlier than in a more established system, and the Griffith University partnership brings a teaching-hospital culture from day one. A system still being built The Gold Coast went from a modest regional service to a full tertiary teaching campus in barely a decade. Everything distinctive about working here — good and less good — comes from that pace. What the growth gives you Responsibility earlier New departments need senior people. Roles open here that a settled system would fill from within, and they open sooner in a career. A teaching culture from day one The Griffith University health precinct sits alongside the hospital, so students, trainees and research are part of the ordinary week. Scale without the eastern-capital price One of the country’s largest hospitals, in a city where you can still live near the beach.

chunks.t: Healthcare on the Gold Coast
chunks.x: A department you help shape Services still forming are services you can influence — rare in a mature tertiary hospital. What it asks of you A bench still catching up The specialist bench is younger than the population it serves. Ask how many consultants sit alongside you in your specialty, not how many are in the hospital. A short referral list to Brisbane A small number of highly specialised tertiary cases go north. Check which ones touch your work before you start. Comfort with change Rosters, structures and reporting lines move faster in a growing service than a settled one. If your field is very narrow, tell us early and we will be straight with you about whether the bench here is wide enough yet. A clinical precinct Photography to come

chunks.t: Healthcare on the Gold Coast
chunks.x: What’s the growth trajectory of the specific department you’d join? Which cases get referred to Brisbane, and how is that handled day to day? What teaching and research involvement comes with the Griffith University partnership? What CPD time and funding is provided? How established is the specialist bench in your specialty specifically? The takeaway The Gold Coast offers real, fast-moving opportunity in a system still building itself out — and it asks you to be comfortable with that pace of change. Ask specifically what’s still maturing in your specialty, and you’ll walk in with likely expectations. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Where clinicians live on the Gold Coast
chunks.x: Where you live on the Gold Coast shapes your day more than almost anywhere else in this collection — the coast runs from high-rise beachfront to canal estates to hinterland acreage, often within a few kilometres of each other. Waterfront canal homes — a Gold Coast signature.

chunks.t: Where clinicians live on the Gold Coast
chunks.h: The Gold Coast at a glance, by area
chunks.x: Area Best for Worth knowing Surfers Paradise & Broadbeach High-rise, the coast’s commercial heart Singles & couples, walk to everything Vibrant but touristy, especially in peak season Burleigh, Miami & Mermaid Beach Trendy, beachy, cafe culture Professionals & young families Popular and priced accordingly Canal estates Sorrento, Mermaid Waters, Broadbeach Waters Families who want water frontage A premium for the waterfront, but part of daily life Robina & Varsity Lakes Planned suburbs near Bond University & the southern hospital campus Families, good schools Purpose-built, less beach-adjacent Southern beach towns Currumbin, Palm Beach, Coolangatta A slower pace, close to the airport & NSW border Further from the tertiary campus; a longer commute north Hinterland acreage Tamborine, Springbrook, Currumbin Valley Space and a cooler climate Longer commute, a car is essential

chunks.t: Where clinicians live on the Gold Coast
chunks.x: Fix your work site first — the tertiary campus (Southport) and the southern campus sit at opposite ends of the strip. Check school catchments if you have children; growth-corridor suburbs sometimes have schools still catching up to demand. Shortlist two or three suburbs and rent short-term in one before committing long-term. Decide how much you value beach access versus space — the trade-off is real and worth testing before you buy. A fast-growing market The Gold Coast’s housing market has grown quickly; prices and rents are no longer the bargain they once were relative to Brisbane. On the open market, expect to apply with ID, references and proof of income, then pay a bond, typically four weeks’ rent. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Getting around the Gold Coast
chunks.x: The Gold Coast is easier to get around than its sprawl suggests, as long as you understand which parts of it the light rail reaches.

chunks.t: Getting around the Gold Coast
chunks.x: Driving Essential for the hinterland and the western growth corridor. The M1 to Brisbane is famously congested on weekends and public holidays. G:link light rail Runs the length of the coastal strip and has extended further south over time — useful if you live and work near it. Heavy rail Connects the coast to Brisbane in around an hour, making the capital commutable for some. Gold Coast Airport At Coolangatta, with domestic and trans-Tasman flights; Brisbane Airport covers the wider international network. The G:link light rail along the coastal strip. How far everything is from the strip Typical off-peak times from the central coast, to scale against each other. The light rail covers the first row; everything below it needs a car or a train — and the marked row is the one that decides whether Brisbane counts as reachable.

chunks.t: Getting around the Gold Coast
chunks.x: Along the strip End to end on the G:link, which is why the strip is the one part of the coast you can live in car-free ~20 min Gold Coast Airport Closer than most capitals manage — a real advantage for trips home ~30 min The hinterland Springbrook, Tamborine and the rainforest — a car, not a tram ~45 min Brisbane Rail, not the M1 — the reliable version of this journey ~1 hour Brisbane Airport The long-haul option, and the reason the drive north is worth timing ~1 hr 30 Indicative off-peak times. The M1 north is famously congested on weekends and public holidays — the rail line is the reliable version of that journey. Sophie’s tip If you can live and work near a light rail stop, do — it changes daily life here. If your role is in the hinterland or the western suburbs, budget for a car as a certainty, not an option, and avoid the M1 on long weekends if you can. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Hinterland, waterfalls & the weekend
chunks.x: The Gold Coast’s best-kept secret isn’t the beach — it’s what sits twenty minutes inland. Rainforest, waterfalls and cool mountain air, all within a weeknight’s reach.

chunks.t: Hinterland, waterfalls & the weekend
chunks.x: Up the range, in driving time To scale against each other. The marked rows are the point of this chapter: two national parks and a mountain village, all close enough to reach after a day shift. Natural Bridge A rock arch and glow-worm cave, especially memorable on an evening walk ~40 min Tamborine Mountain Villages, wineries and lookouts up the range — an easy after-work escape ~45 min Springbrook National Park Ancient rainforest and waterfalls, including Purling Brook Falls ~45 min Lamington & O’Reilly’s Rainforest walks and wildlife — a comfortable half-day or full-day trip ~1 hr 30 Indicative driving times. Hinterland roads wind more than GPS estimates suggest, so allow extra — and some falls run better after rain than in a dry spell. Wildlife in the Gold Coast hinterland is never far from the coast. A note on logistics Hinterland roads wind more than GPS estimates suggest — allow extra time. Some waterfalls run better after rain and can slow to a trickle in a dry spell, so it’s worth checking conditions before a special trip.

chunks.t: Hinterland, waterfalls & the weekend
chunks.x: Burleigh Head National Park’s headland walk is an easy after-work option with a beach at either end of it. Currumbin Wildlife Sanctuary puts native wildlife inside the suburbs, and the Southport Broadwater is where a lot of the coast goes to fish, paddle or simply watch the sunset without leaving town.
