chunks.t: Moving to Hobart: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.x: Hobart is Australia’s most deliberate capital. Nobody drifts to the bottom of an island 240 kilometres off the mainland coast — you choose it, for a mountain that stands over the wards, a harbour that still works for a living, and a health system small enough to know your name.

chunks.t: Moving to Hobart: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.h: A city between the mountain and the harbour
chunks.x: Around 250,000 people live in Greater Hobart, folded between the Derwent estuary and kunanyi / Mount Wellington, whose 1,271-metre summit stands snow-dusted above the office blocks fifteen minutes from town. Founded in 1804, it is Australia’s second-oldest capital after Sydney, and it still runs at that scale — a working harbour city with a fishing fleet, a Saturday market three centuries in the making, and a museum that reshaped how the mainland sees it. Tasmania runs a single statewide health service, and Hobart carries its depth: the principal referral hospital, the widest range of specialist services on the island — including cardiothoracic surgery, neurosurgery and burns — and the university medical school. It is a system you can know personally within a year, which cuts both ways, and this guide says so.

chunks.t: Moving to Hobart: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.h: A city between the mountain and the harbour
chunks.x: The costs are a tight rental market, older housing that wasn’t always built for a cold winter, and the fact that everything — goods, holidays, family visits — crosses Bass Strait. What you get back is proximity: the mountain, the wilderness and the coast are minutes from the wards, not hours. Who wrote this Ethicare is a healthcare recruitment company. This guide is free to read, asks nothing of you, and does not give visa advice. Hobart is the move people romanticise most and research least. This guide takes the winter, the market size and the island logistics as seriously as the scenery — because the clinicians who thrive here knew exactly what they were choosing.

chunks.t: Moving to Hobart: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.x: ~250,000 People in Greater Hobart — the widest job market on the island, and the state’s referral centre. 1804 Founded the same year as the colony itself — Australia’s second-oldest capital city, after Sydney. 1,271 m kunanyi / Mount Wellington, rising straight out of the city — snow on top, wards at its feet, fifteen minutes apart. 1 Statewide health service — Hobart carries the principal referral hospital and the widest range of roles. ~40% Of Tasmania is national park and reserve, including a World Heritage wilderness within a few hours’ drive. 1972 The year Salamanca Market began. It still fills the sandstone waterfront every Saturday. 2011 MONA opened and, more or less single-handedly, changed how the rest of the country sees Hobart. UTC+10 Same clock as Melbourne and Sydney, daylight saving included — island life, mainland time. 100% Of Tasmania, Hobart included, is classed as regional for skilled migration.

chunks.t: Moving to Hobart: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.h: Six things you only learn once you’re here
chunks.x: The cold lives indoors Winter is cold, and older weatherboard homes are draughty. Ask how a house is heated before you sign anything, and budget for warm bedding in month one. The UV doesn’t match the air Cool air, fierce sun. The UV here burns fast even when you need a jumper — sun protection is a year-round habit, not a summer one. You’ll want a car Buses cover the main corridors; everything else wants a car. The ferry from Geelong is the easy way to bring one over. It’s a two-degrees city Everyone knows everyone, faster than you expect. You’ll have a community in a month — and a reputation just as quickly. Winter is embraced, not endured Hobart leans into the dark: Dark Mofo fills June with fire, art and feasting, and the log-fire pub is a genre of its own.

chunks.t: Moving to Hobart: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.h: Six things you only learn once you’re here
chunks.x: The wilderness is close and serious Namadgi-scale wilderness sits an hour or two out, and mobile coverage drops fast beyond the towns. Tell someone your plans on a longer walk. A note on Country Hobart stands on the Country of the muwinina people — nipaluna — and today’s Tasmanian Aboriginal community, the palawa/pakana, carries one of the oldest living cultures on earth. Dual names are official and warmly used: nipaluna (Hobart), kunanyi (Mount Wellington), kanamaluka (the Tamar). Acknowledgement of Country opens meetings, and health services work in partnership with Aboriginal community-controlled organisations. Learn the names early — using them well is noticed and appreciated.

chunks.t: Moving to Hobart: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.x: Nine chapters, all about Hobart specifically. Topics true across the island — Launceston, the north-west coast, the wine and wilderness regions beyond a weekend’s reach — sit in the Tasmania guide . Anything true of Australia generally — Medicare, visas, Ahpra registration, tax, superannuation, schools — lives once in Moving to Australia . If you read nothing else, read Why Hobart for the full case — and what we’d ask you to weigh, and Where clinicians live , because Hobart’s villages are an enjoyable decision rather than a stressful one. chunks.t: Why Hobart: the case for the island capital
chunks.x: Hobart’s photographs undersell the practical case: a walkable harbour city, serious medicine, and wilderness twenty minutes from the ward. Here is what the city gives a working clinician, what a week here plausibly looks like — and when the mainland is the better call.

chunks.t: Why Hobart: the case for the island capital
chunks.x: Start with the working life. Tasmania’s single statewide service means Hobart careers run broad rather than narrow: you see more, carry more, and are known by name in a way the big-city systems can’t manage. Smaller systems tend to look after the people they recruit — relocation help, warm welcomes, rosters negotiated with a human — because every arrival matters. Pay follows Tasmanian enterprise agreements in the national range; we quote no figures here and will always walk you through the current agreement instead. Then the life around the work. Housing costs less than the mainland capitals, even with a tight rental market. Commutes are short everywhere. And the city’s real currency is proximity: the mountain fifteen minutes from the wards, the wilderness an hour or two out, the harbour at the end of the street.

chunks.t: Why Hobart: the case for the island capital
chunks.x: The whole of Tasmania, Hobart included, is classed as regional for skilled migration, which can open extra visa pathways and points. 15 min Hobart’s wards to the mountain road 1 Statewide health service, not several competing networks 100% Of Tasmania counts as regional for migration

chunks.t: Why Hobart: the case for the island capital
chunks.x: A week here can plausibly hold all of this. A shift that starts without traffic, because nowhere in Hobart is far from anywhere else. An after-work walk on kunanyi’s foothill tracks, or a swim at Kingston Beach in the long summer light. Salamanca Market on Saturday morning — produce, makers and half the people you know — then a drive up the Coal River for a cellar-door lunch. Sunday on the Tasman Peninsula under sea cliffs, home by dark. In winter the same week bends rather than breaks: snow on the mountain over breakfast, a log fire in a pub that has kept one burning for a century, and June given over to Dark Mofo’s fires and feasts. People here don’t wait out the seasons. They use them. Sophie’s insight What I love about Hobart is how deliberately people make time for life — a walk up kunanyi, a market on Saturday, a weekend in the wilderness.

chunks.t: Why Hobart: the case for the island capital
chunks.x: And in a smaller, close-knit system, you’re valued and looked after in a way the big cities can’t match. My advice: choose the city on purpose. The clinicians who come for the life it offers — seasons included — are among the happiest placements I have anywhere. Sophie Careem Founder & CEO, Ethicare Resourcing

chunks.t: Why Hobart: the case for the island capital
chunks.h: When the mainland is the better call
chunks.x: The market is the country’s smallest One principal referral centre. A narrow sub-specialty, a very specific career ladder or a two-clinician household may simply need a bigger system. Winter is cold, and so are the houses Cold, dark-by-five winters in a housing stock that can be draughty. If low light flattens you, take that seriously — June here is embraced, but it is still June. Everything crosses the Strait Goods, holidays and family visits all mean a flight or a ferry. If your people are in Sydney or overseas, every reunion is a fare — budget it, emotionally too. It’s quiet Hobart is a small city with a superb food scene, not a metropolis. If big-city churn recharges you, Melbourne is the answer — and it’s 75 minutes away. Rentals are tight A small market with strong demand: good homes go fast. Arrive with your paperwork ready.

chunks.t: Why Hobart: the case for the island capital
chunks.h: When the mainland is the better call
chunks.x: Where we’d steer you instead If you need scale — sub-specialty depth, two careers, big-system progression — Sydney or Melbourne carry more sites. If the dream is warmth rather than wilderness, Brisbane is the answer — Hobart’s winter is the opposite promise. If you want lifestyle-for-money in a bigger market, Adelaide is the closest mainland cousin. In our experience Hobart suits clinicians who’ve realised the thing they want most is scale — a city you can hold in your head, wilderness twenty minutes out, seasons that mean something. The bench is smaller than the mainland’s; the life around it is the argument. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: The cost of living in Mandurah
chunks.x: Mandurah generally costs less to live in than Perth’s coastal suburbs — that is much of the point — with a couple of things that quietly cost more. We do not print dollar figures we have not verified; the tools below build a budget.

chunks.t: The cost of living in Mandurah
chunks.h: What costs less, the same, and more
chunks.x: Housing is the headline: for the same money you are generally closer to the water here than in equivalent Perth suburbs, and the newer estates offer more house again. Groceries, services and the everyday sit broadly where they do across the Perth region. Two things run the other way — keeping a house cool through a long hot summer, and the cost of distance: fuel and time if you commute to Perth, and pricier flights home from a regional base. Housing Generally less than coastal Perth Everyday Broadly similar to Perth Cooling & distance The two that cost more

chunks.t: The cost of living in Mandurah
chunks.x: Set-up costs, rent in advance and bond, the flights and the first months all add up, and they are the same wherever in Australia you land. Build the number with the moving-cost calculator , and read how tax, superannuation and the Medicare levy work in the national money, tax & banking guide before you commit to anything. In one line Cheaper than coastal Perth, especially on housing — just budget for summer cooling and the cost of the distance. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Food, the water and the everyday in Mandurah
chunks.x: In Mandurah the estuary sets the table. The water is not just scenery here — it is where a lot of the food, and the weekends, come from.

chunks.t: Food, the water and the everyday in Mandurah
chunks.x: The Peel estuary is famous for its blue swimmer crabs, and crabbing — by scoop or drop net, to the local size and bag rules — is a local institution. The city throws a festival for it each year. Fresh seafood, the marina’s fish and chips, and waterfront cafes and restaurants along the rebuilt foreshore round it out.

chunks.t: Food, the water and the everyday in Mandurah
chunks.x: Beyond the water, an ordinary week looks like markets and coffee on the foreshore, kids’ sport, and the beach or the estuary after work while the light lasts. It is an outdoors-first, unhurried rhythm — part of the appeal, and part of what people mean when they say it is quieter than a capital. In one line Crabs, the marina and the foreshore — the estuary is the centre of the everyday. If a water-centred, outdoors week is what you are after, this is the draw. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Mandurah at a glance
chunks.x: Mandurah makes sense once you see it is built around an estuary, not a high street. Where people live, which water they use and how long anything takes all follow from that.

chunks.t: Mandurah at a glance
chunks.x: Where Mandurah sits, with the straight-line distance to Perth and Bunbury The city wraps the mouth of the Peel-Harvey estuary, one of the largest in the country, where the Serpentine and Murray rivers meet the sea. Canals thread the newer suburbs, an artificial channel — the Dawesville Cut — flushes the estuary to the ocean, and a long dune coast runs south. The centre and its marina sit on the water; the suburbs spread north and south along both the estuary and the coast. In practice, your side of the water sets your life: canal or estuary for flat water and boats, the ocean side for surf and beaches, the rail corridor for the Perth commute. ~72 km South of Perth ~90,000 Greater Mandurah 2× Sydney Harbour — the estuary

chunks.t: Mandurah at a glance
chunks.x: This is a Mediterranean climate, close to Perth’s: long hot dry summers and mild, wet winters. The estuary and the reliable afternoon sea breeze — the local “Fremantle Doctor” — are what take the edge off January. Summer — Dec to Feb Hot and dry, often well into the 30s, cooled most afternoons by the sea breeze. Autumn — Mar to May The best of it: warm water, settled days and the crowds gone. Winter — Jun to Aug Mild and wet, with storms off the Indian Ocean. Cool, not cold. Spring — Sep to Nov Wildflowers inland and the first swimmable days by the end of it.

chunks.t: Mandurah at a glance
chunks.x: Long before Bindjareb Noongar country The estuary is Bindjareb country, part of the wider Noongar nation of the south-west, lived on and fished for tens of thousands of years. Pinjarra, inland, carries a difficult and important history the region does not hide. 19th century An estuary settlement European settlement followed the fishing and the sheltered water. For a long time Mandurah stayed small — a crabbing and holiday place more than a city. 1990s The Cut, and the canals The Dawesville Cut opened to flush the estuary, and canal estates reshaped the waterfront. Mandurah began to grow in earnest. 2007 onward The railway, and a real city The Perth-to-Mandurah line put the CBD under an hour away, the population climbed, and the holiday town became somewhere to live. Orientation, in one line A city on one of the country’s biggest estuaries, an hour south of Perth, warm and coastal and still growing. Decide which water you want to live near, and the rest of the map follows. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Healthcare in Mandurah
chunks.x: Mandurah gives you a regional healthcare base with Perth’s tertiary system close enough to lean on. What that means for your week depends a lot on your profession and where the work sits.

chunks.t: Healthcare in Mandurah
chunks.x: The Peel region is served by a health campus combining public and private services, alongside community and primary care and a steady private imaging presence across the city. It handles the general and outpatient load of a growing population. What it does not do is the most complex, high-acuity and subspecialty work — that concentrates in Perth’s tertiary hospitals, under an hour north, and referrals move up the line for it. For medical imaging — the area we currently recruit into in Western Australia — that usually means a broad general caseload locally, with the subspecialty and interventional work weighted towards the city.

chunks.t: Healthcare in Mandurah
chunks.h: What to ask before you sign
chunks.x: The title tells you less than the setting. Before you commit, get clear on the modality mix and equipment, the on-call and rostering, the supervision and development available, and how much of the interesting work stays local versus travelling to Perth. A role that looks the same on paper can be a very different week here than in a capital. Registration, in short You will need Ahpra registration through your profession’s National Board before you can practise. Medical radiation professionals also need a Western Australian radiation use licence — a state requirement on top of registration. Both are set out in full, with official sources, in the national eligibility & registration guide, and the pathway checker shows the likely route for your profession. In one line A solid regional and community base with the tertiary system an hour away. Ask what stays local and what travels to Perth — that answer shapes the job more than the location does. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Where clinicians live in Mandurah
chunks.x: The first decision in Mandurah is not which suburb — it is which water, and how far from the train. Everything else follows from that.

chunks.t: Where clinicians live in Mandurah
chunks.x: Canal and estuary. Halls Head, Erskine and Dudley Park put you on flat water, sometimes with a mooring at the door. This is the premium end, and the closest thing to the postcard, but you pay for the frontage. The newer family estates. Madora Bay, Lakelands and Dawesville are where much of the growth — and the more affordable new housing — has gone: bigger blocks, newer schools, a longer run into the centre. Central and the coast. Around the foreshore and the older beachside pockets you trade some space for walkability, the marina and the train.

chunks.t: Where clinicians live in Mandurah
chunks.x: Rank three things in your own order: which water (and how close), value for space, and closeness to the Mandurah line if Perth is part of your plan. It is hard to have all three, and ranking them is what stops you renting or buying in the wrong half of the city. On the water Halls Head, Erskine, Dudley Park — canal and estuary frontage, at a premium. Space and value Madora Bay, Lakelands, Dawesville — newer estates, more house for the money. Walk and commute Central and foreshore — near the marina, cafes and the train. One rule Pick your water and your commute first; the suburb name matters far less. In one line Canal, coast or commuter belt — Mandurah is really three choices. Rank water, value and the train and the shortlist writes itself. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Getting around Mandurah
chunks.x: Mandurah is a car city with one significant exception: the railway that reaches central Perth in under an hour. How much you use each one shapes where you should live.

chunks.t: Getting around Mandurah
chunks.x: The train runs from the city centre to the Perth CBD in around fifty minutes, with park-and-ride at the stations along the corridor. It is what makes a Perth job while living on the coast workable — and the single biggest reason to weight your suburb search towards the rail corridor if the capital is part of your plan.

chunks.t: Getting around Mandurah
chunks.x: Off the rail line, Mandurah runs on cars. The Kwinana Freeway and Forrest Highway carry you north to Perth and south into the South West, and getting around town is a fifteen-to-twenty-minute affair rather than a commute. The rebuilt foreshore and marina are walkable; most of the rest of the city is not, which is worth planning for if you would rather not run two cars. Mandurah → Perth CBD About 50 minutes by train, or a similar drive outside peak. Across town Typically 15–20 minutes by car; traffic is not a daily event. South West Bunbury about an hour further south on the highway. The car question One car works on the rail corridor; two is the norm in the outer estates. In one line A car city with a fast train to the capital. If you will use Perth often, live near the line; if not, the coast opens up. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Dwellingup, Yalgorup and the weekend from Mandurah
chunks.x: From Mandurah the weekend goes three ways: jarrah forest inland, a national park and beaches to the south, and Perth and Fremantle an easy hour north.

chunks.t: Dwellingup, Yalgorup and the weekend from Mandurah
chunks.x: Dwellingup, about forty minutes into the hills, is the gateway to the northern jarrah forest and a hub for the Munda Biddi cycle trail and the Bibbulmun walking track, with mountain biking, whitewater on the Murray and cool green forest that feels a world away from the coast. It is the classic Mandurah escape when summer gets serious.

chunks.t: Dwellingup, Yalgorup and the weekend from Mandurah
chunks.x: South, Yalgorup National Park holds quiet beaches and the thrombolites at Lake Clifton — living rock structures among the oldest records of life on earth. North, Perth and Fremantle are close enough for a spontaneous day: markets, the port city’s cafes and bars, galleries and the things a capital does that a coastal city does not. In one line Forest one way, a national park the other, the capital an hour north. Mandurah’s weekends are wider than the city itself. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Welcome to Mandurah
chunks.x: Mandurah is a city built around water — an estuary twice the size of Sydney Harbour, a network of canals, and a long ocean coast — sitting under an hour south of Perth. For years it was where Perth went to holiday or retire. That is changing fast, and the reasons matter before you decide.

chunks.t: Welcome to Mandurah
chunks.x: ~90,000 people in Greater Mandurah, and among the fastest growth of any Western Australian city. ~50 min to central Perth on the Mandurah line, and a similar drive on the freeway. 2× the size of Sydney Harbour — the Peel-Harvey estuary the city sits on. ~72 km south of the Perth CBD, at the northern end of the South West. Two coasts the sheltered estuary on one side, the open Indian Ocean on the other. Year-round a Mediterranean climate — hot dry summers, mild wet winters.

chunks.t: Welcome to Mandurah
chunks.x: Before you decide The “retirement town” label is out of date — the growth now is young families and commuters. Summer is hot and dry; the estuary and the sea breeze are what make it comfortable. Complex and subspecialty care is in Perth. Day-to-day work is here; the tertiary centre is an hour north. The train changed the city. A Perth job while living on the coast is an option, not a fantasy. Crabbing is a local institution here, not a tourist gimmick — the estuary is full of blue swimmers. Which water you live near — canal, estuary or ocean — shapes your budget and commute more than the suburb name. In one line A fast-growing waterside city under an hour from Perth, cheaper than the capital and built for an outdoor life — as long as you are clear-eyed that the big-hospital work is up the road, not on the doorstep. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Why Mandurah
chunks.x: Mandurah earns a look for a specific kind of move: coast and space at a lower cost than Perth, with the capital still close enough to use. It is not for everyone, and the trade-offs matter as much as the appeal.

chunks.t: Why Mandurah
chunks.x: The draw is a waterside life — estuary, canals and ocean — at a price Perth’s coastal suburbs no longer offer. The city is growing, so housing and services are being built rather than stretched, and the family estates north and south are among the more affordable new housing within reach of a capital. For work, the Peel region carries a real community and outpatient caseload, and private imaging has a steady presence. And because the train reaches central Perth in under an hour, a role in the city while living on the coast is a legitimate plan rather than a stretch.

chunks.t: Why Mandurah
chunks.x: The trade is clinical breadth. The complex, high-acuity and subspecialty work concentrates in Perth’s tertiary hospitals, so if that is the centre of your career, Mandurah is a base near it rather than a substitute for it. You also take on a hot, dry summer, a car-dependent everyday outside the rail corridor, and a city still growing into itself — some services and culture are thinner than a capital’s. Mandurah suits you if… You want the coast and the estuary without a Perth coastal-suburb price. Your work is community, outpatient or imaging-based — or you are happy to commute to Perth for it. You are moving with family and want space, newer housing and the outdoors close by. You value a slower, water-centred life over the density and options of a capital. The version Mandurah trades clinical breadth for space, coast and cost. If Perth is close enough to use when you need it, that can be a very good trade. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Cost of living in Melbourne: what a clinical salary buys
chunks.x: Melbourne sits second on every Australian cost table: clearly below Sydney, clearly above Brisbane, Adelaide and Perth. The version is that you are paying for system depth and city life, and the two lines newcomers underestimate are heating and the second car.

chunks.t: Cost of living in Melbourne: what a clinical salary buys
chunks.x: We used to print a weekly rent and a monthly budget table here. We have taken them out. A figure that was true when a page was written is misleading a year later, and a candidate who plans a move around a stale number is worse off than one who plans around none. What does not go stale is the shape of a month, and the judgement about which lines will surprise you. For today’s actual numbers use the calculators at the foot of the page, and use them to compare Melbourne against the city you are leaving. That is the only comparison that decides anything.

chunks.t: Cost of living in Melbourne: what a clinical salary buys
chunks.x: 2nd Dearest capital — below Sydney, above the rest Tram Living on a line can remove a whole car from the budget Winter A heating bill that Brisbane and Perth never see The structural point: an inner-ring family house here is a serious financial commitment, while an inner-ring flat on a tram line is very achievable on a clinical salary. Which of those you need changes the whole calculation.

chunks.t: Cost of living in Melbourne: what a clinical salary buys
chunks.x: Where a month goes The proportions, for one person on a mid-range budget. Proportions move slowly; prices move every quarter. Rent takes just under sixty per cent — clearly below Sydney, clearly above Brisbane, Adelaide and Perth. Rent 57% Groceries 17% Entertainment 9% Power, gas & water 8% Transport (Myki or fuel) 7% Internet 3% The line that decides it Rent · 57% Two of these lines are the ones newcomers underestimate: heating, because older terraces and weatherboards are poorly insulated, and the second car. Inside the tram rings you may run none; in the outer corridors most households run two.

chunks.t: Cost of living in Melbourne: what a clinical salary buys
chunks.x: Heating, and gas Melbourne homes use gas heating widely, and older terraces and weatherboards are poorly insulated. A cold July in a draughty house is the bill that surprises people from warmer countries most. The second car Inside the tram rings you may run none. In the outer corridors most households run two, with tolls on the cross-city routes on top. This is the single biggest swing in a Melbourne budget. The city itself Melbourne is very good at separating you from money: restaurants, festivals, the football, the theatre. Budget for using the city, because using it is the reason you came.

chunks.t: Cost of living in Melbourne: what a clinical salary buys
chunks.x: Public transport is the big one — a car-free life is possible here in a way it is not in Brisbane, Perth or Adelaide, and that is thousands a year. Then the free city: the gardens, the galleries with free entry, the laneways, the beach on the bay, and a festival calendar that runs most of the year. Groceries at the markets beat the supermarkets, and Victoria grows most of what it eats an hour or two away. On the income side, public-health and not-for-profit roles here can salary-package part of your pay before tax — ask payroll on day one. How packaging, tax and superannuation work is national and lives in Pay & conditions . The bottom line Plan the bridge as well as the destination: temporary accommodation, a bond of about four weeks’ rent plus rent in advance, winter bedding and heating, and either a car or a Myki.

chunks.t: Cost of living in Melbourne: what a clinical salary buys
chunks.x: Then decide whether you need the inner-ring house or the inner-ring flat — in Melbourne that one choice moves the budget more than anything else. Get today’s numbers, and compare them to home These are live and updated continuously. Put the city you are leaving in the other box. Numbeo cost-of-living calculator — the most complete comparison tool, and the one most clinicians already use. Crowd-sourced, so treat it as a ballpark. Expatistan — the same idea with a cleaner side-by-side. Worth running as a sanity check when Numbeo looks off. Australian Bureau of Statistics — official and slower, and the one to trust on the direction of travel. If what you find differs from what we say here, tell us and we will correct it. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Food, coffee & the everyday in Melbourne
chunks.x: Melbourne’s food culture is not a marketing line, it is the product of a century of migration — Italian, Greek, Vietnamese, Lebanese, Ethiopian, Chinese — layered onto a city dense enough to support small, specific places. It is the best-fed city in Australia, and the coffee is the entry point.

chunks.t: Food, coffee & the everyday in Melbourne
chunks.x: The standard here is high and unpretentious: espresso brought by Italian and Greek migrants in the 1950s, refined by a generation of local roasters, and now so normal that a mediocre cup is a scandal. Order a flat white, a long black or a magic (a short double ristretto with steamed milk — a local invention) and expect it to be good almost anywhere with a queue. The corollary: chains barely register. Your loyalty will be to a specific place within four hundred metres of your front door, and you will defend it. The markets Queen Victoria Market in the city, Prahran and South Melbourne for the serious cooks, Footscray and Dandenong for the best value and the widest range in the state. The laneways The rule is simple: no signage, no bookings, up a staircase or down an alley. Ask a colleague; nobody publishes the good ones.

chunks.t: Food, coffee & the everyday in Melbourne
chunks.x: The neighbourhood streets Lygon Street for Italian, Sydney Road for Lebanese and Turkish, Victoria Street for Vietnamese, Box Hill and Glen Waverley for Chinese, Footscray for East African. The parma rule Chicken parmigiana is the pub standard, and calling it a "parmi" marks you instantly as being from anywhere else. It is a parma here.

chunks.t: Food, coffee & the everyday in Melbourne
chunks.x: This is the easiest Australian city in which to find whatever you grew up eating. About four in ten residents were born overseas, and the food infrastructure follows: halal butchers across the north and west, kosher grocers and bakeries in Caulfield and Balaclava, South Asian shops in the eastern and south-eastern suburbs, African grocers in Footscray and Dandenong, and Asian supermarkets essentially everywhere. Very little needs ordering online. For newcomers the practical upside is community, not just ingredients: the shops are usually attached to the associations, places of worship and weekend gatherings that make a city feel liveable within a month rather than a year.

chunks.t: Food, coffee & the everyday in Melbourne
chunks.x: Melbourne lives outdoors when it can and indoors well when it cannot — which is the whole trick of the place. Summer means rooftop bars, the beach at the bay and the tennis in January. Winter means the football, long lunches, wine bars, and galleries with free entry. Spring is the racing carnival and the comedy festival; autumn is the food-and-wine festival and the best weather of the year. There is always something on, and most of it is walkable from a tram stop. The everyday, in one list Find your local coffee place in week one. It matters more than the supermarket. Serious shop: Queen Victoria, Prahran or South Melbourne markets. Best value: Footscray or Dandenong. Learn one neighbourhood food street properly — Lygon, Sydney Road, Victoria Street, Box Hill. Say parma. Book nothing on a laneway. Accept that you will discuss coffee. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Melbourne at a glance: the grid, the rings and four seasons in a day
chunks.x: Before the practical chapters, orientation. Melbourne is unusually legible for a city of five million: a grid at the centre, rings of suburbs around it, and a tram network that makes the whole inner city navigable within a week of arriving.

chunks.t: Melbourne at a glance: the grid, the rings and four seasons in a day
chunks.h: How the city is laid out
chunks.x: Where Melbourne sits, with the straight-line distance to Geelong and Ballarat

chunks.t: Melbourne at a glance: the grid, the rings and four seasons in a day
chunks.x: The centre is the Hoddle Grid, laid out in 1837 and still doing its job: numbered blocks, main streets with laneways behind them, and the Yarra along the southern edge. Southbank and Docklands extend it across and down the river; the gardens ring it on three sides. Most of the tertiary hospital work sits either inside this ring or immediately north and east of it.

chunks.t: Melbourne at a glance: the grid, the rings and four seasons in a day
chunks.x: North: Carlton, Fitzroy, Brunswick and Northcote — terraces, students, live music and the best of the food. East: Richmond, Hawthorn and Kew, leafier and dearer as you go. South: South Melbourne, Albert Park, St Kilda and Prahran, with the bay at the bottom. West: Footscray, Yarraville and Williamstown, the fastest-changing part of the city and still the best value inside ten kilometres.

chunks.t: Melbourne at a glance: the grid, the rings and four seasons in a day
chunks.x: Beyond about fifteen kilometres, Melbourne becomes a different proposition: large growth corridors north, west and south-east, newer housing, bigger blocks, longer commutes and their own regional hospitals. The bay curls south to the Mornington Peninsula; the Dandenong Ranges rise to the east; and Geelong sits an hour south-west as a city in its own right.

chunks.t: Melbourne at a glance: the grid, the rings and four seasons in a day
chunks.x: The cliché is accurate, and it comes from geography: cold fronts arrive off the Southern Ocean and cross the city in an hour. Summer brings serious heat — a run of 40-degree days most years, with total fire ban days across the state — and winter is cool, grey and damp rather than freezing, with dark mornings. Spring and autumn are the best of it, and unpredictable. Summer Dec – Feb 14–26° Heatwaves · fire danger Autumn Mar – May 11–20° The city’s best season Winter Jun – Aug 7–14° Grey, damp, dark early Spring Sep – Nov 10–20° Unpredictable · racing season Two practical notes. Heating matters here in a way it does not further north — ask what a rental has, because older terraces and weatherboards can be cold and expensive to run. And take fire-danger days seriously if you live on the city’s fringe or plan weekends in the ranges: the warnings are precise and worth obeying.

chunks.t: Melbourne at a glance: the grid, the rings and four seasons in a day
chunks.x: Melbourne Airport is about half an hour north-west of the city, with direct flights across Asia, the Middle East and the Pacific and constant shuttles to Sydney — one of the busiest air routes in the world. There is no train to the terminals yet, so budget for a bus or a taxi. Overland, Geelong is an hour, the Great Ocean Road starts ninety minutes away, Sydney is a full day’s drive or a 90-minute flight, and the overnight ferry to Tasmania sails from Geelong.

chunks.t: Melbourne at a glance: the grid, the rings and four seasons in a day
chunks.h: Words you’ll hear in week one
chunks.x: Naarm The Woi Wurrung name for Melbourne, used widely including by health services Myki The tap-on card for trams, trains and buses across the city Hook turn Turning right from the left lane, to keep the trams moving. Alarming once, then normal The G The MCG — the cricket ground that is also the winter football cathedral Parma Chicken parmigiana, the pub standard. Do not call it a parmi here The Peninsula Mornington — beaches, wineries and hot springs, an hour south Total fire ban A statewide summer declaration. It means exactly what it says Footy Australian rules, not rugby. Choosing a team is a social act Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Healthcare in Melbourne: the deepest system in Australia
chunks.x: Registration is national; hiring here is service by service. Melbourne’s distinction is depth — the widest range of tertiary, quaternary and specialist services in the country, with an internationally significant research precinct beside them. This chapter explains the shape of it without naming employers.

chunks.t: Healthcare in Melbourne: the deepest system in Australia
chunks.x: Victoria runs its public system through a large number of separately governed health services, each employing in its own right. In Melbourne that means several major metropolitan services, each with a tertiary campus and a group of community and specialist sites around it, plus standalone specialist services covering areas such as paediatrics, women’s health, cancer, eye and ear, and mental health. There is also a substantial private hospital sector and a large private imaging and pathology market. The practical consequence: “a job in Melbourne” is a job in one service, in one part of a city fifty kilometres across, and moving between services later is a fresh application. Get the service and the campus straight before you start looking at suburbs. Quaternary depth The widest range of highly specialised services in Australia — including work that takes referrals from other states.

chunks.t: Healthcare in Melbourne: the deepest system in Australia
chunks.x: Standalone specialist services Paediatrics, women’s health, cancer, eye and ear and mental health run as their own services here, which creates career paths that do not exist in smaller systems. A research precinct Medical research institutes clustered around the inner-city hospital campuses, with established clinician-researcher pathways and joint university appointments. One national register Ahpra registration works everywhere in Australia. The process, English evidence and assessment live once in Eligibility & registration . The services that only exist at this scale In most systems these sit as departments inside a general hospital. In Melbourne five of them run as health services in their own right — own governance, own recruitment, own career ladder — and that is the concrete version of “depth”.

chunks.t: Healthcare in Melbourne: the deepest system in Australia
chunks.x: Paediatrics A standalone specialist service taking referrals well beyond the city, so a whole career can be built in children’s work without moving between employers to get the case mix. Women’s health Obstetrics, gynaecology and neonatal care run as their own service rather than a wing of a general hospital — which changes what a senior post in the field looks like. Cancer A dedicated service with the research institutes beside it. If you want treatment, trials and teaching in the same week, this is the structure that allows it. Eye and ear Narrow, high-volume specialist work concentrated in one place — the kind of bench that a general hospital in a smaller system simply cannot carry. Mental health Runs as its own service, which means clinical leadership and specialist pathways that sit outside the general acute hierarchy. Each of these employs in its own right, alongside the major metropolitan services — so “a job in Melbourne” is a job in one of them, and a later move is a fresh application. Registration itself is national: Eligibility & registration .

chunks.t: Healthcare in Melbourne: the deepest system in Australia
chunks.h: What that means for a career
chunks.x: If your field is narrow, or you want research and teaching braided into clinical work, Melbourne gives you more options than anywhere else in the country. Higher training posts, fellowships and joint appointments are more plentiful here simply because there are more services competing for and creating them. The flip side is scale. More layers of governance, more competition for the sought-after posts, and a longer path to the specific role you want — where a smaller system might hand you breadth and responsibility immediately. That is a trade, not a criticism; decide which you want. Why Melbourne weighs it properly. Two structural notes. Regional Victoria — Geelong, Ballarat, Bendigo, the Latrobe Valley — runs substantial services with their own recruitment and, in many cases, regional migration advantages the capital does not have; the Victoria guide covers those.

chunks.t: Healthcare in Melbourne: the deepest system in Australia
chunks.h: What that means for a career
chunks.x: And metropolitan Melbourne is not classed as regional for skilled migration, which changes the visa arithmetic — see Visas & the move . “ If the career needs room, Melbourne has the most of it. Everything else here is the price of that. The one-line version

chunks.t: Healthcare in Melbourne: the deepest system in Australia
chunks.x: Pay follows Victorian awards and enterprise agreements — we deliberately quote no figures in this guide, and will walk you through the current agreement for your profession instead. What you can pin down at interview: Salary packaging — public-health roles can package part of your pay pre-tax; ask how much and how to start it on day one Which service, and which campus — the same title means different work across this city The roster reality — shift patterns, penalties, on-call frequency and how gaps get covered Research and teaching time — whether it is protected, funded, and how joint appointments work CPD — funded time and money, and what conference travel is covered Supervision and support in your first year, especially if you trained overseas Parking and the commute at your shift times — inner-city campus parking is scarce and expensive Professional indemnity — what the employer cove

chunks.t: Healthcare in Melbourne: the deepest system in Australia
chunks.x: rs and what stays yours Two things to do early Start registration as soon as Melbourne is on your shortlist — paperwork, not ambition, is what moves start dates. And fix your campus before you fix your suburb: in a city this size with this many services, the commute you sign up for is the one you will live with for years. Prefer it on paper? chunks.t: Where clinicians live in Melbourne: the inner rings explained
chunks.x: In Melbourne the tram line decides the life. Get within walking distance of one that runs to your campus and the city becomes small and easy; get it wrong and you join a freeway every morning. Here is the map as we’d draw it over coffee. On the map The inner north Carlton Fitzroy Collingwood Brunswick Northcote Coburg Preston The inner east Richmond Hawthorn Camberwell Kew Box Hill Doncaster The south & the bay South Melbourne Albert Park Middle Park Port Melbourne St Kilda Elwood Brighton Hampton The west Footscray Seddon Yarraville Williamstown The outer corridors Craigieburn Werribee Melton Dandenong Pakenham Parks & nature Beaches Landmarks Shaded areas are the suburbs named in this chapter. Arrows point to places beyond the map edge, with the straight-line distance from the city centre. Suburb boundaries © Geoscape Australia, CC BY 4.0 · Natural Earth

chunks.t: Where clinicians live in Melbourne: the inner rings explained
chunks.x: Carlton, Fitzroy, Collingwood, Brunswick and Northcote: bluestone lanes, Victorian terraces, live music, and the densest concentration of good food in the country. Close to the inner-city and northern hospital campuses, well served by trams, and the natural first landing for clinicians without children. Prices climb steeply as you approach the parks; Coburg and Preston further out are the value versions of the same idea.

chunks.t: Where clinicians live in Melbourne: the inner rings explained
chunks.x: Richmond, Hawthorn, Camberwell and Kew — leafier, quieter, more expensive, and the traditional family answer. Excellent state and independent schools, big trees, and a straightforward run into the eastern hospital campuses. Beyond them Box Hill and Doncaster are more affordable and increasingly well connected, with a large and long-established Chinese-Australian community and the food that comes with it.

chunks.t: Where clinicians live in Melbourne: the inner rings explained
chunks.x: South Melbourne, Albert Park, Middle Park and Port Melbourne put you between the city and the water, with trams both ways and the bay at the end of the street. St Kilda and Elwood are livelier and better value; Brighton and Hampton further south are family territory with the bathing boxes and the good schools. The bay is calm rather than surf — pleasant for a morning swim, not a substitute for a coast.

chunks.t: Where clinicians live in Melbourne: the inner rings explained
chunks.x: Footscray, Seddon, Yarraville and Williamstown are the best value inside ten kilometres of the city, and the west has spent a decade shedding its old reputation: Vietnamese and East African food, a village feel in the smaller pockets, and Williamstown’s waterfront looking straight back at the skyline. The trade is fewer trams and more reliance on the train line, plus industrial neighbours in places. If your campus is in the west or the inner north, this is where your money goes furthest.

chunks.t: Where clinicians live in Melbourne: the inner rings explained
chunks.x: Beyond fifteen kilometres, Melbourne turns into large growth areas — north around Craigieburn, west around Werribee and Melton, south-east through Dandenong and Pakenham. New houses, big blocks, young families, their own regional hospitals, and prices that make family life possible on one clinical salary. The cost is the commute, which can be long, and a thinner public transport offer. Say the hard thing: if you take an inner-city campus and an outer-corridor house, you will spend ten hours a week travelling.

chunks.t: Where clinicians live in Melbourne: the inner rings explained
chunks.x: Tram The single most important housing variable here 4 wks Typical bond, lodged with the state authority Ask What the heating is — old terraces run cold If you want… Consider Because Food, music and no car Carlton, Fitzroy, Brunswick Trams everywhere, walk to everything Family space and schools Hawthorn, Camberwell, Kew Leafy, established, eastern campuses close The bay at the end of the street Albert Park, Elwood, Brighton Trams and water, family-shaped Best value inside 10 km Footscray, Yarraville, Williamstown The west, on the train line, changing fast Value with a tram Coburg, Preston, Northcote Inner-north life a few stops further out A house on one salary The growth corridors New, big, affordable — and a long commute Renting itself — applications, bonds, rights, the documents that win a competitive inspection — works the same across Australia and lives once in Living in Australia .

chunks.t: Where clinicians live in Melbourne: the inner rings explained
chunks.x: Two Melbourne-specific habits: ask what the heating is and what it costs to run, and check the tram or train route to your actual campus at your actual shift times before you sign. Before you sign a lease Which tram or train line, and does it reach your campus without a change? What heating does it have — and is there any insulation? Old terraces can be brutal in July. Is it in the state-school zone you need? Zones matter here and are checked by address. What is the commute at 6.30am and 10pm, not at 9am? Would a short-term rental first be wiser? Most people re-choose once they know the rings. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Getting around Melbourne: trams, trains and the hook turn
chunks.x: Melbourne is the one Australian city where living without a car is easy — if you live in the right ring. The tram network is the largest on earth, the trains radiate properly, and the whole thing runs on one card. Outside the tram zone, the arithmetic changes.

chunks.t: Getting around Melbourne: trams, trains and the hook turn
chunks.x: Myki One tap-on card across trams, trains and buses, with a daily fare cap. The Free Tram Zone covers the city centre entirely — no touch on, no charge. Trams 250 km of track, 24 routes, the largest network in the world. Frequent, slow-ish, and the reason inner Melbourne works without a car. Trains Radial lines from the city loop out to the suburbs and on to the regional centres. Fast where trams are slow, and the backbone of outer-suburban commuting. Bikes Flat, gridded and well served by separated lanes along the Yarra and the inner north — one of the better Australian cities for a bike commute. Car-free life is practical anywhere inside about ten kilometres, especially north, east and south. In the growth corridors it is not: those are car suburbs with a train line, and most households run two.

chunks.t: Getting around Melbourne: trams, trains and the hook turn
chunks.x: Australians drive on the left, and Melbourne adds one local specialty: the hook turn. To keep the tram tracks clear, you turn right from the left-hand lane, waiting in front of the intersection until the lights change. It is alarming exactly once. The other rule that matters: never pass a stationary tram on the near side when its doors are open. The city has toll roads on its main cross-city routes, so a toll account is worth setting up early. Licence transfer and buying a car work the same across the country and live in Living in Australia . Inner-city hospital parking is scarce and expensive — ask about staff parking at interview rather than assuming.

chunks.t: Getting around Melbourne: trams, trains and the hook turn
chunks.x: From the CBD to… Roughly How The inner north (Fitzroy, Brunswick) 10–20 min Tram The inner east (Richmond, Hawthorn) 15–25 min Tram or train The bay (Albert Park, St Kilda) 15–25 min Tram The west (Footscray, Williamstown) 10–25 min Train Melbourne Airport ~30 min Bus or road — no train yet Growth corridors 45–75 min Train or freeway Geelong / Mornington Peninsula ~1 hr Train or drive Sydney ~90 min Fly — one of the world’s busiest routes The takeaway Choose your home by the line that reaches your campus, not by the suburb’s reputation. Inside the tram rings you may never need a car; outside them you will need two. That decision is worth more to your quality of life here than almost anything else in this guide. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Weekends in Melbourne: the bay, the ranges and the Great Ocean Road
chunks.x: Melbourne’s weekends work outward in rings, and the ring you pick sets the day: the bay for a morning, the ranges or the valley for a Sunday, and the Great Ocean Road for the weekend everyone does at least twice a year.

chunks.t: Weekends in Melbourne: the bay, the ranges and the Great Ocean Road
chunks.x: Port Phillip is calm, shallow water rather than surf — good for a morning swim, a paddle or a walk, and lined with piers from Williamstown round to Brighton’s bathing boxes. An hour south, the Mornington Peninsula turns it into a full weekend: cellar doors, hot springs, calm bay beaches on one side and proper Southern Ocean surf on the other at Portsea and Sorrento. The ferry across the heads to Queenscliff makes a neat loop of it.

chunks.t: Weekends in Melbourne: the bay, the ranges and the Great Ocean Road
chunks.x: East of the city the Dandenong Ranges rise into mountain ash and tree ferns forty minutes from the CBD — cool, wet, quiet, with a steam railway and a lot of tea rooms. North-east, the Yarra Valley is the wine country: an hour out, world-class cool-climate pinot and chardonnay, and long lunches with a view back toward the ranges. Further out again, the High Country delivers real alpine weekends with snow in winter.

chunks.t: Weekends in Melbourne: the bay, the ranges and the Great Ocean Road
chunks.x: It starts ninety minutes from the city and runs for two hundred kilometres along the Southern Ocean: surf breaks at Torquay and Bells Beach, the rainforest and waterfalls behind Lorne and Apollo Bay, koalas at Kennett River, and then the limestone stacks of the Twelve Apostles standing offshore. It is one of the world’s great coastal drives, and it is a weekend rather than a holiday from here. The rings, in driving time Melbourne’s weekends work outward in rings, and the ring you pick sets the day. The marked row is the far end of the Great Ocean Road — the drive everyone here does at least twice a year.

chunks.t: Weekends in Melbourne: the bay, the ranges and the Great Ocean Road
chunks.x: The bay Calm, shallow water rather than surf — piers from Williamstown round to Brighton 15–20 min The Dandenong Ranges Mountain ash and tree ferns; cool, wet and quiet ~40 min The Yarra Valley Cool-climate pinot and chardonnay, and a view back toward the ranges ~1 hour The Mornington Peninsula Hot springs and bay beaches on one side, Southern Ocean surf on the other ~1 hour The Great Ocean Road begins Torquay and Bells Beach — then two hundred kilometres of coast ~1 hr 30 The Twelve Apostles The far end of one of the world’s great coastal drives — a weekend from here, not a holiday ~3 hours Indicative driving times, direct. The Great Ocean Road itself is the point rather than the distance — most people stay overnight at Apollo Bay rather than turning round.

chunks.t: Weekends in Melbourne: the bay, the ranges and the Great Ocean Road
chunks.x: Summer The Australian Open in January, cricket at the G, rooftop bars and the beach. The city empties briefly and then fills again. Winter Football from March to September, and the whole city arranges its Saturdays around it. Plus galleries, wine bars and long lunches. Spring & autumn The racing carnival, the comedy festival, the food and wine festival, the Grand Prix — and the best weather of the year for all of them.

chunks.t: Weekends in Melbourne: the bay, the ranges and the Great Ocean Road
chunks.x: The Great Ocean Road to Apollo Bay, staying overnight rather than rushing The Twelve Apostles at dusk, when the tour buses have gone A Yarra Valley cellar-door lunch and the drive back over the ranges The Dandenongs: Sherbrooke Forest, the steam railway and tree ferns The Mornington Peninsula — hot springs, then surf at Sorrento back beach Wilsons Promontory for a proper walk and empty white beaches Phillip Island: the penguin parade and a surf beach without the crowds A day on the bay — Williamstown, the ferry, Brighton’s bathing boxes The High Country in winter for snow, or in summer for the rivers A Saturday at the football, whichever team a colleague talks you into That’s the guide Nine chapters on Melbourne. Statewide and regional topics live in the Victoria guide , and everything national in Moving to Australia . When you’re ready to talk about roles here, send us your CV . Prefer it on paper? chunks.t: Moving to Melbourne: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.x: Melbourne is the choice for clinicians who want the system, not the beach. Australia’s deepest concentration of tertiary and quaternary medicine, the country’s largest medical research precinct, and a city built on trams, laneways and an argument about coffee. It asks you to accept the weather.

chunks.t: Moving to Melbourne: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.h: A city that rewards people who like cities
chunks.x: Birrarung Marr, a five-minute walk from the CBD Around five million people live here, spread across a grid that Hoddle laid out in 1837 and a tram network that never got torn up — the largest in the world. The centre is dense and walkable, wrapped in gardens, and ringed by inner suburbs of Victorian terraces: Carlton, Fitzroy, Brunswick, Richmond, South Melbourne. Beyond them the city runs out to Port Phillip Bay in one direction and the Dandenong Ranges in the other. For clinicians the draw is depth. Melbourne carries more tertiary and quaternary services than any other Australian city, an internationally significant biomedical research precinct clustered around them, and specialist centres that take referrals from across the country. If your sub-specialty is narrow, or you want research alongside clinical work, this is the strongest market in Australia.

chunks.t: Moving to Melbourne: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.h: A city that rewards people who like cities
chunks.x: The costs are the weather and the price. Four seasons in a day is not a joke: a July morning can be cold and a February afternoon dangerous. And Melbourne is expensive — less brutal than Sydney, well above Brisbane or Adelaide — so the housing arithmetic needs doing carefully before you commit. Who wrote this Ethicare is a healthcare recruitment company. This guide is free to read, asks nothing of you, and does not give visa advice. Melbourne is where we send clinicians who want the deepest system and the richest city life, and it is the city where the housing sums matter most. Where we think somewhere else fits you better, we say so.

chunks.t: Moving to Melbourne: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.x: ~5M People in Greater Melbourne — neck and neck with Sydney for the title of Australia’s largest city. 250 km Of tram track, the largest network on earth — and free travel inside the City Circle zone. Deepest Concentration of tertiary, quaternary and specialist services in the country, with the research precinct beside them. 4 Seasons in a day, reliably. The cliché exists because the weather turns in an hour. 1837 The Hoddle Grid — which is why the centre is legible, walkable and full of laneways behind the main streets. ~100 km Of bay shoreline on Port Phillip, from Williamstown round to the Mornington Peninsula. 1 hr To the Yarra Valley’s vineyards, the Dandenongs, or the start of the Great Ocean Road. UTC+10 With daylight saving — long summer evenings, and dark winter mornings. ~40% Of residents were born overseas. Few cities absorb newcomers as easily, or feed them as well.

chunks.t: Moving to Melbourne: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.h: Six things you only learn once you’re here
chunks.x: The weather is the price Cold, grey stretches in winter and 40-degree days in summer, sometimes the same week. Everyone owns layers and nobody trusts a forecast. Trams organise everything Where you live, how you commute, what you pay in rent. Living on a tram line is the single best housing decision here. Coffee is taken seriously Not a joke and not a pose — the baseline is higher than almost anywhere in the world, and the local roaster matters more than the chain. The laneways are the point The best bars and restaurants are down alleys with no signage. Nobody will tell you where; you find them by walking. Sport is the civic religion The football fills the city from March to September, and the Cup, the Open and the Grand Prix each stop it for a week. You will pick a team. It is a suburbs city Five million people over a huge footprint.

chunks.t: Moving to Melbourne: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.h: Six things you only learn once you’re here
chunks.x: The inner ring is superb and the outer growth corridors are a different life — know which one you are choosing. A note on Country Melbourne stands on the lands of the Wurundjeri Woi Wurrung and Boon Wurrung peoples of the Kulin Nation, and Naarm is the name you will see used widely alongside Melbourne, including by health services. Acknowledgement of Country opens meetings, and Victoria’s treaty and truth-telling processes are further advanced than any other state’s — so this is live, current context, not history. Take the cultural induction seriously.

chunks.t: Moving to Melbourne: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.x: Nine chapters, all about Melbourne specifically. Topics that are true across the state — regional Victoria, the state health structure — sit in the Victoria guide . Anything true of Australia generally — Medicare, visas, Ahpra registration, tax, superannuation, schools — lives once in Moving to Australia . If you read nothing else, read Why Melbourne for the full case — and what we’d ask you to weigh, and Where clinicians live , because in a city this size the tram line decides the life. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Why Melbourne: the case for system depth
chunks.x: Melbourne wins on one argument more decisively than any other Australian city: the depth of the system. This chapter sets that against what it costs you — in rent, in weather, and in commute — and names the five reasons people choose somewhere else.

chunks.t: Why Melbourne: the case for system depth
chunks.x: If your career needs a big system, Melbourne is the answer. More tertiary and quaternary services than anywhere else in the country, specialist centres that take national referrals, and a biomedical research precinct of international standing sitting next to the hospitals that feed it. For sub-specialty work, higher training, research time or an academic thread alongside clinical practice, no other Australian city offers as many doors. Around that sits a city that is good at being a city: trams that go everywhere, a food culture built by successive waves of migration, the best sporting calendar in the country, and gardens wrapped around a legible grid. Pay follows Victorian awards and enterprise agreements — we quote no figures here and will walk you through the current agreement for your profession instead. Deepest Tertiary and research system in Australia 250 km Of tram network — the world’s largest ~40% Of residents born overseas

chunks.t: Why Melbourne: the case for system depth
chunks.x: A tram to work from an inner-north terrace, twenty minutes and no parking problem. A registrar teaching session in the afternoon and a research meeting you could join. Coffee that is quietly excellent from a place with eight seats. Friday night down a laneway with no sign on the door. Saturday at the market, then the football with ninety thousand other people. Sunday in the Dandenongs under tree ferns, or on the bay at Williamstown, or up in the Yarra Valley among the vines. That is the trade in one paragraph: you give up the beach at the end of the street and reliable sunshine, and you get a city with great depth in every direction — clinical, cultural and culinary. Sophie’s insight Melbourne is where I send people whose careers need room — the sub-specialists, the ones who want research alongside the clinical work, the ones who will be bored in a smaller system.

chunks.t: Why Melbourne: the case for system depth
chunks.x: It delivers that better than anywhere in Australia. Weigh two things first: the winter, and the rent. The clinicians who struggle here are the ones who came for the lifestyle photographs rather than the system. Sophie Careem Founder & CEO, Ethicare Resourcing

chunks.t: Why Melbourne: the case for system depth
chunks.h: When we’d point you north instead
chunks.x: The winter is real Grey, wet stretches from May to August, dark mornings, and a wind off the Southern Ocean. If sunshine is what you are moving for, this is the wrong city. It is expensive Cheaper than Sydney, well above Brisbane and Adelaide. A family house in a good inner suburb is a serious financial commitment here. The footprint is enormous Five million people over a huge area. Get the suburb wrong and you will spend hours a week in traffic on a freeway. The beach is a bay, not a coast Port Phillip is calm, brown-sanded and cold. Real surf means the Peninsula or the Great Ocean Road, an hour-plus each way. Big-system politics Depth comes with scale: more layers, more competition for training posts, longer waits for the role you want. Smaller systems can move faster for you.

chunks.t: Why Melbourne: the case for system depth
chunks.h: When we’d point you north instead
chunks.x: Where we’d steer you instead If winter sun and housing arithmetic matter most, read Brisbane — tertiary work with a far gentler climate and price. If you want a major-hospital career at the lowest cost of living, South Australia is the answer. If it is regional Victoria that appeals rather than the capital, the Victoria guide covers the state’s regional centres. In our experience Melbourne suits clinicians building a career with range — the system’s depth means the next sub-specialty, fellowship or research post is usually a tram ride away, not an interstate move. Buy a good coat and it’s the most complete city in the country. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Cost of living in Nelson Tasman: the numbers
chunks.x: Nelson is one of two regions in this collection where the housing market asks something real of you. It is not Queenstown — but it costs more than a city of fifty-five thousand people should, and for exactly the reason you would guess.

chunks.t: Cost of living in Nelson Tasman: the numbers
chunks.x: We used to print a weekly rent and a monthly budget table here. We have taken them out. A figure that was true when a page was written is misleading a year later, and a candidate who plans a move around a stale number is worse off than one who plans around none. What does not go stale is the relationship between places — which suburb, ring or region you choose — and the judgement about which costs catch people out. For today’s actual numbers use the calculators at the foot of the page, and use them to compare Nelson Tasman against the city you are leaving. That is the only comparison that decides anything.

chunks.t: Cost of living in Nelson Tasman: the numbers
chunks.h: Why it costs what it does
chunks.x: Thirty years of people from the rest of New Zealand deciding they would like to live in the sunniest, most beautiful small city in the country. Retirees selling in Auckland and Wellington, lifestyle buyers, and a finite amount of flat land between the hills and the sea. Local wages have not kept pace, so Nelson regularly appears among the less affordable places in New Zealand relative to income. Clinical pay is national. You arrive on the same salary you would earn in Palmerston North or Invercargill, into a materially more expensive market. There is no regional loading to close the gap. What you are buying is 2,400 hours of sunshine and three national parks, and that is a real thing to buy — but go in knowing the price. The good news is the lever: Richmond . Twenty minutes out, on the flat, newer and warmer housing, closer to the hospital than parts of Nelson itself, and meaningfully cheaper. Wakefield, Brightwater and Motueka relax the numbers further.

chunks.t: Cost of living in Nelson Tasman: the numbers
chunks.x: Britannia Heights & the Port Hills The premium end — views over the bay, and the region’s highest prices. Limited stock. The Wood & central Nelson Character villas, walkable to everything. Charming, sought-after, and often cold — check the insulation. Tahunanui & Atawhai Coastal but better value than the hills. Tahunanui in particular offers beach living at a sensible price. Stoke & Nelson South The middle ground, and among the better value inside the city. Handy for the hospital and the schools. Richmond, Hope & Brightwater Materially cheaper for the same size of house, twenty to twenty-five minutes out. This is the lever. Wakefield & Motueka Cheaper again, with more land. Real towns with their own services, thirty to forty-five minutes out. Nelson, or twenty minutes down the road The same small place to live, priced by whether it has a Nelson address.

chunks.t: Cost of living in Nelson Tasman: the numbers
chunks.x: This is the one decision in this chapter that moves real money. ~1.3× Nelson city ~20% a month less Baseline Richmond / Wakefield Monthly rent for a room or small one-bedroom, expressed against Richmond as the baseline. Over a year the gap is worth more than two months’ rent. Richmond is twenty to twenty-five minutes from Nelson Hospital and Wakefield thirty to forty-five — which is why the area you choose is the first thing we raise with clinicians moving here. Indicative prices that change over time. The two rent lines are the most useful comparison in this chapter — model both before you choose a postcode.

chunks.t: Cost of living in Nelson Tasman: the numbers
chunks.x: The extra flight leg Every long-haul trip starts with a domestic hop. Over a few trips home a year that adds up, so budget for it. Cold villas Nelson’s older housing is charming and frequently under-insulated. Paying more rent for a warm, well-insulated home is usually cheaper overall. Water restrictions Normal in dry summers on the Waimea plain. An adjustment rather than a cost, unless you had plans for a garden. The outdoor habit Bikes, kayaks, boots, a season of trips into three national parks. It is why you came, and it belongs in the budget.

chunks.t: Cost of living in Nelson Tasman: the numbers
chunks.x: Compare cities Numbeo · cost of living Nelson prices for rent, groceries, transport and dining, against your current city. Plan your budget Sorted budget planner New Zealand’s free, government-backed budgeting tool. Official data Stats NZ living costs The Household Living-Costs Price Index, updated quarterly. Property realestate.co.nz Compare Nelson, Stoke, Richmond and Motueka side by side. Do this early. Sanity check Expatistan A cleaner side-by-side of two cities. Worth running when Numbeo looks off. Official rents Tenancy Services market rent Bond-lodgement data by area — the most reliable rent figure in New Zealand. How pay, tax, IRD numbers, KiwiSaver and sending money home work is national, and covered in Money, tax & banking . The summary You’ll live well here and rent comfortably. Buying in central Nelson or the hills on one income is hard. The answer most clinicians reach is Richmond or the Waimea plain — twenty minutes out, thousands cheaper, and a warmer house. Model it properly before you fall in love with a villa. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Food, craft and everyday life in Nelson Tasman
chunks.x: Nelson has two things a city of this size has no right to: a serious craft-beer culture and an active community of working artists. Both come from the same place — decades of people choosing to live here and then having to make something.

chunks.t: Food, craft and everyday life in Nelson Tasman
chunks.x: Almost all of New Zealand’s hops are grown on the Waimea plain, and that is not an incidental fact — it is why Nelson became the centre of the country’s craft-brewing industry. There are more breweries per head here than anywhere else in New Zealand, and a local culture around them rather than a tourist one. The region also grows excellent aromatic wine — sauvignon blanc, chardonnay, pinot noir and particularly good rieslings and pinot gris — with cellar doors through the Moutere hills and out towards Māpua. Marlborough is next door if you want more.

chunks.t: Food, craft and everyday life in Nelson Tasman
chunks.x: Apples and pears from the Motueka and Moutere districts, berries, kiwifruit, hops, and olives. Roadside stalls and orchard gates through the season, sold cheaply because there is so much of it. The Nelson Market on Saturday morning is the region’s fixture and unusual in the country for being as strong on craft as on produce — pottery, jewellery, glass, wood and textiles alongside the vegetables. The Motueka and Māpua markets are smaller and worth the trip. And the sea: Tasman Bay is a working fishery, with scallops, mussels, snapper and blue cod. Golden Bay is known for its shellfish. Rules on gathering are real and enforced.

chunks.t: Food, craft and everyday life in Nelson Tasman
chunks.x: This is a real thing rather than a brochure line. Nelson has been a centre for potters, glass artists, jewellers, painters and weavers since the 1960s, drawn by cheap land and good light, and the community has compounded ever since. There are working studios throughout the region, a strong gallery scene, the Suter art gallery in the city, and the World of WearableArt originated here. Practically, for a clinician: it means a small city with a lively cultural life, evening classes and studios you can join, and a social world that is not only sport. That is rarer in New Zealand’s small cities than you might expect.

chunks.t: Food, craft and everyday life in Nelson Tasman
chunks.x: Central Nelson A good, compact scene — Hardy and Trafalgar Streets for restaurants, wine bars and cafés, plus the breweries. Better than the city’s size suggests. Māpua & Motueka The wharf at Māpua for a long lunch, Motueka for good cafés and a strong alternative streak. Both worth the drive. Groceries All the main chains across Nelson and Richmond. Prices around the national average, with local produce noticeably cheaper. Specialist ingredients The weak point. Some Asian and Indian grocers, but the range is narrow compared with a main centre. Check before you commit if a particular cuisine matters — see Finding your feet & your people .

chunks.t: Food, craft and everyday life in Nelson Tasman
chunks.x: Summer is busy Abel Tasman, Kaiteriteri and the campgrounds fill from Boxing Day to late January. Locals use the quieter beaches and enjoy February onwards. Harvest runs autumn Apples, hops and grapes, and a seasonal workforce arriving with them. The region smells of fruit. Winter is mild and quiet The coast rarely does anything harsh, the parks empty out, and the region belongs to residents again. Joining in is easy Tramping and cycling clubs, sailing, sport, studios and classes. A small city where turning up is enough. Limitations Retail is limited. Serious shopping means Christchurch, Wellington or online. Big touring acts and major exhibitions mean a flight. The region’s own festivals fill part of the gap. Specialist imported groceries are hard to find. Most people build up an order a few times a year. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Nelson Tasman at a glance: the sunniest climate in New Zealand
chunks.x: Nelson sits in a rain shadow at the head of a sheltered bay, with mountains taking the weather before it arrives. That single fact explains the sunshine, the orchards, the vineyards and why so many people want to live here.

chunks.t: Nelson Tasman at a glance: the sunniest climate in New Zealand
chunks.x: Where Nelson sits, with the straight-line distance to Blenheim and Motueka Nelson city curls around the eastern end of Tasman Bay, hemmed in by hills, with Tahunanui beach and the Boulder Bank on its seaward side. Twenty minutes south-west, Richmond sits on the flat Waimea plain — the region’s growth area and, for many, its practical centre. From Richmond the Tasman District runs west: Māpua on its inlet, Motueka among the orchards, and Kaiteriteri’s golden sand at the edge of Abel Tasman National Park . Beyond that the Tākaka Hill climbs over into Golden Bay — Mohua — a separate world with its own famously independent community. Inland and south, the land rises into Kahurangi and Nelson Lakes national parks: beech forest, alpine lakes, and the start of the Heaphy Track. South-east, the road to Blenheim and the Marlborough Sounds crosses the Whangamoa and Rai hills.

chunks.t: Nelson Tasman at a glance: the sunniest climate in New Zealand
chunks.x: Summer Dec – Feb 22–26°C Hot, dry, brilliant Autumn Mar – May 17–22°C Settled and golden Winter Jun – Aug 12–14°C Mild coast, frosty inland Spring Sep – Nov 15–20°C Blossom, then warm Indicative daytime highs on the coast. Inland on the Waimea plain and towards Nelson Lakes, winter frosts are routine and summer days are hotter.

chunks.t: Nelson Tasman at a glance: the sunniest climate in New Zealand
chunks.h: What the numbers don’t tell you
chunks.x: The sunshine is the best in New Zealand. Around 2,400 hours a year — Nelson takes the national title most years. The ranges to the west and south strip the prevailing weather of its rain before it reaches the bay, which is why this corner is so consistently bright. Dry summers mean water restrictions. The Waimea plain is intensively horticultural and the region has had real water-supply pressure in dry years. Restrictions in summer are normal, and worth knowing if you are planning a garden. Winters are mild on the coast and cold inland. Nelson itself rarely does anything severe. Twenty minutes inland on the plain, frost is a regular winter feature, and the alpine parks get proper snow. The housing stock needs checking, as everywhere. Older Nelson villas are charming and frequently under-insulated.

chunks.t: Nelson Tasman at a glance: the sunniest climate in New Zealand
chunks.h: What the numbers don’t tell you
chunks.x: Ask about insulation, ventilation and a heat pump, and check the Healthy Homes compliance statement, which is a legal requirement and covered in the national Renting in New Zealand chapter. The Tākaka Hill is a real piece of road. The only route to Golden Bay, and a steep winding climb over marble country. It closes occasionally in bad weather, which isolates the communities beyond it.

chunks.t: Nelson Tasman at a glance: the sunniest climate in New Zealand
chunks.h: Where things are, in driving time
chunks.x: Nelson → Richmond 20 minutes across the plain. The region’s most-driven route. Nelson → Māpua 30 minutes, to the inlet and the wharf. Nelson → Motueka 45 minutes west through the orchards. Nelson → Kaiteriteri / Abel Tasman About an hour to the park’s southern gateway. Nelson → Tākaka / Golden Bay 1 hr 30 over the hill. A different world when you get there. Nelson → Blenheim / Picton / Christchurch 1 hr 45, 2 hr and 5–6 hr respectively. Picton is the ferry to Wellington.

chunks.t: Nelson Tasman at a glance: the sunniest climate in New Zealand
chunks.x: Whakatū Nelson in te reo Māori. Te Tau Ihu The top of the South Island — the prow of Māui’s canoe. Mohua Golden Bay, over the Tākaka Hill. The Hill The Tākaka Hill. The only way to Golden Bay, and a conversation topic. Tahuna Tahunanui — the city’s beach and its suburb. The Māitai The river through Nelson, and its swimming holes. The Great Taste Trail The region’s cycle trail, linking cellar doors, orchards and coast. Centre of NZ The hill walk in Nelson marking the old survey datum. Everyone does it once. The short version A sheltered, sunlit bay with three national parks and the best sunshine hours in the country . Mild on the coast, frosty inland, dry in summer.
