chunks.x: Expatistan — the same idea with a cleaner side-by-side. Worth running as a sanity check when Numbeo looks off. Tenancy Services market rent — official bond-lodgement data by area, and the most reliable rent figure in New Zealand. Stats NZ — official and slower, and the one to trust on the direction of travel. If what you find differs from what we say here, tell us and we will correct it. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Food, shopping and the everyday in Northland
chunks.x: Northland’s food is better than its size suggests and worse than a city’s, and both halves matter. The produce is exceptional; the choice on a wet Tuesday night is not.

chunks.t: Food, shopping and the everyday in Northland
chunks.x: An ordinary evening out in Whāngārei. The choice is smaller than a city’s, and the tables still fill. Town Basin, Whāngārei The rebuilt marina precinct and the best of the city’s eating — restaurants and cafés along the water, the Hundertwasser Art Centre, and a Saturday growers’ market nearby. Kerikeri Punches well above its weight. A serious food town — orchards and growers on the doorstep, good restaurants, a strong Sunday market, and several established wineries within a short drive. Paihia & Russell Waterfront dining aimed partly at visitors, and good for it in summer. Russell in particular has a couple of long-standing places worth the ferry. Farmers’ markets The region’s real strength. Whāngārei on Saturday, Kerikeri on Sunday, and smaller ones through the Bay of Islands. Subtropical fruit, avocados, citrus, kumāra, fish, and prices that will surprise you.

chunks.t: Food, shopping and the everyday in Northland
chunks.x: Roadside stalls part of life here. Honesty boxes with avocados, feijoas, citrus and eggs at farm gates all over the region. Keep coins in the car. The seafood Northland is a fishing region and it shows. Fish and chips here are a different proposition, and if you know someone with a boat you will eat very well indeed.

chunks.t: Food, shopping and the everyday in Northland
chunks.x: Groceries in New Zealand are expensive by international standards, and rural Northland is no cheaper. Knowing the chains helps. Pak’nSave The cheapest of the big chains — warehouse format, bulk buying, bag your own. Whāngārei is the main one; worth the trip from surrounding towns for a big shop. Woolworths & New World Across the larger towns, with Woolworths offering the best online ordering. New World is dearer but better for fresh and specialty ranges. Four Square The small-town workhorse. In much of Northland this is the only supermarket, and you pay for the convenience. Fine for top-ups, expensive for a full shop. The strategy Most Northland households do a large fortnightly shop in Whāngārei or Kerikeri, top up locally, and buy produce and fish from markets and stalls. It works out well. Bring reusable bags. Single-use plastic bags are banned nationwide.

chunks.t: Food, shopping and the everyday in Northland
chunks.x: This is where a small region shows. Restaurant choice outside Whāngārei and Kerikeri is limited, and many places close early or don’t open Mondays and Tuesdays. Cuisines that a city takes for granted — good Vietnamese, Ethiopian, Korean — are thin on the ground or absent. Specialty grocery is the bigger gap. Northland does not have the concentrated South Asian, East Asian or African grocers that Auckland does. Most people manage with a combination of the supermarket’s international aisle, online ordering from Auckland suppliers, and a stock-up whenever they’re in the city. None of this is a reason not to come. It is a reason to arrive with a plan for the things you can’t do without. Finding what you grew up with Online is your friend. Auckland’s specialty grocers ship north, and several halal, South Asian and African suppliers deliver nationwide. Ask the community groups.

chunks.t: Food, shopping and the everyday in Northland
chunks.x: Northland’s international health workforce has been solving this for years and people share sources readily — it is the fastest route to what you need. Stock up in Auckland. Most people combine a specialist shop with an airport run or a specialist appointment. A chilly bin in the boot is standard equipment.

chunks.t: Food, shopping and the everyday in Northland
chunks.x: Whāngārei has the big-box retailers for whiteware and flat-pack. Beyond that, Trade Me and Facebook Marketplace are how Northland buys furniture, and the market is good because people move in and out of the region constantly. Check the delivery position before you order anything large to a rural address — surcharges are common and some retailers won’t come north of the city. If you remember three things Markets, roadside stalls and the sea are the region’s real food strength — the produce is exceptional. Restaurant and specialty-grocery choice is limited. Plan for the things you can’t do without. One big shop in Whāngārei or Kerikeri, top up locally, buy produce at markets. That is how everyone does it. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Northland at a glance: two coasts, one long peninsula
chunks.x: Northland is one long peninsula with two completely different coasts. Understanding that — and the single road that runs down the middle — tells you most of what you need about living here.

chunks.t: Northland at a glance: two coasts, one long peninsula
chunks.x: Where Whangārei sits, with the straight-line distance to Auckland and Kerikeri Three hundred kilometres from Auckland’s northern boundary to Cape Rēinga, and rarely more than eighty wide. State Highway 1 runs the length of it, and almost everything hangs off that spine. The east coast faces the Pacific: sheltered, island-scattered, warm and calm, with the Bay of Islands at its centre. This is the postcard Northland and where most of the population lives. The west coast faces the Tasman: wild, exposed, black-sand, with the Hokianga harbour and the great kauri forests behind it. Fewer people, harder beauty. Whāngārei sits on the east coast about two hours north of Auckland, wrapped around a harbour, and is the only place in the region with city-scale services. North of it, Kerikeri and Paihia in the Bay of Islands; further north, Kaitaia and the Far North. West and south, Dargaville and the Kaipara.

chunks.t: Northland at a glance: two coasts, one long peninsula
chunks.h: The four parts of the region
chunks.x: Whāngārei & the heads The region’s only city, around 55,000, on a harbour with a rebuilt waterfront at Town Basin. The base hospital is here. Twenty minutes east, Whāngārei Heads and a string of beaches under Mount Manaia. The Bay of Islands Kerikeri, Paihia, Russell and Waitangi, an hour north. Subtropical, historically the founding place of the nation, and the region’s tourism heart. Kerikeri is the prosperous horticultural town; Paihia and Russell are on the water. The Far North Kaitaia, Doubtless Bay, Ninety Mile Beach and Cape Rēinga. Remote, beautiful, and the most deprived part of the region. Rural health services matter enormously here. The Kauri Coast & Kaipara The west — Dargaville, the Hokianga, and Waipoua Forest with the great kauri Tāne Mahuta. Farming and forestry country, black-sand beaches, and the quietest part of Northland.

chunks.t: Northland at a glance: two coasts, one long peninsula
chunks.x: Northland has the warmest, most humid climate in New Zealand. Two seasons dominate: a long warm summer and a mild wet winter. Spring and autumn are both pleasant and short. Summer Dec – Feb 24–26° Hot, humid, and the sea at its warmest. Long evenings. The region fills with holidaymakers over the Christmas period. Autumn Mar – May 20–23° Arguably the best of the year. The sea stays swimmable into April, the crowds have gone, and the light is beautiful. Winter Jun – Aug 15–16° Mild and wet. Frost is rare near the coast. The problem is rain and humidity, not cold — damp houses, not frozen ones. Spring Sep – Nov 18–21° Warming fast, and everything grows. Windy at times. The sea is usable again by late October. Damp, and how to handle it Humidity is the housing issue here.

chunks.t: Northland at a glance: two coasts, one long peninsula
chunks.x: Mould, condensation and musty cupboards are the common complaints, and they affect health — particularly for children with asthma. What matters in a house: ventilation, extractor fans in the kitchen and bathroom, a dehumidifier, and insulation that is dry. Heating matters far less than it does in the South Island. When you view a rental, look for mould around window frames and in wardrobes, and ask what ventilation there is. Landlords must meet the Healthy Homes standards, which include ventilation — see Renting in New Zealand .

chunks.t: Northland at a glance: two coasts, one long peninsula
chunks.x: This is not decoration — it shapes how healthcare is practised here. The Bay of Islands is where Māori and Europeans first sustained contact, where the first mission stations were established, and where Te Tiriti o Waitangi was signed in 1840. Around a third of Northlanders identify as Māori, the highest of any region, and iwi and hapū are significant providers and partners in health services. You will encounter te ao Māori in clinical practice here more directly and more often than anywhere else in the country — karakia, whanaungatanga, working with whānau rather than individuals, and services delivered by Māori health providers. Clinicians who engage with that find it the most rewarding part of practising in Northland. It is worth arriving prepared to learn.

chunks.t: Northland at a glance: two coasts, one long peninsula
chunks.x: Whāngārei and Kerikeri both have small airports with connections to Auckland. Everything else goes by road: two and a quarter hours to central Auckland from Whāngārei, closer to four from Kaitaia. Auckland Airport, and therefore every international flight, is a further hour beyond the city. Practically: a trip home to Europe or Africa is a long day before you even board. Plan for it, and budget for the Auckland leg. If you remember three things Two coasts that feel like different countries — sheltered and populated in the east, wild and quiet in the west. Subtropical means damp, not cold. Ventilation matters more than heating when you choose a house. Te ao Māori is central to healthcare here in a way it isn’t elsewhere. Arrive ready to learn. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Healthcare in Northland: hospitals, rural care and generalism
chunks.x: Northland healthcare is generalist, geographically spread, and unusually close to the community it serves. For a clinician who wants breadth and autonomy, it is one of the most interesting places in the country to work. For one who wants a narrow subspecialty, it isn’t.

chunks.t: Healthcare in Northland: hospitals, rural care and generalism
chunks.x: Health New Zealand | Te Whatu Ora runs public healthcare across the country. In Northland that means one base hospital in Whāngārei, a network of smaller rural hospitals and community services down the peninsula, and a strong presence of Māori health providers delivering care in partnership. Whāngārei Hospital is the region’s acute centre — emergency, medical and surgical inpatient services, maternity, intensive care, and the outpatient base for most specialties. Complex tertiary work is referred to Auckland, two and a quarter hours south. Beyond the city, rural hospitals and community sites at Kaitaia, Bay of Islands, Dargaville and Rawene cover local acute presentations, maternity, older persons’ care and outpatient clinics. Some roles are based at one site; many rotate. Whāngārei Hospital The base hospital and the region’s acute centre.

chunks.t: Healthcare in Northland: hospitals, rural care and generalism
chunks.x: Emergency department, inpatient medicine and surgery, maternity, ICU, and the hub for regional outpatient services. Rural hospitals Kaitaia in the Far North, Bay of Islands at Kawakawa, Dargaville on the Kauri Coast, and Rawene on the Hokianga. Rural generalist practice, with retrieval and transfer as everyday considerations. Māori health providers Iwi and hapū-led services deliver a significant share of primary and community care across the region, particularly in the Far North and Hokianga. Working alongside them is a normal part of practice here. Primary & community care General practices, community nursing, mobile services and outreach clinics covering long distances. Primary care carries more here than it does in a city, because the alternative is a two-hour drive. Private provision Limited compared with the main centres.

chunks.t: Healthcare in Northland: hospitals, rural care and generalism
chunks.x: Some private surgical and diagnostic capacity in Whāngārei and Kerikeri; most private work of any complexity goes to Auckland. Retrieval to Auckland Road and air retrieval south is part of the job. Knowing when to transfer, and how long it will take in bad weather, becomes clinical judgement rather than logistics. One employer, named Health New Zealand | Te Whatu Ora is the national public health employer. Pay and conditions come from national collective agreements — your salary is the same here as in Auckland. What changes is the work: broader scope, smaller teams, more autonomy, longer distances, and a patient population with more unmet need.

chunks.t: Healthcare in Northland: hospitals, rural care and generalism
chunks.x: What a generalist region does to a career Four things come up repeatedly from clinicians we have placed in Northland. They are the same four things, read from two directions.

chunks.t: Healthcare in Northland: hospitals, rural care and generalism
chunks.x: Your scope widens Fewer subspecialists on site means you handle more yourself and refer less reflexively. Clinicians consistently describe becoming more capable generalists here, and many call it the most professionally interesting work they have done. Equity is the daily work Not a policy or a training module. If closing that gap is why you came into healthcare, the work here is substantial and it is real. Te ao Māori is embedded Karakia, whanaungatanga, working with whānau rather than the individual in front of you, and partnership with Māori providers as normal clinical practice. Your patients are your neighbours In a region of two hundred thousand you will see people you know. Most clinicians find that grounding.

chunks.t: Healthcare in Northland: hospitals, rural care and generalism
chunks.x: A narrow subspecialty won’t fit If you want to narrow and deepen rather than broaden, Auckland is the answer — two and a quarter hours south. The work is heavy as well as meaningful Later presentations and more social complexity than a city. People come here specifically for that, and it still costs something. Engagement, not tolerance Engaging properly with te ao Māori is the difference between working in Northland and belonging in it. Comfort with distance Road and air retrieval south is part of the job, and bad weather is part of the calculation. Pay comes from national collective agreements, so your salary here is the same as in Auckland. What changes is the work — broader scope, smaller teams, more autonomy, longer distances.

chunks.t: Healthcare in Northland: hospitals, rural care and generalism
chunks.h: Everyday care, for you and your family
chunks.x: The national system — how public and private fit together, what ACC covers, what you pay — is set out in Healthcare in New Zealand . What follows is Northland-specific. Enrolling with a GP Do it in your first fortnight, and expect it to be harder than in a city. Northland has real primary care workforce pressure and some practices have closed books. Ask colleagues, and be prepared to enrol slightly further from home than you’d like. Urgent care Accident and medical services in Whāngārei; elsewhere the local hospital or GP covers urgent presentations. Know your nearest option before you need it — distances make this matter more here. Emergency Dial 111. The emergency department is at Whāngārei Hospital. Healthline on 0800 611 116 gives free 24/7 nurse advice and is useful when you’re rural and unsure. Specialist care for your own family Worth planning for.

chunks.t: Healthcare in Northland: hospitals, rural care and generalism
chunks.h: Everyday care, for you and your family
chunks.x: Some specialties are not available in the region, and an appointment may mean a day trip to Auckland. Not a reason to avoid Northland, but a reason to know. If you remember three things Generalist practice with real breadth and autonomy — the best argument for working here, and the wrong fit for a narrow subspecialty. Equity and te ao Māori are the daily substance of the work, not a training module. Enrol with a GP early; primary care is under pressure and books close. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Where clinicians live in Northland: fourteen places compared
chunks.x: Northland asks you a question the cities don’t: how rural do you want to be? A Whāngārei suburb, a coastal village, a Bay of Islands town or the Far North are four different lives, and the drive between them is measured in hours.

chunks.t: Where clinicians live in Northland: fourteen places compared
chunks.x: One · City, coast or country? Whāngārei gives you the short commute, the hospital and the services. Whāngārei Heads and the east coast give you a beach at the end of the street and a twenty-five minute drive. Kerikeri and the Bay of Islands give you a prosperous small town an hour north. The Far North gives you space, deprivation and real remoteness. These are not variations on a theme. Two · Damp or dry? The Northland housing question. Older weatherboard houses near the coast can be persistently damp; newer builds and well-ventilated homes are fine. This matters more than insulation here — look for mould at window frames and in wardrobes, and ask what extraction the kitchen and bathroom have. Three · How far will you really drive? Everyone overestimates this. An hour each way to Kerikeri sounds romantic in February and wears thin by July, especially on a winding road in the rain.

chunks.t: Where clinicians live in Northland: fourteen places compared
chunks.x: If you’re rostered on call, be conservative. Rent before you buy Six months of renting tells you whether the coast is idyllic or isolating, and whether the drive is scenic or tedious. Northland’s rental market is small. Listings are fewer than you’re used to and good ones move fast — start looking earlier than feels necessary. Renting in New Zealand covers the application pack, the bond and the Healthy Homes standards — the ventilation requirement matters here.

chunks.t: Where clinicians live in Northland: fourteen places compared
chunks.h: Pick your site, then read down
chunks.x: Places reorder by commute to whichever site you select. Rents are indicative weekly figures for a three-bedroom house as at July 2026 — treat them as a shape, not a quote. Commuting to Show Commutes are typical door-to-door driving times. Northland has no real peak outside Whāngārei, but roads wind and summer holiday traffic adds significantly. Rents move; check current listings before budgeting.

chunks.t: Where clinicians live in Northland: fourteen places compared
chunks.x: Whāngārei city Where most clinicians start. Suburbs spread around a harbour, ten to twenty minutes to the hospital, with the region’s only city-scale services. Kensington, Maunu, Onerahi, Kamo and Tikipunga cover most of the range from established to affordable. The Heads & the east coast Twenty-five minutes east of the city — Parua Bay, Ocean Beach, and the villages under Mount Manaia. Beaches, boats and a strong community, at the cost of a real commute on a winding road. The Bay of Islands An hour or more north. Kerikeri is the prosperous horticultural town with good schools and a busy high street; Paihia and Russell are on the water and busy with tourism in summer. The Far North & the west Kaitaia, Dargaville, the Hokianga. Cheapest housing in the region, the most rewarding rural clinical work, and the most remote living.

chunks.t: Where clinicians live in Northland: fourteen places compared
chunks.x: Practical mainly for people based at those sites rather than commuting. If you remember three things City, coast, Bay of Islands or Far North are four different lives — decide which one you want before you look at houses. Damp, not cold, is the housing problem. Check ventilation and look for mould before you sign. Be conservative about how far you’ll drive. Winding roads in winter change the calculation. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Getting around Northland: driving, distance and State Highway 1
chunks.x: Northland has one road spine, no trains, and long distances between everything. A reliable car is not a lifestyle preference here — it is a condition of living in the region.

chunks.t: Getting around Northland: driving, distance and State Highway 1
chunks.h: State Highway 1, and everything hanging off it
chunks.x: SH1 runs the length of the peninsula from Auckland to Cape Rēinga. Almost every journey you make will use part of it. The section from Auckland to Whāngārei has been progressively improved and is the fastest stretch; north of Whāngārei it becomes a two-lane rural highway, and stays that way. The thing that surprises people: Northland roads wind. A distance that looks like forty minutes on a map is frequently an hour, because the road follows hills and harbour edges rather than cutting through them. Locals quote everything in driving time, and within a month you will too. Everything, in driving time from Whāngārei To scale against each other, because in this region the map lies. A distance that looks like forty minutes is frequently an hour — the road follows hills and harbour edges rather than cutting through them. The marked row is the one that governs every trip home.

chunks.t: Getting around Northland: driving, distance and State Highway 1
chunks.h: State Highway 1, and everything hanging off it
chunks.x: The Heads The beaches under Mount Manaia — the everyday escape ~25 min Dargaville West to the Kauri Coast and the Tasman side ~1 hour Kerikeri Through Kawakawa — the main north–south hop within the region ~1 hr 15 Auckland city On a good run. Add an hour for the airport, and longer on a Friday or a holiday weekend ~2 hr 15 Kaitaia The Far North is far ~2 hr 30 Cape Rēinga Worth every minute once. Not a casual day trip from the south of the region ~4 hours Indicative times on a good run. From Boxing Day to late January the highways north fill with holiday traffic, and a two-hour run in June can take three and a half.

chunks.t: Getting around Northland: driving, distance and State Highway 1
chunks.x: New Zealand drives on the left, and most overseas licences are valid for twelve months before conversion — the process is national and set out in Driving & licences . What is specific to Northland is the conditions. Winding, narrow, undulating Most of the region’s roads. Overtaking opportunities are limited and passing lanes are the exception. Allow more time than the map suggests and don’t plan tight connections. Unsealed roads are normal Many beaches, rural addresses and forest tracks are reached on gravel. It is not four-wheel-drive territory, but a low-slung car will suffer and you will wash it constantly. Rain and slips Northland gets heavy subtropical rain, and slips close roads. In a big weather event a route can be shut for days, with a long detour. Rural staff plan around this. Logging trucks and stock Forestry and farming are major industries.

chunks.t: Getting around Northland: driving, distance and State Highway 1
chunks.x: Expect heavy trucks on rural roads, and occasionally stock being moved. Patience is the local driving culture. Summer traffic From Boxing Day to late January the highways north fill with holiday traffic. A run that takes two hours in June can take three and a half in January. Fuel Budget for more of it than you’re used to. Distances are long, and fuel in rural Northland is generally dearer than in the cities. Do you need a car? Yes. This is one of the few chapters in these guides with an unqualified answer. There is no meaningful public transport outside Whāngārei and no rail. Everything — work, school, shopping, the beach — assumes a car. Most households run two , particularly outside the city. Second-hand cars are plentiful and cheap in New Zealand. Buy something reliable rather than something nice. Gravel, salt air and distance are hard on vehicles, and a breakdown an hour from anywhere is a serious problem.

chunks.t: Getting around Northland: driving, distance and State Highway 1
chunks.x: Whāngārei has a small local bus network covering the main suburban routes; useful if you live on one, not a substitute for a car. Intercity coaches run the SH1 corridor to Auckland and up to the Bay of Islands. Whāngārei and Kerikeri both have small airports with regular short flights to Auckland. For a day of meetings in the city, or connecting to an international departure, flying can be worth the fare over four and a half hours of round-trip driving. And a local one: on the east coast, boats are transport as well as recreation. The Paihia–Russell passenger ferry is the ordinary way between those two towns, and a car ferry crosses the Hokianga at Rawene, saving a long inland detour. If you remember three things One highway, no trains, and roads that wind — always allow more time than the map says. A reliable car is essential, and most households need two. Buy for durability, not looks. Auckland is 2 hrs 15 from Whāngārei, plus another hour to the airport. Factor that into every trip home. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Weekends in Northland: the Bay of Islands, the Kauri Coast and the water
chunks.x: This is what Northland is for. Two coasts, two hundred beaches, the oldest forest in the country, and the founding place of the nation — all within an easy drive of wherever you live.

chunks.t: Weekends in Northland: the Bay of Islands, the Kauri Coast and the water
chunks.x: 15 min · Whāngārei Falls & the kauri parks A twenty-six metre waterfall on the edge of the city, and the A.H. Reed park with a canopy walkway through mature kauri. Both are ordinary after-work destinations, not expeditions. 25 min · Whāngārei Heads The harbour road out to Parua Bay, Ocean Beach and Mount Manaia — a steep, short climb with one of the best views in the north. Surf, sheltered swimming and boat ramps all along the way. 40 min · The southern beaches Ruakaka and Waipu Cove — long, safe, patrolled surf beaches. Waipu Caves nearby have glow-worms and cost nothing to visit. 1 hr · Tutukaka & the Poor Knights The Poor Knights Islands are among the best dive sites in the world, reached from Tutukaka. Even if you don’t dive, the coast road out there is worth the drive. 1 hr 15 · The Bay of Islands Paihia, Russell, Waitangi and 144 islands.

chunks.t: Weekends in Northland: the Bay of Islands, the Kauri Coast and the water
chunks.x: Sailing, dolphins, the Treaty Grounds, and the country’s history in one bay. The region’s centrepiece. 1 hr 30 · Waipoua Forest Tāne Mahuta, the largest living kauri, and a forest that has stood since before human settlement. moving, and a short walk from the road. 2 hrs · The Hokianga The west coast harbour — giant sand dunes at Ōpōnoni, the Rawene car ferry, and a quiet, deeply Māori part of the country that feels a world away. 4 hrs · Cape Rēinga Where the Tasman meets the Pacific, and in te ao Māori where spirits depart. Ninety Mile Beach on the way. A long day, and everyone does it once. Kererū in the bush reserves — ordinary here in a way they aren’t in most of the country. Photograph by Emad Kabiri, anaesthetic technician

chunks.t: Weekends in Northland: the Bay of Islands, the Kauri Coast and the water
chunks.x: This is the thing that most distinguishes Northland from anywhere else in this guide. Boat ownership here is ordinary rather than aspirational — a modest trailer boat is within reach on a clinical salary, ramps are everywhere, and the sheltered east coast is forgiving water. Fishing is good and accessible; snapper off the Heads is a normal Saturday. Diving at the Poor Knights is world-class. Kayaking the mangrove estuaries, sailing in the Bay of Islands, and swimming from October through to May in water that stays warm long after the rest of the country has given up. If you have never been a water person, Northland is where you become one. If you already are, this is probably the best region in New Zealand for it.

chunks.t: Weekends in Northland: the Bay of Islands, the Kauri Coast and the water
chunks.x: Waitangi is forty minutes from Kerikeri, and the Treaty Grounds are the most significant historical site in the country — the meeting house, the waka, and the ground where Te Tiriti was signed in 1840. Kerikeri has the oldest surviving buildings in New Zealand, the Stone Store and Kemp House, on a river basin that has barely changed. Russell, across the water from Paihia, was the country’s first European settlement and briefly its capital. Ruapekapeka pā south of Kawakawa is one of the best-preserved battle sites of the New Zealand Wars. For clinicians working in a region where te ao Māori shapes practice daily, understanding this history is not a tourist activity. It is context for the job.

chunks.t: Weekends in Northland: the Bay of Islands, the Kauri Coast and the water
chunks.x: A summer Saturday Early to the Heads, swim, fish or surf, back for the market, and a barbecue while it’s still light. The whole day costs almost nothing. A winter Saturday Waipoua or the A.H. Reed canopy walk in the rain — the forest is better wet. Then Town Basin for lunch. A Bay of Islands day Kerikeri market, the Stone Store, the ferry to Russell, and back over the hill in the evening light. A long weekend The Hokianga and the Kauri Coast, or the whole run to Cape Rēinga and Ninety Mile Beach. Two nights is enough for either. Being sensible outdoors West coast beaches are dangerous — strong rips, steep drop-offs, and often unpatrolled. The east coast is far safer. Swim between the flags where they exist, and treat the Tasman with real respect. Clean your footwear at every kauri dieback station.

chunks.t: Weekends in Northland: the Bay of Islands, the Kauri Coast and the water
chunks.x: The disease is spread on soil, the forests are irreplaceable, and this is taken seriously here. The subtropical sun is fierce. The UV index in Northland is among the highest in the country and burns happen fast, including on overcast days. Heavy rain closes roads. Check before you set out in bad weather, particularly heading west or into the Far North. No city glow to speak of — the night sky is one of the things people who move here mention first. Photograph by Emad Kabiri, anaesthetic technician

chunks.t: Weekends in Northland: the Bay of Islands, the Kauri Coast and the water
chunks.x: The Waipu Caves glow worms, forty minutes south of Whāngārei Northland has almost no live music, theatre or nightlife by city standards, and what exists is concentrated in Whāngārei. Big concerts, exhibitions and international sport mean Auckland. Sunday in a small town is very quiet. And the region empties and fills with the seasons. January is crowded, roads are busy and everything is booked; June is beautiful, empty and a little melancholy. Some people love that rhythm and some find the winters long. If you remember three things Two coasts, warm water half the year, and the best accessible boating and fishing in the country. The forests and the history are on your doorstep, and both are worth taking seriously. Culture and nightlife mean Auckland. If that’s central to you, weigh it carefully. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Moving to Northland: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.x: Nau mai, haere mai ki Te Tai Tokerau. Northland is where New Zealand’s story starts — the first meeting place of Māori and Europeans, the site of the Treaty, and the warmest, greenest, most coastline-heavy region in the country.

chunks.t: Moving to Northland: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.x: Northland is a long peninsula, three hundred kilometres from Auckland’s northern edge to Cape Rēinga, with the Pacific on one side and the Tasman on the other. Nowhere in the region is more than about forty kilometres from the sea. The climate is subtropical. Winters are mild enough that a frost is unusual near the coast, and the growing season runs most of the year. People call it the winterless north and it is not marketing — if you have moved from a cold country, or from a cold New Zealand house, the difference is the first thing you notice. What that buys you is a life lived largely outdoors, on some of the best coastline in the country, at a fraction of Auckland’s housing cost. What it costs you is scale: this is a rural region with one small city, long driving distances, and thinner services than anywhere else in this guide. Both halves are true; weigh them now.

chunks.t: Moving to Northland: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.x: Who wrote this Ethicare is a healthcare recruitment company. This guide is free to read, asks nothing of you, and does not give visa advice. Northland is the region we most often talk people out of, because it suits a particular kind of clinician and not everyone. Where we think it’s the wrong answer, we say so.

chunks.t: Moving to Northland: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.x: ~200,000 People across the whole region — fewer than a single Auckland suburb cluster, spread over an area the size of a small country. ~55,000 In Whāngārei, the only city. Everything else is a town, a village or farmland. 2 hrs 15 Whāngārei to central Auckland on a good run. Close enough for a weekend, far enough to be a different life. Same Clinical pay as Auckland — national collective agreements — on housing that costs a fraction as much. ~35% Of Northlanders identify as Māori, the highest proportion of any region. Te ao Māori is part of daily life and clinical practice here, not an add-on. Rare Frost, near the coast. Winter days sit around fifteen or sixteen degrees and the sea stays swimmable well into autumn. 2 coasts The sheltered Pacific east with its islands and bays, and the wild Tasman west with its black sand and kauri forest. They feel like different countries.

chunks.t: Moving to Northland: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.x: ~15 min From most of Whāngārei to a swimmable beach. From Kerikeri or Paihia, less. 1 base hospital In Whāngārei, supported by rural hospitals and community services across the peninsula. Tertiary referrals go to Auckland.

chunks.t: Moving to Northland: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.h: Six things you only learn once you’re here
chunks.x: Distance is measured in hours, not kilometres Northland roads wind. A journey that looks like forty minutes on a map is often an hour. Locals quote everything in driving time and you will start to as well. Te reo is everyday More so than anywhere else in the country. Place names, greetings, karakia at the start of meetings, and te ao Māori woven into how health services are delivered. You will learn faster here than you would elsewhere. Humidity, not cold, is the winter problem Houses here fight damp rather than frost. Mould and condensation are the common complaint, so ventilation, extractor fans and a dehumidifier matter more than heating. Summer triples the population The Bay of Islands and the east coast beaches fill with holidaymakers from Boxing Day to late January. Roads, restaurants and the emergency department all feel it.

chunks.t: Moving to Northland: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.h: Six things you only learn once you’re here
chunks.x: Kauri dieback is taken seriously Cleaning stations at the entrance to every forest track, and you use them. The kauri forests are a taonga and the disease is spread on footwear. Everyone knows everyone In a region of 200,000 with one hospital, your patients are your neighbours and your colleagues are your friends. That is the best and the hardest thing about practising here. A note on te reo Te Tai Tokerau is Northland’s name in te reo Māori. Whāngārei, Kerikeri, Kaitaia, Kaikohe, Dargaville — the map here is overwhelmingly Māori, and pronouncing it properly matters more in this region than anywhere else in the country. You’re not expected to arrive fluent. You are expected to try. Te ao Māori at work covers pronunciation and the words you’ll hear on the ward.

chunks.t: Moving to Northland: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.x: Nine chapters, all of them about Northland specifically. Anything true of New Zealand generally — visas, registration, tax, renting law, driving licences, schools — lives once in Moving to New Zealand . If you read nothing else, read Why Northland for the full case including the reasons people leave, and Where clinicians live for the fourteen towns and suburbs compared. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Why Northland: the case for the winterless north
chunks.x: Northland is the region clinicians either fall for completely or rule out in a week. It rewards a particular temperament, and this chapter describes both.

chunks.t: Why Northland: the case for the winterless north
chunks.x: Clinical pay in New Zealand is set nationally. A nurse, physiotherapist or radiographer on a given step earns the same in Whāngārei as in Auckland. What changes is what the money buys and what the day feels like. Northland housing is among the cheapest in the country. A family home with a garden, within fifteen minutes of the hospital and twenty of a beach, is an ordinary purchase here on a single clinical salary. That is not true in Auckland, and it is barely true in Christchurch. The offsets are real and worth naming: you will drive more and spend more on fuel, the retail and services market is thinner so some things cost more or take longer, and a specialist appointment for your own family may mean a trip to Auckland.

chunks.t: Why Northland: the case for the winterless north
chunks.x: Monday to Friday Ten to twenty minutes to work in Whāngārei, and parking is free and easy. If you’re at a rural site, longer — but on empty roads. After work Long light evenings most of the year. A swim, a walk up Mount Manaia, or the harbour at Town Basin. The water is warm enough to use from October to May. Saturday A beach on the east coast, the farmers’ market, or the boat if you have one. Boat ownership is far more common here than anywhere else in New Zealand, and much cheaper than you’d expect. Sunday The Waipoua kauri forest, the Hokianga, or nothing at all in a garden that grows year-round. Gardening here is different — subtropical, fast, productive. A long weekend The Bay of Islands is on your doorstep, Cape Rēinga is a full day, and Auckland is close enough for a concert or an international flight. Summer The best of it. Warm sea, long evenings, and a region that empties out to the beaches. Also the busiest stretch clinically — the population swells and the department feels it.

chunks.t: Why Northland: the case for the winterless north
chunks.h: The six things people ask us
chunks.x: Will my clinical skills narrow up here? The opposite, usually. Northland is generalist practice — fewer subspecialists means you carry a broader scope and make more decisions yourself. Clinicians who want to deepen a narrow subspecialty should be in Auckland; clinicians who want to be a capable generalist often find this the best place in the country to do it. Chapter four covers what that means day to day. Is it isolated? Yes, and that is the answer. Whāngārei is a small city and the rest of the region is rural. Auckland is two and a quarter hours away, which is close enough for a weekend but not for a casual evening. If you need a dense city within reach, this will wear on you. What is the deprivation picture? Northland has some of the highest deprivation in New Zealand, and a large rural Māori population with significant unmet health need.

chunks.t: Why Northland: the case for the winterless north
chunks.h: The six things people ask us
chunks.x: Clinically that means more advanced presentations, more social complexity and more work that is about equity. Many people come here specifically for that. Others find it heavy. It is the single most important thing to weigh. Is the housing any good? Cheap and variable. Damp and mould are the region’s housing problem — not cold. Older houses without ventilation or insulation get unpleasant in a humid winter. Newer builds and well-maintained homes are fine. Chapter five covers what to check. Is it a good place with children? For young children, exceptionally — space, beaches, warmth, safety and a slower pace. For teenagers it depends on the child: schooling is good but the range of activities, sports and subjects is narrower than in a city, and some families move south when children reach secondary age. Worth thinking about in advance.

chunks.t: Why Northland: the case for the winterless north
chunks.h: The six things people ask us
chunks.x: How international is it? Less than Auckland, but more than people expect — Northland’s health workforce has drawn internationally for decades and you will not be the only overseas clinician on the ward. Diaspora communities are small, though. If having your own community around you is central, check what exists here first.

chunks.t: Why Northland: the case for the winterless north
chunks.h: Who we’d steer to a main centre
chunks.x: You want a city Whāngārei is a pleasant small city with a good harbourside, but it is not a city in the sense most people mean. Restaurants, culture, nightlife and shopping are all limited compared with Auckland. Your specialty needs volume Some subspecialties simply don’t exist here, and complex work is referred to Auckland. If you need high volumes of a narrow procedure to stay sharp, this is the wrong region. You don’t want to drive There is no meaningful public transport outside Whāngārei, and no trains. Everything here assumes a car, and often two. You need frequent international flights Everything goes through Auckland, two and a quarter hours away, then long-haul from there. Travelling home is a longer day than from anywhere else in this guide. The deprivation would weigh on you The clinical work here is often about the consequences of poverty and distance.

chunks.t: Why Northland: the case for the winterless north
chunks.h: Who we’d steer to a main centre
chunks.x: That is meaningful work, but it is heavy, and it is fair to know that before you commit. Where we’d steer you instead Want warmth and coast with more city around it? Bay of Plenty or Hawke’s Bay . Want a small city with the same value but more services? Waikato or Palmerston North . Want the widest range of roles and the biggest international community? Auckland . In our experience Northland suits clinicians who want generalist breadth and a beach they don’t share — the work is needed, which is its own kind of job satisfaction. The distances are real; the people who thrive treat the driving as part of the life, not a tax on it. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Cost of living in Palmerston North: the best value in the North Island
chunks.x: In most of this collection the cost chapter is where we manage expectations. Here it is the argument. Palmerston North has the best housing value of any North Island city with a base hospital, and on a clinical salary that changes what your life looks like.

chunks.t: Cost of living in Palmerston North: the best value in the North Island
chunks.x: We used to print a weekly rent and a monthly budget table here. We have taken them out. A figure that was true when a page was written is misleading a year later, and a candidate who plans a move around a stale number is worse off than one who plans around none. What does not go stale is the shape of a month, and the judgement about which lines will surprise you. For today’s actual numbers use the calculators at the foot of the page, and use them to compare Palmerston North against the city you are leaving. That is the only comparison that decides anything.

chunks.t: Cost of living in Palmerston North: the best value in the North Island
chunks.x: Clinical pay is national. You arrive on the same salary you would earn in Auckland, Tauranga or Wellington, into a housing market that costs a fraction of theirs. That is the entire proposition, and it is unusually clean. Concretely: a three or four-bedroom family home with a garden, in an established suburb, in a decent school zone, ten minutes from the hospital, is an ordinary purchase on one clinical income here. In Tauranga that is difficult on two. In Auckland it is out of reach for most people we place. If home ownership is part of why you are moving countries, this city does it faster than anywhere else in the North Island. Go twenty minutes further — Feilding, Ashhurst, Foxton — and the numbers relax again.

chunks.t: Cost of living in Palmerston North: the best value in the North Island
chunks.x: Hokowhitu & Aokautere The premium end of a modest market. Expect to pay the top of the local range for an established riverside or hillside home — still well below the national city average. West End, Fitzroy & Fitzherbert Mid-range, close in, walkable. Character housing, which means checking the insulation. Milson, Awapuni, Takaro, Terrace End The best value inside the city. Ordinary, comfortable family suburbs at prices that surprise people arriving from anywhere larger. Kelvin Grove & the newer edges Modern, warm, well-insulated houses — worth a premium in this climate, and often cheaper to run. Feilding & Ashhurst Cheaper again, for more house and more land, twenty minutes out. viable given the commute. Foxton & the coast The cheapest housing in reach. Small towns, dune coast, thirty minutes to work. Where a month goes The proportions, for one person on a mid-range budget.

chunks.t: Cost of living in Palmerston North: the best value in the North Island
chunks.x: Proportions move slowly; prices move every quarter. Rent takes just over half — the smallest absolute rent line of any North Island city with a base hospital. Rent 52% Groceries 19% Entertainment & leisure 9% Power & water 8% Public transport / petrol 6% Internet 3% Mobile phone plan 2% The line that decides it Rent · 52% A flat, compact city is the reason the transport line is this small — most households here run one car rather than two. National agreement pay against the lowest rent in the North Island is the rest of the argument. Indicative prices that change over time. Note the power line — it is higher here than in the warm north, and that is the one place this city costs you more.

chunks.t: Cost of living in Palmerston North: the best value in the North Island
chunks.x: Winter heating The local cost. Frosty nights and older housing stock mean higher power bills than the north. A well-insulated house with a heat pump is worth paying more rent for. A car, but maybe only one Most households here run one car rather than two, because the city is flat and short. That is a real annual saving most people don’t think to count. Getting home Long-haul goes via Auckland or Wellington, so add the domestic leg or the drive to the annual trip home. Weekends away The flip side of being central: you will travel more, because so much is within reach. Budget for petrol you’ll happily spend.

chunks.t: Cost of living in Palmerston North: the best value in the North Island
chunks.x: Compare cities Numbeo · cost of living Palmerston North prices for rent, groceries, transport and dining, against your current city. Plan your budget Sorted budget planner New Zealand’s free, government-backed budgeting tool. Official data Stats NZ living costs The Household Living-Costs Price Index, updated quarterly. Property realestate.co.nz Current Palmerston North rentals and homes for sale, suburb by suburb. Sanity check Expatistan A cleaner side-by-side of two cities. Worth running when Numbeo looks off. Official rents Tenancy Services market rent Bond-lodgement data by area — the most reliable rent figure in New Zealand. How pay, tax, IRD numbers, KiwiSaver and sending money home work is national, and covered in Money, tax & banking . The summary On a clinical salary you will live comfortably here and buy a family home sooner than almost anywhere else in the North Island . The one place it costs you more is heating a cold house in winter — so spend on insulation, not on postcode. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Food, shopping and everyday life in Palmerston North
chunks.x: The city’s food reputation lags well behind the reality, and the reason is the university. Twenty thousand students and a research community make a market for good, cheap, varied food that a city of ninety thousand would not otherwise support.

chunks.t: Food, shopping and everyday life in Palmerston North
chunks.x: George Street The city’s dining lane — a good strip of small restaurants and bars a minute from The Square, and the answer when someone asks where to go. Broadway Avenue & The Square Cafés, bakeries and bistros around the green centre. The everyday lunch and coffee territory. Student value Asian, Indian, Middle Eastern and Pacific food at prices that reflect who eats it. Some of the best-value eating in New Zealand. Coffee Take this seriously: New Zealand coffee is excellent and Palmy holds its own. Local roasters, and a flat white in a suburban café will beat the best in most British cities.

chunks.t: Food, shopping and everyday life in Palmerston North
chunks.h: Markets and what the region grows
chunks.x: The Manawatū is a farming plain, and the food culture follows from it. The Saturday farmers’ market in the city is the weekend fixture — produce, meat, bread, cheese and coffee, and half the neighbourhood. Twenty minutes north, Feilding is a proper country town with a famous Friday market and working saleyards. It is worth going once as an outing and then repeatedly for the food. Between the two you can eat almost entirely from within thirty kilometres. The coast half an hour west gives you the other half of the larder: fishing off the beach, whitebait in season on the river mouths, and a strong local culture around both. Rules on species, size and quantity are real and enforced.

chunks.t: Food, shopping and everyday life in Palmerston North
chunks.x: All the main supermarket chains, plus large-format retail on the northern edge of the city. Food in New Zealand is expensive by British or Australian standards — that is national rather than local, and it is the adjustment people mention most. For specialist ingredients, the student population is your ally: there are Asian, Indian and halal grocers here well out of proportion to the city’s size, and a reasonable range beyond that. It is not Auckland, so if a particular cuisine is central to how your family eats, check before you commit — the national chapter Finding your feet & your people covers where to look and which communities are established here. Onam at home in Palmerston North: Rezon and friends from the hospital, with their families, around a sadya on banana leaves. Read their story →

chunks.t: Food, shopping and everyday life in Palmerston North
chunks.x: Term time and summer are different cities In term the place hums — live music, sport, events, full cafés. From December to February it empties and slows right down. Locals rather like both. Shops close early Most retail winds down by 5.30 or 6pm, supermarkets run later, and Sunday is quieter than you’ll be used to. Sport is the social glue This is a rugby city with a national rugby museum to prove it, but also netball, cycling, hockey, football, running and cricket. Joining a club is the fastest way to know people. Culture is closer than you think Te Manawa — museum, art gallery and science centre in one — plus a real calendar of theatre, festivals and touring shows at the arena. For the biggest acts, Wellington. Limitations Retail is functional rather than exciting. Serious shopping means Wellington or online.

chunks.t: Food, shopping and everyday life in Palmerston North
chunks.x: The best touring music and major exhibitions stop at Wellington, an hour and fifty minutes’ drive away. Very specific imported groceries can need an order in. Most people end up with a Wellington or Auckland run a few times a year. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Palmerston North at a glance: climate, geography and seasons
chunks.x: A flat city in the middle of a river plain, with a mountain range twenty-five minutes east and a wild dune coast half an hour west. The geography is the whole explanation: for the wind, for the cycling, and for how easy everything is to reach.

chunks.t: Palmerston North at a glance: climate, geography and seasons
chunks.x: Where Palmerston North sits, with the straight-line distance to Wellington The Manawatū River comes down through the ranges and out across a wide alluvial plain to the Tasman. Palmerston North sits on that plain, just south of the river, laid out on a grid around a central square. There are almost no hills in the city; the only meaningful rise is on the southern edge towards Aokautere and Massey. East, the Tararua and Ruahine ranges wall off the Wairarapa and Hawke’s Bay, split by the Manawatū Gorge — Te Āpiti. West, the plain runs out through Feilding and Foxton to a thirty-kilometre stretch of dunes and black-sand surf beach. North lie farmland and the Rangitīkei; south, Horowhenua and the road to Wellington. Practically, this means everything is within about twenty-five minutes: the airport, the ranges, Feilding, the university, and every suburb in the city. The ranges at the edge of the plain, twenty-five minutes from town

chunks.t: Palmerston North at a glance: climate, geography and seasons
chunks.x: Summer Dec – Feb 22–25°C Warm, long, breezy Autumn Mar – May 17–21°C Still and golden Winter Jun – Aug 11–13°C Frosty, snow on the tops Spring Sep – Nov 14–19°C Windy, then lovely Indicative daytime highs. Nights are considerably cooler than the northern regions, and winter frosts are normal rather than notable.

chunks.t: Palmerston North at a glance: climate, geography and seasons
chunks.h: What the numbers don’t tell you
chunks.x: The wind is the local signature. The Manawatū sits in a gap between two mountain ranges, which funnels the prevailing westerly straight across the plain. That is why there is a large wind farm on the hills above the gorge, and it is why the region is one of the windiest in the country. In practice: most days a breeze, a few days a year strong. People arriving from Wellington think it is calm. Four real seasons, which the north does not get. Proper frosts, cold clear winter mornings, snow visible on the Tararua tops, and a distinct autumn. If you have come from northern Europe this will feel familiar and welcome. If you came for subtropical warmth, this is the wrong end of the island. Cold houses, not damp ones. The regional housing problem here is heating rather than mould — older houses on a frosty plain.

chunks.t: Palmerston North at a glance: climate, geography and seasons
chunks.h: What the numbers don’t tell you
chunks.x: Ask about insulation, double glazing and a heat pump, and check the Healthy Homes compliance statement, which is a legal requirement and covered in the national Renting in New Zealand chapter. It is drier than you would guess. Rainfall on the plain is moderate — noticeably less than Wellington, Auckland or the West Coast. The ranges take most of it.

chunks.t: Palmerston North at a glance: climate, geography and seasons
chunks.h: Where things are, in driving time
chunks.x: Across the city 10–15 minutes, corner to corner, at any hour. → Feilding 20 minutes north. An award-winning country town with a famous Friday market. → The coast 30 minutes west to Himatangi or Foxton Beach — dunes, driftwood and black sand. → Te Āpiti / the gorge 25 minutes east, for the tracks, the wind farm lookout and the ridgeline. → Wellington 1 hr 50 by road, or a commuter train on weekdays. Your nearest big city and international airport. → Whanganui / Napier / Taupō 1 hr 15, and about 2 hr 30 for each of the other two. The middle of the island has its advantages.

chunks.t: Palmerston North at a glance: climate, geography and seasons
chunks.x: Palmy The city. Used by everyone, including the council. Te Papaioea Palmerston North in te reo Māori. The Square Te Marae o Hine, the green centre of the city. All directions start here. Te Āpiti The Manawatū Gorge, and the tracks and wind farm around it. He Ara Kotahi The shared path and bridge linking the city to the river’s south bank and Massey. The Esplanade Victoria Esplanade — the riverside gardens, playground and miniature railway. Massey The university, just south of the river. Shapes the city’s character. The ranges The Tararua and Ruahine, east of the city. Snow on them means winter. The short version A flat, green, temperate city with distinct seasons, wind, and mountains and coast half an hour apart in opposite directions. The climate asks for a warm house rather than a dry one. What makes the place work is that nothing is far away — Where clinicians live is the next practical read. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Healthcare in Palmerston North: working as a clinician
chunks.x: This is the chapter that changes people’s minds about Palmerston North. The clinical offer here is materially larger than the size of the city would lead you to expect, and for some professions it is one of the more interesting places in the country to work.

chunks.t: Healthcare in Palmerston North: working as a clinician
chunks.x: Public hospital and specialist services are delivered by Health New Zealand | Te Whatu Ora. The hospital in Palmerston North is the base hospital for a large catchment — the Manawatū, Horowhenua, Tararua and out towards the Kāpiti coast — carrying acute medicine and surgery, an emergency department, maternity, paediatrics, intensive care, imaging and outpatient services. Around it sit community and district services, primary care, iwi and Māori health providers, and rural services reaching into some remote country east of the ranges. Complex and highly specialised work — neurosurgery, cardiothoracics, the most complex paediatrics — is referred south to Wellington, under two hours away.

chunks.t: Healthcare in Palmerston North: working as a clinician
chunks.x: The detail that makes this city unusual: it is one of a small number of centres in New Zealand delivering radiation oncology, serving a region far wider than the city itself. For radiation therapists, medical physicists, oncology nurses, medical imaging technologists and oncology-adjacent allied health, that means tertiary-level cancer work in a city where you can buy a house on one salary. There are very few places in the country where those two things are true at once. It also means an unusually collegial, close service. A smaller centre delivering complex work tends to produce clinicians who know each other’s names across disciplines, and a lot of people tell us that is the part they did not anticipate.

chunks.t: Healthcare in Palmerston North: working as a clinician
chunks.x: The detail that makes this city unusual 1 Of a small number of NZ radiation oncology centres Tertiary-level cancer work, serving a region far wider than the city itself, in a place where you can buy a house on one salary ten minutes from the hospital. For radiation therapists, medical physicists, oncology nurses and medical imaging technologists, there are very few places in New Zealand where both of those are true at once. It also makes for an unusually collegial service: a smaller centre delivering complex work produces clinicians who know each other’s names across disciplines — the part people tell us they did not anticipate.

chunks.t: Healthcare in Palmerston North: working as a clinician
chunks.x: Broad scope Outside the tertiary centres you carry a wider caseload and make more of the decisions yourself. Clinicians who want to be capable generalists do well here. A large rural catchment The service reaches into Tararua, Horowhenua and the Rangitīkei. Distance, access and rural health inequity are part of the daily picture. An academic edge A large university in the same city, with health sciences, nursing and research activity. Useful if teaching, research or postgraduate study matters to you. Real progression A mid-sized service delivering complex work gives you visibility. People move into senior and leadership roles here faster than they would in a large centre. An ageing catchment Expect a caseload weighted towards age-related medicine, orthopaedics, oncology and chronic disease, particularly from Horowhenua. Pressure A regional base hospital with a wide catchment is a busy hospital. Waiting lists and workforce gaps are real here as everywhere.

chunks.t: Healthcare in Palmerston North: working as a clinician
chunks.x: This is the rohe of Rangitāne o Manawatū, with Ngāti Kahungunu, Muaūpoko, Ngāti Raukawa and others across the wider catchment. Iwi-led health providers are an established part of care delivery, particularly in Tararua and Horowhenua where deprivation and distance compound. Practically: karakia at the start of meetings, te reo used on the ward, whānau in the room and involved in decisions. You are not expected to arrive fluent — you are expected to try. The national chapter Te ao Māori at work covers pronunciation, the words you will hear and marae etiquette.

chunks.t: Healthcare in Palmerston North: working as a clinician
chunks.x: What to ask at interview What is the catchment for my service, and how much rural or outreach work is involved? What is the on-call or rostered-hours pattern, and how is it paid under the relevant collective agreement? What gets referred to Wellington in my specialty, and how much of that pathway do I stay involved in? What orientation, supervision and cultural induction is there for clinicians new to New Zealand? Is there any link with the university — teaching, research or postgraduate study support? What does professional development funding look like, and is there relocation support? Sophie Sophie’s insight Palmerston North is the one I have to talk people into looking at, and the one they thank me for afterwards. Complex cancer work in a city where you can buy a house on one salary, ten minutes from the hospital — that combination barely exists anywhere else in New Zealand. Sophie Careem Founder, Ethicare Resourcing
