chunks.x: Sea breeze The variable that prices the whole coast 4 wks Maximum bond, plus rent in advance ~20 min A normal commute here, coast to campus If you want… Consider Because The beach at the end of the street Cottesloe, City Beach, Trigg The coast, the breeze, the sunset — at a price Beach life with family value Scarborough, Sorrento, Hillarys Newer housing, surf clubs, north of the river River, schools and the campuses Nedlands, Applecross, South Perth Established, leafy, minutes from tertiary work Café strips and character Mount Lawley, Leederville, Highgate The closest Perth gets to inner-city living Somewhere with its own soul Fremantle and around it Port heritage, markets, arts, southern campuses Space, trees and cooler air Kalamunda, Mundaring Semi-rural hills — and fire-season planning Maximum affordability The rail corridors, north and south Newest housing, own hospitals, train commu

chunks.t: Where clinicians live in Perth: coast, river, inner north and the hills
chunks.x: te Renting itself — applications, bonds, rights — works the same across Australia and lives once in Living in Australia . Perth-specific: rents move with the resources cycle, so ask locals what the market has done in the last year, and check how far inland you are before assuming the sea breeze reaches you. Before you sign a lease How far inland is it, and does the afternoon sea breeze reach? It is worth several degrees. What is the commute to your campus — and is there a train line, or is it car-only? Air conditioning: what kind, and how does the house handle a run of 38-degree days? If you are looking at the hills: what is the bushfire rating and the evacuation plan? Is it in the school catchment you need? Zones are checked by address. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Getting around Perth: rail spines, short commutes and a bike city
chunks.x: Perth is the easiest Australian capital to get around. The rail lines run down the middle of the freeways to the growth corridors, the roads are wide and uncongested by east-coast standards, and the city is flat and sunny enough that cycling is practical.

chunks.t: Getting around Perth: rail spines, short commutes and a bike city
chunks.x: SmartRider One tap-on card across trains, buses and ferries, with free travel inside the central city zone. Trains Fast lines running north, south and east along the freeway medians to the growth corridors, plus the Fremantle line. Excellent if you live on one. Buses and CAT A wide bus network, plus the free CAT buses that circulate through the CBD, Fremantle and Joondalup. Bikes Flat terrain, 3,000 hours of sunshine and a good network of separated paths along the river and rail lines. One of Australia’s better cycling cities. Car-free life works near a train line or in the inner suburbs. Elsewhere Perth is a car city — but an easy one, with short commutes and parking that costs a fraction of Sydney’s.

chunks.t: Getting around Perth: rail spines, short commutes and a bike city
chunks.x: Australians drive on the left. Perth is the least stressful capital to drive in: wide roads, light congestion, free-flowing freeways outside peak, and only one tolled crossing to worry about — there are effectively no toll roads in the state. Licence transfer and buying a car work the same across the country and live in Living in Australia . Two local notes. Distances between towns outside the metropolitan area are enormous, so country driving means fuel planning, wildlife at dawn and dusk, and telling someone your route. And the summer sun is brutal on a parked car — a windscreen shade is not optional here.

chunks.t: Getting around Perth: rail spines, short commutes and a bike city
chunks.x: From the CBD to… Roughly How The western beaches (Cottesloe, City Beach) 15–20 min Drive or train + bus Scarborough / Trigg ~20 min Drive Fremantle ~25 min Train Perth Airport ~20 min Train or drive The Perth Hills 30–40 min Drive Swan Valley ~25 min Drive Rottnest Island ~30 min by sea Ferry from Fremantle or the city Margaret River ~3 hrs Drive One number worth internalising: Sydney and Melbourne are around five hours by air, and there is no practical alternative. Perth’s airport does, however, fly direct to South-East Asia in about five hours and to Europe direct — which for many international clinicians is a better flight map than the east coast offers. The takeaway Transport will be the least of your worries here. Pick a home near a rail line or within twenty minutes of your campus, buy a bike, and accept that the one long journey in your life is the flight east. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Weekends in Perth: Rottnest, the coast and Margaret River
chunks.x: Perth’s weekends are unusually good and unusually close. An island half an hour by ferry, nineteen beaches inside the city, wine country twenty-five minutes away, and a three-hour drive to one of the best corners of Australia. Four ways out of Perth The city is famously isolated and its weekends are not. Four directions, and something at the end of each that Western Australians will tell you about at length. West, offshore No cars, bikes only, sixty-three beaches — and close enough that Perth families treat it as an extension of the city rather than a holiday. The city Fremantle Rottnest · 30 min ferry Up the river, then into the hills The shortest run to wine country of any Australian capital, and hills villages noticeably cooler than the plain in summer.

chunks.t: Weekends in Perth: Rottnest, the coast and Margaret River
chunks.x: The city Swan Valley · 25 min Perth Hills South, to the south-west World-class wine, surf along a limestone coast, karri forests and caves — the classic Perth long weekend, and it earns the reputation. The city Dunsborough Margaret River · ~3 hr Augusta North, up the Coral Coast Limestone spires in the desert, then reef you can swim off the beach, then whale sharks in season. The city The Pinnacles · ~2 hr Kalbarri Ningaloo Each of the four gets its own section below. Indicative times, and all four are drives you would do on an ordinary weekend rather than plan a holiday around.

chunks.t: Weekends in Perth: Rottnest, the coast and Margaret River
chunks.x: Rottnest Island — Wadjemup — sits nineteen kilometres offshore: no cars, bikes only, sixty-three beaches and twenty bays, and the quokkas that made it internet-famous. It is a half-hour ferry from Fremantle and an easy day trip, which is why Perth families treat it as an extension of the city rather than a holiday. On the mainland coast, the metropolitan beaches run for a hundred kilometres: Cottesloe for the sunset crowd, Scarborough for the surf and the pool, Trigg for the waves, Mettams for snorkelling over the reef, City Beach for families, and quieter sand the further north or south you go. Each has its own character and its own regulars.

chunks.t: Weekends in Perth: Rottnest, the coast and Margaret River
chunks.x: The Swan River is the city’s other playground: kayaking, sailing, the foreshore paths, and the ferry across to South Perth. Twenty-five minutes upriver, the Swan Valley is the shortest run to wine country of any Australian capital — cellar doors, breweries and produce, easily done in an afternoon. East, the Perth Hills give you bushwalking, waterfalls in winter and villages that are noticeably cooler than the plain in summer.

chunks.t: Weekends in Perth: Rottnest, the coast and Margaret River
chunks.x: Three hours south is the region that makes Western Australians insufferable about their state: Margaret River, with world-class wine, surf breaks along a limestone coast, karri forests, caves and a food culture to match. Around it, Dunsborough, Yallingup and Augusta anchor a coastline that runs from the Indian Ocean to the Southern. It is the classic Perth long weekend, and it earns the reputation.

chunks.t: Weekends in Perth: Rottnest, the coast and Margaret River
chunks.x: Four ways out of Perth The city is famously isolated and its weekends are not. Four directions, and something at the end of each that Western Australians will tell you about at length. West, offshore No cars, bikes only, sixty-three beaches — and close enough that Perth families treat it as an extension of the city rather than a holiday. The city Fremantle Rottnest · 30 min ferry Up the river, then into the hills The shortest run to wine country of any Australian capital, and hills villages noticeably cooler than the plain in summer. The city Swan Valley · 25 min Perth Hills South, to the south-west World-class wine, surf along a limestone coast, karri forests and caves — the classic Perth long weekend, and it earns the reputation.

chunks.t: Weekends in Perth: Rottnest, the coast and Margaret River
chunks.x: The city Dunsborough Margaret River · ~3 hr Augusta North, up the Coral Coast Limestone spires in the desert, then reef you can swim off the beach, then whale sharks in season. The city The Pinnacles · ~2 hr Kalbarri Ningaloo Wildflower season from August cuts across all four — thousands of species, many found nowhere else, and people plan road trips around it. The Kimberley is further again and belongs to the WA guide . North of the city the Coral Coast runs a long way: limestone spires in the desert at the Pinnacles, then Kalbarri, then the Ningaloo reef — where you can swim off the beach onto coral, and with whale sharks in season. From August the state produces one of the world’s great wildflower displays, thousands of species and many found nowhere else, and people plan road trips around it. The Kimberley is further again and worth the trip of a lifetime; the WA guide covers the state properly.

chunks.t: Weekends in Perth: Rottnest, the coast and Margaret River
chunks.x: Rottnest by ferry, bikes hired, a beach to yourself by mid-morning Margaret River: cellar doors, a surf beach and the karri forest Fremantle — markets, the fishing boat harbour, a brewery in the afternoon Snorkelling at Mettams Pool, then breakfast at Trigg The Swan Valley on a Sunday, twenty-five minutes from town Kings Park at sunset with the city and the river below The Pinnacles at dusk, two hours north Wildflower season in the wheatbelt or the south-west, from August A hills walk to a winter waterfall at Mundaring or Kalamunda Sculpture by the Sea at Cottesloe, then a sundowner on the sand That’s the guide Nine chapters on Perth. Statewide and remote topics live in the Western Australia guide , and everything national in Moving to Australia . When you’re ready to talk about roles here, send us your CV . Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Moving to Perth: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.x: Perth is the trade nobody quite explains properly: you accept isolation, and in return you get the best weather and beaches in Australia, a deep tertiary system, and housing costs that make a family life straightforward rather than a spreadsheet exercise.

chunks.t: Moving to Perth: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.h: The most isolated capital on earth
chunks.x: Around 2.3 million people live on the Swan Coastal Plain, closer to Jakarta and Singapore than to Sydney. That isolation is the defining fact: a five-hour flight to the east coast, a time zone two or three hours behind it, and a city that has spent its history being self-sufficient because there was no alternative. What it produces is a capital with an unusual character — relaxed, outdoors, and quietly wealthy from the resources industry that funds much of the state. The Swan River runs through the middle of it, Kings Park sits on the escarpment above the city, and the Indian Ocean beaches run north and south for a hundred kilometres of white sand. For clinicians the draw is a full tertiary system in a city small enough to know, combined with a state health service that recruits internationally as a matter of routine — and pays attention to relocation because it has to.

chunks.t: Moving to Perth: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.h: The most isolated capital on earth
chunks.x: The cost is the distance: from your family, from the eastern states, and from anywhere else at all. Who wrote this Ethicare is a healthcare recruitment company. This guide is free to read, asks nothing of you, and does not give visa advice. Perth is the city people either love immediately or find too far from everything. Work out which you are before you fly; this guide takes the isolation as seriously as the beaches.

chunks.t: Moving to Perth: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.x: ~2.3M People in Greater Perth — Australia’s fourth-largest city, and the most isolated capital in the world. ~2,100 km To the nearest city of comparable size, Adelaide. The east coast is a five-hour flight. ~19 Beaches along the metropolitan coast, most of them white sand facing an Indian Ocean sunset. ~3,000 Hours of sunshine a year — the sunniest capital in Australia by a clear margin. 400 ha Kings Park, on the escarpment above the city — larger than Central Park, and free. UTC+8 No daylight saving. Two hours behind Sydney in winter, three in summer — and the same clock as much of Asia. ~3 hrs To Margaret River, one of Australia’s great wine regions, with surf beaches and karri forest attached. ~35% Of residents were born overseas — a strongly international city, with large British, South African and South-East Asian communities. The Fremantle Doctor The afternoon sea breeze that arrives most summer days and drops the temperature noticeably. It has a name for a reason.

chunks.t: Moving to Perth: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.h: Six things you only learn once you’re here
chunks.x: The isolation is real Not a talking point — a five-hour flight to Sydney, and a long-haul flight to anywhere else. Weekend trips east do not happen. The beaches are the point Nineteen metropolitan beaches, white sand, warm water and a sunset over the ocean. This is what people mean when they say Perth is underrated. Everything is newer Perth grew late and fast. The housing stock, the hospitals and the infrastructure are noticeably newer than the eastern capitals. The mining cycle matters The resources industry shapes the state economy, rents and the job market. Ask locals about the last boom and the last downturn. Same clock as Asia Perth runs on Singapore and Hong Kong time. It changes the feel of the city, and the flight map, more than people expect. Summer is long and dry Months of hot, dry, cloudless weather with a fire season attached. Beautiful, and relentless by March.

chunks.t: Moving to Perth: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.h: Six things you only learn once you’re here
chunks.x: A note on Country Perth stands on Whadjuk Noongar boodja — Noongar Country, which covers the whole south-west of the state. Boorloo is the Noongar name for the Perth area, and Derbarl Yerrigan for the Swan River. The Noongar seasonal calendar has six seasons rather than four, and you will see it used in schools, parks and health services. Acknowledgement of Country opens meetings; take the cultural induction seriously, particularly if you work in the regions.

chunks.t: Moving to Perth: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.x: Nine chapters, all about Perth specifically. Topics true across the state — the Pilbara, the Kimberley, remote and regional practice — sit in the Western Australia guide . Anything true of Australia generally — Medicare, visas, Ahpra registration, tax, superannuation, schools — lives once in Moving to Australia . If you read nothing else, read Why Perth for the full case, including the isolation question, and Where clinicians live , because the coast-versus-river-versus-hills choice shapes everything here. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Why Perth: the case for the western capital
chunks.x: Perth divides people faster than any other Australian city. Some clinicians arrive and never seriously consider leaving; others count the months until they can move east. This chapter is about working out which you are likely to be, before you commit.

chunks.t: Why Perth: the case for the western capital
chunks.x: Start with the daily life, because that is what wins people over. The beaches are the best of any Australian capital — white sand, clear water, an ocean sunset, and rarely crowded. The weather is the sunniest in the country. Commutes are short, housing is affordable by east-coast standards, and a family house within twenty minutes of a tertiary hospital is an achievable plan. Professionally, the state runs a full tertiary system with newer facilities than most of the country, and it recruits internationally as standard practice — which means the process is well-worn and relocation support is common rather than exceptional. Pay follows WA awards and enterprise agreements; we quote no figures here and will walk you through the current agreement instead. ~3,000 Hours of sunshine a year — the sunniest capital ~19 Metropolitan beaches, most of them uncrowded 100% Of WA counts as regional for skilled migration

chunks.t: Why Perth: the case for the western capital
chunks.x: A twenty-minute drive to work, or a train that arrives. A swim at Cottesloe or Trigg before a late start, in water warm enough for most of the year. Coffee in Leederville or Mount Lawley. Friday evening watching the sun drop into the Indian Ocean, which locals still stop for. Saturday at Fremantle’s markets or on a ferry to Rottnest with the bikes. Sunday in the Swan Valley among the vines, twenty-five minutes from the CBD. The counterweight is what is not in that week: no weekend in another city, no quick flight to see family, and a five-hour journey to reach the rest of your own country. Perth people build their lives locally because the alternative is expensive and exhausting. Sophie’s insight Perth is the city candidates dismiss on the map and then love in person.

chunks.t: Why Perth: the case for the western capital
chunks.x: The beaches, the weather and the housing are all better than the east coast, and the health service is good at welcoming international staff because it has been doing it for decades. The question I always ask is about family. If you need to be able to reach people quickly, the distance will wear on you. If your life travels with you, Perth is one of the best places in Australia to build it. Sophie Careem Founder & CEO, Ethicare Resourcing

chunks.t: Why Perth: the case for the western capital
chunks.h: Who we’d ask to think twice
chunks.x: The distance from family This is the one that decides it. Five hours to the east coast, long-haul to anywhere else, and expensive flights. If someone at home is unwell, you are a long way away. The market is smaller A good tertiary system, but fewer sites than Sydney or Melbourne. A very narrow sub-specialty may have one or two possible employers in the whole state. Summer is relentless Months of dry heat with a serious fire season. The sea breeze helps on the coast; twenty kilometres inland it is a different proposition. The mining cycle The state economy rides the resources cycle, and rents and the job market move with it. It is not unstable, but it is cyclical in a way the east coast is not. It is a quiet city Relaxed and outdoors rather than dense and urban. If big-city energy is what recharges you, Perth will feel underpowered.

chunks.t: Why Perth: the case for the western capital
chunks.h: Who we’d ask to think twice
chunks.x: Where we’d steer you instead If system scale is what your career needs, Melbourne or Sydney carry more sites and more sub-specialty depth. If you want warmth and beaches without the isolation, Brisbane is the direct comparison — and two hours from the east coast, not five. If the regional and remote work is what interests you, the Western Australia guide covers the Pilbara, the Kimberley and the south-west properly. In our experience Perth suits clinicians who want the big-city career with the pressure dialled down — the beaches are better, the commutes shorter. The isolation is the one thing we never talk anyone out of feeling; you either make the west home, or you don’t. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Cost of living in Queensland: the numbers
chunks.x: Queensland’s value case survived the boom, but the corner is no longer cheap — it is cheaper. The regional cities still are cheap, and the gap between the two is the most useful thing in this chapter.

chunks.t: Cost of living in Queensland: the numbers
chunks.x: We used to print a weekly rent and a monthly budget table here. We have taken them out. A figure that was true when a page was written is misleading a year later, and a candidate who plans a move around a stale number is worse off than one who plans around none. What does not go stale is the relationship between places — which suburb, ring or region you choose — and the judgement about which costs catch people out. For today’s actual numbers use the calculators at the foot of the page, and use them to compare it against the city you are leaving. That is the only comparison that decides anything.

chunks.t: Cost of living in Queensland: the numbers
chunks.x: Clinical pay is set by state awards and is broadly comparable with the southern states; we don’t print figures until we’ve verified them against the current instruments. The outgoings side is where Queensland argues: south-east housing runs clearly below Sydney and below Melbourne, and the regional cities run at half the corner or better — with incentives often stacked on top. The interstate migration that made the state famous also moved its prices: Brisbane’s boom years closed some of the old gap, and the premium pockets — Noosa, beachfront Burleigh, the best canals — now price on southern money. The middle of the market held: ordinary suburbs, both coasts included, remain buyable on clinical incomes , which is the sentence that matters. The sunshine hides two costs worth naming early: summer electricity, because air conditioning is infrastructure here; and insurance, which prices flood and cyclone even when nobody mentions them at the open home — markedly so in the north.

chunks.t: Cost of living in Queensland: the numbers
chunks.x: Inner Brisbane The state’s top of range for apartments and Queenslanders alike — a clear step below equivalent Sydney, roughly level-pegging with middle Melbourne. Middle-ring Brisbane & Ipswich corridor The family value belt — where the buy-within-two-years plan still computes. Gold Coast Beach suburbs price confidently, the canal premium is real, and the towers offer the corner’s most accessible rents. Wide spread; choose deliberately. Sunshine Coast Risen hardest of the three — the family-coast reputation now carries a price. Still below the southern capitals for the same postcode-to-beach maths. Toowoomba & the regional cities Bundaberg, Rockhampton, Mackay — family homes at prices that end the housing conversation, frequently paired with incentives. Townsville & Cairns The north’s cities remain affordable; insurance is the line that bites back. Net-net still firmly ahead.

chunks.t: Cost of living in Queensland: the numbers
chunks.x: No longer cheap. Still cheaper. Monthly rent for the same room or small one-bedroom, at true relative scale. The gap between the corner and the regional cities is the most useful number in this chapter. Inner Brisbane The boom closed some of the old gap Baseline Middle ring & the coasts The part of the market that held ~0.8× A regional city Still cheap ~0.6× Cheaper than Sydney and Melbourne, not cheap — that distinction is the whole chapter. One line runs in your favour whichever tier you choose: south-east Queensland’s flat fare is currently the cheapest urban transport in the country. Indicative prices that change over time. The transport line is not a typo — SEQ’s flat-fare policy is currently the cheapest urban transport in the country; check the current scheme.

chunks.t: Cost of living in Queensland: the numbers
chunks.x: Summer power Air conditioning through a humid January is a real bill. Solar is everywhere for a reason — ask whether the rental has it and who gets the benefit. Insurance, north of Bundaberg Cyclone and flood risk price into premiums sharply in the north. Get quotes before committing to buy; renters feel it more gently. School fees on a temporary visa Queensland generally charges nothing: 482 dependants are waived, with a small annual application fee. The rule and the other states sit in the master’s School fees on a visa . Health cover for your visa Many visas require private cover, separate from Medicare — national detail, covered in Immigration & visas .

chunks.t: Cost of living in Queensland: the numbers
chunks.x: Compare cities Numbeo · cost of living Brisbane, Gold Coast and Cairns prices against your current city. Plan your budget Moneysmart budget planner The Australian government’s free budgeting tool. Property realestate.com.au Live rents and sales — compare the corner and the regions early. Master guide The cost of relocating Flights, shipping, bonds and the first ninety days — budgeted once, properly. Sanity check Expatistan A cleaner side-by-side of two cities. Worth running when Numbeo looks off. Official data ABS price indexes Slower than the comparison sites, and the one to trust on the direction of travel. The summary The corner is cheaper than Sydney and Melbourne, not cheap — and still the best big-city buying maths in the country. The regional cities halve the housing line and add incentives . The hidden lines are summer power and northern insurance ; budget both and the sunshine is priced. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Food, shopping and everyday life in Queensland
chunks.x: Queensland’s everyday life is built around its weather the way Melbourne’s is built around its coffee: outdoors, early, and unbothered. The food scene has grown into the climate — markets, seafood and verandah dining — and the state’s real speciality is the shape of an ordinary day.

chunks.t: Food, shopping and everyday life in Queensland
chunks.x: No daylight saving plus subtropical light means the state runs early: beaches busy at five, gyms full at six, 7am meetings unremarkable, school drop-off in sunglasses. Evenings are short in summer and glorious in winter — the barbecue season inverts here, peaking in July when the south shivers. Newcomers fight the rhythm for a month and then convert; fighting it longer is the one reliable way to dislike Queensland.

chunks.t: Food, shopping and everyday life in Queensland
chunks.x: Brisbane has grown up The river city’s dining precincts — Howard Smith Wharves, South Bank, the James Street end — now hold their own against the southern capitals, at a friendlier bill. The coasts do casual brilliantly Burleigh’s headland dinners, Noosa’s river restaurants, surf-club bistros the whole coast long — the surf club is the state’s defining institution: cheap, licensed, and pointed at the ocean. Seafood is the local produce Moreton Bay bugs, mud crab, tiger prawns, reef fish north of Rocky — the fish-and-chips baseline here embarrasses most countries’ fine dining. No tipping, clear menu prices The price is the price and waitstaff earn a wage. Same national rule, same pleasant surprise at the till.

chunks.t: Food, shopping and everyday life in Queensland
chunks.h: Markets and what the state grows
chunks.x: Queensland grows the country’s tropical larder: mangoes and avocados that make the southern supermarkets look apologetic, bananas from the north, strawberries through winter, sugar the whole coast long. The weekend farmers’ markets — Jan Powers in Brisbane, the coast markets at Burleigh and Noosa, Rusty’s in Cairns — are produce-first and cheap in season. The Granite Belt behind Toowoomba is the state’s quiet wine country — high-altitude reds and apple-country autumns — and the hinterlands of both coasts keep a full calendar of food festivals between them.

chunks.t: Food, shopping and everyday life in Queensland
chunks.x: The two big chains and the discounter anchor everywhere down the coast; independent grocers thin out north of the corner but the markets compensate. Whatever your community eats, Brisbane’s south side and the Gold Coast sell it — the multicultural depth is newer than Sydney’s or Melbourne’s but growing fast, and the master’s Finding your feet & your people maps where communities cluster.

chunks.t: Food, shopping and everyday life in Queensland
chunks.x: Nippers is the social engine Sunday-morning surf lifesaving for kids is how coastal families meet everyone they will ever know here. Joining is the fastest shortcut in the state. Sport, both codes, all year League is the religion, union and AFL run deep, netball and touch fill the weeknights. State of Origin nights empty the streets — pick Queensland; it’s safer. The pool is a room of the house Backyard pools are ordinary infrastructure, pool fencing is strict law, and summer social life happens half-submerged. Winter is festival season The dry months carry the calendar — outdoor cinemas, shows, the Ekka in August — because the state schedules its culture for its best weather. Limitations High culture is thinner than the southern capitals — good and growing in Brisbane, a flight away from the regions. Summer curbs the outdoor life it advertises: January is for pools, aircon and early mornings, not long lunches outside. North of the corner, specialist ingredients need planning — every community keeps its list and its Brisbane order. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Queensland at a glance: climate, geography and seasons
chunks.x: Queensland runs from subtropical river city to monsoonal tropics to red-dirt outback — a state so long that its two ends have different seasons. Understanding the three Queenslands is the fastest way to understand which one is yours.

chunks.t: Queensland at a glance: climate, geography and seasons
chunks.x: Where Brisbane sits, with the straight-line distance to Cairns and Townsville The south-east corner is where two-thirds of the state lives: Brisbane on its river, the Gold Coast’s forty-kilometre beach strip south to the border, the Sunshine Coast’s surf towns north, and the Scenic Rim’s green hinterland behind. Subtropical — hot wet summers, warm dry winters, storm season as the soundtrack. The coast runs north for two thousand kilometres: Bundaberg and the southern reef gateways, Rockhampton and Mackay serving cattle and coal country, then the true tropics — Townsville, dry and garrison-tough; Cairns, wet and rainforest-green, where the reef meets the Daintree. Monsoon wet seasons, glorious dry winters, cyclone watch from November. The inland climbs the range to Toowoomba’s gardens, then runs west through farm and cattle country into the outback proper — Longreach, Mount Isa’s mining city, and distances where medicine is flown, not driven.

chunks.t: Queensland at a glance: climate, geography and seasons
chunks.x: Summer Dec – Feb 29–32°C Hot, humid, stormy Autumn Mar – May 24–28°C The humidity breaks Winter Jun – Aug 21–23°C Dry, blue, the payoff Spring Sep – Nov 25–29°C Warming, jacarandas Indicative Brisbane daytime highs. Cairns and Townsville run hotter with a true wet season (roughly December–April); the inland west adds real heat in summer and cold clear nights in winter.

chunks.t: Queensland at a glance: climate, geography and seasons
chunks.h: What the numbers don’t tell you
chunks.x: Winter is the season the state is famous for. Dry, cloudless, twenty-two degrees — from June to August the south-east has arguably the best city weather on earth, and the north has its "dry", which is the tourist season for a reason. The storm season is pure theatre. South-east summer afternoons build purple thunderheads that break at four with hail warnings and drenching rain, then clear by dinner. Download the radar app early; locals treat it as a spectator sport with rules. The wet season is a different contract. North of about Mackay, December to April means monsoonal rain, road cuts, and the cyclone watch. It is well-managed and locals plan around it — but it is real, and the induction your service gives you is not a formality. No daylight saving changes the shape of days. Summer light starts before five and ends by seven.

chunks.t: Queensland at a glance: climate, geography and seasons
chunks.h: What the numbers don’t tell you
chunks.x: The state runs early: 6am gyms full, 7am meetings normal, evening barbecues in winter rather than summer. Sun protection is clinical-grade serious here. Queensland has the world’s highest melanoma rates. Hats, rash shirts and 50+ are school policy and should be yours — the master’s Living in Australia covers the everyday rules.

chunks.t: Queensland at a glance: climate, geography and seasons
chunks.h: Where things are, in travel time
chunks.x: Brisbane → Gold Coast About an hour by road or train to the southern end’s health precinct. Brisbane → Sunshine Coast A little over an hour north to the new hospital spine. Brisbane → Toowoomba 90 minutes up the range. Brisbane → Bundaberg / Rockhampton 4.5 / 7 hours by road — or short flights, which is how the state works. Brisbane → Townsville / Cairns 2-hour flights. Driving is 13–16 hours and a road trip, not a commute. Brisbane → Sydney / Melbourne 1.5 / 2-hour flights, constantly.

chunks.t: Queensland at a glance: climate, geography and seasons
chunks.x: SEQ South-east Queensland — Brisbane plus the two coasts. The corner. The wet / the dry The north’s two seasons. The calendar up there. FNQ Far North Queensland — Cairns and beyond. Straddie / Moreton The bay islands — Brisbane’s weekend sand. The hinterland The green ranges behind either coast — waterfalls and lookouts. Stinger season Box-jellyfish months in the north — swim between the nets. Go Card SEQ’s transport card — trains, busways, ferries, trams. The Isa Mount Isa — the outback mining city, and shorthand for "properly remote". The short version Three Queenslands: the subtropical corner, the tropical coast, the outback west . Winter is the universal payoff; summer asks more the further north you go. Which Queensland you choose decides everything else — Where clinicians live is next. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Healthcare in Queensland: working as a clinician
chunks.x: Queensland runs the most geographically spread public health system in Australia: sixteen hospital and health services covering everything from a capital-city tertiary cluster to islands in the Torres Strait. For a clinician, that spread is the story — the state’s depth is not all in one place.

chunks.t: Healthcare in Queensland: working as a clinician
chunks.x: Public care is organised into sixteen hospital and health services (HHSs) — each with its own board, geography and recruitment. The south-east corner holds several metropolitan services covering Brisbane’s hospital cluster, the Gold Coast’s precinct and the Sunshine Coast’s new spine. Then the map opens out: services centred on Toowoomba, Bundaberg, Rockhampton, Mackay, Townsville, Cairns — and beyond them the truly remote services covering the west and the Torres Strait and Cape. Registration is national through Ahpra; hiring is service by service . The practical consequence: "moving to Queensland" is really choosing an HHS, and the same profession can mean a tertiary team in Brisbane, a regional department in Mackay, or a fly-in clinic run out of Cairns.

chunks.t: Healthcare in Queensland: working as a clinician
chunks.x: What makes Queensland unusual is that tertiary-level medicine exists outside the capital: Townsville anchors tertiary services for the north, and Cairns runs major-hospital medicine at the rainforest’s edge. The state built it that way because Brisbane is simply too far from its own north. How Medicare and the public–private split work is national, and lives once in the master’s How the health system works .

chunks.t: Healthcare in Queensland: working as a clinician
chunks.x: Growth is the constant The south-east is adding people — and hospital capacity — faster than anywhere in Australia, with the 2032 build-up compounding it. New units, new roles, constant recruitment. The north is a career, not a posting Townsville and Cairns offer tertiary and major-hospital medicine with tropical, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health at the centre — work that exists nowhere else in the country at this scale. Rural and remote, properly The western services and the Torres Strait run medicine by air and telehealth across enormous distances — broad scope, strong incentives, real isolation. The master’s Regional life is the account. Retrieval is a system, not an exception Aeromedical transfer knits the state together. Wherever you work, stabilise-and-fly is part of the clinical culture, and the further out, the more of it you own.

chunks.t: Healthcare in Queensland: working as a clinician
chunks.x: Seasonal rhythms are clinical rhythms Storm season in the south-east, the wet and stinger season in the north, tourist surges on both coasts — the caseload has a calendar here. Pay is set by state awards Each profession has its own instruments, with allowances, packaging and — distinctively here — remote-area incentives layered on top. We quote figures only after verifying them against the current award; see Pay & conditions . The state, read as a coastline Queensland’s depth is not all in one place, and this is why: the state is long enough that Brisbane is too far from its own north to serve it. So the north got its own tertiary medicine. Up the coast Each of these is a separate hospital and health service with its own board and its own recruitment — and the two at the far end run tertiary and major-hospital medicine in their own right.

chunks.t: Healthcare in Queensland: working as a clinician
chunks.x: Brisbane Sunshine Coast Rockhampton Mackay Townsville Cairns And away from it Inland and island services where medicine runs by air and telehealth — broad scope, strong incentives, real isolation. Toowoomba & the Darling Downs The western services Torres Strait & Cape “Moving to Queensland” is really choosing one of these — and the same profession means a tertiary team in the south-east, a regional department in the middle, or a fly-in clinic run out of the far north.

chunks.t: Healthcare in Queensland: working as a clinician
chunks.h: Working with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities
chunks.x: Queensland is the only state whose health system serves two distinct First Nations peoples — Aboriginal nations across the mainland, and Torres Strait Islander communities in the islands and the northern coast. Community-controlled health organisations are major partners, and in the northern and western services, First Nations health is much of the daily work rather than a programme beside it. You are not expected to arrive expert. You are expected to take the cultural induction seriously — in the far north it is core clinical preparation — and to learn whose Country and whose islands your service stands on.

chunks.t: Healthcare in Queensland: working as a clinician
chunks.h: Working with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities
chunks.x: What to ask at interview Which HHS and which facility — and does the role involve outreach, fly-in clinics or telehealth to outlying communities? What is the roster pattern, and how are on-call, penalties and allowances handled under the relevant award? For regional and remote roles: exactly what incentives, accommodation and leave provisions apply — and for how long? What is the wet-season / cyclone operational plan, and what does it mean for my roster? (North of Bundaberg, ask this seriously.) What supervision, orientation and CPD support exists for clinicians new to Australia — and how does CPD work this far from the southern cities? Where does complex work refer to, and how much of the retrieval pathway do I own? Sophie Sophie’s insight Queensland is where I place the most families, and the pattern is always the same: they come for the winter and stay for the mortgage. My advice is to take the north seriously — Townsville and Cairns offer careers the southern capitals can’t, and the clinicians who try them almost never come back early. Sophie Careem Founder, Ethicare Resourcing

chunks.x: Ahpra registration, English-language evidence and the visa that goes with your role are national processes, identical in every state. chunks.t: Where clinicians live in Queensland: fifteen places compared
chunks.x: Queensland’s first decision is which Queensland: the south-east corner, the tropical north, or the regional coast between. Within the corner, the second decision — Brisbane, Gold Coast or Sunshine Coast — is happily low-stakes, because they’re an hour apart. First pick your Queensland The state runs on three housing markets, not one. The good news sits in the note underneath. The south-east corner Brisbane, the Gold Coast and the Sunshine Coast — most of the jobs, most of the choice, and city prices that still sit visibly under Sydney and Melbourne equivalents. The tropical north Townsville and Cairns run their own tertiary-grade systems with housing a fraction of the corner’s — the trade is distance and a wet season, not career ceiling. The coast between Mackay, Rockhampton, Bundaberg and their neighbours: hospital towns where a family home costs least of all, and recruitment rarely closes. Within the corner, a wrong guess barely costs you — Brisbane and both coasts sit roughly an hour from each other, so a wrong guess is a move, not a migration.

chunks.t: Where clinicians live in Queensland: fifteen places compared
chunks.x: The inner ring New Farm, Paddington, West End — Queenslander houses on stilts, river walks, and the café-and-market life. The premium end, and still visibly below equivalent Sydney or Melbourne. The middle north and south Ashgrove to Chermside, Camp Hill to Mount Gravatt — the family value ring, on busways and train lines, where most relocating households land. The riverside east Bulimba, Hawthorne, Manly’s bayside — ferries to work, sailing clubs, weekend markets. Family-scaled with water attached. The growth corridors North Lakes, Springfield, Ripley — new estates, new schools and the most house for the money in the metro area; commute and summer heat are the trade. Ipswich The historic city inside the corridor — its own hospital, heritage streets and prices that startle southerners. Rising fast.

chunks.t: Where clinicians live in Queensland: fifteen places compared
chunks.x: Gold Coast — the beach city Australia’s sixth-largest city behind forty kilometres of surf: high-rise energy at Surfers, family suburbs at Burleigh and Palm Beach, hinterland villages behind. A major health precinct of its own, and the light rail stitching it together. Gold Coast — the canals The waterfront-home suburbs — boats at the back fence at prices that still undercut Sydney’s harbour dreams by multiples. Sunshine Coast Caloundra to Noosa — the family-scaled coast: surf towns, the new hospital spine at Birtinya, and a hinterland of market villages. Calmer than the Gold Coast, priced increasingly confidently. Noosa & the premium pockets The exception to Queensland value — Noosa, Burleigh’s beachfront and the best canal addresses run on southern money. Lovely; budget accordingly.

chunks.t: Where clinicians live in Queensland: fifteen places compared
chunks.x: Toowoomba The garden city atop the range, ninety minutes inland — a regional hub with its own hospital, cool nights, and the state’s most settled four-season feel. Bundaberg & the southern reef coast Sugar-town scale with Bargara’s beaches attached, turtles nesting up the road, and family homes at prices that end conversations. Rockhampton & Mackay The central coast’s working cities — beef and mining country with solid hospitals, islands offshore, and strong incentive packages. Townsville The north’s capital in the dry belt — tertiary-level medicine, a garrison-city spine, Magnetic Island twenty minutes offshore. The serious northern career move. Cairns The tropical one — major-hospital medicine between reef and rainforest, an international workforce, and the wet season as the annual contract.

chunks.t: Where clinicians live in Queensland: fifteen places compared
chunks.x: The far west & the Torres Strait Mount Isa’s mining medicine and the island clinics of the Strait — the remotest postings in this collection, with the incentives and the isolation to match. Three things to check before you sign Air conditioning and orientation, not just the address. A Queensland summer in a west-facing rental without decent aircon is a lesson learned once. Ask what’s installed and what the power bills run. Flood mapping, at the exact address. River and creek flooding is part of the state’s history — check the council flood map and ask about the property’s record before signing; insurance prices it even when agents don’t mention it. The school catchment — and the visa fee question. Catchments bind here as everywhere; and on a temporary visa, read the master’s School fees on a visa before you budget.

chunks.t: Where clinicians live in Queensland: fifteen places compared
chunks.x: Most clinicians we move rent for six to twelve months first — long enough to learn whether they’re corner people, coast people or north people. In Queensland those are different lives, and the state is generous enough to let you test them. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Getting around Queensland: trains, ferries, flights and the distances
chunks.x: Queensland transport is two systems: a connected south-east corner of trains, busways, ferries and light rail — currently the cheapest urban transport in the country — and a state beyond it that runs on aircraft and long, straight highways.

chunks.t: Getting around Queensland: trains, ferries, flights and the distances
chunks.x: Brisbane’s rail network radiates through the suburbs and runs the spine of the corner — one line south to the Gold Coast, one north toward the Sunshine Coast — while the busways (grade-separated bus motorways, a Brisbane speciality) cover the corridors trains miss. The CityCat ferries make the river a commute: if your hospital sits near a terminal, the boat is the best journey to work in Australia. The Gold Coast adds its light rail down the beach spine; everything runs on one Go Card (or contactless), and Queensland’s flat-fare experiment has made public transport almost free — check the current fare policy, but budget approximately nothing.

chunks.t: Getting around Queensland: trains, ferries, flights and the distances
chunks.x: One toll network, mild by Sydney standards Brisbane’s tunnels and the airport link are tolled; the coasts largely aren’t. A tag sorts it; the monthly bill is a fraction of NSW’s. The M1 is the pressure point Brisbane–Gold Coast at peak is the corner’s one bad drive. The train exists; use it. Storm-season driving is a skill Flash flooding closes underpasses fast. "If it’s flooded, forget it" is the state’s road-safety mantra, and it is not decorative. Parking is easy outside the centre Hospital and suburban parking is far more forgiving than the southern capitals. Ask at interview anyway.

chunks.t: Getting around Queensland: trains, ferries, flights and the distances
chunks.h: The rest of the state: fly
chunks.x: Brisbane Airport The third gateway — direct to Asia, the Pacific and the Gulf, and the domestic hub the state’s health system quietly runs on. The regional network Townsville, Cairns, Mackay, Rockhampton and Bundaberg all fly to Brisbane multiple times daily. Regional clinicians treat the 6am flight as a bus. Cairns international The north’s own gateway — direct to Asia in season, which changes the trip home for FNQ clinicians. The highways The Bruce runs the coast for 1,700 kilometres — a road trip with a cult following and roadhouse rituals. Inland, distances are long and fuel stops are planned, not assumed.

chunks.t: Getting around Queensland: trains, ferries, flights and the distances
chunks.x: Journey Typical time Brisbane CBD → hospital cluster (Herston / South Brisbane) 10–15 min by busway or ferry Brisbane → Gold Coast ~1 hr by train or road Brisbane → Sunshine Coast ~1 hr 15 by road Brisbane → Toowoomba ~1 hr 30 by road Brisbane → Bundaberg ~4 hr 30 by road, or a 1-hr flight Brisbane → Rockhampton / Mackay 7 / 10 hr by road — fly Brisbane → Townsville / Cairns 2-hr flights; 13–16 hr drives Cairns → the Torres Strait 2-hr flight to Horn Island, then boats Brisbane → Sydney / Melbourne 1.5 / 2-hr flights, constantly Off-peak estimates. Add for the M1 at commuter hours, and treat wet-season road closures in the north as a when, not an if. Licence conversion, buying and registering a car, and the practicalities of Australian driving are national topics, covered once in the master’s Living in Australia . Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Weekends in Queensland: reef, rainforest and the coast
chunks.x: Queensland’s weekend argument is unfair: the world’s largest reef offshore, the world’s oldest rainforest behind it, and a coastline where the ordinary Saturday options would headline other countries’ tourism campaigns. You will live where the rest of the world queues to visit. When to do what, up here Queensland’s weekends are governed by a calendar rather than a map, and it runs opposite to the one most arrivals bring with them. Winter is the season for everything. The wet, and the heat Dec – Mar Humid, storm-heavy and the peak of the northern stinger months. The hinterland waterfalls are at their best, and the crowds are at the coast rather than inland. The turn Apr – May Humidity drops, the water is still warm and the crowds have gone home. Arguably the best few weeks of the year, and the ones locals keep quiet about.

chunks.t: Weekends in Queensland: reef, rainforest and the coast
chunks.x: The dry — peak season Jun – Sep Dry, blue and mild statewide: the reef at its clearest, the interior at its kindest, and the one stretch of the year when every part of this chapter is at its best at once. Building again Oct – Nov Warming up and quiet, with turtles nesting up the regional coast — the last comfortable window before the wet returns. Winter being peak season is the single most useful thing to know about living here — it inverts the leave calendar you arrive with. The season notes below fill in the detail.

chunks.t: Weekends in Queensland: reef, rainforest and the coast
chunks.x: Whitehaven Beach in the Whitsundays The reef, as a habit From Cairns, Townsville or the southern gateways, the Great Barrier Reef is a day boat — snorkelling stops feeling like a bucket-list item and becomes what you do when family visits, and then just what you do. The beaches, all of them Forty kilometres of Gold Coast surf, the Sunshine Coast’s point breaks, Four Mile at Port Douglas, and the empty regional stretches between — patrolled, learnable and warm most of the year. The bay islands Moreton and Straddie are Brisbane’s weekend sand — ferries from the suburbs to wild beaches, sand tobogganing and winter whales off the headlands. The Whitsundays Seventy-four islands and the country’s most famous sail-yourself waters, off Airlie Beach — the long weekend that converts visitors into residents.

chunks.t: Weekends in Queensland: reef, rainforest and the coast
chunks.x: Stinger season North of about Gladstone, November to May means netted swimming enclosures and stinger suits offshore. Managed, signposted, and part of the northern contract. Whales in winter The humpback highway runs the whole coast May to November — Hervey Bay is the world capital of watching them rest.

chunks.t: Weekends in Queensland: reef, rainforest and the coast
chunks.x: The Daintree & the wet tropics The world’s oldest rainforest, World Heritage from Townsville to Cooktown — cassowaries, swimming holes and canopy walks, all within FNQ’s weekend range. The hinterlands Both coasts keep green ranges twenty minutes behind the sand — Springbrook and Tamborine behind the Gold Coast, the Blackall Range behind the Sunshine — waterfalls, lookouts and Sunday-drive villages. The Scenic Rim Brisbane’s crater-rim backdrop — national parks, farm gates and lodge weekends an hour from the city. Fraser / K’gari The world’s largest sand island — four-wheel-drive beaches, perched lakes and dingo country, off Hervey Bay. The outback Longreach’s stockman history, dinosaur country at Winton, and night skies worth the drive — the state’s other half, one proper road trip a year.

chunks.t: Weekends in Queensland: reef, rainforest and the coast
chunks.x: Tourism Queensland.com The state’s official visitor site — regions, the reef and what’s on. Outdoors Queensland National Parks Tracks, camping permits and alerts — K’gari and the islands book out early. The city Visit Brisbane Events, festivals and the river city’s calendar. Practical Translink SEQ journey planning, the Go Card and the flat-fare scheme. That’s the guide Nine chapters on Queensland. Everything national — Medicare, visas, registration, tax, super, schools — lives once in Moving to Australia . When you’re ready to look at roles, see what’s open now . Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Moving to Queensland: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.x: Queensland is the state Australians themselves move to: winter sun, beaches that work all year, and housing that still lets an ordinary salary buy an ordinary house. For clinicians it adds the country’s fastest-growing health demand — and a decentralised system that means real careers far beyond the capital.

chunks.t: Moving to Queensland: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.h: The state people move to on purpose
chunks.x: Brisbane holds around two and a half million people and has grown out of its big-country-town reputation into a confident river city — a rebuilt centre, a strong hospital cluster, and the 2032 Olympics on the calendar. An hour south, the Gold Coast is Australia’s sixth-largest city and its most famous beach strip; an hour north, the Sunshine Coast pairs surf towns with one of the newest hospital precincts in the country. Then the state keeps going — for two thousand kilometres. Townsville and Cairns anchor the tropical north; Toowoomba sits atop the range inland; Rockhampton, Mackay and Bundaberg serve the long central coast. Queensland is the most decentralised state in Australia: one person in two lives outside the capital’s orbit, and the health system is built to match. The costs are heat and distance.

chunks.t: Moving to Queensland: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.h: The state people move to on purpose
chunks.x: Summer is hot and humid everywhere and properly tropical in the north, with a real cyclone season; and the state’s size means the far-flung postings are far. But the value case is the strongest of the big three states: south-east Queensland delivers coast-city life at prices Sydney and Melbourne stopped offering a decade ago. Who wrote this Ethicare is a healthcare recruitment company. This guide is free to read, asks nothing of you, and does not give visa advice. Queensland is where we send the most families, and the state where "which part?" matters most — Brisbane and Cairns are as different as London and Lisbon. Where we think it’s the wrong answer, we say so.

chunks.t: Moving to Queensland: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.x: ~5.6M People, in Australia’s most decentralised state — nearly half live outside greater Brisbane. ~2.5M In Greater Brisbane — the river city, rebuilt and growing toward its 2032 Olympics. 120+ Public hospitals across sixteen hospital and health services — the most geographically spread system in the country. ~7,000 km Of coastline, from the NSW border to the Cape — with the Great Barrier Reef offshore for 2,300 of them. ~650,000 On the Gold Coast — Australia’s sixth-largest city, an hour south of Brisbane by road or rail. ~400,000 On the Sunshine Coast, with one of Australia’s newest hospital precincts. 300+ Days of sunshine a year in the south-east. Winter is the season people move here for. UTC+10 No daylight saving — Queensland opts out. Summer evenings run earlier than the southern states’. 2032 The Brisbane Olympics — a decade of hospital, transport and housing investment already under way.

chunks.t: Moving to Queensland: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.h: Six things you only learn once you’re here
chunks.x: Winter is the payoff Twenty-two degrees, dry and blue, June through August — while Melbourne shivers. It resets what you think a year feels like, and it is why the southerners keep arriving. Summer is the price Hot, humid and stormy in the south-east; monsoonal in the north. Air conditioning is infrastructure, the afternoon storm is theatre, and January errands happen before ten. No daylight saving is a real thing Summer light from 4.45am, dark by seven. Early starts come naturally; long summer evenings don’t. Queenslanders vote to keep it this way and enjoy the argument. "Queensland" is several places The south-east corner is one life; the tropical north another; the outback west a third. The state is a direction, not a destination — choose your hundred kilometres. The regions carry real hospitals Townsville and Cairns run tertiary-level services a full day’s drive from Brisbane.

chunks.t: Moving to Queensland: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.h: Six things you only learn once you’re here
chunks.x: Regional Queensland is not a compromise posting; it is where much of the state’s medicine happens. Cyclone season is managed, not mythical North of about Bundaberg, November to April brings watches and the occasional real one. Building codes, warning systems and local habits are built around it — take the induction seriously. A note on Country Queensland spans hundreds of Aboriginal nations — Yuggera and Turrbal around Brisbane, Kombumerri on the Gold Coast, Yidinji and Djabugay in the far north — and the Torres Strait Islands, whose peoples are a distinct First Nations culture. Torres Strait Islander health is a significant part of the state’s system, particularly in the north. Acknowledgement of Country opens meetings, and health services work in partnership with community-controlled organisations. Take the cultural induction seriously; in the north it is central to the job.

chunks.t: Moving to Queensland: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.x: Nine chapters, all of them about Queensland specifically. Anything true of Australia generally — Medicare, visas, Ahpra registration, tax, superannuation, schools — lives once in Moving to Australia . If you read nothing else, read Why Queensland for the full case — and what we’d ask you to weigh, and Where clinicians live , because the south-east corner and the tropical north are decisions of a completely different kind. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Why Queensland: the case for the sunshine state
chunks.x: Queensland’s case is the one Australians vote for with removal trucks: the same national salary buys more house, more sunshine and more weekend here than in either of the bigger states. The counterweights are summer, storms and sheer distance.

chunks.t: Why Queensland: the case for the sunshine state
chunks.x: Public-sector clinical pay is set by state awards, and we don’t quote figures until we’ve verified them against the current instruments. The structure is what matters: Queensland pay is broadly comparable with the southern states, while south-east Queensland housing runs clearly below Sydney and visibly below Melbourne. That gap is the state’s whole pitch, and it survives the recent boom — narrower than it was, still real. Go regional and the multiplier stacks: Townsville, Cairns, Mackay, Rockhampton and Bundaberg price family homes at a fraction of the south-east, and the further and more remote the posting, the stronger the incentives attached. Queensland is where the regional package system works hardest, because the state needs it most. What you trade: summers that ask something of you, a cyclone season in the north, and distances that make "popping down to Sydney" a flight, always.

chunks.t: Why Queensland: the case for the sunshine state
chunks.x: Monday to Friday Brisbane: 25–45 minutes, train or busway if you’re wise. Gold or Sunshine Coast: 15–25. Regional cities: ten, with parking. Before work The 5am beach swim or river run — the no-daylight-saving dawn makes early exercise a mass habit, not a virtue. After work Winter: barbecue weather all through July. Summer: the pool, the aircon, and the 4pm storm rolling in like scheduled entertainment. Saturday Nippers or netball in the morning, markets after, the beach or the river the rest. The outdoor family weekend is the state’s default setting. Sunday Hinterland waterfalls, a national park, the bay islands — or in the north, the reef, which stops feeling like a bucket-list item and becomes a day out. School holidays You live where the rest of the country goes on holiday. Visitors will find you; budget for the spare room being popular.

chunks.t: Why Queensland: the case for the sunshine state
chunks.h: The six things people ask us
chunks.x: Is there enough work? The fastest-growing demand in the country. The south-east corridor is adding population — and hospital capacity — faster than anywhere in Australia, and the regional services recruit constantly, often with incentives. Healthcare in Queensland explains the sixteen hospital and health services and where the depth sits. Can I buy a house? Yes — and this is the state where that answer is still straightforward. Middle-ring Brisbane, most of the coasts and all the regional cities remain buyable on clinical incomes, singly or jointly. Cost of living runs the numbers, including where the boom has bitten. How bad is summer, really? The south-east: hot, humid, stormy — think six warm months with a sweaty core, made civilised by air conditioning and pools. The north: properly tropical, with a wet season and a cyclone watch.

chunks.t: Why Queensland: the case for the sunshine state
chunks.h: The six things people ask us
chunks.x: People acclimatise faster than they expect; the ones who struggle are those who pretended it wasn’t real. Winter is the repayment, everywhere. Brisbane, Gold Coast or Sunshine Coast? Brisbane for the deepest job market and the river-city life; the Gold Coast for beach-city energy and a big, busy health precinct of its own; the Sunshine Coast for the family-scaled version with a brand-new hospital spine. They’re an hour apart — plenty of clinicians live in one and never regret not choosing the others, and some commute between. Where clinicians live compares all three properly. What about the tropical north? Townsville and Cairns are major centres: tertiary-level hospitals, the reef and rainforest at weekends, a strong international workforce, and Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health careers.

chunks.t: Why Queensland: the case for the sunshine state
chunks.h: The six things people ask us
chunks.x: The trades are the wet season, the distance south, and communities that take a season to open up — then hold you properly. Is it good with children? Arguably the best of the big states: space, sport, beaches, and an outdoor childhood that runs all year. The notes: summer school runs are sweaty, pool fencing is law and vigilance, and if you’re on a temporary visa, read the master’s School fees on a visa chapter before budgeting.

chunks.t: Why Queensland: the case for the sunshine state
chunks.x: You’d wilt in the humidity If a sticky February sounds unbearable, believe yourself. Victoria and the southern coasts exist. You want the deepest subspecialty pool Brisbane’s is strong and growing; Sydney’s and Melbourne’s are deeper. Quaternary careers may still point south. Big-city culture is the point Brisbane’s scene is good now and still a size down. If nightly theatre and headline acts matter most, the southern capitals win. Cyclone season would keep you up North of Bundaberg it is a real annual rhythm. If that maths doesn’t sit, stay south-east — or south. Family is elsewhere The eternal rule: proximity to your people beats sunshine. Perth is five hours; Auckland is four. Where we’d steer you instead Want the biggest market and the harbour? New South Wales . Want the culture city at a discount? Victoria .

chunks.t: Why Queensland: the case for the sunshine state
chunks.x: Weighing the Tasman? The master’s Australia vs New Zealand chapter is the place to start. In our experience Queensland suits clinicians who want the salary to buy a life, not just a postcode — and who’d rather spend winter outdoors. Our one firm piece of advice: visit in February before you commit, not July. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Cost of living in South Australia: the value capital, audited
chunks.x: The picture is a happy one, so let’s audit it anyway. Adelaide is the most affordable mainland capital, the regions cost less again — and there are three costs the sunshine hides that deserve to be weighed before you commit.

chunks.t: Cost of living in South Australia: the value capital, audited
chunks.x: We used to print a weekly rent and a monthly budget table here. We have taken them out. A figure that was true when a page was written is misleading a year later, and a candidate who plans a move around a stale number is worse off than one who plans around none. What does not go stale is the relationship between places — which suburb, ring or region you choose — and the judgement about which costs catch people out. For today’s actual numbers use the calculators at the foot of the page, and use them to compare it against the city you are leaving. That is the only comparison that decides anything.

chunks.t: Cost of living in South Australia: the value capital, audited
chunks.x: What doesn’t change is the relationship: like-for-like housing runs hundreds of dollars a week below Sydney and well below Melbourne, and it is housing that decides whether a salary feels big.

chunks.t: Cost of living in South Australia: the value capital, audited
chunks.x: The costs the sunshine hides Adelaide is the most affordable mainland capital and the regions cost less again. These three lines are the ones worth pricing before you commit — none of them shows up in a rent comparison. Power SA electricity is among the dearest in the country, and summer cooling is non-negotiable. An efficient home and a deliberately chosen energy plan are worth real money a year — compare retailers before you sign anything. The car you’ll probably own Inner-ring and tram-corridor life can be car-free; most SA lives aren’t. Price a reliable used car, registration and insurance into your arrival budget rather than discovering it in month two. Flights east If your people are in Sydney, Melbourne or overseas via the east, visits mean flights. Two or three trips a year is where most families settle — budget it.

chunks.t: Cost of living in South Australia: the value capital, audited
chunks.x: The rent gap against the eastern capitals is the big one — for many households it covers the whole grocery bill. The small ones accumulate: no tolls, cheap parking by capital standards, commutes short enough to save childcare hours, the Central Market beating supermarket prices on produce, and the 10-cent container deposit quietly funding the coffee habit. On the income side, public-health and not-for-profit roles here can salary-package part of your pay before tax — in a lower-cost city the effect on real quality of life is significant, and many international staff don’t set it up until far too late. How packaging, tax and superannuation work is national and lives in Pay & conditions ; the SA habit to copy is simply asking payroll about it on day one.

chunks.t: Cost of living in South Australia: the value capital, audited
chunks.x: The bottom line Plan the bridge, not just the destination: temporary accommodation, a bond of up to four weeks’ rent plus up to two weeks in advance, a first car, and setting up a home. In Adelaide that bridge costs far less than in the eastern capitals — but the people who arrive calm are the ones who priced it anyway. Get today’s numbers, and compare them to home These are live and updated continuously. Put the city you are leaving in the other box. Numbeo cost-of-living calculator — the most complete comparison tool, and the one most clinicians already use. Crowd-sourced, so treat it as a ballpark. Expatistan — the same idea with a cleaner side-by-side. Worth running as a sanity check when Numbeo looks off. Australian Bureau of Statistics — official and slower, and the one to trust on the direction of travel. If what you find differs from what we say here, tell us and we will correct it. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Food, wine & the everyday in South Australia
chunks.x: South Australia’s everyday food culture runs through one building: the Central Market, trading since 1869 in the middle of the city grid. Around it sit the fiercely local supermarket, the surviving corner deli, and — because this is SA — the assumption that decent wine is a grocery, not a luxury.

chunks.t: Food, wine & the everyday in South Australia
chunks.h: The Market and the weekly shop
chunks.x: The Adelaide Central Market is one of the best fresh-food markets in the country — seventy-odd stalls of produce, cheese, seafood, bread and world cuisines under one roof, cheaper and better than the supermarkets for most of what matters. Hospital staff treat Thursday evening or early Saturday as the serious shopping windows; go late Saturday afternoon for the closing-time bargains. For the rest: Woolworths and Coles run full-range stores everywhere, ALDI is the cheapest weekly shop, and the local pride is real — Drakes and Foodland are South Australian institutions, and in the regional towns the independent grocer still anchors the main street. The corner deli — part milk bar, part grocer, part sandwich counter — survives in Adelaide as it does nowhere else in the country. Bring your bags SA was the first state to ban lightweight plastic bags, and the checkout assumes you came prepared.

chunks.t: Food, wine & the everyday in South Australia
chunks.h: The Market and the weekly shop
chunks.x: Save your bottles The 10-cent container deposit has run since 1977. A crate in the boot and a monthly depot run is a local rhythm. Farmers’ markets Willunga on Saturday morning is the flagship; the Hills, Barossa and regional towns all keep their own. The fritz order At the deli counter, fritz and sauce on white bread is the childhood taste of the state. Order it once, for citizenship.

chunks.t: Food, wine & the everyday in South Australia
chunks.x: For its size, Adelaide feeds its communities well. The western suburbs carry the Italian and Greek heritage — delis, continental grocers, the long Sunday lunch; the north and north-east are the centre of gravity for Asian, African and Middle-Eastern groceries; halal butchers are easy to find across the northern suburbs; and kosher supplies, while more limited than Sydney or Melbourne, are available through the long-established community in the east. The Market fills most gaps in one visit. In the regional centres the range narrows — a good independent grocer, a local butcher, sometimes a specialist aisle. Families in the Riverland, the South-East and on the gulfs tend to stock up on city trips or order online, and it works better than newcomers expect.

chunks.t: Food, wine & the everyday in South Australia
chunks.x: Adelaide eats above its weight. The laneway small-bar scene — Peel Street, Leigh Street and their neighbours — arrived a decade ago and stayed; the pub is still the default meeting place; and the cellar doors of McLaren Vale, the Hills and the Barossa double as the state’s best long lunches, forty minutes to an hour from town. Coffee is taken seriously without Melbourne’s theology about it. The heritage list is cheerfully odd: the pie floater — a meat pie upturned in pea soup — is the late-night institution, fritz is the deli order, and every March the whole food city moves outdoors into the festival gardens. Eating out costs noticeably less than Sydney; the wine list is where SA quietly shows off. The everyday, in one list Serious shop: Central Market Thursday evening or Saturday morning; supermarkets for the rest.

chunks.t: Food, wine & the everyday in South Australia
chunks.x: Cheapest basket: ALDI; local loyalty: Drakes and Foodland; regional towns: the independent. Specialist ingredients: west for Italian and Greek, north and north-east for Asian, African, Middle-Eastern and halal. Bags in the car, bottles in a crate, fritz at least once. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: South Australia at a glance: geography, climate & the half-hour clock
chunks.x: Before the practical chapters, orientation. South Australia is the driest state on the driest inhabited continent, and it divides — for a newcomer’s purposes — into three quite different places sharing one capital, one climate pattern and one eccentric clock.

chunks.t: South Australia at a glance: geography, climate & the half-hour clock
chunks.x: Where Adelaide sits, with the straight-line distance to Mount Gambier

chunks.t: South Australia at a glance: geography, climate & the half-hour clock
chunks.x: The capital, the Hills behind it, the Barossa and Clare to the north, McLaren Vale and the Fleurieu Peninsula to the south. Nine in ten of the state’s health jobs sit inside this circle, and nearly everything in it is within an hour of everything else. If you take a city post, this ring is your whole life map — beaches, vines, hills and wards.

chunks.t: South Australia at a glance: geography, climate & the half-hour clock
chunks.x: The Limestone Coast runs to the Victorian border — the coolest, wettest, greenest corner of the state, built on pine forests, vineyards and dairy country around the state’s largest regional city with its famous volcanic Blue Lake. It looks and feels closer to rural Victoria than to the outback, and its referral hospital serves a wide catchment.

chunks.t: South Australia at a glance: geography, climate & the half-hour clock
chunks.x: North and west of Adelaide the country opens out: the Yorke Peninsula’s quiet farming coast, the industrial towns of the Upper Spencer Gulf betting big on steel and hydrogen, the Eyre Peninsula’s seafood ports facing the Southern Ocean, and beyond them the Flinders Ranges and the arid far north, where health care runs on small teams, aviation and telehealth.

chunks.t: South Australia at a glance: geography, climate & the half-hour clock
chunks.x: The climate is Mediterranean: hot, dry summers and mild, green winters, with the rain arriving May to September. Summer brings real heatwaves — runs of days past 40° most years — which end, theatrically, with a cool change rolling in off the Southern Ocean. The Hills sit several degrees cooler and greener; the South-East is the mildest corner; the far north is properly arid. Summer Dec – Feb 17–29° Dry heat · 40° runs Autumn Mar – May 12–23° Mad March · vintage Winter Jun – Aug 8–16° Cool, green, wet Spring Sep – Nov 11–22° Jacarandas · festivals Two practical notes. Older housing stock often has thin insulation and patchy heating — make a good split system a rental-search criterion, for both ends of the year. And take the heat itself seriously: hydration, sun protection and a plan for very hot days matter, especially with children or older family members.

chunks.t: South Australia at a glance: geography, climate & the half-hour clock
chunks.x: South Australia runs on Australian Central Standard Time — UTC+9½, thirty minutes behind Sydney and Melbourne — and, unlike Queensland, it does observe daylight saving, becoming UTC+10½ each summer. The practical effects are small but constant: national meetings land at five past the half-hour, broadcast times shift, and Perth sits ninety minutes behind you in winter. You adjust within a month; your phone adjusts instantly.

chunks.t: South Australia at a glance: geography, climate & the half-hour clock
chunks.x: Adelaide Airport is unusually close to the city — about fifteen minutes from the CBD, on the way to the beach. It flies direct to every Australian capital and to a handful of international hubs, so most of the world is one stop away; and regional services reach Port Lincoln, Whyalla, Mount Gambier and Kangaroo Island. Melbourne is a day’s drive down the coast or up the highway; everywhere else east is a flight.

chunks.t: South Australia at a glance: geography, climate & the half-hour clock
chunks.h: Words you’ll hear in week one
chunks.x: Tarntanya Kaurna name for the Adelaide Plains — “place of the red kangaroo”; widely used in dual naming Mad March The month the Fringe, Festival, WOMADelaide and the motorsport all happen at once The cool change The southerly front that ends a heatwave — you can feel the temperature drop ten degrees in minutes Stobie pole SA’s concrete-and-steel power pole, invented here because termites eat wooden ones Fritz The luncheon sausage every SA childhood runs on — ask for it at the deli, on white bread with sauce Heaps good High praise, delivered flat. The state’s unofficial motto The Riverland The Murray River fruit-and-wine country in the state’s east Pie floater A meat pie upturned in pea soup — a heritage-listed Adelaide late-night institution Prefer it on paper?
