chunks.x: Monday to Friday Fifteen minutes to the hospital from most of the city. Home in daylight for most of the year. Wednesday A run or a ride on the riverside paths, which stretch for kilometres in both directions from the centre. Friday Dinner in the centre or in Cambridge, fifteen minutes down the expressway and a completely different evening. Saturday Raglan for the surf, Hamilton Gardens for the morning, or an hour’s drive to the caves, the lake or the coast. Sunday Slow. Markets, the river, and the kind of afternoon that is hard to have in a bigger city.

chunks.t: Why the Waikato: the case for the heartland
chunks.h: The six things people ask us
chunks.x: Is the tertiary hospital a serious place to work? Yes. It is a tertiary centre serving the central North Island — roughly a million people from the Coromandel to the King Country and across to the Bay of Plenty for some services. That catchment gives a mid-sized city a case mix and complexity that its population alone would not generate. Chapter four covers what that means day to day. Isn’t Hamilton just an Auckland overflow town? It has grown fast partly because of Auckland’s prices, and the expressway made the commute possible for some. But it is a real city with its own university, hospital, arts scene and identity, and most people who live here work here. The comparison locals resent is being treated as a suburb of somewhere else. How close is Auckland, really? About ninety minutes to the southern edge on the expressway, closer to two hours to the city centre.

chunks.t: Why the Waikato: the case for the heartland
chunks.h: The six things people ask us
chunks.x: Close enough for a concert, an international flight or a specialist appointment; far enough that you are not accidentally living an Auckland life at Waikato prices. What about the fog? Real, and worth knowing about. The Waikato basin gets still, cold mornings in autumn and winter where fog sits until mid-morning. It affects driving and occasionally flights from Hamilton Airport. Most people stop noticing after a year; a few find the grey stretches wearing. Is it a good place with children? It is one of the best in the country for it. Space, gardens, short commutes, a full range of schooling, and both beaches and mountains within a couple of hours. The household budget stretches a long way. As everywhere in New Zealand, check school zones before you sign a lease — Schools & education explains how zoning works. Will I be bored? it depends what you want.

chunks.t: Why the Waikato: the case for the heartland
chunks.h: The six things people ask us
chunks.x: Hamilton has good food, decent live music and a university crowd, but it is not Wellington and it is not Auckland. What it has instead is reach — Raglan, the Coromandel, Rotorua, Taupō, Waitomo and the mountains are all inside two hours. People who fill their weekends love it here; people who want a Tuesday night out sometimes don’t.

chunks.t: Why the Waikato: the case for the heartland
chunks.x: It is not a beautiful city Hamilton’s setting is lovely and its architecture largely is not. People arriving from older cities find the streetscape underwhelming, and some never get past it. Auckland’s gravity Being ninety minutes away means some people treat the Waikato as a dormitory rather than a home. If you spend every weekend in Auckland, you will not settle here. Winter is grey and damp Not cold, but persistently overcast and often foggy. The Waikato winter is milder than the South Island’s and considerably less bright. You will need a car Public transport within Hamilton is workable; getting anywhere else in the region is not. Most households run two cars. The region is big and the work spreads out If your role covers rural sites, the driving is real. Some people find it the most rewarding part of the job; others find it wearing.

chunks.t: Why the Waikato: the case for the heartland
chunks.x: Where we’d steer you instead Want the same value with a coastline? Bay of Plenty or Hawke’s Bay . Want a compact, walkable city? Wellington . Want the widest range of roles? Auckland — ninety minutes up the expressway, and a very different proposition. Who it suits Clinicians who want tertiary complexity and rural breadth in the same job, families who want a house and a garden, and anyone who values being an hour and a half from almost everything in the upper North Island. In our experience The Waikato suits clinicians who want the rare combination — tertiary referral work and rural medicine inside the same week. Hamilton doesn’t sell itself hard, which is exactly why the people who move here on the numbers tend to stay on the life. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Cost of living in Wellington for healthcare professionals
chunks.x: Same salary as Auckland, meaningfully lower rent — and one bill that will surprise you in July.

chunks.t: Cost of living in Wellington for healthcare professionals
chunks.x: We used to print a weekly rent and a monthly budget table here. We have taken them out. A figure that was true when a page was written is misleading a year later, and a candidate who plans a move around a stale number is worse off than one who plans around none. What does not go stale is the shape of a month, and the judgement about which lines will surprise you. For today’s actual numbers use the calculators at the foot of the page, and use them to compare Wellington against the city you are leaving. That is the only comparison that decides anything. Because clinical pay sits on national collective agreements, your gross salary here is identical to Auckland’s. Housing costs less. That gap is the quiet financial case for Wellington, and it doesn’t appear on any job advertisement.

chunks.t: Cost of living in Wellington for healthcare professionals
chunks.x: Indicative New Zealand dollars per month as at July 2026, for a household living moderately. Your own numbers will differ — treat this as a shape to sanity-check against, not a quote. Single clinician, inner suburb Rent is over half of it. Everything else put together is smaller than the roof over your head — which is exactly why the Wellington rent gap matters more than any other line here. Rent 54% Food & groceries 54% Metlink, or a car 14% Everyday life 10% Power, winter 10% Internet 9% Mobile 3% The line that decides it Rent · 54% Bar widths are proportions of the month, not amounts. In summer the power line roughly halves, and the whole month eases with it. Excludes tax, KiwiSaver, student loan repayments, a deposit and flights home. Money, tax & banking works out what lands in your account.

chunks.t: Cost of living in Wellington for healthcare professionals
chunks.h: The one bill that catches everyone out
chunks.x: Your power bill in July can be two or three times what it was in February. This isn’t a New Zealand pricing quirk — it’s what happens when a poorly insulated timber house meets a cold, damp winter and a heat pump running most of the day. People arriving in summer sign a lease based on a February bill, then get a July one and think something has gone wrong. Nothing has. Budget for the winter figure from the start and treat the summer months as the discount. The same house, six months apart Baseline February 2–3× The July jump 2–3× July Column heights are to scale, using the midpoint of each range. A well-insulated house narrows the gap considerably — which is the whole argument for the checklist below. Five ways to keep it down Prioritise insulation and double glazing when you choose a house, above almost every other feature. It’s worth more than a second bathroom.

chunks.t: Cost of living in Wellington for healthcare professionals
chunks.h: The one bill that catches everyone out
chunks.x: Ask for the Healthy Homes compliance statement on any rental — landlords must meet minimum heating and insulation standards. Buy a dehumidifier in your first month. It costs less to run than heating damp air, and it protects your belongings from mould. Compare retailers properly — the market is competitive and switching is easy. Powerswitch is the free comparison tool people use. Heat the room you’re in and shut the door. Whole-house heating is rare and expensive here.

chunks.t: Cost of living in Wellington for healthcare professionals
chunks.x: Unfurnished here can mean empty — no fridge, no washing machine, sometimes no curtains. Budget for the first fortnight properly. What the first fortnight costs Bars are to scale against each other, so you can see where the money goes before you’ve bought a kettle. Bond & rent in advance Four weeks’ bond plus two weeks’ rent, up front. The single largest thing to have ready. 1× Whiteware Fridge, washing machine, sometimes a dryer. Second-hand from Trade Me is normal and unsnobbish. ~0.4× Heating & drying A dehumidifier and a decent heater. In Wellington these aren’t optional. ~0.1× Then a car, if you need one — reliable is affordable here, thanks to the used Japanese import market. It sits off this scale because it dwarfs everything else on it. See Driving & licences .

chunks.t: Cost of living in Wellington for healthcare professionals
chunks.x: Rent The big one. A three-bedroom house in a good Wellington suburb costs meaningfully less than the Auckland equivalent, on identical pay. Commuting Shorter distances, less fuel, and the option to run one car instead of two. Parking & tolls No motorway tolls, and if you walk to work the whole line disappears.

chunks.t: Cost of living in Wellington for healthcare professionals
chunks.x: Power in winter The one line where Wellington costs more than Auckland, and the one people forget. Flights Every long-haul trip carries a connection through Auckland or Sydney. Budget for it. Get today’s numbers, and compare them to home These are live and updated continuously. Put the city you are leaving in the other box. Numbeo cost-of-living calculator — the most complete comparison tool, and the one most clinicians already use. Crowd-sourced, so treat it as a ballpark. Expatistan — the same idea with a cleaner side-by-side. Worth running as a sanity check when Numbeo looks off. Tenancy Services market rent — official bond-lodgement data by area, and the most reliable rent figure in New Zealand. Stats NZ — official and slower, and the one to trust on the direction of travel. If what you find differs from what we say here, tell us and we will correct it. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Food and coffee in Wellington: where the culture started
chunks.x: New Zealand’s coffee culture started here and the city has never got over it. More cafés and bars per head than New York, in a place you can walk across.

chunks.t: Food and coffee in Wellington: where the culture started
chunks.h: The city that taught New Zealand to drink coffee
chunks.x: In the late 1980s a handful of Wellington roasters started taking espresso seriously, and the habit spread outward from here to the rest of the country. The roastery names are local institutions, and most cafés will tell you whose beans they pull without being asked. The practical consequence for you is that mediocre coffee is hard to find, and that your morning flat white becomes a small daily pleasure rather than a transaction. It also means Wellingtonians are insufferable about it, and you’ll become one within about four months. The claim, and it holds up 300 + Cafés, bars and restaurants in the centre More per head than New York, inside a centre you can walk across in twenty minutes. It is why a flat white here is a daily pleasure rather than a transaction — and why nobody in this city will let you drink a bad one quietly. 1980s When the roasteries started NZ$5.50 A flat white, roughly 1 hr 15 To the Martinborough vineyards

chunks.t: Food and coffee in Wellington: where the culture started
chunks.h: The vocabulary, so your first order goes smoothly
chunks.x: Not a joke section. The words differ from the UK, the US and the Gulf, and getting them right on day one saves a small daily awkwardness. Flat white Espresso with steamed milk, less foam than a latte, in a smaller cup. The default order. Long black Closest to an Americano — espresso poured over hot water, in that order. Short black An espresso. Ask for a double if you want a double. Trim Skim milk. "Trim flat white" is a complete order. Fluffy Warm frothed milk with chocolate dust, for small children. Usually free. Takeaway Not "to go". Bring your own cup and you’ll usually get a small discount. Three local habits Bring your own cup. A reusable cup is completely normal here and usually earns a discount. Some cafés run cup-lending schemes. It’s the local default rather than a statement. No tipping.

chunks.t: Food and coffee in Wellington: where the culture started
chunks.h: The vocabulary, so your first order goes smoothly
chunks.x: Hospitality staff are paid a proper wage and tipping isn’t expected anywhere — cafés, restaurants or taxis. Kitchens close early. Cafés often stop serving food mid-afternoon, and many kitchens close by nine. If you finish a late shift hungry, learn which places serve late before you need them.

chunks.t: Food and coffee in Wellington: where the culture started
chunks.h: Six parts of the city, six different evenings
chunks.x: Districts rather than individual restaurants — places change, and Sophie’s own list is coming. This is what each part of town is for. Cuba Street The heart of it. Independent, scruffy, excellent — bars, cheap eats, live music and the best people-watching in the country. Go for a long evening that starts without a plan. Courtenay Place Louder and later. Theatres at one end, bars along the length, and where the city goes after a show. Go for a Friday. The waterfront & Queens Wharf Harbour-edge dining and the walk home along the water. Go for a summer evening or when family visit. Newtown The most diverse eating in Wellington — Ethiopian, Malaysian, Middle Eastern, and the grocers that supply them. Go for something you can’t get anywhere else. Hannahs Laneway A short lane of small producers — chocolate, coffee roasting, cheese. Go on a Saturday morning.

chunks.t: Food and coffee in Wellington: where the culture started
chunks.h: Six parts of the city, six different evenings
chunks.x: The Hutt & Petone Jackson Street’s strip of cafés and restaurants, and increasingly where the interesting new places open. Go when you want somewhere the city hasn’t found yet. Awaiting Sophie’s list Named recommendations are coming. This is her own list — specific cafés, bars and the walk to do after Sunday brunch.

chunks.t: Food and coffee in Wellington: where the culture started
chunks.x: The supermarkets Pak’nSave for the bulk shop, New World for the fresh counters, Woolworths for delivery. The same two groups as the rest of the country — see the Auckland chapter for how they differ. Harbourside Market Sunday mornings by Te Papa. Produce, fish and coffee, and the closest thing the city has to a weekly ritual. Newtown & Kilbirnie Specialist grocers for South Asian, Middle Eastern, East Asian and Pacific ingredients, usually cheaper than the chains for anything you buy in quantity. Moore Wilson’s The wholesaler the city’s chefs use, open to everyone. Worth one trip just to see the scale of it.

chunks.t: Food and coffee in Wellington: where the culture started
chunks.x: Over the Remutaka Hill sits the Wairarapa, and at its centre Martinborough — a village surrounded by vineyards, small enough to cycle between them in an afternoon. Martinborough An hour and fifteen minutes by car, or the train to Featherston and a short hop. Pinot noir, cellar doors within cycling distance of the square, and the classic Wellington weekend. Greytown & Carterton On the way. Bakeries, antiques and a slower afternoon than you planned. Marlborough Three hours by ferry across the strait. A serious wine region and a good long weekend. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Wellington at a glance: the harbour, the hills and the wind
chunks.x: A harbour in a drowned river valley, ringed by hills, sitting on a plate boundary at the windiest point in the country. The geography explains almost everything about this city.

chunks.t: Wellington at a glance: the harbour, the hills and the wind
chunks.h: Everything here is explained by the hills and the strait
chunks.x: Where Wellington sits, with the straight-line distance to Masterton Wellington sits at the southern tip of the North Island, on a harbour formed when a river valley flooded. Steep hills rise directly from the water on three sides, and Cook Strait — a forty-kilometre gap between two mountainous islands — opens to the south. That single arrangement produces the compact walkable centre, the houses stacked up hillsides with a hundred steps to the door, the absence of motorways through town, the four rail lines threading up the only flat corridors, and the wind. Understand the geography and the rest of this guide reads as consequence. The harbour A deep natural port that made the city and still runs it. Oriental Bay for swimming, the waterfront promenade for walking, Matiu / Somes Island in the middle.

chunks.t: Wellington at a glance: the harbour, the hills and the wind
chunks.h: Everything here is explained by the hills and the strait
chunks.x: The town belt A ring of protected bush and open land encircling the inner city, set aside in the 1840s. It’s why a capital city has native forest fifteen minutes from most front doors. The south coast Wild, exposed and facing Antarctica. Lyall Bay for surf, Island Bay for families, Red Rocks for a seal colony an hour’s walk from the road end. Two valleys north The Hutt Valley and the western corridor to Porirua — the only flat land in the region, which is where the rail lines, the motorways and most of the family housing went.

chunks.t: Wellington at a glance: the harbour, the hills and the wind
chunks.x: People say Wellington and mean the city. The region is larger, and which part you live in changes your rent, your commute and your weekends considerably. Four Wellingtons, by how far they are from work Same salary in all four. What changes is your rent, your commute and what you do on a Saturday — which is the whole decision, compressed into one chart. Wellington City The compact centre and the hill suburbs around it. Walkable, characterful, the highest rents in the region. Suits people who want to walk to work. 10 min The Hutt Valley Lower and Upper Hutt, by train. Flat land, family houses, gardens, considerably better value, and its own hospital. Suits families who want space. 20 – 40 min Porirua & the western corridor North by rail. Diverse, well-served by trains, strong Pacific and Māori communities, and among the best value in the region. 25 min Kāpiti Coast Beaches, a slower pace and a commuter rail line. Suits people trading commute for coastline. 45 – 60 min Rail and road times to the central city at peak. Off-peak is quicker; a southerly is not.

chunks.t: Wellington at a glance: the harbour, the hills and the wind
chunks.h: Mild, changeable, and windier than anywhere you’ve lived
chunks.x: The temperature range here is narrow. Winters rarely freeze and summers rarely get properly hot — a mean around thirteen degrees, and a good summer day in the low twenties. If you’re coming from northern Europe the winters will feel mild; from the Middle East or India, the summers will feel cool. The wind is the real story. Cook Strait funnels air between two mountain ranges, and Wellington sits in the gap. 173 days a year see gusts above sixty-three kilometres an hour. It isn’t constant — there are still, golden days that are among the best anywhere — but it’s frequent enough to shape how people dress, where they park and which side of the harbour they choose to live on. Two winds to learn The northerly is warm, blustery and persistent. The southerly comes off Antarctica, drops the temperature several degrees within an hour, and closes the airport.

chunks.t: Wellington at a glance: the harbour, the hills and the wind
chunks.h: Mild, changeable, and windier than anywhere you’ve lived
chunks.x: Locals check which one is coming the way people elsewhere check rain. The year Summer Dec – Feb The best of it. Long evenings, swimming at Oriental Bay, and the northerly rather than the southerly. Still not reliably hot — bring a jumper to a January barbecue. Autumn Mar – May Often the finest weather of the year — settled, warm, calmer than summer. Locals will tell you autumn is when Wellington is at its best, and they’re right. Winter Jun – Aug Wet, windy and dark by half past five. The houses matter more than the forecast — see Renting in New Zealand for what to check at a viewing. Spring Sep – Nov Changeable and blustery, with the first properly good days arriving in October. Spring here is a negotiation rather than a season. A mean around thirteen degrees, and a good summer day in the low twenties. From northern Europe the winters will feel mild; from the Middle East or India, the summers will feel cool.

chunks.t: Wellington at a glance: the harbour, the hills and the wind
chunks.x: Wellington sits on a plate boundary and everyone knows it. You’ll feel small earthquakes; most people stop noticing within a year. What that means in practice Buildings are engineered for it, and the standards are among the strictest anywhere. Newer and strengthened buildings are safe. Ask about a building’s seismic rating when you rent or buy — it’s a normal question here, not a rude one. Sort a grab bag and stored water in week one, then stop thinking about it. That’s what locals do.

chunks.t: Wellington at a glance: the harbour, the hills and the wind
chunks.x: Te Whanganui-a-Tara — the great harbour of Tara. Taranaki Whānui and Ngāti Toa Rangatira are the mana whenua of the region, and both are visible in the city’s institutions, place names and the way the health service works. You’ll hear te reo daily, in meetings and on signage. What that means at work — pronunciation, the words you’ll hear on the ward, Te Tiriti and marae etiquette — is national, and covered in Te ao Māori at work . Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Healthcare in Wellington: the hospitals and the catchment
chunks.x: A tertiary hospital serving the lower half of the North Island, ten minutes from the harbour — and the national health bodies down the road. How the New Zealand system is funded and organised nationally is covered in How the health system works . This chapter is Wellington specifically.

chunks.t: Healthcare in Wellington: the hospitals and the catchment
chunks.h: A small city doing tertiary work for a large region
chunks.x: This is the thing that surprises clinicians most about Wellington. The city is modest — around 215,000 people, 440,000 across the region — but the region’s tertiary hospital serves the lower North Island and parts of the upper South Island, a catchment of roughly nine hundred thousand. The practical effect is a case mix considerably more complex than the population suggests, delivered by teams considerably smaller than you’d find in Auckland. You get subspecialty exposure with the intimacy of a district hospital, which is either the ideal combination or an uncomfortable stretch depending on how you like to work. Why the case mix outruns the city Three numbers, at true relative scale. The hospital is sized for the third one, the city you live in is the first — and that gap is the whole character of clinical work here.

chunks.t: Healthcare in Wellington: the hospitals and the catchment
chunks.h: A small city doing tertiary work for a large region
chunks.x: Wellington city The place you live ~215,000 The wider region Four hospitals, city to farmland ~440,000 Tertiary catchment Lower North Island and the top of the South ~900,000 Catchment is the population the tertiary hospital serves for tertiary care, not the number of people living in the city. ~900k Tertiary catchment, across two islands 4 Public hospitals across the region 10 min From the CBD to the regional hospital 2 Universities with health campuses in the city Retrieval is part of the job here Patients arrive from Wairarapa, Whanganui, Palmerston North, Nelson and Blenheim — some by road, some by air. Air ambulance and retrieval work is routine rather than exceptional, and if that interests you, Wellington is one of the better places in the country to do it.

chunks.t: Healthcare in Wellington: the hospitals and the catchment
chunks.x: Four public hospitals serve the greater Wellington region. Which one you join shapes your commute, your caseload and how far you live from the city. The four hospitals, north to south They sit along one line of geography — up the western corridor, through the city, out along the valley and over the hill. Where you join decides which end of it you live at.

chunks.t: Healthcare in Wellington: the hospitals and the catchment
chunks.x: A community hospital Porirua, twenty-five minutes north · day surgery, maternity, outpatients and community services for the northern suburbs and the western corridor The tertiary centre Newtown, ten minutes from the CBD · intensive care, cardiothoracic, neurosurgery, oncology, a children’s hospital and the region’s emergency department A busy secondary hospital Lower Hutt, about twenty-five minutes from the city · serving the valley, with its own emergency department and a strong reputation for burns and plastics A rural hospital Masterton, over the Remutaka Hill · serving a wide farming catchment — broad generalist work, and a very different pace from Newtown Most inner suburbs are a short commute to Newtown; the valley, the north and the Wairarapa each pull your search in a different direction. Where clinicians live reorders every suburb by the hospital you pick.

chunks.t: Healthcare in Wellington: the hospitals and the catchment
chunks.h: A private sector that’s easier to move within
chunks.x: Wellington’s private sector is compact — a handful of hospitals doing planned surgery, endoscopy, diagnostics and day procedures, funded by insurance, by ACC, by patients directly and increasingly by Health New Zealand outsourcing elective lists. Because everything is close together, working across both sectors is unusually practical. A public list in Newtown in the morning and a private list nearby in the afternoon is a short drive, not a cross-town expedition. For theatre nurses, anaesthetic technicians, radiographers and sonographers, the private hospitals are a substantial employer in their own right — and generally offer more regular hours than a tertiary roster. Newtown The largest private hospital in the region sits close to the regional hospital, which makes cross-sector work about as convenient as it gets anywhere in the country.

chunks.t: Healthcare in Wellington: the hospitals and the catchment
chunks.h: A private sector that’s easier to move within
chunks.x: Crofton Downs Surgical and medical private care on the north-western side of the city, close to Karori, Khandallah and the Johnsonville line suburbs. Across the region Day-stay, endoscopy and imaging facilities, alongside community radiology networks with clinics through the city, the Hutt Valley and Porirua. A sketch of the landscape; sites and ownership change.

chunks.t: Healthcare in Wellington: the hospitals and the catchment
chunks.x: Hospitals are the obvious employer. Three more account for a great deal of the clinical work in the region. Primary care General practices grouped into Primary Health Organisations, plus after-hours accident and medical clinics. GPs here are independent businesses rather than hospital employees. Community radiology Clinics through the city, the Hutt and Porirua running their own MRI, CT, ultrasound and mammography. Often more regular hours than a hospital roster. National bodies Being the capital means Health New Zealand’s national office, the Ministry of Health, Pharmac and Te Aho o Te Kahu are all here. If policy, quality or research interests you, no other city comes close.

chunks.t: Healthcare in Wellington: the hospitals and the catchment
chunks.x: A small clinical world, both ways Almost everything clinicians tell us about working in Wellington traces back to one fact: the teams are small. That is the appeal and the cost, and it is worth reading both columns before you decide.

chunks.t: Healthcare in Wellington: the hospitals and the catchment
chunks.x: You’ll know everyone Within a month you’ll know the consultants, the radiographers and the ward clerks by name. Decisions happen in corridors. Retrieval and telehealth are routine Geography is part of clinical practice when your catchment crosses a strait — both are everyday work here rather than exceptional, and if that interests you, few places do more of it. Policy is next door The people writing the guidelines are in the same city, often the same room. Unusually easy to get involved. You can walk to work More Wellington clinicians walk or bus to work than anywhere else in New Zealand. It changes the shape of the day.

chunks.t: Healthcare in Wellington: the hospitals and the catchment
chunks.x: Your reputation travels fast A small professional world cuts both ways. Good work is noticed quickly; so is the other kind. Fewer subspecialists In the narrowest fields there may be two or three people in the country doing what you do. Excellent for autonomy, harder for peer support. Smaller teams, tertiary load The case mix is a nine-hundred-thousand catchment; the rota is a city of two hundred thousand. Ask how the on-call is staffed. What ACC covers, how enrolment works and what everyday care costs are national — see How the health system works . A note on names We don’t name hospitals, trusts or private providers as places of work anywhere on this site — a named employer implies a relationship, and the post and the package get confirmed with you directly. Where a public body is named on this page, it is there as a reference point for how the system is organised. It is not an employer reference, and it does not imply we recruit for it. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Where clinicians live in Wellington: 14 suburbs compared
chunks.x: Fourteen suburbs, sorted by commute to whichever hospital you’ll work at. In Wellington the variables are unusual: sun, wind exposure and how many steps to your front door.

chunks.t: Where clinicians live in Wellington: 14 suburbs compared
chunks.x: Settle these before you look at a single listing. In a city this small, getting the order right saves you from a lease you regret. One · Which hospital? Everything follows from this. Newtown for the regional hospital, the valley for Hutt, the northern suburbs for Kenepuru, over the hill for Wairarapa. Wellington is small but the harbour and the hills make some journeys much longer than the map suggests. Two · Car, train, or on foot? If you want to be car-free you need an inner suburb or a rail line — those are different sets of suburbs. If you’re driving, off-street parking becomes the thing you fight for, and many older houses simply don’t have it. Three · Sun or space? The Wellington trade nobody warns you about. North-facing, sunny and sheltered costs a premium and the houses are smaller. South-facing or wind-exposed gets you more room for less money, and a much colder winter.

chunks.t: Where clinicians live in Wellington: 14 suburbs compared
chunks.x: Rent for a year before you commit to a suburb Wellington’s microclimates vary street by street in a way that’s hard to believe until you live it. One valley is still and sunny; the next ridge is in cloud and wind. A year of renting tells you which side of the hill you want. Renting in New Zealand covers the application pack and the bond.

chunks.t: Where clinicians live in Wellington: 14 suburbs compared
chunks.h: Pick your hospital, then read down
chunks.x: Suburbs reorder by commute to whichever hospital you select. Rents are indicative weekly figures for a three-bedroom house as at July 2026 — treat them as a shape, not a quote. Character homes on the hill — and the steps that come with them Commuting to Show Commutes are typical door-to-door driving times outside peak, and Wellington peak adds meaningfully to the longer ones. Rents move — check current listings before budgeting.

chunks.t: Where clinicians live in Wellington: 14 suburbs compared
chunks.h: The three things that decide a Wellington house
chunks.x: Anywhere else you look at bedrooms, schools and the commute. Here those matter too, but three local variables will affect your daily life more, and none of them appear on a listing in any useful form. Locals assess a house on these before they look at the kitchen. It takes newcomers about one winter to understand why. Which way it faces North-facing is the single most valuable feature a Wellington house can have. Winter sun into the living room, a dry interior and a heating bill you can live with. South-facing on a hillside can mean no direct sun for months. Visit at eleven in the morning in winter if you possibly can — a photograph taken in January tells you nothing. How exposed it is Ridge tops and the south coast take the full force of the southerly. A sheltered valley three hundred metres away can be a different climate entirely.

chunks.t: Where clinicians live in Wellington: 14 suburbs compared
chunks.h: The three things that decide a Wellington house
chunks.x: Ask which way the prevailing wind hits, and stand outside for ten minutes before you decide. How many steps Houses on the hills are reached by staircases — sometimes a hundred or more from the street. Charming at a viewing, less so with shopping, a pram, or after a night shift. Count them, and plan for the next ten years. How renting works nationally — applications, bond, tenancy rights and the Healthy Homes standards — is the same everywhere, and set out in Renting in New Zealand . Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Getting around Wellington: trains, buses and do you need a car
chunks.x: The only New Zealand city where "do I need a car?" has an interesting answer. Four rail lines, a cable car, a harbour ferry, and a walkable centre. Converting your licence, buying a car, WOF and rego are all in Driving & licences . This chapter is about moving around Wellington specifically.

chunks.t: Getting around Wellington: trains, buses and do you need a car
chunks.h: Probably not for work. Probably yes for weekends.
chunks.x: This is the answer and it holds for most clinicians here. If you live in an inner suburb or on a rail line, getting to work without a car is straightforward and often faster than driving. Plenty of Wellington staff don’t own one. But the things people move to Wellington for — the south coast in a swell, a trailhead in the Remutakas, Martinborough on a Saturday, the ferry terminal at seven in the morning — mostly need a vehicle. Many households here run one car between two adults rather than none or two. You can skip the car if You live in Newtown, Mount Cook, Mount Victoria, Aro Valley or Te Aro. You work at the regional hospital and are happy to walk or cycle. You’re on a rail line and your shifts fit the timetable. You’re willing to rent or borrow for the occasional weekend trip. You’ll want one if You work nights, and the timetable thins out when you finish.

chunks.t: Getting around Wellington: trains, buses and do you need a car
chunks.h: Probably not for work. Probably yes for weekends.
chunks.x: You live in Karori, Brooklyn, Miramar or anywhere hilly off a main route. You have children, sports bags and a school run to manage. Weekends in the Wairarapa, the coast or the ranges are the point of moving. Night shifts are the deciding factor for most people. Services run late but thin considerably after midnight, and a 3am finish isn’t a public transport journey. If your roster includes nights, plan for a car, a taxi budget, or a suburb you can walk home from. It’s the thing new arrivals most often get wrong.

chunks.t: Getting around Wellington: trains, buses and do you need a car
chunks.h: Six ways around a small city
chunks.x: Wellington has more transport options than anywhere else in the country, mostly because the geography left no room to build motorways through it. Walking The most Wellington answer. The CBD is about two kilometres end to end, and Newtown to the city is a twenty-five minute walk along a flat road. Invest in a proper coat rather than an umbrella — the wind destroys them within a fortnight, and locals find them mildly funny. Trains Four suburban lines converge on Wellington Station at the north end of the CBD — the best commuter rail network in New Zealand, and the reason the valley and northern suburbs are viable. Frequent at peak, sparser off-peak. Check the timetable against your actual roster, not the advertised frequency. Buses The network that reaches the hills. Metlink runs the whole region, and the routes through Newtown and the hospital are among the busiest in the city.

chunks.t: Getting around Wellington: trains, buses and do you need a car
chunks.h: Six ways around a small city
chunks.x: Reliability has been a live public complaint for years — locals allow more time than the app suggests. The cable car Everyday commuter infrastructure as well as a tourist attraction. Lambton Quay to Kelburn in five minutes, and the reason the university suburb feels close to town. The harbour ferry Queens Wharf to Days Bay and Seatoun. Slower than driving and infinitely more pleasant, and the reason some people live on the eastern bays. Cycling Improving quickly, and e-bikes have changed what the hills mean. The waterfront route is flat and good; the hill suburbs are for the committed.

chunks.t: Getting around Wellington: trains, buses and do you need a car
chunks.x: If you’re choosing a suburb for a car-free life, this is the map that matters. Four lines out of Wellington Station Hutt Valley Line The busiest line, and the one that makes the valley a practical option for hospital staff. Wellington Petone Lower Hutt Upper Hutt Kāpiti Line Fast, frequent, and the reason the Kāpiti Coast is a commute rather than a move. Wellington Porirua Paraparaumu Waikanae Johnsonville Line Suburban, leafy, and a fifteen-minute run into town. Wellington Ngaio Khandallah Johnsonville Melling Line Limited service, but useful if you land in the right part of the valley. Wellington Melling, central Lower Hutt Indicative — each line has more stops than shown. Check Metlink for the full timetable, and check it against your roster rather than the advertised peak frequency.

chunks.t: Getting around Wellington: trains, buses and do you need a car
chunks.x: Four things to know Off-street parking is a valuable amenity. Many older houses have none, and inner-suburb street parking is resident-permit and competitive. Check before you sign. There’s no motorway through the middle. Traffic funnels through a small number of routes, and an incident on one of them affects everything. The Terrace and Mount Victoria tunnels are the pinch points. Locals plan around them the way Aucklanders plan around the bridge. Hill driving in winter is narrow, wet and steep. Nothing dramatic, but a small car with good tyres beats a large one.

chunks.t: Getting around Wellington: trains, buses and do you need a car
chunks.x: How far away everything is Travel time from the city, to scale against each other. The airport is the outlier that makes Wellington feel small; the road north is the one that reminds you the country is long. The airport One of the most convenient in the country — but the runway is short, so international flights reach Australia and the Pacific only. 10 min Over the Remutakas The Wairarapa — vineyards, farmland and a slower weekend. The hill road is winding and closes occasionally in high wind. 1 hr Palmerston North North by road, and the first city of any size on the way up. 2 hrs The Interislander to Picton Take the car. One of the great ferry crossings anywhere — and cancelled in a strong southerly. 3 hrs Taupō The middle of the North Island, and a long-weekend drive. 6 hrs Auckland Driving it once is part of living here. Most people fly it after that. 8 hrs Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Weekends and the outdoors in Wellington
chunks.x: Bush tracks fifteen minutes from most front doors, a wild coast facing Antarctica, and a predator-free valley in the middle of the city. This is what the short commute is for.

chunks.t: Weekends and the outdoors in Wellington
chunks.h: A capital city where you get woken by a parrot
chunks.x: Zealandia is a fenced, predator-free sanctuary in a valley in the middle of Wellington — 225 hectares of regenerating forest where rats, stoats and possums have been eradicated. Native birds were reintroduced, and then they did something nobody fully planned for: they spread out into the city. Kākā — large, loud, intelligent forest parrots — now nest in suburban trees and shout from rooftops at dawn. Tūī and kererū are everywhere. Suburbs run their own trapping groups, and it’s entirely normal for a neighbour to ask whether you want a rat trap for your garden. It’s one of the distinctive things about living here, and it’s the reason a walk through the town belt sounds nothing like a park anywhere else. Kākā Large olive-brown parrots with a flash of red under the wing. Raucous at dawn and dusk, and increasingly common in the suburbs. Tūī Iridescent black with a white throat tuft.

chunks.t: Weekends and the outdoors in Wellington
chunks.h: A capital city where you get woken by a parrot
chunks.x: An extraordinary range of clicks, chimes and whistles — some of it beyond human hearing. Kererū A wood pigeon the size of a small cat. You’ll hear the wingbeats before you see it, and it will eventually fall out of a tree. Kiwi, at night Zealandia runs guided evening tours where you can see and hear kiwi in the wild, ten minutes from the CBD. The thing to take visiting family to.

chunks.t: Weekends and the outdoors in Wellington
chunks.h: Two coasts, and one of them is dangerous
chunks.x: Wellington has a sheltered harbour side and an exposed southern side, and the difference matters for your safety rather than just your comfort. The harbour is calm, warmer and where families swim. The south coast faces Cook Strait, with strong currents, cold water and surf that arrives fast. New Zealand’s drowning rate is high for a developed country, and a disproportionate share involves people newly arrived who underestimated the water. This isn’t a scare paragraph — it’s the single most useful safety thing in this guide. Two coasts, two sets of rules Which side of the city you swim on matters more than the temperature. The harbour is where families go; the south coast faces Cook Strait and asks something of you.

chunks.t: Weekends and the outdoors in Wellington
chunks.x: Oriental Bay A city beach a ten-minute walk from the CBD. Calm, warmer than the coast, and where the whole city swims in February. Days Bay Reachable by ferry, which makes the trip half the point. Sheltered, family-friendly, with a wharf to jump off.

chunks.t: Weekends and the outdoors in Wellington
chunks.h: The south coast — treat with respect
chunks.x: Lyall Bay The surf beach, right beside the airport. Cold, exposed, and good waves. Check conditions before you go in. Island Bay More sheltered than Lyall by a good margin, with a marine reserve alongside. Still the south coast — treat it with respect. Strong currents, cold water and surf that arrives fast are south-coast facts, not south-coast warnings. The panel below is the practical version. Before your first south-coast swim Swim between the flags where there are any. On the south coast, patrols are limited and seasonal. Learn to spot a rip — calmer, darker, flatter water between breaking waves is the current heading out, not the safe bit. Caught in one, don’t fight it. Float, raise an arm, let it carry you out until it weakens, then swim parallel to shore. Never swim alone on the south coast, whatever your ability. Check safeswim.org.nz before you drive out.

chunks.t: Weekends and the outdoors in Wellington
chunks.h: When you’ve got an hour, or a day
chunks.x: An hour · the town belt Bush tracks from almost any inner suburb. Mount Victoria for the harbour view, the Botanic Garden for the easy version, Polhill for something steeper. Half a day · the south coast Red Rocks to the seal colony — an hour’s walk each way along the shore, with fur seals hauled out from May to October. Half a day · Zealandia Ten minutes from town. Two hours of walking, or a whole afternoon if the birds are cooperating. A day · the Remutakas or Ōtaki Proper tramping within an hour. Ridge lines, huts, and views back over the strait. A day · the Wairarapa Over the hill for vineyards, Castlepoint lighthouse, or Cape Palliser and the seal colony at the bottom of the North Island. A weekend · the Marlborough Sounds Three hours on the ferry and you’re somewhere that feels like a different country. The crossing is worth doing at least once in good weather.

chunks.t: Weekends and the outdoors in Wellington
chunks.x: Some weekends the weather simply wins. Wellington is unusually good at this, because a small city with a capital’s institutions means a lot of indoors worth going to. Te Papa The national museum, free, on the waterfront, and excellent. Locals go repeatedly rather than once. Theatre & live music More per head than anywhere else in the country. Circa, BATS and the Opera House, plus small venues most nights of the week. The film scene A serious production industry sits in Miramar, and the city takes cinema seriously — independent screens, festivals and a long season. A long lunch The most Wellington answer of all. Somewhere on Cuba Street, three hours, and the weather is somebody else’s problem. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Moving to Wellington: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.x: Nau mai, haere mai ki Te Whanganui-a-Tara. If you’re reading this you’re somewhere between curious and committed. Either is a good place to be, and this guide is written for both.

chunks.t: Moving to Wellington: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.h: A city small enough to belong to quickly
chunks.x: Oriental Bay. The hills come down to the water, which is why the city never sprawled Wellington is the smallest capital most people have lived in, and that’s the whole character of the place. It has a tertiary hospital, a parliament, a national museum, a theatre scene and a working port — all inside a city you can walk across in an afternoon. The effect on a newcomer is unusual. You’ll run into the same people. Your registrar will know your neighbour. Within two months you’ll have a coffee place where they start your order when you walk in. In a bigger city that takes years, and for a lot of people moving countries alone, it’s the thing that makes the move survivable. The same smallness is why some people leave. Fewer specialists, less anonymity, and a professional world where your reputation travels fast. We’ll be straight about all of that as we go.

chunks.t: Moving to Wellington: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.h: A city small enough to belong to quickly
chunks.x: Who wrote this Ethicare is a healthcare recruitment company. This guide is free to read, asks nothing of you, and does not give visa advice. Where we think Wellington is the wrong answer for someone, we say so. That’s more useful to you and, better for us than a placement that doesn’t last.

chunks.t: Moving to Wellington: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.x: Not a fact sheet. These are the nine figures that shape a week here. 8 km Across at its widest. The whole city, hills to harbour. ~215,000 People in the city, around 440,000 across the wider region. 15 min A typical commute. The single biggest lifestyle variable between NZ cities. Same Clinical pay as Auckland — national collective agreements, lower housing costs. 1 tertiary hospital Serving the lower North Island and the top of the South. 20 min From most suburbs to a hill track or the south coast. 12–20° The usual range. Rarely freezing, rarely hot, never still for long. 2 flights To reach Europe. The runway is short, so long-haul means a connection. One coffee Per capita, more cafés than almost anywhere. It isn’t a boast, it’s a fact of the street.

chunks.t: Moving to Wellington: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.h: Six things you only learn by living here
chunks.x: Small, specific, and the sort of thing that makes the first month feel less foreign if you know it in advance. Nobody uses an umbrella The wind turns them inside out within a fortnight and you’ll feel conspicuous carrying one. Buy a proper hooded rain jacket before you arrive — the single most useful thing in a Wellington wardrobe. The southerly is a forecast, not a mood People will say "there’s a southerly coming" and mean it practically — flights, the ferry, whether the barbecue happens. Learn the difference between a northerly (warm, blustery) and a southerly (cold, straight off Antarctica) in your first week. Everyone works in government, sort of At a party you’ll meet policy analysts, select committee staff and ministry advisors. Politics is discussed the way sport is elsewhere, and it’s entirely normal to see a minister buying coffee.

chunks.t: Moving to Wellington: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.h: Six things you only learn by living here
chunks.x: Houses have heat pumps, not heating Central heating is rare. A heat pump in the living room and nothing in the bedrooms is standard, so bedrooms get cold. A dehumidifier is a normal appliance here, not a sign something is wrong. The city walks Far more people walk to work than in any other New Zealand city. Good shoes matter more than a good car. Earthquakes are ordinary You’ll feel one. Buildings are engineered for it, everyone has a plan, and the fuss is much smaller than you’d expect. Sort your grab bag in week one and then stop thinking about it. A note on te reo Te Whanganui-a-Tara is Wellington’s name in te reo Māori — the great harbour of Tara. You’ll see and hear both, and increasingly the Māori name first in official use. You’re not expected to arrive fluent. You are expected to try. Te ao Māori at work covers pronunciation and the words you’ll hear on the ward. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Why Wellington: the case for the capital
chunks.x: The case for the capital comes down to one number: twenty minutes. What you do with the hours that buys you is the actual argument.

chunks.t: Why Wellington: the case for the capital
chunks.h: Small is the feature, not the compromise
chunks.x: The Beehive: Parliament, in a city small enough to walk across Wellington is hemmed in by hills on one side and the harbour on the other, which means it never sprawled. The city that resulted is roughly eight kilometres across at its widest, with a tertiary hospital, a university campus, the seat of government, a theatre district and a working port all inside that. The consequence for you is arithmetic. A thirty-five-minute commute each way, five days a week, is roughly six hours. Fifteen minutes each way is two and a half. That difference — most of a working day, every week — is the single largest lifestyle variable between New Zealand cities, and it compounds over years. The arithmetic of twenty minutes Hours spent commuting in a five-day week, at true relative scale. The difference is most of a working day — every week, for as long as you stay.

chunks.t: Why Wellington: the case for the capital
chunks.h: Small is the feature, not the compromise
chunks.x: ~6 hrs 35 min each way 3.5 hrs back, every week ~2.5 hrs 15 min each way Roughly a working month a year. What you do with it is the actual argument for the capital — the week below is one shape it tends to take. 8 km Across, at the widest 3.5 hrs A week, saved against a big-city commute 20 min From most suburbs to a hill track Same Salary as Auckland — national agreements The same pay, a smaller outgoing Because clinical pay sits on national collective agreements, your salary here is identical to what it would be in Auckland — while housing costs meaningfully less. That gap is the quiet financial case for Wellington, and it doesn’t appear on any job advertisement. Money, tax & banking works through what lands in your account.

chunks.t: Why Wellington: the case for the capital
chunks.x: One clinician’s week, in the shape it tends to take here. Not a promise — an illustration of what becomes possible when the commute stops eating the evening. Monday Walk to work along the waterfront. Home by six, and the evening is still an evening. Tuesday Late finish, but the drive home is fifteen minutes and there’s no motorway in it. Wednesday Football or a hill run straight from the office. The trailhead is inside the city. Thursday Theatre, a gig or a talk. A small city with a capital’s cultural calendar. Friday Cuba Street, and the walk home takes twenty minutes past the harbour. Weekend The south coast, the Wairarapa or a ferry to the Sounds. All of it inside two hours.

chunks.t: Why Wellington: the case for the capital
chunks.h: The six things people ask us
chunks.x: Is the clinical work as good as Auckland’s? For most specialties, yes. Wellington Regional is a tertiary centre serving the lower North Island and the top of the South, and it holds several national and supra-regional services. Auckland has more volume; Wellington has a catchment that pulls complex work to a compact, well-connected campus. How bad is the wind? It is the most exaggerated and the most real thing about Wellington at the same time. There are perhaps twenty days a year when it is unpleasant, a lot of days when it is simply present, and stretches in autumn that are among the most beautiful weather in the country. Most people acclimatise within a year; a small number never do. What about the earthquake risk? Wellington sits on a fault line and everyone knows it.

chunks.t: Why Wellington: the case for the capital
chunks.h: The six things people ask us
chunks.x: Building standards are among the strictest in the world, public buildings have been strengthened extensively, and preparedness is part of ordinary civic life rather than a background anxiety. Newer apartments and workplaces are built for it. It is a real consideration and it is well managed. Can I really live without a car? More easily than anywhere else in New Zealand. Wellington is the one city here where a car is optional — the inner suburbs are walkable, buses are frequent, and the commuter rail is good. Many hospital staff walk to work. If you want to explore the region at weekends you will want a car, but you may not need to own one. Is it expensive? Less than Auckland, more than everywhere else in this guide. Housing is the pressure point — the geography means the city cannot sprawl, so inner-suburb rents are high and the stock is often old.

chunks.t: Why Wellington: the case for the capital
chunks.h: The six things people ask us
chunks.x: What you get back is time: a fifteen-minute commute and a walkable life. Is it good with children? Good, with one caveat. The city is safe, compact and full of things to do, and schools are strong. The caveat is housing — family-sized homes with flat sections near the centre are scarce and expensive, which is why many families end up in the Hutt Valley or Porirua. Both are a longer commute, and both are covered in chapter five.

chunks.t: Why Wellington: the case for the capital
chunks.h: What we’d ask you to weigh
chunks.x: Every one of these is a real reason people leave. Read them properly — it’s cheaper to decide against Wellington now than in eighteen months. The wind is relentless Not a quirky local detail. Wellington sits in a strait that funnels southerlies and northerlies through the city, and gusts over a hundred kilometres an hour arrive several times a year. Flights get cancelled, the ferry stops, and umbrellas are pointless. People either stop noticing within a year or never stop resenting it, and you can’t tell which you’ll be until you live here. Cold, damp housing Much of the stock is old timber on a hillside, built for a climate nobody has. Winter interiors can be unpleasant, and mould is a common complaint rather than an unlucky one. Healthy Homes standards set a floor, not a good outcome — view in winter if you can.

chunks.t: Why Wellington: the case for the capital
chunks.h: What we’d ask you to weigh
chunks.x: A smaller professional world Fewer specialists in your field, fewer people to learn from, and fewer options if you want to change roles without changing city. In the narrowest subspecialties there may be two or three people in the country doing what you do. If your career plan needs a large department to move around inside, Auckland is the better answer. Long-haul means a connection The runway is short, so international flights are limited to Australia and the Pacific. Everything else goes via Auckland or Sydney, which adds hours and a transfer to every trip home. Earthquake risk is real Wellington sits on a fault line and everyone knows it. Buildings are engineered for it and the practical risk to you is low, but if the idea keeps you awake, weigh that now. Weighing Wellington against Auckland or somewhere smaller is a sensible thing to do properly.

chunks.t: Why Wellington: the case for the capital
chunks.h: What we’d ask you to weigh
chunks.x: Our New Zealand destination guides cover each region in the same detail. Where we’d steer you instead If you need the largest system in the country, Auckland carries more sites and deeper sub-specialty cover. If the wind and the seismic question weigh on you Hawke’s Bay and Nelson Tasman are calmer in both senses. If you want materially more house for the money within reach of the capital, Palmerston North is two hours north. In our experience Wellington suits clinicians who want a capital’s culture without a capital’s commute — twenty minutes door to door buys back a working month every year, and the city fills it well. Respect the wind, rent before you buy, and it’s the easiest big small city in the country. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Cost of living in Western Australia: the numbers
chunks.x: Perth runs the friendliest big-capital arithmetic in Australia: housing below Sydney and Melbourne, no tolls, shorter commutes, and salaries that stretch accordingly. The west’s hidden cost lives on the flight line east — and this chapter prices both sides.

chunks.t: Cost of living in Western Australia: the numbers
chunks.x: We used to print a weekly rent and a monthly budget table here. We have taken them out. A figure that was true when a page was written is misleading a year later, and a candidate who plans a move around a stale number is worse off than one who plans around none. What does not go stale is the relationship between places — which suburb, ring or region you choose — and the judgement about which costs catch people out. For today’s actual numbers use the calculators at the foot of the page, and use them to compare it against the city you are leaving. That is the only comparison that decides anything.

chunks.t: Cost of living in Western Australia: the numbers
chunks.x: Clinical pay is set by state awards and is broadly comparable with the eastern capitals; we don’t print figures until we’ve verified them against the current instruments. On the outgoings side Perth’s advantage compounds quietly: the rent line runs below the big eastern capitals, the transport line has no tolls in it at all, and the mining state’s one everyday gift is among the cheaper household energy on the grid. The line that pushes back is travel . Every east-coast wedding, conference and grandparent visit is a five-hour flight; every European trip is long even with the nonstop. Families who fly often should budget it as a standing annual item, not an exception — it is part of the west’s cost of living, and leaving it out is how the isolation surprises people.

chunks.t: Cost of living in Western Australia: the numbers
chunks.x: Up north, the arithmetic inverts into something unique: remote packages — loadings, provided or subsidised housing, extra leave, airfare assistance — against mining-town prices for everything else. Gone into deliberately, a northern chapter is the fastest financial reset in Australian healthcare. Every package is verified case by case before we quote it.

chunks.t: Cost of living in Western Australia: the numbers
chunks.x: Cottesloe & the western suburbs The premium strip — Perth’s top of range, still visibly below the eastern equivalents for the same postcode-to-sand maths. The beach belt & river suburbs Scarborough to Hillarys, Subiaco to South Perth — the comfortable middle, where most relocating clinicians land. Fremantle Character carries a modest premium; the port town remains gettable in a way its eastern equivalents are not. The corridors & the hills Joondalup north, Rockingham south, Kalamunda east — the value ring, on train lines, with the most house for the money. Bunbury & the south-west Regional prices with coast attached — the corridor’s hub resets expectations; the capes price their postcard. The north Karratha, Hedland and Broome rents run mining-town high — which is exactly why packages include housing. Never take a northern role without the housing line settled.

chunks.t: Cost of living in Western Australia: the numbers
chunks.x: The friendliest big-capital arithmetic Monthly rent for the same room or small one-bedroom, at true relative scale. Perth’s tiers sit closer together than the eastern capitals’ — the west’s real cost is not on this chart. Inner Perth Below Sydney and Melbourne for the same postcode Baseline Corridor & hills Shorter commutes, no tolls anywhere ~0.7× Bunbury & the south-west A regional city with the coast attached ~0.6× The rent line runs below the big eastern capitals, the transport line has no tolls in it at all, and power is among the cheaper on the grid. The west’s real cost is the flight line east — five hours to the east coast, and worth budgeting as a standing annual item. Indicative prices that change over time. The flights line is deliberate — most budgets leave it out until December forces it in.

chunks.t: Cost of living in Western Australia: the numbers
chunks.h: The costs particular to the west
chunks.x: The flight fund East-coast family means two to four crossings a year at five hours each way. Name it in the budget and the isolation stays theoretical. Northern groceries Remote-town freight prices everything up sharply — part of why the loadings exist. Budget the north on its own terms. School fees on a temporary visa WA charges circa $4,000 per family rather than per child for certain skilled subclasses — indicative, with hardship waivers. The rule and the other states sit in the master’s School fees on a visa . Health cover for your visa Many visas require private cover, separate from Medicare — national detail, covered in Immigration & visas .

chunks.t: Cost of living in Western Australia: the numbers
chunks.x: Compare cities Numbeo · cost of living Perth and Bunbury prices against your current city. Plan your budget Moneysmart budget planner The Australian government’s free budgeting tool. Property REIWA The west’s own property portal — live rents and sales, suburb by suburb. Master guide The cost of relocating Flights, shipping, bonds and the first ninety days — budgeted once, properly. Sanity check Expatistan A cleaner side-by-side of two cities. Worth running when Numbeo looks off. Official data ABS price indexes Slower than the comparison sites, and the one to trust on the direction of travel. The summary Perth hands you the easiest big-capital budget in Australia — below-eastern rent, no tolls, cheaper power. The west’s true cost is the flight line east : name it as a standing budget item and the isolation stays a fact, not a regret. The north is its own arithmetic — packages verified case by case, housing line settled first. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Food, shopping and everyday life in Western Australia
chunks.x: Perth’s everyday life is built on a simple luxury the east never gets: the day ends with the sun going down over the sea. Around that daily show sits a food scene that has grown up fast, markets with real produce behind them, and the most unhurried big-city rhythm in the country.

chunks.t: Food, shopping and everyday life in Western Australia
chunks.x: The small-bar decade Perth’s licensing reforms turned the city’s lanes into a small-bar and bistro scene that surprises visitors who knew the old, early-closing town. The CBD and Northbridge carry it; the suburbs followed. Fremantle does the weekend The markets, the fishing-boat harbour’s fish and chips, craft breweries in heritage warehouses — the port town is the state’s default good afternoon. The Indian Ocean menu Crayfish from Geraldton, snapper and whiting off the coast, and the state’s obsession: fresh crays at Christmas. The fish-and-chips baseline is set high. No tipping, clear menu prices The price is the price and waitstaff earn a wage — same national rule, same pleasant surprise.

chunks.t: Food, shopping and everyday life in Western Australia
chunks.h: Markets and what the state grows and pours
chunks.x: The Swan Valley is the city’s own wine country — twenty-five minutes from the CBD, all cellar doors, breweries and long lunches — and Margaret River three hours south is the serious one: cabernet and chardonnay with global reputations, among surf breaks and karri forest. Between them the south-west grows truffles, olives, citrus and the state’s famous marron. Perth’s market culture runs from Fremantle’s institution through suburban growers’ markets, with the wheatbelt and south-west supplying local produce. Whatever your community eats, the eastern corridor’s food strips and the northern suburbs’ grocers cover more of it than Perth’s isolation would suggest — the master’s Finding your feet & your people maps where communities cluster.

chunks.t: Food, shopping and everyday life in Western Australia
chunks.x: The morning belongs to the ocean Swim squads at dawn, the coast path full by six, coffee after — Perth’s beach-before-work culture is the most committed in the country, and joining it is the fastest way in. Sunset is the appointment The only capital where the sun sets over the sea — the coast fills every clear evening, and "sundowners" is a schedule, not a word. Sport, both codes, and the Derby AFL rules the west — two teams, one Derby, allegiances expected. Cricket at the new stadium, netball, surf clubs: the club is the social engine here as everywhere. FIFO shapes the social week Half the state’s social calendar works around mining rosters — the Thursday-night flight north and the week-on week-off rhythm are part of how friendships schedule themselves. Limitations Headline tours and blockbuster exhibitions reach Perth last or not at all — the east’s cultural depth is a flight away.

chunks.t: Food, shopping and everyday life in Western Australia
chunks.x: Late-night everything is thinner than the east; the city runs early because the ocean does. Specialist imported groceries can need planning; every community keeps its list and its favourite importer. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Western Australia at a glance: climate, geography and seasons
chunks.x: Western Australia is three climates stacked on one coastline: a Mediterranean capital, a green and gentle south-west, and a tropical north that runs on wet and dry seasons. Knowing which west you’re moving to matters more here than in any state except Queensland.

chunks.t: Western Australia at a glance: climate, geography and seasons
chunks.x: Where Perth sits, with the straight-line distance to Bunbury and Broome Perth and its coast is the Mediterranean west: hot dry summers cooled every afternoon by the Fremantle Doctor, mild green winters when the rain comes, and a metro area that runs seventy kilometres down a white-sand shore from Yanchep to Mandurah, with the Swan River and Kings Park at its heart. The south-west corner is the green west: Bunbury’s harbour hub, Busselton’s long jetty, the Margaret River capes with their surf and vineyards, and karri forests to Albany’s southern granite coast. Cooler, wetter, and the state’s holiday heart — the one part of WA where "regional" means gentler, not harsher. The north is the tropical west: the Pilbara’s red iron country and company towns, then the Kimberley — gorges, boab trees, tides that swallow islands, and a wet season that closes roads from December to March. Broome faces the Indian Ocean sunset; inland, distances are measured in flight hours. The Kimberley — the north’s scale, in one tide

chunks.t: Western Australia at a glance: climate, geography and seasons
chunks.x: Summer Dec – Feb 30–33°C Hot, dry, sea-breeze cooled Autumn Mar – May 24–29°C Long, warm, settled Winter Jun – Aug 18–20°C Mild, green, showery Spring Sep – Nov 22–27°C Wildflowers, everywhere Indicative Perth daytime highs. The south-west runs a few degrees cooler and wetter; Broome and the north swap all of this for a wet (Nov–Apr) and a dry (May–Oct).

chunks.t: Western Australia at a glance: climate, geography and seasons
chunks.h: What the numbers don’t tell you
chunks.x: The Fremantle Doctor is real infrastructure. The afternoon sea breeze arrives most summer days with clockwork reliability, dropping the coast ten degrees. Locals schedule around it, cyclists curse it, and it is why Perth’s dry 33° beats the east’s humid 28°. Winter is the green season. The rain comes June to August, the state turns green, and spring answers with the world’s largest wildflower bloom — a spectacle from the city’s parks to the outback. Perth winter is mild enough that the beach walk never stops. The north’s wet season is a contract, not a mood. Cyclone watches, road closures, air-only access to some communities, and a build-up humidity that tests everyone. The dry season repays it with perfect blue months. If you’re heading north, the induction is clinical preparation. The sun is serious here too. Perth’s UV matches Queensland’s. Hats, rash shirts and 50+ are school policy and should be yours — the master’s Living in Australia covers the everyday rules.

chunks.t: Western Australia at a glance: climate, geography and seasons
chunks.h: Where things are, in travel time
chunks.x: Perth → Fremantle 30 minutes by train down the river. Perth → Bunbury ~1 hr 45 by road or the regional train. Perth → Margaret River ~3 hr south to the wine capes. Perth → Kalgoorlie ~6.5 hr by road, 1-hr flight — the Goldfields hub. Perth → Karratha / Broome 2 / 2.5-hr flights. Driving is 16–22 hours and an expedition. Perth → Sydney / Bali / London 5 hr / 3.5 hr / 17 hr nonstop — the flight map that explains the west.

chunks.t: Western Australia at a glance: climate, geography and seasons
chunks.x: The Doctor The Fremantle Doctor — the afternoon sea breeze with a schedule. Freo Fremantle — the port town at the river mouth. Rotto Rottnest Island — quokkas, snorkelling, the ferry day out. FIFO Fly-in-fly-out — the mining roster that shapes half the state’s rhythms. Down south The south-west corner — Bunbury to the capes. The weekend direction. Up north The Pilbara and Kimberley. The other direction, and the other life. The wheatbelt The farm country inland of Perth — wildflowers in spring, salt lakes beyond. SmartRider Perth’s transport card — trains, buses, ferries. The short version Three wests: the Mediterranean capital, the green south-west, the tropical north . Perth’s climate is the country’s most pleasant; the north’s is a contract with a payoff. Which west you choose decides everything — Where clinicians live is next. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Healthcare in Western Australia: working as a clinician
chunks.x: Western Australia organises its health system the way its geography demands: metropolitan services running Perth’s tertiary network, and a single country service spanning a third of the continent. For a clinician, the choice of which is the choice of career.

chunks.t: Healthcare in Western Australia: working as a clinician
chunks.x: Perth’s public care runs through metropolitan health service groups — north, south, east and children’s — covering the capital’s tertiary and general hospitals. Everything beyond the metro boundary belongs to the country health service : the largest single health geography in the world, running regional hospitals in Bunbury, Albany, Geraldton, Kalgoorlie, Karratha, Port Hedland and Broome, and district and remote-clinic care across everything between. Registration is national through Ahpra; hiring is service by service. The practical grammar: Perth roles compete like any capital’s; south-west roles blend regional pace with reachable city; and the north recruits constantly, with packages built to compete against mining wages — the strongest loadings in Australian healthcare, described structurally here and verified case by case before we quote anything.

chunks.t: Healthcare in Western Australia: working as a clinician
chunks.x: Aeromedical retrieval is the connective tissue — the flying-doctor tradition began in country like this — and telehealth carries more of the everyday than anywhere in the country. How Medicare and the public–private split work is national, and lives once in the master’s How the health system works .

chunks.t: Healthcare in Western Australia: working as a clinician
chunks.x: Perth: a complete tertiary system Full subspecialty coverage, major teaching hospitals and a children’s service — a step smaller than Sydney’s or Melbourne’s at the quaternary edge, with correspondingly saner competition. The south-west: regional with a safety net Bunbury anchors the state’s gentlest regional medicine — real scope, a growing hub, and Perth ninety minutes away when complexity needs it. The north: the serious posting Karratha, Hedland, Broome and the Kimberley districts — broad scope, thin backup, heavy Aboriginal health caseload, and the packages to match. A defined chapter that changes careers and finances alike. Aboriginal health is central, not adjacent In the Kimberley and Pilbara it is much of the work, led in partnership with community-controlled organisations. Cultural preparation is clinical preparation.

chunks.t: Healthcare in Western Australia: working as a clinician
chunks.x: FIFO shapes the caseload Mining rosters drive occupational health, mental health and emergency patterns across the state — a distinctively western clinical rhythm. Pay is set by state awards Each profession has its instruments, with district allowances and packaging layered by remoteness. We quote figures only after verifying them against the current award; see Pay & conditions . Four Western Australias Everything past the metropolitan boundary belongs to a single country service — the largest health geography in the world. Within it, these are four different careers, and the loadings rise as you read down. Perth and the metro A complete tertiary system across metropolitan service groups: full subspecialty coverage, major teaching hospitals and a children’s service. A step smaller than Sydney or Melbourne at the quaternary edge, with correspondingly saner competition.

chunks.t: Healthcare in Western Australia: working as a clinician
chunks.x: The south-west The state’s gentlest regional medicine. Real scope and a growing hub, with Perth about ninety minutes away when complexity needs it — the usual first step for clinicians testing whether regional life suits them. The Goldfields and mid-west Regional hospitals a long way inland and up the coast, recruiting steadily. Wide scope, small teams, and a step up in responsibility from a metropolitan equivalent. The north The Pilbara and the Kimberley: broad scope, thin backup, a heavy Aboriginal health caseload led in partnership with community-controlled organisations, and packages built to compete with mining wages. A defined chapter that changes careers and finances alike. District allowances and remote loadings vary by town and by profession — we describe them structurally here and verify every figure against the current award before we quote it. See Pay & conditions .

chunks.t: Healthcare in Western Australia: working as a clinician
chunks.x: Perth stands on Noongar country, and the state’s north is home to some of the oldest continuous cultures on earth. Community-controlled health organisations lead substantial care delivery in the Kimberley, the Pilbara and the Goldfields, and the state system works in formal partnership with them. You are not expected to arrive expert. In the north especially, the cultural induction is core preparation: learn whose Country your service stands on, and treat the partnership as clinical business. What to ask at interview Which service and which site — and for country roles, exactly which town, because the north’s postings differ enormously.

chunks.t: Healthcare in Western Australia: working as a clinician
chunks.x: What is the roster pattern, and how are on-call, penalties and district allowances handled under the relevant award? For the north: what precisely does the package include — housing provided or subsidised, leave loading, airfares, and for how long? What is the wet-season operational plan, and what does it mean for my roster and my exits? What supervision, orientation and cultural induction exists — and how does CPD work this far from the eastern cities? Where does complex work refer to, and how much of the retrieval pathway do I own? Sophie Sophie’s insight The west is where I ask about the east-coast family first, because the flight is the only thing people regret. For the right family, Perth is the easiest good life in Australia — and a Broome or Hedland chapter, gone into with open eyes, resets finances in a way no eastern posting can. Sophie Careem Founder, Ethicare Resourcing

chunks.t: Healthcare in Western Australia: working as a clinician
chunks.x: Ahpra registration, English-language evidence and the visa that goes with your role are national processes, identical in every state. They are explained once, properly, in the master’s Eligibility & registration and Immigration & visas . Ethicare Live roles & professions What we’re recruiting for now, by profession and by state. Master guide Pay & conditions How awards, allowances and remote loadings work — and what to verify before you sign. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Where clinicians live in Western Australia: fourteen places compared
chunks.x: Perth’s geography hands you the choice plainly: the coast, the river, or the hills — with Fremantle as its own answer. Beyond the metro, the south-west corridor is the gentle regional option and the north is a different decision entirely. Coast, river or hills Perth’s three home geographies, each with its own line of stops — and Fremantle standing slightly apart as its own answer. Up the coast The sunset side: premium sand first, family esplanades next, the growth corridor’s newer estates beyond. Cottesloe Scarborough–Hillarys Joondalup & north Along the river to the port Kings Park terraces and hospital-adjacent inner suburbs, running down the line to heritage-street Fremantle.
