Subiaco & South Perth Victoria Park Fremantle · 30 min Up into the hills Tall-timber shade, cool nights and land — the tree change that keeps a forty-minute run to the wards. Kalamunda Mundaring South of the metro, Rockingham’s shore and the run toward Bunbury carry the same trade further: more house, more minutes on the train.

chunks.t: Where clinicians live in Western Australia: fourteen places compared
chunks.x: Cottesloe & the western beaches The postcard — Norfolk pines, the ocean pool light, sunset over the sea. Perth’s premium strip, priced like it, and still below eastern equivalents. Scarborough to Hillarys The family beach belt — renewed esplanades, surf clubs, newer apartments and the northern train line behind. Where the 6am-swim life is most affordable. The northern corridor Joondalup and beyond — the growth spine with its own hospital hub, new estates and beaches all the way up. The most house for the money on the coast. Rockingham & the south coast The southern mirror — penguin-island shores, naval-town roots, and value that surprises. The train makes it a real commute.

chunks.t: Where clinicians live in Western Australia: fourteen places compared
chunks.x: Fremantle The port town that stayed itself — heritage streets, markets, working docks and a fierce local identity. Perth’s most characterful address, thirty minutes down the line. The riverside inner suburbs Subiaco, Mount Lawley, South Perth — terraces and art-deco flats near Kings Park and the hospitals, with the river as the morning run. The eastern corridor Victoria Park through to the foothills — the value ring near the big hospital campuses, multicultural food strips included. The hills Kalamunda and Mundaring — jarrah forest, cooler nights, wineries and space, forty minutes from the wards. Perth’s answer to a tree change without leaving town.

chunks.t: Where clinicians live in Western Australia: fourteen places compared
chunks.x: The kind of house the corridor is built on — and what the same budget looks like outside Perth. Mandurah Canals, estuary dolphins and the end of the metro line — technically regional, practically commutable, priced accordingly. Bunbury The regional hub — a working port city with its own hospital, beaches on three sides and house prices that reset expectations. The state’s gentlest regional posting. Busselton & the capes The jetty town and the Margaret River coast beyond — wine, surf and forests, with growing health services and lifestyle demand pricing the best of it. Albany The southern granite coast — cooler, wilder, historically the state’s first settlement, with a solid regional hospital and the south coast to itself.

chunks.t: Where clinicians live in Western Australia: fourteen places compared
chunks.x: Karratha & Port Hedland The Pilbara’s iron towns — company-town economics, serious heat, and packages built to compete with mining wages. Two-to-three-year chapters, entered deliberately. Broome & the Kimberley Cable Beach camels and wet-season contracts — the most beautiful hard posting in the country, with Aboriginal health at the centre of the work. Three things to check before you sign The train line, then the beach. Perth’s lines run the coast and the corridors — a suburb on the right one makes the hospital commute painless; the wrong one means the freeway. Afternoon sun and the Doctor. West-facing rooms cook until the sea breeze lands; ask about orientation, shading and air conditioning like a local. School catchments — and the visa fee question. Catchments bind here as everywhere; on a temporary visa, read the master’s School fees on a visa before you budget.

chunks.t: Where clinicians live in Western Australia: fourteen places compared
chunks.x: Most clinicians we move rent for six to twelve months first — long enough to learn whether they’re coast, river, Freo or hills people. Perth is generous with all four; the north is a separate conversation we have properly, package in hand. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Getting around Western Australia: trains, freeways and flights
chunks.x: Perth transport is a good-news story the east rarely hears: a modern, expanding rail network, freeways that mostly flow, no toll roads at all — and beyond the metro, a state that runs on regional flights and long, straight, empty highways.

chunks.t: Getting around Western Australia: trains, freeways and flights
chunks.x: Perth’s trains run the coast and the corridors — north to the beaches and Joondalup, south to Mandurah, east through the hills line, with new extensions still opening under the state’s rail programme. The system is clean, fast and cheap by eastern standards, and everything runs on a SmartRider card with daily caps. Buses fill the grid — including free city-centre routes — and the ferries cross the river as commute and pleasure alike. The practical rule matches the suburbs chapter: choose your line before your suburb , and test it at shift hours.

chunks.t: Getting around Western Australia: trains, freeways and flights
chunks.x: No tolls. None. WA is the only mainland state without a toll road — the freeway bill is zero, forever, and easterners take a month to believe it. The freeway has a rhythm The Kwinana and Mitchell freeways bunch at peak like anywhere — but "peak" here is forty minutes, not ninety, and it clears. Parking is manageable Hospital and suburban parking is kinder than any eastern capital’s. City parking costs; everywhere else mostly doesn’t. Country driving is its own skill Road trains, roos at dusk, and fuel stops you plan rather than assume. North of the wheatbelt, distance is the hazard — rest, fuel, water, always.

chunks.t: Getting around Western Australia: trains, freeways and flights
chunks.x: Perth → Bunbury Forrest Highway makes it ~1 hr 45; the regional train shadows it. The corridor commute is workable. Beyond Bunbury Busselton, the capes and Albany are road trips — easy, beautiful, and busiest on long weekends when half of Perth heads down south. Regional coaches & trains The state’s regional network links the south-west and the Goldfields — useful, not roster-compatible. Country life assumes a car. The wildflower detours August to October, the wheatbelt roads become the attraction. Locals plan spring drives around the bloom maps.

chunks.t: Getting around Western Australia: trains, freeways and flights
chunks.h: Flying: the state’s real transport system
chunks.x: Perth Airport Direct London and Rome — the country’s only nonstop Europe links — plus Asia in three to five hours, and the east coast in four to five. The intrastate network Karratha, Hedland, Broome, Kalgoorlie and Geraldton fly to Perth multiple times daily — the north’s clinicians treat the flight south as the bus. FIFO air traffic Mining charters make Perth’s regional terminals among the busiest in the country at 5am. Book popular routes early in roster season. The holiday map inverts Bali in 3.5 hours beats Sydney in 5 — South-East Asia is the west’s weekend-away shelf, and it reshapes how families holiday.

chunks.t: Getting around Western Australia: trains, freeways and flights
chunks.x: Journey Typical time Perth CBD → QEII / Murdoch hospital precincts 10–20 min by train or road Perth → Fremantle 30 min by train Perth → Joondalup / Mandurah ~30 / ~50 min by train Perth → Bunbury ~1 hr 45 by road or rail Perth → Margaret River ~3 hr by road Perth → Albany ~4.5 hr by road Perth → Kalgoorlie ~6.5 hr by road, or a 1-hr flight Perth → Karratha / Broome 2 / 2.5-hr flights Perth → Sydney / Bali / London 5 hr / 3.5 hr / 17 hr nonstop Off-peak estimates. North of the wheatbelt, check road conditions in the wet season and carry water always. Licence conversion, buying and registering a car, and the practicalities of Australian driving are national topics, covered once in the master’s Living in Australia . Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Weekends in Western Australia: beaches, forests and the north
chunks.x: The west’s weekends run on its own scale: an island of quokkas offshore, the world’s largest wildflower bloom inland, wine capes and karri forests down south — and, once a year if you’re wise, the Kimberley, which makes everywhere else look small. The bloom that organises spring 12,000 Wildflower species, August to October Every spring the state stages the largest wildflower bloom on earth, and it reaches the suburbs as surely as the interior — Kings Park puts on its September show without you leaving town. Locals plan one proper drive around it every year. The rest of the chapter works outward in rings — the Rottnest ferry first, the far north last and annual.

chunks.t: Weekends in Western Australia: beaches, forests and the north
chunks.x: Rottnest / Wadjemup The ferry-and-bicycle island — quokkas, snorkelling bays and no cars. Perth’s signature day out, and better midweek. The beach ladder Cottesloe’s pines, Scarborough’s esplanade, Mettams’ lagoon, and forty more — the city’s coast alone could fill a year of Saturdays. Kings Park Bigger than Central Park, wilder at its edges, and the city’s rooftop — the September wildflower display alone earns the visit. The Swan Valley Cellar doors, breweries and chocolate at twenty-five minutes — the lazy Sunday, institutionalised. The hills Kalamunda’s trails, Mundaring’s forest and the Bibbulmun Track’s northern trailhead — a thousand kilometres of walking starts here. Penguin & Seal Islands Rockingham’s wildlife ferries south of the city — the family default that visitors never expect.

chunks.t: Weekends in Western Australia: beaches, forests and the north
chunks.x: Margaret River & the capes World-class wine among world-class surf, caves under the ridge, and Cape to Cape walking between two lighthouses — the state’s great long weekend. Bunbury & Busselton Dolphins in Koombana Bay, the mile-long jetty with its underwater observatory — the corridor’s easy family stops. The tall timber Karri and tingle forests around Pemberton and the Valley of the Giants treetop walk — cathedral country, four hours south. Albany & the south coast Granite headlands, whale season, and The Gap’s ocean drama — the wilder, cooler weekend. Wave Rock & the wheatbelt The granite wave inland, salt lakes and silo art — the odd, wonderful interior day trip. The wildflower spring August to October the state hosts the world’s largest bloom — twelve thousand species from the city’s parks to the outback tracks. Plan one drive around it.

chunks.t: Weekends in Western Australia: beaches, forests and the north
chunks.x: Ningaloo The other reef — whale sharks in season, coral off the beach, no boats required. A flight or the great coastal road trip. Kalbarri & the Coral Coast River gorges, sea cliffs and the pink lake — the accessible north, six hours up the coast. The Kimberley Broome’s Cable Beach, the Gibb River Road’s gorges, Horizontal Falls, the Bungle Bungles — Australia’s last great wilderness, and the dry-season expedition that resets your sense of scale. Karijini The Pilbara’s slot canyons and red gorges — the inland masterpiece most easterners never see.

chunks.t: Weekends in Western Australia: beaches, forests and the north
chunks.x: Tourism Tourism Western Australia The state’s official visitor site — regions, road trips and what’s on. Outdoors Explore Parks WA Parks, trails and campgrounds — Karijini and the capes book out in season. The island Rottnest Island Ferries, bikes and bays — the Perth day out. Practical Transperth Journey planning, SmartRider and the new rail lines. That’s the guide Nine chapters on Western Australia. Everything national — Medicare, visas, registration, tax, super, schools — lives once in Moving to Australia . When you’re ready to look at roles, see what’s open now . Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Moving to Western Australia: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.x: Western Australia is a third of the continent with one city holding most of its people: Perth, the most isolated capital on earth, and one of the most pleasant places on it. For clinicians the west offers the country’s best city beaches, an easier housing market than the east, and — beyond the city — the strongest incentives in Australian healthcare.

chunks.t: Moving to Western Australia: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.h: One city, one third of a continent
chunks.x: Spring in the south west. The wildflower season runs August to October, and it is a major event here Perth sits on the Swan River between an endless white-sand coast and its own Mediterranean climate — two million people, a rebuilt riverfront, Kings Park looking over it all, and Fremantle’s port-town streets at the river’s mouth. It runs on its own clock, two or three hours behind the east coast, and closer to Jakarta than to Sydney — a fact that shapes everything from flight times to the evening news. Beyond the city, the south-west corner is the liveable west: Bunbury’s regional hub ninety minutes down the freeway, Busselton and the Margaret River wine coast beyond it, and tall-timber country to the southern capes.

chunks.t: Moving to Western Australia: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.h: One city, one third of a continent
chunks.x: Then the state opens into its other identity — the Wheatbelt, the Goldfields around Kalgoorlie, and the vast north: the Pilbara’s iron country and the Kimberley’s gorges, where medicine is flown, salaries carry serious loadings, and the nearest tertiary hospital is a four-hour flight south. The costs are distance and daylight: every east-coast conference, wedding and family visit is a five-hour flight, and the time gap makes cross-country calls a planning exercise. What the west gives back is the country’s easiest big-city life — and the sunsets, because this is the only capital where the sun sets over the sea. Who wrote this Ethicare is a healthcare recruitment company. This guide is free to read, asks nothing of you, and does not give visa advice. WA is the state people choose deliberately rather than drift into — and the one where the "will the distance bother you?" conversation matters most. Where we think it’s the wrong answer, we say so.

chunks.t: Moving to Western Australia: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.x: ~2.9M People in a state covering a third of Australia — the emptiest map in this collection. ~2.2M In Greater Perth — three-quarters of the state lives in the capital’s coastal strip. 90+ Public hospitals and health campuses, from metropolitan tertiary centres to remote clinics a day’s drive apart. ~12,500 km Of coastline — more than the rest of the mainland states combined, most of it empty. 3,200 hrs Of sunshine a year in Perth — the sunniest capital in Australia. ~100,000 In Greater Bunbury, the south-west’s regional hub, ninety minutes from Perth. UTC+8 Perth’s clock — two to three hours behind the east coast, and aligned with Asia’s business day. 5 hrs Flying to Sydney or Melbourne. The isolation is real, and so is direct London — the only nonstop to Europe in the country. 2–4× The scale of remote-area incentives in the north against a city package — the strongest loadings in Australian healthcare. Verified case by case.

chunks.t: Moving to Western Australia: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.h: Six things you only learn once you’re here
chunks.x: The isolation cuts both ways Five hours to Sydney means weddings, conferences and grandparents are a commitment. It also means Perth built everything it needs — and Bali is closer than Brisbane, which reshapes the holiday map entirely. The beaches really are better White sand, clear Indian Ocean water, and forty minutes of coast inside the metro area. The 6am swim-then-work routine is a mass habit, and the evening sea breeze — the Fremantle Doctor — is a daily institution with a name. The time zone is a stealth feature Aligned with Asia, awkward with the east coast: national meetings happen at 7am or not at all, and calls to Europe land in your evening — better than the east manages. The mining economy sets the rhythm Fly-in-fly-out rosters shape families, suburbs and Monday-morning flights north.

chunks.t: Moving to Western Australia: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.h: Six things you only learn once you’re here
chunks.x: It also underwrites the state’s wages and the demand for health services in places you’ve never heard of. "Regional WA" means something different In the east, regional means two hours from the capital. Here it can mean Karratha or Broome — a flight, a loading, and a different life. The south-west is the gentle version; the north is the serious one. Perth is easier than it looks from afar The housing runs below Sydney and Melbourne, the commutes are shorter, the trains are new, and the lifestyle-per-effort ratio is the best of any Australian capital. People arrive sceptical and stay decades. A note on Country Perth stands on Whadjuk Noongar country, and the south-west is Noongar land from the coast to the wheat line. The north is different Country entirely — Yamatji, Pilbara nations and the Kimberley’s many peoples, where Aboriginal health is central to the clinical work and community-controlled organisations lead much of it. Acknowledgement of Country opens meetings, and in the north cultural safety is core clinical preparation, not a slide deck. Take the induction seriously.

chunks.t: Moving to Western Australia: a guide for healthcare professionals
chunks.x: Nine chapters, all of them about Western Australia specifically. Anything true of Australia generally — Medicare, visas, Ahpra registration, tax, superannuation, schools — lives once in Moving to Australia . If you read nothing else, read Why Western Australia for the full case including the distance question, and Healthcare in WA , because the north is a different career from the city and deserves a clear-eyed look. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: Why Western Australia: the case for the west
chunks.x: Western Australia’s case rests on one question: how much does distance from the east coast matter to you? If the answer is "not much", Perth offers the best lifestyle-per-effort of any Australian capital — and the north offers packages the east can’t match.

chunks.t: Why Western Australia: the case for the west
chunks.x: Public-sector clinical pay is set by state awards, and we don’t quote figures until we’ve verified them against the current instruments. The structure: Perth pay is broadly comparable with the eastern capitals while Perth housing runs clearly below Sydney and below Melbourne — closer to Brisbane’s market, with less competition at inspections and shorter commutes to go with it. Then there is the west’s real differentiator: remote loadings . The Pilbara and Kimberley carry the strongest incentive packages in Australian healthcare — district allowances, housing subsidies or provided housing, additional leave, airfare assistance — because the state must compete with mining wages for every professional it sends north. For a defined chapter of two or three years, the north can reset a family’s finances. We verify every package against the current award before quoting it, and the variation between postings is real. What you trade: the five-hour flight to everything eastern, a time zone that makes national meetings awkward, and — in the north — heat, wet seasons and remoteness.

chunks.t: Why Western Australia: the case for the west
chunks.x: Monday to Friday Perth: 20–40 minutes, with new train lines doing the heavy lifting. Bunbury: fifteen. The north: five, plus the airstrip. Before work The ocean swim — Cottesloe, Scarborough, Mettams Pool — then the commute. Perth’s beach-before-work culture is the country’s most committed. After work The Fremantle Doctor arrives mid-afternoon, the temperature drops, and the coast fills: sunset over the sea, the only capital that gets it. Saturday Kings Park, the river, sport — and Fremantle’s markets and port-town streets for the afternoon. Sunday Rottnest by ferry for quokkas and snorkelling, the Swan Valley’s cellar doors, or the national parks north and south of the city. A long weekend Margaret River — wine, surf and tall forests three hours south — or Bali, which is the shorter flight.

chunks.t: Why Western Australia: the case for the west
chunks.h: The six things people ask us
chunks.x: Is there enough work? Yes — Perth runs a full tertiary system with the state’s growth concentrated in its northern and southern corridors, and regional WA recruits constantly with incentives attached. The depth is a step below Sydney or Melbourne at the quaternary end; for most professions the practical answer is that the west is short of clinicians, not opportunities. Healthcare in WA explains the structure. Will the isolation get to me? The key question, and it splits people cleanly. If your family and social gravity are eastern-states or European, budget the flights and the time gap — they are the reason people leave. If your life builds where you are, Perth’s self-sufficiency, its Asia-facing clock and its direct London flight make the distance mostly theoretical. Know which person you are before you sign. Can I buy a house? More easily than in any other big Australian capital.

chunks.t: Why Western Australia: the case for the west
chunks.h: The six things people ask us
chunks.x: Perth’s market runs below Sydney and Melbourne with less competition, and the middle suburbs remain buyable on clinical incomes. Bunbury and the south-west go further. Cost of living runs the numbers. What is the north really like? A different job in a different country: heat, wet seasons, mining towns and remote Aboriginal communities, enormous scope, thin backup, and the strongest packages in the system. The clinicians who thrive go in curious, take the cultural preparation seriously, and treat it as a defined chapter with an exit plan. The master’s Regional life chapter is the full account. Is it good with children? Excellent in the way Queensland is excellent — space, beaches, sport, sunshine — with Perth’s schools well-regarded and less zone-frenzied than the east’s.

chunks.t: Why Western Australia: the case for the west
chunks.h: The six things people ask us
chunks.x: The notes: grandparents are a five-hour flight away, and on a temporary visa, read the master’s School fees on a visa before budgeting. How international is it? More than its isolation suggests: WA has Australia’s highest overseas-born share, with deep British, South African, Indian and South-East Asian communities — the time zone and flight map make it the natural Australian home for families with Asian or European ties.

chunks.t: Why Western Australia: the case for the west
chunks.x: Your people are on the east coast Five hours each way turns every visit into an event. The eternal rule: proximity to your people wins. You need the deepest subspecialty pool Perth’s tertiary system is complete but smaller; the quaternary edge lives in Sydney and Melbourne. You want big-city culture at scale Perth’s scene is good and growing; the east’s is bigger. If headline acts weekly matter, look east. The time zone would grind If your work or family life runs on eastern-states hours, the two-to-three-hour offset is daily friction. You want four seasons Perth does hot dry summers and mild green winters — beautiful, but if autumn colour and frost matter, look to Victoria or Tasmania. Where we’d steer you instead Want the sunshine with east-coast proximity? Queensland . Want the biggest markets? New South Wales or Victoria .

chunks.t: Why Western Australia: the case for the west
chunks.x: Weighing the Tasman? The master’s Australia vs New Zealand chapter is the place to start. In our experience WA suits clinicians who want Australia’s most liveable everyday — beaches, commutes, weather — and are clear-eyed about the distance from everywhere else. The ones who thrive stop flying east for weekends and start exploring their own coast. Prefer it on paper? Request the printed guide →

chunks.t: About Australia: land, culture & life
chunks.x: ~26.6m People on a single continent 6 + 2 States & territories each with its own feel 200+ Languages spoken one of the most multicultural nations 65,000+ Years of culture the world’s oldest, still living A first impression

chunks.t: About Australia: land, culture & life
chunks.h: A vast country with an easy warmth
chunks.x: Australia is the world’s largest island and its smallest continent, roughly the size of mainland Europe, home to around twenty-six million people. Nearly all of them live around the coastal edge. What strikes most newcomers first is the ease of it. The light is bright, the days are outdoors, and people are relaxed, direct and quick to include you. Underneath that easygoing surface sit two things to know early: a First Nations culture tens of thousands of years old, and a modern nation built by people from every corner of the world. You’ll feel both, often in the same day. You don’t need to know any of this before you arrive, but a little understanding goes a long way. The people who settle most happily are those who come curious , ready to learn the land’s stories and customs rather than expecting it to be just like home. The land

chunks.t: About Australia: land, culture & life
chunks.x: Australia is big enough to hold the tropics, the desert and cool green coastlines all at once. Where you settle shapes your whole experience of it. Where life happens

chunks.t: About Australia: land, culture & life
chunks.x: Most Australians live on the eastern and southern coasts: Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane, Adelaide and Perth. Big, easy cities where the beach, the café and the office are rarely far apart. The interior

chunks.t: About Australia: land, culture & life
chunks.x: Beyond the cities lies the vast interior: red earth, endless sky and sacred places like Uluru. Remote, spectacular, and central to how Australia sees itself. The climate

chunks.t: About Australia: land, culture & life
chunks.x: From the tropical north to the temperate south, it’s a sunlit country, and its seasons are flipped from the northern hemisphere. Summer runs December to February; Christmas is a beach day. A short history

chunks.t: About Australia: land, culture & life
chunks.x: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have lived on this land for more than sixty-five thousand years, the world’s oldest continuous living cultures, with hundreds of distinct nations, languages and deep connection to Country. 1770 & 1788

chunks.t: About Australia: land, culture & life
chunks.x: James Cook charted the east coast in 1770; in 1788 the First Fleet established a British colony at Sydney Cove. What followed was profound and often painful upheaval for First Nations peoples, a history the country continues to reckon with. 1901

chunks.t: About Australia: land, culture & life
chunks.x: Six self-governing British colonies united to form the Commonwealth of Australia, one nation, one Parliament, and the states and territories you’ll recognise today. 1967

chunks.t: About Australia: land, culture & life
chunks.x: More than ninety per cent of Australians voted to count Aboriginal people in the census and allow national laws for them, a landmark moment in a long journey toward recognition and equality. 1992

chunks.t: About Australia: land, culture & life
chunks.x: The High Court recognised that Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples held rights to their land before colonisation, overturning the idea that Australia had belonged to no one, a turning point in law and national understanding. 1970s–today

chunks.t: About Australia: land, culture & life
chunks.x: The end of restrictive immigration policy opened Australia to the world, and waves of migration made it one of the most diverse societies on earth. In 2008 the nation formally apologised to the Stolen Generations, and the work of reconciliation continues today. The oldest living culture on earth

chunks.t: About Australia: land, culture & life
chunks.x: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have cared for this continent for more than sixty-five thousand years. Australia has no national treaty; the relationship is expressed through recognition, custom and an ongoing process of reconciliation. You’ll hear it often

chunks.t: About Australia: land, culture & life
chunks.x: Meetings, events and school assemblies frequently open by acknowledging the Traditional Owners of the land. A Welcome to Country is a similar ceremony offered by Traditional Owners themselves. A different worldview

chunks.t: About Australia: land, culture & life
chunks.x: For First Nations peoples, land, kinship, language and identity are woven together as “Country”, a living relationship of care, not ownership, across some 250 language groups. The work continues

chunks.t: About Australia: land, culture & life
chunks.x: A national effort to heal historic wrongs and close the gap in health, education and life outcomes, including, very directly, in the health system you’ll work in. This is a live and sometimes complex national conversation, in 2023 a referendum on an Indigenous Voice to Parliament did not pass, and questions of treaty and recognition remain open. For healthcare workers it matters in practice: the system places real emphasis on culturally safe care and on better outcomes for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people, and you’ll see that reflected in policy, training and everyday practice. You don’t need to be an expert, an open, respectful willingness to understand is exactly what’s hoped for. Aussie English

chunks.t: About Australia: land, culture & life
chunks.h: A few words you’ll hear every day
chunks.x: English is the everyday language, though Australians shorten almost everything. Arvo Afternoon: “see you this arvo”. Brekkie Breakfast, often eaten out, at a café. Servo A petrol (service) station. Bottle-o The bottle shop, where you buy alcohol. Chemist The pharmacy, where you fill a script. Doona A duvet or quilt for the bed. Thongs Flip-flops: footwear, not underwear! Heaps Lots, or very: “heaps good”, “thanks heaps”. No worries You’re welcome, it’s fine, the national motto. Esky A cool box for keeping drinks and food cold. Ute A utility vehicle, a pick-up truck. Snag A sausage, the star of any “barbie” (barbecue). Many Australian place names come from Aboriginal languages, Canberra, Wollongong, Parramatta, Bendigo, so it’s worth learning to say where you live correctly. Getting it right is warmly appreciated, and locals are happy to help. People & culture

chunks.t: About Australia: land, culture & life
chunks.x: Loyalty and looking out for one another run deep. Neighbours, colleagues and other families who’ve made the move tend to fold you in quickly: many newcomers are surprised how at home they feel within months. The great outdoors

chunks.t: About Australia: land, culture & life
chunks.x: Weekends are for the beach, the bush, the backyard barbecue or the footy. Sunshine and the coast are woven into ordinary life, and an easy, shared way to make friends and feel you belong. A fair go

chunks.t: About Australia: land, culture & life
chunks.x: Hierarchy is downplayed and first names are the norm, even at work. People value fairness, humility and not taking yourself too seriously. Everyone, in the Australian ideal, deserves “a fair go”. Many cultures, one home

chunks.t: About Australia: land, culture & life
chunks.x: Nearly half of all Australians were born overseas or have a parent who was. Large communities from every continent mean you’ll rarely be the only one who has come from somewhere else.

chunks.t: About Australia: land, culture & life
chunks.x: Life here is comfortable and modern, but more relaxed and more spread out than many are used to: cities are low-rise and car-friendly, coffee is taken seriously, and sport is a shared language. For most people that easy, outdoor rhythm is precisely the appeal, and it’s one our clinicians rarely regret. Sophie’s insight When we began working in Australia, the thing that struck me most was how easily people made room for us. Say yes to the barbecue and the early swim. Learn to acknowledge the Country you’re standing on, and to say your town’s name the way the locals do. None of it is hard, and all of it tells Australia you’ve come to belong, not just to work. That openness, more than the sunshine, is what turns a posting into a home. Sophie CEO & Founder, Ethicare Resourcing Common questions

chunks.t: About Australia: land, culture & life
chunks.h: The things people ask us first
chunks.x: Will I understand the accent and all the slang? Very quickly, yes. English is the everyday working language, so you’ll never be stuck, the accent and the habit of shortening words just take a week or two to tune into. Picking up a few local expressions is a lovely, easy way to show you’ve settled in, and colleagues will happily translate anything that catches you out at first. How should I engage with First Nations culture respectfully? Come open and curious. You’ll encounter Acknowledgement of Country at work and around the community, and in healthcare you’ll meet a real emphasis on culturally safe care and on closing the gap in outcomes for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people. You don’t need to be an expert, listening, learning and treating the culture with respect is exactly what’s hoped for, and your workplace will guide you.

chunks.t: About Australia: land, culture & life
chunks.h: The things people ask us first
chunks.x: Is Australia very different culturally from home? It depends where you’re coming from, but most newcomers find it familiar enough to settle quickly and different enough to feel new. It’s a modern, English-speaking democracy with a relaxed, outdoorsy, egalitarian culture and a deeply multicultural society. The adjustments tend to be gentle: more sunshine, more space and a slower pace rather than anything jarring. Will my family fit in? Most families settle well, though it takes time. Australia is welcoming and diverse, with well-established communities from all over the world. Children in particular settle fast, helped by friendly schools and an outdoor childhood of sport and the beach. Our community guide lists groups you can join before you arrive. Keep exploring

chunks.x: Whether you’re weighing up the move or want to understand the country better, we’re always glad to talk about the land, the lifestyle, and whether it could be the right home for your family. chunks.t: About New Zealand: Te Tiriti & te reo
chunks.h: A small country with a big heart
chunks.x: Aotearoa is a nation of around five million people at the bottom of the South Pacific, closer to Antarctica than to most of the world. What strikes most newcomers first is the contrast between the dramatic and the gentle. Soaring mountains, deep fiords and wild coastlines sit beside an unhurried, friendly way of life. People are direct but warm, proud but unshowy, and quick to make room for you. Underpinning it all is a bicultural foundation, the partnership between Māori, the indigenous people, and those who came later, layered today with communities from every corner of the world. You don’t need to know any of this before you arrive, but a little understanding goes a long way. The people who settle most happily are those who come curious , ready to learn the land’s stories and customs rather than expecting it to be just like home. The land

chunks.t: About New Zealand: Te Tiriti & te reo
chunks.h: Two islands, and never far from nature
chunks.x: New Zealand stretches long and narrow, so wherever you settle the coast, the bush and the mountains are close. Te Ika-a-Māui

chunks.t: About New Zealand: Te Tiriti & te reo
chunks.x: Warmer and more populous, home to Auckland and the capital, Wellington. Rolling green farmland, volcanic plateaus, geothermal Rotorua and long surf beaches define it. Te Waipounamu

chunks.t: About New Zealand: Te Tiriti & te reo
chunks.x: Wilder and more spacious, with the Southern Alps running down its spine, the lakes and fiords of the south, and Christchurch and Dunedin as its main cities. The climate

chunks.t: About New Zealand: Te Tiriti & te reo
chunks.x: Mild rather than extreme, with four real seasons, and reversed from the northern hemisphere. Summer is December to February; the far south can be properly cold in winter. A short history

chunks.t: About New Zealand: Te Tiriti & te reo
chunks.x: New Zealand was one of the last large landmasses on earth to be settled by people. c.1300s

chunks.t: About New Zealand: Te Tiriti & te reo
chunks.x: Polynesian voyagers navigated vast distances of open ocean to reach Aotearoa, becoming the tāngata whenua, the people of the land, and developing distinct iwi (tribes) with rich language, custom and oral history. 1642 & 1769

chunks.t: About New Zealand: Te Tiriti & te reo
chunks.x: Dutch explorer Abel Tasman sighted the coast in 1642; more than a century later, British navigator James Cook mapped the islands, opening the way to wider European contact and trade. 1840

chunks.t: About New Zealand: Te Tiriti & te reo
chunks.x: The Treaty of Waitangi was signed between the British Crown and many Māori rangatira (chiefs), the document still considered New Zealand’s founding agreement, and central to public life to this day. 1860s–1900

chunks.t: About New Zealand: Te Tiriti & te reo
chunks.x: Rapid settlement, the New Zealand Wars and large-scale land loss profoundly affected Māori, a difficult history the country continues to reckon with and openly. 1893

chunks.t: About New Zealand: Te Tiriti & te reo
chunks.x: New Zealand became the first self-governing country in the world to grant women the right to vote, an early mark of the egalitarian streak it still prizes. 1970s–today

chunks.t: About New Zealand: Te Tiriti & te reo
chunks.x: A Māori cultural renaissance revitalised te reo and tikanga, Treaty settlements began addressing historic wrongs, and waves of migration made New Zealand the diverse, outward-looking democracy it is now. The founding document

chunks.t: About New Zealand: Te Tiriti & te reo
chunks.x: Signed on 6 February 1840, Te Tiriti o Waitangi is an agreement between the Crown and Māori. It shapes law, public services and the health system you’ll work in. Article one

chunks.t: About New Zealand: Te Tiriti & te reo
chunks.x: Governance, the Crown’s role in governing the country, establishing settled law and order. Article two

chunks.t: About New Zealand: Te Tiriti & te reo
chunks.x: Chieftainship: Māori authority over their lands, resources and taonga (treasures), including language and custom. Article three

chunks.t: About New Zealand: Te Tiriti & te reo
chunks.x: Equity, the same rights, protections and citizenship for Māori as for all New Zealanders. The English and te reo Māori texts differ in important ways, and those differences sit at the heart of New Zealand’s ongoing conversation about partnership. For healthcare workers this matters in practice: the principles of Te Tiriti underpin the health system’s commitment to equity and to better outcomes for Māori, something you’ll see reflected in how care is delivered. Te reo Māori

chunks.t: About New Zealand: Te Tiriti & te reo
chunks.h: A few words you’ll hear every day
chunks.x: Te reo Māori is an official language, woven through greetings, place names, signage and the workplace. No one expects fluency. Kia ora Hello, and a warm “be well”, used constantly. Aotearoa New Zealand: “land of the long white cloud”. Whānau Family, in the broad, extended sense. Tāngata whenua People of the land: Māori as indigenous people. Manaakitanga Hospitality, kindness and care for others. Kaitiakitanga Guardianship and care of the environment. Tikanga Customs, the right and proper way of doing things. Marae Communal meeting grounds, the heart of a community. Pākehā New Zealanders of European descent. Haere mai Welcome: come in, come here. Ngā mihi Thanks and warm regards: common at the end of emails. Kia kaha Stay strong, an everyday word of encouragement. Place names are often te reo too, so it’s worth learning to say where you live correctly. Locals will warmly help you. Pronunciation is consistent once you learn the vowels, and getting it right is appreciated. People & culture

chunks.t: About New Zealand: Te Tiriti & te reo
chunks.x: Hospitality runs deep. Neighbours, colleagues and other families who’ve made the move tend to fold you in quickly: many newcomers are surprised how at home they feel within months. Tūrangawaewae

chunks.t: About New Zealand: Te Tiriti & te reo
chunks.x: Weekends are for the beach, the bush, the boat or the rugby. Connection to the land is central, and an easy, shared way to make friends and feel you belong. Mahi tahi

chunks.t: About New Zealand: Te Tiriti & te reo
chunks.x: Hierarchy is downplayed and first names are the norm, even at work. People value humility, fairness and pitching in, the “number eight wire” knack for practical problem-solving is a point of pride. Kanorau

chunks.t: About New Zealand: Te Tiriti & te reo
chunks.x: Alongside its bicultural foundation, New Zealand is home to large Pacific, Asian, South African, British and many other communities, so you’ll rarely be the only one who has come from somewhere else.

chunks.t: About New Zealand: Te Tiriti & te reo
chunks.x: Life here is comfortable and modern but a little more low-key than some are used to: shops close earlier, cities are smaller, and the pace is gentler. For most people that’s precisely the appeal. The trade is a simpler, more spacious kind of life, and it’s one our clinicians rarely regret. Sophie’s insight When my own family arrived, the thing that moved me most wasn’t the scenery, it was how readily people made space for us. Learn a few words of te reo, say yes to the invitation to the beach, ask people how to pronounce their town’s name properly. None of it is hard, and all of it tells New Zealand you’ve come to belong, not just to work. That openness, more than anything, is what turns a posting into a home. Sophie CEO & Founder, Ethicare Resourcing Common questions

chunks.t: About New Zealand: Te Tiriti & te reo
chunks.h: The things people ask us first
chunks.x: Do I need to speak te reo Māori? Not at all. English is the everyday working language, and you’ll get by perfectly without a word of te reo. That said, learning a handful of common greetings and saying place names correctly is warmly received, and it’s a lovely, easy way to show you respect where you’ve come to live. You’ll absorb plenty just by being here. Why does the Treaty matter for my work in healthcare? Te Tiriti o Waitangi underpins how public services, including health, are designed and delivered. In practice that means the system places real emphasis on equity and on improving outcomes for Māori, and you’ll see that reflected in policy, training and day-to-day care. You don’t need to be an expert, an open, respectful willingness to understand it is exactly what’s hoped for.

chunks.t: About New Zealand: Te Tiriti & te reo
chunks.h: The things people ask us first
chunks.x: Is New Zealand very different culturally from home? It depends where you’re coming from, but most newcomers find it familiar enough to settle quickly and different enough to feel new. It’s a modern, English-speaking democracy with a relaxed, outdoorsy, egalitarian culture and a strong bicultural heart. The adjustments tend to be gentle, a slower pace, smaller cities and earlier nights rather than anything jarring. Will my family fit in? Most families settle well, though it takes time. New Zealand is welcoming and diverse, and there are well-established communities from all over the world. Children in particular settle fast, helped by friendly schools and an outdoor childhood. Our community guide lists groups you can join before you arrive. Keep exploring

Ask Ethicare Back to New Zealand Ethicare Resourcing · your guide to a life and career in New Zealand.

chunks.t: Aotearoa in short
chunks.x: A country of extraordinary landscapes — from the towering Southern Alps to tranquil fiords, geothermal marvels and pristine coastlines. Kettle on. A longer read — about 4 min 2 Main islands — North & South 15K km Of stunning coastline 5.2 M Friendly residents (Kiwis) New Zealand sits in the south-western Pacific, around 1,900 km south-east of Australia. Its geography has sculpted a playground for outdoor enthusiasts and a haven for those who appreciate nature’s splendour. Whether you’re drawn to snow-capped mountains or pristine coastlines, every corner of the country is a visual masterpiece. This diversity is mirrored in a climate that shifts from the subtropical north to the alpine south. Four climate zones at a glance Subtropical — Northland & Auckland: warm, humid summers, mild winters Temperate — most of the North Island: warm dry summers, cooler wet winters Continental — Canterbury & Otago: hot dry summers, cold frosty winters Alpine — the Southern Alps: cold year-round with heavy winter snowfall

chunks.t: Aotearoa in short
chunks.x: The average temperature decreases as you travel south. January and February are the warmest months; July is the coldest. Summer Dec – Feb 20–25° Avg daytime Autumn Mar – May 17–21° Avg daytime Winter Jun – Aug 12–16° Avg daytime Spring Sep – Nov 16–19° Avg daytime

chunks.t: Aotearoa in short
chunks.x: New Zealanders — Kiwis — are known for being warm, direct and easy-going, with a deep love of the outdoors and a strong respect for work-life balance. You’ll feel welcomed quickly, and family life is given real room to breathe. Aotearoa weaves together Māori heritage and influences from across Europe, the Pacific and Asia. Te reo Māori, tikanga (customs) and manaakitanga (care for others) are woven through everyday life — not a museum piece, but a living part of how the country works. “ Māori make up over 14% of the population — their language and culture shape every facet of New Zealand life. Te Tiriti o Waitangi & the Tiaki Promise Te Tiriti o Waitangi (1840) — the founding agreement between the Crown and Māori, widely understood today as the document that guides the partnership between government and Māori. You’ll hear it referenced often.

chunks.t: Aotearoa in short
chunks.x: The Tiaki Promise — a shared commitment to care for New Zealand’s land, sea and culture. "Tiaki" means to care for; the idea is simple — treat the place, and its people, with respect. Three official languages — English, te reo Māori and New Zealand Sign Language. Stable & progressive — a parliamentary democracy with a strong culture of human rights, environmental care and dependable public services.

chunks.t: Aotearoa in short
chunks.h: Ten small things that make New Zealand, New Zealand
chunks.x: A few of the quirks and claims to fame you’ll pick up not long after you arrive. 01 The kiwi — a flightless, nocturnal bird found nowhere else, and the affectionate name locals give themselves. 02 The haka — the Māori ceremonial dance the All Blacks perform before every match, known the world over. 03 Geothermal country — sitting on the Pacific Ring of Fire, Rotorua bubbles with geysers, hot springs and mud pools. 04 Adventure capital — Queenstown is the birthplace of the bungee, with skydiving, skiing and jet-boating on tap. 05 Votes for women — in 1893 New Zealand became the first self-governing country to grant women the vote. 06 No snakes — there are no native snakes anywhere in the country, on land or in its waters. 07 Middle-earth — the Lord of the Rings and Hobbit trilogies were filmed across its landscapes.

chunks.t: Aotearoa in short
chunks.h: Ten small things that make New Zealand, New Zealand
chunks.x: 08 Dark skies — the Aoraki Mackenzie Dark Sky Reserve offers some of the Southern Hemisphere’s best stargazing. 09 A very long name — Taumatawhakatangihangakoauauotamateaturipukakapikimaungahoronukupokaiwhenuakitanatahu , a Hawke’s Bay hill, is among the world’s longest place names. 10 Few land mammals — apart from bats, New Zealand has no native land mammals, and no native land snails or frogs either. chunks.t: Community & belonging in Australia
chunks.h: Belonging is what makes a move last
chunks.x: Australia is one of the most multicultural countries in the world. Almost half its people were born overseas or have a parent who was, and the big cities are a true mix of cultures, faiths and languages from every corner of the earth. The healthcare workforce itself is wonderfully international. The important part: that diversity is not spread evenly across the country. The capitals are among the most cosmopolitan cities anywhere; large regional cities are reasonably mixed; and small country towns and the remote outback are predominantly Anglo-Australian, where a newcomer who looks or worships differently can feel far more visible. None of that means a place is unwelcoming, but it changes the day-to-day, and you deserve to know before you choose where to live. Our promise in this guide is simple: we’ll tell you the truth about a town before you move there. Where your community already exists, what life tends to feel like for people from your background, and whether somewhere is likely to suit your family. Faith & places of worship

chunks.t: Community & belonging in Australia
chunks.h: A place to worship, whatever your faith
chunks.x: Freedom of religion is protected in law. The cities have established congregations across many traditions; in smaller towns the choice narrows, sometimes sharply. Kirtan at a Melbourne gurdwara. Whatever your tradition, the congregation is usually already there — the question is how far from the hospital it is. Christian

chunks.t: Community & belonging in Australia
chunks.x: From Catholic, Anglican and Uniting to Pentecostal, Orthodox and a wide range of ethnic-specific congregations, Christian communities are found in every city and most towns: many with services in languages other than English. Muslim

chunks.t: Community & belonging in Australia
chunks.x: Long-established Muslim communities in the major cities run mosques, Islamic centres and schools, and halal food is easy to find. In regional and remote areas, mosques and halal options are far fewer and worth checking before you move. Hindu

chunks.t: Community & belonging in Australia
chunks.x: A large, active Hindu community supports temples and cultural associations in the cities, with festivals such as Diwali celebrated publicly, often as major city-wide events. Sikh

chunks.t: Community & belonging in Australia
chunks.x: A fast-growing Sikh population maintains gurdwaras across the cities and a number of regional centres, offering worship, langar and a strong, practical welcome for new arrivals. Buddhist

chunks.t: Community & belonging in Australia
chunks.x: Buddhist temples and meditation centres reflect Australia’s diverse Asian communities, welcoming both heritage practitioners and newcomers to the practice. Jewish & others

chunks.t: Community & belonging in Australia
chunks.x: Well-established Jewish communities are concentrated in Sydney and Melbourne, with synagogues, schools and kosher food. Many other faith communities are present too, mostly in the larger cities. Faith communities are often the fastest route to friendship and practical help when you arrive: many run welcome groups, share local knowledge and lend a hand with the early settling-in. It’s worth reaching out before you even land. If your faith matters to you, tell us; it can shape which town is the right one. Cultural & diaspora communities

chunks.t: Community & belonging in Australia
chunks.h: Chances are, your community is already here, in the cities
chunks.x: Communities form where people settle, mostly around the capitals. Knowing where yours is established can help when you’re choosing a base. Holi in Melbourne. The festivals travel with the people who keep them, which is usually the first sign that a community is properly established rather than just present.

chunks.t: Community & belonging in Australia
chunks.x: Large, active communities from the UK, Ireland, India, the Philippines, South Africa, China, Vietnam, the Middle East and across the Pacific mean cultural associations, social events and familiar faces are rarely far away in the cities.

chunks.t: Community & belonging in Australia
chunks.x: Because so many clinicians have made this exact move, from the UK, South Africa, the UAE and beyond, you’ll find others in your profession who share your background and understand both the work and the journey.

chunks.t: Community & belonging in Australia
chunks.x: Diwali, Eid, Lunar New Year, Holi, Vaisakhi and many more are celebrated openly and often city-wide: public, joyful occasions that make it easy to stay connected to your heritage and share it.

chunks.t: Community & belonging in Australia
chunks.x: Many communities run weekend language and culture schools so children stay connected to their heritage language and traditions while they grow up as young Australians.

chunks.t: Community & belonging in Australia
chunks.x: Active online groups for almost every nationality and city are where newcomers ask questions, find housing, swap recommendations and arrange the first real-life catch-ups.

chunks.t: Community & belonging in Australia
chunks.x: Cricket, football, netball, cultural dance, choirs and hobby clubs are some of the easiest, most natural ways to meet people who share your interests and, often, your background. Worth knowing

chunks.t: Community & belonging in Australia
chunks.x: If your faith or culture is central to your life, where you settle matters as much as the job. Most diverse

chunks.t: Community & belonging in Australia
chunks.x: Sydney · Melbourne · Perth · Brisbane · Adelaide Among the most multicultural cities on earth. In many suburbs the majority of residents were born overseas, you’ll hear dozens of languages, and almost every faith, cuisine and community is well represented. For most people from any background, the capitals feel cosmopolitan and easy to belong in. This is where established diaspora communities, places of worship, cultural grocers and international schools are concentrated, and where being from somewhere else is completely ordinary. Mixed

chunks.t: Community & belonging in Australia
chunks.x: e.g. Newcastle · Geelong · Townsville · Cairns · Toowoomba The bigger regional centres are reasonably diverse and growing more so, partly because healthcare and universities draw people from everywhere. You’ll usually find at least one mosque, temple or cultural association, some international groceries, and other migrant families, though less choice than a capital, and it varies a lot from town to town. Least diverse

chunks.t: Community & belonging in Australia
chunks.x: Inland NSW/QLD/SA · remote WA & NT communities Small country towns and remote areas are predominantly Anglo-Australian, alongside significant Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander populations in parts of the outback. There may be no mosque, temple or gurdwara for hundreds of kilometres, little or no halal or cultural food, and you may be one of very few people of your background in town. In practice: most people find country Australians warm, direct and welcoming, and many newcomers thrive in the close-knit pace. But as a visible minority you will be more conspicuous, and a minority of people do encounter staring, awkward assumptions or, occasionally, outright prejudice. It’s not the norm, but it’s real, and it weighs differently for a family than for a single clinician on a fixed contract.

chunks.t: Community & belonging in Australia
chunks.x: So a Black clinician from South Africa, a Muslim family from the UK or a Hindu radiographer from India might love a busy Perth or Melbourne suburb, and find a tiny outback town isolating. That’s exactly the kind of trade-off we’ll talk through with you, town by town, before you accept anything. Sometimes the answer is a regional city rather than a remote one; sometimes it’s choosing the suburb carefully. There’s almost always a way to get both the role and the community, it just takes a clear conversation first. The culture you’re joining

chunks.t: Community & belonging in Australia
chunks.x: Australia has the world’s oldest continuous living cultures, cared for by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples for more than 60,000 years. In remote and regional areas you may work closely with Aboriginal communities. In healthcare this matters practically. Many services place real emphasis on cultural safety : care that respects a patient’s culture, history and identity, and you may take part in cultural awareness training, hear an Acknowledgement of Country at the start of meetings, or work alongside Aboriginal Health Workers. You don’t need to know all of this on arrival; a willingness to learn and to show respect goes a very long way, and it’s one of the quiet privileges of working here. Australians talk a lot about a “fair go” , the idea that everyone deserves a fair chance regardless of background.

chunks.t: Community & belonging in Australia
chunks.x: It’s part of the national character and you’ll feel it in how flat, first-name and unpretentious workplaces tend to be. Like any ideal it isn’t lived out perfectly everywhere, but it’s a real and widely-held value, and it sits behind much of the warmth newcomers describe. If you’re considering a remote role with a large Aboriginal community, we’ll talk you through what the work and the cultural context are like, so you arrive prepared and respectful rather than surprised. An inclusive welcome

chunks.t: Community & belonging in Australia
chunks.h: A country that welcomes you as you are
chunks.x: Australia has strong anti-discrimination law covering race, religion, sex, sexual orientation and disability, at work and in everyday life. The protections apply everywhere; the lived experience is warmest in the cities.

chunks.t: Community & belonging in Australia
chunks.x: Marriage equality has been law since 2017, protections are nationwide, and the cities have visible, thriving communities and major events such as Sydney’s Mardi Gras. Smaller towns are often quieter and more conservative, but the law protects you everywhere.

chunks.t: Community & belonging in Australia
chunks.x: Workplaces, including across the health system, take inclusion and anti-discrimination seriously under the Fair Work framework. You should expect to be treated with respect and fairness as a matter of course.

chunks.t: Community & belonging in Australia
chunks.x: Single parents, blended families, same-sex parents and multi-generational households are all an ordinary, accepted part of Australian life. A taste of home

chunks.t: Community & belonging in Australia
chunks.h: The small comforts that matter most
chunks.x: In the cities most foods from home are surprisingly close; in the regions, most people end up planning ahead and ordering online.

chunks.t: Community & belonging in Australia
chunks.x: The big supermarkets, Woolworths, Coles and ALDI, carry growing world-food aisles, and the cities have large Asian, Indian, Middle Eastern, African and European grocers. Halal, kosher and a huge range of cultural foods are easy to find in metro areas; online ordering fills most gaps elsewhere.

chunks.t: Community & belonging in Australia
chunks.x: From South Indian and Filipino to Lebanese, Vietnamese, Korean and beyond, city restaurants serve the real thing, and community events where home cooking is shared generously are some of the best ways to meet people.

chunks.t: Community & belonging in Australia
chunks.x: The celebrations you grew up with are very likely marked here too, often publicly in the cities. Keeping your own traditions alive, and being invited into others’, is part of what makes life here rich.

chunks.t: Community & belonging in Australia
chunks.x: Halal food is widely available in the cities: many mainstream supermarkets and butchers stock halal-certified meat, and metro areas have dedicated halal butchers, grocers and restaurants. In regional and remote areas the choice narrows considerably, so it’s worth checking what’s available in a specific town before you commit.

chunks.t: Community & belonging in Australia
chunks.x: Kosher options are concentrated in Sydney and Melbourne, which have kosher stores, butchers and delis alongside established Jewish communities. Elsewhere it’s mostly online or through the local community, the peak Jewish bodies in the useful links are the best people to point you to current suppliers.

chunks.t: Community & belonging in Australia
chunks.x: Biltong, boerewors and braai staples, plus West and East African groceries, are available through specialist stores in the cities and a number of online retailers that ship Australia-wide, a real comfort if you’re moving from South Africa or elsewhere on the continent. Practical first steps

chunks.t: Community & belonging in Australia
chunks.x: Search online for groups linked to your nationality, faith or city. Introducing yourself early means a friendly contact or two before you even land.

chunks.t: Community & belonging in Australia
chunks.x: In a big city the suburb shapes everything: community, schools, places of worship, the food shops. We’ll help you pick one that fits your family, not just your commute.

chunks.t: Community & belonging in Australia
chunks.x: Colleagues are often your first community, and many have made the same move. Ask them where to worship, shop and gather, they’ll know.

chunks.t: Community & belonging in Australia
chunks.x: A weekly class, sports team, choir or place of worship gives your week an anchor and the same faces each time, which is how acquaintances become friends.

chunks.t: Community & belonging in Australia
chunks.x: Cook for new neighbours, share your festivals, contribute what’s yours. Belonging flows both ways, and people love being welcomed into something new.

chunks.t: Community & belonging in Australia
chunks.x: We know the makeup of the towns we place people in, and we’ll tell you where you’re likely to find your community, and where you might not. Communities & support networks

chunks.t: Community & belonging in Australia
chunks.x: Moving abroad doesn’t mean leaving your faith or your support behind. Places of worship, accessibility services and mental-health support, the networks that help you look after yourself and the people you love. Faith & worship National Council of Churches Find a Church Australian National Imams Council Hindu Council of Australia Sikh Council of Australia Executive Council of Australian Jewry Buddhist Council of NSW Accessibility & disability Disability Gateway Government information & services People with Disability Australia Carers Australia Disability Sports Australia Wellbeing & mental health Lifeline Australia 24/7 crisis support · 13 11 14 Beyond Blue Anxiety, depression & support Head to Health Black Dog Institute These are starting points, not endorsements: each link opens an external site we don’t control, and communities come and go.

chunks.t: Community & belonging in Australia
chunks.x: If you can’t find yours, or you’d like a warm introduction to people who’ve walked the same path, tell us where you’re moving and what matters to you. See also our Useful contacts guide. If you need help now Relocating is hard, and the months after arriving are when it tends to land. Both of these are free, and neither is a last resort. 13 11 14 Lifeline Crisis support and suicide prevention, 24 hours a day. Call, or text 0477 13 11 14. 000 Emergency services Police, fire or ambulance, anywhere in Australia. Ask for the service you need. Sophie’s insight People worry, quietly, about whether they’ll fit in, whether they’ll find somewhere to pray, food that tastes like home, friends who understand them, and whether they’ll be made to feel welcome. I take those worries seriously, because the answer depends on where you go.

chunks.t: Community & belonging in Australia
chunks.x: A family might feel completely at home in a diverse city suburb and quite isolated in a remote town with the same job title. My job is to tell you that before you decide, not after. There is almost always a way to find both the right role and the right community. It just starts with a frank conversation, and I’d much rather have it early. Sophie CEO & Founder, Ethicare Resourcing Common questions

chunks.t: Community & belonging in Australia
chunks.h: The questions people ask us about belonging
chunks.x: What’s it like as a person of colour or visible minority in a small town? It depends a lot on the town, and we’ll always give you a clear read on a specific one. In the big cities, being from anywhere is completely ordinary and most people feel very much at home. In small country towns and remote areas, which are predominantly Anglo-Australian, you’ll be more visible, and while most country Australians are warm and welcoming, a minority of people do experience staring, clumsy assumptions or occasional prejudice. It’s not the norm, but it’s real. For many single clinicians on a fixed contract it’s a non-issue; for a family putting down roots it can matter more. If it’s a concern, a diverse regional city or a well-chosen city suburb is often a better fit than a remote posting, and we’ll help you weigh it up. Will I be able to practise my religion freely? Yes.

chunks.t: Community & belonging in Australia
chunks.h: The questions people ask us about belonging
chunks.x: Australia has freedom of religion, and active communities exist across all the major faiths, especially in the cities. Places of worship, religious schools and cultural associations are well established in metro areas. In regional and remote places the nearest mosque, temple or gurdwara may be a long way off, so if regular worship is important to you, it’s worth checking what’s available in a particular town before you move. Is there a community of people from my country? Almost certainly, particularly in and around the capitals. Australia’s healthcare workforce is highly international, with established communities from the UK, Ireland, India, the Philippines, South Africa, China, the Middle East and many more, with social groups, festivals and online networks.

chunks.t: Community & belonging in Australia
chunks.h: The questions people ask us about belonging
chunks.x: These cluster in the cities, so even if your role is regional, many people choose a city base or visit regularly to stay connected. How welcoming is Australia to LGBTQ+ people? Marriage equality has been law since 2017, anti-discrimination protections are nationwide, and the cities have visible, thriving communities and major events. Smaller towns are often quieter and more conservative in feel, but the legal protections apply everywhere. As with everything on this page, we’re happy to be candid about what a particular community is likely to feel like. Can you help me choose somewhere I’ll belong? That’s one of the most valuable things we do. Tell us your background, your faith if it’s part of your life, what matters to your family and the kind of role you want, and we’ll tell you which places are likely to suit, and which probably won’t. The goal is a move that lasts, not just a job that’s filled. Keep exploring
