chunks.t: Driving & licences in Australia
chunks.h: The deadline nobody mentions until it has passed
chunks.x: You can almost certainly drive on your overseas licence when you arrive. What varies is how long for, and when the clock starts. Like tenancy law, and unlike income tax, driver licensing in Australia is state and territory business . Eight jurisdictions, eight road authorities, eight sets of conversion rules and eight different grace periods. There is no national driving licence and no federal answer to “how long can I use mine”. The trap is subtler than a different number, though. In several states the clock is tied not to your arrival date but to when you become a permanent resident , so a clinician on a temporary work visa may drive on an overseas licence for years quite legally, then have a short window after their permanent residency is granted, at exactly the moment they are least likely to be reading road authority websites.

chunks.t: Driving & licences in Australia
chunks.h: The deadline nobody mentions until it has passed
chunks.x: Driving on a licence that has quietly stopped being valid is not a technicality. It can void your insurance cover in an accident, which turns an ordinary bad day into a financial catastrophe. This is the one thing on this page worth checking in your first week rather than your first year. What to do about it Find your state’s road authority in the table below, read its page on overseas licence holders, and write your own deadline in your calendar with a reminder a month before . If your visa status changes later, and for most clinicians it eventually does, check the rule again on the day it changes. That single reminder is the whole of the advice. The primary source

chunks.t: Driving & licences in Australia
chunks.x: These are the authoritative answers on your deadline, your conversion route and how CTP works where you live. State or territory Road authority How CTP insurance works here New South Wales Transport for NSW Service NSW handles licence transactions You choose a CTP insurer separately — the “green slip” — before you can register a vehicle. Victoria VicRoads Licensing and registration Included in your registration, administered through the state injury insurer. Nothing separate to arrange. Queensland Department of Transport and Main Roads Licences, registration, CTP Bundled with registration, but you nominate which licensed insurer provides it. Western Australia Department of Transport WA Driver and vehicle services Included in your registration through the state insurer. Nothing separate to arrange.

chunks.t: Driving & licences in Australia
chunks.x: South Australia Service SA Licensing and registration Bundled with registration, with a choice of approved insurer. Tasmania Transport Tasmania Registration and licensing Included in registration through the state motor accidents scheme. Australian Capital Territory Access Canberra Road transport services Bundled with registration; you select from the licensed insurers. Northern Territory NT Motor Vehicle Registry Licences and registration Included in registration through the territory scheme. Authorities occasionally reorganise and rename. If a link here does not resolve, search the authority name plus “overseas licence” and tell us, and we will correct the page. The process

chunks.t: Driving & licences in Australia
chunks.x: For most of the clinicians we place this is paperwork rather than a test. It depends on where your licence was issued. Australia treats a list of countries as having comparable licensing standards . If you hold a full licence from one of those, you can generally convert by application, identity, evidence of your licence, an eyesight check, a fee, without sitting a practical driving test. The United Kingdom, Ireland and a number of others sit on those lists. If your licence is from a country not on your state’s list, expect to sit some combination of a knowledge test, a hazard perception test and a practical driving test. That is a normal and passable process, not a rejection, but it takes time and needs booking, which is the other reason to find out early rather than late. Because the lists are maintained state by state, a country recognised in one jurisdiction is not automatically recognised in another. Check the list held by your road authority, not a general one.

chunks.t: Driving & licences in Australia
chunks.x: This single answer determines whether the rest is paperwork or an exam. Do it first.

chunks.t: Driving & licences in Australia
chunks.x: Your overseas licence, an official English translation if it is not in English, your passport and visa, and proof of your Australian address. A licence that has expired complicates things considerably, so convert before yours lapses.

chunks.t: Driving & licences in Australia
chunks.x: Some authorities take walk-ins, most now prefer an appointment. Appointments in the larger cities can be weeks out, which is a very common reason people miss a deadline they knew about.

chunks.t: Driving & licences in Australia
chunks.h: Expect to surrender your overseas licence
chunks.x: Many states keep it when they issue yours. If you want it as a keepsake or for driving in a third country later, ask what the policy is before you hand it over.

chunks.t: Driving & licences in Australia
chunks.x: Ask your home authority for a letter confirming your licence history and any claims record before you leave. It is what lets an Australian insurer treat you as an experienced driver rather than a beginner, and it is much harder to obtain once you have gone. In our experience

chunks.t: Driving & licences in Australia
chunks.h: The document people wish they had brought is a letter about their driving history
chunks.x: Your Australian licence will say you passed a check. It says nothing about the fifteen years you drove without a claim, and insurers price on exactly that. A one-page letter from your home licensing authority or your current insurer, obtained before you fly, routinely saves more on premiums in the first two years than the whole conversion costs. Almost nobody thinks of it. The compulsory one

chunks.t: Driving & licences in Australia
chunks.x: If you are arriving from New Zealand or the UK, this is unfamiliar, and getting it wrong means driving illegally rather than merely uninsured.

chunks.t: Driving & licences in Australia
chunks.x: It covers injury to people in a motor accident, other drivers, passengers, pedestrians. Not vehicles, not property. It is compulsory everywhere. You cannot legally register or drive a vehicle in Australia without it. This is not the optional-but-sensible category. It attaches to the vehicle , not to you as a driver, which is why it is tied to registration rather than sold as a personal policy. How you buy it varies by state. In some it arrives inside your registration bill; in others you must choose an insurer yourself before you can register at all. The table above says which applies where you are.

chunks.t: Driving & licences in Australia
chunks.h: Why New Zealand arrivals find this odd
chunks.x: New Zealand has no CTP because ACC covers accidental injury on a no-fault basis for everyone, funded partly through levies including one on petrol and registration. Australia has no ACC. Injury cover comes through this compulsory motor insurance instead, and it works on a fault-based model in most states. The practical consequence: in New Zealand car insurance is not legally compulsory at all. In Australia part of it is. Advice carried across the Tasman is wrong in both directions. And it is only part. CTP leaves your own car, and everyone else’s, entirely uncovered, which is what the next section is about. The optional ones

chunks.t: Driving & licences in Australia
chunks.h: The other car insurances, and which you need
chunks.x: CTP is the floor. Above it sit three tiers, and which to buy depends on what your car is worth. Third party property. Covers damage you do to other people’s vehicles and property, and nothing of your own. This is the minimum most drivers should hold above CTP, because the risk it covers is unlimited: a modest older car can write off something expensive, and you would be liable for the whole of it. Third party fire and theft. The middle tier. Other people’s property, plus your own car if it is stolen or burns. Worth considering for a car with some value but not enough to comprehensively insure. Comprehensive. Covers your own vehicle as well, whoever was at fault. Sensible for anything newer or financed, and the default for most households.

chunks.t: Driving & licences in Australia
chunks.h: The other car insurances, and which you need
chunks.x: The reasonable approach for an arriving clinician: hold third party property from the day you own a car, and choose between the higher tiers based on what the car is worth and how much you could absorb losing it. Nothing about your visa status changes what is available to you. Home contents cover is a separate matter and sits with renting in Australia . Life, disability and income protection are usually held inside your super fund, which is covered in money, tax and banking . Practical

chunks.t: Driving & licences in Australia
chunks.x: Run a written-off vehicle and finance check. Every state provides or points to a register showing whether a car has been written off, stolen, or still has money owing on it. A car with finance owing can be repossessed from you even after you have paid the seller. Get an independent inspection. The state motoring clubs offer pre-purchase inspections and they are worth every cent on a private sale. Check the roadworthy requirement. Several states require a roadworthy or safety certificate for a private transfer, and whose job it is differs. Confirm the registration transfers properly. Registration is state-based, and a car registered interstate needs re-registering where you live, sometimes with an inspection.

chunks.t: Driving & licences in Australia
chunks.x: Dealer or private is a real trade-off. Dealers cost more and carry statutory warranty obligations; private sales are cheaper and sold as-is. Stamp duty applies on transfer , set by each state, on top of the purchase price. Budget for it rather than discovering it. Interstate moves need re-registration , so if you expect to move states within a year, factor that in. Buying with no Australian credit history is fine for cash but harder for finance, the same blank-slate problem as renting. Paying cash for a modest first car avoids the issue entirely. Utes and large SUVs dominate the market and hold value well. Small cars are cheaper to buy and run, and perfectly adequate for city work. Told straight

chunks.t: Driving & licences in Australia
chunks.h: Should you ship your own car?
chunks.x: Almost certainly not. Australia has strict vehicle import rules, and a personally imported car generally needs an import approval before it is shipped and compliance work after it arrives. Add sea freight, quarantine cleaning, duty and taxes, any modifications required to meet Australian design rules, and the delay while all of that happens, and the total commonly exceeds what the same car is worth on the local market. There are narrow exceptions, a rare or classic vehicle, or a personal import concession that fits your circumstances exactly. If you think you are in one of those, get proper advice from a customs broker rather than a shipping company’s sales team, because their interests differ from yours. In our experience

chunks.t: Driving & licences in Australia
chunks.h: The clinicians who ship a car regret it. The ones who sell up and buy on arrival do not.
chunks.x: It is an emotional decision more than a financial one, and we understand why. A car is one of the few large familiar objects you could theoretically bring. But it arrives weeks after you do, needs work before it can be driven, and by then you have already had to solve the problem another way. Sell at home while you are there to manage it, and buy something modest and second-hand in your first month. Upgrade once you know your commute. The road itself

chunks.t: Driving & licences in Australia
chunks.x: Australians drive on the left. Beyond that, a few things are different and one of them is dangerous. Enforcement

chunks.t: Driving & licences in Australia
chunks.x: Fixed cameras, mobile cameras, average-speed enforcement and low tolerances. Australian enforcement is stricter than many arrivals expect, penalties are real, and demerit points accumulate against your new licence quickly. Assume the limit is the limit. The dangerous one

chunks.t: Driving & licences in Australia
chunks.h: Distance is not what it looks like on a map
chunks.x: The single most underestimated risk. Journeys between regional towns are longer, emptier and more tiring than the distance suggests, phone coverage disappears, and fuel stops can be hundreds of kilometres apart. Plan long drives properly, carry water, and tell someone your route. Wildlife

chunks.t: Driving & licences in Australia
chunks.h: Dawn and dusk are the risk
chunks.x: Kangaroos and livestock on regional roads are a serious hazard, worst at first and last light. Many locals avoid driving country roads at those hours, and that is sound advice rather than folklore. Alcohol

chunks.t: Driving & licences in Australia
chunks.x: Police stop drivers at random as a matter of course, not on suspicion. The limit is low, the enforcement is constant, and for a registered health practitioner a drink-driving conviction is a professional problem as well as a legal one. Cities

chunks.t: Driving & licences in Australia
chunks.x: Sydney, Melbourne and Brisbane have extensive toll networks needing an electronic tag or a pass; Perth and Adelaide have none. Inner-city parking is expensive and hospital staff parking is often limited and waitlisted. Worth asking about before you assume you will drive to work. Conditions

chunks.t: Driving & licences in Australia
chunks.x: Summer heat is hard on older cars and on tyres. Low sun at either end of the day is worse than in higher latitudes. And in the north, a road that is fine in June may be cut in February. Never drive into floodwater, which is advice locals repeat every single wet season for good reason. Before you buy anything

chunks.t: Driving & licences in Australia
chunks.x: A car is one of the largest costs of the first year, and for some people it is optional. In the inner suburbs of Sydney, Melbourne and Brisbane, plenty of households manage without one: public transport is decent, parking is expensive, and car-share and ride-hailing fill the gaps. If you will live centrally and work at a well-connected site, try the first two months without buying and see. Almost everywhere else the answer is yes, and in outer-suburban and regional Australia a household often needs two, which is a cost that a salary comparison will not show you. The deciding factor is usually your roster, not your suburb. Public transport that works perfectly for a nine-to-five does not help at the end of a late shift when services have stopped, and a taxi home several nights a week is worse than owning something modest. If you work nights, weekends or on-call, assume you need a car.

chunks.t: Driving & licences in Australia
chunks.x: Which is the argument for deciding after you arrive rather than before. Give it a month, learn the actual commute, then buy, the same logic as not signing a lease from photographs. What a car costs to run in a specific city, and whether a second one is affordable there, is covered in the cost chapter of each destination guide . Where to check the current rules Your state or territory road authority, from the table above, the only authoritative source on your deadline, your conversion route and CTP. Department of Infrastructure and Transport . Federal vehicle import rules, if you are still considering shipping. The motoring club in your state, pre-purchase inspections, roadside assistance and written-off vehicle checks. Common questions

chunks.t: Driving & licences in Australia
chunks.h: The things people ask us first
chunks.x: Can I drive on my overseas licence? Usually yes at first, but the period is set by each state and in several it starts when you become a permanent resident rather than when you land. That is the trap. Check your own road authority in your first week and put your deadline in your calendar with a reminder a month before. Driving on a lapsed licence can void your insurance. Will I have to sit a driving test? Only if your licence is from a country not on your state’s recognised list. Holders of a full licence from a recognised country generally convert by application, with no practical test. The lists are maintained state by state, so check the one held by your own authority rather than a general list. What is CTP and is it compulsory? Compulsory third party insurance covers injury to people in a motor accident, and yes, you cannot legally drive without it anywhere in Australia.

chunks.t: Driving & licences in Australia
chunks.h: The things people ask us first
chunks.x: In some states it arrives inside your registration; in others you must choose an insurer before you can register. It does not cover damage to any vehicle, which is why most drivers also hold third party property or comprehensive cover. Is car insurance compulsory like in New Zealand? The comparison runs the other way. New Zealand has no compulsory motor insurance at all, because ACC covers accidental injury on a no-fault basis. Australia has no ACC, so injury cover comes through compulsory CTP instead. If you are moving between the two countries, do not carry either assumption across. Should I ship my car? Almost never. Import approval, compliance work, freight, duty and any modifications commonly add up to more than the same car costs locally, and it arrives weeks after you do. Sell at home while you are there to manage it and buy something modest second-hand in your first month.

chunks.t: Driving & licences in Australia
chunks.h: The things people ask us first
chunks.x: Do I need a car at all? In the inner suburbs of the biggest cities, often not. Almost everywhere else yes, and frequently two per household in regional areas. Your roster decides it more than your suburb: if you finish late shifts after the buses stop, a car stops being optional. Decide after a month here rather than before you arrive. What should I bring from home? A letter from your licensing authority or current insurer confirming your driving history and claims record. Your Australian licence will not carry your fifteen claim-free years, and insurers price on exactly that. It is easy to get before you leave and awkward afterwards. Read a little deeper

chunks.t: Education & schools in Australia
chunks.x: Education is run by each state and territory, so starting ages, year-level names and term dates vary. All follow a common Australian Curriculum. Schooling is compulsory from around age six until at least sixteen, and most children attend from the year they turn five. For newcomers, the practical headline is simple: places are generally easy to access, support for new arrivals is well established, and children tend to settle quickly. The stages

chunks.t: Education & schools in Australia
chunks.x: Long day care, preschool and kindergarten programs in the years before formal school: widely available, and a gentle on-ramp for younger children. Primary

chunks.t: Education & schools in Australia
chunks.x: The first year (called Prep, Foundation, Kindergarten or Reception depending on the state) through to Year 6, the grounding years, usually from around age five. Secondary

chunks.t: Education & schools in Australia
chunks.x: High school through to a senior secondary certificate. The final years lead to the ATAR, the rank used for university entry, though it’s far from the only pathway. The early years

chunks.t: Education & schools in Australia
chunks.x: If you’re moving with little ones, childcare is often the first thing to arrange. The options

chunks.t: Education & schools in Australia
chunks.x: Long day care (centre-based, from babies to school age), family day care in a carer’s home, occasional care, and preschool or kindergarten in the year or two before school. School-age children can use outside-school-hours care before and after school and in the holidays. The cost

chunks.t: Education & schools in Australia
chunks.x: Childcare is a real household cost. The federal Child Care Subsidy lowers fees for eligible families, but eligibility depends on your residency and visa status, so many families on a temporary visa (including the 482) don’t qualify and pay full fees. It’s worth budgeting for, and checking your position early. Getting a place

chunks.t: Education & schools in Australia
chunks.x: Popular centres. Especially in cities and inner suburbs, can have waiting lists. Registering your interest before you arrive, with a couple of options in mind, takes the pressure off those first few weeks. Whether the Child Care Subsidy applies to you comes down to your visa, so we’ll help you understand where you stand, and factor childcare into the bigger picture of the move, before you commit. Three sectors

chunks.t: Education & schools in Australia
chunks.x: Families choose between three broad sectors. All follow the national curriculum; the right one depends on your priorities, your budget and where you live.

chunks.t: Education & schools in Australia
chunks.x: Public schools, funded by the state, free or low-cost (small fees and costs apply). The large majority of children attend them, and places are usually tied to your home address.

chunks.t: Education & schools in Australia
chunks.x: A large, well-established system open to families of many backgrounds, with modest fees. A popular middle path for many relocating families.

chunks.t: Education & schools in Australia
chunks.x: Private and faith-based schools with higher fees, offering particular philosophies, facilities or programs. Many have waiting lists, so it’s worth enquiring early. What it costs

chunks.t: Education & schools in Australia
chunks.h: School fees, and the part that depends on your visa
chunks.x: What you’ll pay depends on the sector and on your residency status. For most relocating families the biggest variable is the visa.

chunks.t: Education & schools in Australia
chunks.x: Free or low-cost for citizens and permanent residents. You’ll still meet voluntary contributions, uniforms, excursions and materials, but tuition itself is covered.

chunks.t: Education & schools in Australia
chunks.x: Modest tuition fees that rise gradually through the year levels, an affordable middle path for many families.

chunks.t: Education & schools in Australia
chunks.x: Higher fees that vary widely by school, reflecting facilities, programs and philosophy. Worth enquiring early, as many have waiting lists.

chunks.t: Education & schools in Australia
chunks.h: Residents and temporary residents pay differently
chunks.x: On a permanent visa, government schooling is free or low-cost and you are generally eligible for the Child Care Subsidy. On an employer-sponsored 482 you are a temporary resident, and two things change: your children may pay an annual tuition contribution at a government school, which varies by state and is waived for many of the occupations we place, and you usually will not qualify for the Child Care Subsidy. Because the amounts and exemptions are set state by state and revised each year, they live in one place rather than three: School fees on a visa holds the current figures by state, who is exempt, and the official page for each. Out-of-school and holiday programmes run through the long summer break and each term break, and they book out early in the popular suburbs. The practical part

chunks.t: Education & schools in Australia
chunks.x: For public schools, where you live usually decides which school your child can attend, which is why the suburb decision and the school decision go hand in hand. Most government schools have a catchment zone , and living within it gives your child a place. That makes it worth researching schools before you choose a rental, especially if a particular school matters to you. Catholic and independent schools enrol more broadly but may have waiting lists and their own application timelines. Newly arrived children whose first language isn’t English are usually well supported through English as an Additional Language programs, so a language gap is rarely a barrier to settling in. The specifics, zones, fees and what’s available near you, differ by state and suburb, so we’ll point you to the relocation guide for your state and the right state education department as those are published. After school

chunks.t: Education & schools in Australia
chunks.x: Australia has a well-regarded university sector and a parallel vocational system (TAFE) for hands-on, industry-focused training. Entry to university is most often via the ATAR from Year 12, but there are many alternative pathways too.

chunks.t: Education & schools in Australia
chunks.x: Here the visa matters again, and it’s worth knowing early if you have older teenagers. Citizens and permanent residents are treated as domestic students , eligible for government-subsidised Commonwealth Supported Places, and (for citizens) the HECS-HELP loan that lets you defer fees. Temporary-visa holders, including dependents on a 482 , are generally treated as international students : full international fees, and no access to HELP loans. If your family moves to permanent residency before or during study, that picture can change, so the timing of a teenager’s university start is worth planning around. Moving with a teenager close to university age? Check this early: whether you’re on a temporary or permanent pathway can make a difference to tertiary fees, and it’s worth weighing alongside the rest of the move.

chunks.t: Education & schools in Australia
chunks.x: Sophie’s insight School is the worry I hear most from parents, and almost always the one that resolves most happily. Children settle faster than their parents expect, schools are welcoming to new arrivals, and the support for kids finding their feet is real. My one piece of practical advice: if a particular public school matters, check its zone before you sign a lease. That single step saves families a lot of stress. Sophie CEO & Founder, Ethicare Resourcing The end of the day is where a lot of settling happens: sport, clubs and the walk home with people your children will know by the second week. Common questions

chunks.t: Education & schools in Australia
chunks.h: The things parents ask us first
chunks.x: Will my child get a place easily? Generally yes. Government schools must provide a place for children living in their catchment zone, and Catholic and independent schools enrol from a wider area (sometimes with waiting lists). The main thing is to align your housing choice with the school you’d like. What if English isn’t my child’s first language? Schools are well set up for this through English as an Additional Language support. Children pick up the language quickly, and a language gap rarely holds them back from settling and making friends. How much do schools cost? Government schools are free or low-cost for residents (with contributions for uniforms, excursions and materials). Catholic schools charge modest fees; independent schools charge more and vary widely. See what school costs for the full picture, including how it changes on a temporary visa. We’re on a 482 visa.

chunks.t: Education & schools in Australia
chunks.h: The things parents ask us first
chunks.x: Do we pay for a government school? Possibly. This is the key thing to check. On an employer-sponsored 482 you’re a temporary resident, and several states and territories charge an annual tuition contribution for temporary residents’ children at public schools, while others exempt skilled or sponsored visas. It varies a lot by state and changes over time, so check the current policy with the state education department where you’re heading before you budget. Can we get the Child Care Subsidy on a 482? Usually not. The Child Care Subsidy depends on residency and visa status, and most temporary-visa families, including many on a 482. Don’t qualify, so they pay full childcare fees. Permanent residents and citizens are generally eligible. It’s worth budgeting for either way and checking your position early.

chunks.t: Education & schools in Australia
chunks.h: The things parents ask us first
chunks.x: Will my child’s year level transfer? Usually children are placed by age into the corresponding year level, with schools assessing where they’ll fit best. Because starting ages and year names vary by state, it’s worth confirming the equivalent with your destination’s education department. Read a little deeper

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: What will my partner do? Two careers move, not one, and their work rights depend on their own visa grant and its conditions, not on a job offer of their own. Can my partner work? on this page sets out what decides it, what to ask before you accept, and what to do if they are a clinician too. Immigration & visas explains how a partner fits the main application. Will we pay school fees? It depends on your state and your visa: public schooling is not automatically free for every temporary-visa family, and the rules differ meaningfully between states. Will I have to pay school fees? answers it properly, read it before you choose a state, not after. What will childcare cost? Under-fives are a different budget line entirely, and in popular suburbs the constraint is places rather than price.

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: Childcare covers the options, the waiting lists, the subsidy question and what a clinical roster does to all three. Can we manage on one income at first? Don’t guess. Do the subtraction: net salary, minus rent, childcare, school costs, insurance, a car and the weekly shop. If the result works before a second income arrives, everything that follows is easier. Salary & pay and the cost of relocating give you the pieces. Will my family have healthcare cover? Medicare is not automatic on every temporary visa, and private health cover can be a visa condition in its own right. Check your family’s position early, bring enough regular medication for the first weeks, and carry copies of medical records. Understanding healthcare covers Medicare and the private system.

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: When in the school year should we move? Aim for the long summer break and children get a clean start, though schools handle mid-year joins well too. Teenagers approaching their senior assessment years need the most care, plan around exam cycles, not flight prices. Does my child need extra learning support? Support does not transfer automatically with overseas paperwork. Get current reports and assessments before you leave, contact shortlisted schools before you commit to an address, and ask each one directly what support it can offer and how long assessments take to arrange. Can our parents and grandparents join us? Visits are usually possible. Longer stays and permanent residence are much harder, with sponsorship, caps and long waits.

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: Family-stream visitor visas (subclass 600) cover regular visits; the Sponsored Parent (Temporary) visa (subclass 870) allows stays of three or five years at a time, up to ten years in total, with sponsorship and health-insurance conditions, an annual cap and no work rights, and no pathway to residence. Permanent routes exist too: the Parent visa (subclass 103) carries a queue measured in decades, while the Contributory Parent visa (subclass 143) moves far faster in exchange for substantially higher contribution charges. Caps, charges and processing change, check the official Home Affairs parent visa pages before promising anything to the grandparents. Temporary first, or permanent residence? For families this is the quiet big one, because residence status, not the job, drives the school-fee, Medicare and subsidy answers above.

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: Most clinicians arrive on the employer-sponsored Skills in Demand visa (subclass 482) with the family as secondary applicants; some roles support the permanent Employer Nomination Scheme (subclass 186) sooner, and regional classifications open further routes. Reaching permanence flips several of the costs on this page. Immigration & visas covers the pathways. What if someone in the family has a health condition or disability? This is the hardest question on the page, and the one to face earliest. Every applicant. Dependants included, must meet Australia’s migration health requirement, and the test is projected cost, not diagnosis: a Medical Officer of the Commonwealth assesses whether a condition is likely to cost more than the Significant Cost Threshold, currently A$86,000.

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: For temporary visas costs are assessed over your stay; for provisional and permanent visas generally over five years, and up to ten years for a permanent condition with a predictable course. Being able to pay privately does not change the test. Classic triggers include high-cost PBS medicines (biologics such as adalimumab), dialysis- or transplant-level care, and some high support needs in children. Having a condition does not automatically mean the requirement is not met; each case is assessed individually. If one family member fails, the whole application can be refused; health waivers exist on some visa subclasses only, and are discretionary. Declare everything, and gather specialist reports and costed treatment plans before you apply. For anything borderline, read the Home Affairs health requirement guidance closely first.

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: The official Home Affairs health requirement pages carry the current rules; whether a particular medicine is PBS-funded is a separate question again, see Understanding healthcare . We’re recruitment specialists, not registered migration agents, and none of this is immigration, tax or financial advice. Visa conditions and eligibility rules change, so confirm the current position with the Department of Home Affairs and the schools themselves before committing. The reassuring part

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.h: Children travel further than we give them credit for
chunks.x: Children take their cue from you. If the move is framed as an adventure and the practicalities are quietly handled in the background, most children adapt remarkably quickly, often faster than the adults. Australia’s outdoor, friendly, sport-loving culture is good for kids, and schools are well used to welcoming children from all over the world. This guide walks through both halves: getting there in one piece, and helping everyone feel at home once you’ve arrived. If there’s one thing to hold onto, it’s this: a few unsettled weeks are completely normal and almost always temporary. Wobbles, clinginess and the odd tearful evening don’t mean you’ve made the wrong decision, they mean a small person is doing something brave. The question the move turns on

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: Two salaries or one changes what you can afford and where you can live. The short version: your partner’s work rights depend on their own visa grant and its conditions. Partners are usually included in your application as secondary applicants, so what they can do follows from the visa they are granted, not from a job offer of their own. That is why the answer is never a flat yes or no, but check it against the route you are on — and check it before you accept, not after. Whose visa decides it

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: Work rights depend on the visa your partner is granted and its conditions, usually as part of your application. Change route — temporary to permanent — and theirs changes with it. Read the conditions on the visa you are granted, not the one you applied for. Will the qualification count?

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: Permission to work and recognition to practise are two different processes. Regulated professions run through the Australian regulator or assessing authority for that field; everything else is judged by employers. Start it early. Assessments take longer than anyone expects. How long until they earn?

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.h: Budget the first months on one income
chunks.x: Even with full work rights, job-hunting while unpacking, enrolling children and learning a new city takes time. Families who plan for one income and are pleasantly surprised do far better than families who plan for two. If they are a clinician too

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: Theirs may well be the longer one. Run both from the start rather than in sequence — a second timeline discovered late is the most common reason a family ends up arriving months apart. Check their pathway alongside yours.

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.h: What to settle before you accept
chunks.x: Ask the employer which visa they intend to sponsor and what conditions come with it. Ask what support, if any, extends to a partner. Then have the conversation at home about what six months on one income looks like. None of this is awkward at the offer stage; all of it is expensive later. Visa conditions are set and changed by government, so we point you at the source rather than paraphrasing it: Department of Home Affairs . Ethicare is not an immigration adviser. See also visas and immigration . Under five

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: The binding constraint is places rather than price. In popular suburbs the waiting list starts long before you land. 1

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: Long day care covers the full working day. Family day care is a smaller setting in an educator’s own home, and is often the more flexible option. Preschool and kindergarten are the year or two before school, run by each state under its own name and its own rules — which is why advice from a friend in another state may not apply to you. 2

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.h: Join waiting lists before you fly
chunks.x: You can enquire and be listed from overseas. Do it as soon as you have a suburb in mind, and list at more than one centre. A place you do not need is easy to decline; a place that does not exist is not. 3

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.h: Check the subsidy against your own visa
chunks.x: Fees are quoted per day, and the Child Care Subsidy reduces what families pay — but eligibility depends on your residency status, so a temporary-visa family should confirm their position before budgeting on the subsidised figure. This is the single most expensive assumption we see families make. 4

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.h: Test it against a clinical roster
chunks.x: Standard centre hours were not designed around a 7am start or a late finish. Ask about the earliest drop-off and the latest pick-up, ask what happens when you are held past handover, and plan for the gap — a nanny share or family day care often covers what a centre cannot. Official sources: Child Care Subsidy (Services Australia) for eligibility and rates, and your state education department for preschool. For school-age children, schools and education covers enrolment, catchments and fees. Doing it on your own

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: Two things need handling early, and both are easier to do at home than from the other side of the world.

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.h: Consent to take a child abroad
chunks.x: Where someone else holds parental responsibility, you will generally need their written consent or a court order — and it can be asked for twice: once by the visa application, and again by an airline or a border officer. Get it in writing, get copies certified, and carry them in your hand luggage rather than the shipping container. Full birth certificates showing both parents, not the short form. Any parenting or custody orders, certified. A signed consent letter with the other parent’s contact details, or evidence of sole parental responsibility. Where a parent has died, the death certificate. Immunisation records and medical notes, which schools and clinics will ask for. One income, two costs

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.h: Childcare is the line that decides it
chunks.x: Work the numbers on your own salary with care included at full price, and check the subsidy question above before you rely on it. The first three months are the most expensive of the whole move. No second adult

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.h: Build the network before you need it
chunks.x: Before and after-school care, school-holiday programmes, a neighbour, and one colleague who will swap a shift. Set these up in the first fortnight, not the first emergency. The roster

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: Nights, weekends and on-call are a different proposition without another adult at home. Say so at offer stage — it is a normal conversation, and a far harder one to start once you have arrived. School holidays

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.h: Longer than you are used to
chunks.x: The summer break is substantial and falls over Christmas. Holiday programmes book out early. Check the term dates for your state before you plan your leave for the year. Consent and documentation requirements are set by government: see Department of Home Affairs . Before you fly

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: Share the news in good time and keep the conversation going. Look at photos and maps of where you’re heading, watch videos together, and let them ask the same questions as many times as they need to. Make it real

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: Explore the new town online, find the local beach, park or pool, and if you can, look at their school’s website together. The more they can imagine the everyday, the less frightening it feels. Honour the goodbye

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: A proper goodbye matters. Help them mark leaving friends, family and a familiar home, a small party, a memory book, swapping addresses, so the move feels like a beginning, not a loss.

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: A favourite toy, blanket or pillow should travel in the hand luggage, never the hold. Familiar things are anchors when everything else is new.

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: Reassure them that grandparents and friends are a video call away. The time difference takes some juggling, but knowing loved ones haven’t disappeared makes the distance easier.

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: Let older children choose a few of their own things to bring. A little ownership over the move turns something happening to them into something they’re part of.

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: Carry passports, visas, and copies of immunisation records, medical notes and any prescriptions in your hand luggage. Australia’s biosecurity rules are strict, so check what food and items you can bring before you pack. The big one

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: It’s usually 20 to 24 hours with a stop somewhere. Break the journey

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: A night’s stopover en route (common hubs include the Gulf, Singapore, Hong Kong or Kuala Lumpur) can split an overwhelming trip into two manageable ones and let small bodies stretch, sleep and reset. Ask for help

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: Request bassinets, children’s meals and seats together when you book, and use family boarding. Cabin crew are well used to travelling children and will lend a hand if you ask. Beat the boredom

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: Snacks, headphones, downloaded shows, and a few small wrapped activities handed out across the hours work wonders. Novelty buys you precious quiet stretches.

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: Comfy layers and familiar pyjamas signal bedtime even at 35,000 feet, and layers cope with cabins that swing from warm to chilly.

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: Feeding, a drink or a chew during take-off and landing helps with pressure. Pack more nappies, wipes and spare clothes than feels sensible.

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: The time difference is large, so nudge towards local time over the first few days with daylight, fresh air and patience. Expect early starts and odd-hour wakings for a week or so.

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: Declare any food, and don’t pack fresh produce. Australia’s arrival biosecurity is strict. Knowing this in advance saves a stressful first hour at the airport with tired children. When you land

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: Most families find the first couple of days are best kept small: rest, food, a gentle look around.

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: Don’t fight the jet lag with a packed schedule. Let everyone sleep, eat simply, and surface slowly, and in the heat, get the children drinking water, slip-slop-slapping on sunscreen and out of the midday sun.

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: A trip to the local supermarket, park or beach in the first day or two makes the new place feel ordinary and knowable, fast, for children especially.

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: The familiar bedtime story, the same breakfast, the favourite cup. Tiny rituals carried from home are how children feel safe somewhere new. Finding your feet

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: Routine and friends are the fastest cure for homesickness, so enrol and start school or early learning sooner rather than later. Our education guide walks through how it works, including the bits that depend on your visa.

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: Playdates, birthday parties, Nippers at the surf club, weekend sport: these are where Australian childhood friendships form. Accepting invitations, for parents too, is how a family puts down roots.

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: A few weeks in, the novelty fades and the missing-home feelings can arrive, for children and adults alike. It’s a normal stage, not a setback. Keep routines steady and it passes. The decision that shapes the rest

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.h: Choosing where to live, with the family in mind
chunks.x: For families, where you settle often matters as much as the role. In the cities, you’ll find the widest choice of schools, the most established communities, and classmates from every background, so a child who’s a visible minority is one of many. In small country towns and the remote outback, the pace is gentler and the welcome often warm, but there’s less diversity, fewer services and a child may be one of very few from their background. For some families that closeness is a gift; for others it can feel isolating. It’s worth thinking about with your children’s needs in the picture. There’s a practical layer too: in most states, a government school place is tied to your home address through a catchment zone , so the suburb and the school decision go hand in hand. It’s well worth researching schools before you choose a rental.

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.h: Choosing where to live, with the family in mind
chunks.x: Our community guide goes deeper on how diversity changes by place. Once you’re applying for a role through us, this is exactly the kind of thing we’ll talk through with you: your children’s ages, what matters to your family, and the character of the places you’re considering. We’d far rather help you choose well up front than watch a family settle somewhere that was never going to suit them. Different ages, different needs

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: 0–4 The easiest to relocate and the quickest to settle: their world is you. Protect sleep and feeding routines, keep their comfort items close, and routines help them settle wherever you are. Primary age

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: 5–11 Many settle quickly, though every child is different. Friendly, outdoor, sporty Australian classrooms make friends easy to come by. Tweens

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: 12–13 Old enough to feel the loss of friends keenly, young enough to make new ones readily. Help them stay in touch with old friends while gently encouraging clubs and activities that build new circles. Teenagers

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.h: The ones who need a say
chunks.x: 14+ Moving at a decisive age is hard, and they need more time and more involvement. Bring them into decisions, take homesickness seriously, mind how the senior-school years (and the ATAR) line up, and give the first term or two before judging how it’s going. Told straight

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: Give yourself permission to find it hard. You’re holding down a new job, running an unfamiliar household and being everyone’s reassurance, often without your usual support network nearby, and the distance from family back home can feel further from Australia than almost anywhere. Build your own footholds early: say yes to the school-gate chat, find one or two other parents, and lean on the communities who’ve made the same move. You don’t have to do it perfectly, and you certainly don’t have to do it alone. If you ever feel you’re struggling more than seems normal, reach out, to your GP, to a helpline, or to us. Asking for support is part of doing this well, not a sign you’ve got it wrong. Sophie’s insight I’ve sat with so many parents who lay awake over this exact question, the flight, the schools, whether they’re doing the right thing by their children.

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: Here’s what I’ve seen, again and again: the kids are usually fine, and often more than fine. They take to the beach and the outdoor life, they make friends at the park, and within a term this is home. My advice is to look after yourselves as carefully as you look after them, and to choose where you live with the whole family in mind, not just the commute. Pointing families towards the right town, the right school and the right people is one of the parts of this work I love most. Sophie CEO & Founder, Ethicare Resourcing Common questions

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: When’s the best time of year to move with school-age children? The Australian school year runs from late January to mid-December, in four terms, so arriving around late January lets children begin with everyone else. That said, schools take new arrivals throughout the year and are well practised at it, the right time is mostly the one that fits your job and visa, so don’t force it to line up perfectly. How long until the children really settle? Every child is different, but a common pattern is an exciting first few weeks, a dip as the novelty fades and home is missed, and a gradual settling over the following months. Every child is different; teenagers in particular may need longer. Steady routines and getting into school quickly are the things that help most.

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: What about childcare while we’re both finding our feet? Australia has a well-established early childhood system: long day care, family day care and preschool or kindergarten. The federal Child Care Subsidy lowers fees for eligible families, but eligibility depends on your residency and visa: many families on a temporary visa (including the 482) don’t qualify and pay full fees. Popular centres can have waitlists, so it’s worth enquiring before you arrive. Our education guide covers this in detail. Will being on a temporary visa affect my child’s schooling? It can, and it’s worth checking early. Government schooling is free or low-cost for citizens and permanent residents, but several states charge an annual tuition contribution for temporary residents’ children at public schools, while others exempt skilled or sponsored visas.

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: It varies a lot by state and changes over time, so check the current policy with the state education department where you’re heading. The education guide has an indicative state-by-state breakdown. Can you help us choose where to live with the family in mind? Yes. For families moving with a role through us, it’s one of the most useful things we do. Tell us your children’s ages, what matters to your family and any schools you’ve got your eye on, and we’ll help you weigh up suburbs, school zones, commutes, community and the everyday feel of an area, before you commit to anywhere. Keep exploring

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: How schooling works, enrolment zones, fees and the part that depends on your visa. Read the guide Reference

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: A look at faith, culture and how diversity changes by place. Read the guide Stage 07

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: The practical countdown: shipping, timing and getting the family move organised. Read Stage 07 Free, any time

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: Tell us who is coming with you and where you’re thinking of settling, and we’ll help you plan a move that works for everyone — your partner’s work, childcare or schools, the timing, the journey itself, and the soft landing on the other side. Ask Ethicare about moving as a family Browse current opportunities Ethicare Resourcing · your guide to a life and career in Australia.

chunks.t: Understanding healthcare in Australia
chunks.h: A universal system, with private care alongside
chunks.x: Reviewed July 2026 · checked against current Services Australia and Department of Health guidance. Eligibility rules and thresholds change, always confirm your own position at the source. Australia runs a universal public system, funded through taxation and a Medicare levy, alongside a substantial private sector. Most people use a mix of the two across their lives. Healthcare is delivered by the states and territories but underpinned by national funding and a national medicines scheme, which is why standards are broadly consistent wherever you live. For clinicians, that scale and that public–private mix are part of the appeal: broad experience, and real choice over where and how you work. There are two questions on most people’s minds when they read a page like this.

chunks.t: Understanding healthcare in Australia
chunks.h: A universal system, with private care alongside
chunks.x: Will my family be looked after? And what will it cost us? This guide answers both including the parts Medicare doesn’t cover, which are the parts newcomers are most often surprised by. The short version. If you arrive as a permanent resident, you enrol in Medicare and most of your care is free or heavily subsidised. If you arrive on a temporary work visa, your position depends on your passport, and for many of our clinicians it’s better than they expect. Either way, plan for dental, ambulance and optical, which sit outside Medicare for most adults. The backbone

chunks.t: Understanding healthcare in Australia
chunks.x: Medicare is the national scheme that subsidises or covers much of the cost of care. For your family, it’s the thing to sort early. What it covers

chunks.t: Understanding healthcare in Australia
chunks.x: Free treatment as a public patient in a public hospital, and rebates toward GP visits, tests and many specialist services. Some services are bulk-billed (nothing to pay); others carry a gap fee, which is the difference between the rebate and what the clinic charges. Who’s eligible

chunks.t: Understanding healthcare in Australia
chunks.x: Citizens and permanent residents enrol. Many temporary visa holders qualify through a reciprocal health care agreement between Australia and their home country. Others rely on private cover, sometimes as a condition of the visa itself. The levy

chunks.t: Understanding healthcare in Australia
chunks.x: Most taxpayers pay a Medicare levy through income tax, a proportion of income, deducted like any other tax. Higher earners without private hospital cover may also pay a surcharge on top. Rates change; check the current figures with the ATO. The question everyone asks first

chunks.t: Understanding healthcare in Australia
chunks.h: Where you’ll stand, by how you arrive
chunks.x: This is the difference between arriving covered and arriving exposed. There are broadly three positions. 1

chunks.t: Understanding healthcare in Australia
chunks.h: Permanent resident or citizen, full Medicare
chunks.x: You enrol and you’re in: public hospital care, GP rebates, PBS medicines, the lot. Your dependent children are enrolled alongside you. This is the simplest position and the one most of our clinicians reach eventually, whether they arrive that way or transition later. 2

chunks.t: Understanding healthcare in Australia
chunks.h: Temporary work visa, from a reciprocal-agreement country
chunks.x: Australia holds reciprocal health care agreements with eleven countries : the United Kingdom, the Republic of Ireland, New Zealand, Belgium, Finland, Italy, Malta, the Netherlands, Norway, Slovenia and Sweden. If you hold a passport from one of these and you’re here on an eligible visa, you can enrol for Medicare access to medically necessary treatment. What that covers varies by country, and the differences matter. Most agreements include subsidised GP visits and public hospital treatment; the New Zealand and Ireland agreements are narrower and don’t extend to GP visits in the same way. Check your own country’s agreement at the source before you assume. 3

chunks.t: Understanding healthcare in Australia
chunks.x: If your passport isn’t on that list, South Africa, the UAE, India, the Philippines and many others aren’t, you won’t enrol in Medicare on a temporary visa. You’ll hold private health insurance instead, and for most sponsored work visas maintaining adequate cover is a formal condition of the visa (you may see it written as condition 8501). Your employer sometimes contributes; often they don’t. Budget for it. We raise this early with everyone, because it changes the family budget and occasionally the choice of route. It is never a reason not to come, but it should never be a surprise either. And to be clear: we’re recruiters, not migration or insurance advisers. We’ll tell you what to check and where; the answer has to come from the official source or a licensed adviser. First fortnight

chunks.t: Understanding healthcare in Australia
chunks.x: Enrolment is administrative rather than difficult. Arrive with the paperwork already in a folder. 1

chunks.t: Understanding healthcare in Australia
chunks.x: You generally enrol after you land, in person at a service centre or online, depending on your circumstances. It isn’t something to do from abroad, so don’t worry that you’re behind before you fly. 2

chunks.t: Understanding healthcare in Australia
chunks.x: Passports for every family member, and evidence of your visa grant. If you’re enrolling under a reciprocal agreement, you’ll usually need to show you’re enrolled in your home country’s system too. 3

chunks.t: Understanding healthcare in Australia
chunks.x: A card has to be posted somewhere. Temporary accommodation is generally fine, but a rental agreement or a utility bill makes everything faster, another reason to sort housing early. 4

chunks.t: Understanding healthcare in Australia
chunks.x: MyGov is the front door to most government services here, Medicare included. Linking Medicare to it means claims, records and your digital card all sit in one place. Do it in your first week. 5

chunks.t: Understanding healthcare in Australia
chunks.x: There can be a short window between landing and your card arriving. Travel or private cover across those first weeks is cheap peace of mind, particularly with children. 6

chunks.t: Understanding healthcare in Australia
chunks.x: Card in hand, register the family with a local practice. Don’t wait for someone to be unwell. New-patient appointments can take a fortnight or more in busy areas. Two systems, working together

chunks.t: Understanding healthcare in Australia
chunks.x: State-run hospitals and services provide emergency, acute and much elective care, free or heavily subsidised through Medicare. It’s where a great deal of teaching, training and complex work happens, and where most of the roles we recruit for sit.

chunks.t: Understanding healthcare in Australia
chunks.x: Private hospitals and clinics offer choice of provider and often shorter waits for elective care, funded by insurance and out-of-pocket fees. Many clinicians work across both, and some build a portfolio deliberately.

chunks.t: Understanding healthcare in Australia
chunks.x: The same specialist may see you publicly or privately; the same scan may be bulk-billed at one clinic and charged at another. Elective waits are the usual reason families take out cover, urgent care doesn’t wait for anyone in either system. Told straight

chunks.t: Understanding healthcare in Australia
chunks.x: Whether you need it depends on your visa, your income and your family. If it’s a visa condition, it isn’t optional. Many temporary work visas require you to hold and maintain adequate health cover for yourself and every family member for the whole time you’re here. Letting it lapse is a visa problem, not just a health one. If you’re Medicare-eligible, it’s your choice. The public system will look after you. Families choose cover for shorter elective waits, a choice of doctor, a private room, and “extras” policies that put something back toward dental, optical and physiotherapy, the things Medicare largely doesn’t fund for adults. Two rules are worth knowing before you decide. Higher earners without private hospital cover pay an additional surcharge at tax time, so for some households cover costs less than not having it.

chunks.t: Understanding healthcare in Australia
chunks.x: And there’s a loading that increases premiums for people who take out hospital cover later in life, with concessions for recent arrivals, so the timing of your first policy can matter for years. Both are threshold-and-percentage rules that change; get the current numbers from the ATO and the government’s comparison site rather than from a broker’s brochure. Policies also carry waiting periods . Months before some services can be claimed, longer for pregnancy and pre-existing conditions. If a baby or a known procedure is on the horizon, that timing deserves real attention before you pick a policy. Our view: don’t buy the first policy you’re shown, and don’t let anyone tell you the public system isn’t good enough. It is. Cover buys convenience, choice and the extras, which for some families is worth a great deal and for others isn’t. Everyday care

chunks.t: Understanding healthcare in Australia
chunks.x: Day-to-day healthcare runs through general practice, with a national medicines scheme keeping prescriptions affordable. Your GP is the front door: the first stop for most concerns and the gatekeeper for referrals to specialists and many tests. Unlike some systems you may know, you don’t register with one practice for life. You can see any GP anywhere, but continuity is worth having, so most families settle on one. Bulk billing and gap fees. A bulk-billing practice accepts the Medicare rebate as full payment, so you pay nothing at the desk. Many others charge a fee and Medicare refunds part of it, leaving you a gap. Bulk billing is more common for children, concession-card holders and in some regional areas; it has become less common generally, so ask when you book rather than assuming.

chunks.t: Understanding healthcare in Australia
chunks.x: Specialists usually charge a gap, sometimes a substantial one, and you’ll want to ask the cost before the appointment. Nobody minds the question. The PBS. Prescription medicines are subsidised through the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme , which caps what most people pay for listed medicines, with a lower cap for concession-card holders and a safety net once a household’s spending passes a yearly threshold. Not every medicine is listed, and brand names differ from what you may be used to, so check your family’s regular prescriptions against the PBS before you move, and bring a written summary of your medical history and current doses. Ask if a clinic bulk-bills Ask a specialist’s fee up front Check prescriptions against the PBS Bring a written medical summary Register the family early The part people don’t expect

chunks.t: Understanding healthcare in Australia
chunks.x: Largely private and out of pocket. There is public dental care for eligible concession-card holders, usually with long waits, and schemes that help with children’s dental for eligible families. For most working adults, plan to pay, and factor it into the year’s budget, especially if anyone is due significant work.

chunks.t: Understanding healthcare in Australia
chunks.x: This one catches people out. Ambulance cover is arranged state by state rather than nationally, in some places it’s provided, in others you subscribe or insure, and an uncovered call-out can be a unpleasant bill. Check the arrangement in your state in your first week.

chunks.t: Understanding healthcare in Australia
chunks.x: Glasses, contact lenses, most physiotherapy, psychology beyond limited referred sessions, podiatry and similar sit largely outside Medicare, or attract only partial rebates. These are what “extras” insurance is designed for. None of this is a reason for alarm, it’s a reason to plan. Families who know about ambulance and dental before they arrive absorb them easily. Families who find out via a bill do not. If something goes wrong

chunks.t: Understanding healthcare in Australia
chunks.x: Triple zero reaches ambulance, fire and police. It’s the number to teach your children on day one. Emergency departments at public hospitals treat anyone who needs them, regardless of cover, care first, paperwork later. Urgent, not an emergency

chunks.t: Understanding healthcare in Australia
chunks.x: Between a GP appointment and an emergency department sit urgent care clinics and after-hours services, with growing bulk-billed provision. For a sprain, a fever or stitches, they’re usually the faster, kinder option. Not sure

chunks.t: Understanding healthcare in Australia
chunks.x: A national free health advice line and website staffed by health professionals, available around the clock. When you’re new and unsure whether something warrants a hospital, it’s exactly the right first call. Where you come in

chunks.t: Understanding healthcare in Australia
chunks.x: For clinicians, the system offers broad experience and a collaborative, patient-centred culture, with national registration that lets you move between states without starting again. You might work in a public health service, a private provider, or community and primary care, and many roles offer a mix of the two. Practice tends to be team-based and relatively flat : your professional opinion is expected, not merely permitted, and being asked “what do you think?” by a senior colleague is normal rather than a test. Clinicians arriving from more hierarchical systems tell us this takes a few weeks to trust and then becomes the thing they’d least want to give up.

chunks.t: Understanding healthcare in Australia
chunks.x: That said, it’s a tendency rather than a guarantee: culture varies from one workplace and team to the next, so it’s worth asking what a particular department is really like when you interview, and talking to people already doing the job. There is a strong emphasis on culturally safe care , including for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander patients, and you’ll meet it in induction, in documentation and in how teams talk about patients. It is treated as clinical quality, not as an add-on. The other side: services are busy, some regions carry real workforce pressure, and distance is a clinical factor in a country this size, retrieval, telehealth and outreach are ordinary parts of practice rather than exceptions. Your profession guide goes deeper into scope, demand and what the day-to-day is really like for your role. Ready to see how your role fits? Stage 04 · Can I work in Australia? sets out the registration pathway, and each profession page covers scope, demand and pay. Told straight

chunks.t: Understanding healthcare in Australia
chunks.h: Bulk billing is less universal than it sounds
chunks.x: “Free GP visits” is how Medicare gets described abroad. In practice many clinics charge a gap. Ask when you book. 2

chunks.t: Understanding healthcare in Australia
chunks.x: Urgent care is prompt and excellent. Non-urgent surgery in the public system can mean a long wait, which is precisely why many families hold cover. 3

chunks.t: Understanding healthcare in Australia
chunks.x: There is no single national answer, and an uncovered call-out is expensive. Check your state, not the internet’s general advice. 4

chunks.t: Understanding healthcare in Australia
chunks.h: Your visa condition is yours to maintain
chunks.x: If cover is required by your visa, keeping it current is your responsibility for the whole stay, including through job changes. 5

chunks.t: Understanding healthcare in Australia
chunks.x: The levy, the surcharge, PBS caps and insurance loadings all move. Anything you read anywhere, here included, should be checked against the current official figures. 6

chunks.t: Understanding healthcare in Australia
chunks.h: We don’t give insurance or tax advice
chunks.x: We’ll tell you what to look into and flag what usually applies to clinicians in your position. The advice itself must come from the official sources or a licensed adviser. Sophie’s insight Two things reassure most families fastest: that healthcare here is good and universal, and that sorting their own access is simpler than they feared. Get your Medicare position clear before you accept the role, choose a family GP early, check your prescriptions before you fly, and find out how ambulance works in your state. That’s most of it. The one I always raise unprompted is dental. It’s the cost people don’t plan for, and it’s much easier to absorb when you knew it was coming. For your work, the public–private mix is a real strength, it’s part of why clinicians find the experience here so broad. Sophie CEO & Founder, Ethicare Resourcing Official sources

chunks.t: Understanding healthcare in Australia
chunks.x: Enrolling, cards & agreements Services Australia · Medicare Reciprocal health care agreements myGov · link your services The authority on whether you can enrol, and on what your country’s agreement covers.

chunks.t: Understanding healthcare in Australia
chunks.x: The costs side PBS · subsidised medicines privatehealth.gov.au · compare cover ATO · levy & surcharge Check whether your medicines are listed, compare policies without a broker, and get current thresholds.

chunks.t: Understanding healthcare in Australia
chunks.x: When you need help, and how you register healthdirect · free health advice Department of Health & Aged Care Ahpra · professional registration In an emergency call 000 . For anything you’re unsure about, healthdirect is the right first call. Common questions

chunks.t: Understanding healthcare in Australia
chunks.h: The things people ask us first
chunks.x: Will my family be covered by Medicare? It depends on your visa and your passport. Citizens and permanent residents enrol in Medicare and so do their dependent children. Many temporary visa holders qualify through one of Australia’s eleven reciprocal health care agreements, the UK, Ireland, New Zealand, Belgium, Finland, Italy, Malta, the Netherlands, Norway, Slovenia and Sweden. If your passport isn’t on that list, you’ll hold private cover instead, often as a condition of the visa. We flag this early, because it affects your budget. Do I need private health insurance? If your visa requires it, yes, and you must maintain it for your whole stay. If you’re Medicare-eligible it’s a real choice: the public system will look after you, and cover buys shorter elective waits, choice of doctor, and extras toward dental, optical and physiotherapy.

chunks.t: Understanding healthcare in Australia
chunks.h: The things people ask us first
chunks.x: Two tax rules can tip the maths, a surcharge for higher earners without hospital cover, and a loading for taking out cover later in life, so it’s worth checking the current thresholds before deciding. How soon can I enrol after arriving, and what do I bring? You enrol once you’re here, not before. Bring passports for everyone, evidence of your visa grant, an Australian address, and, if you’re enrolling under a reciprocal agreement, evidence you’re in your home country’s system. Set up a myGov account in your first week and link Medicare to it. Hold interim cover across the gap between landing and your card arriving. How do I see a doctor as a newcomer? Register the family with a local GP practice, they’re the front door for most care and referrals. Do it before anyone is unwell, because new-patient appointments can take a fortnight or more in busy areas.

chunks.t: Understanding healthcare in Australia
chunks.h: The things people ask us first
chunks.x: Ask whether the clinic bulk-bills (nothing to pay) or charges a gap fee. You’re not tied to one practice, but continuity is worth having. Is everything really free? No. Public hospital care as a public patient is free, and Medicare rebates cover much of everyday care. But many GPs charge a gap, specialists often charge a significant one, and adult dental, ambulance in some states, optical and most allied health sit largely outside Medicare. The big frightening costs are covered; the everyday ones need a modest budget. What about ambulance cover? This is the one that surprises people most. Ambulance is arranged state by state rather than nationally, in some places it’s provided, in others you subscribe or insure, and an uncovered call-out can be a serious bill. Find out how it works in your state in your first week; it’s usually a small annual cost to fix.

chunks.t: Understanding healthcare in Australia
chunks.h: The things people ask us first
chunks.x: Will my regular medication be available? Usually there’s an equivalent, but brand names and availability differ and not every medicine is listed on the PBS. Check your family’s prescriptions against the PBS before you move, bring a written summary of your history and current doses, and carry enough supply for the transition and your first GP appointment. Are waiting lists long? For anything urgent, no. Emergency and acute care are prompt and of a high standard. For non-urgent elective surgery, public waits can be long, and they vary by state and by procedure. That gap is the main reason many families hold private hospital cover, and it’s worth weighing against your own circumstances rather than a national average. How different will practising here feel? Clinically familiar; culturally a little flatter.

chunks.t: Understanding healthcare in Australia
chunks.h: The things people ask us first
chunks.x: Teams are collaborative, your opinion is expected rather than tolerated, and culturally safe care is treated as clinical quality. Registration is national, so you can move between states without starting again. Services are busy, and distance shapes practice, retrieval, telehealth and outreach are ordinary rather than exceptional. Your profession guide covers the day-to-day properly. Read a little deeper
