chunks.t: CV & interview preparation for Australia
chunks.x: Australian healthcare CVs are clean and factual: what you can do and have done, backed by evidence. A busy manager should see your fit in under a minute. A few things employers here look for that may differ from where you trained: Your registration or accreditation status up front, registered, in progress, or eligible. Clinical competencies and modalities stated plainly, with caseload or volume where it helps. Reverse-chronological roles with dates, settings and responsibilities, with gaps explained briefly. No photo, date of birth or marital status, they’re not expected and best left off. We help every candidate shape a CV that reads naturally to Australian employers, not by changing your experience, but by framing it the way the people hiring expect to see it. Practical

chunks.t: CV & interview preparation for Australia
chunks.h: What goes in, section by section
chunks.x: There’s no official format, but there is a shape Australian hiring managers are used to reading. 1

chunks.t: CV & interview preparation for Australia
chunks.x: Top of page one. Whether you’re registered, in progress or eligible is often the first thing a manager looks for, so don’t bury it on page three. 2

chunks.t: CV & interview preparation for Australia
chunks.x: Three or four lines: your profession, years of experience, the settings you’ve worked in and what you’re looking for. Not a personal statement, a précis. 3

chunks.t: CV & interview preparation for Australia
chunks.x: Stated plainly, ideally with an indication of volume or independence. “Independent reporting across x and y” tells a manager more than a list of nouns. 4

chunks.t: CV & interview preparation for Australia
chunks.x: Employer type rather than brand (many managers won’t know the hospital), setting, dates, and what you were responsible for. Brief explanations for any gaps. 5

chunks.t: CV & interview preparation for Australia
chunks.x: Your qualifying award, where and when, then relevant post-qualification training. Recent CPD signals someone who keeps current. 6

chunks.t: CV & interview preparation for Australia
chunks.x: Two is standard, ideally including a recent clinical supervisor. Ask them before you list them, and warn them about the time difference. Learned the hard way

chunks.t: CV & interview preparation for Australia
chunks.x: Naming your registration status in the first few lines Describing settings and systems, not just job titles Two or three specific stories you can tell naturally Being clear about what you want next, and why Australia Explaining a career gap briefly and without apology Asking your own questions at the end

chunks.t: CV & interview preparation for Australia
chunks.x: A photo, date of birth or marital status, leave them off Assuming a manager knows your hospital, region or grading system Untranslated local acronyms and banding shorthand Ten pages when four would do, or one page when four are needed Rehearsed answers that don’t quite answer the question asked Treating “why Australia?” as small talk, it’s a question What to expect

chunks.t: CV & interview preparation for Australia
chunks.x: Interviews for overseas candidates are usually done by video, and are often more conversational than formal. Format

chunks.t: CV & interview preparation for Australia
chunks.x: A panel of one to three people, typically a manager and a senior clinician, by Teams or Zoom, allowing for the time difference. Usually one or two stages. Tone

chunks.t: CV & interview preparation for Australia
chunks.x: Friendly and on first-name terms. They’re assessing competence, but also whether you’ll be a good colleague, so it’s as much a two-way conversation as a test. Focus

chunks.t: CV & interview preparation for Australia
chunks.x: Expect questions grounded in practice: how you handled something, how you work in a team, how you keep patients safe, rather than abstract puzzles. The week before

chunks.t: CV & interview preparation for Australia
chunks.x: A video interview across time zones has a few practical failure modes. Close those off and you can concentrate on the conversation. 1

chunks.t: CV & interview preparation for Australia
chunks.x: In their time zone and yours, in writing. Australia spans several zones and only some observe daylight saving, which catches people out every year. 2

chunks.t: CV & interview preparation for Australia
chunks.h: Test the link, not just the laptop
chunks.x: Open the actual meeting link a day early. Check camera, microphone, and that whatever’s behind you is something you’re happy for a panel to look at. 3

chunks.t: CV & interview preparation for Australia
chunks.h: Prepare three stories, not thirty answers
chunks.x: One about a difficult clinical situation, one about a team or a disagreement, one about improving something. Most behavioural questions can be answered from those three. 4

chunks.t: CV & interview preparation for Australia
chunks.h: Know the service you’re applying to
chunks.x: Not trivia, just context: what kind of service it is, the population it serves, and where your role sits in it. We’ll brief you on this properly beforehand. 5

chunks.t: CV & interview preparation for Australia
chunks.h: Have your own questions written down
chunks.x: Nerves erase them. A short list on paper, next to you, is completely acceptable and makes you look considered rather than unprepared. 6

chunks.t: CV & interview preparation for Australia
chunks.x: Agree a fallback in advance: a phone number to call, or who reconnects first. It happens often enough to be worth a sentence beforehand. Be ready for these

chunks.t: CV & interview preparation for Australia
chunks.x: Most questions fall into a few families. Have a couple of real examples ready for each; the "tell me about a time…" style rewards specifics.

chunks.t: CV & interview preparation for Australia
chunks.x: Your scope, the modalities or cases you’re confident with, how you stay current, and how you’d handle an unfamiliar situation safely.

chunks.t: CV & interview preparation for Australia
chunks.x: Working in a multidisciplinary team, raising a concern, handling a difficult interaction with a colleague or patient.

chunks.t: CV & interview preparation for Australia
chunks.x: Why Australia, why this role, and whether you’ve thought the relocation through, they want to know you’ll stay and settle. Worth rehearsing out loud: “Tell me about a time something went wrong and what you did.” “How do you raise a concern about a colleague’s practice?” “What would you do on a shift where you were asked to work outside your scope?” “Why Australia, and why now?” Four questions, in some form, come up in most interviews we sit in on. It goes both ways

chunks.t: CV & interview preparation for Australia
chunks.x: An interview where you ask nothing reads as an interview where you didn’t care.

chunks.t: CV & interview preparation for Australia
chunks.x: What does a typical week look like? What’s the case mix? How is the team staffed at the moment, and what’s the plan? What does support look like in the first few months?

chunks.t: CV & interview preparation for Australia
chunks.x: How do people develop here? Is there protected time for CPD? What have previous international clinicians in this team gone on to do?

chunks.t: CV & interview preparation for Australia
chunks.x: What relocation support exists? Who helps with the practical side of landing? Is there anyone in the team who’s made the same move? The thing that sets candidates apart

chunks.t: CV & interview preparation for Australia
chunks.x: Australian healthcare is collaborative and patient-centred, with a strong emphasis on respectful, culturally safe care. Employers hire people who’ll add to that, not just tick the clinical boxes. You don’t need to perform, just be ready to show, with examples, that you communicate openly, work flatly within a team, ask when you’re unsure, and treat patients and colleagues with respect. A little awareness of the local context (that you’ve thought about practising in a new system and culture) goes a long way. And then?

chunks.t: CV & interview preparation for Australia
chunks.x: Decisions rarely come the same day. A panel usually needs to reconvene, and public services often have an approval step after that, so a few days to a couple of weeks is normal rather than ominous. We chase on your behalf, and we’ll tell you what we’re hearing even when what we’re hearing is “not yet”. If an offer comes, read it properly before you celebrate: the role and its level, hours, on-call expectations, start date, and what relocation support is included. Ask about anything unclear now, because it’s far harder to raise once you’ve accepted. And if the answer is no, ask for feedback. It’s usually given generously here, and it’s often about timing or scope rather than you. One thing we’d say plainly: don’t resign anything, or give notice on a home, until your offer and your visa are both real. We’ll tell you when that point has arrived.

chunks.t: CV & interview preparation for Australia
chunks.x: Sophie’s insight The clinicians who interview well are rarely the ones with the slickest answers, they’re the ones who’ve prepared two or three specific stories and can talk about them naturally. We’ll do a proper prep call before any interview: the likely questions, the panel, the role, and the small cultural things that make a difference. You’ll walk in knowing what to expect, which is most of the battle. Sophie CEO & Founder, Ethicare Resourcing Common questions

chunks.t: CV & interview preparation for Australia
chunks.h: The things people ask us first
chunks.x: How long should my CV be? For most clinical roles, two to four pages is right: long enough to evidence your experience and modalities, short enough to stay readable. We’ll help you trim or expand it to suit the role and your seniority. Will the interview be in person? Almost never for an overseas candidate, they’re done by video, scheduled around the time difference. We’ll make sure you’re set up and comfortable with the format beforehand. What if I’m asked something I don’t know? Say so, and say how you’d find out or who you’d ask. In Australian healthcare, knowing your limits and seeking help is seen as a strength, not a weakness, it’s exactly the safe behaviour they’re looking for. Do you help with references? Yes. We’ll guide you on who to ask and when, since references and certificates of good standing are often on the critical path for both the job and your registration.

chunks.t: CV & interview preparation for Australia
chunks.h: The things people ask us first
chunks.x: Should I explain a gap in my CV? Yes, briefly and without apology. Parental leave, caring, study, illness, a move, all completely normal. A one-line explanation stops a reader guessing, and guessing is worse than the truth in almost every case. Can I ask about pay in the interview? You can, though for public roles the answer is usually set by an agreement rather than negotiable, so there’s often less to discuss than you’d expect. It’s generally easier to let us handle the pay conversation while you concentrate on the role. What if I interview badly on the day? Tell us afterwards. Sometimes there’s a second stage where it can be put right, sometimes there’s another role that suits better. What doesn’t help is pretending it went well, we can only advocate for you properly if we know what happened. How many roles should I apply for at once? Fewer, better-matched applications beat a scattergun. Two or three serious possibilities is plenty to manage alongside registration and a visa, and it means every interview gets proper preparation. chunks.t: Money, tax & banking in Australia
chunks.h: The order to do things in
chunks.x: Almost all of this is straightforward if done in sequence. The commonest mistake is starting work before the tax office knows you exist. Before you fly

chunks.t: Money, tax & banking in Australia
chunks.x: The major banks let you open a transaction account from overseas, then verify your identity at a branch when you arrive. It costs nothing and it means your bond and your first salary have somewhere to land. Week one

chunks.t: Money, tax & banking in Australia
chunks.h: Apply for your Tax File Number
chunks.x: Free, online, and only possible once you are in the country with work rights. Until your employer has it, they are obliged to withhold tax at the top rate. Week one

chunks.t: Money, tax & banking in Australia
chunks.h: Verify your identity at a branch
chunks.x: Passport and, ideally, a local address. This activates the account you opened from overseas and usually gets you a card the same week. Before your first pay run

chunks.t: Money, tax & banking in Australia
chunks.x: Your employer will ask, or will quietly default you. This is the one decision on this page that compounds for forty years, and the section below is about why it deserves ten minutes. First month

chunks.t: Money, tax & banking in Australia
chunks.h: Sort out Medicare, or your exemption
chunks.x: Either enrol if you are entitled, or get the statement that lets you claim an exemption from the levy. Both routes need doing; neither happens automatically. First month

chunks.t: Money, tax & banking in Australia
chunks.x: Not a lifestyle question but an arithmetic one, because of the surcharge. Explained below. Ongoing

chunks.t: Money, tax & banking in Australia
chunks.x: Arrival date, visa grant, any foreign income, and the date you started work. Your first tax return is the one where residency and part-year thresholds matter, and the paperwork makes it painless. The one that unlocks everything

chunks.t: Money, tax & banking in Australia
chunks.x: A TFN is your permanent personal reference with the Australian Taxation Office, issued once and yours for life, even if you leave and come back. You apply after you arrive, online, once you hold a visa with work rights. It is free . There are commercial sites that will charge you to submit the same form, and there is no version of the process where paying is faster or better. Apply through the ATO directly. Give the number to your employer as soon as it arrives, and to your bank and your super fund. Until your employer has it they are legally required to withhold tax at the highest rate, which you would get back eventually through your return, but it makes your first month or two considerably leaner than it needs to be. One habit worth keeping from day one: your TFN is a sensitive identifier. Legitimate parties who ask for it are your employer, your bank, your super fund and the ATO. Nobody else needs it, and no legitimate organisation will ever ask for it by email or text. Practical set-up

chunks.t: Money, tax & banking in Australia
chunks.x: Easier than in most countries, and one of the few things worth doing before you get on the plane.

chunks.t: Money, tax & banking in Australia
chunks.x: Apply online from overseas. The major banks all offer a migrant or newcomer account you can open before arrival, months ahead if you like. Verify in a branch on arrival with your passport. Bring your visa grant notice too; it saves questions. Everyday banking is app-first and payments between accounts are near-instant, including to businesses and individuals. You will need a BSB and account number to give your employer, the two numbers that together identify an Australian account. Cheques are effectively extinct. Do not budget any part of your move on being able to pay by cheque.

chunks.t: Money, tax & banking in Australia
chunks.x: Monthly account fees are common but usually waived above a modest monthly deposit, which a salary comfortably clears. Ask rather than assume. Give your bank your TFN when it arrives. Without it, tax is withheld from any interest you earn. Tap-and-go is universal , and a surcharge for card payment is legal and common in cafés and taxis. Keep your home-country account open for at least the first year. Closing it early makes transfers, pensions and any lingering direct debits harder than they need to be. Credit history does not travel. You start from nothing here, which matters for borrowing later but not for everyday banking. The decision that compounds

chunks.t: Money, tax & banking in Australia
chunks.h: Superannuation, and the choice most people accept by default
chunks.x: Superannuation is Australia’s compulsory retirement saving, and it is one of the better features of working here. Your employer pays a legislated percentage of your earnings into a fund on top of your salary. The rate is set by law rather than negotiated, it has been rising in steps, and you should check the current figure, but the important point is structural: it is additional to your pay, not deducted from it. When you compare a package here against one at home, super is real money that a salary comparison alone will miss. In most cases you can choose the fund . If you do not choose, one of two things happens: your existing fund is used if you already have one, or your employer’s default applies.

chunks.t: Money, tax & banking in Australia
chunks.h: Superannuation, and the choice most people accept by default
chunks.x: Health sector employers commonly offer an industry fund, and industry funds are generally low-fee and perfectly reasonable, but there is a difference between choosing that and being defaulted into it without looking. What to look at, in order: the fees, the long-run net performance, the insurance built into the default option and whether you need it, and the investment mix relative to your age and your plans. Ten minutes on the government’s comparison tool is enough to make a defensible choice, and small fee differences compound into large numbers across a career. In our experience

chunks.t: Money, tax & banking in Australia
chunks.h: The one thing clinicians most often regret is ending up with several small super accounts
chunks.x: It happens quietly: a locum stint here, a fixed-term contract there, each one defaulting you into a different fund. Every account charges its own fees and often its own insurance premiums, and the total quietly erodes. Keep one fund and tell each new employer where to pay. Consolidating later is possible and worth doing, but check what insurance cover you would lose before you close anything, because that is the one part of consolidation that can bite.

chunks.t: Money, tax & banking in Australia
chunks.h: The insurance you probably do not know you have
chunks.x: This is the part that surprises almost every arriving clinician. Most Australian super funds include default insurance inside the fund, with the premiums deducted from your balance rather than billed to you. Typically that means life cover , total and permanent disability cover , and sometimes income protection . Two consequences to know. The first is that you may already be insured for more than you assume, which matters if you were about to buy a separate policy. The second is the reason for the warning above: consolidating several accounts into one closes the others, and closes their cover with them. If you have developed a health condition since that cover started, you may not be able to replace it on the same terms. So the order matters. Find out what cover each fund provides, decide what you need against your mortgage and dependants, and only then consolidate.

chunks.t: Money, tax & banking in Australia
chunks.h: The insurance you probably do not know you have
chunks.x: If the default cover is more than you need you can usually reduce or cancel it and stop paying the premiums, and if it is less than you need, a super fund is often not the cheapest place to top it up. Neither of those is a decision we are licensed to make for you, but both are worth ten minutes of a licensed adviser’s time. If you eventually leave Australia permanently on a temporary visa, you may be able to claim your super back through the departing Australia superannuation payment, taxed at a rate set for that purpose. It is not a reason to plan differently, but it is worth knowing the money is not lost. How it works

chunks.t: Money, tax & banking in Australia
chunks.x: Australian income tax is progressive and administered federally; there is no state income tax. We do not print rates or thresholds, because they change with each federal budget. Tax is withheld from your pay by your employer under a system called PAYG. Pay as you go, so for most employed clinicians the amount arriving in your account is already net. The financial year runs from 1 July to 30 June , which catches people out in a small but persistent way: it is not the calendar year and it is not the April year some of you are used to. You lodge a return after 30 June, and for a straightforward salaried position this is simple: much of it arrives pre-filled, and the ATO’s own online service is free. Most clinicians in their second year onwards do it themselves in under an hour.

chunks.t: Money, tax & banking in Australia
chunks.x: Two things that are worth an accountant in your first year specifically: a part-year residency position, and any income or assets still generating money in your home country. Both are ordinary situations, both have a right answer, and both are easier to get right once than to unpick later. Where to get the current numbers Australian Taxation Office , the primary source for rates, thresholds, the residency tests and lodging your return. Free, and more current than any guide. Moneysmart . The government’s independent money guidance, including a pay calculator and a super fund comparison tool. No products sold. ATO: superannuation , the current employer contribution rate, choice-of-fund rules and consolidation. Services Australia — Medicare , enrolling, reciprocal agreements, and applying for a Medicare Entitlement Statement. A distinction that matters

chunks.t: Money, tax & banking in Australia
chunks.h: “Resident for tax purposes” is not the same as your visa
chunks.x: Tax residency has nothing to do with citizenship and only an indirect relationship with your visa. It turns on your actual circumstances: where you live, where you work, where your family is, what you have set up, and whether you intend to stay. Someone on a temporary employer-sponsored visa who takes a twelve-month lease and starts a permanent clinical role is very often a resident for tax purposes, despite the word “temporary” on the visa. It matters because residents generally get a tax-free threshold and resident rates, while non-residents are taxed from the first dollar at higher rates. The gap is not trivial. Most arriving clinicians who move properly. Job, home, family, intention to stay. Are residents for tax purposes from close to their arrival date, which is usually the better outcome.

chunks.t: Money, tax & banking in Australia
chunks.h: “Resident for tax purposes” is not the same as your visa
chunks.x: But it is your circumstances that decide it, not a form you fill in, so confirm your own position with the ATO’s residency tests or an accountant in year one. Where this goes wrong Two mistakes we see. The first is assuming that a temporary visa means non-resident for tax , and paying more than necessary for a year before anyone notices. The second is the reverse: assuming residency and forgetting that as a resident you generally need to declare worldwide income , including rent from a property you kept at home. Both are fixable. Both are much easier to get right at the start. The levy, and the refund people miss

chunks.t: Money, tax & banking in Australia
chunks.h: The Medicare levy and the surcharge
chunks.x: Two separate things with confusingly similar names. One of them is a refund routinely left unclaimed.

chunks.t: Money, tax & banking in Australia
chunks.x: What it is: a percentage of taxable income paid by most residents, funding the public health system. It appears in your tax return rather than as a separate bill. If your country has a reciprocal health care agreement with Australia, you may be enrolled in Medicare and liable for the levy in the ordinary way. If you are not entitled to Medicare , you can apply to Services Australia for a Medicare Entitlement Statement and claim an exemption in your return. This is the missed refund. Plenty of arriving clinicians pay a levy for a health system they were not entitled to use, because nobody told them the statement exists.

chunks.t: Money, tax & banking in Australia
chunks.x: What it is: an additional charge on higher earners who do not hold an appropriate level of private hospital cover. Why it matters to you: many clinical salaries sit above the threshold, so this is likely to apply. The arithmetic: a basic hospital policy frequently costs less than the surcharge it avoids. That is precisely why so many Australian households hold cover they rarely claim on. Extras is not hospital cover. Dental and optical extras do not exempt you from the surcharge, and this is the most common expensive misunderstanding. Run your own numbers against your actual income rather than taking a rule of thumb, including ours. How the public and private systems fit together, and what Medicare covers, is explained properly in how the health system works . This section is only about the money. Getting your money here

chunks.t: Money, tax & banking in Australia
chunks.x: Transferring your savings is one of the largest financial events of the move, and the default option is usually the expensive one. The cost of an international transfer is rarely the advertised fee. It is the exchange rate margin. The gap between the rate you are given and the real mid-market rate, and on a sum large enough to fund a bond, a car and three months of living, a poor margin costs meaningfully more than any fee. Compare your bank against a specialist transfer service, on the same day, for the same amount, and look only at how many Australian dollars arrive. That is the whole comparison. Banks are convenient and often not competitive; specialists are usually better on rate and require a little setup. Two practical points.

chunks.t: Money, tax & banking in Australia
chunks.x: Split your transfer rather than moving everything on one day, because you have no way of knowing whether today’s rate is good and splitting removes the need to guess. And expect to be asked to document the source of large sums. That is ordinary anti-money-laundering compliance, not suspicion, and having a payslip or sale document ready makes it a five-minute conversation. In our experience

chunks.t: Money, tax & banking in Australia
chunks.h: Nobody regrets keeping a buffer at home for the first six months
chunks.x: Moving everything at once feels decisive and occasionally goes wrong. A delayed start date, a rental application that falls through, a family reason to fly home unexpectedly. A reserve in your home currency is not indecision, it is what makes the first months calm. The other end

chunks.t: Money, tax & banking in Australia
chunks.h: What you leave behind at home
chunks.x: We are not qualified to advise on the tax system you are leaving. These are the questions to ask while local advisers are still a phone call away. Your pension. Whatever scheme you are in, find out before you leave what happens to it when you stop contributing, whether it can be transferred, and whether transferring is a good idea. Frequently it is not. Get this in writing while you are still in the country. Property you are keeping. If you rent out a home at home, that income may be declarable in both countries. Double tax agreements exist precisely so you are not taxed twice, but they do not apply themselves. Your final part-year return. Most systems require one for the year you leave, and it is often the year you are owed a refund. Easy to forget from twelve thousand miles away. Student loans.

chunks.t: Money, tax & banking in Australia
chunks.h: What you leave behind at home
chunks.x: Many countries require continued repayment from abroad, on a different basis from at home, and some charge a fixed amount rather than an income-linked one. Check the rule for your own scheme before you go. One accountant conversation in your last month at home and one in your first Australian year will cost less than either mistake. This is the part of the move where paying a professional is straightforwardly worth it. Common questions

chunks.t: Money, tax & banking in Australia
chunks.h: The things people ask us first
chunks.x: What is a TFN and when should I apply? Your permanent tax reference with the ATO, one number, yours for life. Apply online once you have arrived and hold a visa with work rights. It is free, and no commercial site can get it faster. Until your employer has it, they must withhold tax at the top rate, so week one is the right time. Can I choose my own super fund? In most cases yes, and you should. If you do not choose, you are defaulted, either into an existing fund of yours or your employer’s default. Health employers commonly offer a low-fee industry fund, which is a perfectly good answer, but there is a difference between choosing it and being placed in it without looking. Compare fees and long-run net performance on the government’s tool. Do I have to pay the Medicare levy? It depends on whether you are entitled to Medicare.

chunks.t: Money, tax & banking in Australia
chunks.h: The things people ask us first
chunks.x: If your country has a reciprocal agreement you may be enrolled and liable in the ordinary way. If you are not entitled, apply to Services Australia for a Medicare Entitlement Statement and claim an exemption in your return. This is the refund arriving clinicians most often miss. Is private health insurance worth it? Often, and for an unromantic reason: above a certain income you pay the Medicare levy surcharge if you do not hold private hospital cover, and a basic policy frequently costs less than the surcharge. Extras cover does not count. Run it against your own income rather than trusting a rule of thumb. Am I a resident for tax purposes? Probably, if you have moved properly. Job, home, family, intention to stay, even on a temporary visa. Tax residency follows your circumstances, not your visa label, and residents generally get a tax-free threshold and lower rates.

chunks.t: Money, tax & banking in Australia
chunks.h: The things people ask us first
chunks.x: Confirm your own position with the ATO’s residency tests in year one, because it changes what you pay. Do I need life insurance or income protection? Check what you already have first. Most Australian super funds include default life and total-and-permanent-disability cover, sometimes income protection, with premiums taken from your balance rather than billed to you. Find out what each of your funds provides before buying a separate policy, and before consolidating accounts, because closing a fund closes its cover. What about professional indemnity insurance? Ahpra requires professional indemnity arrangements to be in place as a condition of registration. In an employed public role you are generally covered by your employer; if you take on private sessions or any independent practice, that usually needs your own cover.

chunks.t: Money, tax & banking in Australia
chunks.h: The things people ask us first
chunks.x: It belongs with eligibility & registration rather than here, because it is a registration requirement rather than a money question. When is the tax year? 1 July to 30 June. Not the calendar year, and not the April year some arrivals are used to. You lodge after 30 June, and for a salaried role much of the return arrives pre-filled. What is the cheapest way to move my savings over? Compare your bank against a specialist transfer service on the same day for the same amount, and look only at how many Australian dollars arrive. The exchange rate margin matters far more than the advertised fee. Split the transfer over several dates rather than betting on one, and keep a buffer at home for the first six months. chunks.h: Not sure what applies to you?
chunks.x: We are recruiters, not accountants, and we will not pretend otherwise, but we have walked a lot of clinicians through this first month and we know which questions are worth paying someone to answer. Ask Ethicare The full move, step by step Ethicare Resourcing · your guide to a life and career in Australia.

chunks.t: Moving to Australia with pets
chunks.x: Moving pets to Australia works from many countries, but it requires considerably more planning than booking an extra seat on the flight. Australia operates strict biosecurity requirements designed to protect their unique environments and animal health. That means your pet’s move needs to be planned alongside your own, not a few weeks before departure. For most owners, a pet isn’t cargo to be transported after the move. They’re part of who’s moving. Section 01 · Timing

chunks.t: Moving to Australia with pets
chunks.x: The process your pet follows depends on the country you are moving from . Requirements can include microchipping, vaccinations, rabies testing, parasite treatments, veterinary examinations, official documentation, import permits and quarantine. And the order matters: where a test or treatment has to happen within a specified window, getting the sequence wrong can delay the whole move. When to start As soon as Australia becomes a serious possibility, not when the removal boxes are packed. You don’t need a signed contract to start researching your pet’s requirements, and starting early is the cheapest thing you can do. Section 02 · The rules

chunks.t: Moving to Australia with pets
chunks.x: Requirements follow the biosecurity risk of your country of export, so the same breed can face different processes from different countries. Australia

chunks.t: Moving to Australia with pets
chunks.h: Among the strictest in the world
chunks.x: Requirements depend on the country your pet is travelling from and the type of animal. Dogs and cats from approved countries may need to complete a series of veterinary and biosecurity steps before departure. Identification by microchip Rabies vaccination and testing Parasite treatments Veterinary certification An import permit Some animals will also need to spend time in post-entry quarantine after arriving. There are additional restrictions affecting certain breeds and circumstances, so don’t assume that because somebody else’s dog moved successfully, yours follows the same route. The regulator is the Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry . It sorts countries of export into groups by rabies risk and publishes a separate step-by-step guide for each group, so the first thing to establish is which group your country sits in.

chunks.t: Moving to Australia with pets
chunks.h: Among the strictest in the world
chunks.x: That guide is then your checklist: agriculture.gov.au — step-by-step guides . Check the source Regulations change. A checklist somebody used a few years ago, or even relatively recently, should never replace current government guidance. Check the source, not the forum post. Section 03 · Quarantine

chunks.t: Moving to Australia with pets
chunks.h: Will my pet have to quarantine?
chunks.x: Possibly. It depends on the animal and the country it is travelling from — Australia sorts countries into groups by rabies risk, and that determines the process. If quarantine is required, availability becomes part of your relocation timeline . Facilities book up, and that’s one of the clearest reasons pet travel shouldn’t be left until the end of the process. Three dates, not one Your employment start date, your family’s flights and your pet’s travel date may not be the same. Plan them as three linked decisions rather than assuming everyone arrives together. Section 04 · Sequencing

chunks.t: Moving to Australia with pets
chunks.h: Your pet doesn’t necessarily have to travel with you
chunks.x: A clinician might travel first, begin work, move out of temporary accommodation and secure a pet-friendly long-term rental before their partner, children and pets follow. Other families move together and arrange for the pet to arrive separately. There isn’t one correct way. Think about what makes the transition easiest for both your family and your animal, and remember that arriving into a settled home is a much gentler landing for a dog than arriving into a serviced apartment and a house-hunt. Section 05 · Somewhere to live

chunks.t: Moving to Australia with pets
chunks.x: Getting your pet into the country is only half the problem. You also need somewhere to live that will have them. Check the rules around pets before assuming a property is suitable, and pay particular attention to temporary accommodation. A serviced apartment or short-term let that works perfectly for a family may not accept a dog or cat. If your pet is arriving after you, use that window to find suitable long-term accommodation. Then think beyond whether the landlord permits pets: Is there enough space? Is there a secure garden, if you have a dog? Are there good places nearby for walking? How long will your pet be alone while you’re working? The right home for your family needs to work for them too. Section 06 · Cost

chunks.t: Moving to Australia with pets
chunks.x: The total depends on where you’re travelling from, the size and type of animal, veterinary requirements, transport and whether quarantine is required. Potential expenses include veterinary appointments, vaccinations, blood tests, official certification, permits, airline transport, travel crates, pet relocation companies and quarantine. For a large dog or multiple animals, the total can become a significant part of the family’s relocation budget. Get quotes early It is far easier to plan for this six months out than to discover it once you’ve committed most of your savings to flights, accommodation and setting up the new home. Our relocation cost guide shows where this sits against everything else you’ll be paying for. Section 07 · The journey

chunks.t: Moving to Australia with pets
chunks.h: Ask for it stage by stage
chunks.x: Depending on the route and airline arrangements, your pet may travel in a specially designed crate in an appropriate part of the aircraft rather than alongside you in the cabin. There may also be stopovers or transfers. A reputable pet transport specialist or airline should be able to explain the journey clearly, including where your animal will be during each stage. If your pet is elderly or has a medical condition, discuss the proposed route with your vet well in advance. Medication & sedation

chunks.t: Moving to Australia with pets
chunks.h: Not your decision to make alone
chunks.x: If you’re worried about how your pet will cope, speak to your vet and the company responsible for transporting them. Sedation can create additional risks during air travel and may not be permitted or recommended in some circumstances. The right approach depends on the individual animal and the requirements of the carrier, so ask both, and follow the advice. Should you use a pet relocation company? You don’t have to manage all of this alone. Specialists can coordinate veterinary timelines, documentation, travel crates, flights and quarantine arrangements. At a cost. Some families value having someone run a complicated process while they’re simultaneously dealing with visas, registration, jobs, schools and their own move; others prefer to manage it themselves. If you do use one, establish exactly what the quote includes and what you’ll still need to arrange separately. Section 08 · Check before you spend

chunks.t: Moving to Australia with pets
chunks.h: Older pets, restricted breeds & other animals
chunks.x: Three situations where the answer needs checking before you spend any money on the process. Older pets

chunks.t: Moving to Australia with pets
chunks.x: Moving a healthy three-year-old dog and moving a fourteen-year-old dog are very different decisions. For an older animal, the length of the journey, underlying conditions and ability to cope with transport all need careful thought. That doesn’t automatically mean an older pet can’t relocate. It means the decision belongs with your vet, rather than resting on whether the paperwork permits it. Breeds & species

chunks.t: Moving to Australia with pets
chunks.x: Australia restricts the importation of certain dog breeds or types, and there can be restrictions affecting hybrid animals. If there’s any possibility your dog falls within a restricted category, check the official rules first, don’t rely on appearance, breeder descriptions or informal advice. For pets other than dogs and cats, birds, rabbits, reptiles, don’t assume the dog-and-cat process applies. Check whether your animal can legally be imported before making any plans. For some species and countries of origin, it may not be possible at all. Section 09 · Settling in

chunks.t: Moving to Australia with pets
chunks.h: The first few weeks after arrival
chunks.x: The journey is only one part of your pet’s transition. Establish a predictable routine as quickly as you can. Find a local vet, update identification details where required, and learn the local rules for registration, microchipping and dog control. Then do the enjoyable part. Find the walks. Find the parks. Find the beach. For a lot of families, exploring the new neighbourhood with the dog is the first thing that makes the place feel like home. Section 10 · The package

chunks.t: Moving to Australia with pets
chunks.x: Pet relocation isn’t normally a standard employment benefit, but that isn’t quite the end of the question. If your employer is providing a general relocation allowance rather than paying only specified expenses, you may have some flexibility over how that money is used. Never assume pet transport is covered. Ask what the relocation contribution can and cannot be used for before making any bookings. Our offer guide covers how to raise this well, and relocation support is often more negotiable than the salary itself. Useful contacts

chunks.t: Moving to Australia with pets
chunks.x: Specialist relocation companies can coordinate veterinary requirements, documentation, flights, travel crates and quarantine. For candidates relocating from the UK, established providers include:

chunks.t: Moving to Australia with pets
chunks.x: A vet-led international pet relocation company providing services to Australia and New Zealand.

chunks.t: Moving to Australia with pets
chunks.x: Heathrow-based international pet transport specialist with veterinary and animal-handling facilities.

chunks.t: Moving to Australia with pets
chunks.x: UK pet relocation company arranging international transport for dogs, cats and other animals. Quarantine in Australia

chunks.t: Moving to Australia with pets
chunks.x: Cats and dogs requiring post-entry quarantine in Australia are accommodated at the Australian Government’s Post Entry Quarantine Facility at Mickleham, near Melbourne. Requirements for importing animals depend on the country your pet is travelling from, and they change without notice — always check the current Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry guidance before making arrangements. Ethicare does not receive commission from any of the providers listed here. We’d recommend obtaining several quotes and confirming current government requirements directly before you book anything. Sophie’s insight I should declare an interest: we are all completely soft about animals here, and there are two dogs in the Ethicare office on any given day. So when someone tells me they won’t move without their dog, I don’t treat that as a complication to be worked around.

chunks.t: Moving to Australia with pets
chunks.x: It’s just one of the things that has to work. What I’d say is that this is the part of a relocation people leave latest and regret most, because the timings are fixed by regulation and no amount of goodwill speeds them up. Raise it with us in the first conversation, not the last. It’s far easier to build the whole move around your pet’s timeline than to discover six weeks before departure that the sequence doesn’t work. Sophie Founder, Ethicare Resourcing Common questions

chunks.t: Moving to Australia with pets
chunks.h: The questions we’re asked about moving with pets
chunks.x: How far in advance should I start? As soon as the move becomes a serious possibility. Several of the veterinary steps have to happen in a particular order and within specified windows, and quarantine facilities have finite availability, so the timeline is set by regulation rather than by how organised you are. Starting early costs nothing and prevents the most common delays. Will my dog definitely have to go into quarantine? Not necessarily, it depends on the destination, the animal and your country of origin, since Australia categorises countries by biosecurity risk. Where quarantine does apply, treat facility availability as part of your relocation timeline rather than an afterthought. Can my pet travel on the same flight as me? Sometimes, but don’t assume it.

chunks.t: Moving to Australia with pets
chunks.h: The questions we’re asked about moving with pets
chunks.x: Depending on the route and airline, your pet may travel in a specially designed crate in an appropriate part of the aircraft rather than in the cabin, and there may be stopovers or transfers. A reputable specialist or the airline should walk you through where your animal will be at each stage. Should my pet be sedated for the journey? That’s a decision for your vet and the transport company, not something to arrange yourself. Sedation can carry additional risks in air travel and may not be permitted or recommended depending on the animal and the carrier’s requirements. My dog is a restricted breed, is that the end of it? Check the official rules before assuming either way, and before spending anything. Australia restricts certain breeds or types, and there can be restrictions on hybrid animals. Don’t rely on appearance, breeder descriptions or informal advice.

chunks.t: Moving to Australia with pets
chunks.h: The questions we’re asked about moving with pets
chunks.x: This is one to confirm at the source. What about a rabbit, bird or reptile? Considerably more complicated, and for some species and countries of origin importing isn’t possible. The dog-and-cat process doesn’t transfer. Confirm whether your animal can legally be imported before making any relocation plans around it. Will an employer pay for pet relocation? It isn’t a standard benefit, so never assume it. But if the employer offers a general relocation allowance rather than reimbursing only specified expenses, you may have flexibility over how it’s used. Ask what the contribution can and can’t cover before you book. Free, any time

chunks.t: Moving to Australia with pets
chunks.h: Tell us about them in the first conversation
chunks.x: Where you’ll live, where the children will go to school, when the family should travel, and how and when your pets make the journey. These aren’t small details to sort out once the job is secured. They’re part of whether the relocation works for everybody. chunks.t: Practising in Australia
chunks.x: Kettle on. A longer read — about 11 min Medicare, the public and private split and the PBS are explained properly in how healthcare works in Australia . This is the clinician’s summary of it. Who pays

chunks.t: Practising in Australia
chunks.x: Medicare, the state or territory health service, the disability scheme, private health insurance and the person themselves. Which one is paying shapes your caseload, your paperwork and how much intervention you have available. The structural one

chunks.t: Practising in Australia
chunks.x: Registration is national, so you can move states without starting again. Public hospitals are not: each state and territory runs its own services on its own enterprise agreements. The job travels; the terms and conditions do not. The scale of private

chunks.t: Practising in Australia
chunks.x: A very large share of care — particularly imaging, allied health, mental health and elective surgery — happens in private and community practice on Medicare-funded referrals rather than inside a hospital. Distance

chunks.t: Practising in Australia
chunks.h: A clinical factor, not a lifestyle one
chunks.x: Australia is the size of Europe with a fraction of the population. Outreach, fly-in services, retrieval and telehealth are ordinary practice rather than specialist interests. Before you search Ask which state, and ask who funds the role. Two jobs with the same title in Perth and in Hobart are different jobs on different agreements, and a Medicare-funded private caseload is a different working life from a state-run hospital one. Nothing in a job advert makes either obvious. Ask us — we find out before you apply.

chunks.t: Practising in Australia
chunks.x: Equality is giving everyone the same. Equity is giving people what they need to reach the same outcome — and here the distance between the two is measured, published and acted on, most visibly through Closing the Gap. In practice Extra time, an interpreter or outreach for the person who needs it is the standard here, not favouritism.

chunks.t: Practising in Australia
chunks.x: Shared goals, real choice, informed decisions — and family in the room by default rather than by invitation. In practice Write goals in the person’s own words — the plan that means something to them is the one that gets followed.

chunks.t: Practising in Australia
chunks.x: Teams run flat. You are expected to know what the other professions contribute, and to ask when something sits outside your scope. In practice Being new is not a reason to stay quiet in a case conference.

chunks.t: Practising in Australia
chunks.h: Prevention and keeping people out of hospital
chunks.x: Avoiding an admission counts as an outcome in its own right, and a great deal of funding follows care delivered in the community rather than on a ward. In practice Hospital-avoidance targets and community contracts will shape your caseload from week one.

chunks.t: Practising in Australia
chunks.x: Demand is shifting towards rehabilitation, chronic conditions, aged care and disability support. That is where the growth in most professions sits, and where a large share of the funding now goes. In practice More of your week is about function and independence than cure — and the funding follows it.

chunks.t: Practising in Australia
chunks.x: Australia holds the oldest continuing cultures on earth and is one of the most multicultural countries in the world. Nobody expects you to arrive expert. The history and the culture are covered properly in community and culture in Australia . Here is what they mean in a clinic by your second week.

chunks.t: Practising in Australia
chunks.h: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health
chunks.x: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have cared for this continent for more than 60,000 years. Colonisation and its continuing effects are part of the clinical picture, not a historical aside — and health outcomes remain measurably unequal. Connection to family, community, culture and Country is understood here as part of health rather than context around it. The culture you would be joining

chunks.t: Practising in Australia
chunks.x: The national agreement to close the gaps in life expectancy, health and wellbeing outcomes. You will hear the term constantly, in service plans, funding and appraisals. At a caseload level it asks a practical question: what would equitable access to your profession require for someone living hundreds of kilometres from the nearest service? What that looks like in remote practice

chunks.t: Practising in Australia
chunks.x: Aboriginal Community Controlled Health Organisations deliver care designed and governed by the communities they serve, usually with family and Country at the centre of the model rather than at its edge. You will refer to them, work alongside them, and in some roles be employed by them. Where they sit, by state Cultural safety, plainly Clinical competence is performing the technique correctly. Cultural safety is the patient’s judgement of whether your care was safe for them — which is why you cannot self-certify it, and why it sits in the codes of conduct rather than in an induction folder. Day to day it is unremarkable good practice: learn whose Country your service stands on, take the cultural induction seriously, ask who should be part of the conversation, explain before you touch, notice when someone has gone quiet, and accept correction without defending yourself. Nobody expects fluency on arrival. People do notice effort. Acknowledgement of Country opens the meeting. Take it as clinical business, not ceremony.

chunks.t: Practising in Australia
chunks.h: Where you practise changes the job
chunks.x: Metropolitan Melbourne and a remote community in the Northern Territory are the same registration and not remotely the same work. What “regional” can mean Alice Springs, Northern Territory. A small town that is also the referral centre for an area larger than many countries. A post here means outreach, travel and a scope far broader than the metropolitan version of the same job.

chunks.t: Practising in Australia
chunks.x: Workforce shortages, very long distances, outreach and fly-in services, and a scope of practice far broader than the metropolitan version of your job. This is where the most autonomy, often the best pay, and the country’s most persistent workforce need all sit — along with professional isolation and distance from family, which are worth weighing before month three. Often true: one contact instead of six · a broader caseload · decisions you make rather than escalate · telehealth as core practice · a community that knows exactly who you are

chunks.t: Practising in Australia
chunks.x: Subspecialty depth, teaching, research and the largest teams, concentrated in the capitals and carrying the state’s tertiary and quaternary work.

chunks.t: Practising in Australia
chunks.x: Medicare-funded referrals, booked lists, commercial throughput and often the newest equipment. A career route in its own right here, and a large employer in several professions.

chunks.t: Practising in Australia
chunks.x: Work funded through the disability scheme or aged care rather than through health, focused on function, capacity and daily living rather than episodes of treatment.

chunks.t: Practising in Australia
chunks.x: Aboriginal Community Controlled Health Organisations and regional outreach programmes, where your profession sits inside a wider model of care and cultural safety is the clinical standard.

chunks.t: Practising in Australia
chunks.x: Enterprise agreements, progression, rostering and how services are structured are all set state by state. Your registration moves with you; your pay and conditions are renegotiated by geography.

chunks.t: Practising in Australia
chunks.x: Medicare, state health, the disability scheme, private insurance or an employer. Each buys a different job under the same professional title — different caseload, different documentation, different amount of time per person.

chunks.t: Practising in Australia
chunks.x: What catches experienced clinicians out here is rarely clinical. It is the structure around the work. These are the differences every profession meets. The version specific to your discipline sits on your own profession’s page. Who funds the care Where many clinicians trained One payer, one set of rules, invisible to you at the bedside. Often here Five, sometimes two for the same person. The funder decides your documentation, your session limits and how long you have — and you are expected to know which one applies. National or state Where many clinicians trained One national employer, one set of terms wherever you work. Often here National registration, state employment. Pay, progression and rostering change when you cross a border, and comparing two offers means comparing two agreements. Terminology Where many clinicians trained Familiar shorthand and familiar service names.

chunks.t: Practising in Australia
chunks.x: Often here Different words for the same thing, a wall of acronyms for funding schemes, and Acknowledgement of Country opening meetings. Learn whose Country your service stands on early. Referral pathways Where many clinicians trained Access is referral-gated, and the referral defines the episode. Often here Direct access is common in several professions, and a referral often comes with a funded session count attached — which changes how you plan an episode of care. Autonomy Where many clinicians trained Decisions are escalated for approval. Often here You make the call and justify it afterwards, and the further from a capital city you work, the more true that becomes. Most clinicians name this as the best part of the job and the hardest month of the first year. Distance Where many clinicians trained A tertiary centre is a bus ride away. Often here It may be a flight.

chunks.t: Practising in Australia
chunks.x: Retrieval, outreach and telehealth are ordinary parts of the job rather than specialist interests, and travel time is in your diary. Cultural expectations Where many clinicians trained A module, completed once at induction. Often here Written into the national codes of conduct you practise under, and a professional expectation from your first shift. None of this is expected of you on day one. But the clinicians who settle fastest understood the system before they signed.

chunks.t: Practising in Australia
chunks.x: Most clinicians describe the start as a runway rather than a cold plunge. This is what the runway usually contains.

chunks.t: Practising in Australia
chunks.x: A structured orientation to the service, its systems and its documentation before you carry a full load. In public services it is formal and measured in days, not an hour, and the funder-specific paperwork from the previous section is learned here rather than before you arrive.

chunks.t: Practising in Australia
chunks.h: Supervision, where your registration carries it
chunks.x: Depending on your profession and route, registration can come with a period of supervised practice attached. It is a registration condition, not a judgement on your experience. Whether it applies to you, and for how long, is on your profession page and in the registration guide .

chunks.t: Practising in Australia
chunks.x: First names, open communication and multidisciplinary teamwork are the norm, and clinicians arriving from more hierarchical systems often describe care as a touch less rushed. Not universal — healthcare is healthcare — but it is the common experience.

chunks.t: Practising in Australia
chunks.h: One registration, wherever you go next
chunks.x: Registration is national. Once you are settled you can develop, specialise or move between states without starting the paperwork again — though pay and terms change at the border, as the previous section says. Three to six months is the usual figure before the systems, the shorthand and the referral pathways stop taking conscious effort. The wobble that tends to arrive around the third month is rarely about the work. What we do in those months is set out once, on the About page ; the life around the job has its own guides, community and culture and moving with your family .

chunks.t: Practising in Australia
chunks.h: Learn whose Country you are moving to
chunks.x: The traditional owners of the place you will work, and how to say the name. It takes an evening, it will come up in your first week, and getting it wrong without having tried is what people notice.

chunks.t: Practising in Australia
chunks.h: Read the community and culture guide
chunks.x: Once before you fly and once after your first fortnight — it reads differently the second time. Community and culture in Australia

chunks.t: Practising in Australia
chunks.x: How it funds care, what bulk billing means and where the private system sits. Knowing it signals you have done more than skim a job advert. How healthcare works here

chunks.t: Practising in Australia
chunks.h: Ask which state agreement covers the role
chunks.x: And what step you would start on. Two offers with the same headline title can be materially different once the agreement is on the table, and this is the question candidates most often forget to ask.

chunks.t: Practising in Australia
chunks.h: Decide what the move is for
chunks.x: Adventure, scope, pay, family — the answer changes which state, which setting and which roles we should be showing you. One boundary. We are not migration agents and we are not your regulator — those decisions sit with the board and with the Department of Home Affairs. What we do is explain, sequence and keep your file moving, and tell you plainly what we do not know. And make sure the system holds no surprises before your family is committed to it.

chunks.t: Practising in Australia
chunks.x: Tell us your profession and where you trained, and we will give you a clear read on the system — and which state fits — before you spend money on anything. chunks.t: Life in regional Australia
chunks.h: Regional Australia is not remote Australia
chunks.x: Regional rarely means the outback. In many cases it means a modern city with a major hospital, good schools and a beach. Many regional cities are home to well over 50,000 people. Some pass 100,000, or even 250,000. For many internationally trained clinicians, they feel like medium-sized cities rather than isolated towns. They have: Major public hospitals Private healthcare providers Universities Airports Modern shopping centres Sporting facilities Restaurants and cafés Coastline or countryside on the doorstep Geelong Bunbury Toowoomba Ballarat Launceston Albury–Wodonga Orange Mackay The first thing you notice

chunks.t: Life in regional Australia
chunks.x: In many regional cities, a commute of 10–20 minutes is completely normal. Instead of spending two hours a day in traffic, you could be: Walking the dog before work Having breakfast with your children Going for a swim after your shift Home for dinner every evening Over a year, that adds up to hundreds of hours outside work. For many families, it becomes the single biggest change after relocating, bigger than the job, bigger than the weather. The professional side

chunks.t: Life in regional Australia
chunks.h: Healthcare sits at the heart of the community
chunks.x: Many clinicians tell us they feel they make a more visible difference.

chunks.t: Life in regional Australia
chunks.x: Healthcare professionals often become well-known within their local communities. Your work is visible, and so are you, in a way that’s easy to lose in a city of five million.

chunks.t: Life in regional Australia
chunks.x: You work closely with colleagues across specialties and often know your referring clinicians personally, rather than as a name on a request form.

chunks.t: Life in regional Australia
chunks.x: Patients tend to stay with the same services for longer, so stronger professional relationships have room to develop. Everyday life

chunks.t: Life in regional Australia
chunks.h: The pace is different. You don’t give things up.
chunks.x: Life moves a little more slowly, and everyday life feels less rushed. Parking isn’t an event. Shopping takes twenty minutes rather than an afternoon. Many people leave work and are at the beach, the river or a walking trail within half an hour. For people relocating from London, Johannesburg or Dubai, the change can feel remarkable. And the biggest misconception is that regional means missing out. Many regional centres have: Excellent coffee culture Independent restaurants Farmers’ markets Live music Sporting clubs and gyms Cinemas The difference is that everything is closer together. Before work, not instead of it Where you live

chunks.t: Life in regional Australia
chunks.x: Property prices vary considerably across Australia, but many regional locations offer homes that would cost significantly more in the largest cities. That might mean: A larger garden An extra bedroom Space for children to play A home office A shorter drive to work For families, this is often the biggest practical advantage of regional living. Our relocation cost guide shows how housing decisions shape your first three months, wherever you land. Saturday, rewritten

chunks.t: Life in regional Australia
chunks.x: Weekends get their shape back. A typical Saturday might be: Breakfast at a local café Children’s sport A trip to the beach Lunch with friends An afternoon barbecue Sunset by the water Not because you’re on holiday. Because that’s where you live. For families

chunks.t: Life in regional Australia
chunks.x: Class sizes can sometimes be smaller, children often spend less time travelling to and from school, and parents frequently comment on the strong sense of community around local schools. One thing to check early: if you’re relocating on a temporary visa, public school fees for temporary residents vary between states , and in some states, regional moves are treated differently from metropolitan ones. Our school fees guide covers it state by state, and the education guide explains how Australian schooling works. The money question

chunks.t: Life in regional Australia
chunks.x: Not necessarily. Regional doesn’t mean lower paid, particularly in professions experiencing workforce shortages. Some regional positions offer stronger overall packages than their metropolitan equivalents, which can include: Relocation assistance Housing support Visa sponsorship Professional development funding Recruitment incentives The advice: compare the whole package, and the whole cost of living, rather than assuming anything from the postcode. Our salary guide explains how Australian pay is structured, and the negotiation guide covers what’s movable in an offer. The limits

chunks.t: Life in regional Australia
chunks.h: Is there anything you’ll miss? Probably.
chunks.x: If you love living in the centre of a major international city, hundreds of restaurants, extensive nightlife, big sporting events every week. Regional living will feel quieter than you’re used to. Some specialist shopping or entertainment may mean travelling to a larger city. And depending on where you live, visiting family overseas may involve a domestic flight before your international one. These aren’t reasons not to move. They’re part of making an informed decision. From our experience, the people who settle best are those who value more time outside work, space for their family, outdoor living, community and strong professional relationships. Many arrive planning to stay for two years. A surprising number are still there ten years later. Before you say no

chunks.t: Life in regional Australia
chunks.h: Don’t judge a role by its postcode
chunks.x: Don’t dismiss a role because you’ve never heard of the town. Before saying no, ask: How far is it from the beach? What is the hospital like? How long is the commute? What are the schools like? Could my family have a better quality of life there? Sometimes the places you’ve never heard of become the places you never want to leave. Different, not less

chunks.t: Life in regional Australia
chunks.h: The best move isn’t always the biggest city
chunks.x: We’ve helped healthcare professionals settle across Australia, coastal cities, regional hubs, places many people outside Australia have never heard of. Time and again, we hear the same thing: “We only wish we’d realised what regional Australia was actually like sooner.” Sometimes the right move is the place that gives you more time, more space and a better life outside work. See where the roles are Free, any time

chunks.t: Life in regional Australia
chunks.h: Tell us what matters to your family
chunks.x: The beach, the schools, the commute, the mortgage, everyone weighs them differently. The destination finder asks what matters most and shows which places fit, including the ones you haven’t heard of yet. See live roles Is Australia right for us?
