chunks.t: Australia or New Zealand? A guide
chunks.x: New Zealand Australia The decision guide Australia or New Zealand? Two countries, one comparison A side-by-side look at building a healthcare career, and a life, in each country: health systems, registration, pay, visas, family life and how to decide. Kettle on. About 9 min Read the comparison → Ask Ethicare 9 sections Updated October 2026 Section 01 · The headline

chunks.t: Australia or New Zealand? A guide
chunks.h: The two countries at a glance
chunks.x: Australia is the bigger market. New Zealand is smaller, with one national health service. Beyond that, the employer, the town and the role often matter as much as the country. Topic Australia New Zealand Health system State and territory public systems, plus a very large private sector. One national public service, Health New Zealand – Te Whatu Ora, plus a smaller private sector. Jobs market Larger, with more employers and settings. Smaller; openings vary by profession and region. Registration A national scheme run by Ahpra for the professions it regulates. Some, such as sonography and social work, sit outside it. Each profession has its own regulator, with a practising certificate renewed every year. Pay Often higher in headline terms, varying by state, setting and role. Employers add superannuation. Public pay set mostly by national collective agreements.

chunks.t: Australia or New Zealand? A guide
chunks.h: The two countries at a glance
chunks.x: Living costs Big differences between the major cities and regional areas. Auckland and the regions differ a lot, mainly on housing. Family Partner work rights, school fees and healthcare depend on the visa and, for schools, the state or territory. Visas for your partner and children, and school and healthcare eligibility, depend on your visa, occupation and pay. Lifestyle Huge variation between states, cities and regions. Huge variation between regions, from Auckland to small rural towns. Look past the country A radiographer in regional Western Australia lives a very different life from one in central Sydney, and a busy New Zealand emergency department is not a quiet place to work. Compare the places and roles you would actually take. Section 02 · The systems

chunks.t: Australia or New Zealand? A guide
chunks.x: Both countries run universal public healthcare funded largely through taxation, with a private sector alongside. How that’s organised is where they differ. Topic Australia New Zealand Public system Run at state and territory level, each jurisdiction manages its own public hospitals and services, within a national framework and Medicare. One national service, Health New Zealand – Te Whatu Ora, delivering public hospital and community care across the country. Private sector Very large and well established, especially in imaging, surgery and diagnostics, a major source of roles. Present and growing, but smaller; most acute care sits within the public service. Scale Large population spread across big cities and vast regional areas. Smaller population concentrated in a handful of cities, plus high-demand regional centres.

chunks.t: Australia or New Zealand? A guide
chunks.x: What it means for you More employers and settings to choose between; you’ll often weigh public against private. One employer for most public roles, so terms are more consistent between regions. Ethicare insight In Australia, part of your decision is often public or private , two quite different working cultures. In New Zealand, the bigger question is usually which part of the country , because the system itself is more consistent from place to place. Section 03 · Registration

chunks.t: Australia or New Zealand? A guide
chunks.x: You can’t work as a clinician in either country until the relevant regulator has registered you. The principle is the same; the machinery differs. Australia

chunks.t: Australia or New Zealand? A guide
chunks.h: A national scheme, for most professions
chunks.x: For the professions it covers, Australia regulates through a national scheme run by Ahpra (the Australian Health Practitioner Regulation Agency), with a national board for each profession. That registration applies Australia-wide. Some professions sit outside Ahpra and have their own arrangements: sonographers are accredited through the Australian Sonographer Accreditation Registry, for example, and social workers through the Australian Association of Social Workers. For several professions, qualifications from comparable overseas regulators (for example the UK’s HCPC or Ireland’s CORU) can be recognised through a faster pathway. Otherwise the relevant board assesses your qualification, and a national examination is sometimes required. Registration and a migration skills assessment are separate processes ; you may need one, the other, or both. New Zealand

chunks.t: Australia or New Zealand? A guide
chunks.x: New Zealand regulates each profession through its own responsible authority or board , and once registered you hold an Annual Practising Certificate (APC) that you renew each year. The board assesses your qualification, recent clinical experience and competence against New Zealand standards. Routes are often a comparable-country pathway (more streamlined) or a qualifications-assessed pathway. You’ll typically need verified qualifications, evidence of recent practice, a criminal-history check and, where required, English-language evidence. The trade-off Neither country is simply easier. For some professions New Zealand’s route is shorter; for others, Australia’s is. Your profession and where you trained decide it. Can you actually work in either country? Check your registration pathway → Section 04 · Pay & living costs

chunks.t: Australia or New Zealand? A guide
chunks.x: A single number would mislead you here. This is how pay works in each country, and what to weigh alongside it. Australia

chunks.t: Australia or New Zealand? A guide
chunks.x: Public-sector pay is set by state-based enterprise agreements and awards, which also define progression, overtime and allowances. On top of pay, employers pay compulsory superannuation (retirement contributions). The very large private sector, with high volumes in some specialties, can support strong earning potential, but figures vary by state, setting and role. New Zealand

chunks.t: Australia or New Zealand? A guide
chunks.x: Public pay is largely set by national collective agreements, which give clear bands and progression across the country. Private work can add to this for some roles. "What will I earn?" is a per-role question, so we answer it per role. Cost of living matters just as much as headline pay. Both countries have affordable regional areas and pricier big cities; housing is the biggest variable in each. The right comparison is always take-home pay against local costs for the specific place you’d live , not one country’s average against another’s. Topic Australia New Zealand Retirement savings Employers pay superannuation on top of your pay: 12% of ordinary earnings since 1 July 2025. If you leave Australia for good on a temporary visa, you can usually claim it, minus tax. KiwiSaver is for people entitled to live in New Zealand indefinitely, so it usually starts once you hold residence.

chunks.t: Australia or New Zealand? A guide
chunks.x: From 1 April 2026 the default is 3.5% from you, matched by 3.5% from your employer. Tax Income tax comes out of your pay, plus a 2% Medicare levy for most taxpayers. Income tax and the ACC earners’ levy come out of your pay. Housing Usually the biggest cost. Sydney and Melbourne cost far more than most regional towns. Usually the biggest cost. Auckland and Queenstown cost far more than most regional towns. What could you earn? See published pay rates → What might the move cost your family? Calculate your moving budget → Section 05 · Visas

chunks.t: Australia or New Zealand? A guide
chunks.x: Both countries have routes for eligible healthcare professionals to move with their families. Partner work rights, schooling, healthcare and their costs depend on the visa and your circumstances, so check them before you decide. Topic Australia New Zealand Common work route Employer-sponsored temporary work visas are the usual entry for skilled clinicians, with skilled and nominated pathways alongside. The Accredited Employer Work Visa is the usual route, tied to an accredited employer and a skilled role. Residence Employer-nomination and skilled-migration routes can lead to permanent residence, depending on your occupation, visa and circumstances. Many healthcare roles are on the Green List, with straight-to-residence or work-to-residence routes. Eligibility depends on your occupation and registration. Your family Partner work rights depend on the visa granted.

chunks.t: Australia or New Zealand? A guide
chunks.x: Public school fees for the children of temporary visa holders vary by state and territory. Which visas your partner and children can get depends on your visa, occupation and pay. School and healthcare eligibility depend on the visa too. Good to know Some visa routes also require a migration skills assessment, separate from professional registration. Registration and visa steps are best sequenced together, usually a job offer first, then the visa. Ethicare insight Both countries reward getting the order right: registration, offer and visa need to happen in the correct sequence, and small timing details (like the validity window on certificates) trip people up. Ethicare is not an immigration adviser. Check your visa with the Department of Home Affairs or Immigration New Zealand. Section 06 · Life & family

chunks.t: Australia or New Zealand? A guide
chunks.x: Both are English-speaking and outdoors-oriented, but they feel different to live in. Australia

chunks.t: Australia or New Zealand? A guide
chunks.x: A warm climate across much of the country, several large coastal cities, and everything from beaches to outback. Distances are big, which shapes travel and where you settle. Life in a regional town is very different from life in Sydney or Melbourne. New Zealand

chunks.t: Australia or New Zealand? A guide
chunks.x: A cooler, greener landscape, with mountains, coast and lakes rarely far away. Auckland is the one large city; most people elsewhere live in smaller cities and regional towns, where commutes are usually shorter. Māori culture is woven through everyday life in New Zealand; Australia’s draw is often its range of places to live. For schools, healthcare and settling in, read moving to Australia with your family and moving to New Zealand with your family . Picture an ordinary Tuesday, not just the holiday photos, that’s the life you’re choosing. Where could you see yourself living? Explore destinations that suit you → Section 07 · Career

chunks.t: Australia or New Zealand? A guide
chunks.x: Topic Australia New Zealand Market size Large, major public systems plus one of the world’s biggest private sectors, so more roles and settings. Smaller, with workforce shortages in many professions. Specialisation Broad scope to sub-specialise, with clear career ladders in bigger centres. Broad general scope with room to develop expertise; often more autonomy earlier. Ways of working Choice between public and private cultures; high volumes in some private settings. Mostly public; the private sector is smaller. The trade-off Australia’s scale gives you more directions to grow and more private options. New Zealand often gives broader scope earlier. Either way, the service you join shapes your week more than the flag does. Section 08 · Deciding

chunks.t: Australia or New Zealand? A guide
chunks.x: Choose what matters most. This is a reflection exercise, not an eligibility assessment. 1 What matters most for your career? More employers and specialist opportunities A particular team, role or working environment I’m flexible 2 What kind of lifestyle appeals to you? A larger city with lots happening A smaller city or regional community Either could suit me 3 What’s your biggest financial priority? Maximising earning potential Balancing earnings with living costs Keeping initial moving costs manageable 4 What matters most to your family? Partner employment and schools Being close to nature and outdoor activities Finding the right community 5 How certain are you about your destination? Leaning towards Australia Leaning towards New Zealand Still exploring both Explore my preferences What your answers point to

chunks.t: Australia or New Zealand? A guide
chunks.x: Compare places in the Destination Finder Check your registration route Save this to my plan Nothing here is sent to Ethicare. Your answers stay on this page. You don’t have to choose forever Plenty of clinicians start in one country and move to the other later. The goal now is the next good step for you and your family. Sophie’s insight People often come to us convinced they have to get this "right" the first time. You don’t. Both countries value your skills, so the question isn’t which is better, it’s which fits the life you want next. Sometimes that’s Australia, sometimes New Zealand, and sometimes it’s starting where the door opens first. Sophie Founder, Ethicare Resourcing Section 09 · Questions

chunks.t: Australia or New Zealand? A guide
chunks.x: Is it easier to get registered in Australia or New Zealand? Neither is simply easier. It depends on your profession and where you trained: for some professions New Zealand’s route is shorter, for others Australia’s is. Some Australian routes also need a national exam or a separate migration skills assessment. The pathway checker shows the likely route in each. Where will I earn more? There’s no single answer. It varies by role, setting, state and agreement, and must be weighed against local living costs. What could I earn? shows published rates for some professions. Can my family come with me? Both countries have routes for eligible healthcare professionals to move with their families. Partner work rights, schooling, healthcare and their costs depend on the visa and your circumstances, so check them before you decide. Ethicare is not an immigration adviser.

chunks.t: Australia or New Zealand? A guide
chunks.x: Do I have to choose one forever? No. Many clinicians move between the two over a career, and the systems have a lot in common. The goal now is the next good step. I’m not from the UK, does this still apply to me? Yes. We work with clinicians trained across the UK, Ireland, South Africa, the UAE and beyond. Both countries recognise a wide range of international qualifications; the pathway checker shows how yours is likely to be assessed. Your next step

chunks.t: Before you leave home
chunks.h: The three that matter most for a clinician
chunks.x: Registration You cannot work until your board has registered you and, where it applies, issued a practising certificate. If any step is outstanding, know who is waiting on what, and tell your employer. Some new registrants start under supervision; find out before you arrive. Visa conditions A work visa is usually tied to a named employer and role. Read the conditions on the grant letter, and check the start date on your contract matches what you told Immigration New Zealand. The first shift Ask your employer for a list of what they need before day one: ID, registration evidence, bank account and IRD number for payroll, police check status, uniform sizes, and your induction dates. Your first weeks after landing are in Your first month ; the full list of everything in the move is in the relocation checklist . Ethicare Resourcing

chunks.t: Cost of relocating to Australia or NZ
chunks.x: New Zealand Australia The relocation cost guide What does it really cost to get there? The cash you need in hand, stage by stage Not what you’ll earn, and not what it costs to live. The cash you need in hand to execute the move, and the bit that catches people out. Kettle on. A longer read — about 14 min See the seven stages → Work out what the move costs 14 sections Updated August 2026 Free The money, in order

chunks.t: Cost of relocating to Australia or NZ
chunks.h: Seven stages, and the cash each one needs
chunks.x: Relocation costs arrive in a sequence, not all at once. Jump to any stage. And then one more thing After all seven comes the stage nobody budgets for: the gap before your first pay day . It lands at exactly the moment the other seven have emptied your account. The practical question

chunks.t: Cost of relocating to Australia or NZ
chunks.h: Flights are the obvious cost. They’re rarely the whole story.
chunks.x: Professional registration, visas, medicals, temporary accommodation, rental deposits, transport and setting up a new home add up surprisingly quickly. So before accepting a role, it’s worth asking a very practical question: How much money will we need to make the move? There isn’t one figure that works for everybody. But there are costs you can anticipate, and a few that regularly catch people by surprise. This guide walks the sequence, then helps you build your own number rather than borrowing somebody else’s, and if you would rather do the arithmetic than read it, the cost of moving calculator builds the same budget from your answers. Stage 01

chunks.t: Cost of relocating to Australia or NZ
chunks.x: For healthcare professionals, the cost of relocating often begins long before the flight. Depending on your profession and pathway, you may need to pay for some combination of: Registration or application fees Qualification assessments English language testing Certificates of good standing Police checks Certified documents and translations Examinations or competency assessments Annual practising or registration fees A radiologist, GP, psychologist and radiographer can have completely different registration journeys. Your individual circumstances matter too, two people in the same profession may face different requirements depending on where they trained and what they’ve done since. Do this first Establish your likely registration pathway before you budget anything else, because it’s the cost that varies most between two apparently similar clinicians. Stage 02

chunks.t: Cost of relocating to Australia or NZ
chunks.x: What you pay depends on the country, the visa route, and whether you’re relocating alone or with family. There may also be associated costs for medical examinations, police certificates, document certification or immigration advice. Some employers cover or contribute towards these. Others don’t. The assumption that costs people money Don’t assume “visa sponsorship” means every immigration-related expense is covered. Before accepting an offer, ask exactly what the employer will pay for and what remains yours. Stage 03

chunks.t: Cost of relocating to Australia or NZ
chunks.x: Prices vary significantly with the time of year, departure country, baggage requirements and how much flexibility you have over dates. And remember luggage: moving internationally on the standard airline allowance is difficult, particularly with children, so additional baggage or freight may need to be part of the budget. Ask how, not just whether If your employer offers a flight allowance, establish whether they book directly, reimburse afterwards, or provide a fixed contribution. That distinction matters enormously for cash flow before departure, a reimbursement you receive in month two doesn’t help you buy the tickets. Stage 04

chunks.t: Cost of relocating to Australia or NZ
chunks.x: The assumption that an international move requires a shipping container costs some families thousands they didn’t need to spend. Ship it

chunks.t: Cost of relocating to Australia or NZ
chunks.x: International shipping can be expensive and slow, and large items may be less practical in your eventual home than they were in your current one. But replacing the contents of a whole family home isn’t cheap either. Start again

chunks.t: Cost of relocating to Australia or NZ
chunks.x: Many families take personal belongings and a few important possessions, then buy furniture after arriving. Some clinicians move ahead of their family with a couple of suitcases and arrange everything later. Work out what suits you Some families ship almost everything and are glad they did. Others arrive with four suitcases and never miss the rest. Decide from your circumstances, not from what an international move is supposed to look like. Stage 05

chunks.t: Cost of relocating to Australia or NZ
chunks.x: This is the cost people underestimate most often. You may not be able, or want, to sign a long-term rental agreement before seeing a property. That can mean spending your first few weeks in a hotel, serviced apartment or short-term let, and the longer it takes to find a suitable home, the more expensive it becomes. Families with requirements around bedrooms, schools and location often take longer. Find out exactly how long If an employer provides temporary accommodation, establish precisely how many nights. Two weeks disappears very quickly when you’re starting a new job at the same time as house-hunting in a city you don’t know. Stage 06

chunks.t: Cost of relocating to Australia or NZ
chunks.x: Finding the property is only part of the expense. You need enough money available to move into it. Upfront rental requirements differ between Australia and New Zealand and are subject to local rules, but expect to need money available for a rental bond and rent around the start of the tenancy. Then comes everything the house needs at once: Bedding and towels Kitchen equipment, down to a kettle Cleaning products Internet and utilities connection And the dozens of small purchases that look trivial individually None of these are significant on their own. All of them arriving in the same fortnight is a different matter, and if you’re relocating with children, the list grows. Stage 07

chunks.t: Cost of relocating to Australia or NZ
chunks.h: You may need a car sooner than expected
chunks.x: Whether you need one depends heavily on where you live and work. In many locations, particularly with children, a car makes everyday life considerably easier. Potential costs include buying or financing the vehicle, registration, insurance, fuel, and converting or obtaining the appropriate driving licence. If both adults will be working in different locations, you may eventually need two. Decide this before the house, not after Transport and accommodation are one decision, not two. Choosing a home without working out how you’ll get to work is how a cheaper rent becomes an expensive year. Running alongside

chunks.t: Cost of relocating to Australia or NZ
chunks.h: Three costs that don’t sit in the sequence
chunks.x: These run underneath all seven stages, and they’re where a budget usually springs a leak. Your costs back home

chunks.t: Cost of relocating to Australia or NZ
chunks.h: They don’t stop when you land
chunks.x: You may still have a mortgage or rent, insurance, storage, loan repayments, professional memberships, the costs of selling or letting your property, and other existing commitments. If your family follows several months later, you may temporarily be funding households in two countries. That can be the most financially demanding way to relocate, even though for some families it’s the most practical. Map that overlap before committing to a start date. Your partner’s income

chunks.t: Cost of relocating to Australia or NZ
chunks.x: Particularly important for families who normally rely on two incomes. Your partner may need time to find work, may have their own registration requirements if they’re in a regulated profession, or you may decide one parent concentrates on settling the children first. Don’t build your first-year budget around both adults earning immediately. If the second income arrives quickly, excellent. If it doesn’t, you don’t want the whole move to become financially stressful. And if you’re moving with children Budget differently from an individual: school uniforms, stationery, devices, childcare, before- and after-school care, sports equipment and activities. Even where individual amounts are modest, they arrive together. The first few weeks of a relocation are often a period when money seems to leave the account constantly, that’s normal when you’re establishing an entire household, and it’s exactly why a buffer matters. The gap nobody budgets for

chunks.t: Cost of relocating to Australia or NZ
chunks.h: Your first salary may be further away than you think
chunks.x: Starting work doesn’t mean being paid. Depending on your employer’s payroll cycle and your start date, there can be a real gap before your first full salary reaches your account. It arrives at precisely the wrong moment. At the same time, you may be paying for temporary accommodation, a rental bond, furniture, transport and everyday living. One question, asked early “When will I receive my first payment?” It is a very simple question, almost nobody asks it, and the answer makes budgeting the first two months dramatically easier. The other side of the ledger

chunks.t: Cost of relocating to Australia or NZ
chunks.h: What will your employer pay for?
chunks.x: Depending on the employer, profession and how hard the vacancy has been to fill, support ranges from very little to substantial. What might be covered

chunks.t: Cost of relocating to Australia or NZ
chunks.x: Relocation support might include contributions towards flights, visa costs, professional registration, temporary accommodation, shipping, general relocation expenses or immigration assistance. Some employers offer a fixed relocation allowance. Others reimburse specified expenses up to a maximum. Some offer very little, and some particularly hard-to-fill positions come with a great deal. So don’t ask “is there relocation assistance?” Ask “what exactly does the relocation package cover?” Watch for repayment clauses

chunks.t: Cost of relocating to Australia or NZ
chunks.x: An employer may require you to repay some or all of the contribution if you leave within a specified period. That isn’t necessarily unreasonable, they’re investing significant money in your move. But you need to understand the terms before accepting. Read the contract carefully, ask what the period is, and ask what happens if you leave for reasons outside your control. Relocation support is also one of the most negotiable parts of an offer, sometimes more so than the salary itself. Our guide to negotiating an offer covers how to raise it. Your number, not somebody else’s

chunks.t: Cost of relocating to Australia or NZ
chunks.h: How much should you have saved?
chunks.x: A single clinician with flights and temporary accommodation covered may need relatively little upfront; a family shipping belongings may need many thousands more. So rather than borrowing an arbitrary number, build your own relocation fund in three parts. Part one

chunks.t: Cost of relocating to Australia or NZ
chunks.x: Registration, immigration, medicals and documentation, flights, and shipping if you’re shipping. Everything you pay while still at home. Part two

chunks.t: Cost of relocating to Australia or NZ
chunks.x: Temporary accommodation, rental bond and initial rent, transport, and furnishing and equipping the house. Part three

chunks.t: Cost of relocating to Australia or NZ
chunks.x: Enough accessible money to cover everyday life until your salary, and potentially your partner’s, is properly established. Then do the subtraction Take off anything the employer has confirmed in writing that they will cover. What’s left is a far more meaningful figure than anyone else’s relocation budget, and it’s specific enough to plan against. Build it with your own figures

chunks.t: Cost of relocating to Australia or NZ
chunks.h: The cost of moving calculator does this arithmetic for you
chunks.x: Answer a few questions about your profession, your household and where you are going. It applies the published registration and visa fees, works the bond and rent in advance out of the tenancy rules where you are moving, subtracts what your employer is contributing, and gives you a figure you can print. Every number editable Official fees sourced and dated Nothing personal asked Work out my moving budget → The last rule

chunks.t: Cost of relocating to Australia or NZ
chunks.x: If you possibly can, don’t spend every available dollar getting there. International moves don’t always go to plan. A property may take longer to find than you expected. A partner’s job may take longer to arrive. Your belongings may be delayed in transit. The car may need repairing. You may need to fly home unexpectedly. Money that remains untouched after the move makes every one of those situations considerably less stressful, and none of them less likely. Don’t let the total put you off Added together, this can sound daunting. But not everybody pays for everything themselves. Employers contribute. Families relocate in stages. Some people sell furniture rather than shipping it. Others arrive in furnished accommodation and take their time. The important thing is knowing the likely costs before you commit.

chunks.t: Cost of relocating to Australia or NZ
chunks.x: A well-planned move is a completely different experience from discovering that your first salary needs to cover a bond, furniture, a car and six weeks of living all at once. Sophie’s insight We see relocation as more than securing a job and obtaining a visa. The moment that worries me for people isn’t the flight. It’s week three, when the temporary accommodation is ending, the bond is due, the house is empty and the first pay day hasn’t arrived. Almost nobody plans for that fortnight, and it colours how the whole move feels. Ask the unglamorous questions early: what the employer will cover in writing, when you’ll be paid, and what you need in the bank before you get on the plane. Getting the job is only the beginning. Arriving with financial breathing room is what lets you start the new life well. Sophie Founder, Ethicare Resourcing Common questions

chunks.t: Cost of relocating to Australia or NZ
chunks.h: The questions we’re asked about relocation costs
chunks.x: Can you give me a single figure to save? no, and anyone who does is guessing. A single clinician whose employer covers flights and temporary accommodation needs a fraction of what a family of five shipping belongings and furnishing a house needs. Build the three-part fund above, subtract what your employer has confirmed in writing, and you’ll have a number that means something. Does “visa sponsorship” mean my immigration costs are paid? Not necessarily. Sponsorship refers to the employer’s role in the visa process, not automatically to who pays for what. Medicals, police certificates, document certification and advice may all still be yours. Ask for the split explicitly, before you accept. Should I ship my furniture? There’s no universal answer.

chunks.t: Cost of relocating to Australia or NZ
chunks.h: The questions we’re asked about relocation costs
chunks.x: Shipping is slow and can be expensive, and large items sometimes suit your new home less well than your current one, but replacing a whole household isn’t cheap either. Many families take personal belongings and buy furniture after arriving. Price both properly rather than assuming a container is required. How long should I expect to be in temporary accommodation? Longer than you hope, particularly with children and school considerations. It’s the most commonly underestimated cost of the whole move. If an employer is providing it, get the exact number of nights in writing and budget for the possibility of needing more. What if I have to repay relocation assistance? Repayment clauses are common and not unreasonable. The employer is investing real money.

chunks.t: Cost of relocating to Australia or NZ
chunks.h: The questions we’re asked about relocation costs
chunks.x: What matters is understanding the terms before you sign: how long the period is, whether it reduces over time, and what happens if you leave for reasons outside your control. Ask, and get it in writing. Is relocation support negotiable? Often yes, and sometimes more readily than the salary. Particularly where pay sits on a fixed scale. For a family moving halfway around the world, meaningful relocation support can be worth more in year one than a modest increase to base pay. Our offer guide covers how to raise it well. chunks.t: Driving in New Zealand
chunks.x: New Zealanders drive on the left, and outside the main cities most people need a car. Three questions decide your first months: can you drive when you arrive, how you convert your licence, and how to buy a reliable car. Kettle on. About 5 min

chunks.t: Driving in New Zealand
chunks.h: 01 · Can I drive when I arrive?
chunks.x: Yes, on your valid overseas licence, for a limited time that depends on when you last arrived in New Zealand: Arriving before 1 November 2026 You can drive on your overseas car licence for up to 18 months from that arrival. Arriving on or after 1 November 2026 The limit is 12 months from that arrival. This applies to car licences; overseas motorcycle and truck licences are limited to 12 months whenever you arrived. Your licence must be current and in English, or carried with an approved English translation or an international driving permit. The permit is a translation, not a licence: it only works alongside your overseas licence. Carry your licence whenever you drive. If you leave and come back, the clock does not restart; it runs from your last arrival as a new resident. Confirm the current rule on the NZ Transport Agency’s page for new residents .

chunks.t: Driving in New Zealand
chunks.x: Before your time runs out, convert to a New Zealand licence. How much testing that involves depends on where your licence is from. Exempt countries Includes the United Kingdom, Ireland, South Africa, Australia, Canada, the United States and most of Western Europe. If you have held a full licence from one of these for two years or more, you can usually convert without a theory or practical test. Less than two years: a practical test. Non-exempt countries Includes the Philippines, India and many others. You sit the theory test and then a practical test, and may hold a learner licence with conditions in between. Book early; practical test slots can be scarce. To apply, take the conversion form, your overseas licence, your passport, proof of your New Zealand address and, if your licence is not in English, an approved translation to a driver-licensing agent such as the AA. You will have an eyesight check on the spot. The NZ Transport Agency’s conversion page has the current list of exempt countries, forms and fees.

chunks.t: Driving in New Zealand
chunks.x: What catches new arrivals Drive on the left. Roundabouts run clockwise and you give way to the right. Roads are often narrow, winding and unlit, with one lane each way. Journey times are longer than the distance suggests, so trust the map’s time, not the kilometres. The open-road limit is 100 km/h, and lower limits are enforced. Speed cameras are common. Drink-driving limits are low and strictly enforced. Plan ahead on nights out. One-lane bridges are common in rural areas; the signs show who gives way. Winter brings ice, fog and snow on inland and South Island roads. Carry chains where the signs say so. Read the Road Code . If you are converting from a non-exempt country, the theory test is based on it.

chunks.t: Driving in New Zealand
chunks.x: Most people buy second-hand. Trade Me Motors and dealers’ yards are where most cars are listed; Japanese imports are everywhere and parts are cheap. Three pieces of paper matter: WoF The warrant of fitness is a regular safety inspection: tyres, brakes, lights, rust. It must be current to drive, and a car being sold needs one issued within the last month. It is not a mechanical health check. Rego Vehicle licensing, paid to the NZ Transport Agency for 3, 6 or 12 months. The label is on the windscreen. Check it is current before you buy. Diesel cars also pay Road User Charges, bought in advance by the kilometre, so a cheap diesel costs more to run than it looks. Pre-purchase inspection A mechanic’s check of the engine, gearbox and body before you pay. The AA and independent garages offer them. Worth it on anything you cannot afford to be wrong about.

chunks.t: Driving in New Zealand
chunks.x: Insurance Not compulsory in New Zealand, but a crash without it is yours to pay for. Third-party cover is the minimum; most people take comprehensive. Compare a few quotes. Before you buy a car Check the WoF and rego are current, and ask when the WoF was last issued. Pay for a pre-purchase inspection on anything you are serious about. Check for money owing on the car. If there is finance against it, the lender can repossess it from you. When you buy, you must tell the NZ Transport Agency you are the new owner (the seller does the same). You can do it online or at an agent. Arrange insurance before you drive it away. Trade Me and the AA are commercial organisations. We don’t endorse them; they are simply where most people look and where many conversions are done.

chunks.t: Driving in New Zealand
chunks.x: Shift work shapes the commute. Early starts and late finishes mean driving in the dark, often on rural roads, and sometimes between sites. A few things to settle before your first week: Do the drive to the hospital once in daylight before you do it at 6am. Ask your department about staff parking: where it is, what it costs and whether night-shift parking is close to the entrance. Check your route for winter. Some inland roads ice over; your colleagues will know which ones. In Auckland, Wellington and Christchurch, buses and trains can cover a day-shift commute. For nights and weekends, a car is usually the only option. If you are not driving yet, a bike or e-bike covers a lot of regional towns, and a colleague on the same roster will often share lifts.

chunks.t: Living & thriving in Australia
chunks.h: Finding your feet in a new system
chunks.x: Australian teams are used to welcoming international clinicians and describe a runway rather than a cold plunge. Expect a proper induction, supportive colleagues and, where relevant, a period of orientation or supervision as you find your rhythm. The culture tends to be collaborative and relatively flat: first names, open communication, multidisciplinary teamwork, and many clinicians say care feels a touch less rushed than they were used to. Within a few months, the unfamiliar becomes ordinary. One national registration means your career isn’t fixed to one place: as you settle, you can develop, specialise or move between states without starting your paperwork over. You won’t arrive to strangers

chunks.t: Living & thriving in Australia
chunks.x: The families who thrive build connection early, and Australia, one of the most multicultural countries on earth, makes that easier than most. Your community

chunks.t: Living & thriving in Australia
chunks.x: Whatever your background, there’s likely an established community from home: cultural associations, events and networks that make the first months feel familiar. Faith

chunks.t: Living & thriving in Australia
chunks.x: Churches, mosques, temples, gurdwaras and faith communities of every kind are part of the fabric of Australian cities and towns. Through the kids

chunks.t: Living & thriving in Australia
chunks.x: Children’s schools and weekend sport are, for many parents, where friendships form fastest, for the whole family. The reason many came

chunks.t: Living & thriving in Australia
chunks.x: Beaches, parks, bush and sport are woven into normal life. An early swim, a weekend hike, a barbecue in the park, the climate makes the outdoors a default, not an effort.

chunks.t: Living & thriving in Australia
chunks.x: Outside the biggest-city centres, space and shorter commutes give time back. For many, that reclaimed time is the single biggest change.

chunks.t: Living & thriving in Australia
chunks.x: Families consistently say it’s a wonderful place to raise children: safe, active and outdoors, with strong schools and a gentler pace. Making it last

chunks.t: Living & thriving in Australia
chunks.h: From a long stay to a home
chunks.x: The distance from family is the hard part, and most people plan trips home and regular calls to manage it. But belonging tends to creep up quietly: a local you’re a regular at, neighbours who know your name, a team that feels like yours, children who sound like locals. Give it a year, keep saying yes to invitations, and the place stops being somewhere you moved to and starts being home. What we do after you land

chunks.t: Living & thriving in Australia
chunks.h: You’ll hear from us when it’s hardest
chunks.x: Almost everyone hits a wobbly stretch around the third month, and our support is timed for it. 1

chunks.t: Living & thriving in Australia
chunks.x: We know your arrival date, and you have a mobile number that a person answers. Not a duty line or a ticket, the same people you’ve dealt with all along, who know your name and your situation. 2

chunks.t: Living & thriving in Australia
chunks.x: We call once the adrenaline wears off, when the admin arrives all at once: tax file number, bank account, Medicare, school enrolment. We’ll also introduce you to a family who made the same move to your area, if you’d like that. 3

chunks.t: Living & thriving in Australia
chunks.x: A deliberate check-in, timed for the dip, because we know it’s coming. It’s the call people are most surprised to get and most glad of. Not a satisfaction survey, just a clear conversation about how it’s going. 4

chunks.t: Living & thriving in Australia
chunks.h: A year on, and after that
chunks.x: There’s no end date on it. A contract question, a move interstate, work for your partner, a reference years later. Call us. We measure this work by how you’re living a year on, not by the placement. The settling in is yours to do. What we promise is that you’ll always know who to call, and they’ll already know your story. Sophie’s insight We measure a good move in years, not weeks, which is why we don’t disappear once you’ve landed. The clinicians we placed are the ones we check in on, introduce to others, and help when the next decision comes around. Settling takes a season or two; thriving takes saying yes to the place. If you keep us posted, we’ll keep helping. That’s rather the point of doing this properly. Sophie CEO & Founder, Ethicare Resourcing Common questions

chunks.t: Living & thriving in Australia
chunks.h: The things people ask us first
chunks.x: How long until it feels like home? For most people, the practical side settles within weeks and the emotional side within a year. The turning point is usually social: once you have a few real friendships and a routine that’s yours, it stops feeling like a move and starts feeling like life. Will I keep progressing in my career? Yes. Australia’s health system is large and modern, with room to develop, specialise and take on senior or lead roles. National registration means you can also change setting or state as your goals evolve. How do people manage the distance from home? Planned trips back, regular video calls, and leaning on the community here. It’s the hardest part for close families, and naming it rather than pretending it’s nothing, is how most people make peace with it. Can I move to a different state later? Generally yes. Your national registration travels with you; you’d just sort housing, schools and any state radiation licence for the new location. Many clinicians move once or twice as they find the pace and place that suits them. That’s the journey

chunks.t: Living & thriving | New Zealand
chunks.h: Settling in is a season, not a switch you flip
chunks.x: Most of what people mean by “the lifestyle” is this ordinary: a walk after work, twenty minutes from home. Nobody feels completely at home on day one, and nobody should expect to. Belonging is built slowly, out of small ordinary things: a regular coffee spot, a colleague who becomes a friend, the first weekend that feels like fun rather than admin. This step is about giving that process room, and knowing what helps it along. The truth we share with everyone: the first few months are a mix of wonderful and wobbly, and that’s completely normal. The families who thrive aren’t the ones who never find it hard, they’re the ones who expected the dip, and kept going. Why people choose New Zealand

chunks.x: Verified and dated. A national ranking describes the country, not any one family, workplace or week. 2 nd Most peaceful country in the world — and first in the Asia–Pacific Global Peace Index 2026 1 st Life–work balance, three years running Global Life-Work Balance Index 2025, Remote 11 th World happiness — the highest-ranked English-speaking country World Happiness Report 2026 Above average 15-year-olds in maths, reading and science OECD PISA 2022 Life in Aotearoa New Zealand

chunks.t: Living & thriving | New Zealand
chunks.h: More than a job, a life
chunks.x: Monday Hospital Saturday Coast Sunday Trails Evening Family BBQ The role is why you come. The life is why you stay. What to expect

chunks.t: Living & thriving | New Zealand
chunks.x: Most people move through a recognisable emotional arc in their first year, including a middle stretch when the novelty fades before the belonging arrives. First weeks

chunks.t: Living & thriving | New Zealand
chunks.x: excited & busy Everything is new and a little thrilling, the scenery, the accents, the supermarket. You’re busy setting up a life, and the adrenaline carries you. Enjoy it, take the photos, and don’t worry that it won’t always feel this heightened. First months

chunks.t: Living & thriving | New Zealand
chunks.x: wobbly & homesick This is the part nobody warns you about. Once the novelty fades, the distance from home, the small frustrations and the effort of starting over can catch up with you. It’s not a sign you made a mistake, it’s a normal, well-documented stage. Naming it takes away most of its power. Around 6 months

chunks.t: Living & thriving | New Zealand
chunks.x: settling Routines form. You have a GP, a favourite beach, people you’d call on a bad day. Work feels familiar, the children have friends, and the place stops feeling like somewhere you’re visiting. The wobble eases almost without you noticing. The first year

chunks.t: Living & thriving | New Zealand
chunks.x: belonging One day you realise you’ve stopped converting prices, you know the back roads, and you’re the one welcoming the next new arrival. It rarely happens in a moment, but somewhere in the first year, New Zealand quietly becomes home. What we do after you land

chunks.t: Living & thriving | New Zealand
chunks.h: You’ll hear from us when it’s hardest
chunks.x: Our support is timed for that arc, because the months after you arrive decide whether the move lasts. 1

chunks.t: Living & thriving | New Zealand
chunks.x: We know your arrival date, and you have a mobile number that a person answers. Not a duty line or a ticket, the same people you’ve dealt with all along, who know your name and your situation. 2

chunks.t: Living & thriving | New Zealand
chunks.x: We call once the adrenaline wears off, when the admin arrives all at once: IRD number, bank account, GP enrolment, school forms. We’ll also introduce you to a family who made the same move to your region, if you’d like that. 3

chunks.t: Living & thriving | New Zealand
chunks.x: A deliberate check-in, timed for the dip, because we know it’s coming. It’s the call people are most surprised to get and most glad of. Not a satisfaction survey, just a clear conversation about how it’s going. 4

chunks.t: Living & thriving | New Zealand
chunks.h: A year on, and after that
chunks.x: There’s no end date on it. A contract question, a move to another region, work for your partner, a reference years later. Call us. We measure this work by how you’re living a year on, not by the placement. What this isn’t: we’re a small team, not a concierge service. We won’t organise your weekends or pretend to be your friendship circle, and the settling-in itself is still yours to do. What we do promise is that you’ll always know who to call, and they’ll already know your story. The whole picture

chunks.t: Living & thriving | New Zealand
chunks.h: Home is a long way away
chunks.x: Flights to the UK, South Africa or the Gulf take the best part of a day and are a real annual cost. Most people plan one trip home every year or two and budget for it deliberately. Video calls across a twelve-hour time difference take some working out, and the first Christmas away is usually the hardest one. Housing

chunks.t: Living & thriving | New Zealand
chunks.h: Quality varies as much as price
chunks.x: Auckland and Wellington are expensive to buy in and competitive to rent in, while many regions are markedly cheaper. Less expected is the housing stock itself: a good deal of it is older and less insulated than new arrivals assume, so winter indoors can feel colder than the climate suggests. Ask about insulation, heating and whether a home meets the Healthy Homes standards. Renting in New Zealand covers what to look for. Scale

chunks.t: Living & thriving | New Zealand
chunks.h: A smaller country means smaller services
chunks.x: Highly complex and subspecialty work is concentrated in the main centres, so if your practice depends on high volumes of rare cases you may see fewer of them than in a large tertiary centre abroad. Many clinicians find the trade-off worthwhile: broader scope, more autonomy and more continuity. Some find the narrower case mix a loss. Be clear with yourself about which you are. Pay

chunks.t: Living & thriving | New Zealand
chunks.x: Salaries generally sit below Australia and well below the Gulf. They are also set by national collective agreements, which means the rate is the same in Invercargill as in Auckland, and progression is transparent rather than negotiated. Set against the cost and pace of life it works out differently for different people. Pay agreements sets out the mechanism, and your profession guide gives indicative bands. Timing

chunks.t: Living & thriving | New Zealand
chunks.x: Between assessing your qualification, verifying documents, English evidence where it applies and the regulator’s own queue, think in months. Nothing about it is unusually difficult, but it rewards starting early and gathering paperwork before you think you need it. Registration has the sequence for your profession. Work culture

chunks.t: Living & thriving | New Zealand
chunks.x: Practice here tends to be collaborative and less hierarchical than many systems, and most people find leave gets taken. It is not universal, and healthcare is healthcare: there are pressured departments, short-staffed weeks and shifts that overrun. What people report is a different default, not a different profession. What helps

chunks.t: Living & thriving | New Zealand
chunks.x: Find your everyday anchors fast, a café, a gym, a running route, a Saturday market. Ordinary routines are what make a new place feel like yours, and they’re the quickest antidote to the unsettled early weeks. People

chunks.t: Living & thriving | New Zealand
chunks.x: Kiwi friendliness is real, but friendships still take effort on both sides. Accept the after-work drink, the school-gate chat, the neighbour’s BBQ. The people who connect quickly are the ones who say yes more often. Outdoors

chunks.t: Living & thriving | New Zealand
chunks.x: Nothing roots you here faster than the land. Walk the local track, learn to fish, take up a water sport, explore your region on weekends. The outdoors is where New Zealand life happens, and where friendships are made. When everyone settles

chunks.t: Living & thriving | New Zealand
chunks.h: The career matters. The life around it does too.
chunks.x: Up the mountain in the gondola, a winter weekend for one of the families we placed in the Manawatū. Often it’s a partner or a teenager who finds it hardest, and who needs the most room to find their own footing.

chunks.t: Living & thriving | New Zealand
chunks.x: The trailing partner often has the hardest adjustment, no ready-made colleagues, a career to rebuild. Their settling matters enormously, so protect time for them to find work, purpose and friends of their own. Don’t underestimate how much it shapes the whole family’s happiness.

chunks.t: Living & thriving | New Zealand
chunks.x: Younger children usually adapt within weeks; teenagers may grieve the friends and life they left and need longer. Keep talking, stay patient through the ups and downs, and lean on schools, they’re well used to helping new arrivals find their place.

chunks.t: Living & thriving | New Zealand
chunks.x: Big moves test relationships as well as strengthen them. Be kind to each other through the wobbly months, share the load of settling, and make time for the things you enjoy together, not just the endless to-do list of a new life. You won’t be on your own

chunks.t: Living & thriving | New Zealand
chunks.x: Belonging often comes through the communities that already feel familiar: your faith, your culture, your people, even the foods of home. Your community

chunks.t: Living & thriving | New Zealand
chunks.x: South African, Filipino, Indian, British and many other communities are well established across New Zealand. Connecting with families who’ve made the same move means a ready-made circle who understand exactly what you’re going through. Finding your community Faith & worship

chunks.t: Living & thriving | New Zealand
chunks.x: Churches, mosques, temples and faith communities are part of life here, and often among the warmest welcomes a newcomer receives. Wherever you settle, there’s likely a community of your faith close by. Faith & community A taste of home

chunks.t: Living & thriving | New Zealand
chunks.x: From biltong and spices to your favourite groceries, the small tastes of home matter more than you’d expect. We can point you to where to find them, and the cafés and shops that become familiar comforts. Useful contacts Groups & networks

chunks.t: Living & thriving | New Zealand
chunks.x: Local Facebook groups, parents’ networks and profession circles are where the small questions get quick, kind answers, from the best dentist to where to buy a good heat pump. They’re a quiet lifeline in the early months. Groups & networks Tell us where you’re moving from and what matters to your family, and we’ll connect you with the partners, communities and contacts we trust. Few things make us happier than helping a family find their place. Worth knowing

chunks.t: Living & thriving | New Zealand
chunks.x: Missing home doesn’t mean you chose wrong. It means you loved what you left. Let yourself feel it, talk about it, and trust that it softens as your new life fills in around you. 2

chunks.t: Living & thriving | New Zealand
chunks.x: Regular calls home are a comfort, but living entirely online keeps one foot in the old life. Plan your trips back, then give yourself permission to be fully here in between. 3

chunks.t: Living & thriving | New Zealand
chunks.h: Give it a full year before judging
chunks.x: The first year has seasons, literally and emotionally. Try not to make any big "was this a mistake?" decisions in the dip. Almost everyone who pushes through comes out the other side glad they did. 4

chunks.t: Living & thriving | New Zealand
chunks.x: Whether it’s a GP, a community group, a colleague or us, you don’t have to white-knuckle the hard days alone. Reaching out early is what settled, thriving people do, not a sign of struggling. Sophie’s insight I tell everyone the same thing before they fly: there will be a Tuesday, a few months in, when you wonder what on earth you’ve done. It passes. For my own family, home crept up quietly, one day I was giving a newcomer directions without thinking, and I realised I’d stopped feeling like a visitor. Be patient with the dip, say yes to the invitations, and let the small routines do their work. Thriving here isn’t a moment you arrive at. It’s a life you build, one ordinary good day at a time. Sophie CEO & Founder, Ethicare Resourcing Common questions

chunks.t: Living & thriving | New Zealand
chunks.h: The things people ask us first
chunks.x: How long does it take to feel settled? For most people, somewhere around six months things start to click, and by the end of the first year New Zealand feels like home. Everyone’s different, some settle faster, some need longer, but if you’re still finding it hard at three or four months, that’s completely normal and not a sign anything’s wrong. The dip is part of the process, not the end of it. What if I get homesick? You almost certainly will at some point, and that’s healthy rather than a problem. Stay in touch with home, plan a trip back to look forward to, but also pour energy into building your life here: routines, friendships, getting outdoors. Homesickness fades fastest when your new life has enough in it to hold your attention. And if it weighs heavily, talk to someone; you don’t have to carry it quietly. How do I make friends as an adult? Through repetition and showing up.

chunks.t: Living & thriving | New Zealand
chunks.h: The things people ask us first
chunks.x: Say yes to work invitations, join something you’d enjoy anyway, a club, a class, a sport, and be the one who suggests the coffee. School gates, neighbours and other migrant families are natural starting points. It can feel slow at first, but Kiwis are welcoming, and a few months of saying yes usually leaves you with a real circle. My partner is struggling more than me. Is that normal? Very. The person with the job arrives to a ready-made structure and colleagues, while a trailing partner often has to build everything from scratch. It’s one of the most common strains on a move, and the answer is to take it seriously: protect time and support for them to find work, purpose and people of their own. Their settling is every bit as important as yours. Can I still lean on Ethicare once I’ve arrived? Always. Our relationship doesn’t end when you start your job.

chunks.t: Living & thriving | New Zealand
chunks.h: The things people ask us first
chunks.x: That’s rather the point of how we work. Whether you need an introduction to a community, a steer on something practical, or just a familiar voice on a wobbly week, we’re here. We measure our success by how well you’re living a year on, not by the placement itself. The end of the journey, and the start of a life

chunks.t: Money, tax and banking in New Zealand
chunks.x: A handful of early tasks will get your finances running smoothly. Most can be started before you arrive and completed in your first few weeks. Kettle on. A longer read — about 4 min Bank account Receive your salary and pay bills locally — start before arrival where possible IRD number Your tax identifier — needed to be paid correctly. Apply as soon as you arrive KiwiSaver Voluntary retirement savings, with employer contributions, auto-enrolled when you start work ACC No-fault accident cover for everyone in NZ — funded automatically via levies

chunks.t: Money, tax and banking in New Zealand
chunks.x: The major banks are ANZ, ASB, BNZ, Kiwibank and Westpac. You can usually start the process online before you arrive and activate the account in person once here. You’ll typically need your passport, work or resident visa, and proof of a New Zealand address. Ask for online banking and a debit card at the same time.

chunks.t: Money, tax and banking in New Zealand
chunks.x: Every worker needs an IRD number from Inland Revenue. Apply online once you have a NZ address and bank account; processing usually takes around 7–10 working days. Give the number to your payroll team as soon as it arrives so the correct PAYE tax code is applied. Wages are commonly paid fortnightly into your NZ account.

chunks.t: Money, tax and banking in New Zealand
chunks.x: KiwiSaver is a government-supported retirement scheme. On a work visa you can usually opt in or out; contributions are a set percentage of your pay (commonly 3%, 4%, 6%, 8% or 10%), with employers contributing at least 3%. Funds can be withdrawn if you permanently leave New Zealand. Sending money overseas: banks can transfer internationally, but specialist services such as Wise or OFX are often cheaper and faster. Always compare the exchange rate and fees before moving larger amounts. Do this first Apply for your IRD number as soon as you arrive — almost everything else in your financial setup depends on it.

chunks.t: Money, tax and banking in New Zealand
chunks.x: Income tax is deducted automatically through PAYE, so for most people there’s nothing to file. You’re taxed on income from New Zealand and overseas once you’re a tax resident — Inland Revenue (IRD) has clear calculators if you want to check where you’ll sit. ACC — the Accident Compensation Corporation — gives everyone in New Zealand no-fault cover for injuries, whether they happen at work, at home or on the ski field. It’s funded through levies and government, and applies to residents and visitors alike. Worth sorting early Insurance — ACC covers injury, but not illness or your belongings. Many newcomers take out health, contents and life cover; Immigration New Zealand publishes a migrants’ guide to what’s worth considering. KiwiSaver — you become eligible once you’re a resident, and it’s one of the simplest ways to build long-term savings.

chunks.t: Money, tax and banking in New Zealand
chunks.h: Work for a partner or family member
chunks.x: If a partner is job-hunting, New Zealand has a healthy market and a few trusted places to start. Healthcare Kiwi Health Jobs ↗ The national site for health and care vacancies across Aotearoa. All industries Seek ↗ The largest general job board in New Zealand. All industries Trade Me Jobs ↗ Broad listings across most sectors and regions. Government Work and Income ↗ Job listings plus advice and support for new arrivals. chunks.x: Safe communities, strong schools and easy access to parks, sport and the outdoors are, again and again, the reasons families decide to stay. Childhood here tends to involve a lot of being outside. Career

chunks.t: Is Australia right for me & my family?
chunks.h: The things people ask us first
chunks.x: Will my partner be able to work? In many cases, yes. Partners on skilled and many employer-sponsored visas are often eligible to work, frequently with open work rights. The bigger question is usually about their world rather than their visa, finding their own purpose and people. Home Affairs sets out each partner’s work rights in full. Will my children settle? Most do, and often faster than their parents. Australian schools are generally welcoming to new arrivals, and a childhood here involves a lot of outdoor time and sport, which helps children find their feet. Younger children tend to settle within weeks; teenagers usually need more time and more involvement in the decision. Is it expensive to live there? Australia isn’t cheap, and housing in Sydney and Melbourne is the part that surprises people most.

chunks.t: Is Australia right for me & my family?
chunks.h: The things people ask us first
chunks.x: That said, pay is fair and many families find the trade (more sun, space and time for a different kind of life) is exactly what they were after. We’d always encourage planning around real numbers, which the cost-of-living and destination guides will help with. How far is it really from home? Far. There’s no softening that. Long-haul flights and the cost of them are the main downside for close families. Many people manage it well with planned trips home and regular calls, but it’s worth being clear-eyed about before you decide, rather than discovering it afterwards. Do I need to decide now? Not at all. This first step is about exploring. Plenty of people sit with it for months, talk it over as a family, and only then start looking at the practical side. When you’re ready, the next steps are clear, and you won’t be working through them alone. Next · Stage 03
