chunks.t: Moving with children and teenagers
chunks.x: New Zealand Australia A reality check Moving with children and teenagers What childhood can look like here, and what you would be leaving More room. More outdoors. Shorter distances. A childhood that can feel a little less hurried — and, at the same time, further from the people who know them best. Both sides of it → Ask Ethicare 11 sections Reviewed September 2026 Free Answer first

chunks.t: Moving with children and teenagers
chunks.h: More room. More outdoors. Shorter distances.
chunks.x: A childhood that can feel a little less hurried, and a week where finishing work still leaves some day in it. Away from

chunks.t: Moving with children and teenagers
chunks.h: The people who know them best
chunks.x: A new school, new friendships, and a completely new sense of home — built from scratch, at whatever age they are when you go. That trade is the question most parents are really asking, and it is not one a salary comparison can answer. Two things decide how well it goes more than the country does: where each child sits in their qualification years , and whether they had any real part in the decision . The practical detail on schooling — enrolment zones, year levels, fees on a visa — lives in the country guides: education in New Zealand and education in Australia . This page is about deciding, not about enrolling. Section 01 · What a week can look like

chunks.t: Moving with children and teenagers
chunks.h: Children’s lives can spill outside more
chunks.x: After school might mean kicking a ball around, swimming, heading to the beach, riding bikes or being in someone’s garden — rather than every activity feeling like a planned expedition. Weekends can feel less dominated by shopping and indoor entertainment, and more by “shall we go somewhere?” The distinction parents describe is not that there is more to do, but that less of it needs organising in advance. Unpolished

chunks.t: Moving with children and teenagers
chunks.h: Muddy, barefoot, outside in imperfect weather
chunks.x: School camps, swimming, sport, bare feet in summer. There is something practical about childhood here, and less pressure to make it look curated. Club sport

chunks.t: Moving with children and teenagers
chunks.h: Saturday morning is the social structure
chunks.x: Rugby, football, netball, cricket, athletics, surf lifesaving and nippers all run at junior level through local clubs. It is where a good deal of the settling happens — for parents on the sideline as much as for children. Water

chunks.t: Moving with children and teenagers
chunks.h: Swimming is treated as a life skill
chunks.x: With this much coastline, learning to swim is closer to a requirement than a hobby, and holiday programmes lean heavily on the water — kayaking, sailing, surf skills. Section 02 · The part that changes most

chunks.t: Moving with children and teenagers
chunks.h: Space and time, and the geography of an ordinary day
chunks.x: In many places, the geography of everyday life becomes much simpler. Home, school, the hospital, the sports club and the supermarket can all sit within a relatively small radius. You might finish work and still have some day left. It is not everywhere. Auckland traffic is not idyllic, and neither is a long Sydney or Melbourne commute. But in Palmerston North, Christchurch, parts of Wellington, or the regions in either country, the distances are shorter — and that changes family life in ways a pay figure cannot describe. Worth checking against a specific address This is the one claim on the page you can verify before you commit to anything. Take a real suburb in the town you are considering, and measure the actual distances: to the hospital, to two schools, to a supermarket, to the nearest beach or park. A ten-minute commute is a different life from a fifty-minute one, whichever country it is in. The destination guides set out what each place is like at that level of detail. Section 03 · The calendar inverts

chunks.t: Moving with children and teenagers
chunks.h: Summer falls at Christmas, and the year has a different shape
chunks.x: School finishes, Christmas arrives, and families head into the long summer break — all in the same fortnight. Christmas can mean barbecues, beaches, camping and children outside until late, rather than darkness at four in the afternoon. The school year then runs from late January or early February through to December, which is also why a family arriving from a September-start system often lands mid-year. Parents who grew up with a northern Christmas describe this as the change that took longest to stop feeling strange, and the one their children adapted to immediately. Section 04 · Two different offers

chunks.t: Moving with children and teenagers
chunks.h: Australia has a different feel again
chunks.x: If New Zealand can feel smaller, greener and a little gentler, Australia can feel bigger, brighter and more energetic. New Zealand

chunks.t: Moving with children and teenagers
chunks.x: Small communities, nature at the doorstep, and a slightly slower rhythm. Bare feet, school camps, and weather you go out in anyway. Australia

chunks.t: Moving with children and teenagers
chunks.x: Houses opening onto outdoor areas, children in and out of the water, school sport, eating outside, and Christmas Day in the heat. In places such as Perth, Brisbane, the Gold Coast and the coastal regional cities, outdoor life can be woven into the ordinary week rather than saved for holidays. Pools, beaches, parks, barbecues, sports grounds and eating outside are simply part of the environment, and the sporting culture is strong. Parents describe the rhythm as: school, home, swimmers on, down to the beach or the pool. Weekends might be junior sport in the morning, breakfast somewhere afterwards, then friends, beach or a barbecue. Not only a stereotype, and not a screen-free utopia either The Australian Institute of Family Studies describes parks, beaches and other natural spaces as important settings for children’s outdoor and nature play.

chunks.t: Moving with children and teenagers
chunks.x: The same body also cautions that Australian children are spending increasing amounts of time indoors and on devices. Both things are true at once, which is why we would not write “move to Australia and get your children off their iPads.” Primary source: Australian Institute of Family Studies (aifs.gov.au). Reviewed September 2026.

chunks.t: Moving with children and teenagers
chunks.h: Australia gives you far more choice of what kind of family life you want
chunks.x: Melbourne can feel sophisticated and metropolitan. Brisbane is subtropical and increasingly big-city. Perth offers city infrastructure alongside an enormous coastline. Adelaide can feel manageable and family-oriented. Then there are regional coastal places where life becomes considerably smaller and slower. Bundaberg is a completely different proposition from Melbourne. Moving a child to Bundaberg is not selling them “Australia” — it is a regional Queensland childhood. Which is why it is worth deciding on a place rather than a country. The Australian destination guides are written at that level.

chunks.t: Moving with children and teenagers
chunks.x: The heat can be intense , and sun protection becomes part of daily life rather than a holiday habit. Distances are enormous. Depending on where you live, a car is essential rather than optional. Housing in some major cities is very expensive , and it is the item most likely to change which suburb, or which city, works for you. What could childhood look like here? Not a permanent holiday. School runs still happen, parents still work late, and children still want their screens. What changes is that family life has the opportunity to move outside — into the garden, the pool, the park, the sports club and, for many families, the beach. The biggest change may not be what your children do. It may be where they do it. Section 05 · The practical constraint

chunks.t: Moving with children and teenagers
chunks.x: Qualification systems do not line up between countries, and mid-course transfers are where families most often say they wish they had known earlier. New Zealand

chunks.t: Moving with children and teenagers
chunks.h: NCEA, awarded across the senior years
chunks.x: Senior secondary students work towards the National Certificate of Educational Achievement, gathered through internal and external assessment across the final school years rather than in one terminal exam series. Some schools also offer Cambridge International or the International Baccalaureate. Because credits accumulate, the timing of a move within a senior year matters. Schools can advise on what transfers and what has to be repeated. Primary source: NZQA (nzqa.govt.nz). Reviewed September 2026. Australia

chunks.t: Moving with children and teenagers
chunks.h: A senior certificate set by each state
chunks.x: The senior secondary certificate is a state matter — the HSC in New South Wales, the VCE in Victoria, the QCE in Queensland, and their equivalents elsewhere — each with its own subject rules and assessment pattern, feeding a nationally comparable university rank. Moving between Australian states mid-certificate is its own question, not only moving into Australia from abroad. If you have a choice of state, and a child in their final two years, that is worth factoring in. Primary source: each state curriculum authority, and the Australian Curriculum (australiancurriculum.edu.au). Reviewed September 2026. The pattern we see Families who move before the senior qualification years, or after them, describe far fewer academic problems than families who move partway through. Where the timing cannot be chosen, the schools themselves are the ones to ask — before you accept a role, not after.

chunks.t: Moving with children and teenagers
chunks.h: A senior certificate set by each state
chunks.x: Ask what your child’s current course maps onto, what is credited, and what would need repeating. Two schools in the same city can answer differently. We are not qualified to advise on curriculum equivalence, and neither is any recruiter who tells you otherwise. What we can do is help you ask the right question of the right school early enough for the answer to change your plan. Section 06 · What changes at this age

chunks.t: Moving with children and teenagers
chunks.h: Why this age is different from moving a seven-year-old
chunks.x: A younger child’s world is largely the one you provide. By thirteen or fourteen, a good deal of it is theirs. Friendships are the structure, not an accessory. Younger children make friends through proximity; teenagers have chosen theirs, often over years, and rebuilding that takes a term or two rather than a fortnight. Qualifications are already in progress. A move mid-course has consequences a primary-school move simply does not have — the section above is about exactly that. Sport, music and clubs are commitments with a history. A place in a squad or an orchestra took time to earn, and it does not transfer. Identity is under construction. Being the new person with an accent lands differently at fifteen than at eight. They can see the trade-off you are making. Younger children take a move on trust; teenagers form a view about whether it is fair, and they will tell you.

chunks.t: Moving with children and teenagers
chunks.h: Why this age is different from moving a seven-year-old
chunks.x: None of that makes it a bad idea. It means the move is a negotiation with another person rather than a piece of logistics — and the outdoor, sporty week described earlier is often what a teenager gains in exchange for what they give up. Section 07

chunks.t: Moving with children and teenagers
chunks.x: The move was announced rather than discussed. The most common regret we hear, and the one with the longest tail. The timing was set by the job alone. A start date that suits an employer can land in the middle of a qualification year. Term dates were not checked. The southern-hemisphere school year starts in late January or early February. Arriving mid-year means joining classes already underway. The house was chosen before the school. In New Zealand, enrolment zones mean the school your child can attend is often decided by where you sign a tenancy. Nobody planned for the friendships left behind. Time zones make staying in touch harder than families expect; the UK is eleven to thirteen hours behind New Zealand depending on the season. One parent wanted it much more than the rest of the household. Teenagers notice, and it shapes how they read every difficulty that follows. The families who found it manageable were surprised by very little of it. Section 08 · What we hear works

chunks.t: Moving with children and teenagers
chunks.h: Give them something real to look at
chunks.x: Not a brochure. The actual school website, the actual suburb on a map, the club that plays their sport, what a Saturday looks like. Families say the decision landed better when their teenager could picture a specific life rather than a country. Before you fly

chunks.t: Moving with children and teenagers
chunks.h: Line up one thing they already do
chunks.x: A club, a squad, a teacher, a class. Arriving with one fixed point in the week comes up more often than anything else as the thing that shortened the settling. On arrival

chunks.t: Moving with children and teenagers
chunks.h: Let the first fortnight be small
chunks.x: Most families find the early days are best kept quiet — sleep, food, the local shops — rather than filled with sightseeing that everyone is too tired to enjoy. The first term

chunks.t: Moving with children and teenagers
chunks.h: Expect a dip, and know roughly when
chunks.x: Families describe a harder stretch somewhere around the second or third month, once the novelty has gone and the friendships have not yet arrived. Knowing it is a stage rather than a verdict is what people say helped. Keeping the old life

chunks.t: Moving with children and teenagers
chunks.x: A standing weekly call at a time that works in both hemispheres tends to survive; ad-hoc messaging across a twelve-hour gap tends not to. Several families budget for one trip home in the first two years and say it changed how the move felt. Sport and the outdoors

chunks.t: Moving with children and teenagers
chunks.h: It does a lot of the work
chunks.x: Club sport runs at every age and level in both countries, and it is where a good deal of the settling happens — for teenagers and for the parents standing on the sideline. There is more on this in moving with your family . Section 09 · At your own kitchen table

chunks.t: Moving with children and teenagers
chunks.x: Where is each child in their qualification years, and what would a move cost them academically? Is there a start date that would sit between stages rather than inside one? What would each of them be giving up that cannot be replaced — a squad place, a grandparent nearby, a course? What would have to be true for them to think this was a good idea? What is the plan if it is not working after a year? Saying it out loud changes the conversation. Who else are you bringing, or leaving — a parent, a sibling at university, a pet? These are not questions we answer for you. Answer them before an offer needs a decision in five days. Section 10 · The harder case

chunks.t: Moving with children and teenagers
chunks.h: If they don’t want to come
chunks.x: Some teenagers will say no, and mean it. That is an answer rather than an obstacle to be managed. Some families go anyway, and the young person settles. Some delay by a year or two until an exam series is finished. Some decide it is not the right moment and revisit it later — the roles will still exist, and so will the registration you have already earned. Some arrange for an older teenager to stay on with family to finish a course. We are not going to tell you which of those is right for your household. What we will say is that we have seen all four work, and that the one which tends not to work is proceeding as though the objection was not made. Worth knowing about registration and visas Registration, once granted, generally does not evaporate if you delay a move by a year, though maintenance requirements and fees continue to apply. Visa conditions and dependant age limits are a different matter and do have deadlines. If timing is the question in your household, ask us before you assume either way — the sequencing is the part we do. Common questions

chunks.t: Moving with children and teenagers
chunks.x: Is there a worst age to move a child? There is no single answer, but the constraint families run into most is the qualification years rather than age itself. A move partway through a senior certificate carries academic consequences that a move a year either side does not. Beyond that, what people report matters more is how much say the young person had. Will my child have to repeat a year? Sometimes, and it depends on the system, the school and where your child is in their course. The school year runs late January to December in both countries, so a family arriving from a September-start system often lands mid-year, and placement is decided school by school. Ask the specific schools you are considering, before you accept a role.

chunks.t: Moving with children and teenagers
chunks.x: Can we choose the school before we choose the house? In New Zealand this is the order we would suggest thinking in: many popular schools manage demand with an enrolment zone, so where you rent can decide where your child can go. The detail is in education in New Zealand . In Australia, government schools also use catchments, set state by state. Do we pay school fees on a temporary visa? In New Zealand, children of parents on longer work visas can usually attend state schools as domestic students; schools still ask for donations and activity costs. In Australia it depends on the state and often on your occupation — the current position by state is in school fees on a visa . What about university afterwards? Domestic or international tuition status depends on your visa and residency at the time your child enrols, not on when you arrived, and the thresholds differ between the two countries.

chunks.t: Moving with children and teenagers
chunks.x: It is a question worth asking early if you have a fifteen or sixteen-year-old, because it can be worth a great deal of money. Is one country easier than the other for teenagers? Not in a way we would generalise. Australia has more large cities and more choice of school and pathway; New Zealand is smaller, and a sporty, outdoor school culture comes up often when families describe why their children settled. The bigger variable is the specific town and school, not the country.

chunks.t: Moving with children and teenagers
chunks.h: Want to talk it through before you decide anything?
chunks.x: Have these answers before you face a five-day deadline. There is no fee to you at any stage. Ask Ethicare → Work out what the move costs Read a little deeper

chunks.t: Should you negotiate your salary?
chunks.x: New Zealand Australia The offer guide Should you negotiate? How to ask well, and when not to You’ve received the offer. The role is right, the location works, your family is excited, and the salary is slightly lower than you expected. Work through it → Check your offer 10 sections Updated August 2026 Free The uncomfortable bit

chunks.t: Should you negotiate your salary?
chunks.h: Asking a reasonable question rarely has to be confrontational
chunks.x: The good news is that a well-framed question about salary is a normal professional conversation, not a confrontation. But whether you can negotiate, and how much flexibility the employer has, depends heavily on your profession, your employer and your employment model. So the first job isn’t deciding what to ask for. It’s working out which situation you’re in. Section 01 · Before you respond

chunks.t: Should you negotiate your salary?
chunks.h: Find out how the salary was determined
chunks.x: Healthcare salaries aren’t all set the same way, and these are different conversations rather than variations on one. A public hospital may employ clinicians according to a collective agreement, award or established salary scale. A private provider may have considerably greater discretion. A GP may be discussing an hourly rate or a percentage of billings rather than a traditional salary. A senior specialist may be negotiating sessions, on-call commitments and private work alongside base remuneration. Sometimes the employer has real flexibility. Sometimes they don’t. Establishing which should come before you decide how to respond, because the same request lands very differently in each case. Section 02 · Room to move

chunks.t: Should you negotiate your salary?
chunks.x: The public and private answers are different, and so is the question worth asking in each. Public sector

chunks.t: Should you negotiate your salary?
chunks.h: Less flexible than you expect, but ask about placement
chunks.x: If you’re joining a public healthcare organisation, your salary may be linked to an established scale. That doesn’t mean there is nothing to discuss. The important question is usually where you enter the scale . Previous experience can influence placement, depending on the profession, agreement and employer. If you have twelve years of relevant post-qualification experience, it’s entirely reasonable to ask whether all of it has been recognised in determining your starting point. That is a different conversation from “I’d like another $15,000.” You’re asking the employer to check whether the offer accurately reflects your experience, which is a question they can act on. Private sector

chunks.t: Should you negotiate your salary?
chunks.x: Private healthcare employers often have greater freedom over remuneration, although this varies enormously. It’s particularly relevant in private radiology, general practice, allied health and diagnostic imaging. The employer may be weighing the scarcity of your skills, local workforce demand, your experience, subspecialty expertise and how difficult the vacancy has been to fill. An experienced MSK radiologist is entering a very different negotiation from someone applying for a position with numerous suitable local candidates. Your position depends partly on the value and scarcity of what you bring. Don’t negotiate because you think you should Plenty of generic career advice says never accept the first offer. Healthcare recruitment isn’t that simple.

chunks.t: Should you negotiate your salary?
chunks.x: If an employer has offered the top of the applicable range and has correctly recognised your experience, pushing further because negotiating is supposedly expected may achieve very little. Equally, accepting an offer you’re uncomfortable with creates a different problem later. The aim isn’t to win, it’s to be comfortable before you move your life to another country. Section 03 · Your benchmark

chunks.t: Should you negotiate your salary?
chunks.h: Know what you’re worth, but use the right comparison
chunks.x: Comparing the wrong two things is worse than not researching at all, because it gives you false confidence. A private Australian salary shouldn’t automatically be compared with a public New Zealand one. Sydney shouldn’t necessarily be compared with regional Western Australia. A contractor rate isn’t equivalent to an employee salary. A package inclusive of superannuation isn’t the same as a base salary plus super. A role with substantial on-call or weekend work shouldn’t be compared with one built around predictable weekday sessions. Before deciding an offer is too low, be certain what you’re measuring it against. Our money guide works through the comparisons that hold up. Section 04 · The rest of the package

chunks.t: Should you negotiate your salary?
chunks.h: Salary isn’t the only thing you can negotiate
chunks.x: Sometimes an employer cannot increase the base, and that doesn’t mean the conversation is finished. Depending on the employer and role, there may be scope to discuss: Relocation assistance, flights and temporary accommodation Professional registration or licensing costs Immigration or visa-related support CPD or professional development funding, and professional memberships Start date Working pattern, or number of sessions Flexible working arrangements Additional annual leave On-call or overtime arrangements The timing of your first salary review Not every employer will offer these, and some organisations have strict policies about what they can fund. But when you’re moving internationally, relatively small changes to the package can make a significant difference.

chunks.t: Should you negotiate your salary?
chunks.h: Salary isn’t the only thing you can negotiate
chunks.x: Relocation support can be worth more than a rise Imagine an employer can’t move on salary but can contribute towards flights, temporary accommodation and relocation expenses. For someone moving alone, that’s useful. For someone relocating a family of four, it could materially reduce the cost and stress of the move. Consider the total first-year value of an offer. A slightly higher base isn’t the better package if another employer is meaningfully helping you get established. Section 05 · Focus

chunks.t: Should you negotiate your salary?
chunks.h: There’s a difference between negotiating and producing a shopping list
chunks.x: If salary, leave, relocation, working hours, start date and every other part of the offer are challenged at once, an employer may reasonably start to wonder whether you want the job. So prioritise. Ask yourself one question: what matters to me? If salary is the issue, concentrate on salary. If the salary is acceptable but the cost of relocating your family is the worry, relocation assistance is the more important conversation. If your priority is spending Fridays with your children, negotiating your working pattern may be worth considerably more to you than a small increase. One clear ask lands. Six diffuse ones sound like doubt. Section 06 · Other offers

chunks.t: Should you negotiate your salary?
chunks.h: Be careful about using another offer as use
chunks.x: If you have another offer, it can be relevant. Handle it carefully. There is a considerable difference between saying: “I’ve received another offer at a higher salary, although this remains my preferred role. Is there any flexibility within the package?” …and attempting to create a bidding war. Healthcare communities in Australia and New Zealand can be surprisingly small, particularly within specialist professions, and your professional reputation travels with you. Never invent another offer, or exaggerate its value. It is a small world, the claim is easier to check than people assume, and the cost of being caught is out of all proportion to the gain. Section 07 · The conversation

chunks.t: Should you negotiate your salary?
chunks.x: Usually once you have a clear offer. Trying to negotiate hard before an employer has decided they want to appoint you tends to be counterproductive. By offer stage, both sides have invested in the process. The employer knows your experience, you know more about the role, and there is something concrete to discuss. If you’re working with a recruiter, this is also where they earn their place. A good one already understands the employer’s salary structure, whether flexibility is likely, and where your experience sits relative to other appointments. You don’t need a complicated strategy. Something like this is enough: “Thank you — I’m genuinely pleased to receive the offer and really enthusiastic about the role.

chunks.t: Should you negotiate your salary?
chunks.x: Before I formally accept, could I ask whether there is any flexibility on the salary? Based on my experience in [area], I was hoping we might look at something closer to [figure].” That’s a professional conversation. You’ve expressed enthusiasm, explained your reasoning, and given the employer a chance to respond. They may agree. They may meet you in the middle. Or they may explain the offer is already at the maximum available. All three are useful answers. Section 08 · The answer

chunks.t: Should you negotiate your salary?
chunks.x: If the employer has clearly demonstrated you’re already at the maximum available under the relevant agreement, asking repeatedly won’t change the outcome. Likewise, if an employer has already improved the offer significantly to meet your requests, think carefully before returning with another. The question becomes simply: is this opportunity right for you at the package available? If they say no

chunks.t: Should you negotiate your salary?
chunks.x: A declined salary request doesn’t mean the employer doesn’t value you. They may be constrained by a collective agreement, internal parity, budget or organisational policy. None of which is about you. You can then look at the whole opportunity and decide. If it works, accept it confidently. If it doesn’t, far better to recognise that before relocating halfway around the world. Section 09 · The point of all this

chunks.t: Should you negotiate your salary?
chunks.h: Don’t accept a salary you’re already unhappy with
chunks.x: If you accept an offer while privately feeling underpaid or undervalued, that feeling rarely disappears once you’ve moved. It waits, and it surfaces in your first difficult month. So ask reasonable questions before you commit. Understand the salary. Understand the package. Understand what is and isn’t negotiable. Then decide on the full opportunity. Negotiation isn’t just about earning more A successful negotiation doesn’t have to end with the biggest possible salary. It might mean having your previous experience properly recognised. Help with the cost of moving your family. Eight sessions rather than ten. Additional professional development. Or understanding that the original offer was already a fair one. Sophie’s insight Our role isn’t to push every offer higher.

chunks.t: Should you negotiate your salary?
chunks.h: Don’t accept a salary you’re already unhappy with
chunks.x: If an employer has recognised your experience properly and the figure is at the top of what they can do, I’d rather tell you that than manufacture a negotiation to look useful. Where there is room, we’ll have the conversation with the employer on your behalf, which is often easier for everyone than doing it yourself in the same week you’re trying to make a good first impression. What I care about is that both sides understand exactly what’s being agreed, and that the opportunity still feels right once the excitement of receiving the offer has passed. Sophie Founder, Ethicare Resourcing Common questions

chunks.t: Should you negotiate your salary?
chunks.h: The questions candidates ask us at offer stage
chunks.x: Will negotiating make me look difficult, or risk the offer? A single, well-framed question asked with enthusiasm for the role does not put a sensible offer at risk. What can cause friction is challenging six things at once, negotiating before the employer has decided to appoint you, or pushing again after they’ve already moved significantly. Ask once, ask clearly, and be ready to accept the answer. Can I negotiate in the public sector at all? Often not the rate itself, because it sits on a published scale. But you can and should ask about placement on that scale. Whether all your relevant post-qualification experience has been recognised in your starting step. That’s a question with a factual answer, and it’s where most value is found.

chunks.t: Should you negotiate your salary?
chunks.h: The questions candidates ask us at offer stage
chunks.x: What if they can’t move on salary? Ask about the rest of the package: relocation assistance, flights, temporary accommodation, registration and visa costs, CPD funding, start date, working pattern, leave, or the timing of your first review. For an international move, those can be worth more in year one than a modest increase to base pay. Should I tell them about another offer? Only if it’s real, and only framed as a question rather than an ultimatum. Making clear this is still your preferred role. Never invent one or inflate it. Specialist healthcare communities in both countries are small, and your reputation outlasts any single negotiation. Will you negotiate on my behalf? Where it’s appropriate, yes, and it’s often easier that way, since we already know the employer’s structure and whether there’s flexibility.

chunks.t: Should you negotiate your salary?
chunks.h: The questions candidates ask us at offer stage
chunks.x: We’ll also tell you when there isn’t, rather than putting you through a conversation that won’t change anything. How do I know whether the offer is fair in the first place? Start with how the figure was set and what it should be compared against, award floor, collective agreement step, or a private-market rate. Our Australian and New Zealand pay guides explain the mechanics of each, and we’ll confirm the specific position for any role we discuss with you. Free, any time

chunks.t: Should you negotiate your salary?
chunks.h: Got an offer in front of you?
chunks.x: Send us the detail and we’ll tell you how the figure was set, whether there’s likely to be room, and what else in the package is worth asking about. Even if the role isn’t one of ours. chunks.t: The New Zealand relocation checklist
chunks.x: Everything in the guide, as a list you can tick off. It saves as you go. Six stages, from three months before you leave to three months after you land. Nothing here is urgent on its own — the point is that none of it arrives as a surprise. Not every line applies to every household; skip what doesn’t. 0 of 0 done Print my list Start again Saved in this browser only — it doesn’t leave your device and we can’t see it. Use the same browser and it will be here when you come back. “A list this long looks like a mountain when you are standing at the bottom of it. It is not. It is roughly forty small errands spread over six months, and most of them take under an hour. Do the ones with a lead time first — pets, schools, the bank account — and let the rest arrive in their own order. Nobody has ever done all of this perfectly, and everybody has still arrived.” Sophie Careem — Founder & CEO, Ethicare Resourcing Ethicare Resourcing

chunks.t: The New Zealand relocation checklist
chunks.h: This chapter is part of a bigger guide — and we’re here for the rest of it
chunks.x: We place healthcare professionals across New Zealand and Australia, and stay with the move through registration, visas and the first months after you land. Careers in New Zealand → Ask Ethicare A different question

chunks.t: The New Zealand relocation checklist
chunks.h: This checklist answers when . There’s another for what applies to me .
chunks.x: The list above is the timeline — around forty errands in the order they need doing. If you’d rather start from who’s moving, our moving checklist builds itself around your household: partner work rights, school-age children, under-fives, a pet, or moving out ahead of the family. chunks.t: Community & belonging in New Zealand
chunks.h: Belonging is what makes a move last
chunks.x: The second friendliest country in the world. New Zealand came second, just behind Costa Rica, in Condé Nast Traveller’s 2026 Readers’ Choice Awards, voted for by its readers (October 2026). Source → A family festival at Victoria Park, Palmerston North. Small towns run more of these than cities do, and they are usually where newcomers meet people first. New Zealand is a multicultural country. Its cities and towns are home to long-established Māori and Pacific communities alongside large Asian, Middle Eastern, African and European populations, and the healthcare workforce itself is wonderfully international. Whatever your faith, culture or background, there is a good chance a community already exists. How large it is, and how close, depends on where you settle: Auckland has almost everything; a small town may have one congregation and a WhatsApp group.

chunks.t: Community & belonging in New Zealand
chunks.h: Belonging is what makes a move last
chunks.x: Friendships take time anywhere, and some people do experience loneliness, a hard cultural adjustment or, occasionally, discrimination. Knowing that in advance makes the slow months easier. If there’s one promise in this guide, it’s this: you will not have to leave who you are behind to move here. Belonging takes a little time and a little effort, but the ingredients are all here, waiting. Faith & places of worship

chunks.t: Community & belonging in New Zealand
chunks.h: A place to worship, whatever your faith
chunks.x: Freedom of religion is protected in law. The cities have established congregations, and many smaller towns have more than newcomers expect. Christian

chunks.t: Community & belonging in New Zealand
chunks.x: From Anglican, Catholic and Presbyterian to Pentecostal and a wide range of ethnic-specific congregations, Christian communities are found in every city and most towns: many with services in languages other than English. Muslim

chunks.t: Community & belonging in New Zealand
chunks.x: Established Muslim communities in the main centres run mosques, Islamic centres and schools, with halal food increasingly easy to find. Smaller cities have growing congregations and prayer spaces too. Hindu

chunks.t: Community & belonging in New Zealand
chunks.x: A large and active Hindu community supports temples and cultural associations, with major festivals such as Diwali celebrated publicly in the cities, often as city-wide events. Sikh

chunks.t: Community & belonging in New Zealand
chunks.x: A growing Sikh population maintains gurdwaras in the main centres, offering worship, langar and a strong sense of community for new arrivals. Buddhist

chunks.t: Community & belonging in New Zealand
chunks.x: Buddhist temples and meditation centres reflect New Zealand’s diverse Asian communities, welcoming both heritage practitioners and newcomers to the practice. Jewish & others

chunks.t: Community & belonging in New Zealand
chunks.x: Long-established Jewish congregations and a range of other faith communities are present, particularly in the larger cities. If your faith is part of your life, it can stay that way here. A practical tip Faith communities are often the fastest route to friendship and practical help when you arrive: many run welcome groups, share local knowledge and lend a hand with the early settling-in. It’s worth reaching out before you even land. Cultural & diaspora communities

chunks.t: Community & belonging in New Zealand
chunks.h: Chances are, your community is already here
chunks.x: Where people settle, communities form: cultural associations, social groups and informal networks. Rezon and his wife celebrating Onam with colleagues in Palmerston North: the sadya served on banana leaves, and the family dressed for the day. Rezon, Neethu and Anu’s first year in Palmerston North →

chunks.t: Community & belonging in New Zealand
chunks.x: Large and active communities from the UK and Ireland, India, the Philippines, South Africa, China and across the Pacific mean cultural associations, social events and familiar faces are rarely far away.

chunks.t: Community & belonging in New Zealand
chunks.x: Because so many clinicians have made this exact move, you’ll find others in your profession who share your background: people who understand both the work and the journey, and are generous with advice.

chunks.t: Community & belonging in New Zealand
chunks.x: Diwali, Eid, Lunar New Year, Pasifika and many more are celebrated openly and often city-wide: public, joyful occasions that make it easy to stay connected to your heritage and share it with new friends.

chunks.t: Community & belonging in New Zealand
chunks.x: Many communities run weekend language and culture classes so children stay connected to their heritage language and traditions while they grow up as young New Zealanders.

chunks.t: Community & belonging in New Zealand
chunks.x: Active online groups for almost every nationality and city are where newcomers ask questions, find housing, swap recommendations and arrange the first real-life catch-ups.

chunks.t: Community & belonging in New Zealand
chunks.x: Cricket, football, rugby, cultural dance, choirs and hobby clubs are some of the easiest, most natural ways to meet people who share both your interests and, often, your background. “I was surprised by how strong the Keralan community is in Manawatū. There are lots of families here and people were incredibly welcoming when we arrived. Having people around who understand where you’ve come from, while you’re also building a new life in New Zealand, really helped us settle.” A clinician’s family on settling in Manawatū An inclusive welcome

chunks.t: Community & belonging in New Zealand
chunks.h: A country that welcomes you as you are
chunks.x: People are protected by law from discrimination on the grounds of race, religion, gender, sexual orientation and more.

chunks.t: Community & belonging in New Zealand
chunks.x: New Zealand is widely regarded as one of the most welcoming places in the world for LGBTQ+ people, with legal equality, visible communities and Pride events in the main centres.

chunks.t: Community & belonging in New Zealand
chunks.x: Workplaces, including across the health system, take inclusion and anti-discrimination seriously, and the law backs that up. If you are treated unfairly, your employer, your union and the Human Rights Commission are the places to go.

chunks.t: Community & belonging in New Zealand
chunks.x: Single parents, blended families, same-sex parents and multi-generational households are all an ordinary, accepted part of New Zealand life. Te ao Māori

chunks.t: Community & belonging in New Zealand
chunks.h: Manaakitanga, the welcome at the heart of it
chunks.x: One of the first Māori words you’ll come across is manaakitanga: caring for others, hospitality and generosity towards newcomers. As a newcomer you’ll be welcomed into a country shaped by Te Tiriti o Waitangi and the relationship between Māori and the Crown. Understanding a little of this, the role of te reo Māori, the customs of a pōwhiri (welcome) or a karakia (blessing) you may encounter at work is part of settling in respectfully and well. It’s also one of the quiet privileges of making your life here. You don’t need to know everything on arrival. A willingness to learn and to show respect goes a long way , and our About New Zealand guide covers the history, Te Tiriti and te reo in more depth. A taste of home

chunks.t: Community & belonging in New Zealand
chunks.h: The small comforts that matter most
chunks.x: Most foods from home are closer than you’d think, especially in the cities. These are the suppliers people tell us about.

chunks.t: Community & belonging in New Zealand
chunks.x: Big world-food ranges and dedicated Asian grocers. Tai Ping Asian Supermarket The Asian Grocer (online) New World, world-food aisles

chunks.t: Community & belonging in New Zealand
chunks.x: Biltong, boerewors, braai & pantry staples. Something From Home The South African Shop Biltong & Wors Shop

chunks.t: Community & belonging in New Zealand
chunks.x: British groceries, sweets, biscuits & tea. UK Foods NZ A Little Bit of Britain British Food Imports The big supermarkets — New World, PAK’nSAVE and Woolworths. All carry growing international aisles, and most cities have large Asian grocers such as Lim Chhour and Da Hua alongside Indian, Korean, Middle Eastern and Pacific specialists. These are commercial businesses we don’t endorse; links open external sites we don’t control, and range and availability vary by region.

chunks.t: Community & belonging in New Zealand
chunks.x: Halal food is widely available, especially in the main centres. Many mainstream supermarkets and butchers stock halal-certified meat (FIANZ is the country’s main halal certifier), and cities have dedicated halal butchers, grocers and restaurants. In smaller towns the choice narrows, but it’s rarely far away.

chunks.t: Community & belonging in New Zealand
chunks.x: Kosher options are more limited but present — Auckland has the widest range, including a kosher store and deli, and Wellington has some too. Elsewhere it’s mostly online or through the local Jewish community. The New Zealand Jewish Council and local congregations are the best people to point you to current suppliers. Practical first steps

chunks.t: Community & belonging in New Zealand
chunks.x: Search for groups linked to your nationality, faith or city, email the nearest congregation or association, and introduce yourself. A friendly contact or two before you land changes the first weekend.

chunks.t: Community & belonging in New Zealand
chunks.x: The first invitations, a coffee, a barbecue, a community event, are how roots begin. Accepting them, even when you’re tired, pays off quickly.

chunks.t: Community & belonging in New Zealand
chunks.x: Colleagues are often your first community, and many have made the same move. Ask them where to worship, shop and gather, they’ll know.

chunks.t: Community & belonging in New Zealand
chunks.x: A weekly class, sports team, choir or place of worship gives your week an anchor and the same faces each time, which is how acquaintances become friends.

chunks.t: Community & belonging in New Zealand
chunks.x: Cook for new neighbours, share your festivals, contribute what’s yours. Belonging flows both ways, and people love being welcomed into something new.

chunks.t: Community & belonging in New Zealand
chunks.x: Each destination guide covers the local groups, places of worship and cultural associations in that place. Read the one for where you are considering before you decide. Where to start

chunks.t: Community & belonging in New Zealand
chunks.x: The national organisations for the major faiths, each with regional centres in the main cities, plus a couple of practical ways to find local groups wherever you settle.

chunks.t: Community & belonging in New Zealand
chunks.x: National churches with parishes nationwide. Catholic Church in New Zealand Anglican Church in Aotearoa, NZ & Polynesia Presbyterian Church of Aotearoa NZ

chunks.t: Community & belonging in New Zealand
chunks.x: National peak bodies, with centres in each main city. Federation of Islamic Associations of NZ Hindu Council of New Zealand New Zealand Jewish Council

chunks.t: Community & belonging in New Zealand
chunks.x: Local groups, societies and a friendly introduction. Citizens Advice Bureau directory Ask Ethicare about community Sikh, Buddhist and many other faith communities also have well-established gurdwaras, temples and centres across the main cities, as do a great many cultural and national societies. If you can’t find yours, tell us where you’re moving and what matters to you, and we’ll point you to the nearest community. For newcomer networks and a region-by-region list of local groups, see Useful contacts . Links open on external sites we don’t control. Sophie’s insight People worry, quietly, about whether they’ll fit in, whether they’ll find somewhere to pray, food that tastes like home, friends who understand them. I understand that worry completely. What I’ve seen is how much is already here, and how warmly people are received once they reach out.

chunks.t: Community & belonging in New Zealand
chunks.x: The clinicians who thrive are the ones who let New Zealand welcome them and who keep hold of their own culture at the same time. You don’t have to choose. Helping a family find their community, the temple, the grocer, the weekend cricket, is some of the most rewarding work we do. Sophie CEO & Founder, Ethicare Resourcing Common questions

chunks.t: Community & belonging in New Zealand
chunks.h: The questions people ask us about belonging
chunks.x: Will I be able to practise my religion freely? Yes. New Zealand has freedom of religion, and active communities exist across all the major faiths, especially in the cities. Places of worship, religious schools and cultural associations are well established, and faith communities are often among the warmest and most practical sources of support for newcomers. Is there a community of people from my country? Almost certainly, particularly in the larger centres. New Zealand’s healthcare workforce is highly international, and there are established diaspora communities from the UK, Ireland, India, the Philippines, South Africa, China, the Pacific and many more, with social groups, festivals and online networks that make it easy to connect. How welcoming is New Zealand to LGBTQ+ people? Very.

chunks.t: Community & belonging in New Zealand
chunks.h: The questions people ask us about belonging
chunks.x: New Zealand is consistently ranked among the most accepting countries in the world for LGBTQ+ people, with full legal equality, visible communities and Pride events. Inclusion is taken seriously both in law and in everyday life, including across the health system. Can I find the food and ingredients I’m used to? Mostly, yes, especially in the cities, where international supermarkets and specialist grocers stock ingredients from across the world, and halal and other cultural foods are increasingly easy to find. In smaller towns the range is narrower, but online ordering fills most gaps, and you’ll quickly learn where to look. What if I’m moving somewhere smaller and quieter? Smaller regions have less variety than the big cities, but they often make up for it with a closeness that’s harder to find in a metropolis: people notice newcomers and make an effort. We’ll tell you what to expect in any region you’re considering, and help you weigh community alongside everything else. Keep exploring

chunks.t: Education & schools in New Zealand
chunks.h: A welcoming system where children settle fast
chunks.x: The system will feel broadly familiar to anyone from a comparable country, with a few differences in structure, qualifications and the way you enrol. This guide walks through all of it, so you can picture your children’s school days clearly and choose the right place with confidence. If there’s one practical thing to take away, it’s this: school enrolment and where you live are closely linked. Many good schools have enrolment zones, so it pays to research schools before you settle on a neighbourhood, often the school decides the postcode. From toddlers to teenagers

chunks.t: Education & schools in New Zealand
chunks.x: Schooling runs from age 5 through to around 18, divided into clear stages. Most children start school on or around their fifth birthday, and education is compulsory from 6 to 16. Under 5

chunks.t: Education & schools in New Zealand
chunks.x: birth–5 Optional but popular early learning: kindergartens, daycare, playcentres and kōhanga reo (Māori-language). Government funding subsidises a set number of hours a week for children aged 3 to 5, so it’s more affordable than many expect. Years 1–6

chunks.t: Education & schools in New Zealand
chunks.x: ages 5–10 The foundation years, starting when your child turns five. Warm, play-informed and broad, with a strong focus on literacy, numeracy and learning to belong in a classroom community. Years 7–8

chunks.t: Education & schools in New Zealand
chunks.x: ages 11–12 A two-year bridge between primary and secondary in many areas, easing the step up. In some places these years sit within a full primary or a middle school instead, it varies by region. Years 9–13

chunks.t: Education & schools in New Zealand
chunks.x: ages 13–17 Where students work towards their national qualifications in the senior years, with a widening choice of subjects and pathways into work, training or university. How the year is shaped

chunks.t: Education & schools in New Zealand
chunks.x: The New Zealand school year runs from late January to mid-December, divided into four terms of roughly ten weeks each. Between terms are two-week breaks, with a long summer holiday over Christmas and New Year. Term 1

chunks.t: Education & schools in New Zealand
chunks.x: The year begins, usually in the first week or two of February, followed by a two-week autumn break. Term 2

chunks.t: Education & schools in New Zealand
chunks.x: The longest stretch of settled learning, rounded off by the two-week winter holidays. Term 3

chunks.t: Education & schools in New Zealand
chunks.x: Through the heart of winter into early spring, then a two-week spring break. Term 4

chunks.t: Education & schools in New Zealand
chunks.x: The final term, ending before Christmas and the long summer holiday of around six weeks. A few things worth knowing: exact dates are set each year by the Ministry of Education and vary slightly between schools (start days, the odd teacher-only day). Public holidays and your region’s anniversary day also fall within term time. For care over the breaks, holiday programmes are widely available, see childcare & out-of-school care above. Your choices

chunks.t: Education & schools in New Zealand
chunks.x: Most children attend free, government-funded state schools, but there are three main types to know about: each with a different character and cost. Most common

chunks.t: Education & schools in New Zealand
chunks.x: Government-funded and free for domestic students, these educate the large majority of children. Quality is generally high and consistent, and they follow the national curriculum. Special character

chunks.t: Education & schools in New Zealand
chunks.x: State-funded schools with a particular character, often faith-based (such as Catholic) or a specific philosophy. They follow the national curriculum but usually charge modest attendance dues. Fee-paying

chunks.t: Education & schools in New Zealand
chunks.x: Independently run and funded mainly through fees. A smaller part of the system, chosen by some families for particular programmes, facilities or smaller classes. The thing to get right early

chunks.t: Education & schools in New Zealand
chunks.h: Enrolment zones, why where you live matters
chunks.x: Many popular schools manage demand with an enrolment zone. Inside it, a place is generally guaranteed; outside it, places are limited and offered by ballot — which is the single biggest reason to research schools before choosing where to live.

chunks.t: Education & schools in New Zealand
chunks.x: Living within a school’s zone usually guarantees enrolment, which is why families often choose the neighbourhood for the school.

chunks.t: Education & schools in New Zealand
chunks.x: Out-of-zone places at popular schools are limited and typically allocated by a ballot, so they’re never guaranteed.

chunks.t: Education & schools in New Zealand
chunks.x: You can look up any school’s zone online before signing a lease. A few minutes here saves a lot of stress later. “Ethicare advised us to choose our children’s school before looking for a home, because many schools in New Zealand are zoned. It was really useful advice. We found that rental prices could vary quite a bit depending on the school zone, although we were pleasantly surprised by how good the standard of schools was generally. It definitely helped us narrow down where we wanted to live.” A family we supported, on choosing the school before the suburb Getting enrolled

chunks.t: Education & schools in New Zealand
chunks.x: You enrol with the individual school rather than a central authority. Reach out before you arrive if you can: many will start the conversation by email.

chunks.t: Education & schools in New Zealand
chunks.x: Have passports, visas, immunisation records, and your children’s previous school reports and any learning-support paperwork ready, they help with the right placement.

chunks.t: Education & schools in New Zealand
chunks.x: Children are generally placed by age rather than by exactly where they were in their old system, which keeps them with their peers.

chunks.t: Education & schools in New Zealand
chunks.x: Schools provide English-language learning support where it’s needed, so children who are still building their English are well looked after. What they’ll learn & earn

chunks.t: Education & schools in New Zealand
chunks.x: A broad, inclusive curriculum runs through the school years, and senior students work towards a national qualification, with some schools offering international alternatives too. The curriculum

chunks.t: Education & schools in New Zealand
chunks.x: Schools follow the New Zealand Curriculum, with te reo Māori and Aotearoa’s bicultural heritage woven through. The emphasis is on well-rounded learning, not just exams, including plenty of time outdoors and on sport. The main qualification

chunks.t: Education & schools in New Zealand
chunks.x: The National Certificate of Educational Achievement is the principal secondary qualification, taken across the final three years (Levels 1–3). It’s flexible, combining internal and external assessment across a wide range of subjects. Other options

chunks.t: Education & schools in New Zealand
chunks.x: Some schools also offer Cambridge International or the International Baccalaureate alongside or instead of NCEA, worth asking about if your child is mid-pathway or you’d like an internationally portable qualification. NCEA is assessed in credits across the senior years rather than in one set of final exams, which is the biggest adjustment for a teenager arriving mid-schooling. Told straight

chunks.t: Education & schools in New Zealand
chunks.x: State schooling is free for domestic students, but there are everyday extras to budget for, and your visa decides whether your children are treated as domestic or international students. State school tuition Free for domestic students, which children of many longer-term work-visa holders are, depending on the visa. School donations State schools may request a voluntary donation to top up funding. It’s optional, though many families contribute. Uniforms, stationery & devices Practical costs you’ll budget for: uniforms, stationery, a device for older students, and trips or activities. State-integrated dues Integrated schools typically charge modest compulsory attendance dues on top of the free tuition. Private school fees Independent schools charge full tuition fees, which vary widely by school.

chunks.t: Education & schools in New Zealand
chunks.x: International student fees If your visa means your children are international students, state schools charge fees, so it’s worth confirming your status early. Whether your children count as domestic or international students depends on your visa. Confirm it with Immigration New Zealand or the school. Rules and costs change, so always check the current position at the source. Ethicare are recruitment specialists, not an education authority. What they’ll wear

chunks.t: Education & schools in New Zealand
chunks.x: As a rule, the older the student, the more likely a uniform, and the more formal it tends to be. Primary years

chunks.t: Education & schools in New Zealand
chunks.x: Many primary schools have a relaxed, inexpensive uniform. Usually a polo and shorts, skirt or trousers in the school colours, and some have none at all. Summers are casual, and it’s common for young children to go barefoot on warm days. Intermediate & secondary

chunks.t: Education & schools in New Zealand
chunks.x: From intermediate and especially at secondary school, a uniform is normally required, often with a separate PE kit. State-integrated and private schools tend to be more formal, sometimes including a blazer. Sun-smart

chunks.t: Education & schools in New Zealand
chunks.x: New Zealand takes sun protection seriously. Many schools run a “no hat, no play” rule through the summer terms, so a wide-brim or bucket hat is usually part of the kit.

chunks.t: Education & schools in New Zealand
chunks.x: The school’s own uniform shop or office . The first stop, and where compulsory branded items are sold. The school’s approved uniform supplier , many schools nominate a specialist supplier for items like blazers, jerseys and the PE kit. Big-box retailers such as The Warehouse , handy and affordable for generic basics: plain polos, shorts, socks, hats and shoes. Second-hand uniform sales , run by most schools or their parents’ association, and by far the cheapest way to kit children out. For the under-fives & after the bell

chunks.t: Education & schools in New Zealand
chunks.x: Funded early learning, before- and after-school care, and clubs cover the gaps around your shifts.

chunks.t: Education & schools in New Zealand
chunks.x: The government’s 20 Hours ECE scheme funds up to 20 hours a week of early childhood education for eligible children aged three to five (and some younger children at certain services), at participating providers. It makes pre-school care far more affordable than many newcomers expect.

chunks.t: Education & schools in New Zealand
chunks.x: Beyond the funded hours, families may be able to get further help, such as a Childcare Subsidy through Work and Income, depending on income, hours worked and circumstances. It’s worth checking what you’re eligible for once you’ve arrived.

chunks.t: Education & schools in New Zealand
chunks.x: Options include kindergartens, daycare (education & care centres), home-based care, playcentres and kōhanga reo. Popular centres can have waitlists, so enquire early. Ideally before you arrive, to line something up for your start date.

chunks.t: Education & schools in New Zealand
chunks.x: Some hospital and healthcare sites have an onsite or nearby early learning centre, though it isn’t universal. If childcare close to work matters for your shifts, tell us, we can check what’s available at a specific site.

chunks.t: Education & schools in New Zealand
chunks.x: Many schools take part in a national breakfast programme, providing a free, healthy breakfast before class. It’s a quiet help on busy mornings and a warm start to the day for children settling in.

chunks.t: Education & schools in New Zealand
chunks.x: Out of School Care and Recreation (OSCAR) programmes run before school, after school and through the holidays, often onsite or nearby. A Work and Income OSCAR Subsidy can help with the cost for eligible families, useful when your hours don’t match the school bell. Funding rules, hours and subsidies change and depend on your circumstances and visa, always confirm the current detail with the Ministry of Education, Work and Income or the provider. Ethicare are recruitment specialists, not an education authority, but we’re glad to help you weigh up options near a role. Early learning here is play-based and part-funded from age three — the constraint is usually places rather than price, and the waiting list starts before you land. More than logistics

chunks.t: Education & schools in New Zealand
chunks.x: Tend to settle within weeks. Friendly classrooms, lots of outdoor play and sport make it easy to make friends fast, often before their parents have unpacked the last box.

chunks.t: Education & schools in New Zealand
chunks.x: May need more time and more say. Leaving friends at a decisive age is hard, so involve them in school choice, keep talking, and give the first term or two to find their feet.

chunks.t: Education & schools in New Zealand
chunks.x: Schools are experienced at welcoming new arrivals and often pair newcomers with a buddy. Get to know teachers early, and the school gate is a great place for parents to make friends too. Sophie’s insight The children are so often the part parents worry about most, and so often the ones who settle first. My one piece of practical advice is to start with the school, not the suburb: find schools you’d be happy with, check their zones, and let that guide where you look to live. And don’t underestimate a Kiwi childhood: the outdoors, the sport, the easygoing classrooms. Plenty of families tell me their kids ended up happier here than they ever expected. Sophie CEO & Founder, Ethicare Resourcing Common questions

chunks.t: Education & schools in New Zealand
chunks.x: Will my children need a school uniform, and what does it cost? It depends on the school and the age. Primary schools are often relaxed, a simple, inexpensive uniform or none at all, while intermediate and secondary schools usually require one, sometimes with a separate PE kit. It’s a cost worth budgeting for upfront, but most schools run second-hand uniform sales that bring it right down. See our uniforms section above for the detail. Can my children go to state school for free on my visa? Children of New Zealand citizens and residents are domestic students, so state schooling is free. Children of many work-visa holders. Including the Accredited Employer Work Visa (AEWV), are also generally treated as domestic students where the parent holds an eligible work visa, which means free state schooling too.

chunks.t: Education & schools in New Zealand
chunks.x: Eligibility hinges on your specific visa and its conditions, and the rules can change, so confirm your children’s status with Immigration New Zealand, the Ministry of Education or the school before you enrol. If they’re classed as international students, state schools charge fees. What childcare is available for under-fives, and is it subsidised? Early childhood education (ECE) is well established, kindergartens, daycare (education and care centres), home-based care, playcentres and kōhanga reo (Māori-language). The government’s 20 Hours ECE scheme subsidises a set number of hours each week for eligible children aged three to five, so it’s often more affordable than newcomers expect. Popular centres can have waitlists, so it’s worth researching and contacting them before you arrive. Confirm what funding your children are eligible for based on your visa.

chunks.t: Education & schools in New Zealand
chunks.x: When in the year should my child start school? The school year runs from late January to mid-December across four terms, so starting at the beginning of the year lets children begin alongside everyone else. That said, schools enrol new arrivals throughout the year and are well practised at it. The right time is usually the one that fits your job and visa, so don’t force it to line up perfectly.
