chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: What will my partner do? Two careers move, not one. Whether a partner can work depends on the visas you each hold, check the official Immigration New Zealand guidance directly rather than assuming. Whether your partner can get an open work visa of their own depends on your visa, job and pay, so check Immigration New Zealand’s current partner rules for your role. Before you fly: rework their CV for the local market, check whether their profession needs its own registration here, and treat the first months as one-income planning. Immigration & visas explains how partner visas fit the main application. Will we pay school fees? State school places depend on your children counting as domestic students, which follows from your visa.

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: Children holding a student visa based on a parent’s work visa can usually enrol as domestic students, but confirm it before you commit — Education & schools walks through eligibility and the everyday costs that apply either way. What will childcare cost? Under-fives are a different budget line entirely. Funded hours, extra charges and subsidies are explained in Childcare , and a partner staying home changes the sum in both directions. Can we manage on one income at first? Don’t guess. Do the subtraction: net salary, minus rent, childcare, school costs, insurance, a car and the weekly shop. If the result works before a second income arrives, everything that follows is easier. Salary & pay and the cost of relocating give you the pieces. Will my family have healthcare cover? Publicly funded care depends on each family member’s immigration status, not just yours.

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: Updated eligibility regulations take effect on 1 December 2026; most existing rules, including the two-year work visa test, stay the same. Enrol with a GP early, bring enough regular medication to cover the first weeks, and carry copies of medical and vaccination records. Understanding healthcare covers the system, ACC and what care costs. When in the school year should we move? Aim for the long summer break and children get a clean start, though schools handle mid-year joins well too. Teenagers approaching NCEA years need the most care, plan around exam cycles, not flight prices. Does my child need extra learning support? Support does not transfer automatically with overseas paperwork.

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: Get current reports and assessments before you leave, contact shortlisted schools before you commit to an address, and ask each one directly what support it can offer and how long assessments take to arrange. Can our parents and grandparents join us? Visits are usually possible; longer stays are harder. A Parent and Grandparent Visitor Visa allows repeat visits of up to six months at a time, and the newer Parent Boost Visitor Visa lets sponsored parents stay for up to five years at a stretch, with health-insurance, sponsorship and financial conditions attached, and no pathway to residence. Residence routes exist too (Parent Resident, Parent Retirement) but run on ballots, caps or substantial funds. Start with the official Immigration New Zealand family pages before promising anything to the grandparents.

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: Temporary first, or straight to residence? For families this is the quiet big one, because residence, not the job, is what settles the school, healthcare and subsidy questions above. Green List Tier 1 professions can apply Straight to Residence , with partner and children included in the same application from day one; Tier 2 runs Work to Residence after two years. If your profession qualifies, it changes the whole family’s first years. Immigration & visas covers the pathways. What if someone in the family has a health condition or disability? This is the hardest question on the page, and the one to face earliest. Every applicant — children included — must meet New Zealand’s “acceptable standard of health”. For residence, Immigration New Zealand may decline an application if a person’s health costs are likely to be more than NZ$81,000.

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: For temporary visas there is no dollar figure: it looks at whether someone is likely to need hospital care, residential care, high-cost medicines or high-cost disability services during their stay. A diagnosis on its own is not an automatic barrier; each case is assessed individually, and one family member not meeting the standard can affect the whole application. Medical waivers exist but are discretionary. Declare everything, and gather specialist reports and costed treatment plans before you apply. For anything borderline, read Immigration New Zealand’s health requirement guidance closely first. The official INZ health requirements page carries the current criteria; whether a particular medicine is funded here is a separate question again, see Understanding healthcare . We’re recruitment specialists, not licensed immigration advisers, and none of this is immigration, tax or financial advice. Visa conditions and eligibility rules change, so confirm the current position with Immigration New Zealand and the schools themselves before committing. The reassuring part

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.h: Children travel further than we give them credit for
chunks.x: The weekends are the part people underestimate, and the part their children remember. Children take their cue from you. If the move is framed as an adventure and the practicalities are quietly handled in the background, many children adapt well, though every child moves at their own pace. This guide walks through both halves: getting there in one piece, and helping everyone feel at home once you’ve arrived. If there’s one thing to hold onto, it’s this: a few unsettled weeks are completely normal and almost always temporary. Wobbles, clinginess and the odd tearful evening don’t mean you’ve made the wrong decision, they mean a small person is doing something brave. The question the move turns on

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: Two salaries or one changes what you can afford and where you can live. The short version: your partner’s right to work comes from your visa rather than from a job offer of their own, and what they are permitted to do depends on the route you are granted, the role you hold and the conditions attached. That is why the answer is never a flat yes or no, but check it against the route you are on — and check it before you accept, not after. Real story · the partner’s job “Finding work for Jonathan took a full year, and saying it was tough would be an understatement. That experience taught us how important it is to research the job market properly before making a move like this.” Janita, nuclear medicine technologist, Auckland. Jonathan came with her from South Africa in January 2024. What the move was like → Whose visa decides it

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: A partner’s work rights follow from your visa and the terms of your job. Move from a work visa to residence and their position changes with it. Read the conditions on the visa you are granted, not the one you applied for. Will the qualification count?

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: Permission to work and recognition to practise are two different processes. Regulated professions run through the New Zealand regulator for that field; for everything else, recognition of an overseas qualification is judged by employers or assessed by NZQA. Start it early. Assessments take longer than anyone expects. How long until they earn?

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.h: Budget the first months on one income
chunks.x: Even with full work rights, job-hunting while unpacking, enrolling children and learning a new city takes time. Families who plan for one income and are pleasantly surprised do far better than families who plan for two. If they are a clinician too

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: Theirs may well be the longer one. Run both from the start rather than in sequence — a second timeline discovered late is the most common reason a family ends up arriving months apart. Check their pathway alongside yours.

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.h: What to settle before you accept
chunks.x: Ask the employer which visa they intend to support and what conditions come with it. Ask what help, if any, extends to a partner. Then have the conversation at home about what six months on one income looks like. None of this is awkward at the offer stage; all of it is expensive later. Visa rules are set and changed by government, so we point you at the source rather than paraphrasing it: Immigration New Zealand . Ethicare is not an immigration adviser. See also visas and immigration . Under five

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: The binding constraint is places rather than price. In the popular suburbs the waiting list starts long before you land. 1

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: Early childhood education covers several quite different things: education and care centres open across the working day, kindergartens often running school-like hours, home-based educators caring for a few children in their own home, and kōhanga reo, where the day is conducted in te reo Māori. They differ in hours, cost and character, not just in name. 2

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.h: Join waiting lists before you fly
chunks.x: You can enquire and be listed from overseas. Do it as soon as you have a suburb in mind, and list at more than one centre. A place you do not need is easy to decline; a place that does not exist is not. 3

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.h: Understand what is funded, and what isn’t
chunks.x: Three different things affect what you pay. 20 Hours ECE: for children aged 3 and 4, the government funds up to 20 hours a week at participating services. Extra charges: hours beyond that, and some optional extras such as meals or trips, are charged by the service, and prices vary widely. Help with costs: Work and Income’s Childcare Subsidy and Inland Revenue’s FamilyBoost help some households, but both have income and residence rules. Ask each centre for its fees and which funding your child qualifies for on your visa before you budget on a subsidised figure. 4

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.h: Test it against a clinical roster
chunks.x: Standard centre hours were not designed around a 7am start or a late finish. Ask about the earliest drop-off and the latest pick-up, ask what happens when you are held past handover, and plan for the gap — a home-based educator or a nanny share often covers what a centre cannot. Official sources: Ministry of Education — early learning for how it works, and help paying for early childhood education for funded hours and subsidies. For school-age children, schools and education covers enrolment zones, the school year and settling in. Doing it on your own

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: Two things need handling early, and both are easier to do at home than from the other side of the world.

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.h: Consent to take a child abroad
chunks.x: Where someone else holds guardianship or parental responsibility, you will generally need their written consent or a court order — and it can be asked for twice: once by the visa application, and again by an airline or a border officer. Get it in writing, get copies certified, and carry them in your hand luggage rather than the shipping container. Full birth certificates showing both parents, not the short form. Any parenting, guardianship or custody orders, certified. A signed consent letter with the other parent’s contact details, or evidence of sole responsibility. Where a parent has died, the death certificate. Immunisation records and medical notes, which schools and clinics will ask for. One income, two costs

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.h: Childcare is the line that decides it
chunks.x: Work the numbers on your own salary with care included at full price, and check the funding question above before you rely on it. The first three months are the most expensive of the whole move. No second adult

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.h: Build the network before you need it
chunks.x: Before and after-school care, school-holiday programmes, a neighbour, and one colleague who will swap a shift. Set these up in the first fortnight, not the first emergency. The roster

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: Nights, weekends and on-call are a different proposition without another adult at home. Say so at offer stage — it is a normal conversation, and a far harder one to start once you have arrived. School holidays

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.h: Longer than you are used to
chunks.x: The long summer break falls over Christmas and the New Year, exactly when a new arrival has no family nearby and holiday programmes book out early. Check the term dates before you plan your leave for the year. Consent and documentation requirements are set by government: see Immigration New Zealand . Before you fly

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: Share the news in good time and keep the conversation going. Look at photos and maps of where you’re heading, watch videos together, and let them ask the same questions as many times as they need to. Make it real

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: Explore the new town online, find the local playground or beach, and if you can, look at their school’s website together. The more they can imagine the everyday, the less frightening it feels. Honour the goodbye

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: A proper goodbye matters. Help them mark leaving friends, family and a familiar home, a small party, a memory book, swapping addresses, so the move feels like a beginning, not a loss.

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: A favourite toy, blanket or pillow should travel in the hand luggage, never the hold. Familiar things are anchors when everything else is new.

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: Reassure them that grandparents and friends are a video call away. Knowing the people they love haven’t disappeared makes the distance much easier to bear.

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: Let older children choose a few of their own things to bring. A little ownership over the move turns something happening to them into something they’re part of.

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: Carry passports, visas, and copies of immunisation records, medical notes and any prescriptions in your hand luggage, you may need them sooner than you think. The big one

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: It’s usually 24 hours or more with at least one stop. Break the journey

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: A night’s stopover en route (common stops include the Gulf, Singapore or Australia) can split an overwhelming trip into two manageable ones and let small bodies stretch, sleep and reset. Ask for help

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: Request bassinets, children’s meals and seats together when you book, and use family boarding. Cabin crew are well used to travelling children and will lend a hand if you ask. Beat the boredom

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: Snacks, headphones, downloaded shows, and a few small wrapped activities handed out across the hours work wonders. Novelty buys you precious quiet stretches.

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: Comfy layers and familiar pyjamas signal bedtime even at 35,000 feet, and layers cope with cabins that swing from warm to chilly.

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: Feeding, a drink or a chew during take-off and landing helps with pressure. Pack more nappies, wipes and spare clothes than feels sensible.

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: Nudge towards local time over the first few days with daylight, fresh air and patience. Expect early starts and odd-hour wakings for a week or so.

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: Screen-time rules and perfect manners can take the week off. Your only job on the plane is to arrive: everyone, frazzled but together. When you land

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: Keep the first couple of days deliberately small: rest, food and a gentle first look around.

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: Don’t fight the jet lag with a packed schedule. Let everyone sleep, eat simply, and surface slowly. The to-do list can wait a day or two.

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: A trip to the local supermarket, park or beach in the first day or two makes the new place feel ordinary and knowable, fast, for children especially.

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: The familiar bedtime story, the same breakfast, the favourite cup. Tiny rituals carried from home are how children feel safe somewhere new. Real story · arriving in stages Amanda started work in medical imaging in Gisborne five months before her husband and children could follow. They landed the week before this photograph; the children started school the week after it. Plenty of families arrive in two stages, one person starting the job while the rest finish visas, a school year or a house sale. It is a normal way to do this, and the months in between are the hardest part of the whole move. Decide before you go how you will handle them: a fixed call each day, a date in the diary for the second flight, and someone at each end who knows the plan. Finding your feet

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: Routine and friends are the fastest cure for homesickness, so enrol and start school or early childhood education sooner rather than later. Our education guide walks through how it works.

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: Playdates, birthday parties, the local sports club, the swimming lessons: these are where Kiwi childhood friendships form. Accepting invitations, for parents too, is how a family puts down roots.

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: A few weeks in, the novelty fades and the missing-home feelings can arrive, for children and adults alike. It’s a normal stage, not a setback. Keep routines steady and it passes. How families meet people

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: For a lot of New Zealand parents this is the rite of passage: an early start, a coffee from the club rooms and an hour on the sideline. Club sport runs at every age and level here, and it is not only for the children — plenty of parents end up playing too. The winter codes

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: Junior grades start young and run on Saturday mornings through the winter terms, organised by local clubs rather than by schools in most places. Subs are usually modest, and second-hand boots circulate freely. The summer ones

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: Swimming lessons are close to universal — with this much coastline, learning to swim is treated as a life skill rather than a hobby. Cricket, athletics and touch fill the summer terms. And beyond the field

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: Gymnastics, dance, martial arts, Scouts and Guides all run in term time, most of them within a short drive. School newsletters are where these are advertised, so read the first few properly. Water safety is taught early here, and school holiday programmes lean heavily on it — kayaking, sailing, surf lifesaving and swimming all run through the summer break. Worth knowing for a first term: sign-ups tend to happen in the weeks before a season starts rather than during it, and most clubs are run by parent volunteers — which is also why the sideline is where people get to know each other. Different ages, different needs

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: Every child is different. Personality, developmental needs, family circumstances and past moves all shape how quickly they settle, so treat these as starting points. Babies & toddlers

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: 0–4 Often the simplest to move, because their world is you, though sleep and feeding can take a while to recover. Protect routines and keep comfort items close. Primary age

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: 5–10 Many settle well once school starts, though some take longer. Clubs, sport and outdoor activities are an easy way into new friendships. Tweens

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: 11–13 Old enough to feel the loss of friends keenly, young enough to make new ones readily. Help them stay in touch with old friends while gently encouraging clubs and activities that build new circles. Teenagers

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.h: The ones who need a say
chunks.x: 14+ Moving at a decisive age is hard, and they need more time and more involvement. Bring them into decisions, take homesickness seriously, and give the first term or two before judging how it’s going. Told straight

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: Give yourself permission to find it hard. You’re holding down a new job, running an unfamiliar household and being everyone’s reassurance, often without your usual support network nearby. That’s a lot. Build your own footholds early: say yes to the school-gate chat, find one or two other parents, and lean on the communities who’ve made the same move. You don’t have to do it perfectly, and you certainly don’t have to do it alone. If you ever feel you’re struggling more than seems normal, reach out, to your GP, to a helpline, or to us. Asking for support is part of doing this well, not a sign you’ve got it wrong. Sophie’s insight I’ve sat with so many parents who lay awake over this exact question, the flight, the schools, whether they’re doing the right thing by their children. Here’s what I’ve seen, again and again: the kids are usually fine, and often more than fine.

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: They make friends at the park, they take to the outdoors, and within a term this is home. My advice is to look after yourselves as carefully as you look after them, the calmer you are, the faster they settle. And lean on us. Pointing families towards the right school, the right neighbourhood and the right people is one of the parts of this work I love most. Sophie CEO & Founder, Ethicare Resourcing Common questions

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: When’s the best time of year to move with school-age children? The New Zealand school year runs from late January to mid-December, so arriving around the start of the year lets children begin with everyone else. That said, schools take new arrivals throughout the year and are well practised at it, the right time is mostly the one that fits your job and visa, so don’t force it to line up perfectly. How long until the children really settle? Every child is different, but a common pattern is an exciting first few weeks, a dip as the novelty fades and home is missed, and a gradual settling over the following months. Every child is different; teenagers in particular may need longer. Steady routines and getting into school quickly are the things that help most.

chunks.t: Moving with your family
chunks.x: What about childcare while we’re both finding our feet? New Zealand has a well-established early childhood education system, kindergartens, daycare and home-based care, and government funding subsidises hours for children aged three to five, so it’s more affordable than many expect. It’s worth researching and contacting providers before you arrive, as popular centres can have waitlists. Can you help us choose where to live with the family in mind? Yes. For families moving with a role through us, it’s one of the most useful things we do. Tell us your children’s ages, what matters to your family and any schools you’ve got your eye on, and we’ll help you weigh up neighbourhoods, school zones, commutes and the everyday feel of an area before you commit to anywhere. Keep exploring

chunks.t: Your first month in New Zealand
chunks.x: A flexible plan for your first four weeks: what to organise early, what can wait, and what to expect along the way. Kettle on. A longer read — about 7 min

chunks.t: Your first month in New Zealand
chunks.x: Most forms, appointments and rental applications ask for at least one of these, so sort them out first. The best order depends on your visa and how you apply. 1 · A New Zealand address Everything else is asked in relation to it. A short-term rental, serviced apartment or a friend’s spare room all count — you don’t need the permanent one yet. 2 · A bank account Open it before you fly if you can; most banks let you start the process from overseas and finish it in branch with your passport and proof of address. 3 · An IRD number Apply as a new arrival, ideally before your visa’s travel date passes, as that route can be faster. You’ll need a New Zealand bank account or Inland Revenue’s IR997 identity form. Your employer needs the number before your first pay run. Inland Revenue’s steps 4 · A phone number Asked for by almost every form, appointment and rental application you’ll make.

chunks.t: Your first month in New Zealand
chunks.x: A prepay SIM at the airport is enough to start. The one that costs real money Your employer will ask you to complete an IR330 tax code declaration before your first pay run. If you have no IRD number yet, you’re taxed at the no-notification rate — considerably higher than your real rate — until you produce one. It’s refunded eventually, but "eventually" can mean the end of the tax year. Apply for the IRD number as soon as you can, and give it to your employer as soon as it arrives.

chunks.t: Your first month in New Zealand
chunks.x: Use it as a guide, not a timetable. Move things around to fit your start date, your visa and who is arriving with you. Week one · Land and anchor Sleep, a SIM card, the bank account finished in branch, the IRD application in. Walk your temporary neighbourhood. Register the household with a GP near where you’ll live. Feels: disorienting, and faster than you expected. Week two · Wheels and paperwork Start the licence conversion, rent or buy a car, get a local public transport card. First shifts and orientation. If children are with you, contact schools and check the zone for any address before you sign. Feels: busy, productive, tiring. Week three · Viewings and the dip Serious house-hunting, references ready, applications in the same day. For many people, this is when the adrenaline runs out. Feels: harder than week one, and completely normal. Week four · Settle and join Lease signed, utilities and broadband connected. If you hold residence, decide on KiwiSaver. Join one thing that isn’t work. Feels: like the beginning of an ordinary life rather than a very long trip.

Real story · day one What Janita’s new department left on her desk in her first week in Auckland: a bag of New Zealand things and a card from the team. It cost them almost nothing and it is the part she mentioned first. If a team does this for you, that is a fair signal about the team. Janita’s first two years →

chunks.t: Your first month in New Zealand
chunks.h: Six things that won’t be done in a month
chunks.x: A month is enough to be functional, not settled. These usually take longer, and the timings vary a lot from person to person. Feeling at home in the department Three to six months before the systems, the shorthand and the referral pathways stop taking conscious effort. A settled circle of friends Six to twelve months, and it depends almost entirely on what you joined in month one. Knowing the city A year, and a few wrong turns. You’ll pick the right beach for the conditions eventually. The right house Most people move once. Renting first and choosing properly second is the sensible plan, not a failure. Residency, if that’s the plan Measured in years rather than months, and worth starting the paperwork trail early. Not converting every price Six months or so before you stop doing mental exchange-rate arithmetic in the supermarket. “Do one non-essential thing in your first week.

chunks.t: Your first month in New Zealand
chunks.h: Six things that won’t be done in a month
chunks.x: A walk up a volcano, a swim, a ferry to nowhere in particular. It will feel indulgent when you have a hundred jobs on a list — that is exactly why it works. The admin will still be there on Monday, and you will have one memory of the place that is not a queue or a form. Start collecting those early.” Sophie Careem — Founder & CEO, Ethicare Resourcing Each of these has a chapter of its own when you need the detail: Money, tax & banking for your IRD number, first payslip and KiwiSaver; Driving & licences for converting your licence and buying a car; and Schools & education for zoning and enrolment.

chunks.t: Your first month in New Zealand
chunks.h: If your family is with you
chunks.x: A first month with a partner and children looks different from one on your own. Five things to plan for: School enrolment State schools usually enrol by home zone, so check the zone before you sign a lease. Whether your children count as domestic students depends on your visa. Schools & education Childcare Early childhood places can have waiting lists, so contact centres before you arrive. Ask each one how your visa affects fees and funded hours. Your partner’s work Whether they can work, and for whom, depends on the visa they were granted. If they work in a regulated profession, their registration can take months, so start early. Getting around Work out the school run and your commute before you choose where to live. Routines A regular mealtime, bedtime and weekend plan helps children settle while everything else is new. There is more in moving to New Zealand with your family .

chunks.t: Your first month in New Zealand
chunks.h: The shape of the first year
chunks.x: Many people describe something like these four phases, though the timing varies a lot. Knowing the shape in advance takes much of the alarm out of the middle of it. First weeks The honeymoon Everything is new — the scenery, the accents, the supermarket — and the adrenaline of setting up a life carries most of it. It does not stay this heightened, and that is not a loss. First months The dip Once the admin list runs out and the novelty thins, the distance from home, the small frustrations and the effort of starting over tend to arrive together. For some people it comes within weeks; for others, months. It says nothing about whether the decision was right. Having something in the calendar that isn’t admin helps. Around six months Finding your feet Routines form: a GP, a favourite beach, people you would call on a bad day.

chunks.t: Your first month in New Zealand
chunks.h: The shape of the first year
chunks.x: Work stops taking conscious effort, the children have friends, and the place stops feeling like somewhere you are visiting. The first year Home You stop converting prices, you know the back roads, and you are the one giving the next arrival directions. It rarely happens in a moment. Somewhere in the first year, it has happened.

chunks.t: Your first month in New Zealand
chunks.x: Admin and friendships are only part of it. Four things people who have been through it often say they wish they had known earlier. Homesickness is normal, not failure Missing home does not mean the decision was wrong; it means you valued what you left. It softens as the new life fills in around it, and saying it out loud shortens the process. Stay connected, and be here Regular calls home help. Living entirely online keeps one foot in the old life. Plan the trips back, then let yourself be fully here in between. Judge it at a year, not at month three The first year has seasons, literally and emotionally. A “was this a mistake?” decision taken in the dip is taken on the worst evidence you will ever have. Ask for help early A GP, a community group, a colleague, or us. Reaching out early is what the people who settled did, not a sign of struggling. The people side has a chapter of its own, finding your community , What we do in those months is set out once, on the About page . Ethicare Resourcing

chunks.t: Your first month in New Zealand
chunks.h: This chapter is part of a bigger guide — and we’re here for the rest of it
chunks.x: We place healthcare professionals across New Zealand and Australia, and stay with the move through registration, visas and the first months after you land. Careers in New Zealand → Ask Ethicare

chunks.t: Healthcare in New Zealand explained
chunks.h: A publicly funded system, built on care for everyone
chunks.x: New Zealand’s health system is largely public, funded through taxation, and free or low-cost for residents and many people on longer work visas. For you, this matters in two ways. As a new resident, it shapes how you and your family will access care. And as a healthcare professional, it shapes the system you’ll practise within: its values, its structure and its priorities. A little orientation now makes both feel far less unfamiliar. Check your eligibility first. Publicly funded care is for citizens, residents and people whose work visa lets them stay for two years or more (or who have already been here lawfully for two years in a row). Your partner and children are not covered because you are: each person’s eligibility depends on their own visa. If someone in the family is not eligible, they pay for care at full price unless they have insurance, so settle this before you fly.

chunks.t: Healthcare in New Zealand explained
chunks.h: A publicly funded system, built on care for everyone
chunks.x: Use Health New Zealand’s eligibility guide . Updated eligibility regulations take effect on 1 December 2026. Most existing rules are unchanged, including the two-year work visa test, and lawful time already spent in New Zealand can count towards the two years in some cases. Reviewed 14 October 2026; confirm the current position at the source. How it’s structured

chunks.t: Healthcare in New Zealand explained
chunks.h: Health New Zealand | Te Whatu Ora
chunks.x: The national organisation that runs publicly funded health services, hospitals, specialist and community care, across the country. Recent reforms brought services under one national body to make care more consistent wherever you live. Primary care

chunks.t: Healthcare in New Zealand explained
chunks.x: General practitioners are the front door to most healthcare. You enrol with a local practice, and your GP handles everyday care and referrals onward to hospital or specialist services when needed. Accident cover

chunks.t: Healthcare in New Zealand explained
chunks.x: A uniquely New Zealand feature: a national scheme that covers treatment for injuries from accidents, for everyone, regardless of fault, including visitors. More on this below. The private system

chunks.t: Healthcare in New Zealand explained
chunks.x: A private sector runs alongside the public one. Many people hold private health insurance for faster access to elective procedures and more choice, while relying on the public system for emergencies and complex care. The one that surprises people

chunks.t: Healthcare in New Zealand explained
chunks.x: ACC is a no-fault scheme covering treatment and rehabilitation for accidental injury, for residents and visitors alike. In return you generally cannot sue for personal injury — one of the things newcomers find most unfamiliar.

chunks.t: Healthcare in New Zealand explained
chunks.x: If you’re injured in an accident, you’re covered regardless of who was to blame, at work, on the road, on the ski field or at home.

chunks.t: Healthcare in New Zealand explained
chunks.x: Cover extends to everyone in New Zealand, including international visitors and people on any visa, not only residents.

chunks.t: Healthcare in New Zealand explained
chunks.x: It helps with treatment costs, and can contribute to rehabilitation and lost income while you recover from a covered injury.

chunks.t: Healthcare in New Zealand explained
chunks.x: Illness, most gradual-process conditions, some treatments and part of the cost of others. It is not a substitute for health or travel insurance if you are not eligible for public care. Everyday healthcare

chunks.t: Healthcare in New Zealand explained
chunks.x: One of the first things to do on arrival. Enrolling makes everyday visits cheaper and gives you a regular doctor who knows your family’s history.

chunks.t: Healthcare in New Zealand explained
chunks.x: Primary care is subsidised rather than free for adults, so you pay a part-charge per visit. Care for children is heavily subsidised, and often free.

chunks.t: Healthcare in New Zealand explained
chunks.x: Pharmac, a government agency, decides which medicines are publicly funded, keeping the cost of most prescriptions low at the pharmacy counter.

chunks.t: Healthcare in New Zealand explained
chunks.x: Public hospital and emergency treatment is free for eligible residents. In an emergency, call 111 for an ambulance.

chunks.t: Healthcare in New Zealand explained
chunks.x: A free 24/7 phone line staffed by nurses for health advice when you’re unsure whether to see a doctor, useful in the early days before you have a regular GP.

chunks.t: Healthcare in New Zealand explained
chunks.x: Urgent care clinics handle the things that can’t wait for a GP appointment but aren’t emergencies, handy to know where your nearest one is. Told straight

chunks.t: Healthcare in New Zealand explained
chunks.x: The big, frightening costs are covered, while everyday primary care carries modest charges. Public hospital & emergency Free for eligible residents and citizens, including surgery, specialist and emergency care. Accident-related treatment Largely covered by ACC for everyone, including visitors, with some part-charges depending on the care. GP visits A subsidised part-charge per visit for adults; care for children is heavily subsidised and frequently free. Prescriptions Low cost for funded medicines, thanks to Pharmac subsidies at the pharmacy. Dental & optical (adults) Mostly private and paid for out of pocket, though dental care is free for children and teenagers. Private healthcare Optional: private insurance buys faster access to elective procedures and more choice, on top of public cover. Exact charges vary by practice, region and your eligibility, and the rules can change. Always confirm current detail with the practice or the official sources below. Ethicare are recruitment specialists, not a health authority. Two questions everyone asks

chunks.t: Healthcare in New Zealand explained
chunks.h: Dental care, and whether you need private insurance
chunks.x: Dental is mostly private for adults, and private health insurance is a choice rather than a must. Dental · children

chunks.t: Healthcare in New Zealand explained
chunks.x: Basic dental care is free for children and teenagers up to their 18th birthday, through school dental services and enrolled community providers. It’s one of the quieter things families appreciate here. Dental · adults

chunks.t: Healthcare in New Zealand explained
chunks.x: Adult dental isn’t generally publicly funded, so you pay privately, check-ups, fillings and the rest. Costs vary between practices, so it’s worth comparing and booking a first check-up once you’ve settled. Dental · the exceptions

chunks.t: Healthcare in New Zealand explained
chunks.x: Dental treatment for an accidental injury is covered by ACC, public hospitals handle some acute and emergency dental, and limited grants exist for people on low incomes. Outside those, plan for adult dental as a private cost. Private insurance

chunks.t: Healthcare in New Zealand explained
chunks.x: You don’t need private health insurance to be cared for: the public system covers emergency, hospital and essential care for eligible residents, and ACC covers accidents for everyone. Many people still take out cover for faster elective surgery, more choice of specialist, and sometimes dental and optical extras, and some employers offer it as a benefit. It sits on top of the public system, it doesn’t replace it. Eligibility, funding and grants change over time and depend on your visa and circumstances, confirm the current detail with a practice or the official sources below. Ethicare are recruitment specialists, not a health authority.

chunks.t: Healthcare in New Zealand explained
chunks.h: “Optional” depends on what you are used to
chunks.x: For a clinician arriving from the UK or Ireland, not holding cover is the obvious default. For many of the people we place, it is not. If you are coming from South Africa , a medical aid scheme is close to how a professional household gets care at all; the premium is a fixed, substantial line in the monthly budget, and stopping it would be unthinkable. The same is broadly true arriving from the United States , and from parts of the Gulf and Asia where employer cover is the mechanism rather than a benefit. So families arrive and buy a comprehensive policy on day one, because that is what a responsible parent does where they come from. The difference here is that, for eligible residents, the two things insurance protects you against elsewhere are already largely covered: acute and emergency hospital care through the public system, and treatment for accidental injury through ACC.

chunks.t: Healthcare in New Zealand explained
chunks.h: “Optional” depends on what you are used to
chunks.x: What private insurance adds is choice and speed: elective surgery in weeks rather than months, your choice of specialist, a private room, and sometimes dental and optical extras. If you are weighing Australia too: Australia gives higher earners a tax reason to hold private hospital cover; New Zealand gives none. Here the decision is only about what you want. How the Australian system works explains the difference. Our suggestion: compare cover before you travel rather than after. Check first whether everyone in your family is eligible for public care; anyone who is not needs insurance from day one. If you are all eligible, you may not need comprehensive cover, but look at the policies before you leave, because pre-existing conditions and waiting periods are usually assessed when you join, not when you claim. If your employer offers cover as a benefit, take it.

chunks.t: Healthcare in New Zealand explained
chunks.h: Your first healthcare steps in New Zealand
chunks.x: 0 of 5 Check each family member’s eligibility for publicly funded care How Find a local GP practice taking enrolments How Arrange any ongoing prescriptions or specialist referrals Save Healthline (0800 611 116) and your nearest urgent care Decide on private health and travel insurance before you fly How Save this checklist to my plan Ticks are saved on this device only. Sophie’s insight The clinicians we place often tell me the system here lets them practise the way they always wanted to, with time to know their patients and a team that pulls together. The bits that feel foreign at first, like ACC or enrolling with a GP, become second nature within weeks. My advice is to get your family enrolled with a local practice early, and to come curious about the emphasis on equity and Māori health. It’s one of the things that makes practising here feel meaningful.

chunks.t: Healthcare in New Zealand explained
chunks.h: Your first healthcare steps in New Zealand
chunks.x: One caveat, though: “a team that pulls together” is true of many of the places our clinicians land, not a promise about every one. Team culture varies as much between workplaces here as it does anywhere — so it’s worth asking what a particular team and department are really like when you interview, and talking to people already doing the job. Sophie CEO & Founder, Ethicare Resourcing Official sources

chunks.t: CV & interview preparation | New Zealand
chunks.h: You’ve done the work. This step is about making it easy for someone here to see it.
chunks.x: Most people aren’t overlooked for lack of experience, but because their CV was written for a different health system. And remember: you don’t prepare for this alone. We brief you on the role, the employer and the people you’ll meet, help shape your CV, and run through likely questions before the day. By the time you log on, there are very few surprises left. What employers are reading for

chunks.t: CV & interview preparation | New Zealand
chunks.x: Exactly what you do, where, and at what level: modalities, settings, patient groups and caseload. Specifics reassure; vague job titles don’t travel well across systems. Currency

chunks.t: CV & interview preparation | New Zealand
chunks.x: Evidence you’ve been practising and keeping up to date. A short, plain summary of your most recent roles matters more than a decade-by-decade history. Fit

chunks.t: CV & interview preparation | New Zealand
chunks.h: A sense of who you are
chunks.x: New Zealand teams hire people, not just skill sets. A brief sense of your values, your reasons for moving and how you work helps them picture you in the room. Building your CV

chunks.t: CV & interview preparation | New Zealand
chunks.h: A CV that reads well to a Kiwi eye
chunks.x: This is the structure we find works best for healthcare roles here: clean, scannable and no longer than it needs to be. 1

chunks.t: CV & interview preparation | New Zealand
chunks.x: Three or four lines at the top: who you are, your profession and years of experience, your key strengths, and a sentence on why New Zealand. This is the part most likely to be read in full. 2

chunks.t: CV & interview preparation | New Zealand
chunks.x: Your profession’s registration status (or where you are in the process), your qualifications and any specialist credentials. Employers look for this early. Don’t bury it on page two. 3

chunks.t: CV & interview preparation | New Zealand
chunks.x: For each role: your title, the organisation, dates, and a few bullet points of what you did: modalities, systems, responsibilities and scale. Lead with the relevant, trim the ancient. 4

chunks.t: CV & interview preparation | New Zealand
chunks.x: Equipment, modalities, software and any specialist techniques. For imaging and technical roles especially, naming the systems you’ve worked on tells an employer a great deal at a glance. 5

chunks.t: CV & interview preparation | New Zealand
chunks.x: Recent courses, training and CPD. It signals you’re current and invested, and it reassures boards and employers alike that you keep your practice fresh. 6

chunks.t: CV & interview preparation | New Zealand
chunks.x: You don’t need to print referees on the CV, but have two or three lined up and forewarned. Quick, willing references keep an offer moving. Slow ones are a common, avoidable hold-up. A few small things that matter

chunks.t: CV & interview preparation | New Zealand
chunks.x: Keep it to two or three clean pages, with plenty of white space. Use plain, consistent formatting, no photos, no graphics, no clutter. Spell out acronyms a New Zealand reader may not know. Tailor your summary slightly to each role you apply for. Proofread, then have someone else proofread again.

chunks.t: CV & interview preparation | New Zealand
chunks.x: A ten-page CV listing every course since graduation. Dense paragraphs where clear bullet points would do. Local jargon or system names with no explanation. Gaps left unexplained, a brief note is always better than a mystery. Sending the same generic CV to every single employer. The interview

chunks.t: CV & interview preparation | New Zealand
chunks.h: What to expect on the day
chunks.x: Most first interviews are by video call, often conversational. They want to know you can do the job, fit the team and have thought the move through. S

chunks.t: CV & interview preparation | New Zealand
chunks.x: Set the scene briefly, where you were and what was happening. T

chunks.t: CV & interview preparation | New Zealand
chunks.x: What you were responsible for, or the challenge you faced. A

chunks.t: CV & interview preparation | New Zealand
chunks.x: What you did, the specific steps you took, not the team’s. R

chunks.t: CV & interview preparation | New Zealand
chunks.x: How it turned out, and what you learned or improved. Come ready for these

chunks.t: CV & interview preparation | New Zealand
chunks.x: Have a real example ready for the behavioural questions. That’s where STAR earns its keep. About your practice Talk me through your clinical experience and scope. What modalities, systems or caseloads are you strongest in? How do you keep your skills and knowledge current? Describe a clinically challenging case and how you handled it. About working together Tell me about a time you handled a difficult patient or colleague. How do you cope when a shift gets busy or stressful? Describe a mistake or near-miss and what you did next.

chunks.t: CV & interview preparation | New Zealand
chunks.x: How do you fit into and support a team? About the move Why New Zealand, and why now? What do you know about our region and service? How are you planning the practical side of relocating? Where do you see yourself settling for the longer term? Te Tiriti, cultural safety & equity How would you contribute to improving health equity for Māori patients in your clinical practice? How does Te Tiriti o Waitangi apply to your practice? How do you provide culturally safe care? Tell us about a time you involved a patient’s whānau in a decision. Your questions for them What does induction and support look like for new arrivals? How is the team structured, and who would I work with? What does a typical week or roster look like? What are you hoping the right person brings to this role?

chunks.t: CV & interview preparation | New Zealand
chunks.h: The question to prepare for: health equity for Māori
chunks.x: Most New Zealand clinical interviews now ask about Māori health equity, cultural safety or Te Tiriti o Waitangi, and often all three. Nobody expects an overseas candidate to be an expert. The panel is listening for three things: that you know why equity matters, that you can name something practical you would do, and that you will keep learning. “How would you contribute to improving health equity for Māori patients in your clinical practice?” A model answer, in four beats. What you understand. “Māori have poorer outcomes across many measures and more barriers to getting care on time, so giving everyone the same care doesn’t produce the same outcomes. I’ve read the Ministry’s Te Tiriti framework and your service’s equity priorities. That’s a start, not expertise.” What you would do. “I’d look for the barriers I can affect: transport, cost, language, appointment times.

chunks.t: CV & interview preparation | New Zealand
chunks.h: The question to prepare for: health equity for Māori
chunks.x: When a Māori patient misses an appointment I’d want to find out why before anyone is discharged from the list, and ring rather than re-send a letter.” An example of your own. One time you removed a barrier for a patient anywhere in the world: an interpreter instead of a relative, a double appointment, asking who they wanted in the room. What you would ask of them. “I’d want to know who the Māori health team are and how I refer, in my first week, and I’d want to be told when I get something wrong.” What makes it work: it names the inequity plainly, spends most of its time on something concrete, and ends by asking for help, which reads as humility rather than weakness. Read Te ao Māori at work first; it covers the ground in about seven minutes. Then practise the answer in the interview preparation tool , which has a worked example from a radiographer.

chunks.t: CV & interview preparation | New Zealand
chunks.h: The question to prepare for: health equity for Māori
chunks.x: Sophie’s insight The clinicians who interview best aren’t the slickest, they’re the ones who sound like themselves. New Zealand employers can spot a rehearsed answer a mile off, and what wins them over is warmth, honesty and a clear reason for wanting to be here. So prepare your examples, yes, but don’t over-polish. Tell me a real story from your work and let your care for patients show. That, far more than a perfect CV, is what gets the offer. Sophie CEO & Founder, Ethicare Resourcing Common questions

chunks.t: CV & interview preparation | New Zealand
chunks.h: The things people ask us first
chunks.x: How long should my CV be? Two to three pages is the sweet spot for most healthcare roles. Long enough to show your experience and registration clearly, short enough that a busy hiring manager reads it all. Lead with your most recent and relevant work, and don’t feel you must document every course you’ve ever done, a focused CV reads as confident. Will the interview be in person or online? Almost always a video call for the first round, since you’ll likely still be overseas. They’re usually relaxed and conversational. We’ll tell you who you’ll be meeting and what to expect, and it’s always worth testing your camera, sound and a quiet, well-lit spot beforehand so the tech is one less thing to think about. What if I’m asked something I don’t know? Honesty lands far better than bluffing.

chunks.t: CV & interview preparation | New Zealand
chunks.h: The things people ask us first
chunks.x: It’s completely fine to say you haven’t met that exact situation, then talk through how you’d approach it or relate it to something similar you have done. Thoughtfulness and self-awareness reassure an employer much more than a confident guess that doesn’t ring true. How do I talk about wanting to move? Simply. Employers know New Zealand is a lifestyle move and they’re glad of it. What they want to hear is that you’ve thought it through and you’re likely to stay. A clear, real reason, whether that’s family, balance or the kind of practice you’re after, is exactly the right answer. Can you help me prepare? Absolutely, it’s a core part of what we do. We brief you on the role and the employer, help shape your CV, talk through likely questions, and answer anything you’re unsure about before the day. The downloadable interview guide above is a good place to start, and then we pick up from there together. Next · Stage 07

chunks.t: Which agreement sets your pay in New Zealand
chunks.h: Everything here is public. Almost nobody reads it.
chunks.x: Every one of these agreements is published in full. You are entitled to read the document that will govern your salary before you accept a job. What people struggle with is knowing which one. There are more than a dozen in circulation, several professions sit under agreements with names that do not match their job title, and a few of the documents you will find first have expired. So this is the register: what covers each profession, how long it runs, and where to read it yourself. This page is deliberately a register, not an explainer. How pay works . Steps, progression, what sits on top of base salary, tax and take-home, is explained once, in Salary & pay, explained . The register

chunks.t: Which agreement sets your pay in New Zealand
chunks.x: When an agreement expires its terms continue to apply until a replacement is ratified, so nobody’s pay stops. But we will not print a figure from an expired document, and neither should anyone else. Profession Agreement Runs to Status Psychologists Cover depends on the employer Confirm which agreement applies before relying on a figure, the independent-provider agreement we hold expired on 30 June 2026 Psychologist roles → Expired In bargaining Sonographers, private sector An APEX agreement with an independent provider Expired 31 Jul 2026 In bargaining Radiology, private sector An APEX agreement with an independent radiology provider Expired 31 Mar 2026 In bargaining General practice is the one gap. There is no single collective agreement for GPs . Pay depends on whether you are salaried by a practice, employed through a primary health organisation, or contracting, and it is negotiated individually. It is the one area where the number really does depend on the conversation. The thing that surprises people

chunks.t: Which agreement sets your pay in New Zealand
chunks.x: Open the physiotherapy, occupational therapy, dietetics, social work, radiation therapy and anaesthetic technology agreements side by side and you find the same ten steps, to the dollar. That is the allied pay equity settlement: your step sets your salary, not your profession. Step 10 Recognition step $119,300 Step 9 Recognition step $116,133 Step 8 Additional progression step, by agreed objectives $112,965 Step 7 Top automatic step $110,290 Step 6 $107,414 Step 5 $102,667 Step 4 $96,754 Step 3 $90,843 Step 2 $84,927 Step 1 Entry, on registration $79,014 Radiation therapy Occupational therapy Physiotherapy Dietetics Social work Anaesthetic technology Steps 1 to 7 are automatic , one a year on your anniversary date. Step 8 depends on objectives you set with your manager when you reach step 7.

chunks.t: Which agreement sets your pay in New Zealand
chunks.x: Steps 9 and 10 are recognition steps for experienced practitioners who are not in a designated role. Designated roles sit above this. Team leader, section head and professional advisor positions run on a separate six-grade scale reaching into the $150,000s. The figures above are the rates payable from the 2026 anniversary in the radiation therapy, occupational therapy, dietetics, social work and anaesthetic technology agreements. Physiotherapy is one increase round behind on the calendar and runs a few hundred dollars lower until its next anniversary; every agreement steps up again during 2027. Where you land on this ladder is the single biggest decision in your offer, and it is set by how your overseas experience is counted. That is worth getting right rather than accepting. Imaging, sonography, nursing and midwifery run on their own scales, not this one. Sonography in particular sits well above it , and reporting sonographers higher again, on a separate scale in the same agreement. Read the documents yourself
