chunks.t: Which agreement sets your pay in New Zealand
chunks.x: Every agreement Health New Zealand | Te Whatu Ora is party to, including nursing and the senior medical agreements. The salary scales live in the appendices at the back of each document. tewhatuora.govt.nz The two lists do not always agree. Where a newly settled agreement appears on one and not the other, the more recent document is usually the operative one, but if a figure matters to a decision you are making, ask us or ask the union rather than guessing between them. The limits

chunks.t: Which agreement sets your pay in New Zealand
chunks.h: What a collective agreement will not tell you
chunks.x: It sets the scale. It does not settle your salary, and reading it will leave four questions open.

chunks.t: Which agreement sets your pay in New Zealand
chunks.x: The agreement says the employer will take your years of experience in the occupation into account, and may go higher where recruitment is difficult. That is discretion, and discretion is where an offer is won or lost.

chunks.t: Which agreement sets your pay in New Zealand
chunks.x: Penal rates, on-call, call-back, allowances and overtime are all in the agreement, but what you will earn depends on the roster you are given. Two people on the same step can take home materially different amounts.

chunks.t: Which agreement sets your pay in New Zealand
chunks.x: Designated positions run on their own grades and are graded by the employer against the responsibilities of the post. Whether a job is designated is a question about that specific job, not about your profession.

chunks.t: Which agreement sets your pay in New Zealand
chunks.h: What it means where you are going to live
chunks.x: Clinical pay is national. The cost of living is not. The same step is a comfortable salary in one region and a stretch in another, and no agreement addresses that. All four of these are things we work out with you before you decide, against the agreement and in writing. Apply and we’ll give you the number for your role . Profession, years of experience, and where you are thinking of going is enough to start. Common questions

chunks.t: Which agreement sets your pay in New Zealand
chunks.h: Questions we get about the agreements
chunks.x: Do I have to join the union to be paid on the agreement? No. Your terms are set by the agreement that covers your role, and you do not have to be a member to be employed on it. Membership is your decision. Some agreements do provide that a new member is placed on the scale from the point they join, so if you are weighing it up, ask the relevant union directly rather than your employer. My agreement has expired. Has my pay stopped rising? Your existing terms continue to apply until a replacement is ratified, so nothing lapses and your annual step progression continues. What pauses is the across-the-board increase that a new agreement usually brings. Back pay to an agreed date is common when one settles, but it is negotiated rather than guaranteed.

chunks.t: Which agreement sets your pay in New Zealand
chunks.h: Questions we get about the agreements
chunks.x: Why will you not quote me a salary until you have checked? Because a figure from the wrong column of the right document is still wrong, and it is the sort of wrong that surfaces on someone’s first payslip in a new country. Most of these agreements carry three dated columns and a separate designated scale. We take a day and give you the number you will be paid. Does my overseas experience count towards my step? Experience in the occupation is what the agreements direct the employer to take into account, and that is not limited to New Zealand. How much of it is recognised in practice varies, and it is one of the few negotiable parts of a clinical offer. Come to that conversation with your years set out clearly and evidenced. Is the private sector paid on these agreements? Some independent providers hold their own collective agreements, and several appear in the register above.

chunks.t: Which agreement sets your pay in New Zealand
chunks.h: Questions we get about the agreements
chunks.x: Many do not, in which case pay is individually negotiated. If you are considering a private role, ask at the outset whether a collective agreement applies. The answer changes what there is to discuss. Keep exploring

chunks.t: Which agreement sets your pay in New Zealand
chunks.x: How the steps work, what sits on top of base pay, tax, take-home and ACC. The whole picture, once. Read the guide Stage 04

chunks.t: Which agreement sets your pay in New Zealand
chunks.x: Your scope and registration decide which agreement covers you, and where you sit on it. Read Stage 04 Professions

chunks.t: Which agreement sets your pay in New Zealand
chunks.x: Profession by profession: registration, how pay is structured, and what the work is like. Browse professions Free, any time

chunks.t: Which agreement sets your pay in New Zealand
chunks.h: Want the number for your role?
chunks.x: Tell us your profession and how long you have been qualified, and we will confirm which agreement covers you, where you would sit on it, and what the full package looks like where you are thinking of living. In writing, before you decide anything. Ask Ethicare about pay Browse current opportunities Ethicare Resourcing · your guide to a life and career in New Zealand.

chunks.t: Practising in Aotearoa New Zealand
chunks.x: Kettle on. A longer read — about 9 min The system itself is explained properly in how healthcare works in New Zealand . This is the clinician’s summary of it. Who pays

chunks.t: Practising in Aotearoa New Zealand
chunks.x: The public system, ACC, private insurance and the person themselves. A single episode of care can involve more than one, and which one is paying changes what you are able to offer. The distinctive one

chunks.t: Practising in Aotearoa New Zealand
chunks.x: A no-fault accident scheme that funds treatment and rehabilitation directly. It has no real equivalent elsewhere, and it is why a large community and private sector exists alongside the public one. Where care happens

chunks.t: Practising in Aotearoa New Zealand
chunks.h: Closer to home than you expect
chunks.x: Homes, workplaces, schools, marae and community clinics carry a real share of the work. Keeping people independent and out of hospital is a funded objective, not an aspiration. Scale

chunks.t: Practising in Aotearoa New Zealand
chunks.x: Fewer specialist services, broader scopes of practice, and a professional community small enough that you are likely to know your national counterparts inside a year.

chunks.t: Practising in Aotearoa New Zealand
chunks.x: Equality is giving everyone the same. Equity is giving people what they need to reach the same outcome — and here the distance between the two is measured, published and acted on. In practice Two people with the same diagnosis may need different amounts of your time. Giving it to them is the standard, not favouritism.

chunks.t: Practising in Aotearoa New Zealand
chunks.x: Care is something done with people rather than to them: shared goals, real choice, informed decisions, and family in the room by default rather than by invitation. In practice Record goals in the person’s own words. A goal that means something to them is far more likely to be met than one that means something to you.

chunks.t: Practising in Aotearoa New Zealand
chunks.x: Teams are flatter and less territorial than in many systems. You are expected to know what the other professions contribute, and to ask when you do not. In practice Handovers and case conferences carry real clinical weight. Being new is not a reason to stay quiet in them.

chunks.t: Practising in Aotearoa New Zealand
chunks.x: Keeping people well is taken as seriously as treating them once they are not. Avoiding an admission counts as an outcome in its own right. In practice You may be asked what you did to prevent the next episode, not only what you did about this one.

chunks.t: Practising in Aotearoa New Zealand
chunks.x: Demand is shifting towards rehabilitation, chronic conditions, disability and supporting independence at home. That is where the growth in most professions sits. In practice More of your caseload will be long-term and community-based than you are used to, and less of it will resolve.

chunks.t: Practising in Aotearoa New Zealand
chunks.x: The split most systems maintain between the two is treated here as a gap to close rather than a boundary to respect. In practice Asking about mood, sleep, work and housing is part of a physical assessment, not a trigger for a referral elsewhere.

chunks.t: Practising in Aotearoa New Zealand
chunks.x: Aotearoa New Zealand has a Treaty relationship at the centre of its health system. You are expected to arrive willing, not expert. We explain each of these once, properly, in the guide that owns it rather than three times in different words. Here is what they are and why they will matter to you by your second week.

chunks.t: Practising in Aotearoa New Zealand
chunks.x: The founding agreement between Māori and the Crown, and a live part of how health services are designed, funded and assessed — not a historical footnote. For a clinician it asks three things: partnership , participation and protection . What each one looks like on a shift

chunks.t: Practising in Aotearoa New Zealand
chunks.h: Māori health and Te Whare Tapa Whā
chunks.x: Improving Māori health outcomes is one of the system’s defining priorities. You will meet Māori models of health early — most often Te Whare Tapa Whā, which understands wellbeing as physical, mental, family and spiritual together, standing on connection to place. The model, and how to use it

chunks.t: Practising in Aotearoa New Zealand
chunks.x: New Zealand’s Pacific population is large, young and diverse — and “Pacific” is not one culture. Samoan, Tongan, Cook Islands, Niuean, Fijian and other communities differ in language, faith and family structure. Family and church are often central both to a decision and to whether a plan is followed at home. Ask; do not assume. Communities and everyday life Cultural safety is a competency, not a module Clinical competence is performing the technique correctly. Cultural safety is the patient’s judgement of whether your care was safe for them — which is why you cannot self-certify it, and why your board assesses it as an ongoing competency rather than something you complete at induction. Day to day it is unremarkable good practice: pronounce names correctly, ask who should be part of the conversation, explain before you touch, notice when someone has gone quiet, and accept correction without defending yourself. The practical checklist sits here .

chunks.t: Practising in Aotearoa New Zealand
chunks.h: Where you practise changes the job
chunks.x: More than the job title does. In New Zealand distance is a clinical factor rather than a lifestyle preference. Why one contact has to count A rural highway in the South Island. Ninety minutes each way is an ordinary journey for an appointment here — which is why rural clinics are designed around a single contact that leaves the person with something they can run themselves, rather than a course of six.

chunks.t: Practising in Aotearoa New Zealand
chunks.x: Dispersed populations, long travel times and fewer specialist services mean broader scope, more autonomy and telehealth as ordinary practice rather than an add-on. Regional recruitment is one of the country’s most persistent workforce priorities — some of the most interesting work is there, and so is the professional isolation. We will tell you about both. Often true: one contact instead of six · a broader caseload · decisions you make rather than escalate · a community that knows who you are

chunks.t: Practising in Aotearoa New Zealand
chunks.x: Sub-specialty depth, teaching, research and the largest teams, concentrated in a handful of cities and carrying national service responsibilities.

chunks.t: Practising in Aotearoa New Zealand
chunks.x: A real share of the work happens in houses, workplaces, schools and on marae. You will drive, you will carry your own diary, and you will see people in the environment they live in.

chunks.t: Practising in Aotearoa New Zealand
chunks.x: Care designed and delivered by and for the community, usually with whānau at the centre of the model rather than at its edge. You will refer to them and work alongside them. The further you are from a main centre, the broader you become.

chunks.t: Practising in Aotearoa New Zealand
chunks.x: Almost everything that catches experienced clinicians out here is structural rather than clinical. These are the differences every profession meets. The version specific to your discipline sits on your own profession’s page. Terminology Where many clinicians trained Familiar shorthand, and familiar names for services and roles. Often here Different words for the same thing, and te reo Māori used routinely in service names, meetings, notes and greetings. Pronunciation is noticed, and learning it is the easiest respect you will ever earn. Referral pathways Where many clinicians trained Access is referral-gated, and the referral defines the episode. Often here Direct access is common in several professions, and accident-funded care can bring someone to you before anyone else has seen them — which brings triage and red-flag responsibility with it.

chunks.t: Practising in Aotearoa New Zealand
chunks.x: Autonomy Where many clinicians trained Decisions are escalated for approval. Often here You make the call and justify it afterwards. Most clinicians name this as the best part of working here, and the hardest month of the first year. Multidisciplinary working Where many clinicians trained Hierarchical, and organised by profession. Often here Flat, informal and collaborative — with an expectation that you contribute beyond the edge of your own discipline and ask when something is outside it. Public, private and ACC Where many clinicians trained One payer, one set of rules. Often here Three, sometimes for the same person. Each changes your documentation, how much intervention is available to you, and how long you have. Cultural expectations Where many clinicians trained A module, completed once at induction. Often here A competency your board assesses you against, and a professional expectation from your first shift. You aren’t expected to arrive knowing any of this. But understanding the system you are joining is part of becoming a good clinician within it.

chunks.t: Practising in Aotearoa New Zealand
chunks.x: Pronunciation of te reo Māori, of place names, and of the iwi whose area you are moving to. Thirty minutes a week is enough to matter, and getting it wrong without trying is what people notice.

chunks.t: Practising in Aotearoa New Zealand
chunks.h: Read the chapter on te ao Māori at work
chunks.x: Once before you fly and once after your first fortnight — it reads differently the second time. Te ao Māori at work

chunks.t: Practising in Aotearoa New Zealand
chunks.x: It will come up, and understanding how it funds treatment and rehabilitation signals that you have done more than skim a job advert. How healthcare works here

chunks.t: Practising in Aotearoa New Zealand
chunks.x: Who else is in it, how decisions get made, and what is expected of you in a case conference in your first month.

chunks.t: Practising in Aotearoa New Zealand
chunks.h: Ask about the setting, not the title
chunks.x: City, regional or rural, and public, private or accident-funded, change the job far more than the job title does. Ask before you accept, not after you arrive.

chunks.t: Practising in Aotearoa New Zealand
chunks.h: Decide what you want the move to give you
chunks.x: The version of your profession available here is broader than in most systems. Choosing well matters more than choosing quickly, so take the time. One boundary. We explain, sequence and keep a file moving, and we will tell you plainly what we do not know. We are not immigration advisers and we are not your regulator — those decisions sit with the board and with the immigration authority. What we can do is make sure you understand the system before you commit your family to it.

chunks.t: Practising in Aotearoa New Zealand
chunks.x: Tell us what you hold and where you trained, and we will give you a clear read on the system you would be joining — before you spend money on anything. Ask Ethicare → Apply and send your CV Find your profession Te ao Māori at work How healthcare works here Registration Practising in Australia New Zealand

chunks.t: MCNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: At a glance Three scopes, a pathway in each General (resident doctors, RMOs, doctors in training), vocational (independent specialists) and special purpose (temporary). Which pathway you use depends on where you trained and where you have practised. A job offer comes first The pathways most international doctors use require one — with supervision for the comparable health system route, at consultant level for the specialist fast-track — and your employer completes part of the application. Verification before submission Your qualifications must be verified at source through EPIC before the Council will start on your file. Begin it early; it is the slowest step you control. Registered in New Zealand, not before A registration meeting after you arrive confirms identity and supervision. Only then is registration granted and a practising certificate issued — and most international graduates start under supervision. Not all: Australian graduates who completed an internship in Australia, and holders of approved Australasian postgraduate qualifications, may not be required to.

chunks.t: MCNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Read it once to understand the shape of the journey, then come back to each section as you reach it. The checklist at the end remembers what you have ticked, on this device. Understanding the Council The three scopes General scope: which pathway is yours Vocational scope: registering as a specialist Primary source verification References, English and fitness Applying with your employer The registration meeting and your practising certificate Working under supervision, and progression Where people get stuck Questions we are asked most The whole journey on one page The checklist — 32 items, tickable Section 01

chunks.t: MCNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: The Medical Council of New Zealand — Te Kaunihera Rata o Aotearoa — registers doctors under the Health Practitioners Competence Assurance Act 2003 and is responsible for their competence, conduct and fitness to practise. Any doctor applying for registration must be fit for registration and fit to practise medicine; the Council determines this as part of assessing every application.

chunks.t: MCNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Registration places you in a scope of practice. A practising certificate is what lets you work, and for international graduates it carries an endorsement naming your approved employment and supervision. You cannot practise until registration is confirmed and the certificate is issued, and you can only work within what the certificate says.

chunks.t: MCNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: The Council publishes an online registration self-assessment tool that points you to the pathway you may be eligible for. It is the right first step before you gather a document or ask an employer for anything. Job offer → Verification and application → Eligibility letter → Registration meeting in New Zealand → Practising certificate — supervised practice → Change of scope Section 02

chunks.t: MCNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: The Council has three main types of registration, which it calls scopes. Within each there are several pathways, and each pathway has its own requirements. Resident doctors, RMOs, doctors in training

chunks.t: MCNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Preceded by a provisional general period under supervision. The scope most international doctors below consultant level register in. Specialists working independently

chunks.t: MCNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Permanent, specialist registration. International graduates enter through a provisional vocational period under supervision, then apply for the change of scope. Temporary, for a specific purpose

chunks.t: MCNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Six categories: locum tenens, teleradiology, visiting expert, postgraduate training, research, and other special purposes such as a disaster or pandemic. Also supervised. Locum tenens, for twelve months or less, is a mainstream clinical route — but none of these is the way into a permanent post. Every international graduate is supervised at first. Whether you enter a provisional general, provisional vocational or special purpose scope, you work under a Council-approved supervisor while you become familiar with the New Zealand health system and its expected standard of practice. Section 03

chunks.t: MCNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.h: General scope: which pathway is yours
chunks.x: Five pathways for doctors who trained outside New Zealand and Australia. Which one applies depends on where you qualified, where you are registered and where you have recently practised. Competent Authority

chunks.t: MCNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: A primary medical degree from the UK or Ireland, with your internship completed there. Comparable health system

chunks.t: MCNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.h: Recent experience in one of 29 recognised countries
chunks.x: At least 33 months of clinical practice, at 20 or more hours a week, in the 48 months before you apply — in the same or a similar area of medicine, at a similar level of responsibility to the New Zealand post — plus current full or general registration in one of those systems. A separate set of prerequisites exists for general practitioners with a recent postgraduate GP qualification. Examinations

chunks.t: MCNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.h: NZREX Clinical, PLAB 1 and 2, or the AMC exams
chunks.x: Passed within the last five years. This route also needs a job offer as a PGY1 in accredited clinical attachments with an accredited training provider, leading into the two-year prevocational training programme. UK general registrants

chunks.t: MCNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.h: PLAB, 12 months of UK practice, full GMC registration
chunks.x: PLAB Parts 1 and 2 passed within the last five years, full GMC general registration, and 12 months of UK practice that must be Foundation Year 1, FY2 stand-alone, or 12 months in an Approved Practice Setting. Progression also needs ACLS certification within the last 12 months and a minimum three-month supervision period before your supervisor can recommend you. Australian general registrants

chunks.t: MCNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Passed the Australian Medical Council examinations and registered with Ahpra. Read the list, not the label. The Council publishes the 29 comparable health systems and its criteria for them, and it adds countries from time to time. Whether your country is on it — and whether your recent months meet the 33-of-48 test at 20 hours a week — is what decides this pathway, not where you were born or trained. Section 04

chunks.t: MCNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.h: Vocational scope: registering as a specialist
chunks.x: Four pathways. Two are for doctors who already hold an approved New Zealand or Australasian postgraduate qualification; the other two are for specialists trained elsewhere. VOC1 and VOC2

chunks.t: MCNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.h: Approved New Zealand or Australasian qualification
chunks.x: VOC1 if you already hold general scope registration; VOC2 if you do not. VOC3 — provisional vocational

chunks.t: MCNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.h: Trained and qualified as a specialist outside New Zealand and Australia
chunks.x: The Council assesses your training and qualifications on their merits, usually with advice from the relevant New Zealand college. VOC4 — the fast-track

chunks.t: MCNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.h: Approved UK, Irish or Australian postgraduate qualification
chunks.x: For specialists intending to work in an approved area of medicine. Prerequisites: an acceptable primary medical qualification; a postgraduate qualification on the Council’s approved list; at least 24 months’ clinical experience at 0.5 FTE or more in the past five years in that area, including 12 months within the last 18, in a comparable health system; and a job offer at consultant or specialist level. The Council states a processing time of 20 working days from a complete application; psychiatry may take longer.

chunks.t: MCNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: A successful international application leads to a provisional vocational period under supervision, during which the Council satisfies itself that you are competent to practise independently in your field. When you have completed the requirements it sets, you apply for the change of scope to vocational registration. Obstetrics and gynaecology, psychiatry and anatomical pathology carry additional information requirements. Check the approved list, and its date. The VOC4 list of approved postgraduate qualifications is a live document — the Council has added chemical pathology, haematology and microbiology to it. Confirm your qualification and area of medicine are on the current version before you plan around the fast-track. Section 05

chunks.t: MCNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Since November 2017 the Council has required key documents to be verified directly with the institution that issued them, through ECFMG’s EPIC service — now accessed via the MyIntealth portal. You must start this before you submit your application. The verification can take time, and the Council cannot begin processing until it has evidence that it is under way. Of everything in this guide it is the step most worth starting the day you decide to apply, because nothing you or your employer do afterwards can shorten it. 1

chunks.t: MCNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Through the MyIntealth portal; ECFMG publishes instructions specific to New Zealand applicants. 2

chunks.t: MCNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: The independent evidence behind your application — and the three things most often left late. References

chunks.t: MCNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.h: Three, on the Council’s referee report form
chunks.x: The Council describes authentic, authoritative and comprehensive references as necessary to its decisions on fitness and competence, and the references go on its own RP6 referee report form. Who verifies them depends on the scope you are applying for : normally your prospective employer must make a declaration and provide evidence of having verified the reference. For provisional vocational and vocational applications the Council contacts the referee directly. Brief your referees either way. English

chunks.t: MCNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Every applicant must satisfy the Council that they can comprehend and communicate effectively in English in the medical workplace. The policy sets out the routes and any test requirement; scores are not reproduced here because the policy is revised. Check it before booking, and time any test to stay valid. Fitness for registration

chunks.t: MCNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: A legal requirement on the Council. Full disclosure of anything relevant — even matters you consider minor or resolved — is always the right approach; non-disclosure is treated far more seriously than the underlying matter usually is. Section 07

chunks.t: MCNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Applications are made online through the Council’s portal, myMCNZ, and you complete them with your employer — some documents can only be completed by them. Your employer applies for approval of the position and of your supervisor on the Council’s form for your pathway, and the Council publishes a checklist for each pathway listing exactly what to submit. Processing times run from the date the Council receives a complete application, so the checklist is worth reading twice. 1

chunks.t: MCNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.h: Work through the Council’s checklist for your pathway
chunks.x: Every document it lists, certified where required, clearly named. 3

chunks.t: MCNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Fees are published on the Council’s forms, fees and checklists page and revised; confirm before you pay. 5

chunks.t: MCNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: The biggest factor within your control once the file is in. 6

chunks.t: MCNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.h: Receive your eligibility for registration letter
chunks.x: It confirms for other agencies — Immigration New Zealand among them — that you can be registered, and gives you instructions for your registration meeting. Section 08

chunks.t: MCNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.h: The registration meeting and your practising certificate
chunks.x: Every international medical graduate coming to practise in New Zealand for the first time attends a registration meeting, and must be able to produce the information the Council has asked for. The meeting confirms your identity, completes the registration formalities, takes your application for a practising certificate and settles your supervision. For the VOC4 fast-track it takes place within two weeks of your intended start date, and only once you have arrived in New Zealand. After the meeting, and once payment for the practising certificate is received, the Council grants registration in your provisional scope and issues the certificate — allow three days. You cannot practise until then. Registration must be confirmed and the practising certificate in your hands, and you may only work within the endorsement and any conditions noted on it. Plan your start date around the meeting, not the flight. Section 09

chunks.t: MCNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: The provisional period is where the Council satisfies itself that you are ready for the scope you applied for. Three rules shape it. 1

chunks.t: MCNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: In every provisional general, provisional vocational and special purpose scope, under a Council-approved supervisor. 2

chunks.t: MCNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Your practising certificate endorses a specific employment, supervision, position and location. If any of them change you apply for a variation at least 20 working days in advance, and wait for the Council’s approval before starting under the new arrangement. 3

chunks.t: MCNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.h: Progression is applied for, not automatic
chunks.x: Provisional general to general depends on which pathway brought you in . On the comparable health system and UK general registrant routes: 12 months full-time equivalent, three satisfactory supervision reports covering the nine months immediately before you apply, and your supervisor’s recommendation. On the Competent Authority pathway for UK and Irish graduates it is shorter — six months full-time equivalent and two consecutive satisfactory reports. If you have not met them within 12 months you continue under supervision until you have. Provisional vocational to vocational: once you have completed the requirements Council set for you.

chunks.t: MCNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Your general scope is limited to the area of medicine you worked in during the provisional period — unless that was general practice, which carries no limitation. An unlimited general scope needs six months full-time equivalent of supervised practice in medicine and six months in surgery during your provisional general scope — and no more than three months of that medicine may be emergency medicine. Once in the general scope you are no longer supervised, but you must meet the Council’s recertification requirements through the Inpractice programme or an accredited vocational training programme. Where people get stuck

chunks.t: MCNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: EPIC runs at the pace of your medical school. The Council cannot start until it is under way.

chunks.t: MCNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.h: Counting months that do not count
chunks.x: The comparable health system test is 33 of the last 48 months, at 20 hours a week, in a similar area and level. Locum weeks or a different specialty may not qualify.

chunks.t: MCNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.h: Assuming the label, not the list
chunks.x: A country you think of as comparable may not be on the Council’s list; a qualification you think of as approved may not be on the VOC4 list.

chunks.t: MCNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: The comparable health system and VOC4 pathways need one — with supervision, or at consultant level.

chunks.t: MCNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: At least three references, on the Council’s RP6 form. Your employer verifies them for general and special purpose scopes; the Council does it directly for vocational. A slow referee is a slow application.

chunks.t: MCNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.h: Booking the flight around the offer, not the meeting
chunks.x: Registration is granted after the meeting in New Zealand, and the certificate follows payment.

chunks.t: MCNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.h: The fix for all of these
chunks.x: Run the self-assessment, start verification the same day, secure the offer, brief your referees, and read the Council’s checklist for your pathway twice before you and your employer submit. Section 11

chunks.t: MCNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.h: The questions we are asked most
chunks.x: Which scope should I apply for? General scope (through a provisional general period) if you will work as a resident doctor, RMO or in vocational training. Vocational scope (through a provisional vocational period) if you will work independently as a specialist. Special purpose is temporary, for research, training or disaster assistance. The Council’s online self-assessment tool points you to the pathway you may be eligible for. I trained in the UK or Ireland. Which pathway is mine? For general scope, the Competent Authority pathway if your primary medical degree and internship were in the UK or Ireland; or UK general registrants if you passed PLAB Parts 1 and 2, completed 12 months of satisfactory UK practice and hold full GMC registration. For specialists, an approved UK or Irish postgraduate qualification may qualify you for the VOC4 fast-track.

chunks.t: MCNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.h: The questions we are asked most
chunks.x: What counts as a comparable health system? The Council keeps a list — currently 29 countries — assessed against health system infrastructure, population health outcomes and the medical regulatory framework. For the general-scope pathway you need at least 33 months of clinical practice, at 20 or more hours a week, in the 48 months before you apply, in one or more of those systems, in a similar area of medicine and at a similar level of responsibility to the New Zealand post. Do I need a job offer before I apply? Yes, on the pathways most international doctors use. The comparable health system pathway requires a job offer that includes supervision, and the VOC4 fast-track requires a job offer at consultant or specialist level. You complete the application with your employer, because some documents can only be completed by them.

chunks.t: MCNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.h: The questions we are asked most
chunks.x: What is primary source verification? The Council requires key documents — your primary medical qualification and, for specialists, your postgraduate qualification — to be verified directly with the institution that issued them, through ECFMG’s EPIC service (accessed via the MyIntealth portal). Start it before you submit: the Council cannot begin processing until it has evidence the verification is under way. How long does the Council take? For a complete VOC4 fast-track application the Council states 20 working days, with psychiatry applications possibly taking longer. For other pathways the Council publishes its own processing times, which run from receipt of a complete application. The slow parts are usually outside the Council — primary source verification and references.

chunks.t: MCNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.h: The questions we are asked most
chunks.x: What is the registration meeting? A meeting with the Council after you arrive in New Zealand — for VOC4 within two weeks of your intended start date — to confirm your identity, complete formalities, apply for your practising certificate and agree your supervision. Registration is granted after the meeting and payment; allow three days for the practising certificate. You cannot practise until you hold it. Will I be supervised? Yes. Every international medical graduate registered in a provisional general, provisional vocational or special purpose scope must work under supervision while they become familiar with the New Zealand health system. Your practising certificate carries an endorsement naming the approved employment and supervision; any change needs a variation approved by the Council, applied for at least 20 working days in advance.

chunks.t: MCNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.h: The questions we are asked most
chunks.x: How do I move from provisional general to general scope? It is not automatic. You apply once you have completed 12 months full-time equivalent in the provisional general scope, received three satisfactory supervision reports for the nine months immediately before applying, and been recommended by your Council-approved supervisor. Your general scope is then limited to the area you worked in, unless it was general practice or you completed six months each of supervised medicine and surgery. Can Ethicare review my application? Yes. We help you identify the pathway, sequence primary source verification and references so nothing waits on anything else, and read the file against what the Council asks for before you and your employer submit. The registration decision always rests with the Medical Council. Section 12

chunks.t: MCNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Scope, pathway and a job offer — in that order. Run the Council’s registration self-assessment tool It points you to the pathway you may be eligible for. Do it before a single document. Decide the scope you are applying for General (resident doctor, RMO, in training) or vocational (independent specialist). Special purpose is temporary. Confirm your pathway within that scope Competent Authority, comparable health system, examinations, UK or Australian general registrant; or VOC1–VOC4 for specialists. Secure a job offer With supervision for the comparable health system pathway; at consultant or specialist level for VOC4. Note the current fees Registration, the practising certificate and third-party costs. Check the Council’s live fees page.

chunks.t: MCNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Each pathway has its own tests. These are the ones most international doctors meet. An acceptable primary medical qualification Check your medical school against the Council’s acceptable-qualifications list. Comparable health system: 33 months in the last 48 Clinical practice at 20 or more hours a week, in one or more of the 29 recognised countries, in a similar area and at a similar level to the New Zealand post. Comparable health system: current full or general registration With the regulator of at least one comparable system worked in during those 48 months. VOC4: an approved postgraduate qualification On the Council’s approved list, in an approved area of medicine. VOC4: 24 months at 0.5 FTE or more in the past five years Including 12 months within the last 18, in a comparable health system, in that area of medicine. Meet the fitness for registration requirements Health, conduct and competence — full disclosure.

chunks.t: MCNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.h: 03 Primary source verification — start this first
chunks.x: The Council cannot begin processing until it is under way. Open an EPIC account via the MyIntealth portal ECFMG’s Electronic Portfolio of International Credentials. Request verification of your primary medical qualification Sent directly from your medical school. Request verification of your postgraduate qualification, if applying for a vocational scope Keep the evidence that verification is under way You upload it with your application.

chunks.t: MCNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: The independent evidence. Three referees on the Council’s referee report form At least three, on form RP6. Your employer verifies them — the Council does so itself only for vocational applications. CV on the Council’s template where one is specified VOC4 has its own CV template. Meet the Council’s English language policy Check the current routes and any test requirement before booking; time a test to stay valid. Additional information for certain specialties Obstetrics and gynaecology, psychiatry and anatomical pathology have extra forms or requests.

chunks.t: MCNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Some documents can only be completed by them. Request a PIN and create your myMCNZ account Employer completes the approval of position and supervisor form Names your position and your Council-approved supervisor. Submit a complete application with the fee Processing time runs from receipt of a complete application. Respond promptly to any Council request Speed of response is the biggest factor within your control. Eligibility for registration letter received Confirms for Immigration New Zealand that you can be registered, and sets out your registration meeting.

chunks.t: MCNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Registration is confirmed in New Zealand, not before. Attend your registration meeting Identity, formalities, practising certificate application, supervision. For VOC4, within two weeks of your start date. Pay for your practising certificate Allow three days after the meeting for it to be issued. Do not practise until registration is confirmed and you hold the certificate Work only within the endorsement and conditions on it.

chunks.t: MCNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: What the provisional period asks of you. Work under your Council-approved supervisor Required in every provisional and special purpose scope. Apply for a variation before anything changes Employment, supervision, position or location — at least 20 working days in advance, and wait for approval. Provisional general: 12 months FTE, three satisfactory supervision reports, supervisor recommendation Then apply for general scope — it is not automatic. Provisional vocational: complete the requirements Council sets Then apply for change of scope to vocational. Meet recertification requirements once in the general scope Inpractice, or an accredited vocational training programme. Print or save as PDF What next?

chunks.t: MRTB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: At a glance Registration comes first In New Zealand you generally need to be registered — or clearly registrable — before an employer progresses your application. Plan everything else on top of it. You register into a scope Medical imaging, MRI, sonography, nuclear medicine or radiation therapy. MRI and sonography are scopes in their own right; mammography is a specialisation inside the imaging scope. Your qualification decides the scope, not your job title. Two questions, one decision Are you suitably qualified, and are you currently competent and safe? Every document you supply answers one of those two. Supervision is normal Many international registrants start with a supervised period. It is a structured settling-in, not a doubt about your ability.

chunks.t: MRTB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Read it once to understand the shape of the journey, then come back to each section as you reach it. The checklist at the end remembers what you have ticked, on this device. Understanding the Board Which professions register Pathways and assessment Eligibility requirements Preparing your application Employment references English language Completing the application After you submit Where people get stuck Questions we are asked most The whole journey on one page The checklist — 36 items, tickable Section 01

chunks.t: MRTB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: The Medical Radiation Technologists Board registers and oversees medical radiation professionals in New Zealand under the Health Practitioners Competence Assurance Act. Its job is to protect the public by making sure everyone practising in a regulated imaging or radiation therapy role is qualified, competent and fit to do so. The titles and clinical roles are legally protected. You cannot practise, or call yourself a registered practitioner, without being registered with the Board and holding a current practising certificate. That is not a formality — it is the mechanism that tells patients, employers and colleagues you have met a national standard.

chunks.t: MRTB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: The Board registers you into a defined scope — medical imaging, MRI, sonography, nuclear medicine or radiation therapy — and you must practise within it. Your qualification and experience are assessed against the scope you apply for, which is why matching your application to the right scope from the start matters so much.

chunks.t: MRTB registration guide and checklist
chunks.h: Registration and the Annual Practising Certificate
chunks.x: Registration confirms you have met the standard. The Annual Practising Certificate (APC) is what permits you to work, year to year. Think of registration as the licence and the APC as keeping it current: you must hold a valid APC while working, renewed annually alongside a declaration about your health, conduct and continuing professional development. The Board can ask for evidence of CPD, so keep records from day one. Qualification → Registration → Annual Practising Certificate → Practise in New Zealand Section 02

chunks.t: MRTB registration guide and checklist
chunks.h: Which professions register with the MRTB
chunks.x: Your scope is determined by your qualification and the work you are trained and experienced to do — not by your job title, which varies from country to country. Scope

chunks.t: MRTB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Diagnostic images across general X-ray, CT, fluoroscopy and theatre imaging. Technical precision with direct patient care, often across many clinical settings. Scope

chunks.t: MRTB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: The Board defines this scope by three modalities — general, vascular and cardiac ultrasound imaging. Highly autonomous and interpretive, needing strong clinical judgement. Scope

chunks.t: MRTB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Functional imaging with radiopharmaceuticals — PET and SPECT — blending imaging with the safe handling of radioactive materials. Scope

chunks.t: MRTB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Planning and delivering radiation treatment, most often within oncology services, across a whole course of treatment. Scope

chunks.t: MRTB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: A gazetted scope of practice in its own right, not part of the imaging scope. There is no mutual-recognition shortcut into it: see Section 03. Not a scope

chunks.t: MRTB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Mammography is a specialisation within the Medical Imaging Technologist scope, not a separate registration. You register as a Medical Imaging Technologist and practise into it with the appropriate training. Not sure which scope applies to you? Ask before you apply, not after. Assessment against the wrong scope costs months. if you apply through Ethicare, we help you map your background to the right scope so the application is judged against the correct standard from the start. Section 03

chunks.t: MRTB registration guide and checklist
chunks.h: Registration pathways and how you are assessed
chunks.x: At its heart, registration asks two questions: are you suitably qualified, and are you competent and safe to practise within the scope you are applying for? The pathway your application takes is simply the route the Board uses to answer those two questions for your background. Qualification assessment. The Board first considers whether your qualification is comparable to the New Zealand standard for the scope. Some countries and institutions are well recognised; others need closer examination of course content and clinical hours. Competence assessment. Beyond the paper, the Board wants assurance you are currently competent — recent practice, employment references and your clinical history. Requests for more information. Common, and not a red flag: a clearer document, an extra reference, clarification of scope. Responding promptly and completely is the single biggest thing within your control. Possible outcomes

chunks.t: MRTB registration guide and checklist
chunks.h: Being registered with a supervised period is normal, not a setback
chunks.x: Most internationally qualified applicants are registered with an initial period of supervised practice. It is a structured way of supporting you while you settle into the New Zealand system, equipment and protocols — not a sign the Board doubts your ability. Expect it rather than hope to avoid it: on the Board’s own pathway table, a qualification from one of its six recognised countries with three or more years’ practice in the five years before you apply still leads to registration with a condition of supervision. Less recent practice than that, and an examination comes first, with supervision on top. The six recognised countries are Australia, Canada, Ireland, South Africa, the United Kingdom and the United States. Registration granted — you meet the standard and proceed to your APC.

chunks.t: MRTB registration guide and checklist
chunks.h: Being registered with a supervised period is normal, not a setback
chunks.x: Registration with supervised practice — you can work, under the supervision of an experienced colleague for an initial period. Conditions or further requirements — pending additional evidence, assessment or an examination. Further assessment required — the Board asks for more before deciding. If a supervised period applies, factor it in early: you will need an employer and a supervisor who can support it. Many employers are used to this and have arrangements ready.

chunks.t: MRTB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: For some applicants the assessment leads to an online examination. The Board’s own policy sets the trigger: the examination applies to applicants who “do not hold a substantially equivalent qualification”. In practice equivalence turns on two things together — where you trained, and how recent your practice is. A qualification from one of the six recognised countries backed by three or more years’ practice in the last five avoids the examination; less recent practice than that, and it is required. It is a recognised, formal pathway, not a penalty, and the Board runs one for every one of its five scopes. This is where scope matters, and it is the single most important thing on this page if you are an MRI technologist or a sonographer.

chunks.t: MRTB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Australian-registered practitioners in diagnostic radiography, nuclear medicine or radiation therapy are exempt from the examination under trans-Tasman mutual recognition. The Board states plainly that those provisions “do not apply to Australian-registered practitioners wanting to register in either the Sonographer or MRI Technologist scopes of practice in New Zealand”. There is no mutual-recognition shortcut into either scope from anywhere. Every applicant goes through the full overseas-trained assessment, so whether you sit the examination comes down to where you trained and how recent your practice is — and for many people in these two scopes, that means sitting it. Anticipate it rather than be caught out. The exam is sat online under remote proctoring: a supervisor verifies your identity (two forms of ID, one a government-issued photo ID, plus your authorisation code) and oversees the session. The fee is paid in advance and forfeited if you are refused access on the day for failing to establish your identity — have your documents in order. 1

chunks.t: MRTB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: The Board confirms your application and begins its review. 2

chunks.t: MRTB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Your references and recent practice confirm your skills are current. ?

chunks.t: MRTB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Confirmed, sometimes with conditions or a supervised period. Section 04

chunks.t: MRTB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Qualifications Required: a recognised qualification appropriate to the scope you are applying for. Why: your qualification is the foundation of safe practice. The New Zealand qualifications that lead to registration are bachelor’s degrees (Level 7 on the New Zealand Qualifications Framework), so that is broadly the benchmark. The Board does not simply count years: it assesses whether your qualification is equivalent to, or as satisfactory as, an approved New Zealand qualification for your scope — content, clinical hours and outcomes, not level alone. If you are not certain how yours compares, check before you apply. Recent practice Required: evidence that you have practised recently and to a sufficient extent. Why: skills fade when unused. If you have had a significant break, flag it early so it is addressed rather than discovered mid-assessment.

chunks.t: MRTB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: English language Required: evidence of English language ability — Section 07. Why: clear communication is a patient-safety issue: referrals, explaining procedures, precise communication with patients and colleagues. Fitness to practise Required: a declaration, and sometimes evidence, about your physical and mental health as it relates to safe practice. Why: this is about practising safely, not about excluding people with health conditions. The vast majority of declarations raise no issues. Professional conduct Required: disclosure of any disciplinary history, conditions or investigations. Why: the Board must protect patients. Full disclosure — even of matters you think minor or resolved — is always right. Non-disclosure is treated far more seriously than the underlying matter usually is.

chunks.t: MRTB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Certificates of Good Standing Required: one from every regulator you have been registered with, sent directly to the MRTB. Why: they are how one regulator tells another you have no unresolved concerns. They have a limited validity window, which makes their timing one of the trickier parts of an application — Section 05. Read every requirement as a question. The Board is asking whether you are safe to practise. Frame each document as the answer to that question and your application becomes far more persuasive. Section 05

chunks.t: MRTB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: The Board describes these documents as a legal requirement and says provision of them is non-negotiable, so treat the list as a list rather than a guide. How it looks matters more than people expect. The Board is forming a picture of you as a professional, and a folder of crooked, half-legible photocopies quietly undermines that picture even when every document is genuine. Clean colour scans, pages straight and square, nothing cut off, consistent file names, certification and translations done properly the first time. Treat it like a portfolio you would be proud to hand over.

chunks.t: MRTB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Why Confirms identity and nationality; underpins your visa and right to work. Where Your existing passport — valid, and not expiring mid-process. Mistake A passport close to expiry, or a scan that crops the machine-readable strip. Tip Scan the full photo page flat, in colour, all four edges visible.

chunks.t: MRTB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Why They prove you hold the qualification registration is based on. Where Your awarding university or college; request certified copies early if originals are missing. Mistake Only the final certificate, when the Board also wants the detail of what you studied. Tip Keep certificates and transcripts together — they are assessed as a pair.

chunks.t: MRTB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Why Course content, clinical hours and modules — often what lets the Board map your training to a scope. Where Your institution’s registry; many issue official transcripts directly. Mistake Missing pages, or transcripts that do not show clinical placement hours. Tip If the transcript is light on clinical detail, add a course outline or syllabus.

chunks.t: MRTB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Why Demonstrates recent practice and the breadth of your experience. Where Compiled by you — accurate and complete. Mistake Unexplained gaps, or dates that do not match the rest of the application. Tip Account for every period. A one-line explanation of a break beats an unexplained hole. Build your CV is written for this.

chunks.t: MRTB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Why Confirm good standing with every regulator you have registered with. Where Requested from each regulator and sent directly to the MRTB — not via you. Mistake Requested too early so they expire before assessment; or a regulator from years ago forgotten. Tip Limited validity, so timing is everything. Line them up to arrive when the application is ready, not months before.

chunks.t: MRTB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Why They verify competence and recent practice — so important they have Section 06 to themselves. Where Current and recent supervisors or managers. Mistake A referee chosen for seniority rather than knowledge of your clinical work. Tip Brief your referees properly — read Section 06 before approaching anyone.

chunks.t: MRTB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Why If your name differs across documents, the Board needs to link them to one person. Where Marriage certificate, deed poll or equivalent. Mistake A name difference between a degree certificate and a passport, overlooked. Tip Check every document carries a consistent name, and include the bridging document if not.

chunks.t: MRTB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Why A separate requirement from good standing, and the one applicants most often miss entirely. The Board asks for two — one personal, one professional. Where A professional colleague and someone who knows you personally. Neither is the same thing as a clinical reference or a certificate of good standing. Mistake Assuming your Certificates of Good Standing cover this. They do not.

chunks.t: MRTB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Why Your record of cases and procedures from training. It evidences the clinical content behind your qualification. Where Your training institution or your own records. Often left behind in a move — look for it before you need it. Mistake Finding out it is in a box in another country, six weeks into the application.

chunks.t: MRTB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Why It lets the Board map what you were taught against the New Zealand standard for your scope. Required, not a nice-to-have. Where Your institution’s registry or course handbook for your year of study — not the current version of the course. Mistake Sending the modern prospectus instead of the curriculum you were taught.

chunks.t: MRTB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Why Where your qualification included one, the Board lists it among the documents it asks for. Where Your institution, or your own copy. Mistake Omitting it because it feels academic rather than clinical.

chunks.t: MRTB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Why The Board’s own form, capturing your practice in the shape it wants to assess. Where Downloaded from the Board, completed from your records. Mistake Filling it from memory so it quietly disagrees with your CV and employment certificates.

chunks.t: MRTB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Why One from every employer you have had in the last five years, confirming the work you have claimed. Where Each employer’s HR department. Start with the oldest — former employers are the slowest part of most applications. Mistake A single summary letter in place of individual certificates.

chunks.t: MRTB registration guide and checklist
chunks.h: Evidence of two years’ overseas employment
chunks.x: Why Where it applies to you, the Board wants start and end dates, contracted weekly hours and job title. Where Your employers — ask for it in exactly that form. Mistake A letter confirming you worked there, with none of the three things the Board asked for.

chunks.t: MRTB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Why Certification confirms a true copy; translation makes non-English documents assessable. Where An approved person such as a notary; a recognised, independent translator. Mistake Wrong or incomplete certification wording; translations not independently certified. Tip Confirm exactly who may certify and the wording required before you spend money. Getting it wrong means doing it twice. One folder, one file per document. When everything is gathered, certified and in date at the same time, the application itself takes a fraction of the effort. Section 06

chunks.t: MRTB registration guide and checklist
chunks.h: References are the part most within your control
chunks.x: Your qualification proves what you were trained to do. Your references prove what you do, now, in clinical practice. The Board relies on them to confirm you practise safely and competently. A vague reference leaves a gap the Board may have to fill by asking for more — which means delay.

chunks.t: MRTB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: The instinct is to ask the most senior person available. Resist it. The best referee has directly supervised or worked alongside your clinical practice recently and can speak to it in specific terms. A clinical lead who knows your work beats a department head who barely does. A poor reference “I have known Sam for some years. Sam is hard-working and a pleasure to work with. I am happy to recommend Sam.” No clinical detail, no dates, no scope, no basis for assessing competence. A strong reference “As Imaging Lead, I have directly supervised Sam for three years. Sam independently performs general X-ray, CT and MRI to a high standard, including complex and emergency cases, and consistently demonstrates safe, patient-centred practice.” Specific, dated, scope-clear, credible.

chunks.t: MRTB registration guide and checklist
chunks.h: What a reference that never prompts a follow-up contains
chunks.x: The referee’s full name, job title and professional relationship to you How long, and in what capacity, they have known your work The specific scope and modalities you work within — settings and responsibilities An assessment of your clinical competence, safety and professionalism, with examples Confirmation of the dates and the hours or extent of the practice described Official letterhead, signature, date and verifiable contact details

chunks.t: MRTB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Most weak references are weak because the referee was not told what was needed. Explain that this is for professional registration in New Zealand, share which scope you are applying for, and tell them what the Board values: clinical detail, dates, scope and a clear assessment of competence. Ask early — a referee on leave when you need them is a common, avoidable delay. We can review references before submission against what the Board looks for and flag anything likely to prompt a follow-up. The content always remains your referee’s own independent assessment. Section 07

chunks.t: MRTB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: This exists for patient safety: the Board needs objective assurance of clear communication in a clinical setting. Test

chunks.t: MRTB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Widely accepted. The Board sets minimums overall and in each component — listening, reading, writing, speaking. A strong overall score does not help if one component falls short, so prepare evenly. Test

chunks.t: MRTB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: The healthcare-specific alternative many clinicians prefer because its tasks are set in medical contexts. Minimum grades apply in each of the four components. Alternative evidence

chunks.t: MRTB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: In some circumstances the Board accepts alternative evidence in place of a test — for example an English-medium education and career, or employer references. Eligibility is specific and decided by the Board; check before assuming you qualify. Results expire. Typically around two years from the test date. Sitting the test early and then taking many months to assemble the rest of the application is a frequent reason for paying to sit it again. Time it to remain valid through to assessment. And even fluent speakers stumble on technique: sit a timed practice test, find your weakest component, book early — centre availability can be limited. Which test should I choose? Either, where accepted. Many clinicians find OET more natural because the content is medical. Pick the one that plays to your strengths. Can I combine scores from two sittings? The Board’s rules on combining sittings are specific — check current guidance before relying on it. What if I narrowly miss one component? You generally need to re-sit. Build a little time buffer into your plan in case. Section 08

chunks.t: MRTB registration guide and checklist
chunks.h: Create your application on the Board’s portal
chunks.x: Work through each section methodically. Read every question carefully — accuracy here saves queries later. 2

chunks.t: MRTB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Clear, high-quality colour scans, named so the Board can see at once what each file is. 3

chunks.t: MRTB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Assessment and registration fees as they apply. Keep your payment confirmation. 4

chunks.t: MRTB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Review everything once more against the requirements. A ten-minute final check is the cheapest delay-insurance there is. 5

chunks.t: MRTB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Expect an acknowledgement, possibly requests for further information, then the decision. Check email, including spam, and the portal. A request that sits unanswered for three weeks adds three weeks. Put yourself in the assessor’s shoes. Could a stranger open this application and find everything they need without emailing you? If yes, you have prepared it well.

chunks.t: MRTB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Depending on your circumstances the Board’s charges can include an application or qualification-assessment fee, the registration fee, your Annual Practising Certificate and — if it applies — an examination fee. On top sit third-party costs: criminal history checks, translation, certification. The examination fee is paid in advance and forfeited if you are refused access on the day, so do not pay it until you are ready and your ID is in order. Amounts are deliberately not printed here. The Board publishes its prescribed fees in a notice on its website and revises them; confirm the current figures on the Board’s own schedule before you budget or pay. Where an Ethicare package applies to your placement, APC costs are reimbursed — ask us what your package includes before you rely on it. Section 09

chunks.t: MRTB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: The Board confirms receipt. Keep your documents and login organised and watch for contact. 2

chunks.t: MRTB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Qualification, competence and recent practice reviewed against your scope. Timeframes vary with your background and how complete the application is. 3

chunks.t: MRTB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Confirmed, sometimes with conditions or a supervised period. The moment the move becomes real. 5

chunks.t: MRTB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: With registration, or clear registrability, you are in a strong position to secure a role. This is where planning the move takes over from registration. Where people get stuck

chunks.t: MRTB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Warm but vague, with no clinical detail, dates or scope. The single most common cause of a follow-up request.

chunks.t: MRTB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Cropped, blurry or greyscale. If the assessor cannot read it, it does not count.

chunks.t: MRTB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: A certificate without the transcript that shows course content and clinical hours.

chunks.t: MRTB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Copies certified by the wrong person or with the wrong wording — redone from scratch.

chunks.t: MRTB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Passport, certificates and references that differ, with no bridging document.

chunks.t: MRTB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Unexplained periods that raise questions about recent practice.

chunks.t: MRTB registration guide and checklist
chunks.h: The fix for all of these
chunks.x: Prepare everything together, check it as a set, and have it read by someone else before you submit. Most of these mistakes are invisible to the person making them. Section 11

chunks.t: MRTB registration guide and checklist
chunks.h: The questions we are asked most
chunks.x: Can I apply for registration before finding a job? Yes — and in most cases you should. Because registration usually comes before employment, starting early puts you in a far stronger position when roles arise. Do I need registration before interviewing? Not always for an initial conversation, but employers want confidence that you are registrable. Being registered, or clearly on track to be, makes you a much stronger candidate. How long does registration usually take? It varies considerably with your background, your scope and — crucially — how complete your application is. A clean, well-prepared application is the single biggest thing you can do to keep the timeline short. Can I submit additional documents later? Yes. If the Board requests further information, you provide it during assessment. Responding promptly and fully is what keeps things moving.

chunks.t: MRTB registration guide and checklist
chunks.h: The questions we are asked most
chunks.x: Can I work while my application is being assessed? You cannot practise in a regulated role until you are registered and hold a current APC. Plan your move around that fact rather than assuming you can begin and sort registration out afterwards. Will I have to work under supervision? Most likely yes, and that is normal. On the Board’s published pathway table, even a qualification from one of its six recognised countries (Australia, Canada, Ireland, South Africa, the UK and the USA) with three or more years’ practice in the last five leads to registration with a condition of supervision. It is not a judgement on your ability. Plan for it: you will need an employer and a supervisor who can support it. Will I need to sit an examination? Many applicants do.

chunks.t: MRTB registration guide and checklist
chunks.h: The questions we are asked most
chunks.x: The Board’s policy applies the examination to anyone who does not hold a substantially equivalent qualification, and equivalence turns on where you trained together with how recent your practice is — a qualification from one of the six recognised countries plus three or more years’ practice in the last five avoids it. If you are an MRI technologist or a sonographer, assume you will sit it unless told otherwise. Trans-Tasman mutual recognition does not reach either scope, so there is no shortcut into them from anywhere, Australia included. The Board runs an examination for all five of its scopes. What if my referee has left the organisation? Common and manageable. A referee can still provide a reference after moving on, provided they knew your clinical work; another suitable supervisor can also step in. Direct knowledge of your work is what matters, not their current employer.

chunks.t: MRTB registration guide and checklist
chunks.h: The questions we are asked most
chunks.x: How much does registration cost? Typically an assessment fee, the registration fee, your APC, an examination fee if one applies, plus third-party costs such as criminal checks and translations. Figures are not quoted here because the Board updates them — always check its current fees notice. Can Ethicare review my application? Yes. We review your documents and references before submission against what the Board looks for and flag likely issues while they are easy to fix. We support and guide; the registration decision always rests with the Board. Section 12

chunks.x: At a glance Two routes in UK-trained and HCPC-registered is streamlined, with course information waived. Every other overseas qualification is assessed individually against the Council’s criteria. Two years’ experience is the benchmark The Council asks for two years’ full-time equivalent post-qualification specialised experience. It publishes no hours figure, so evidence it in years and FTE, the way the Council states it. The scope widened in April 2025 Aligning the role with the UK’s ODP. Understanding the Council Which pathway applies to you The expanded scope, and what it means for ODPs Qualifications and experience Eligibility and documents References and criminal history English language Cultural competence Applying, and what happens next Where people get stuck Questions we are asked most The whole journey on one page The checklist — 35 items, tickable Section 01

chunks.t: MSCNZ registration: anaesthetic technicians
chunks.x: The Medical Sciences Council of New Zealand — Te Kaunihera Pūtaiao Hauora o Aotearoa — registers and oversees anaesthetic technicians, and medical laboratory science practitioners, under the Health Practitioners Competence Assurance Act 2003. Its purpose is to protect the public by making sure everyone practising is qualified, competent and fit to do so.

chunks.t: MSCNZ registration: anaesthetic technicians
chunks.x: You cannot lawfully work as an anaesthetic technician in New Zealand without registration with the Council and a current annual practising certificate. Registration confirms you have met the standard in the scope; the APC is what permits you to work, renewed every year.

chunks.t: MSCNZ registration: anaesthetic technicians
chunks.h: Case-by-case assessment outside the UK route
chunks.x: Overseas qualifications other than recognised UK ones are assessed individually against a standard set of criteria approved by the Council. The quality and completeness of the evidence you provide directly shapes the outcome. Confirm your pathway → Evidence, application and fee → Council assessment → Registration in the AT scope → APC once resident, then practise The APC cannot be issued in advance. You can only apply for your annual practising certificate once you are resident in New Zealand or can evidence your move. Registration can be in hand before you travel; the certificate that lets you work cannot. Plan the start date around that. Section 02

chunks.t: MSCNZ registration: anaesthetic technicians
chunks.x: Two broad routes. The first is streamlined; the second weighs your qualification, registration and experience individually against the Council’s criteria. Route 1 — streamlined

chunks.t: MSCNZ registration: anaesthetic technicians
chunks.x: You hold a United Kingdom qualification in anaesthetic technology and are registered and in good standing with the Health and Care Professions Council. With two years’ full-time equivalent post-qualification specialised anaesthetic technology experience you will generally be eligible, though the Council may require a period of supervised practice once you start. Course information is still required. The Council’s document list applies to all internationally qualified applicants and includes the academic transcript, the syllabus or curriculum in English, and the clinical logbook where applicable. With less than two years’ experience you can still apply and be assessed, which may include a Work-Based Assessment in practice. Route 2 — individual assessment

chunks.t: MSCNZ registration: anaesthetic technicians
chunks.x: You qualified outside the UK. Your qualification, registration and experience are weighed individually against the Council’s standard criteria. Training closer in scope to New Zealand’s — Australia and Ireland, for example — tends to map more readily, but every application is considered on its own merits. Course information is required: transcript, syllabus and clinical logbook where applicable (Section 04). The completeness and clarity of that evidence is what decides the outcome and the timeline. Check eligibility first. Before assembling documents, complete the Council’s Eligible check form. It gives you an early read on whether you can apply, so you know where you stand before investing time and money. Section 03

chunks.t: MSCNZ registration: anaesthetic technicians
chunks.h: The expanded scope, and what it means for ODPs
chunks.x: From 1 April 2025 a new Gazette notice broadened the activities and responsibilities anaesthetic technicians in New Zealand can undertake, aligning the role more closely with international roles such as the UK’s Operating Department Practitioner. The Council has said this reflects the increasing complexity of anaesthetic care and the need for a flexible, highly skilled workforce. Anaesthetic technicians may practise across operating departments, radiology, intensive care, maternity and emergency departments — anywhere anaesthesia is administered or airway emergencies are managed. Expanded scopes, for example post-anaesthetic care and peripherally inserted central catheters, are available on completion of an accredited training pathway and Council approval. For ODPs

chunks.t: MSCNZ registration: anaesthetic technicians
chunks.h: Clearer pathways into the New Zealand system
chunks.x: The expanded scope gives clearer registration pathways for Operating Department Practitioners who meet the relevant competencies. If you hold a recognised UK qualification and HCPC registration in good standing, you apply via the UK route in Section 02. A profession in demand

chunks.t: MSCNZ registration: anaesthetic technicians
chunks.x: Registered anaesthetic technicians sit on Immigration New Zealand’s skill-shortage list, so the role is viewed favourably for visa purposes. Lists change — check the current one before you rely on it. Section 04

chunks.t: MSCNZ registration: anaesthetic technicians
