The two-year full-time equivalent requirement is central to the UK route. Make sure the employer statement puts the full-time-equivalent period beyond doubt — a vague letter is the most common cause of a follow-up query. Section 05

chunks.x: Present it like a professional portfolio: clean, high-resolution colour scans; pages straight and complete; consistent naming; certification done correctly the first time. A well-organised application is read more favourably, and assessed faster, than a disorganised one containing exactly the same facts.

One Certificate of Competence and Experience — professional — ideally from a registered anaesthetic technician. If you have not practised as an AT before, a recent lecturer or employer may be used. Referees complete the Council’s own template and return it directly to the Council. Tell them to expect an email. Criminal history

chunks.t: MSCNZ registration: anaesthetic technicians

Sent directly to the Council from the issuing authority. Third-party pre-employment checks are not accepted. No more than six months old on the day you submit. A conviction is not an automatic bar. The right approach is full disclosure. Non-disclosure is treated far more seriously than most underlying matters. Section 07

chunks.t: MSCNZ registration: anaesthetic technicians
chunks.x: Safe, precise communication with patients and colleagues in a high-stakes clinical environment. Every applicant must meet the Council’s English Language Policy, which sets out several routes — for example evidence that English was the sole language of instruction and assessment throughout your qualification, or a recognised test result. Where a test is required the Council accepts IELTS or the OET. IELTS asks for 7.0 in each of listening, reading and speaking and 6.5 in writing; the OET asks for a B pass. The Council does not accept the IELTS Online test or OET@Home. Confirm the current accepted tests and minimum scores against the Council’s live policy before booking, because the policy is periodically updated. Sitting the test too early. Applications take time to assemble, so an early test risks expiring before you submit. Time it so the result remains valid when your application reaches the Council. Section 08

chunks.x: You must complete the Foundation Course in Healthcare and Te Tiriti o Waitangi, delivered by Mauri Ora Associates, and provide the certificate of completion with your application. It builds your understanding of cultural competence and the obligations that flow from te Tiriti. Practice in New Zealand reflects a system-wide commitment to equitable health outcomes, and particularly to safeguarding the wellbeing of Māori. The Council’s Cultural Competence Standards are part of the competence framework every registrant is expected to meet. Required with the application

chunks.h: The questions we are asked most
chunks.x: Should I do anything before applying? Yes. Complete the Council’s Eligible check form first. It gives you an early read on whether you can apply before you invest time and money. I am a UK-trained ODP. Can I work there? The 1 April 2025 scope change opened clearer pathways for Operating Department Practitioners who meet the relevant competencies. If you hold a recognised UK qualification and are HCPC-registered in good standing, you apply via the UK route. Do I need to provide my course syllabus? Not if you are UK-trained — course information is waived for that route. Applicants from elsewhere provide the transcript, syllabus and, if applicable, the clinical logbook. Will I need supervised practice? Possibly. UK-trained applicants may be required to complete a period of supervised practice, and those with less than two years’ experience may undergo a Work-Based Assessment.

chunks.t: MSCNZ registration: anaesthetic technicians
chunks.h: The questions we are asked most
chunks.x: It is designed to support safe practice in a new system, not to penalise you. How long does registration take? We review your evidence — particularly your experience documentation and pathway choice — against what the Council looks for, and flag likely issues while they are still easy to fix. The registration decision always rests with the Council. Section 12

chunks.x: At a glance An individual assessment, not a pathway The Board assesses fitness, equivalence and competence case by case and makes its own judgement of your qualifications. Your evidence shapes the outcome. Start with the free self-assessment The Board’s online Self-Assessment of Eligibility gives you an early read before you spend a cent or gather a document. 1,500 supervised hours, evidenced in detail Total hours, the dates they run between, what you were doing and who supervised you. The most scrutinised part of the file — gather it first. Registration where you trained and where you live Both are expected. chunks.t: NZPB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Psychology registration is one of the more rigorous allied-health processes, so read this once end to end, then return to each section as you reach it. The checklist at the end remembers what you have ticked, on this device. Understanding the Board The seven scopes of practice How the Board assesses your qualifications The 1,500-hour supervised practice requirement Eligibility and documents References and criminal history English language Cultural competence and the Raka Māui programme Applying, and what happens next Where people get stuck Questions we are asked most The whole journey on one page The checklist — 38 items, tickable Section 01

chunks.t: NZPB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: The New Zealand Psychologists Board — Te Poari Kaimātai Hinengaro o Aotearoa — registers and oversees psychologists under the Health Practitioners Competence Assurance Act 2003. Its purpose is to protect the public by making sure everyone practising as a psychologist is qualified, competent and fit to do so.

chunks.t: NZPB registration guide and checklist
chunks.h: The title is protected by law
chunks.x: You cannot lawfully call yourself a psychologist, or practise, without registration and a current Annual Practising Certificate. Registration confirms you have met the standard in a given scope; the APC is what permits you to work, and is renewed every year.

chunks.t: NZPB registration guide and checklist
chunks.h: An individual assessment, not a checklist
chunks.x: The single most important thing to understand. Unlike regulators that sort applicants into fixed pathways, the Board assesses every overseas application on its own merits — for fitness, equivalence of qualifications and competence — and it does not rely on assessments by the New Zealand Qualifications Authority. It makes its own. The quality and completeness of your evidence directly shapes the outcome. Qualification and 1,500-hour internship → Registration in a scope → Annual Practising Certificate → Practise in New Zealand Start with the self-assessment. First, complete the Board’s free online Self-Assessment of Eligibility for Registration. It gives you an early read on how the Board may view your fitness, the equivalence of your qualifications and your current competence — so you know where you stand before investing time and money. Section 02

chunks.t: NZPB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: You apply for registration in a specific scope. A clinical psychologist will generally apply for the Clinical Psychologist scope; the wrong one is a costly detour. General

chunks.t: NZPB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: The scope most applicants from clinical backgrounds apply for. Requires clinical training and supervised clinical practice. Specialist scope

chunks.t: NZPB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Evidence of counselling-psychology training and supervised practice. Specialist scope

chunks.t: NZPB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Evidence of educational-psychology training and supervised practice. Specialist scope

chunks.t: NZPB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Evidence of neuropsychology training and supervised practice. In training

chunks.t: NZPB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: For those completing the supervised internship stage. In training

chunks.t: NZPB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: For those in structured employer-based training, such as Corrections or Defence pathways. The “psychologist where you trained” test. One principle runs through every scope: the Board asks whether your qualification would lead to registration in the jurisdiction where you obtained it. If you do not meet the registration or licensing requirements where you trained, you are unlikely to be eligible in New Zealand. The Board also expects you to hold registration both where you trained and where you currently live. Section 03

chunks.t: NZPB registration guide and checklist
chunks.h: 1,500 hours of supervised practice as part of your qualification
chunks.x: An internship, closely supervised by a qualified psychologist. Section 04 covers this fully. 4

chunks.t: NZPB registration guide and checklist
chunks.h: An endpoint evaluation of your internship, or a licensing examination
chunks.x: Formal evidence that your supervised practice was assessed, not just completed. 5

chunks.t: NZPB registration guide and checklist
chunks.h: Registration where you trained and where you currently live
chunks.x: As a psychologist, with a government-mandated authority, in good standing.

chunks.t: NZPB registration guide and checklist
chunks.h: If your programme was online or low-residency
chunks.x: Ask before you apply. The Board assesses every overseas application individually for equivalence of qualifications, and a programme delivered substantially at a distance is harder to evidence as equivalent to a six-year, accredited, in-person New Zealand training. The Board does not publish a blanket rule on this, so the answer comes from your own eligibility self-assessment and, if needed, a direct question to the Board — not from a page like this one.

chunks.t: NZPB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: A minimum six-year course of studies in psychology, from an accredited training programme, with the 1,500-hour supervised practice completed as part of it.

chunks.t: NZPB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Start with the Board’s online Self-Assessment of Eligibility. It is the first step in the process and it exists precisely to answer questions like this before you pay a non-refundable fee. Prescribed countries: a note on fees, not a fast track. Canada, Ireland, South Africa, the United Kingdom and the USA are “prescribed countries”. Applications from them tend to be quicker and cheaper to process because their training and regulation closely resemble New Zealand’s. It is not a separate pathway and it does not change the standard you must meet. Psychologists registered in Australia use Trans-Tasman mutual recognition instead. Section 04

chunks.t: NZPB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: You must provide conclusive, clear and reliable evidence of a structured, supervised and formally evaluated practice programme of at least 1,500 hours completed as part of your qualification, approved by the Board or an equivalent registering authority. 1,500

chunks.t: NZPB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: A structured, supervised and formally evaluated practice programme completed as part of your qualification. Semi- independent

chunks.t: NZPB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: The Board counts from when you “actually commenced practising (under appropriate supervision but semi-independently) as a psychologist”, and stops when the placement contract ends. Earlier practica do not count. Closely supervised

chunks.t: NZPB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: The programme must have been structured, supervised and formally evaluated, and completed as part of your qualification rather than alongside it.

chunks.t: NZPB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: The Board counts your internship from when you began practising as a psychologist — supervised, but semi-independently — through to the end of your placement contract. Internships normally come toward the end of training and are distinguished from earlier practica by the greater independence you are given. Practicum hours from early in your training generally do not count toward the 1,500. Gather this evidence first. It is the hardest to reconstruct and the most scrutinised. Aim for documentation showing the total hours, the breakdown of activities, the proportion of direct client contact and the supervision arrangements, ideally confirmed by your training institution or supervisor. A letter that simply states “completed an internship” rarely satisfies the Board. Section 05

chunks.t: NZPB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Present it like a professional portfolio: clean, high-resolution colour scans; pages straight and complete; consistent naming; certification done correctly the first time. A well-organised application is read more favourably, and assessed faster, than a disorganised one containing exactly the same facts.

chunks.t: NZPB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Why Your degrees and diplomas are the foundation of registration, and the Board makes its own assessment of them rather than relying on NZQA. Provide Full detail of the course content of your undergraduate and postgraduate degrees and diplomas, plus everything relating to internships and practical training. Mistake Thin course-content detail, especially from outside the UK, South Africa or the USA — the Board needs it to judge equivalence.

chunks.t: NZPB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Why The Board needs to confirm you are registered or licensed where you trained and where you live, and in good standing. Provide Details of your current registration with a recognised authority, such as a state or national registration body. Mistake A qualification that is not eligible for registration as a psychologist where you trained — the application will be declined.

chunks.t: NZPB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Why Registration is scope-specific. Provide Evidence of the applicable qualifications, internships and practical training for each scope you are applying to register in. Tip Confirm your scope first (Section 02), then gather evidence specific to it.

chunks.t: NZPB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Why To confirm who you are and link your records. Provide Certified identity documents, evidence of any name change if your name differs across documents, and translations of anything not in English. Tip Scan flat, in colour, with all edges visible; confirm who may certify before you pay. Section 06

chunks.t: NZPB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: The Act requires you to be a “fit and proper person”; these two requirements are how the Board confirms it, and a small error means starting again. References

chunks.t: NZPB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Three references, on the Board’s own reference template. At least one should come from a senior psychologist registered, chartered or licensed with a government-mandated registration authority overseas — with a copy of that referee’s own registration certificate or licence. The original document, signed and dated no earlier than three months before the Board receives your application — or emailed by the referee directly to the Board with your name in the subject line. Referees should have known you for at least twelve months, ideally professionally. Family members and friends are not suitable. Criminal history

chunks.t: NZPB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: From each country you have lived in for longer than three months within the past five years. The official source for each country — for example ACRO Police Clearance in the UK, the Australian Federal Police certificate, the South African Police Clearance Certificate, or FBI and state-level checks in the USA. No more than six months old, including all names you are or were known by. Requested directly from the police in the country concerned. Third-party pre-employment checks are not accepted. A conviction is not an automatic bar. The Board considers each case on its merits. The right approach is full disclosure: submit the record and an explanatory letter. Non-disclosure is treated far more seriously than most underlying matters. Section 07

chunks.t: NZPB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Safe, precise communication with clients and colleagues. The Board’s bar is specific, and higher than in some professions. You need a test only if both of these are true. English is not your first language, and your psychology qualifications were not completed in English in Australia, Canada, South Africa, the United Kingdom, Ireland or the United States. If either does not apply to you, you generally will not need a test. 7.5

chunks.t: NZPB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: IELTS Academic is the only English test the Board currently accepts. 7.0

chunks.t: NZPB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: A strong average does not rescue one component below the line. Prepare evenly across all four. 2 yrs

chunks.t: NZPB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Results must have been obtained within two years before you apply. 1

chunks.t: NZPB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: The Board accepts IELTS One Skill Retake results, so narrowly missing one component need not mean sitting the whole test again. Sitting the test too early. Psychology applications can take several months to assemble, so an early IELTS risks expiring before you submit. Time the test so the result is still valid when your application reaches the Board. Section 08

chunks.t: NZPB registration guide and checklist
chunks.h: Cultural competence and the Raka Māui programme
chunks.x: The practice of psychology in New Zealand reflects the world views of both partners to te Tiriti o Waitangi. The Board’s Core Competencies include cultural competencies, and registered psychologists are expected to be culturally competent with all cultures — and particularly to safeguard the wellbeing of Māori, as part of a system-wide effort to address the effects of colonisation on Māori health. You can begin before you relocate, and demonstrating that you have started carries real weight with the Board. You are also welcome to make submissions to the Board about your practice in terms of cultural safety generally. Raka Māui — a condition of your registration

chunks.t: NZPB registration guide and checklist
chunks.h: Not optional, and not a mark against you
chunks.x: This is the part of the process that changed most recently, and it is the one to plan around. The Board’s Raka Māui Competence Programme applies to eligible overseas-trained psychologists whose applications for registration are approved by the Board on or after 1 July 2026 . Completing it is a condition of your registration , and it must be completed within two years of registration . It is not a judgement on your clinical ability. Because overseas applicants have typically not trained or practised with Māori, its express purpose is to build the cultural capability needed to practise safely in a country where tangata whenua have unique and specific needs. Treat it as part of the job you are taking, with two years to do it in — not as paperwork to be avoided. Required, once registered

chunks.t: NZPB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: The Board’s own programme, and a condition of registration for anyone approved on or after 1 July 2026. Two years from registration to complete it. The Board publishes the programme guide on its website. Useful beforehand

chunks.t: NZPB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Nothing replaces Raka Māui, but arriving with some grounding helps. The Board also publishes Cultural Safety Guidelines and a Tangata Whenua reading list, and both are worth working through before you land. Section 09

chunks.t: NZPB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: The Board’s online Self-Assessment of Eligibility gives you an early read before you commit time and money. 2

chunks.t: NZPB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Identify which of the seven scopes your training evidences, and gather evidence specific to it. 3

chunks.t: NZPB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Qualifications and course content, the 1,500-hour internship breakdown, registration evidence, references, criminal-history records, and IELTS results if required. 4

chunks.t: NZPB registration guide and checklist
chunks.h: Read the Board’s cultural safety material
chunks.x: Groundwork before you arrive. The required programme, Raka Māui, begins after you are registered and runs for up to two years. 5

chunks.t: NZPB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Overseas applications go to the Board with the application fee, which is non-refundable. 6

chunks.t: NZPB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: The Board assesses your fitness, equivalence and competence, and sets the conditions your registration will carry. 7

chunks.t: NZPB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Once registered in your scope, apply for your Annual Practising Certificate before you can practise. How long it takes — our experience, not a Board figure

chunks.t: NZPB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Overseas psychology applications commonly take around four to six months, and longer from outside the prescribed countries because the Board examines course content in more depth. The completeness and clarity of your evidence is the biggest factor within your control. Fees

chunks.t: NZPB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: No amounts are printed here deliberately. Application fees are non-refundable, differ between prescribed and non-prescribed countries, and are reviewed periodically. Confirm them on the Board’s Fees and Levy page before you budget or pay. Where people get stuck

chunks.t: NZPB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: The biggest one. Letters that do not show the 1,500 hours, the dates, the nature of the work or the supervision arrangements — or that count practica from before you were practising semi-independently.

chunks.t: NZPB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: A largely online, weekend or summer-intensive qualification that does not meet the one-continuous-year requirement.

chunks.t: NZPB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Applying for a scope your training does not evidence. Confirm your scope first.

chunks.t: NZPB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: No senior overseas-registered referee with their certificate, or references signed more than three months before submission.

chunks.t: NZPB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: A pre-employment background check instead of one requested directly from the police, or one older than six months.

chunks.t: NZPB registration guide and checklist
chunks.h: IELTS too low or too old
chunks.x: Below 7.5 overall or 7.0 in a section, or results expired before submission.

chunks.t: NZPB registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Especially from non-prescribed countries: too little for the Board to judge equivalence.

chunks.t: NZPB registration guide and checklist
chunks.h: The fix for all of these
chunks.x: Do the self-assessment, gather internship evidence first, confirm your scope, and have everything reviewed before you submit. Most of these are invisible to the person making them. Section 11

chunks.t: NZPB registration guide and checklist
chunks.h: The questions we are asked most
chunks.x: Should I do anything before applying? Yes. Complete the Board’s free online Self-Assessment of Eligibility first. It gives you an early read on how the Board may view your qualifications and competence before you invest time and money. Which scope should I apply for? The one your training and supervised practice evidence — most commonly Clinical Psychologist for those from clinical backgrounds. Registration is scope-specific, so applying for the wrong one is a costly detour. My qualification was partly online. Is that a problem? It may be, and it is worth settling before you pay anything. The Board assesses equivalence of qualifications individually against a minimum six-year accredited course with 1,500 supervised hours inside it, and a programme delivered substantially at a distance is harder to evidence against that.

chunks.t: NZPB registration guide and checklist
chunks.h: The questions we are asked most
chunks.x: There is no published blanket rule either way, so use the Board’s Self-Assessment of Eligibility first and ask the Board directly if it is still unclear. Do my practicum hours count toward the 1,500? Generally not. The Board counts internship hours from when you began practising semi-independently under supervision, toward the end of your training — distinct from earlier practica. The hours must also meet the activity and supervision breakdown in Section 04. I am registered in Australia. Does that help? Yes. Under Trans-Tasman mutual recognition you transfer your registration rather than going through the full overseas assessment. The transfer must be complete before you start work. Do I have to do the Raka Māui programme? If your application for registration is approved by the Board on or after 1 July 2026 and you are an eligible overseas-trained psychologist, yes.

chunks.t: NZPB registration guide and checklist
chunks.h: The questions we are asked most
chunks.x: Completing Raka Māui is a condition of your registration and you have two years from registration to finish it. It exists because overseas applicants have usually never trained or practised with Māori, and it is designed to support you into practice here rather than to penalise you. Budget the time for it the way you would budget for any other condition on your registration. Do I need IELTS? Only if English is not your first language and your qualifications were not completed in English in Australia, Canada, South Africa, the UK, Ireland or the USA. Where it is required, it is IELTS Academic, 7.5 overall with 7.0 in each section, obtained within two years. How long does it take? In our experience overseas psychology applications commonly take around four to six months, and longer from outside the prescribed countries because the Board examines course content in more depth.

chunks.x: That is Ethicare experience, not a Board figure. The completeness and clarity of your evidence is the biggest factor within your control. Can Ethicare review my application? Yes. We review your evidence — particularly your internship documentation and scope choice — against what the Board looks for, and flag likely issues while they are still easy to fix. The registration decision always rests with the Board. Section 12

chunks.x: The 1,500-hour requirement is the most scrutinised part of the application. Evidence of 1,500 or more supervised practice hours Structured, supervised and formally evaluated, as part of your qualification. Show at least 50% in service-related activities Treatment, assessment, interviews, report writing, case presentations, consultations. Show what the hours consisted of Assessment, intervention, report writing, consultation — and how much of it was direct client work. Certified translations of any non-English documents At least one senior overseas-registered referee Registered, chartered or licensed — include a copy of their registration certificate. References original, signed and dated within three months Or emailed by the referee directly to the Board, with your name in the subject line. Referees who have known you professionally for 12 months or more Family and friends are not suitable.

chunks.x: Police records with precise rules that are easy to get slightly wrong. Police record from each country you have lived in Any country you lived in for more than three months in the past five years. Requested directly from the police Third-party pre-employment checks are not accepted. No more than six months old, with all your names included Explanatory letter if you have any conviction A conviction is not an automatic bar. Disclose fully and explain.

chunks.x: Raka Māui is a condition of your registration. Groundwork before you relocate makes it easier. chunks.t: OTBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: The Occupational Therapy Board of New Zealand registers and oversees occupational therapists under the Health Practitioners Competence Assurance Act 2003. Its purpose is to protect the public by ensuring everyone practising as an occupational therapist is qualified, competent and of good character. The title “occupational therapist” is protected by law. You cannot use the title or practise — including by telehealth from overseas — without registration and a current practising certificate. Practising, or claiming the title, while unregistered is an offence under section 7 of the Act.

chunks.x: The single most important thing to understand about OTBNZ: overseas applications are assessed on their individual merits — fitness, equivalence of qualifications and competence — by Board-appointed occupational therapists. The quality and completeness of the evidence you provide directly shapes the outcome.

chunks.t: OTBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Registration confirms you have met the standard. The practising certificate is what permits you to work, renewed each year; the APC year runs 1 April to 31 March. You must hold a current practising certificate at all times while practising, even under a different job title or in a voluntary role. Qualification and competence assessment → Registration — general scope → Practising certificate → Practise in New Zealand Section 02

chunks.t: OTBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Which pathway you use depends on where you trained and where you are registered. For many UK-based candidates the abridged pathway is the relevant one. Abridged

chunks.t: OTBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.h: Qualified and registered in the UK, Ireland, Canada or South Africa
chunks.x: Your qualification must be from an education facility accredited by the World Federation of Occupational Therapists (WFOT), and you must be currently registered in that country. The evidence required is streamlined — certificate and transcript rather than the full syllabus — but the standard is not lowered, and the cultural-competence and good-character requirements still apply. Standard overseas

chunks.t: OTBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: The core requirements are the same, with closer scrutiny of your course content so the Board can judge equivalence: qualification certificate, full academic transcript, and a detailed course description or syllabus. Trans-Tasman

chunks.t: OTBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.h: Currently registered with Ahpra in Australia
chunks.x: You register under the Trans-Tasman Mutual Recognition Act 1997 rather than the overseas-trained route — a different and generally faster process. Trans-Tasman registrants are not required to complete the Recertification Programme. Not sure which applies? Choosing the right pathway from the outset avoids rework and makes document-gathering far simpler. For candidates who apply through us, it is one of the first things we confirm. Section 03

chunks.t: OTBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.h: How the Board assesses your qualifications
chunks.x: A relevant occupational therapy qualification, assessed as equivalent to a New Zealand qualification by Board-appointed occupational therapists On the abridged pathway, a qualification from a WFOT-accredited programme and current registration in that country Evidence of your current registration and good standing with the authority where you trained and practise That you are of good character and a fit person to practise — confirmed through references and a criminal-history check That you can communicate effectively in English — Section 07 Primary source verification. The Board may require your identity and qualifications to be confirmed directly with the issuing institution, at your own cost, after your application is assessed. Build the possibility into your timeline. Section 04

chunks.t: OTBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: OTBNZ asks overseas applicants to actively demonstrate competence against its national standards, the part international applicants most often underestimate. You must show you can meet the Board’s Competencies for Registration and Continuing Practice . On the standard pathway this happens through three connected steps in your applicant portal, after your initial application — and your file is not processed until they are in. The Board’s abridged page does not list a self-assessment and instructs applicants to upload a blank page in the cultural competence area instead, so confirm which pathway you are on before you start writing. 1

chunks.t: OTBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: The centrepiece. Against each competency you evidence how your practice meets the New Zealand standard. Vague, general statements rarely satisfy the assessors; specific examples from your practice carry far more weight. 2

chunks.t: OTBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Work history in full, with any significant gap — travel, family leave — briefly explained. Build your CV is written for this. 3

chunks.t: OTBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.h: The Ngā Paerewa Te Tiriti eLearning course
chunks.x: The Board’s cultural-competence requirement — Section 08. On the standard pathway, at least one referee — an occupational therapist who has worked with you — is asked to view your self-assessment and confirm it accurately represents your practice. Choose that referee with care. Draft your self-assessment early. Map your experience to the New Zealand competencies before you submit, using the Board’s published competencies document. Arriving at the portal with your examples already drafted turns the most demanding step into a straightforward one. Section 05

chunks.t: OTBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Clean colour scans, certified correctly the first time and consistently named: a well-organised application is assessed more smoothly.

chunks.t: OTBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Why Your degree is the foundation of registration, and the Board makes its own assessment of it. Provide Certified copies of your occupational therapy qualification certificate and academic transcript; on the standard pathway, also a detailed course description or syllabus.

chunks.t: OTBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Why To confirm who you are and link your records. Provide Two forms of identity documentation, one with a photograph, certified, plus evidence of any name change. Non-English documents need a certified translation alongside a certified copy of the original.

chunks.t: OTBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Why To confirm you are registered and in good standing where you practise. Provide A certificate of good standing from every authority you are currently or were previously registered with, plus details of any disciplinary action taken or pending. Hard copies still matter. Your certified ID, qualification certificate, transcript, certificates of good standing and criminal-history check must also be sent to the Board in hard copy by post or courier, not only uploaded. Plan the postage time into your schedule. Section 06

chunks.t: OTBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Two requirements with precise rules that are easy to get slightly wrong — and a small error means starting that piece again. References

chunks.t: OTBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Each over 18, known you for more than twelve months, not a relative, not living at your address, and a person of good standing in the community. At least one must be an occupational therapist with whom you have worked for more than six months in the last two years. On the standard pathway, that referee also reviews your competence self-assessment and confirms it reflects your practice. Criminal history

chunks.t: OTBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Declare any convictions, and provide a criminal-conviction check for your country of current registration and any other country you have lived in for more than six months in the last ten years. A New Zealand check is arranged for you during processing, unless you have never been to New Zealand. A conviction is not an automatic bar. The Board considers each case individually. Full disclosure with an explanatory note is the right approach; non-disclosure is treated far more seriously than most underlying matters. Section 07

chunks.t: OTBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Safe, precise communication with clients and colleagues. The Board’s rule here is specific. When a test is needed

chunks.t: OTBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.h: If English is not your first language
chunks.x: You are generally exempt if you completed your occupational therapy qualification, and the relevant schooling, taught and assessed in English in a recognised country — New Zealand, Australia, Canada, Ireland, South Africa or the UK. Speakers of te reo Māori or New Zealand Sign Language as a first language are exempt. Test

chunks.t: OTBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: At the time this guide was written: a minimum grade B in each of the four components. Test

chunks.t: OTBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: At the time this guide was written: at least 7.0 in each band. Clubbing is allowed, within limits. You may combine results across more than one sitting, provided the standard is achieved within twelve months of your first test. Results must be no older than twenty-four months when submitted. If you narrowly miss on one component, clubbing may still get you there — mind both windows. Check the Board’s current English policy for the live thresholds. Section 08

chunks.t: OTBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Practice in Aotearoa New Zealand reflects the world views of both partners to te Tiriti o Waitangi. All applicants complete the Board’s Ngā Paerewa Te Tiriti eLearning course, accessed via Ko Awatea LEARN. You request your account once the Board has confirmed your application number has been updated to your registration number — so this one, unlike the physiotherapy courses, waits for the Board’s cue. Engaging with te Tiriti and Māori health early is still worth doing in its own right. Anticipate this

chunks.t: OTBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.h: Everyone new to practice in New Zealand completes the Recertification Programme
chunks.x: Occupational therapists new to practice in Aotearoa New Zealand — which includes overseas-qualified registrants — complete the Board’s Recertification Programme when they first practise here. For overseas-qualified practitioners that means fortnightly supervision and completion of Te Rito. It is not a mark against you. Its express intent is to ensure you begin practice with sufficient support, for your benefit and the protection of the public, and to give the Board assurance of competence before you practise independently. Trans-Tasman registrants are not required to participate. Factor supervision arrangements into your first year’s planning and your choice of employer. Section 09

chunks.t: OTBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Certified qualification, transcript (and syllabus on the standard pathway), ID, certificates of good standing, criminal-history checks, and English results if required. 3

chunks.t: OTBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Desktop competence self-assessment, nominate your referees, upload your CV, and begin Ngā Paerewa Te Tiriti when the Board opens it to you. Your application is not processed until these are provided. 5

chunks.t: OTBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Post or courier the documents the Board requires in physical form. 6

chunks.t: OTBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Board-appointed occupational therapists assess your application. Once registered, apply for your practising certificate before you can work — you can apply for it at the same time as registration through the portal.

chunks.t: OTBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.h: How long it takes, and what it costs
chunks.x: The Board publishes an indicative processing time that runs from the point all information, payment and printed documents have been received — so the bigger variable is usually how quickly you assemble complete, correctly certified evidence, not the Board’s own processing. Fees are payable and non-refundable: the overseas registration fee, then the practising certificate, plus criminal-history checks and any primary source verification paid to the relevant providers. Amounts and timings are deliberately not printed here. The Board publishes both on its website and revises them; confirm the current figures before you budget or pay. Where people get stuck

chunks.t: OTBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: The biggest one. General statements instead of specific, evidenced examples mapped to each competency.

chunks.t: OTBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Standard when you qualify for abridged, or the reverse. Confirm your pathway first.

chunks.t: OTBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Missing the occupational therapist who has worked with you for six months or more in the last two years.

chunks.t: OTBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Uncertified copies, missing translations, or forgetting that several documents must also go by post.

chunks.t: OTBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Below the threshold in one component, or results older than twenty-four months at submission.

chunks.t: OTBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.h: The fix for all of these
chunks.x: Confirm your pathway, draft the self-assessment early, line up the right referees, and have everything read by someone else before you submit. Section 11

chunks.t: OTBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.h: The questions we are asked most
chunks.x: Is there a faster route for UK-trained occupational therapists? Often, yes. If you qualified in the UK, Ireland, Canada or South Africa from a WFOT-accredited programme and are currently registered there, the abridged pathway recognises the similarity in regulation and streamlines the evidence required — though the standard and the cultural-competence requirement still apply. Do I need IELTS, or will OET do? Either is accepted where a test is required. You only need a test if English is not your first language and your training does not meet the recognised-country exemption. What is the desktop competence self-assessment? A written assessment, completed in your applicant portal, in which you evidence how your practice meets each of the Board’s competencies. It is the core of an overseas application — prepare specific examples rather than general statements.

chunks.t: OTBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.h: The questions we are asked most
chunks.x: I’m registered in Australia — does that help? Yes. With current Ahpra registration you transfer under Trans-Tasman Mutual Recognition rather than the overseas-trained route — a different and generally quicker process. What is the Recertification Programme? A support programme for therapists new to practice in New Zealand. As an overseas-qualified registrant you have fortnightly supervision and complete Te Rito — designed to support you into safe independent practice, not to penalise you. Can Ethicare review my application? Yes. We review your evidence — particularly the competence self-assessment and your pathway choice — against what the Board looks for, and flag likely issues while they are still easy to fix. The registration decision always rests with the Board. Section 12

chunks.t: OTBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Map your practice to the Board’s competencies. Section 04 Preparing

chunks.t: OTBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.h: Line up three referees and your criminal-history checks
chunks.x: One referee an occupational therapist, six months in the last two years. Section 06 Preparing

chunks.t: OTBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.h: Recertification Programme, employment and the move
chunks.x: Fortnightly supervision and Te Rito in your first period of practice; where registration hands over to planning your move . The checklist

chunks.t: OTBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.h: Thirty-three items, in the order you will meet them
chunks.x: Ticks are saved on this device only. The list is always current, which a downloaded copy never is. 0 of 33 ticked Clear all ticks

chunks.t: OTBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Get oriented and pick the right pathway before you spend money or gather documents. Confirm which pathway applies to you Standard overseas, abridged (UK, Ireland, Canada, South Africa) or Trans-Tasman (Ahpra). If abridged: confirm your programme is WFOT-accredited Required for the abridged route. Confirm you are currently registered where you trained or practise And that you can obtain a certificate of good standing. Check whether you need an English test Only if English is not your first language and you do not meet a recognised-country route. Note that fees are payable and non-refundable Confirm the current figures on the Board’s fees page before budgeting.

chunks.t: OTBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: The written desktop assessment is the centrepiece of an overseas application. Download the Board’s Competencies for Registration and Continuing Practice Map your experience to each competency before you submit. Draft specific, evidenced examples per competency General statements rarely satisfy the assessors. We read drafts for candidates who apply through us. Line up your OT referee to confirm it On the standard pathway they review and confirm your self-assessment. Note it is completed in the applicant portal After your initial application; your file is not processed until it is done.

chunks.t: OTBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: What the Board’s appointed occupational therapists assess. Certified occupational therapy qualification certificate Original or certified copy. Certified academic transcript Original or certified copy. Detailed course description or syllabus — standard pathway Not required on the abridged pathway. Be ready for primary source verification The Board may require it, at your own cost.

chunks.t: OTBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Confirming who you are and that you are fit and proper. Two certified forms of ID, one with a photo Plus certified evidence of any name change. Certified translations of any non-English documents Alongside a certified copy in the original language. Three referees lined up Over 18, known you twelve months or more, not a relative, not at your address, and a person of good standing in the community. At least one referee is an occupational therapist Worked with you six months or more in the last two years.

chunks.t: OTBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Police checks with precise rules. Criminal-conviction check for your country of registration Plus any country lived in for six months or more in the last ten years. Let the Board arrange the New Zealand check Emailed to you during processing, unless you have never been to New Zealand. Explanatory note if you have any conviction Not an automatic bar — disclose fully.

chunks.t: OTBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Only if English is not your first language and you do not meet a recognised-country route. Sit OET (occupational therapy version) or IELTS Academic Meet the Board’s threshold in every component. Achieve the standard within twelve months if combining sittings You may club results across sittings. Results no older than twenty-four months at submission Time the test so it stays valid.

chunks.t: OTBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Required of every applicant — on the Board’s cue. Note Ngā Paerewa Te Tiriti is required Approved online course via Ko Awatea LEARN. Request your Ko Awatea account at the right time Only after the Board updates your application number to a registration number. Read about te Tiriti o Waitangi and Māori health Worth doing now, ahead of the course.

chunks.t: OTBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Putting it together and what follows. Submit your initial application and fee via MyOTBNZ The applicant portal. Complete the portal steps: self-assessment, referees, CV Your application is not processed until these are in. Post or courier the hard-copy documents Several must be supplied physically, not just uploaded. Respond promptly to any Board queries Speed of response is the biggest factor within your control. Registration confirmed Apply for your practising certificate Before you can work — it can be applied for alongside registration. Begin the Recertification Programme Fortnightly supervision and Te Rito for overseas-qualified registrants. Print or save as PDF What next?

chunks.t: OTBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.h: Registration is one part of the decision
chunks.x: Check my pathway Your profession, where you trained, what you hold — and the route most likely to apply to you. How registration works in New Zealand For every profession — the boards, the sequence, English and timelines. Allied health in New Zealand The family of professions, and the pages for each. Occupational therapist What the work is like, indicative pay, where you could live. Plan your move Registration, visas, family and the order to do it in — personalised, saved in your browser. How we help

chunks.t: OTBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.h: We can read it before the Board does
chunks.x: We review your evidence — particularly the competence self-assessment and your pathway choice — against what the Board looks for, and flag likely issues while they are still easy to fix. We support and guide you through the process; the registration decision always rests with the Occupational Therapy Board of New Zealand. Ask Ethicare The Board’s own site ↗

chunks.t: PBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: At a glance Registration comes first An employer generally wants to see you are registered, or clearly registrable, before progressing your application. Plan everything else on top of it. Four pathways — get yours right first Express (UK, Ireland, Canada, South Africa), Trans-Tasman (Ahpra-registered in Australia) or General (everyone else). The wrong one is the most common avoidable delay. Assessed against the Practice Thresholds A shared Australia–New Zealand set of competencies. Read them before you apply; they are the yardstick for everything you submit. Two cultural competency courses Online, within your control, required. The one part of the application you can finish today.

chunks.t: PBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Read it once to understand the shape of the journey, then come back to each section as you reach it. The checklist at the end remembers what you have ticked, on this device. Understanding the Board Scopes of practice Which pathway is yours The Practice Thresholds and assessment Eligibility requirements Preparing your application Cultural competency English language Completing and submitting After you submit, and your APC Where people get stuck Questions we are asked most The whole journey on one page The checklist — 39 items, tickable Section 01

chunks.t: PBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: The Physiotherapy Board of New Zealand registers and oversees physiotherapists under the Health Practitioners Competence Assurance Act. Its purpose is to protect the public by making sure everyone practising as a physiotherapist is qualified, competent and fit to do so. The title and practice of physiotherapy are legally protected: you cannot practise, or call yourself a physiotherapist, without registration and a current Annual Practising Certificate.

chunks.t: PBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: What sets physiotherapy apart is what you are assessed against. Every application is measured against the Physiotherapy Practice Thresholds in Australia and Aotearoa New Zealand — a shared set of competencies describing what a physiotherapist must be able to do, safely and effectively, to register and practise. Get to know them early; Section 04 covers them in detail.

chunks.t: PBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.h: Registration, the APC and your HPI number
chunks.x: Registration confirms you have met the standard and does not expire. The Annual Practising Certificate (APC) is what permits you to work, renewed each year; the physiotherapy APC year runs to 31 March and is managed through the Board’s MyPBNZ portal. Once registered you are added to the public Register of Physiotherapists and the Ministry of Health issues your Health Practitioner Index (HPI) number. Registration is an ongoing commitment: competence, ethical practice and annual CPD the Board can audit. Qualification → Registration — General Scope → Annual Practising Certificate → Practise in New Zealand Section 02

chunks.t: PBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Three scopes exist. For anyone applying from overseas, one matters to begin with: every physiotherapist must first be registered in the General Scope. Your application is for this

chunks.t: PBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Where every physiotherapist begins. The full breadth of autonomous practice — assessment, diagnosis and treatment — across musculoskeletal, neurological, cardiorespiratory and other areas. Later

chunks.t: PBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: For advanced skills in areas such as musculoskeletal, neurology or cardiorespiratory practice. Not an entry point: it needs unrestricted General Scope registration, a current APC, a relevant postgraduate qualification and experience including time practising in New Zealand. Later

chunks.t: PBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: The most advanced scope, for physiotherapists recognised as specialists in their field. Built on General Scope registration and New Zealand practice — something to progress toward, not a route in. What this means for you. Apply for the General Scope. The other two are progression options once you are registered, hold an APC and have built experience here. Nothing to think about yet — but reassuring that the career pathway exists. Section 03

chunks.t: PBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: PBNZ has four distinct pathways, and which one you use depends entirely on where you trained and where you are registered. Pathway 1

chunks.t: PBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Who: physiotherapists connected to the UK, Ireland, Canada or South Africa — either unrestricted registration there (HCPC, CORU, HPCSA or a Canadian physiotherapy regulator) or a physiotherapy qualification from one of them recognised as pre-registration by that regulator. Why it exists: the Board treats those four jurisdictions as closely aligned with New Zealand, so the Express Pathway removes duplication of what you have already proven. Pathway 2

chunks.t: PBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Who: physiotherapists holding either full or limited registration with Ahpra in Australia. Why it exists: under the Trans-Tasman arrangement, registration in one country is recognised in the other. You apply under TTMR, not as an overseas-trained applicant. Worth knowing: limited registration carries supervision conditions, and those conditions apply in New Zealand too. It is the only supervision requirement on any of the overseas pathways. Pathway 3

chunks.t: PBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Who: Fiji National University qualifications from 2013 onwards, and Hong Kong SAR physiotherapy degrees granted since 2015. Why it exists: you follow the General application process, but the Board has pre-identified which competencies need supplementary evidence — so it is a shorter road than General from a standing start. Pathway 4

chunks.t: PBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Who: everyone else — no recognised qualification or unrestricted registration in the UK, Ireland, Canada, South Africa or Australia. Why it exists: it assesses your qualification and competence directly against the Practice Thresholds, with a structured way to demonstrate any competency your curriculum does not already evidence (Section 04). 1

chunks.t: PBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.h: Qualified at Fiji National University from 2013, or in Hong Kong SAR since 2015?
chunks.x: International General: Fast Track. You use the General application process, but the Board has already identified which competencies need supplementary evidence. 4

chunks.t: PBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: International General Pathway. The wrong pathway costs time. Applying under General when you qualify for Express, or the reverse, is one of the most common avoidable delays. If you are unsure where you fall, check before you start . Section 04

chunks.t: PBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.h: The Practice Thresholds and how assessment works
chunks.x: The Practice Thresholds describe the threshold competence required for initial registration and continuing practice — what you must be able to do, safely and effectively, across assessment, clinical reasoning, intervention, communication, professional behaviour and safety. They are shared across Australia and New Zealand, which is why Australian-registered physiotherapists move so smoothly between the two systems. On the General Pathway, assessment runs through five phases. Knowing them in advance removes most of the anxiety, because you can see exactly where you are at any point. 1

chunks.t: PBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: The Board reviews your application for completeness. If anything is missing or eligibility is in question, you are emailed before it proceeds. 2

chunks.t: PBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: An assessor reviews how well the curriculum of your primary physiotherapy degree aligns with each key competency. Two outcomes: every competency met, and the application goes straight forward; or gaps, and it moves to Phase 3. Neither is unusual — curricula differ between countries. 3

chunks.t: PBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.h: Request for supporting evidence — only if needed
chunks.x: You are told exactly which competencies to demonstrate and have three months to provide evidence. Competencies already shown do not need proving again. 4

chunks.t: PBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: If it meets the criteria you proceed; if not, you can submit more based on the assessor’s feedback. 5

chunks.t: PBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Applications that meet the requirement go to the Registrar for approval, and you receive email confirmation.

chunks.t: PBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.h: Demonstrating competencies, if you reach Phase 3
chunks.x: The Board’s request sets out precisely which competencies need evidencing, and it publishes a Guidance on Providing Supporting Evidence document with templates — a Reflections template and a Validation of Work History form. Read them; they help you choose high-quality evidence. Give specific examples and detail from your training or work, clearly named and well organised. Read the Thresholds before you apply. Map your experience to each competency. If you can already see where your curriculum might be light, start gathering specific, detailed examples now — the evidence phase, if it comes, is then far quicker. Section 05

chunks.t: PBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: A recognised physiotherapy qualification Why: your qualification is the foundation of safe practice. The Board needs confidence your training covered the Practice Thresholds — which is why course content can matter as much as the certificate, particularly on the General Pathway. Registration and good standing Why: if you are, or have been, registered as a physiotherapist anywhere, the Board needs to know you are in good standing with no unresolved concerns. This underpins the Express and TTMR pathways and supports the General Pathway too. Recency of practice Why: skills fade when unused. If you have had a significant break, flag it early — depending on the gap, a Return to Practice process may apply. English language Why: patient safety. Taking histories, explaining treatment, communicating precisely with patients and colleagues. Section 08.

chunks.t: PBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Fitness for registration Why: your physical and mental fitness to practise safely, and your professional conduct history. Full disclosure — even of matters you think minor or resolved — is always right. Non-disclosure is treated far more seriously than the underlying matter usually is. Cultural competency Why: practising safely in New Zealand means understanding its cultural context, including Te Tiriti o Waitangi and Māori health. PBNZ requires evidence of cultural competency training — specific enough to have its own section, 07. Read every requirement as a question. The Board is asking whether you are safe to practise. Frame each document as the answer and your application becomes far more persuasive. Section 06

chunks.t: PBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: The Board is forming a picture of you as a professional, and a folder of crooked, half-legible photocopies undermines it even when every document is genuine. Clean colour scans, pages straight and square, nothing cut off, consistent file names, certification done properly the first time.

chunks.t: PBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Why Confirms who you are; underpins your visa and right to work. Accepted A passport or birth certificate, plus a name-change document (marriage certificate, deed poll) if your name differs across documents. Tip Scan flat, in colour, with all edges visible.

chunks.t: PBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Why Your primary physiotherapy qualification is the basis of registration; on the General Pathway these are what the curriculum assessment works from. Required General Pathway: your degree, academic transcript, curriculum and a clinical hours profile — all four. Express Pathway: the degree or academic transcript for your primary physiotherapy qualification, and certificates of good standing from every regulatory authority you have been registered with. Both are required — registration evidence does not stand in for the qualification document. Mistake Sending only the degree and transcript. The curriculum and clinical hours profile are required and frequently forgotten.

chunks.t: PBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Why Confirm good standing with every physiotherapy regulator you have registered with. Timing Each must be less than three months old on the date you submit. Requesting too early is a frequent, avoidable reason to start again. Tip Line them up to be fresh at submission, not months before.

chunks.t: PBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Why The Board must protect patients, so it checks your background. Required From any country you have lived in for more than twelve months in the last ten years since age eighteen — and, like Good Standing, each less than three months old at submission. Tip They can take time to obtain, so balance starting early against the three-month rule.

chunks.t: PBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Why Evidences your experience and recency of practice. Mistake Submitting your own CV format. The Board requires its own downloadable template and will send yours back. Tip Complete it fully, accounting for every period including gaps. Build your CV helps you assemble the content before you transfer it.

chunks.t: PBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Why Certification confirms a true copy of the original. The rule Each required document is either certified, or sent directly to the Board by the issuing authority. Translations of any non-English document must also be provided. Tip Confirm who may certify and the wording before you spend money. Getting it wrong means doing it twice. Section 07

chunks.t: PBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: A requirement that surprises many international applicants, and one you can begin today. PBNZ requires evidence of cultural competency training as part of registration, typically certificates from two recognised courses. They cover cultural safety, Te Tiriti o Waitangi and its place in healthcare, and working effectively with Māori and New Zealand’s diverse communities. Safe physiotherapy here is not only clinical skill; Te Tiriti is foundational to the health system and cultural safety is treated as a core part of competent practice, not an optional extra. chunks.x: Across two sittings within six months, subject to floors in each component that differ by test. If you narrowly miss one component, that is usually cheaper than re-sitting the whole thing. Results expire. Typically around two years from the test date. Sitting the test early and then taking many months to assemble the rest is a frequent reason for paying to sit it again. Time it to remain valid through to assessment. Sit a timed practice test first, find your weakest component, and book early. Section 09

chunks.t: PBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.h: The questions we are asked most
chunks.x: Which pathway should I use? Ahpra-registered in Australia: Trans-Tasman Mutual Recognition. Trained or registered in the UK, Ireland, Canada or South Africa: the International Express Pathway. Everyone else: the International General Pathway. When in doubt, check before you start. Can I apply for registration before finding a job? Yes — and in most cases you should. Registration usually comes before employment, so starting early puts you in a far stronger position when roles arise. What scope will I be registered in? The General Scope, where every physiotherapist begins. Advanced Practice and Specialist are progression options once you are registered, hold an APC and have New Zealand experience. What are the Practice Thresholds? The shared Australia–New Zealand set of competencies your application is assessed against: what a physiotherapist must be able to do to register and practise.

chunks.t: PBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.h: The questions we are asked most
chunks.x: Read them before you apply. Do I really need the cultural competency courses? Yes. Evidence of cultural competency training, typically two courses, is part of registration. Online and within your control — one of the easiest things to complete early. What if my curriculum does not cover every competency? On the General Pathway the assessment runs in phases. If the curriculum review finds gaps, you are told the specific competencies to demonstrate and have around three months to provide detailed evidence from your training or work. Competencies already shown do not need proving again, and the Board provides guidance and templates. Can I work while my application is being assessed? You cannot practise until you are registered and hold a current APC. Plan your move around that fact rather than assuming you can begin and sort registration out afterwards.

chunks.h: The questions we are asked most
chunks.x: Can Ethicare review my application? Yes. We review documents and competency evidence before submission against what the Board looks for and flag likely issues while they are easy to fix. The registration decision always rests with the Board. Section 13

chunks.t: PBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Two courses required, entirely within your control. Complete a Mauri Ora course Foundations in Cultural Competency, or Healthcare and the Treaty of Waitangi — counts as one of your two. Complete a second, distinct course The other Mauri Ora course, or Ngā Paerewa Modules One and Two. Remember: Ngā Paerewa Modules One and Two count as one course Pair it with a Mauri Ora course. Save all completion certificates You upload these with your application.

chunks.t: PBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: The foundations every application needs. Passport or birth certificate Either is accepted for identity; full, clear colour scan. Name-change documents Only if your name differs across documents. Primary physiotherapy degree Certified copy of your qualifying qualification. Academic transcript Required alongside the degree. Curriculum Required on the General Pathway — often forgotten. Clinical hours profile Required on the General Pathway — often forgotten. Certification done correctly Each document certified, or sent to the Board directly by the issuing authority. Translations, if applicable Certified translation of any non-English document.

chunks.t: PBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Confirmation you are in good professional standing — mind the three-month rule. Evidence of registration — Express and TTMR Degree or transcript from the UK, Ireland, Canada or South Africa, or proof of registration with HCPC, CORU, HPCSA, a Canadian regulator or Ahpra. Certificates of Good Standing requested From every physiotherapy regulator you have registered with. Good Standing less than three months old at submission A hard PBNZ rule — do not request them too early. Police or criminal history certificates From every country lived in for twelve months or more in the last ten years since age eighteen. Police certificates less than three months old at submission The same rule — balance it against how long they take to obtain.

chunks.t: PBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Proof your skills and communication are current. CV on the PBNZ template The Board’s own template, not your format, with every period accounted for. Confirm which English route applies First-language evidence, English-medium education, or a test. Sit IELTS Academic, OET, PTE Academic or TOEFL iBT, if required Meet the minimum in every component, not just overall. Check English test validity dates Results expire, typically after about two years — time it to stay valid through assessment.

chunks.t: PBNZ registration guide and checklist
chunks.x: Only if your curriculum does not cover every competency. Review the assessor’s competency request It lists exactly which competencies still need demonstrating. Read the Board’s supporting-evidence guidance Use its guidance document and templates — Reflections, Validation of Work History. Gather specific examples for each competency Detailed evidence from your training or work; already-met ones do not need repeating. Submit within three months of the request Name files clearly; keep folders short and well organised.

Answer the fitness-for-registration questions English, physical and mental fitness, professional conduct — full disclosure. Upload documents as clean colour scans Straight, square, nothing cut off, clearly named. Pay the applicable fee Keep your payment confirmation. Final check, then submit Could a stranger find everything they need without emailing you?

chunks.x: 1 Check your pathway Your profession and where you trained decide the route. 2 Gather your evidence Qualifications, references, good standing and, if needed, English. 3 Apply to your board With the fee. The board assesses your application. 4 Registration and practice A scope of practice, then an annual practising certificate. Additional examinations, supervision or other requirements depend on your profession and pathway. Practical details

chunks.t: Can I work in New Zealand? Registration
chunks.x: Documents and English Boards ask for degree certificates, transcripts, proof of identity, references and a certificate of good standing from your current regulator. Some must be certified or sent directly between bodies, and they can take weeks to arrive, so start early. Most boards need evidence of English unless you trained and practised in English in a recognised country. Each board publishes its exemptions and required scores. IELTS (Academic) and OET, which is built for healthcare, are the widely accepted tests. If you need to prepare, our endorsed partner Swoosh English offers IELTS and OET preparation for healthcare professionals. Fees and timelines Applications, English tests, assessments, exams and certified documents each carry a cost, and they vary by board and profession. For some candidates the total is significant, so budget for it early with the cost calculator .

chunks.t: Can I work in New Zealand? Registration
chunks.x: Getting documents together usually takes weeks; the board’s assessment usually takes months, depending on your profession and pathway. Your job offer and visa normally progress at the same time, so you do not have to be registered before you apply for roles. Some pathways begin with a period of supervised practice. Sophie’s insight The mistake I see most is leaving registration too late. Documents and good-standing certificates take longer than anyone expects. Check your route first, start the paperwork early and keep everything in one folder. Sophie CEO & Founder, Ethicare Resourcing Common questions

chunks.t: Can I work in New Zealand? Registration
chunks.x: Do I need a job offer before I can register? Usually not to begin the process. For some professions a position or supervisor is part of the registration pathway; for others you can register independently. In practice, registration, a job offer and your visa tend to move together. Will my overseas qualification be recognised? Some overseas qualifications are recognised through established pathways, while others need further assessment, examinations or supervised practice. Eligibility depends on your profession, qualifications and individual circumstances. Your registration board makes the final decision. Do I definitely have to sit an English test? Not necessarily. Many clinicians who trained and practised in English in a recognised country are exempt. Each board publishes who is exempt, so check its policy before you book a test.

chunks.t: Can I work in New Zealand? Registration
chunks.x: Where evidence is needed, IELTS (Academic) and OET are the widely accepted tests. How much does registration cost? Each board sets its own application and annual practising certificate fees, and there can be extra costs for English tests, assessments, exams and certifying documents. For some candidates the total is significant, so budget for it early. The cost calculator helps you set it out. What if my situation is unusual? Career breaks, training in more than one country, a niche specialty or a less common qualification can all change your route, and some situations will not meet the requirements. The pathway checker shows where you are likely to stand; the board makes the final decision. Next · Stage 04

chunks.t: Preparing to move | New Zealand
chunks.h: A big move is just a lot of small, doable things
chunks.x: So this step lays it out as a countdown: what to think about months ahead, what to do in the final weeks, and what waits for your first days on the ground. Work through it at your own pace, tick things off as you go, and let the list carry the worry so you don’t have to. And you’re not project-managing this alone. We’ve helped many families make exactly this move , and we’re on hand for the questions the checklists don’t answer, plus introductions to the relocation and shipping partners we trust. Start with the big rocks

chunks.t: Preparing to move | New Zealand
chunks.x: These three take the longest and matter the most, so get them moving early. A roof

chunks.t: Preparing to move | New Zealand
chunks.x: You don’t need your forever home before you fly, just a sorted first few weeks. Temporary or short-term rental accommodation buys you time to find the right place once you’re here. Money

chunks.t: Preparing to move | New Zealand
chunks.x: Opening a New Zealand bank account and planning how you’ll move your money across are jobs best started early: some banks let you begin the process before you arrive. Children

chunks.t: Preparing to move | New Zealand
chunks.x: If you’re moving with children, school enrolment and zones shape where you’ll want to live. Researching this early often decides the neighbourhood for you. A countdown to departure

chunks.t: Preparing to move | New Zealand
chunks.x: Research regions and neighbourhoods, guided by work and schools. Begin school enrolment enquiries and check zones. Get quotes from international shipping and relocation companies. Start gathering documents: passports, certificates, references, medical and school records. Plan the money side: how and when you’ll transfer funds. 1–2 months out

chunks.t: Preparing to move | New Zealand
chunks.x: Book flights and your first accommodation for arrival. Confirm your shipping or air-freight, and decide what comes and what goes. Arrange travel and contents insurance for the move. Notify schools, landlords, banks and utilities at home of your leaving date. Sort pets early if they’re coming, it has its own long timeline. Final weeks

chunks.t: Preparing to move | New Zealand
chunks.x: Close or redirect accounts, subscriptions and mail. Pack a "first fortnight" bag: essentials you’ll want before shipping arrives. Keep all key documents together in your hand luggage. Confirm someone can meet you or your accommodation is ready on arrival. Say your goodbyes, and let yourself feel them. First days here

Look into transport, a car, or public transport options. Breathe. The hardest part is now behind you. The practical detail
