chunks.t: Why people move, and what they miss
chunks.x: New Zealand Australia Stage 01 · Imagine the possibilities Could life look different? Why healthcare professionals move to Australia or New Zealand — and what they say they miss You have seen the pitch: work-life balance, beaches, space. Much of it is true. This is the rest of the picture — what people gain, what they trade and what they miss — so you can decide whether the trade is right for you. Start with why people go → Ask Ethicare 8 short sections Reviewed September 2026 Free Start here

chunks.t: Why people move, and what they miss
chunks.h: It shouldn’t start with a vacancy
chunks.x: But when you are thinking about moving your life — and possibly your family’s — to the other side of the world, there is more you probably want to know. What do the healthcare professionals who made the move love? What surprised them? And what do they miss, six months or ten years later? Not to persuade you to go, and not to put you off. Deciding whether to move shouldn’t start with a vacancy. It should start with whether you can see a life there. You don’t need to have decided anything yet — not the country, not the timing, not whether you are going at all. This is exploration. Every other part of the site is open without it, and this page is here whenever the question comes back. Section 01 · The reasons

chunks.t: Why people move, and what they miss
chunks.h: More life around the working day
chunks.x: Finishing a shift with daylight left. Weekends that are not spent recovering. Wanting work to take up a smaller share of life. Work

chunks.t: Why people move, and what they miss
chunks.x: Another health system, other ways of working, a specialist opening, or simply a change. Not easier by definition — different. Family

chunks.t: Why people move, and what they miss
chunks.x: Space, schooling, and wanting children to know another country while they are young enough for it to become theirs. Money

chunks.t: Why people move, and what they miss
chunks.x: Real in some Australian professions and places. The headline salary is only part of it — Make the numbers work is where that gets tested. Space

chunks.t: Why people move, and what they miss
chunks.x: A garden. A shorter drive to work. Coast or hills as part of an ordinary week rather than a holiday. Not everyone gets a house by the beach. Adventure

chunks.t: Why people move, and what they miss
chunks.x: Some people simply want to, while they can. Wonder about it for ten years and there comes a point where you either do it or accept you probably never will. The system

chunks.t: Why people move, and what they miss
chunks.h: Tired of the one you are in
chunks.x: Some people are: the workload, the waits, the pay conversation, a service that runs on goodwill. A real reason. A move changes a great deal and does not fix what would travel with you — and both these systems are under pressure too. Different pressure, not none. Precedent

chunks.t: Why people move, and what they miss
chunks.h: Someone you know has done it
chunks.x: A friend, a colleague, a cousin already there. Often the thing that turns an idea into something that feels possible. Section 02 · Not one destination

chunks.t: Why people move, and what they miss
chunks.x: Australia and New Zealand are not one place, and neither is one place inside itself. New Zealand

chunks.t: Why people move, and what they miss
chunks.x: Smaller communities, the outdoors close to ordinary life, and a different scale of living. People come for family life and adventure more than for earning potential. Auckland, Wellington, Christchurch, Palmerston North and rural New Zealand are very different lives. Explore New Zealand → Australia

chunks.t: Why people move, and what they miss
chunks.x: A warmer climate, larger cities, a bigger health system and job market, long-established migrant communities, and stronger earning potential in some professions. Perth, Melbourne, Hobart, Bundaberg and regional Western Australia are not interchangeable. Explore Australia → Weighing the two at once? Australia or New Zealand? sets them side by side. Section 03 · After the move

chunks.t: Why people move, and what they miss
chunks.x: The children being outside — after school, not just on holiday. The barbecue that isn’t saved for the one sunny Saturday in August. A walk after work, in daylight. A beach the tourists don’t know about. Room for a dog. Being known in a smaller community. In parts of Australia, how much of life happens outdoors. In New Zealand, how quickly you are out of the city and into coast, bush or hills. A shorter, calmer commute — for some people, in some places. The first Christmas on a beach. A child’s accent you weren’t expecting. Eventually the extraordinary becomes ordinary. People tell us that is when somewhere starts to feel like home. What is here is what the people we have placed tell us. Named stories appear as people agree to them — Megan’s, from Manchester to the Sunshine Coast , is the first. Section 04 · The other side

chunks.t: Why people move, and what they miss
chunks.h: The things nobody puts in the brochure
chunks.x: Real story · what you leave “Of course, we miss our loved ones and the sunny South African weather, so we feel very fortunate that both of our parents were able to come and visit us here.” Janita, nuclear medicine technologist, Auckland. The airport, January 2024 — both sets of parents have since been out to visit. What the move was like → Written first for people leaving the UK, because that is who most of our candidates are today. Coming from South Africa, Ireland, India or the Philippines? What you would gain and miss is different, and we want to write it with people who have done it. Tell us what you would want here. The ordinary choice

chunks.t: Why people move, and what they miss
chunks.h: Food, and streets that change every few blocks
chunks.x: Chinese, Indian, Turkish, Caribbean or Vietnamese within a walk; the family-run place you have been going to for years. Both countries are multicultural, most of all in the big cities — a smaller city or regional town will feel the difference. Old things

chunks.t: Why people move, and what they miss
chunks.x: Victorian brick, villages where none of the houses line up, a pub that has been there for 300 years. And the pub itself — the local, the fire, the roast — is its own culture. Both countries have pubs; they are not that. Europe

chunks.t: Why people move, and what they miss
chunks.x: Lisbon for a long weekend, Paris by train, the Alps. Even if you rarely went, you could. From here the near world is the Pacific and Asia, and Britain is a day’s flying away. Culture and choice

chunks.t: Why people move, and what they miss
chunks.h: The exhibition, the theatre, the tour
chunks.x: Melbourne and Sydney are major cultural cities and New Zealand has real arts and music scenes — but moving from a global city to a smaller centre is still a trade. If this is part of what makes you happy, it is not superficial. Seasons

chunks.t: Why people move, and what they miss
chunks.x: The first cold day, autumn leaves, long light evenings. Christmas at 28 degrees delights some people and never feels right to others. New Zealand and southern Australia have real seasons; the tropical north does not. “Better weather” isn’t the question — what weather makes you happy is. Familiarity

chunks.t: Why people move, and what they miss
chunks.x: Which supermarket, which form, which queue. For the first while, nothing is instinctive, and that is tiring in a way people don’t expect. It passes; it is worth knowing it is coming. Section 05 · The real trade-off

chunks.t: Why people move, and what they miss
chunks.h: How does being this far from home feel to you?
chunks.x: Food can be found and you can travel for a concert. Family is harder: you will not be there for everything. Worth thinking through now rather than after: A full day in the air each way, and what the flights cost for a family. How much of your annual leave a visit home uses. Long-haul with small children. Ageing parents, and what an emergency would look like from there. Keeping relationships alive across a time difference that turns your evening into their morning. How often you could afford to go back. Video calls help enormously. They are not the same as being there. For some people the life they gain makes the distance worthwhile; for others it eventually brings them home. Neither means the move failed. The cost of visits belongs with everything else that has a number — Make the numbers work . Section 06 · Your own list

chunks.t: Anaesthetic Technician jobs in New Zealand
chunks.h: The detail, when you want it
chunks.x: What changes is your standing and the shape of your role, and for ODPs in particular that needs understanding before you commit. Anaesthetic technology is a registered profession here, with its own council and its own defined scope. You register with the Medical Sciences Council of New Zealand and hold an Annual Practising Certificate, the same as any other regulated clinician. That matters more than it sounds. Your scope is written down, your accountability is your own, and you are not practising as an assistant under someone else's registration. The scope is anaesthesia-focused rather than whole-theatre. If you have trained as an ODP in the UK, this is the difference. New Zealand still separates anaesthetic practice from scrub and recovery roles, so you go deeper into anaesthesia instead of rotating across all three.

chunks.t: Anaesthetic Technician jobs in New Zealand

chunks.x: The 2025 scope update extended the role across the phases of anaesthesia — preparation, induction, maintenance, emergence and handover — rather than across the theatre. Some ATs also work in PACU, but anaesthesia is the core of the job. Theatre teams are smaller and flatter. You will know every anaesthetist you work with by name, and you will be expected to speak up. Lists are generally less rushed than in high-volume overseas systems, handovers are less formal, and the amount of independent preparation and problem-solving expected of you is higher. ATs tell us the trust is the best part and the exposure is the part that takes adjusting to. "You are registered in your own right, and the team treats you that way." For most people that trade lands well: a narrower scope, held with more authority.

chunks.t: Anaesthetic Technician jobs in New Zealand
chunks.x: I'm a UK-trained ODP. Does my qualification count? Yes. The Medical Sciences Council assesses your qualification, your recent clinical practice and your competency against New Zealand standards, and UK ODP training is well recognised. We support internationally trained ATs and ODPs from the UK, South Africa, the UAE and beyond. The adjustment is scope rather than skill. You will narrow into anaesthesia and go deeper, rather than rotating across anaesthetics, scrub and recovery. Will I lose my scrub and recovery skills? some of them. New Zealand keeps anaesthetic practice separate from scrub and recovery, so your scrub work will not be part of the job. Some ATs do work in PACU, and that varies by service, so it is worth asking about specifically if recovery matters to you. What you gain is depth.

chunks.t: Anaesthetic Technician jobs in New Zealand
chunks.x: Most ODPs who move here say the anaesthetic side of their practice got noticeably stronger in the first year, because it is all they do. What did the 2025 scope update change? It extended the role across the phases of anaesthesia — preparation, induction, maintenance, emergence and handover — bringing it closer to the multi-phase perioperative responsibility ODPs hold in the UK. What it did not do is merge anaesthetic practice with scrub and recovery. Practically, it means clearer recognition of what experienced ATs were already doing, and a scope that reads much more familiarly to someone arriving from the UK. What are on-call and out-of-hours patterns like? They depend on the service. Acute theatres run around the clock, so shift work and on-call are part of hospital practice, and in smaller hospitals on-call comes round more often because the roster is shorter.

chunks.t: Anaesthetic Technician jobs in New Zealand
chunks.x: Private surgical centres are largely daytime elective work. Ask about on-call frequency and how it is paid before you accept anything. You will work with the same anaesthetists repeatedly rather than a rotating cast, hierarchies are less formal than in large overseas suites, and you are expected to raise concerns directly. Most ATs find the trust and the visibility go together: good practice gets noticed quickly here. Can I progress, or is it a flat career? There is a proper ladder. Senior AT and charge roles, equipment and clinical lead positions, clinical education and student supervision, and depth in specialties such as cardiac, neuro, obstetric or paediatric anaesthesia.

chunks.x: Getting registered Registration overview Reviewed July 2026 · checked against the Medical Council of New Zealand’s current published guidance To practise in New Zealand you'll register with the Medical Council of New Zealand (MCNZ). Consultant radiologists work towards vocational registration in radiology; we’ll help you understand your pathway from the start. The Council assesses your specialist qualifications and experience against New Zealand standards, often alongside the RANZCR for the vocational (radiology) scope. As part of the process you'll typically need: Verification of your qualification Evidence of recent clinical practice A police / criminal-history clearance Confirmation of English-language proficiency, if required Once registered, you’ll hold an Annual Practising Certificate (APC). We support you from understanding your pathway through to securing the right role.

If you hold a UK, Irish or other overseas fellowship rather than the FRANZCR, your application goes down VOC3 and RANZCR advises the Council on it — so plan for months, not weeks, and start the college paperwork before you apply rather than after. chunks.t: Consultant Radiologist Jobs in New Zealand
chunks.x: Will I need to re-sit exams? No. Consultants from comparable health systems register towards vocational registration in diagnostic radiology without New Zealand exams. It helps that RANZCR is the joint college for Australia and New Zealand, so the training standard your qualification is measured against is a familiar one, and Fellowship routes are well trodden. What you will have is a defined period of supervision first, commonly in the range of six to twelve months, before full vocational registration. It is collegial rather than probationary: a named supervisor, scheduled reviews, and a record that you have settled into practice here. The slowest part of the whole process is usually verifying your primary qualification at source, so we start that before anything else.

chunks.t: Consultant Radiologist Jobs in New Zealand
chunks.x: Will I have to keep general reporting alongside my subspecialty? In most departments, yes — and it is worth being clear-eyed about it. Services here are smaller than the tertiary centres many consultants come from, so even strongly subspecialised radiologists usually carry a share of the general list. In a provincial department, general reporting across plain film, CT, ultrasound and MRI is the backbone of the week, with your subspecialty layered on top. The larger centres come closest to a purely subspecialty practice, with dedicated sessions and enough volume to sustain them. If keeping a narrow focus is essential to you, say so early; it narrows which departments make sense. Many radiologists find the breadth is the part they end up valuing. What is on-call like? Clearly defined and properly paid, which is often the first pleasant surprise.

chunks.t: Consultant Radiologist Jobs in New Zealand
chunks.x: Out-of-hours commitments are set out in the national agreement rather than negotiated role by role, and call attracts penalty rates plus availability allowances on top of base salary. The practical reality varies with department size. Much of the after-hours work is reported remotely from home with full PACS access, and a number of services use overnight teleradiology cover so the on-call burden is lighter than the roster suggests. In smaller centres you are in a shorter rotation with fewer colleagues, and interventional cover is a separate question we always pin down in writing before you accept. How is my salary step decided? By the number of years since you became eligible for specialist registration — not by when you register in New Zealand, and not by negotiation.

chunks.t: Consultant Radiologist Jobs in New Zealand
chunks.x: Public senior-doctor pay sits on the national collective agreement, so the bands, steps and allowances are published and the same wherever you work. There is no advantage to being a strong negotiator, which most consultants find a relief. We confirm your step against the current agreement in writing before you accept a role, along with what on-call, allowances and leave add on top of base. If a figure has not been verified against the agreement, we will tell you it hasn't rather than let you plan around it. Can I do private work or teleradiology alongside a public role? Yes, and in radiology it is common. Private practice outside contracted public hours is permitted, and the private sector is where radiology income rises most sharply. Plenty of consultants hold a public appointment for the teams, teaching and complexity, and take private sessions around it.

chunks.t: Consultant Radiologist Jobs in New Zealand
chunks.x: Teleradiology adds a further option, including reporting for services well outside your own region. Two practical caveats: your work visa, if you are on one, is tied to your employer, so additional work needs checking before you commit to it; and indemnity and any restraint provisions in your contract need reading properly. We go through both with you rather than leaving you to find out later. Could I move to Australia later, or come back? Many radiologists do, in both directions. RANZCR spans both countries, and vocational recognition across the Tasman is well established, so a move later is a paperwork exercise rather than a fresh assessment. Trans-Tasman travel and work rights for New Zealand residents and citizens make the practicalities considerably easier than most international moves. People also come the other way, choosing New Zealand for the balance and the pace of the working week even where Australia pays more at the top end. If Australia turns out to be the better fit, the Australia guides cover it in the same depth. Nau mai, haere mai · If you’re weighing it up

chunks.t: GP Jobs in New Zealand
chunks.x: Will I need to re-sit exams? Almost never. GPs from comparable health systems register towards vocational registration without sitting New Zealand exams — what varies is the supervision that comes first. If your qualification is on the Medical Council's approved list you take the fastest route with no separate college equivalence assessment. If it isn't, RNZCGP assesses your training and the outcome sets the length: broadly around a year of supervision, or longer where an assessment pathway applies. Supervision here is not someone checking your work. It is a named colleague, regular scheduled conversations, and a structured way of showing you have settled into New Zealand general practice. Most GPs describe it as useful rather than onerous — and it ends with permanent vocational registration.

chunks.t: GP Jobs in New Zealand
chunks.x: How different is the funding and consultation model? This is the biggest practical adjustment, so understand it before you arrive. Practices enrol patients and receive capitation funding for that enrolled population, topped up by a patient co-payment at the time of the appointment. Most people pay something to see their GP; children and Community Services Card holders pay less or nothing, and practices in high-need areas are funded differently again. What it means day to day: your list is your list, continuity is real, and the funding follows the relationship rather than the activity. There is no QOF-style points system driving your week. Standard appointments are short by international standards, though longer consultations are widely available and how you structure your day is largely yours to negotiate.

chunks.t: GP Jobs in New Zealand
chunks.x: Salaried, contractor or practice ownership — which should I choose? They are different jobs, not just different pay structures. Salaried is the simplest landing: a known income, employment protections, someone else carrying the business. Contractor arrangements give you more control over sessions and a higher ceiling, with the trade-off that you carry more of your own risk, tax and indemnity admin. Ownership is a business as well as a clinical role, and rewards people who want a say in how the practice is run. Our advice is to arrive salaried or on a simple contract, learn the system for a year, then decide. Almost nobody regrets that order. We'll show you the numbers for a specific role, alongside what living in that town costs, rather than a national average. What is rural general practice like here? Broader than you are probably imagining, and that is the appeal.

chunks.t: GP Jobs in New Zealand
chunks.x: Rural GPs manage presentations that would be referred on in a city — minor trauma, acute medicine, obstetric and emergency care, sometimes inpatient work — with real distance between you and the nearest hospital. Demand is highest here, incentives are often better, and the clinical breadth is why many people never go back to metropolitan practice. It asks something of you in return: fewer colleagues on site, on-call that really is on-call, and a small community where you are the doctor at the supermarket too. Some people find that the best part of the job. We will tell you plainly which category we think a role falls into. Do I have to become an RNZCGP Fellow? Not to work. You practise under vocational registration in general practice; Fellowship of the Royal New Zealand College of General Practitioners is the college qualification alongside it.

General practice sits at the top tier of the Green List, which means a residence application from the outset rather than years on a work visa first. chunks.t: Medical imaging careers in Australia
chunks.x: Australia runs a large public system alongside one of the biggest private imaging markets in the world, and it does not train enough people to staff either. Internationally qualified clinicians are a permanent part of how imaging works here, not a gap-filler. The thing to settle first: three of these professions register with Ahpra, and one does not register at all — sonography is accredited instead. Start on the wrong route and you lose months you cannot get back. Radiographers → Plain film, CT, MRI, mammography, theatre and interventional work across public and private services. Registered with the Medical Radiation Practice Board through Ahpra. Also searched as Mammographer CT radiographer MRI radiographer Interventional radiographer Sonographers → General, obstetric and cardiac scanning, with a private market that pays for it.

chunks.t: Medical imaging careers in Australia
chunks.x: Accredited through ASMIRT and ASAR — not an Ahpra-registered profession. Radiation therapists → Planning and delivering treatment across public cancer centres and a growing private network. Same board, same Ahpra application as radiography. Nuclear medicine technologists → SPECT/CT and PET/CT practice, with theranostics expanding fast. Ahpra registration plus an ANZSNM skills assessment.

chunks.t: Medical imaging careers in Australia
chunks.h: Mammography, CT and MRI are not separate professions
chunks.x: They are scopes within radiography, and one Ahpra registration covers all of them. Australian employers advertise by modality, so we name them above because that is how people search — but the route in is the radiographer route. Can I work there?

chunks.t: Medical imaging careers in Australia
chunks.x: No employer here can shorten this, and neither can we. What we can do is tell you which route you are on before you spend money, and be straight when there is a real obstacle. Radiography · radiation therapy · nuclear medicine

chunks.t: Medical imaging careers in Australia
chunks.h: Ahpra, through the Medical Radiation Practice Board
chunks.x: One national board, one application, three divisions of practice. Your qualification is assessed against the Australian standard; where it falls short you may be asked for supervised practice or further assessment rather than refused outright. Nuclear medicine adds an ANZSNM skills assessment, and radiation licensing is handled state by state on top. How the Ahpra route works → Sonography

chunks.t: Medical imaging careers in Australia
chunks.h: ASAR, after ASMIRT recognises your qualification
chunks.x: Sonography is not a registered profession in Australia. You are accredited instead: ASMIRT assesses your qualification, then you enter the ASAR register. Different body, different evidence, different timeline — and a route that trips up people who assume Ahpra covers everything in an imaging department. How the ASAR route works →

chunks.t: Medical imaging careers in Australia
chunks.h: And it is more than your qualification
chunks.x: Certificates of good standing from every regulator you have held, an English-language test unless you qualify for an exemption, a criminal history check, a health and fitness-to-practise declaration, and recency of practice. These are what usually set the timeline, and they are the same whichever of the four professions you hold. Every gate, in one place → Check my pathway → Registration in Australia, explained The work itself

chunks.t: Medical imaging careers in Australia
chunks.h: What could your week look like?
chunks.x: Australia is not one imaging labour market. The funder shapes the job as much as the employer does, the modality shapes the day, and the state you land in shapes the agreement and the rota. When a vacancy names a title, the useful questions are which rooms, which case mix, who funds it and what the after-hours commitment is.

chunks.t: Medical imaging careers in Australia
chunks.x: The widest door, and where most people start. In a public department that means plain film, fluoroscopy and cross-sectional work in the same week, with the emergency department and theatre lists pulling on the same rooms — run by state and territory health services, so your enterprise agreement, rota and progression are set where you land rather than federally. Private and community imaging is the other half of the picture and a very large employer: referred outpatient work on Medicare-funded requests, booked lists, a great deal of musculoskeletal imaging, and often the newest equipment.

chunks.t: Medical imaging careers in Australia
chunks.x: Depth in one place rather than breadth across many, and the modalities employers ask about most. Cross-sectional experience gained overseas usually transfers well; smaller sites may expect you to cover both.

chunks.t: Medical imaging careers in Australia
chunks.x: National population screening is a defined, high-volume workflow with its own quality requirements and its own mobile services. It carries its own training expectations, so check what will be recognised before you plan around it.

chunks.t: Medical imaging careers in Australia
chunks.x: General, obstetric, vascular and cardiac scanning, much of it in private practice, with a degree of autonomy in reporting that many overseas sonographers have not had. One of the most sought-after corners of the family, and the one with the most distinctive route in.

chunks.t: Medical imaging careers in Australia
chunks.x: SPECT/CT, PET/CT and theranostics, concentrated in fewer centres. Radiation licensing is handled state by state on top of national registration — an extra step rather than a barrier, but one that takes time.

chunks.t: Medical imaging careers in Australia
chunks.x: Its own profession and its own route, not a corner of diagnostic imaging. Treatment is delivered from designated centres rather than every hospital, so the job comes with a location decision attached, and the work is planned, longitudinal and spent with the same patients over weeks.

chunks.t: Medical imaging careers in Australia
chunks.x: This cuts across all of the above. Broader practice, more autonomy and a closer-knit team — you are more likely to be the person on site than one of several, and often better paid, with regional allowances on top. The trade-off can be distance, fly-in services, on-call and fewer specialist services nearby, so weigh them before choosing where to live. Regional does not mean second best. It does mean a different life, so choose it knowing that. One registration covers plain film, CT, MRI and mammography. The rooms you work in are decided by the vacancy, not the regulator.

chunks.t: Medical imaging careers in Australia
chunks.x: Acute and unselected case mix, the widest range of equipment, an on-call commitment, and pay set by the enterprise agreement of the state you work in.

chunks.t: Medical imaging careers in Australia
chunks.x: Booked lists, referred outpatients, commercial throughput and often better equipment for a narrower range of work. Public or private is not the same job with a different employer — it changes your case mix, your hours, your autonomy and what a week feels like. What could I earn? Can we afford it?

chunks.t: Medical imaging careers in Australia
chunks.h: A bigger salary does not automatically mean a better move
chunks.x: Two questions people usually ask as one. The first is about the scale you would be paid on. The second is about what the move costs before that salary arrives, and what is left of it once rent, school and the exchange rate have had their say. Pay is set state by state Public-sector pay runs on state and territory enterprise agreements, so the same job pays differently in Perth and in Hobart. Private practice sits outside those agreements again. Superannuation is paid on top of base salary, and it is a real part of the package rather than a footnote. Seniority, hours, on-call and allowances move the total more than the headline does. chunks.h: The roles are often where you were not looking
chunks.x: Most people picture Sydney or Melbourne. Most of the imaging roles we are asked to fill are in regional Western Australia, regional Queensland, Tasmania and the outer suburbs of the big cities — places with a real shortage, better-paid versions of the job, and a life that suits some households far better than a capital would. Some locations are much more sought after than others. That does not make them better. The destination guides are written for the whole household — commute, schools, partner work, climate, distance from an airport — and they are candid about the disadvantages. chunks.t: Medical imaging careers in Australia
chunks.h: Sometimes we will tell you not yet
chunks.x: Before we talk about jobs we look at what you hold, where you trained and the kind of practice and place you want. If there is a realistic route we set it out, with the steps and the likely timeline. If there is a real obstacle — recency, an assessment that will take a year, a partner whose qualification will not transfer — we say so, rather than let you pay an assessment fee to find out. We do not grant registration and we do not guarantee it; the regulator does that. What we do is keep the file moving, put the steps in the right order, and stay with you after the offer — because most moves that fail, fail at the relocation rather than the interview. chunks.t: Medical imaging careers in New Zealand
chunks.x: New Zealand trains a fraction of the imaging and radiation workforce it needs, so internationally qualified clinicians are not a stopgap here — they are how services run. That shows up in how registration is handled and how quickly a good application moves. All four professions register with the same board, which makes this the most predictable family to move into — and they spend their working lives inside the same patient pathway, which is where this page goes next. Sonographers → General, obstetric and cardiac scanning, with reporting scopes open to experienced clinicians. Radiographers → Plain film, CT and theatre work across the public system and private practice. Radiation therapists → Planning and delivering treatment in the national network of cancer centres. Nuclear medicine technologists → SPECT/CT and PET/CT at the centre of the scope, and one CT boundary worth reading.

chunks.t: Medical imaging careers in New Zealand
chunks.h: Where your work sits in someone’s diagnosis
chunks.x: Imaging is almost never the destination. It is the step where another specialty’s uncertainty turns into a decision — which is why an imaging department is the busiest crossroads in most hospitals, and why the professions in it work to somebody else’s clock as well as their own. Most of the family is invisible in that sentence. One examination can involve a radiographer or sonographer, a radiologist, a medical physicist, a nurse, the person who booked it and the clinician who acts on it. The patient meets perhaps two of them.

chunks.t: Medical imaging careers in New Zealand
chunks.x: A GP, surgeon, oncologist or emergency consultant has a question they cannot answer by looking. Referring teams · booking and administration

chunks.t: Medical imaging careers in New Zealand
chunks.x: Positioning, protocol, dose and image quality — and often the first person to see that something is wrong. Radiographers · sonographers · nuclear medicine technologists · nursing

chunks.t: Medical imaging careers in New Zealand
chunks.x: Images become an opinion, with the responsibility that carries. Increasingly written remotely, and out of hours. Radiologists · reporting sonographers · nuclear medicine physicians

chunks.t: Medical imaging careers in New Zealand
chunks.x: The multidisciplinary meeting, the clinic, the theatre list. Your work is now somebody’s treatment plan. Referring teams · MDT · surgery · oncology

chunks.t: Medical imaging careers in New Zealand
chunks.x: In radiation therapy the imaging is the treatment — planning, verification and delivery, over weeks rather than minutes. Radiation therapists · medical physicists · radiation oncologists Nobody orders a scan for the scan. Worth knowing before you search Your modality shapes your week more than your job title does. A New Zealand radiographer’s core scope covers plain film, CT, mammography and theatre work — one registration, but very different working days. MRI is the exception: it is a separate scope of practice, added to your registration rather than included in it, though it sits under the same board. The same layering applies to general, obstetric and cardiac scanning within sonography. So when a vacancy says “radiographer”, the useful questions are which rooms, which case mix, and what the after-hours commitment looks like — not whether you are eligible. Ask us and we will find out before you apply. Source: Medical Radiation Technologists Board — add a scope of practice . Checked 17 September 2026.

chunks.t: Medical imaging careers in New Zealand
chunks.h: What could your career look like here?
chunks.x: Six routes cover most of what an internationally trained clinician does here. Some you will recognise immediately; one or two work differently enough from other countries to be worth reading before you apply. None of them is a career for life — people move between them, and the scope you hold is what decides how easily.

chunks.t: Medical imaging careers in New Zealand
chunks.x: The widest door, and where most people start. In a public department that means plain film, fluoroscopy, ultrasound and cross-sectional work in the same week, with the emergency department and the theatre lists pulling on the same rooms; in community and private imaging it means booked outpatient lists, a lot of musculoskeletal work, and a steadier pace. The acute, unselected case mix is the part that is hardest to find anywhere else — and the part that takes the most adjusting to if you have worked in a single-modality role. Often in the department: radiography · sonography · radiology · nursing · medical physics · assistants and administration

chunks.t: Medical imaging careers in New Zealand
chunks.x: Deeper work in one place rather than breadth across many, and the modalities employers ask about most often. Cross-sectional experience gained overseas usually transfers well, and smaller sites may expect you to cover both rather than specialise. Worth knowing that MRI is a separate scope of practice under the MRTB — added to your registration, not included in it — so check whether you hold it before applying for MRI roles.

chunks.t: Medical imaging careers in New Zealand
chunks.x: Organised population screening is a defined, high-volume workflow with its own quality requirements — a different day from diagnostic work, and one that suits people who like rhythm and precision. It carries its own training expectations, so check what will be recognised before you plan around it.

chunks.t: Medical imaging careers in New Zealand
chunks.x: SPECT/CT, PET/CT and therapeutic work, concentrated in fewer centres — so this route often comes with a decision about where you live. There is also one CT boundary in the registered scope worth reading before you apply.

chunks.t: Medical imaging careers in New Zealand
chunks.x: Image-guided procedures, angiography and hybrid theatre work, where imaging is part of the intervention rather than a step before it. Closer to the patient and to the surgical team, with on-call attached in most services.

chunks.t: Medical imaging careers in New Zealand
chunks.x: Its own profession and its own route, not a corner of diagnostic imaging. Treatment is delivered from a national network of cancer centres rather than from every hospital, so the job comes with a location decision attached — and the work is planned, longitudinal and spent with the same patients over weeks. Radiation therapy · medical physics · radiation oncology · nursing

chunks.t: Medical imaging careers in New Zealand
chunks.x: This one cuts across all six. Broader practice, more autonomy and often a closer-knit team — you are more likely to be the person on site than one of several. The trade-off can be distance, on-call requirements and fewer specialist services nearby, which are things worth knowing before choosing where to live.

chunks.t: Medical imaging careers in New Zealand
chunks.x: Acute and unselected case mix, the widest range of equipment, collective-agreement pay, an on-call commitment, and the whole multidisciplinary system around you.

chunks.t: Medical imaging careers in New Zealand
chunks.x: Booked lists, referred outpatients, different funding and often better equipment for a narrower range of work. Public or private is not the same job with a different employer — it changes your case mix, your hours, your autonomy and what a week feels like.

chunks.t: Medical imaging careers in New Zealand
chunks.x: The things that are the same whichever of these professions you hold. Who regulates this work? The Medical Radiation Technologists Board (MRTB) is the regulator for these professions, under the Health Practitioners Competence Assurance Act — one application process, with a defined scope of practice for each. Some modalities, MRI among them, are a separate scope of practice , added on top of your core registration rather than included in it. Registration is the first gate, and it runs on its own timeline. How registration works in New Zealand · Check your pathway What does the pay look like? Public-system pay is set by collective agreement rather than negotiated role by role, so your base salary comes from a national scale rather than a negotiation with the hospital. Your step on that scale, your hours and your on-call commitment are what vary.

chunks.t: Medical imaging careers in New Zealand
chunks.x: Private and ACC-funded work sits outside that and varies. Indicative bands sit on each profession’s own guide above. Pay in New Zealand · The agreements, verified Which visa would I need? Most clinicians move on a work visa tied to an accredited employer. Medical imaging technologists, MRI technologists, sonographers, radiation therapists and nuclear medicine technologists all sit in Tier 1 of the Green List — Straight to Residence — which changes the route considerably. Checked against Immigration New Zealand’s Green List (Appendix 13, in force from 9 March 2026); the list changes, so confirm it against your own occupation before you plan around it. The visa can usually run alongside registration. Visas and residence What about the rest of the move? Schools, housing, healthcare, banking, shipping and the first few weeks each have their own guide.

chunks.x: Registration The Medical Council of New Zealand registers all doctors. For specialist recognition, your College assesses whether your training is comparable, and that finding usually decides your pathway. Registration runs on its own timeline and is nearly always the longest part of the move, so it is the thing to settle before you give notice or enrol a child in a school. chunks.t: Medicine careers in New Zealand
chunks.h: Fewer layers between you and the patient
chunks.x: New Zealand is small enough that the same consultant may see a patient in clinic, operate on them, take the call about them at two in the morning and write to their GP afterwards. Sub-specialty depth is thinner than in a large system; generalist breadth is expected, and valued. Referrals

chunks.t: Medicine careers in New Zealand
chunks.h: The GP is the front door, and the loop closes with them
chunks.x: Referrals arrive from someone you may know by name, and continuity is a working structure: general practice holds the long-term relationship, and patients return there after discharge. General practice · outpatient clinics · shared care Acute care

chunks.t: Medicine careers in New Zealand
chunks.x: Smaller departments, consultants on the floor, and air and road retrieval as a routine part of acute care. Emergency medicine · anaesthesia · retrieval · nursing On the ward

chunks.t: Medicine careers in New Zealand
chunks.x: Fewer registrars and thinner sub-specialty cover, and a great deal of care after discharge carried by community teams, district nursing, aged residential care and accident-funded rehabilitation. Senior medical officers · registrars and RMOs · allied health · community nursing What surprises most consultants You will do more of your own work. Fewer registrars, thinner sub-specialty cover, and a service that expects you to be a generalist inside your specialty. For many international consultants that broader responsibility is both the attraction of working here and the biggest adjustment of the first year. The second surprise is the size of the professional community. In most specialties you will know your counterparts around the country by name within a year or two, which makes referral relationships personal and the multidisciplinary meeting less formal and considerably more useful. Settings and regions

chunks.t: Medicine careers in New Zealand
chunks.x: A tertiary post, a regional hospital and a rural generalist role are further apart here than the job titles suggest. Location sets your case mix, your on-call, your sub-specialty support and how far away the nearest scanner is. Hospitals

chunks.t: Medicine careers in New Zealand
chunks.x: Most of it happens outside the main centres. Regional & secondary hospitals Broader case mix, less sub-specialty support, a team small enough that everyone knows each other, and clinical decisions that are yours to make. A good number of consultants arrive intending to take a tertiary post and stay in one of these instead. Often around you: SMO colleagues across specialties · registrars and RMOs · nursing · allied health · imaging · the local GPs Tertiary centres Sub-specialty work, complex referrals, teaching and research, concentrated in a handful of cities, with the national service responsibility that goes with it. Public and private Public hospital services mean unselected acute work, the full multidisciplinary system, collective-agreement pay that is the same wherever you do the job, and the on-call that comes with it. Private practice is elective lists, more control over your week and income outside the agreement, often alongside a public appointment. The two differ in case mix, autonomy and what you are responsible for, and many consultants hold both. Community

chunks.t: Medicine careers in New Zealand
chunks.x: Careers where the working week looks nothing like a ward round. General practice & community Longer consultations and continuity of care, with a business model attached to the clinical one. Rural generalist Broad scope, autonomy, and distance as a clinical factor in every decision. Deeply rewarding, and best entered with a plan for the professional isolation that comes with it. Retrieval, transport & telehealth Geography makes this core work: air and road retrieval, and telehealth that stands in for a clinic. Aged residential care An increasing share of medicine, mostly outside hospital walls, and one of the quieter routes into a portfolio career. Population and portfolio

chunks.t: Medicine careers in New Zealand
chunks.x: Clinical careers where the patient is a population, a cohort or a student. Māori & Pacific health providers Kaupapa Māori and Pacific organisations delivering care on their own terms, with whānau at the centre of the model. Public health & population health Prevention, screening, outbreak and policy work — a clinical career with the patient defined as a population. Academic, teaching & research Joint appointments with the medical schools, trials work and supervision, usually alongside clinical sessions. Locum & fractional work A good way to try the country, and a specialty, before committing your family to either. Sometimes it is the better first step, and we will say so.

Do registration first — the skills assessment comes after it. How registration works → What could I earn? Set state by state Public pay comes from each state’s own enterprise agreement, so the band moves when you cross a border, and private molecular-imaging services set their own. chunks.x: Is the skills assessment done by ASMIRT? Not for nuclear medicine — the migration skills assessment is carried out by ANZSNM (the Australian and New Zealand Society of Nuclear Medicine), the gazetted authority for this profession, and it generally comes after MRPBA registration. The HCPC/CORU comparable-regulator routes apply to radiography and radiation therapy, not nuclear medicine — so most overseas nuclear-medicine qualifications go through individual assessment against the Australian standard. chunks.x: The scope covers imaging with or without sealed sources, so therapeutic work sits inside it rather than beside it. In smaller services you would see the whole caseload rather than a slice of it. The CT question is the one to settle before you accept anything. The Board’s competence standards are explicit: nuclear medicine practitioners operate gamma camera SPECT/CT and PET/CT systems, and the CT within that is for attenuation correction, anatomical fusion and transmission imaging . That is what the scope covers. Diagnostic CT is separate, and needs one of three things. A practising certificate in the medical imaging technologist scope; completion of a Board-approved education programme in CT; or evidence of CT competency obtained elsewhere that the Board deems satisfactory and approves.

chunks.t: Nursing & midwifery careers in New Zealand
chunks.x: Most New Zealand births are led by a midwife rather than an obstetrician. A Lead Maternity Carer holds the whole episode — booking, pregnancy, birth and the weeks after it — with obstetric teams involved when there is a clinical reason for them to be. If you are a midwife, that means more autonomy and more continuity than most systems offer, and a caseload you carry rather than a shift you hand over. It also means being the person the decision rests with at three in the morning, which is worth thinking about before you move for it. If you hold both nursing and midwifery registration elsewhere, the two are assessed separately here. Midwifery here is a distinct profession with its own register and its own scope, rather than a nursing specialty — one of the first things to get clear if you are coming from a system that treats it otherwise. chunks.x: Most pregnancies are carried by a Lead Maternity Carer — usually a midwife — who holds the care from booking to six weeks after birth. chunks.t: Obstetrics & Gynaecology jobs in New Zealand
chunks.h: Both halves of the specialty, in the same week
chunks.x: Outside the tertiary centres a post is obstetric and gynaecological: labour ward, clinics, elective and acute operating. A generalist appetite matters more here than in most specialties, because that is what the job is. The team around you

chunks.t: Obstetrics & Gynaecology jobs in New Zealand
chunks.x: You would know the midwives, the anaesthetists and the theatre teams by name, and consultant presence on the labour ward is expected rather than negotiated. Most consultants describe the working relationship as noticeably flatter than the one they left. The Lead Maternity Carer model is the single biggest adjustment. Referral pathways are defined and the working relationship with midwives is a professional partnership rather than a hierarchy. Your clinical authority is unchanged; what changes is how a woman reaches you, and who holds her care between the times she does. Consultants who expect to run every pregnancy find this harder than those who came looking for a specialist role with a clear edge to it. Sub-specialty work is concentrated. Maternal-fetal medicine, gynaecological oncology, urogynaecology and reproductive medicine sit in a handful of tertiary centres.

chunks.t: Obstetrics & Gynaecology jobs in New Zealand
chunks.x: Elsewhere you would carry a generalist list with an interest attached — which suits some people exactly and frustrates others, so decide early which you are. Abortion care sits in health law here. Since the law changed in 2020 it is regulated as health care rather than under the criminal law, and provision is part of ordinary service planning. Conscientious objection provisions exist and services differ, so this is a question worth asking of a specific post rather than of the country. Private gynaecology operates in the larger centres and sits comfortably alongside a public post. Private obstetrics is a smaller market than in many systems, largely because the public model already delivers the continuity that private care is often bought for.

chunks.t: Obstetrics & Gynaecology jobs in New Zealand
chunks.x: Getting registered Your specialty is one of the quicker ones Reviewed August 2026 · checked against the Medical Council of New Zealand’s current published guidance You register with the Medical Council of New Zealand in the vocational scope of obstetrics and gynaecology. The route is the same one every specialist follows; three details are specific to you. Obstetrics and gynaecology is on the fast-track list. A UK Fellowship or Membership of the relevant Royal College, held together with a CCT issued by the GMC or PMETB or a CCST issued by the STA, sits on the Council’s approved list — as does an Irish Membership or Fellowship held with a CSCST. The Council publishes twenty working days for a complete application on that pathway. A FRANZCOG needs no assessment. If you trained through RANZCOG, your fellowship is an approved Australasian qualification.

chunks.t: Obstetrics & Gynaecology jobs in New Zealand
chunks.x: No comparability exercise, and no college advice to wait on. Trained elsewhere? RANZCOG advises the Council. Qualifications outside those lists are assessed against the FRANZCOG standard, on the college’s own process. Allow considerably longer, and start the college paperwork early rather than after you apply. What the Council will want to see, whichever route you are on: A consultant-level job offer — a listed prerequisite on the fast-track pathway Primary-source verification of your medical degree and specialist qualification Evidence of at least 24 months’ recent practice in the specialty A certificate of good standing from every authority you have registered with Identity, criminal-history and English-language evidence where required The order matters more than the speed.

The Council application is built around both, and the visa runs alongside it rather than after it. chunks.h: What the fast track asks of you
chunks.x: VOC4 has prerequisites the other routes don’t, and one of them surprises people: a job offer in Aotearoa New Zealand at consultant or specialist level is a listed prerequisite , so the role comes first and the application is built around it. You’ll also need 24 months’ practice in obstetrics and gynaecology at 0.5 FTE or more within the past five years — 12 of them in the 18 months before you apply — in a health system the Council treats as comparable, three verified references, and your qualifications already moving through EPIC / MyIntealth. You practise under a named supervisor in an approved position — supervision is a condition of the provisional scope, not a judgement on you. Your registration meeting happens in New Zealand, within two weeks of your intended start date, and you cannot practise until it is done and your practising certificate issued — allow about three days after the meeting for that. And moving to the full vocational scope is an application you make once the Council’s requirements are met, not something that arrives on a date. Where this comes from.

Why New Zealand A system that backs rehabilitation For occupational therapists, New Zealand offers something rare: manageable caseloads, autonomy, and ACC-model funding that lets you focus on helping people recover and return to life. Manageable, person-centred caseloads Clinical autonomy A system built around rehabilitation "The system here backs rehabilitation." Add shorter commutes and the outdoors close by, and the move tends to give back time and headspace as well as a different way of working. What the work is like ACC pays for rehabilitation directly, which shapes the whole caseload Occupational therapy travels well as a clinical skill. What is different here is who pays for the plan, and where the work happens. ACC funds rehabilitation, not just treatment.

chunks.t: Occupational Therapist jobs in New Zealand
chunks.h: The detail, when you want it
chunks.x: New Zealand's no-fault accident scheme pays for OT assessment and intervention directly — equipment, home modifications, vocational rehabilitation, return-to-work planning — for anyone injured here, however it happened. In practice that means funding decisions move faster than you are probably used to, injury-related work makes up a bigger share of most caseloads, and a great deal of OT happens outside hospital walls because someone is paying for it to. Community and home-based practice is the centre of the profession here, not the overflow. You will spend real time in people's houses, workplaces and schools, and you will usually carry your own caseload with the authority to make the call. That is more autonomy than many OTs arrive with. It also means more driving, more lone working, and more of your clinical reasoning happening in someone's kitchen rather than in a team room.

chunks.t: Occupational Therapist jobs in New Zealand
chunks.h: The detail, when you want it
chunks.x: Assessment is whānau-centred, and that is a clinical difference. Te Tiriti o Waitangi obligations and Māori models of health — Te Whare Tapa Whā most commonly — sit inside the competencies you are assessed against rather than alongside them as training. You will formulate around a household, not only an individual. For most OTs arriving from overseas this is the new part of the job, and it changes the plan, not just the paperwork. "The funding follows the person, so the plan can actually happen." That is the part OTs tell us they had stopped expecting: recommending what someone needs and watching it arrive. It is not frictionless, and the caseloads are real. But the system is pointed in the same direction you are.

Scope of practice A broad, flexible scope with real decision-making authority New Zealand OTs work across physical and mental health, rehabilitation, community, paediatric and ACC-funded settings, and usually with more independence than in a heavily tiered service.

chunks.t: Occupational Therapist jobs in New Zealand
chunks.x: You will typically hold your own caseload, own the outcomes, and make independent clinical decisions about assessment, intervention and discharge. Most OTs build depth in an area over time while keeping a generalist base underneath it. Equipment and home modification work carries more weight here. Prescribing equipment and recommending housing modifications is a core part of the job rather than a referral you make to someone else, funded through ACC or through Ministry of Health pathways depending on the person. There is still assessment and accountability, but the decision is far more often yours. Vocational rehabilitation and workplace assessment are a bigger share of practice than in systems where nobody funds them — return-to-work planning, workplace ergonomic assessment and graduated return are routine ACC-funded work rather than a specialist niche.

chunks.t: Occupational Therapist jobs in New Zealand
chunks.x: Sensory-based practice is well embedded, particularly in mental health and paediatrics, and often more so than in the services OTs arrive from. If sensory regulation is an interest, there is an active community of practice here. Hand therapy, neuro rehabilitation, paediatrics, mental health and older-person services all have established specialist routes. Tell us the work you want and we will tell you where it exists. The difference that shapes the work The ACC model, and why it matters New Zealand’s Accident Compensation Corporation (ACC) funds injury-related care, creating a more direct, rehabilitation-focused way of working with fewer barriers between assessment and treatment.

There can be a short adjustment while you get familiar with ACC and a new system, but it’s usually brief, and OTs tend to move quickly into highly autonomous work. chunks.t: Occupational Therapist jobs in New Zealand
chunks.x: Do I need to be an ACC-approved provider? It depends entirely on how you are working. If you are employed by a public service or an established provider, their contracting with ACC covers the work and you do not arrange anything yourself — you will simply notice that funding for equipment and rehab arrives from a different place than you are used to. If you are planning to work privately and invoice ACC directly, that means meeting their provider requirements, so check them before you set anything up. Tell us which you are considering and we will explain what applies. Does my UK or South African experience count? Yes. The Board assesses your qualification, your recent practice and your competency against New Zealand standards, and training from the UK, South Africa, Ireland, Australia and comparable systems is well recognised.

chunks.t: Occupational Therapist jobs in New Zealand
chunks.x: Most internationally qualified OTs come through this route without difficulty. The adjustment when you arrive is rarely clinical. It is the funding system, the amount of community work, and whānau-centred assessment — not your ability to do the job. What does Te Tiriti practice mean day to day? Practical things, mostly. Involving whānau in assessment and planning as a matter of course rather than on request. Working with Te Whare Tapa Whā as a model that includes spiritual and family wellbeing alongside the physical. Getting names and pronunciation right. Asking about a household rather than assuming it. Employers provide induction and ongoing support, and nobody expects you to arrive fluent. They do expect you to arrive willing, and it will come up at interview. Public or private — which gives the better caseload? Different rather than better.

chunks.t: Occupational Therapist jobs in New Zealand
chunks.x: Public gives you structured teams, supervision on tap, breadth of presentation and a clear progression path. ACC-funded private practice gives you more autonomy, more focused rehabilitation work, faster access to funding, and often more control over your diary. A lot of OTs here do some of both over time, and moving between them is normal rather than a career reset. How does equipment and home modification funding work? Through two main routes: ACC for anything injury-related, and Ministry of Health pathways for need arising from disability or illness. Both are assessment-driven, and as the assessing OT you carry considerably more of the decision than in a panel-based system. It is not unlimited and it is not instant. But the gap between what you recommend and what your client receives is much smaller than most OTs are used to.

Sensory practice is well embedded in mental health and paediatrics. Neuro rehabilitation runs across inpatient and community services. Specialisation here tends to be built on a generalist base rather than entered straight from training, so if you are already specialised, tell us early — those roles are fewer and worth timing properly. chunks.x: Getting registered Registration overview Reviewed July 2026 · checked against the Physiotherapy Board of New Zealand’s current published guidance To practise in New Zealand you'll register with the Physiotherapy Board of New Zealand . For most internationally trained physiotherapists the process takes around three to six months, and is simpler than it first appears. The Board assesses your qualifications, clinical experience and overall competency against New Zealand standards, including clinical care, communication and professional practice. As part of the process you'll typically need: Verification of your qualification Evidence of recent clinical practice A police clearance Confirmation of English-language proficiency, if required Once registered, you'll hold an Annual Practising Certificate (APC) , which allows you to work legally. We support you through each stage, from understanding your pathway, to preparing your application, to securing the right role once you're registered.

chunks.t: Physiotherapist jobs in New Zealand
chunks.x: Private and ACC clinics, or the public system — which should I be looking at? This is the real decision, and it matters more than most people expect. Private and ACC-funded clinics give you the most autonomy soonest: your own caseload, mostly musculoskeletal, direct access, and earnings that move with how busy you are. Health New Zealand roles give you complexity and structure instead — inpatient and community rehabilitation, neurology, respiratory, older persons' health, paediatrics, rotations, and a clearer ladder with funded development alongside it. Plenty of physiotherapists do both over a career, and moving between them later is normal. Tell us how you like to work and what you want to be good at in five years, and we'll be straight with you about which fits. Do I need to be an ACC provider myself? Not as an employee.

chunks.t: Physiotherapist jobs in New Zealand
chunks.x: Clinics hold the ACC contract and you treat under it, so the billing and reporting sit with the practice rather than with you personally. What does land on you is the documentation: injury claims, treatment rationale and progress reporting are part of the working day, and they are how funded treatment gets approved and continued. It is simple once you have seen it a few times, and any decent clinic will walk you through their systems in your first fortnight. If you ever go on to run your own practice, becoming a contracted provider is a separate step and we can point you at the right people. I've specialised in neuro, respiratory or paediatrics rather than MSK. Is there work for me? Yes — but be realistic about where it sits.

chunks.t: Physiotherapist jobs in New Zealand
chunks.x: Specialist non-musculoskeletal work is concentrated in hospital services and the main centres, so if neurological rehabilitation or paediatrics is what you want to keep doing, your location options narrow. There is real demand, and specialist experience is valued; there are simply fewer posts and they turn over less often. Provincially, the volume is musculoskeletal and ACC-funded. Many people arriving with a specialist background take a broader role first, then move back towards their area once they know the system and the people. Say early on if your specialty is non-negotiable — it changes which roles we put in front of you. Will my current banding or seniority carry across to the pay scale? Relevant experience is normally recognised, but it is not a direct band-to-step conversion.

chunks.t: Physiotherapist jobs in New Zealand
chunks.x: Public and community roles sit on the APEX physiotherapy scale, and where you start on it is assessed by the employer against your experience and the agreement's own criteria — not by mapping an overseas grade onto a New Zealand one. Private and ACC clinics work differently again, with earnings shaped by caseload as much as by starting rate. Our job is to get your starting point confirmed in writing before you accept anything, alongside what that means in the town you'd be living in. We won't guess at a number to make a role sound better than it is. How different is the way physiotherapy is practised? The clinical knowledge transfers almost entirely. What tends to shift is emphasis.

chunks.t: Physiotherapist jobs in New Zealand
chunks.x: Practice here leans strongly towards active rehabilitation, education and self-management — getting people moving, understanding their injury and taking the work home with them — rather than long courses of passive treatment. If you come from a hands-on tradition, expect to use those skills as part of a plan rather than as the plan. Cultural safety is also treated as core clinical practice, not an add-on. Understanding Te Tiriti o Waitangi and how it shapes health care, and working respectfully with Māori and Pacific patients and their whānau, is part of what the Board expects of you and part of what makes you good here. Nobody expects fluency on day one; they do expect you to take it seriously. Can I locum, work part-time, or split my week between clinics? Part-time is common and generally easy to arrange.

chunks.t: Physiotherapist jobs in New Zealand
chunks.x: Locum and multi-clinic work is more complicated at first, and the reason is the visa rather than the profession: an Accredited Employer Work Visa ties you to one accredited employer and a specific role, so stitching together shifts across several practices usually isn't possible until you have residence. Once you're a resident, the flexibility opens right up and a lot of physiotherapists do build a mixed week. If flexibility is the whole point of the move for you, tell us at the start — it shapes which visa route and which employers make sense. Nau mai, haere mai · If you’re weighing it up

Your registration meeting happens in New Zealand, within two weeks of your intended start date, and you cannot practise until it is done and your practising certificate issued — allow about three days after the meeting for that. chunks.t: Diagnostic Radiographer (MIT) jobs in New Zealand
chunks.h: The detail, when you want it
chunks.x: The scope is drawn wider than UK-style radiography. New Zealand registers the profession as medical imaging technology, and most people you work with will call you an MIT. That is not just a naming difference. The scope you register into covers plain film and CT, but also fluoroscopy, theatre and mobile work, trauma, and in many services DEXA as well. Working across several modalities in the same week is normal here rather than a specialism you apply for. How big the service is decides the shape of your job. In the main centres you will walk into a department that feels familiar: subspecialised rooms, dedicated modality teams, students on placement. In a provincial hospital you might be one of a handful of MITs covering everything that hospital images, on your own overnight, with the radiologist reporting from somewhere else.

chunks.t: Diagnostic Radiographer (MIT) jobs in New Zealand

Reporting-radiographer posts are not an established route here in the way they are in the NHS. Advanced practice runs instead through modality depth, protocol and image-quality leadership, teaching, and clinical lead roles — real progression, just a different ladder. "You do more, in more rooms, with fewer people around you." None of that is a warning. Most MITs tell us the breadth is the best part of the move. It just means choosing your department with your eyes open, and we will be straight with you about which services will stretch you and which will steady you.

chunks.t: Diagnostic Radiographer (MIT) jobs in New Zealand
chunks.x: Computed tomography sits within the medical imaging technologist scope, alongside mammography and angiography. No separate registration, and in most services CT is the backbone of the week rather than a specialism you apply for. Mammography

chunks.t: Diagnostic Radiographer (MIT) jobs in New Zealand
chunks.x: Also within the MIT scope. Screening and symptomatic work are usually service-specific rather than scope-specific, so the question to ask a department is what training and caseload it offers, not whether you are permitted. MRI

chunks.t: Diagnostic Radiographer (MIT) jobs in New Zealand
chunks.x: Magnetic resonance imaging is a separate registered scope in New Zealand, not a modality inside general imaging. Practising in it needs registration in it — not experience alone, and not a manager’s sign-off. If MRI is your whole job, the trans-Tasman exclusion matters more than anything else on this page. Mutual recognition between Australia and New Zealand covers the medical imaging technologist, radiation therapist and nuclear medicine technologist scopes. MRI and sonography are excluded — so an Australian-registered MRI technologist applies as an internationally qualified applicant, and a timeline built on mutual recognition will be wrong by months. There is a published experience route into the MRI scope.

chunks.t: Diagnostic Radiographer (MIT) jobs in New Zealand
chunks.x: A Board-approved undergraduate qualification in medical imaging or radiation therapy, at least 2.5 years full-time equivalent of MRI practice meeting the Board’s clinical experience requirements, and a pass in a Board MRI examination. If you came to MRI from a general radiography background rather than a dedicated MRI qualification, that is the route to read properly. An examination is not automatic. Where the Board decides a qualification is not equivalent it may in some circumstances offer an examination, but whether one is offered is the Board’s decision on your application rather than a right you can plan around. Board fees are published: NZ$922 to register, NZ$510 for the initial practising certificate, and NZ$2,704 for the online examination where required. If your MRI is a sideline of a general list, the MIT scope is usually the right application and MRI a later addition.

Check your own case with the Board before you make a decision on it. Pay & benefits How pay is set One national scale. Common questions

chunks.t: Diagnostic Radiographer (MIT) jobs in New Zealand
chunks.x: I'm HCPC-registered in the UK. Does that transfer to the MRTB? Not automatically — you apply to the Medical Radiation Technologists Board, and they assess your qualification, your recent clinical practice and your competency against New Zealand standards. UK training is well recognised and most UK radiographers come through this route without difficulty — and the same pathway applies wherever you trained, whether that’s South Africa, the UAE or elsewhere: the Board assesses your qualification and recent practice, not your passport. What takes the time is document verification and getting your evidence of recent practice in order, so start collecting it early. We help you work out which pathway applies and what the Board will want to see before you spend money on an application.

chunks.t: Diagnostic Radiographer (MIT) jobs in New Zealand
chunks.x: Will my Australian registration count? There is a trans-Tasman recognition arrangement between the two countries, and in practice AHPRA-registered radiographers usually have a quicker route than someone applying from further afield. It is still an application to the Board rather than an automatic transfer. Tell us where you are registered and we will confirm what applies to you before anything is submitted. What does "general radiography" cover here? More than the phrase suggests. Plain film and CT will be your backbone, with fluoroscopy, theatre and mobile work, trauma and often DEXA around them. In a provincial hospital, general means general: whatever comes through the door on your shift, frequently with you as the only technologist on site. In the main centres the day is more contained, closer to a large overseas department.

chunks.t: Diagnostic Radiographer (MIT) jobs in New Zealand
chunks.x: Can I stay in one modality — MRI or CT only? In the main centres, largely yes. Tertiary departments run dedicated CT and MRI teams and people do build whole careers in one. Bear in mind that MRI is its own registered scope, so a pure MRI role means holding that scope rather than just being rostered there. In smaller services it is not realistic. The department needs everyone able to cover everything, and that is exactly what makes those roles good for building breadth. I want to move into reporting. Is that possible? Not in the way you are thinking. Reporting sits with radiologists here, and reporting-radiographer posts are not an established part of the workforce as they are in the NHS. If a reporting qualification is the point of your next five years, New Zealand may not be the right move.

chunks.t: Diagnostic Radiographer (MIT) jobs in New Zealand
chunks.x: If what you want is more clinical responsibility, the routes here are modality expertise, protocol and quality leadership, teaching, and senior or charge roles. Several MITs also contribute to image interpretation informally within their teams. It is a different ladder, not a shorter one. What are regional and rural roles really like? Busier in scope and quieter in volume. You will cover more modalities, make more decisions on your own, and get to know the clinical teams properly. On-call is usually part of it, and the radiologist may be reporting remotely rather than sitting down the corridor. Before you accept one, ask three things: how often you are on call, who you can phone at three in the morning, and what support the service gives for postgraduate study. chunks.t: Speech & Language Therapy in New Zealand
chunks.x: Speech-language therapy is self-regulated in New Zealand. There is no statutory registration board of the kind physiotherapy and occupational therapy have. What most employers expect instead is Registered Membership of the New Zealand Speech-language Therapists’ Association, which people shorten to NZSTA. Professional body NZSTA holds the professional framework. Membership, not statutory registration, is what employers ask to see. Two overseas routes Mutual Recognition, if your association and your training are both in a signatory country. Otherwise Qualifications Approval. Trained in the UK? The RCSLT is a signatory to the Mutual Recognition Agreement, so certified members who trained in the UK have the shorter route.

In New Zealand the profession writes itself as speech-language therapist, and the official occupation title is Speech Language Therapist. Same job, same training, different house style.
